title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
section: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
content: While language models have become dramatically more capable, retrieval still largely relies on lexical matching or similarity in fixed embedding spaces. This creates a capability asymmetry: what the retriever fails to find, even the strongest generator cannot recover. We propose DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of pretrained language models to retrieval using decision models that jointly evaluate candidate branches in a single forward pass, without generating any tokens, and show that judging candidates in a shared context makes their relevance estimates comparable. Like a person browsing a library, DecisionRAG navigates the corpus’s inherent structure from broad topics down to individual passages, deciding at each level which branches are worth exploring. Without task-specific training or a first-stage retriever, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Across four benchmarks, including a corpus of 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs, retrieval takes just 0.7–1.8 seconds per query.

authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a core component of modern language-model pipelines ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Guu et al., 2020 ; Gao et al., 2023b ) . By fetching evidence from an external corpus at inference time, RAG gives a model access to up-to-date information it never saw during training ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Vu et al., 2024 ) and grounds its responses in verifiable sources ( Shuster et al., 2021 ; Gao et al., 2023a ) .

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Yet, while the language generation models have become dramatically more capable ( OpenAI, 2026b ; Anthropic, 2026 ) , the retrievers that decide what they see have not kept pace. Most retrieval systems still score each passage via heuristics based on term frequencies like BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) , or by nearest neighbors in a fixed embedding space ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Izacard et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . This creates a striking capability asymmetry between the retriever and the generation model (Figure 1 ): whatever the retriever misses, no amount of generator capability can recover ( Barnett et al., 2024 ) .

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Ideally, a model as capable as the generator would decide what to retrieve. Agentic approaches let an LLM navigate the corpus step by step ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) , but generating many tokens at every step in an agentic loop makes them too slow and costly for many applications ( Jeong et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Rerankers offer a cheaper middle ground ( Nogueira and Cho, 2019 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Reddy et al., 2024 ) , but they can only reorder what a first-stage retriever has already returned.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Decision models have emerged as a new paradigm to leverage the power of pretrained language models quickly without sampling any tokens ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026a ; Li and Wagle, 2026 ) . Given a context and a set of questions, a decision model such as Jev ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) returns, for each question, a probability distribution over its answer options (for a yes/no question, P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\mathrm{yes}) ), answering many questions in parallel against a shared context in a single forward pass. This makes them a natural fit for retrieval, bringing the capability of LLMs to the choice of what to retrieve. Furthermore, scoring the candidates jointly makes their decisions comparable with one another ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) . Using decision models to choose what to retrieve thus promises to level the playing field between the retriever and generator.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: We propose DecisionRAG, which retrieves by navigating instead of searching (Figure 2 ). Most corpora have an inherent structure of topics, documents, sections, and passages, which humans exploit to find information efficiently ( Pirolli and Card, 1999 ) . DecisionRAG leverages this structure through hierarchical decisions ( Geva and Berant, 2018 ; Liu et al., 2021 ) : at each level, a decision model jointly evaluates candidates to identify the most promising branches, progressively narrowing the search from broad categories (e.g. topics or document titles) down to individual passages. Each decision requires only a single forward pass without generating any tokens, keeping retrieval fast even for large corpora. DecisionRAG thus brings the capabilities of pretrained language models directly to retrieval, without a first-stage retriever at query time, a precomputed index, or task-specific training.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: We evaluate DecisionRAG on four benchmarks spanning multi-turn dialogue ( Feng et al., 2021 ; Katsis et al., 2025 ) , scenario-based questions ( Sun et al., 2022 ) , and open-domain search over 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Without task-specific training, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Judging candidates in a shared context contributes to these gains, improving accuracy by up to 7.7 points over independent judgments ( Section 6.1 ). Despite harnessing the capabilities of a language model at every stage, DecisionRAG retrieves in just 0.7–1.8 seconds at a cost of 0.2–2.3 cents per query. Compared with an LLM that generates navigation decisions over the same hierarchy token-by-token, it achieves comparable accuracy with 34–145 × \times lower latency ( Section 6.3 ). Training a dedicated 8B decision model on in-domain data further raises R@1 on MultiDoc2Dial to 60.7, surpassing the best compared published task-trained retriever by 5.7 points and suggesting substantial headroom as decision models improve.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Traditional retrieval methods, including BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) and dense retrievers ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) , rank passages using lexical matching or learned embedding similarity. Neural reranking methods refine these rankings using language-model-based relevance estimates. Cross-encoders evaluate individual query–passage pairs ( Nogueira et al., 2020 ) , while LLM-based rerankers perform listwise ranking by generating permutations ( Sun et al., 2023 ) or iteratively selecting candidates from subsets ( Zhuang et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Although reranking can improve retrieval quality, it remains limited by the candidate recall of the initial retrieval stage.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: An alternative line of work integrates language models directly into the retrieval process. Agentic approaches interleave reasoning with the use of search-engines to iteratively identify relevant evidence ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) . Other methods use hierarchical representations to guide retrieval. MemWalker navigates a hierarchy of summaries constructed from long documents ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , while PageIndex uses document tables of contents for LLM-guided navigation ( VectifyAI, 2025 ) . LATTICE extends hierarchical navigation to corpus-level retrieval, constructing a semantic tree and using LLM-generated relevance assessments to select branches at each level ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) . These approaches require generating tokens sequentially at each retrieval step, which can incur substantial latency when navigation involves multiple rounds of reasoning.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Recent work has explored more efficient approaches to language-model-based ranking. FIRST derives listwise rankings from the logits of a single generated identifier ( Reddy et al., 2024 ) , while ICR and BlockRank extract ranking signals from attention patterns over jointly presented candidates ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) . Decision models offer another approach to evaluating multiple candidates without generating tokens ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026a ) . Given a shared context and a set of questions, these models produce probability distributions over the answer options of each question in a single forward pass. This enables parallel relevance judgments over multiple candidates, with each candidate evaluated against the same contextual information.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Hierarchical retrieval has also been studied as a means of reducing the search space in large document collections. DocQN learns to navigate document trees using reinforcement learning ( Geva and Berant, 2018 ) , while dense hierarchical retrieval progressively selects documents and passages using trained encoders ( Liu et al., 2021 ) . RAPTOR constructs a hierarchy of recursively generated summaries to support retrieval at different levels of abstraction ( Sarthi et al., 2024 ) . Related work has also highlighted the importance of document-level context for passage retrieval ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) .

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: DecisionRAG combines hierarchical retrieval with non-generative relevance judgments. It uses existing document structure where available and constructs document groups otherwise ( Section 4.1 ). Unlike conventional reranking pipelines, DecisionRAG does not require a first-stage retriever to construct a candidate pool. Unlike LLM-guided hierarchical search, it evaluates candidates at each level through parallel relevance judgments in a single forward pass, without generating tokens.

section: Judging candidates in a shared context.
content: Because every question sees the same context, each probability is formed in view of the alternatives: a candidate that would look relevant on its own receives a lower P ⁡ ( Yes ) P(\mathrm{Yes}) when a clearly better one is present. The shared context thus puts the individual probabilities into perspective, making them comparable across candidates. Our ablations support this: scoring candidates together rather than separately improves R@1 on MultiDoc2Dial by 7.7 points and Hit@1 on Natural Questions by 6.5 points ( Sections 6.1 and 6.2 ). They also show where the comparison matters: splitting a pool into smaller requests lowers Hit@1 but leaves R@10 unchanged. Scores from separate requests therefore suffice for screening, where recall counts, whereas the final ranking benefits from one shared request.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Rather than scoring every passage in the corpus individually, DecisionRAG progressively narrows the search space by traversing a corpus hierarchy. At each level, a decision model evaluates the candidates under consideration and retains the most promising ones for further exploration. Candidates not selected are pruned, and their descendants are never evaluated.

content: We first evaluate candidate documents using parallel binary judgments ( Equation 2 ). The shared context s D s_{D} contains the query and descriptions of all candidate documents, while each binary question asks whether a particular document is worth exploring for the query. As illustrated in Figure 3(a) , the model evaluates all candidates in a single forward pass, assigning each a relevance score. In our running example, the pages for Christopher Nolan and Memento (film) are retained, while Gladiator (2000 film) is discarded despite the latter’s keyword overlaps with the query. We retain the top k k documents according to their relevance scores and prune the remaining branches.

content: We next expand the retained documents into their passages and evaluate them using parallel binary judgments ( Equation 2 ). The shared context s P s_{P} now contains the query and all candidate passages, allowing the model to assess their relevance in view of one another, so that their probabilities are directly comparable ( Section 3.2 ). We rank the passages by their binary relevance scores and keep the top r r across all selected documents. On Natural Questions, where the paragraph stage spans 30 pages, each paragraph’s score is first multiplied by its page’s ( Section B.5 ). In our running example, a passage from Memento (film) describing its protagonist, Leonard Shelby, provides the evidence needed to answer the query.

content: To refine the final ranking, we optionally apply a multiple-choice judgment over the top m ≤ r m\leq r passages selected by binary scoring ( Equation 3 ). The choice context lists only these m m passages ( Section B.6 ). Their choice probabilities determine their order, while the remaining passages retain their binary ranking. We use m = 20 m=20 , except on Natural Questions, where m = 5 m=5 . On MTRAG, we instead promote only the highest-probability choice to rank one, preserving the relative order of all other passages. As illustrated in Figure 3(b) , the model compares the shortlisted passages as competing alternatives within a single decision.

The multiple-choice judgment is reserved for the end, where it compares the top passages from the binary judgments directly and sharpens the top rank ( Section 6.4 ). content: The document–passage hierarchy is only the simplest instance of DecisionRAG. For larger corpora, documents can be organized into higher-order groups, such as topics, categories, or products, using existing corpus structure or grouping related documents. The same procedure then applies recursively: at each level, parallel binary judgments identify promising groups, and only their children are evaluated at the next level. For example, when searching the full Wikipedia corpus, one could traverse categories related to films and Christopher Nolan before reaching the individual page for Memento . Thus, DecisionRAG extends to deeper hierarchies without requiring all documents to be evaluated at once. When a corpus lacks such structure, a hierarchy can be built offline by clustering document embeddings, e.g., with recursive k k -means ( Nistér and Stewénius, 2006 ) or scalable agglomerative clustering ( Bateni et al., 2017 ; Monath et al., 2021 ; Dhulipala et al., 2023 ) , as we do for Natural Questions ( Section 4.1 ). The tree need not be uniform: on MTRAG, a heading level is inserted only below pages with more than 60 passages.

section: Levels too large for one request.
content: A level may hold more candidates than fit into one request; on Natural Questions, the 150 retained clusters contain about 17,500 page titles. We then split the level into parallel requests, each with its own shared context. This costs little: the benefit of the shared context levels off at about 50 candidates per request ( Section 6.2 ), and pooled scores suffice for screening. Where the top candidates of a split level should be compared more closely, we rescore them in one request, as for the top 50 pages on MTRAG ( Section B.4 ).

content: MultiDoc2Dial ( Feng et al., 2021 ) contains goal-oriented dialogues grounded in US government documentation. ConditionalQA ( Sun et al., 2022 ) contains scenario-based questions about UK government guidance, often requiring evidence from multiple paragraphs. MTRAG ( Katsis et al., 2025 ) evaluates conversational retrieval over technical documentation; we use its IBM Cloud subset. Natural Questions ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) contains real search queries grounded in Wikipedia.

content: Without task-specific training or a conventional retrieval index, DecisionRAG substantially outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker ( Table 2 ): On MultiDoc2Dial, it improves R@1 by 13.8 percentage points, and on Natural Questions, it improves Hit@1 by 17.4 points.

content: Natural Questions also shows that DecisionRAG needs no ready-made hierarchy: Wikipedia’s 108,626 pages, far too many for one top level, are simply clustered into 1,000 groups ( Section 4.1 ). DecisionRAG then reads only 16% of the page titles. Any corpus can be given a hierarchy this way, with a number of sequential stages that grows only logarithmically with its size ( Equations 4 and 6.6 ).

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Even when using a strong language model such as GPT-5 to rerank the dense retrieval results, DecisionRAG achieves comparable or higher rank-one accuracy on MultiDoc2Dial and Natural Questions (65.4 versus 60.8). It also improves ConditionalQA R@10 (71.9 versus 64.0) and MTRAG R@5 (34.2 versus 31.8), although GPT-5 achieves higher ConditionalQA Hit@1 (73.4 versus 69.7). On MTRAG, whose annotated evidence was collected with ELSER, we judge the top five passages of every system, and DecisionRAG ranks first among all eighteen, including last-turn and rewritten-query baselines (R@5 34.2 versus 32.5 for the best baseline; Sections A.3 and 12 ).

content: DecisionRAG can also complement dense retrieval by incorporating dense-retrieved passages into its final ranking stage. This combination improves R@10 from 83.6 to 84.7 on MultiDoc2Dial, from 71.9 to 76.3 on ConditionalQA, and from 86.7 to 88.9 on Natural Questions. These gains suggest that the two approaches recover complementary evidence and can be effectively combined.

section: 6.1 Scoring Candidates in a Shared Context
content: A central design choice of DecisionRAG is to judge candidates against a shared context rather than independently. For Natural Questions design questions, we build pools of 5 to 1,000 candidates from the gold paragraph and hard negatives retrieved by BM25, SPLADE-v3, and e5 ( Figure 5 ). Shared-context binary judgments consistently outperform scoring each candidate in a separate request, and multiple-choice ranking performs best within its 255-option limit. Beyond that limit, multiple-choice ranking of the binary top 255 retains much of this advantage: 53.7% Hit@1 with 1,000 candidates versus 47.6% for binary judgments alone.

content: Prior work also navigates hierarchies with language models, but lets a generative LLM decide at each level via generating tokens ( Chen et al., 2023 ; VectifyAI, 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2026 ) . To isolate the effect of deciding by parallel judgments instead of generation, we keep DecisionRAG’s hierarchy and budgets fixed and replace its decision model by GPT-5 (low reasoning effort), which reads the candidates of each level and writes out the numbers of those to keep, in the style of LATTICE ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) . On ConditionalQA it selects 3 of the 652 pages and ranks their paragraphs; on Natural Questions it selects 150 of the 1,000 clusters (when it lists fewer, we ask for the rest in the same conversation), then 30 pages from their titles, and ranks the paragraphs of the top pages as DecisionRAG does.

We compare this reranker with DecisionRAG.

content: Navigating the hierarchy outperforms reranking the retriever’s candidates ( Table 8 ): Hit@1 rises by 7.7 points on ConditionalQA (95% CI: [2.6, 13.3]) and by 7.0 points on Natural Questions ([3.4, 10.8]), while MultiDoc2Dial and MTRAG are level. Even without any retrieval index, DecisionRAG ( Table 2 ) improves Hit@1 over the reranker by 6.0 points on Natural Questions ([2.4, 9.8]) and by 4.0 points on ConditionalQA. This holds although the dense top 100 contains the gold evidence more often than the navigated candidates (Natural Questions: 98.4% versus 94.0%; ConditionalQA: 98.5% versus 91.1%): when both contain it, navigation ranks it first more often (70.1% versus 61.9% and 76.7% versus 67.3%), plausibly because it presents whole pages in reading order rather than isolated passages.

content: Finally, we examine how the navigation budget affects retrieval.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Pruning at the top level is what keeps navigation cheap on large corpora, but it is also where evidence can be lost: a page in a discarded cluster can never be retrieved. We investigate how many clusters must be kept to match the recall of scoring every page directly, varying the share of the 1,000 Natural Questions clusters that DecisionRAG keeps up to flat scoring of all 108,626 page titles ( Figure 7 ). Recall@10 rises steeply up to about 10% of the clusters and then stays level: keeping 15% matches flat scoring (86.2% versus 84.5%) at a fifth of the cost (2.3¢ versus 12.1¢ per query) and a third of the latency (1.7 versus 4.5 seconds). Below 5%, the cluster holding the gold page is often discarded, and recall@10 falls to 63.7% at 1%.

content: The same trade-off appears one level down, in the page budget. On MultiDoc2Dial, we increase the number of newly retained pages from three to ten, keeping the remaining configuration fixed. R@10 improves from 81.0% to 83.6%, while R@1 increases only from 46.9% to 47.4% ( Table 9 ). The larger budget increases API cost by 83% and median latency by 28%. Exploring more pages therefore primarily improves evidence coverage, with diminishing returns for the top-ranked passage.

authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: DecisionRAG relies on a corpus hierarchy whose structure and node descriptions allow the decision model to identify relevant branches. Poorly organized documents or uninformative descriptions can therefore hurt retrieval quality. Moreover, navigation prunes branches irreversibly, so relevant passages may be missed if their ancestors are discarded; we show that larger exploration budgets and complementary dense retrieval can mitigate this.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: We introduced DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of large language models into retrieval by navigating corpus hierarchies with non-generative decisions. At each level, candidates are evaluated jointly in a shared context, allowing their relevance to be judged in view of one another. By progressively narrowing the search space, DecisionRAG retrieves relevant evidence with a number of sequential decisions that grows only logarithmically with corpus size under a balanced hierarchy. As decision models improve, retrieval can inherit their capabilities directly.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: MultiDoc2Dial ( Feng et al., 2021 ) contains goal-oriented dialogues grounded in 488 documents from four US government help centers. We build a help-center–page–passage hierarchy from the dataset’s metadata. Help centers are given by the domain field, and documents sharing a title after removing the #1/#2 part suffix form one page, giving 413 pages. We use the benchmark’s official structure-based segmentation into 4,110 passages.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Passages are represented by their full text and their page and parent-heading path, pages by their titles and section headings, and the four help centers by one-line descriptions written manually from their names. We evaluate on the official validation split (661 dialogues, 4,201 turns). Each turn has one gold passage containing the grounding span of the agent’s response. The released test split provides no usable evaluation examples.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: ConditionalQA ( Sun et al., 2022 ) contains scenario-based questions about UK government guidance whose answers may depend on several conditions and paragraphs. Its corpus contains 652 guides. We recover their structure from the HTML headings ( h1 , h2 ) and extract 58,483 paragraph-level units from p , li and tr elements. Pages are represented by their titles and top-level part headings, and paragraphs are grouped under their heading paths. Retrieval searches the full corpus rather than assuming the relevant guide is known. We evaluate on the 285 questions of the labeled development split, 271 of which have annotated evidence (about four paragraphs on average).

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: We use the IBM Cloud subset of MTRAG ( Katsis et al., 2025 ) , with 8,578 documentation pages and 72,442 passages, keeping the benchmark’s document files and passage chunks. Pages are grouped into 172 products by the first path segment after /docs/ in their URLs. Because the corpus does not preserve HTML markup, we recover section headings from the text layout (short lines separated by blank lines). Pages are represented by their titles and recovered headings, and passages by their text and heading. Product descriptions are built automatically from the product name, the opening of its landing page and three page titles.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: The held-out evaluation set contains 26 human-written conversations with 205 turns, 188 of which have annotated evidence (one to seven gold passages).

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: MTRAG’s gold passages were selected from the annotators’ ELSER retrieval sessions, so relevant passages that ELSER did not surface cannot be gold. We therefore add LLM-judged relevant passages to the gold passages. For each turn, we pool the top five passages of all 18 systems evaluated on MTRAG, including released ELSER and the last-turn and rewritten-query baselines, together with the gold passages, representing identical texts once. GPT-5 receives the conversation, the reference reply and the shuffled candidates, without knowing which system retrieved them, and grades each passage as needed for the answer (2), related but insufficient (1) or unrelated (0). Grade-2 passages are added to the relevance set, and all original gold passages are kept. GPT-5 grades 87.9% of the gold passages as needed. The expanded labels reduce the dependence on ELSER. Table 12 compares all systems.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: We use the DAPR version ( Wang et al., 2024 ) of Natural Questions ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , whose corpus splits 108,626 Wikipedia pages into 2,682,017 paragraphs. We evaluate on a fixed random sample of 500 of the 3,610 questions in DAPR’s test split, which is drawn from NQ’s development set. A question’s gold paragraphs (one to three) lie on a single page. Since Wikipedia has no structure above the page, we cluster the pages into 1,000 groups with k k -means over e5-base-v2 embeddings ( Wang et al., 2022 ) of each page’s title and first sentence. Groups hold 15 to 350 pages (median 106). Each group is described by one sentence that Qwen3-8B writes from its page titles ( Section B.5 ). Pages are represented by their titles and paragraphs by their text, grouped under their page title.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
section: A.5 Design Sets and Configuration Selection
content: Retrieval configurations (candidate representations, routing rules and retention budgets) are selected on design sets that are disjoint from the evaluation sets. Selection does not update the parameters of Jev. MultiDoc2Dial uses samples of its training split and ConditionalQA 300 training questions. MTRAG has no training split, so we use 50 synthetic IBM Cloud conversations (292 turns) and 131 IBM Cloud turns from MTRAG-UN ( Rosenthal et al., 2026 ) , whose conversations are disjoint from the evaluation set.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: At each stage, the judge receives a context containing the query and the numbered candidate descriptions, followed by one yes/no question per candidate. Candidates are listed in document order and grouped under their parent pages where applicable. Each stage builds a new context; probabilities from earlier stages are not included. Conversational queries contain the six most recent dialogue turns.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: For conversational retrieval, the page and passage questions are “Is the information the agent needs for its next reply on Page n n ?” and “Should the agent’s next reply be based on Passage n n ?” For ConditionalQA and Natural Questions, they are “Is the information needed to answer the user’s question on Page n n ?” and “Does Paragraph n n contain information needed to answer the user’s question?”

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
section: B.2 MultiDoc2Dial and the Conversational Notepad
content: The routing context describes the four help centers, with one question per center. We keep the highest-scoring center, the runner-up if the top probability is below 0.8, and the center of the most recently retrieved page. The page stage scores the pages of the kept centers and keeps ten. All passages of these pages, plus those of the two most recent notepad pages, are scored in one shared context.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
section: B.2 MultiDoc2Dial and the Conversational Notepad
content: The notepad, used on MultiDoc2Dial and MTRAG, lists distinct page identifiers by most recent retrieval. After each turn, the page of the top-ranked passage moves to the front. The page-stage context lists the notepad pages. The notepad is built only from the system’s own retrieval decisions, never from gold evidence, and previously retrieved passages are neither marked nor excluded.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: The page stage scores all 652 guides in one request and keeps three, whose paragraphs are scored together under their heading paths.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: The main configuration scores pages directly instead of routing through products. In a first pass, all 8,578 page titles are split into parallel requests under the input-size limit, keeping each product’s pages together, and the top 50 pages by pooled score are kept. Because these scores come from different contexts, a second pass rescores the 50 together with their product names and headings, and keeps ten.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Pages with more than 60 passages pass through an extra stage that scores their headings and keeps the top eight. At most 60 passages of these headings, in document order, continue to the passage stage.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: Each cluster is described by Qwen3-8B, given its page titles (most typical first, at most 300) and the prompt: “Write one sentence (at most 30 words) describing what the pages in this group are about. Name the main kinds of subjects it covers, including the less typical ones, so that a reader can tell whether a given Wikipedia page would belong to this group.” The judge scores the 1,000 cluster descriptions in eight parallel requests, asking for each whether “the page with the information needed to answer the user’s question [is] likely in Topic n n ”, and keeps 150 clusters. Their page titles, about 17,500 per question, are scored in parallel requests of at most 20k tokens. The paragraph stage scores all paragraphs of the top three pages, the first ten of pages ranked 4–10 and the first three of pages ranked 11–30 in one shared context, about 230 paragraphs per question. Each paragraph’s probability is multiplied by its page’s.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: The multiple-choice question follows binary scoring. Its answer options are the top 20 candidates by P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\mathrm{yes}) (top five on Natural Questions), and its context lists only these candidates, in reading order and formatted as in binary scoring. On MultiDoc2Dial, ConditionalQA and Natural Questions, the choice probabilities reorder the shortlist, and all other candidates keep their binary order. On MTRAG, only the highest-probability choice moves to rank one. Compared with a choice request over the full binary context, the shorter context changes retrieval by at most one point on every dataset and shortens the MTRAG choice request from 0.30–0.37 to 0.14 seconds. Retrieval without the choice step is evaluated in Section 6.4 .

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
content: The generator is Qwen3.5-27B (FP8 weights, thinking disabled, greedy decoding), served with vLLM. Its input is a short task instruction, the passages numbered in each system’s rank order, and the query: the user’s situation and question on ConditionalQA, the question on Natural Questions, and the last six turns on MTRAG. It answers ConditionalQA with “Answer:” followed by yes, no, a short phrase or “not answerable” (optionally with conditions), Natural Questions with a phrase of at most five words, and MTRAG with a reply that says when the passages do not contain the answer. Exact match uses the standard answer normalization; the Natural Questions references are the short answers of NQ-open, available for 334 of the 500 questions. The judge is the same model, shown the query, the reference answer(s) and the generated answer, and asked whether the answer is correct (for MTRAG, consistent with the reference response, and a refusal on unanswerable turns). Part of the generations and verdicts were produced by the same model through the OpenRouter API instead of our local deployment; on 200 prompts answered by both, answer quality matched and the verdicts agreed on 96.5%.

content: The configurations in Table 13 use 297 turns from 50 complete training dialogues, six-turn input, title-only page descriptions, ten newly selected pages, no help-center routing and no choice step, so their scores are not comparable to the main results. Separate scoring builds one context per page, containing the conversation, the page title and its passages with their heading paths; shared scoring lists the passages of all kept pages in one context, grouped by page. Both rank passages by P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\mathrm{yes}) for “Should the agent’s next reply be based on Passage n n ?”. Own notepad is the page memory of Section B.2 , built by each configuration from its own decisions. Paired R@1 differences, resampling whole dialogues, are + 4.0 +4.0 [ 0.7 , 8.0 ] [0.7,8.0] for adding the notepad and + 7.7 +7.7 [ 3.3 , 12.2 ] [3.3,12.2] for shared over separate scoring with notepads.

content: Given the gold page, passage scoring on MultiDoc2Dial design turns reaches 62.7 R@1 and 94.3 R@5. On the ConditionalQA development set, the three-page configuration without multiple-choice ranking misses the gold page for 8.5% of evidence-labeled questions, ranks a paragraph from another page first for 9.6%, and ranks another paragraph of the gold page first for 13.7%. Passage ranking thus remains a substantial source of error even when navigation reaches the relevant page.

title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
section: D.3 Dense candidates and multiple-choice ranking
content: + dense candidates adds the top 20 dense-retrieved passages (top 10 on ConditionalQA) to the navigated candidates, removes duplicates, and groups all candidates by page and section in reading order. Multiple-choice ranking either reorders the top 20 ( order ) or moves only its pick to rank one ( top1 ). Table 14 reports the design-set comparisons, at three pages on MultiDoc2Dial and ConditionalQA and ten pages on MTRAG-UN. The design sets are 1,832 turns from 300 MultiDoc2Dial training dialogues, the 285 of the 300 ConditionalQA design questions that have paragraph evidence, and 86 labeled MTRAG-UN turns, one per conversation. Δ \Delta is the difference in the primary metric to the configuration with neither component, with an unadjusted paired 95% interval. content: The open-weight judges are Qwen3-Base models (1.7B, 4B and 8B) whose language-model head is replaced by a scoring head. Each candidate is posed as its own question with the answer options “no” and “yes”, appended to the shared context. All questions start at the position right after the context and cannot attend to each other, so the judgments of different candidates depend only on the shared context, as in Equation 2 . The head projects the hidden states of the question’s end token and of each option’s end token into a common space, scales their cosine similarity by a learned inverse temperature (capped at 100), and normalizes over the question’s options with a softmax; P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\mathrm{yes}) is the probability of “yes”. Training minimizes the cross-entropy over the options. In the general and MultiDoc2Dial-only checkpoints, the end tokens of a question’s two options can also attend to each other; the LoRA checkpoint does not use this link.

The label of each example is the dataset’s gold option; the alternatives are its own distractors or, for classification, a random subset of the class labels. The mixture contains no MultiDoc2Dial or ConditionalQA data.

content: MultiDoc2Dial training examples are generated from its training split with the routing, page and passage stages of the navigation; 3% of training dialogues are held out for monitoring. The generator simulates the notepad with a gold page with probability 0.65, includes the gold page among three candidates with probability 0.85, and adds a second help-center negative stage with probability 0.17; identical-text copies of the gold passage are never used as negatives. ConditionalQA examples are built by the navigation’s own page and paragraph stages, so their inputs match those at inference. A page-stage example lists all 652 pages with “yes” for the gold page; a paragraph-stage example lists every paragraph of five candidate pages with “yes” for the evidence paragraphs. The gold page’s rank among the five candidates is drawn from Jev’s page-stage ranks on the 300 ConditionalQA design questions, and the remaining candidates are the top BM25 pages; when the gold page is not drawn, all paragraphs are negatives. Paragraphs whose exact text appears as evidence on another page are not asked, and questions without evidence contribute only a page-stage example. Questions on 10% of the training pages are held out for monitoring.

title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. This update is usually presented as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. We present a geometrical interpretation of this update instead. Treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle’s mass. Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population. The physical reading needs nonnegative rewards, which can always be arranged by adding a constant to every reward without changing the update. In the limit of a large population or under antithetic sampling, the centroid sits on the model itself, so ES has an even simpler geometric interpretation: from its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its own population. The same picture explains what subtracting the mean reward does: it changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model to the sampled centroid. Our contribution is an intuitive, geometric way to visualize an ES update, exact for any finite population.

title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: Evolution strategies (ES) have recently returned as a practical alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Abdi et al., 2026 ) . The algorithm is simple. Perturb the current model N N times with Gaussian noise, score each perturbed copy, and merge the perturbations weighted by their rewards. The standard way to understand this update is as a Monte Carlo estimate of the gradient of a smoothed objective ( Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017 ; Salimans et al., 2017 ) . That view is correct, but says little about what a single update does to the model in parameter space.

title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: In this paper, we give the ES update a geometrical interpretation grounded in a physical intuition. Think of the N N perturbed models as particles sitting around the current model (Figure 1 (a)). Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid, which is also its center-of-mass (COM). After scoring, give each particle a mass equal to its reward. The COM then shifts away from the centroid. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population (Figure 1 ). For the masses to be physical, the rewards should be nonnegative with a positive total. This is not a restriction: adding a constant to every reward makes it so and leaves the update unchanged. In the limit of a large population or at any N N under antithetic sampling (mirrored sampling), the centroid sits on the model itself, and the picture becomes simpler and even more intuitive: from its current location in parameter space, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its sampled population.

title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: The center of mass has appeared in the ES literature before, but in a different role. In classical evolution strategies the best offspring are selected and the parent is moved to their centroid, a point that Beyer and Schwefel (2002) describe as a center of mass. CMA-ES does the same with rank-based weights in place of equal ones ( Hansen, 2016 ) , and the selection term of Price’s equation gives the change in a population’s mean trait as the covariance between trait and fitness ( Price, 1970 ) . In each case the object described is the new mean, written as a weighted average of the candidates. The mean-subtracted update used in modern practice, for instance by Qiu et al. (2026) with an additional standard-deviation normalization, is not of this form. It takes a step, and we show that this step is the displacement between two centers of mass of the same population, one computed with equal masses and one with rewards as masses. This is also what makes the role of reward centering visible. Subtracting the mean reward changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model location to the sampled centroid.

content: This is the central observation of the paper. For mean-subtracted ES, the update step has a simple geometric interpretation. The update vector is the displacement from the equal-weight balance point of the system, which is the centroid 𝐩 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{p}} , to its reward-weighted COM 𝐩 COM \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{COM}} , scaled by α ​ r ¯ / σ \alpha\overline{r}/\sigma and applied at the current model 𝜽 \bm{\theta} ( fig. 1 (b,c)). Here, system refers to the sampled population of models around 𝜽 \bm{\theta} . In the infinite population regime, or at any N N under antithetic sampling, the centroid coincides with the current location of the model ( eq. 7 ), which means that the update literally moves the model at 𝜽 \bm{\theta} towards the reward-weighted COM of the population. Put simply, the ES update can be understood with a physical intuition—treat reward as mass, and in the infinite population regime the model moves towards the COM of its own system of particles.

content: This shows that the raw-reward update is the centered-reward update plus an additional term that depends on two things: (1) the total reward obtained by all the perturbations, and (2) the distance between the centroid of the sampled population and the current model, which exists only because the population is finite. This is what mean subtraction does geometrically. It removes the part of the update caused by the sampled centroid not sitting on the model, a part that is dominated by noise. 2 2 2 The term is not pure noise, since its expectation works out to 1 / N 1/N of the expected raw update, but by eq. 6 its typical size is of order α ​ | r ¯ | ​ d / N \alpha|\overline{r}|\sqrt{d/N} , so for d ≫ N d\gg N it is dominated by sampling noise. title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: In this paper, we gave the ES update a geometrical interpretation grounded in physical intuition. We treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle’s mass. Before scoring, all particles have the same mass and the center of mass of the system is simply the centroid of the sampled population. After scoring, the reward-weighted COM shifts away from the centroid, and we show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a factor that depends on the mean reward. This holds for any finite population. In the infinite population regime, or under antithetic sampling, the centroid coincides with the model and the interpretation becomes even simpler. From its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted COM of its own system of particles. The same picture also explains the role of mean subtraction.

title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
authors: Akshat Gupta
content: This paper presents an interpretation of the ES update and not a new method. The identity in eq. 12 is exact and needs no experimental validation. The physical reading of rewards as masses needs nonnegative rewards with a positive total. This is always achievable by adding a constant to every reward, but the identity itself holds without it, so the physical picture is a convenience rather than a requirement. Our analysis of the term removed by mean subtraction assumes independent Gaussian perturbations with a fixed σ \sigma , and does not cover adaptive step sizes or covariance updates such as those in CMA-ES. Finally, the claim that this term is dominated by noise is made for d ≫ N d\gg N , which is the regime of LLM fine-tuning, and may not hold for small problems.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
section: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Thanks: § Work done while interning at Amazon FAR Thanks: † Amazon FAR team co-lead
content: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLoRe , a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/ .

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: Humanoid robots offer a general-purpose embodiment for working in environments built for people. Many tasks in these environments, such as pushing a cart, moving a heavy box, and wiping a surface, require the robot to control contact force as well as motion. However, learned humanoid loco-manipulation is commonly formulated as generating and tracking motion references [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Tracking a demonstrated hand trajectory alone does not reproduce the demonstrated force, which also depends on contact geometry, stiffness, and object motion. Unlike a fixed-base arm, a humanoid must stay balanced under these contact loads, coordinating its hands, torso, and legs while regulating force.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: Two difficulties stand in the way. The first is data: imitation learning requires scalable demonstrations that record contact force alongside motion. Existing robot-free interfaces for whole-body demonstration collection record motion but not force [ 4 , 5 ] . The second is execution: the robot must accurately apply the desired force. Current learned humanoid whole-body controllers track motion alone, or treat force as a disturbance to reject or a stiffness to lower [ 6 , 7 ] . Tracking a commanded contact force has been shown only on quadrupedal manipulators, using estimated rather than measured force [ 8 , 9 ] , which is not accurate enough. A humanoid instead needs to track force at both hands together with whole-body motion while maintaining balance.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: We present FLoRe , a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. Its robot-free force-annotated data collection system records contact force with each demonstration; the policy learns to predict this force, and the controller tracks it. The system pairs two UMI-style handheld grippers [ 10 ] with a chest tracker and two ankle trackers [ 4 , 11 ] . Each gripper carries a wrist camera, a pose tracker, and a six-axis F/T sensor [ 12 , 13 ] . The applied wrench is thus recorded alongside hand, torso, and foot motion. The robot uses the same gripper–sensor assembly.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: For the high-level planner, we propose a force-reactive diffusion policy [ 14 ] . It observes wrist images, robot state, and the measured wrench at each hand, then predicts a chunk [ 15 ] of action, gripper widths, and per-hand desired force. Force enters as both an input and an output. The input lets the policy react to interactions that images do not reveal. The output is commanded to the controller [ 13 ] , rather than used only as an auxiliary target [ 16 ] . This connects the force measured during demonstration to the deployed force.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: To track the commanded forces, we develop a whole-body controller with hybrid compliance. It outputs only joint positions, so each hand’s force command becomes a shift of its position target. In contact, an integral of the force error measured at the wrist adjusts this shift until the hand exerts the commanded force, whatever the contact stiffness. Along uncommanded axes, the same integral lets the hand yield to external pushes. Each hand thus tracks force along the commanded direction and complies along the others, without switching modes. We train the controller in simulation [ 17 ] and deploy it on the robot using wrist F/T measurements.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: We deploy FLoRe on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three whole-body contact-rich tasks: pushing a gantry hanging another robot, bimanual box rotation, and board wiping. In simulation, the controller realises in-contact force error of about 1 N per hand while tracking whole-body motion. On the real robot, FLoRe succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller with force commands disabled. section: II-A Force Sensing for Loco-Manipulation Data Collection and Policy Learning
content: Robot-free data collection builds on UMI [ 10 ] . Force-aware variants add wrist or fingertip sensing, but deploy on fixed-base arms with analytic impedance or admittance control [ 12 , 13 , 18 ] . Humanoid extensions instead collect whole-body motion and execute it with learned trackers, but do not record contact force [ 4 , 11 ] . WT-UMI is the closest interface for humanoids, although it measures only a scalar normal force at each palm and relies on paired teleoperation data [ 19 ] . Our interface records a six-axis wrench at each hand together with torso motion, and its demonstrations require no robot-side data.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
section: II-A Force Sensing for Loco-Manipulation Data Collection and Policy Learning
content: Measured force has been used to condition visuomotor policies [ 20 , 21 ] . Other work predicts stiffness, admittance gains, or virtual position targets that are executed by an impedance controller [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 12 ] . More closely related methods predict a wrench trajectory together with pose, but execute it on fixed-base arms through analytic force controllers [ 13 , 25 , 26 ] . On humanoids, WT-UMI passes a scalar normal-force prediction to an admittance rule [ 19 ] . UniFP is the closest formulation. It predicts 3-D force commands, but deploys end-effector force control only on a quadrupedal manipulator. Its humanoid interface exposes force only at the base [ 9 ] . Our planner instead predicts per-hand pose, gripper, and wrench trajectories from handheld demonstrations, then sends the predicted force to a learned humanoid whole-body controller.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: Learned legged and humanoid controllers usually either withstand external force or yield to it through commanded stiffness or damping [ 6 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 7 , 30 ] , but neither approach directly specifies how hard to press. Direct force tracking has mainly been studied on quadrupedal manipulators, as a separate control mode or through a target-shifting spring law, both using force estimated from proprioception [ 8 , 9 ] . WT-UMI regulates a scalar palm force on a humanoid, but through an analytic admittance rule and inverse kinematics above a separate locomotion controller [ 19 ] . In contrast, our hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking integrates the force error measured at each wrist. One learned policy tracks position in free space and force along the commanded direction, while remaining compliant along the other directions and maintaining balance.

Table I compares FLoRe with FLoRe w/o Force , SONIC [ 3 ] , and SONIC + admittance , all evaluated with 𝐟 cmd = 0 \mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{cmd}}=0 on two held-out motion sets. Relative to FLoRe w/o Force , FLoRe adds 1.3–3.2 cm of global root error and at most 8.0 mm of wrist position error, while its wrist orientation error roughly halves; it also tracks orientation better than SONIC , at a higher root error. section: IV-B Hybrid Compliance Whole-body Low-level Controller
content: Hybrid compliance controller tracks commanded force accurately. Neither SONIC nor FLoRe w/o Force accepts a force command. SONIC + admittance does, but its servo acts outside the balance policy and realizes only 0.67–0.70 of the commanded force, with an in-contact error of about 7.9 N. FLoRe tracks 5–25 N commands with a gain of 1.03–1.06 and about 1 N of in-contact error per hand; lateral and downward commands reach a lower gain and leak partly into the other axes. With nothing commanded the sensor still reads 1.25–1.50 N, so at deployment we zero commands below 1.5 N and cap them at 25 N. Integrating the measured force error removes the dependence on the unknown contact stiffness: Spring-Law , the target-shift law of [ 9 ] without its force-feedback term, cannot detect contact, and its force scales with that stiffness relative to the assumed K K . The same integral makes the hand compliant: while it tracks a force, a push along an uncommanded axis is read by the wrist sensor and builds up the integral, which moves the target with it, so the hand gives way instead of resisting, with no mode switch (real robot, Fig. 4 bottom).

content: Real-world force tracking. We verify force tracking on the robot against an external reference: a rigidly mounted digital force gauge that the hand presses along each of ± x \pm x , ± y \pm y , and ± z \pm z while the humanoid stands freely. The command follows a staircase of 4, 6, 8, and 10 N, repeated across directions and hands. Along the x x axis, the measured steady-state force reaches approximately 91 % 91\% of the commanded magnitude, with a mean absolute steady-state error of about 1.1 N. The response enters a ± 1 \pm 1 N band in 1.8 s on average, while the steady-state fluctuation remains approximately ± 0.3 \pm 0.3 – 0.5 0.5 N. The controller consistently recovers the commanded contact force without loss of stability.

The box remains on the table, so the measured wrench reflects table friction, box inertia, and the internal squeeze between the hands. A rollout succeeds if the box rotates by more than 40 ∘ 40^{\circ} and remains upright after release.

content: Performance. Ours erases the strip in 8/10 rollouts. DP succeeds in 3/10. It usually hovers above the board (Fig. 5 , bottom right). This directly shows that observed motion can be valid supervision in free space but not in contact [ 41 ] . w/o F-cmd succeeds in 4/10. It detects contact but cannot increase a force that is too low. w/o F-in succeeds in 7/10 but continues wiping in free space when the board is farther away. This task also has the largest offline errors: 2.02 cm for pose and 1.59 N for force.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: F1: The force channel costs little motion tracking. Relative to FLoRe w/o Force , FLoRe adds 1.3–3.2 cm of root error and at most 8.0 mm of wrist position error while halving wrist orientation error (Table I ); in return it tracks commanded force with a gain of 1.03–1.06 and about 1 N of in-contact error. The 1.25–1.50 N F = 0 F{=}0 floor bounds the smallest verifiable command, and lateral and downward commands remain weaker.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: F2: Force-reactive policies resolve failures that motion alone cannot distinguish. With the same demonstrations and controller, DP succeeds in 26.7% of rollouts and FLoRe in 80% (Table II ). The position-only policy stalls when a reached pose does not move the object, hovers or presses too hard when the board is displaced, and loses balance against the heavy box (Fig. 5 ). Force also composes with coordination: both hands hold the internal force on Rotate Box, and the push is sustained while walking on Push Gantry.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: F3: Force commands give the larger, significant gain; force observations show a smaller trend. Withholding the predicted force from the controller reduces success from 80% (24/30) to 36.7% (11/30; Fisher’s exact test, p = 0.001 p=0.001 ): the policy senses resistance but can respond only through pose. Removing the force observation reduces success to 66.7%.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
content: We presented FLoRe , a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation from robot-free demonstrations that record both motion and contact wrench. Our hybrid compliance whole-body controller tracks the learned force commands, allowing the humanoid to sustain contact, coordinate both hands, and apply force while walking and balancing. On three tasks, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy. By making force a shared interface between demonstrations, policies, and whole-body control, FLoRe extends robot-free imitation learning to contact-rich skills that motion alone cannot specify.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
section: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
content: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Recently, Large language models (LLM) and agents based on LLM have shown growing promise in clinical medicine, from summarizing patient records and drafting notes to supporting bedside decisions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Now, most medical benchmarks test these models in some closed questions or single-step tasks, such as diagnosis and treatment planning [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . However, clinical care is a multi-step process in which clinicians must adapt their decisions as a patient’s condition and test results evolve. In oncology, for example, patients move from initial diagnosis and treatment planning to toxicity management and long-term surveillance [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Moreover, what guides clinical decisions at each stage depends on the specific disease: resectability and operability guide local treatment in non-metastatic lung cancer [ 19 , 20 ] , while cytogenetic and molecular markers inform risk stratification and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia [ 21 , 22 ] . Because clinical priorities and available evidence shift from one stage to the next, a model that performs well in diagnosis may still fail to adjust treatment appropriately for severe toxicities or monitor for recurrence. This motivates us to design an open-ended disease-specific evaluation organized throughout the care phases to provide a clinically interpretable account of the strengths and limitations of the model in fulfilling the responsibilities in each phase.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Recent benchmarks have taken an important step forward by using structured rubrics to assess open-ended medical responses [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Rather than relying on a single overall score, these frameworks break clinical expectations down into explicit checkable items, making it much easier to spot missing medical facts, misunderstood patient data, or unsafe advice. For example, HealthBench pairs physician-written rubrics with automated grading to evaluate model behavior in various clinical dialogs [ 23 ] . Similarly, Adaptive Precise Boolean rubrics use fine-grained yes-or-no criteria to speed up grading and improve agreement among evaluators in metabolic health [ 25 ] . Despite this progress, current rubric-based systems still fall short of real-world clinical demands in two critical ways [ 23 , 25 ] . First, they evaluate isolated encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities shift across successive decision points for the same patient. Second, they overlook how clinicians phrase their requests differently in daily practice, ranging from broad open-ended questions to highly detailed instructions [ 23 , 5 ] . Because even subtle changes in wording can sharply alter an LLM’s output [ 15 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] , testing a model under a single prompt format cannot tell us whether it remains reliable when a busy clinician asks for help in a more general way. Moving beyond static evaluation thus requires solving two connected challenges: how to measure model performance consistently as patients move through distinct stages of care, and how to test whether that performance holds up when the same clinical problem is framed in different ways.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: To tackle these challenges, we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a longitudinal benchmark centered on the pathway of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Here, we focus on NPC because its management follows a well-defined, radiotherapy-centered pathway in which each stage demands different clinical reasoning and evidence [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] . Based on clinical semantics, we divide the patient journey into six sequential care phase: Work-up, Diagnosis, Staging, Treatment, Toxicity and Follow-up. Each patient–phase unit is assessed at a defined clinical decision point, with model inputs restricted to evidence available at that time and later information excluded. In each phase, we evaluate model responses using rubrics organised around five shared dimensions: Decision Quality (DQ), Evidence Grounding (EG), Status Determination (SD), Evidence Faithfulness (EF) and Safety Adherence (SA). To ensure scalability, we developed reusable templates within these dimensions to link common clinical requirements to individual patient data. Specifically, these templates capture phase-specific clinical requirements, which are then translated into patient-specific atomic criteria anchored in the clinical evidence available at each decision point. To assess sensitivity to task formulation, we pair each focused, phase-specific clinical request with two variants—a broad clinical request and a detailed prompt specifying expected response components—while keeping the patient–phase unit, underlying clinical evidence and evaluation rubric fixed. Together, these approaches enable consistent comparisons across patients and care phases while providing a modular framework that could be adapted to other cancers and chronic diseases.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Following this design, we constructed 941 phase-specific evaluation units and 17,688 case-specific rubric criteria from real-world longitudinal clinical records of 405 patients. With this dataset, we assessed 30 language models and identified distinct performance changes across the care pathway. Although most models demonstrated solid decision quality during initial diagnosis, their reliability dropped sharply in later phases: staging was plagued by explicit decision errors, whereas follow-up suffered from frequent omissions of required clinical actions and evidence. Furthermore, we also found that the performance of some weak models proved to be highly sensitive to task formulation. Specifying the expected elements raised the median quality of decisions, while making the request more general caused a steep drop. This pattern points to a fundamental limitation of current LLMs: they possess substantial medical knowledge, yet may struggle to identify clinical priorities independently without explicit structural guidance. These findings introduce some implications for deploying AI in clinical practice. First, high scores on static diagnostic benchmarks do not guarantee safe performance throughout a patient’s entire treatment journey, since a model that excels at initial diagnosis can still falter during staging or survivorship care. Second, the decline in performance under broad prompts raises concerns about relying on clinical LLMs for autonomous decision-making when busy clinicians ask open-ended questions. Instead, safe clinical integration will require stage-aware guardrails and structured workflow prompts that actively guide models through each phase of care. By identifying where and how models fall short along a longitudinal disease pathway, NPC-RubricBench provides a rigorous foundation for building medical AI systems intended to support patients from their first visit through long-term follow-up.
