content: The scope of the supplied material determines where relevant evidence must be found, while relationships among its parts determine what must be connected. FinanceBench’s long-context setting supplies the relevant filing in the prompt [93]; multi-hop and long-document tasks require linking supporting information across passages, pages, or documents [19, 94–97]. A synthesis must further combine these contributions into an account that preserves their meaning [79, 81]. ConvFinQA extends the dependency to conversation history, with follow-up calculations using values or results established in earlier turns [98]. The requested inference determines how the evidence is used. A numerical answer may require computing with selected values, sometimes through an intermediate program [21, 99, 100], while a legal conclusion may require applying an explicit rule to the facts [101]. Scientific assessments draw on domain knowledge to interpret the evidence [102, 103]. Plans require comparing available options against stated requirements and commonsense feasibility constraints, including whether the proposed choices can be combined into a workable arrangement [78, 83]. An informational response can explain why a report contains an incorrect value. Correcting that value extends the responsibility to changing the relevant workbook entry and checking that the update has taken effect. 3.2 Atomic Action Level This transition from generating information to modifying state defines the Atomic Action Level, which assigns the agent a local objective with a clearly defined target and effect, such as correcting a spreadsheet cell, repositioning a slide element, or updating a record field. Here, the level is determined by the local scope of the work objective rather than the number of low-level execution steps: a single local action may still require several mouse, keyboard, or API operations to complete. Regardless of the interface mechanics, the agent must apply the change to the intended object while preserving any properties that the request leaves unchanged [104]. 3.2.1 Creating and Modifying Local Work Objects A request may add a bounded element to an existing artifact, such as a formula [105, 106], a conditional formatting rule [107], or a chart in WTM-Bench’s single-artifact tasks [108]. String transformations and spreadsheet data manipulation can likewise be specified through examples or natural language [109, 110]. Existing content can also be edited: InstructExcel expresses spreadsheet operations as scripts, PPTC includes individual edits to slide text, styles, and positions, and MiLDEdit specifies design-layer changes that preserve surrounding layout and non-target content [111–113]. The same local scope applies to application records and communication state. WorkArena’s form tasks request records with specified field values, while WorkBench includes scheduling a particular event and replying to or deleting a selected email [9, 114]. Each request supplies a target and an intended change that execution must realize. 3.2.2 Executing and Checking a Local Change To carry out these requests, the agent must identify the target and specify the operation through an available interface. ScreenSpot-Pro isolates target location in professional application screenshots [115]. BFCL’s single- call tasks examine function and argument specifications; MedAgentBench adds patient-specific parameters through a blood-pressure documentation request linked to the intended record [35, 116]. After execution, completion depends on the resulting state: an artifact must contain the requested content or property, and an application record or message must reflect the intended change. In AndroidWorld’s messaging task, the evaluator checks the destination number and message content in the phone’s SMS database [27]. Inspecting the resulting state during execution can likewise tell the agent whether the operation needs correction. 19

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 3.3 Multi-step Level Many work objectives cannot be met by a single local change: they depend on intermediate results that are not available at the start. Preparing a forecast, for example, requires importing data before constructing calculations and checking the resulting workbook. Intermediate operations establish information or state on which later decisions depend. Work at the Multi-step Level coordinates these dependent operations toward a complete objective, adapting subsequent actions to intermediate results and execution feedback [117]. Because only the objective is delegated, completion is assessed on the final result, whichever sequence of actions reaches it. 3.3.1 Completing Objectives through Intermediate Results A complete objective may culminate in a usable artifact, an informational result assembled from acquired evidence, or a change to an operational environment. Intermediate results supply the components and inputs needed to complete that objective. In data-science tasks, data preparation and code execution lead to an executable analysis, as illustrated by DataSciBench and ScienceAgentBench [10, 118]. Artifact production also requires the parts to work together. Slide generation connects content selection and visual planning [119, 120]; each slide must fit the deck’s outline and surrounding narrative [5, 17]. In a financial workbook, a value computed on one worksheet may supply calculations on another [121]. Completion therefore depends on both the individual transformations and the relationships among their results. Intermediate results can also supply the evidence for an answer or plan. TravelPlanner’s two-stage setting requires collecting travel options through tools before assembling an itinerary that satisfies the user’s constraints [83]. GAIA includes questions that require locating a study on the web before recovering the requested fact [40]. For tasks that change an environment, intermediate changes establish the state needed to complete the requested operation. Terminal-Bench 2.0 includes configuring systems and migrating databases [122]. In AIOpsLab’s mitigation tasks, the objective is to restore a running service through interventions such as configuration changes or version rollbacks [123]. Desktop and web tasks carry these intermediate results across applications. In OSWorld, payment records determine the recipients of a reminder email; WebArena’s museum-itinerary example combines reference pages and a map before recording the route in a project README [6, 7]. 3.3.2 Managing Action Dependencies and Feedback These dependencies shape the order and content of subsequent actions. A tool result can supply arguments for a later call, as in MCP-Bench and MCP-Universe [124, 125]. An interpretation of business context can determine which data to join or aggregate before a result is computed, as in DABstep [126]. A change of state can enable a previously unavailable operation: ToolSandbox’s messaging example requires cellular service to be enabled before the message can be sent [127]. TimeArena’s simulations add duration and resource constraints: agents must schedule around unfinished actions and occupied objects while advancing independent work [128]. Feedback from execution can require revising the sequence. Execution feedback guides SheetAgent’s workbook editing loop, while Spreadsheet-RL provides recalculated values during execution in Microsoft Excel [45, 129]. In DeepPresenter, rendered slides guide revisions; VIGA likewise executes candidate programs and inspects the rendered scenes before continuing scene edits in BlenderBench [58, 130]. The agent must retain these observations and changes so later actions use the current state. In many organizational settings, completing a task is only one step within a broader operational process. A finished financial forecast, for example, may need to pass through compliance verification, managerial assessment, and budget allocation before taking effect, where advancing the work depends on procedural rules and interactions with other participants. 20

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 3.4 Workflow Level The Workflow Level widens what is delegated from a single objective to the operational process around it. The process carries the objective through stages with distinct responsibilities and conditions for advancement, and each stage establishes an output, decision, or confirmation on which another stage or participant relies. The agent therefore coordinates the handoffs between stages and the procedural requirements that govern them, including cases where intermediate findings change the remaining work. Because these stages belong to the delegated work, completion covers the process outcome as well as the final output (Section 2.1): a correct forecast still cannot take effect while a required approval is missing. CXBench scores final outcomes and process compliance separately in regulated customer-service tasks, where a run that reaches the correct final state but fails a process check, such as providing a required disclosure or obtaining consent, counts as a false pass [131]. The same criterion separates workflow stages from the stages an agent system introduces into its own execution. Anthropic’s Research system, for example, runs a research stage, in which a lead agent decides how many search subagents to create and adds more when the evidence is insufficient, followed by a citation stage that attaches sources to the final report [132]. The requester, however, asks for a sourced answer to a research question, and even an explicit request for multi-agent execution specifies how the system should work without defining any stage on which the result depends. Any other arrangement of stages that yielded an equally well-sourced report would complete the request just as well, so the research and citation stages organize the execution of a multi-step objective rather than forming part of the delegated work. 3.4.1 Carrying Work through Functional Stages Stages group actions around an output or decision that subsequent work requires. A handoff can make an artifact available under an agreed specification, confirm an input, or authorize further work. In WorkArena++, employee-onboarding tasks connect user creation with ordering and assigning hardware [133]. A similar handoff occurs in an OfficeBench training task: the agent reads an Excel participant list, creates calendar events, and emails the training details to participants [76]. The same dependence on stage outputs appears in artifact production. MetaGPT follows the standard operating procedures of a software team: a requirements document guides architecture and interface design, then implementation and testing [54]. SlideRL uses research findings and an outline to guide slide generation and revision [134]. EXP-Bench links experimental design and implementation to execution and conclusions, while PaperBench requires implementing and executing a paper’s experiments to reproduce its empirical results [135, 136]. DAComp makes the handoffs explicit in pipeline tasks that connect cleaning, entity integration, and aggregation under specified data contracts [137]. 3.4.2 Coordinating Workflow Progress Once a stage has produced its output, assessment, confirmation, and policy conditions determine when work can advance. In CHI-Bench’s healthcare administrative tasks, assessment can yield a decision or a request for missing information [138]; τ-bench requires user confirmation before specified database updates [29]. In EnterpriseOps-Gym, warranty status determines whether the agent records a customer interaction and schedules a warranty discussion [139]. AutomationBench’s meeting-conflict task applies a spreadsheet priority policy, marks the lower-priority meeting for rescheduling, and reports the decision to Slack [140]. Progress also depends on other participants. In τ 2-bench’s telecommunications tasks, the agent coordinates its actions with changes made by a tool-using simulated user [30]. In EntCollabBench, roles with different tools and data access pass intermediate outputs to one another, while TheAgentCompany includes tasks requiring information from simulated coworkers [31, 38]. In Collaborative Gym, the agent’s literature search and the human’s feedback feed revisions to a shared related-work draft [141]. Retaining pending changes and their prerequisites lets the agent integrate each reply into the current workflow. These dependencies can extend across repeated operations: E-Commerce Bench connects procurement, fulfillment, returns, and cash-flow decisions over a simulated year [33]. 21

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 3.5 Workspace Level In the preceding forms, the request or task setup largely specifies which objects the work involves. As agents become able to work across entire code repositories and an organization’s documents, emails, and chats [11, 12, 142], a request can state only the goal. The agent must then establish which objects are relevant and how their relationships affect completion. A report may depend on a particular workbook version, while an approved decision may need to be reflected in several records. The Workspace Level makes discovering and following these relationships part of the delegated responsibility. The agent locates relevant objects, reconciles their evidence and versions, and, when the task requires updates, preserves consistency among the affected objects. 3.5.1 Locating Relevant Objects in a Workspace Relevant material may be distributed across documents and spreadsheets, message histories, code repositories, or linked business records. Workspace-Bench makes identifying relevant objects and their dependencies part of the task [36]. GraphForge constructs assignments requiring comparison, reconciliation, or derivation across files, while WorkGenesis requires drawing on public source files and synthesized companion attachments to produce occupational deliverables [143, 144]. OfficeQA Pro’s full-corpus tasks require finding the pages needed for an answer, while DRBench’s application-based tasks require retrieving enterprise material for a research report [145, 146]. Finding the right page can itself require reading charts and layouts, as in ViDoRe, introduced with ColPali [147]. As a retrieved object points to further sources, the relevant context develops through these connections. 3.5.2 Following Dependencies across Workspace Objects The connections uncovered during search determine how retrieved objects fit into the task. They may be explicit references, shared entities, or relationships of derivation and version. In CRMArena, identifying which order a customer refers to requires relating product information to that customer’s purchase history [148]. LOCA-bench makes these cross-source relationships explicit in a task adapted from Toolathlon: assembling an exam spreadsheet requires matching Canvas announcements and emails to the correct courses [149, 150]. In Loc- Bench, repository tasks similarly require locating the files and functions relevant to an issue description [151]. Repository repair extends this process to modifying code and testing the affected components [3, 16, 152, 153]. Spider 2.0’s DBT tasks extend this dependence to data-transformation projects: the agent reads SQL, YAML, and Markdown files to complete a missing transformation and check the resulting database state [154]. Using related objects together can also require reconciling what they say. Agora tasks require deriving a numerical answer from documents whose terminology, units, and time periods must be reconciled, while HERB queries connect people, products, and release events across heterogeneous enterprise records [155, 156]. APEX-Agents makes source selection concrete in a valuation task that combines the implied share price in a discounted cash-flow model with earnings per share from a financial statement for a specified date [157]. Tracing historical versions and derived-content relationships helps establish which sources support the conclusion [36]. Object relationships also determine what must be rechecked when work changes. In OSWorld 2.0, revised budget and vendor constraints arriving through TeamChat require the agent to reconsider affected entries in a purchase-order form [32]. Linking the updated constraints in the chat to the affected form entries identifies which earlier work needs revision. Discovering these dependencies exercises work openness; maintaining the result as relevant inputs change exercises persistence (Section 2.2). 3.6 Synthesis: Work Scope and Capability Demands Across the five work forms, the foundational capabilities introduced in Section 2 support work over an expanding set of dependencies. As an assignment grows, an interpretation of the evidence can affect decisions and changes across several stages or objects. The agent must carry those dependencies through the work and use feedback from the resulting state to decide what can proceed and what needs revision. Work complexity thus scales through the web of dependencies that these capabilities must manage in concert. 22

content: Table 3 relates the five work forms to the capability requirements introduced in Section 2.3. Work at the Workspace Level requires tracking the sources and dependencies behind a result, with consistency checks extending to affected objects when updates are required. Table 3 Capability demands across the five Work Forms Work Form Perception and Understanding Reasoning and De- cision Making Planning and Co- ordination Execution and State Manage- ment Verification, Re- covery, and Re- planning Conversation Level Interpret supplied ev- idence and context Derive supported an- swers and judgments Organize local rea- soning when needed Produce the re- quested response or specification Check evidence support, constraints, and output validity Atomic Action Level Identify the target object and local state Select an appropriate operation Establish a valid lo- cal action path Commit the intended local change Confirm the target ef- fect Multi-step Level Track intermediate evidence and state Adapt decisions to in- termediate results Decompose a coher- ent objective Maintain state across related actions Check intermediate and final outcomes Workflow Level Identify stages, rules, and shared state Reason about prereq- uisites and policies Coordinate stages, branches, and handoffs Commit consequen- tial state transitions Validate stage tran- sitions and workflow outcomes Workspace Level Discover relevant ob- jects, relations, ver- sions, and authority Reconcile evidence across objects Plan over object and dependency structure Track object state; preserve consistency when updating re- lated objects Check source lineage, freshness, and depen- dencies This dependency-centered view also clarifies where a work agent needs improvement: missing evidence can interrupt a sequence of actions, an incorrect decision can propagate into later stages, and a changed constraint can invalidate dependent outputs. Section 4 examines how experience from such work can improve the model, the harness, and their interaction, while Section 5 considers how to assess the resulting work and the progress made by these improvements. 4 Optimization: From Work Experience to System Capability The capabilities required by work agents must be cultivated via systematic optimization. As discussed in Section 2, this optimization can take place at both the model and harness levels. Model updates improve interpretation, reasoning and action selection, while harness updates enhance the interfaces, tools, memory and execution workflows that support the model. These improvements draw on diverse corpora and experience gathered during work, including observations of the environment, action trajectories and feedback on task outcomes. As illustrated in Figure 5, Section 4.1 examines the environments, data, and feedback that provide learning signals. Section 4.2 examines how pre-training, mid-training, and post-training develop model capabilities, while Section 4.3 explores improvements to interfaces, workflows, and memory. Finally, Section 4.4 examines how models and harnesses can adapt together and support continued self-improvement. 4.1 Training Environments, Data, and Rewards Agents learn to perform work through environments, data and feedback. Environments provide tasks for interaction, while corpora offer relevant knowledge and trajectories show how actions affect task progress. Feedback helps agents identify successful decisions and outcomes. For example, when preparing a report from multiple workbooks, an agent needs to understand how source values relate to calculations and reported findings, and how to update affected results when the source data changes. Table 4 compares methods for constructing environments, curating corpora and trajectories, and designing feedback. 23

Each task includes an initial workspace, available actions, a request, and checks for evaluating the results. These components can be constructed from existing work records. For example, daVinci-Env reconstructs software tasks from repositories, and Spreadsheet-RL uses paired workbooks and an Excel runtime [129, 158]. Real- world tasks often depend on information spread across documents, applications, and people. Therefore, training environments should preserve these dependencies so that agents can learn which actions to take and how to verify their results. Grounding tasks in work materials. Recent pipelines connect work materials to requirements in several ways. NexForge organizes task generation around capabilities and task forms, while WorkGenesis builds occupational requests with supporting resources [144, 159]. GraphForge represents evidence across retrieved files as a graph, then uses it to generate instructions and source-linked rubrics [143]. WorkForge starts from expert workflow plans, retrieves real files, and identifies facts that guide the instructions, solution plans, and programmatic and semantic checks [160]. title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: actor transforms input materials toward reference outputs [161]. Together, these approaches cover different aspects of task construction, from generating realistic requirements to grounding them in evidence and defining the expected results. Constructing shared and changing state. Tasks spanning multiple applications also require consistent states and operations. Agent World Model creates database-backed tool environments, EnvCraft builds sequences of dependent tasks, and AgentMercury constructs business environments with shared entities and constraints [162–164]. CoworkEnv jointly generates requests, service records, completion checks, and permitted actions, then validates their consistency before collecting teacher trajectories [166]. Cowork-Gym introduces a stateful user who can provide information, revise requirements, and modify the shared workspace [167]. Such changes can affect later actions. For example, an updated customer record may change which operation is valid, while a revised workbook may invalidate an earlier analysis. WorkRover repeatedly checks and repairs consistency among the context, task, harness, and verifier [168]. These methods highlight the importance of maintaining a valid and consistent environment as tasks progress. CompoWorld extends environment construction to tasks involving multiple services [165]. It builds reusable services with typed states and common interfaces, uses a world model for tools that are difficult to implement reliably, and samples dependency graphs across services. Each service maintains its own state, while the agent transfers information between services through observations and actions. This allows cross-service dependencies to be controlled alongside the number of services. In a matched comparison using the same backbone, training procedure, and 1K SFT trajectories, AutomationBench success increases from 12.83% with single-service environments to 33.33% with composed environments. Scaling coverage, depth, and validation. Training environments can scale by adding more workspaces, more tasks within each workspace, or more rollouts per task. These choices expose agents to different materials, task dependencies, and ways to complete or recover from work. WorkBorne compares broader artifact coverage with more transitions per corpus under matched trajectory budgets [161]. Broader coverage performs better at 1K, 3K, and 5K trajectories, while both strategies achieve similar results at 8K. WorkForge reports that increasing training data from 1K to 16K trajectories improves ALE by 13.0 points and WildClaw by 8.4 points [160]. Its comparisons using equal numbers of trajectories also favor longer interactions, although these trajectories differ in task content and decision depth. Together, these findings highlight the importance of tracking both task diversity and interaction structure alongside training volume. Reported dataset sizes also refer to different outputs of generation pipelines. WorkForge constructs 16,665 tasks, GraphForge retains 2,169 training trajectories from 2,153 selected tasks, and WorkBorne produces 7,882 task environments and 15,485 trajectories from 1,061 artifact corpora [143, 160, 161]. These counts are difficult to compare without specifying what is measured and at which stage. Thus, we suggest reporting generation attempts, accepted tasks, usable trajectories, and verification costs to assess how efficiently environment construction produces useful training experience. Validation is equally important as environments scale. An executable task may still contain incomplete requirements, inconsistent sources, or a verifier that accepts incorrect results. Validation must establish both that a task can be completed and that its verifier accepts correct solutions while detecting errors. It must also cover any new materials introduced during scaling. In WorkForge’s matched 1K-trajectory ablation, combining programmatic and semantic checks achieves an ALE score of 22.11, compared with 15.62 for semantic-only and 14.89 for programmatic-only selection [160]. GraphForge’s corruption audit shows that deleting a worksheet reduces the target rubric score by 0.377, while finer row-level, numerical, and citation errors change scores by less than 0.03 on a 0–1 scale [143]. These results suggest combining source-based judgments with exact checks of critical values and using deliberate errors to test verifier reliability. Failed checks and their dependencies can also guide environment repairs, as discussed in Section 4.4.3. Beyond scale and validation, training environments vary in difficulty, openness, persistence, and business fidelity. Difficulty reflects the decisions and dependencies involved in completing a task, while openness reflects what the agent must discover during execution. Persistence concerns how long the task state and responsibilities remain relevant, and business fidelity describes how closely the materials and constraints reflect real work. Human participants may also provide clarification, corrections, approvals, or final assessments 26

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: at different stages. A useful training set should combine controlled tasks that expose specific failures with interactive workspaces that require multiple capabilities. Evaluation on new business tasks can then test whether these capabilities transfer to unfamiliar materials and conditions. 4.1.2 Corpus and Trajectory Curation Corpora provide the materials agents work with, while trajectories record how agents use those materials to complete tasks. Documents, code, and completed artifacts offer domain knowledge and examples, while interaction records capture observations, actions, and their results. Curation selects and organizes these sources according to the capabilities being trained. For example, repository-level data can link issues to relevant files and edits, while execution trajectories also capture tool outputs and failed attempts leading to those changes [169]. Preserving this context helps models learn what actions to take and why. Task, workspace, and trajectory identifiers support coverage analysis and data splits based on shared sources. Interactive tasks also require records of changing requirements and actions taken by other participants [167]. CoworkEnv collects teacher demonstrations from validated environments, where SFT improves the mean Claw-Eval score from 46.6 to 64.1. The same environments also support student RL comparisons [166]. Generated trajectories should preserve the dependencies between actions. AgentTrek uses tutorials and guided replay to construct web interaction trajectories [170]. EnterpriseLab derives tool dependencies from enterprise schemas and reuses identifiers returned by earlier calls in later operations [171]. TDScaling organizes tools into business scenarios and generates examples for underrepresented domains and reasoning patterns [176]. Exploration offers another way to collect experience. SEE builds a verified graph of mobile interface transitions and generates tasks involving interruptions and recovery [177]. Scenario-based generation provides workflows with clear goals, while exploration captures states that standard demonstrations may miss. Successful trajectories show how to complete tasks, and recovery segments demonstrate how to proceed when execution is disrupted. Data selection should reflect the capabilities being trained. Artifact checks can filter for successful outcomes, while failed attempts may still provide useful examples for recovery and state tracking. OpenThoughts-Agent evaluates task sources, teachers, data mixtures, and filtering strategies through downstream training, including comparisons under matched token budgets [172]. CurateEvo uses development-set failures to improve data augmentation, filtering, and refinement [173]. As policies improve, repeated easy successes provide less useful information, while errors involving changed inputs, missed requirements, or costly recovery can guide further data collection. Construction and development data should remain separate from held-out evaluation tasks. When tasks share files, splitting data by workspace or source family provides a stronger test of whether models can generalize to unfamiliar materials and requirements. 4.1.3 Feedback Design Feedback turns work requirements into learning signals. When success can be measured from the resulting workspace, direct checks are possible. Spreadsheet-RL recalculates edited workbooks in Excel and compares relevant regions against target workbooks [129]. Anchor derives business tasks and verifiers from constraint programs to check feasibility, solution quality, and relationships among records [174]. Other tasks require judgments about content and presentation. Preference-based reward learning uses human comparisons [178], GraphForge links rubric items to source evidence, and SlideRL evaluates slide structure, rendering, and content [134, 143]. CogEvol also checks rendered content and browser interactions [179]. The appropriate feedback depends on the output, which may require checks of its values, organization, and behavior. Require- ments specify what counts as success, while verifiers assess the supporting evidence. Keeping these roles separate allows missing checks or parsing errors to be corrected without changing the task itself. Feedback can also focus on requirements that agents frequently miss. The Completion-Focused Rubric Reward of CompoWorld assigns greater weight to criteria with lower pass rates within a rollout group [165]. It rewards partial progress but gives the maximum reward only when all criteria are satisfied. This encourages agents to address the remaining steps needed to complete a workflow. Final outcomes alone do not reveal which actions contributed to success. Intermediate feedback helps connect 27

WorkRover’s Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment uses recorded dependencies to assign bounded positive credit to earlier turns that contributed to verified progress [168]. For example, reading a source may receive credit if its information supports a later correct change. Stage checks identify when progress occurs, while dependency records help determine which earlier decisions contributed to it. Both require sufficient records of workspace states and their relationships. Reliable feedback must also account for changing requirements. Cowork-Gym links requirements to success conditions, supporting evidence, and checkers while allowing users to introduce new constraints [167]. Main- taining current requirements alongside relevant artifacts helps agents detect omissions when earlier instructions leave the active context or source data changes. Verification also has a cost. Structural and state checks can detect common errors efficiently, while semantic inspection and human assessment handle requirements that need more context. As execution becomes faster and more parallel, verification may become a bottleneck. Thus, we propose using dependencies among sources and artifacts to determine which checks need to be repeated, which evidence remains valid, and when further assessment is necessary. Feedback design should also account for the verification and rework required before an output can be accepted. 4.2 Model Optimization Model optimization develops the knowledge and decision-making capabilities agents need to perform work. Pre- training builds broad semantic and computational knowledge; mid-training adapts this foundation to domain materials, interaction patterns, and long context; post-training strengthens behavior through demonstrations, execution feedback, and teacher guidance. Figure 6 connects these roles. The model first learns about work objects, then how to use their interaction histories, and how to improve decisions from task outcomes. The stages differ in their data mixtures, prediction targets, and training schedules, while token prediction and agent trajectories contribute across stages. 4.2.1 Pre-training Pre-training establishes the world knowledge and general capabilities that work agents rely on to understand unfamiliar tasks and environments. Through large-scale learning from text, code, mathematics, and other materials, models acquire factual knowledge, domain concepts, common conventions, and computational skills. These are essential for professional work, where requests often assume knowledge that users do not explicitly provide. For example, an agent revising a budget report must understand financial categories and units, interpret relationships between tables and written claims, and recognize how formulas or code produce numerical results. This background knowledge allows agents to interpret workspace materials, understand task requirements, and reason about possible actions before adapting to specific workflows. Work materials can in turn enrich pre-training with structured and multimodal prediction signals. For autoregressive language models, pre-training uses the standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective. Given a token sequence x, the model learns to predict each token from its preceding context by minimizing LNTP(θ) = −Ex∼D |x| X t=1 log pθ(xt | x<t), (3) where D denotes the pre-training corpus. Under this objective, the selection and organization of training data determine what knowledge and relationships the model encounters. DeepSeek-V4, for example, combines web data with mathematics, programming, and long technical documents [182]. Work materials further expose cell addresses, formulas, layout, and relations between inputs and computed outputs. DocLLM uses text-infilling pre-training over document text and bounding-box layout [183]. Such structure can support executable prediction targets: TAPEX pre-trains a model to predict SQL execution results from queries and serialized tables, improving downstream table reasoning [184]. This illustrates how structured data can develop computational skills alongside factual knowledge. Additionally, work agents must recognize relevant knowledge when it appears in different forms. Its early-checkpoint experiment reports 28.94% SimpleQA accuracy for ten distinct rephrasings used once, versus 23.76% for ten repetitions of the original text. content: pre-training data. Mid-training addresses this gap by increasing the density of specialized and long-tail knowledge while preserving the relationships among relevant materials. GLM-5 organizes related files, issues, pull requests, and commits into training sequences, then increases the proportion of long documents and synthetic agent trajectories in later stages [187]. Step 3.5 Flash begins with software engineering and tool-use data at 32K context, retaining 21% pre-training replay, before expanding to 128K with long documents, synthetic reasoning, and agent data [188]. Kimi K2.5 similarly combines high-quality text and multimodal materials while extending context from 32K to 256K [186]. These approaches increase exposure to specialized work knowledge while using replay to preserve broader capabilities. For work agents, organizing knowledge around related files, requirements, and revisions is particularly useful, as understanding a work object often requires information distributed across multiple sources. Agent Interaction Familiarization. Domain knowledge alone cannot prepare an agent for the interactions required to complete work. An agent must also understand what a tool call changes, how to interpret its response, and what to do when an operation fails or produces an unexpected result. Mid-training can introduce these interaction patterns before post-training begins to optimize task behavior. DeepSeek-V4 incorporates agentic coding data at this stage [182]. Nemotron combines repositories, pull requests, edit histories, and build logs in a 500B-token mixture at 256K context, including 10% agent traces and 20% pre-training replay [189]. With subsequent SFT held fixed, this stage improves SWE-bench Verified Pass@1 from 60.7% to 64.5%. daVinci-Dev further combines trajectories reconstructed from pull requests with trajectories collected through actual tool execution [169]. Its mid-training uses both successful and failed executions, while later SFT focuses on test-passing trajectories. This distinction is important for work agents, as unsuccessful interactions can expose errors and intermediate states that success-only demonstrations may omit. Learning from these records helps models become familiar with the observation, action, and state-change patterns involved in execution. This provides a stronger starting point for post-training, where feedback can focus on improving decisions and completing tasks reliably. Long-Context Learning and Post-Training Readiness. Work agents frequently perform tasks in which later decisions depend on information or changes from much earlier interactions. For example, modifying a source workbook may affect several calculations and invalidate parts of a previously generated report. Simply extending the context window does not ensure that a model can identify these dependencies or reconstruct the current workspace state. TrajLong addresses this problem by transforming interaction histories into retrieval, information-combination, and file-state reconstruction tasks using full-token next-token prediction [190]. Under a fixed 40B-token budget and identical later SFT, these tasks outperform raw-trajectory training on all seven reported ablation benchmarks. Function-aware fill-in-the-middle training similarly uses code dependencies to select functions or function groups for reconstruction, improving the mean across SWE-bench Verified and Lite from 13.95 to 15.60 in a controlled 7B comparison [191]. The choice of prediction targets also matters. In Nemotron’s 100B-token ablation, masking tool responses while retaining them as context raises SWE-bench Verified Pass@1 from 27.5% to 37.8% after identical SFT [189]. This distinction is relevant to agent training because tool responses provide evidence for subsequent decisions, even when the model does not need to generate those responses itself. Efficient access to long histories presents another challenge. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next introduces sparse attention during continued training at 256K context to reduce the cost of accessing relevant information [192], connecting this stage to the memory mechanisms in Section 4.3.3. Ultimately, the value of mid-training should be measured by its contribution to later optimization. Step 3.5 Flash reports stronger and more stable RL gains after incorporating task knowledge and tool-use patterns [188], while Nemotron compares recipes through identical SFT runs because intermediate model metrics do not reliably predict downstream agent performance [189]. 4.2.3 Post-training Post-training develops the policies that allow work agents to apply their knowledge to real tasks. Beyond understanding a request, an agent must select appropriate actions, respond to changes in the workspace, and determine whether its results satisfy the requirements. Different training methods provide supervision for these decisions. Demonstrations show how tasks can be completed, execution rewards evaluate the consequences of actions, teacher guidance improves decisions at states encountered by the agent, and retrospective learning extracts useful information from previous attempts. content: learning signals and update mechanisms. Learning from demonstrations. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches agents to follow instructions, use tools, and produce completed work through examples [193–195]. Synthetic instructions provide additional supervision before task-specific interaction [196]. For work agents, demonstrations can capture both the steps taken during execution and the structure of an accepted deliverable. Kimi K2 generates tool-use trajectories by constructing domains, tools, and tasks, simulating interactions, and filtering the results, while also incorporating real execution environments into post-training [185]. Interactive demonstrations teach agents how to respond to observations and tool feedback [197, 198]. Artifact-based supervision instead connects task requirements to completed outputs. CogEvol trains on verified representations of slides and interactive pages [179], while GraphForge uses source-linked rubrics to select generated solutions for rejection fine-tuning [143]. CoworkEnv provides curated teacher executions that improve multi-turn performance on Claw-Eval, with the same executable environments supporting subsequent RL [166]. Together, these approaches teach agents how to carry out tasks and what acceptable results should look like. Learning through execution rewards. Reinforcement learning improves an agent’s policy through the outcomes of its own interactions [199–201]. Web navigation, device control, and repository repair provide different environments in which actions can be executed and evaluated [202–204]. For artifact-producing tasks, Spreadsheet-RL evaluates the resulting workbook, while SlideRL combines structural, visual, and content feedback to assess generated slides [129, 134]. However, work agents often complete tasks through many dependent steps, making it difficult to determine which earlier decisions contributed to the final result. Intermediate rewards and credit assignment help address this problem. ADMIRE derives adaptive milestones from successful GUI trajectories, while HiPER learns hierarchical policies with subgoals and associated value estimates [205, 206]. GiGPO combines episode-level advantages with comparisons of actions taken from repeated environment states [207]. WorkRover uses recorded dependencies to assign credit to earlier turns that support verified progress [168]. These methods provide different ways to connect final outcomes with intermediate decisions, allowing agents to learn from both completed work and progress made along the way. Reliable execution feedback also requires accurate records of the interactions being trained on. Mercor and SkyRL’s knowledge-work recipe uses 1,928 expert-created tasks and emphasizes environment repair, exact token histories, and small-set overfitting tests before scaling RL [208]. Its loss ablations compare weighting at the token, sequence, and prompt-group levels, with prompt-group weighting reducing the influence of unusually long trajectories. The resulting 397B model improves held-out APEX-Agents Pass@1 from 16.11% to 27.29%. These practices are particularly important for work agents, where tool failures, inconsistent environments, and long execution histories can make rewards unreliable. Preserving the exact observations and actions behind each reward helps distinguish policy errors from infrastructure failures and keeps learning aligned with the interaction that actually occurred. Learning from teacher guidance. Demonstrations alone may not cover the states an agent encounters during its own execution, especially after incorrect actions or unexpected tool responses. On-policy distillation addresses this gap by providing teacher guidance at states reached by the student [209]. TCOD gradually increases student-controlled interaction, while Guided-OPD reduces teacher-controlled turns and combines teacher imitation with distillation on student-generated states [210, 211]. This allows supervision to follow the developing policy more closely [212, 213]. Step-wise on-policy distillation adjusts guidance based on student–teacher divergence [214]. Other methods improve supervision at specific decisions. LiteGUI selects a human-verified valid action that matches the student’s attempted action, while Gated Hindsight Distillation uses a later screenshot to guide an earlier decision [215, 216]. Foundation-model training also uses on-policy distillation to combine specialized capabilities or preserve them across training stages [182, 187]. For work agents, these methods are useful because guidance can address errors and partial progress encountered during actual execution, rather than relying only on previously collected demonstrations. Learning from accumulated feedback. Work agents can also learn from information accumulated across attempts, including corrections, execution feedback, and completed results [217–219]. SDPO provides textual feedback to a self-teacher and distills its improved predictions into the acting policy, while Skill-SD additionally conditions the teacher on short summaries of earlier attempts [220–222]. RePro uses completed attempts to teach models which intermediate decisions indicate useful progress [223]. These approaches reuse information 31

content: 4.3 Harness Optimization Work agents rely on external support to inspect information, execute operations, and manage work across multiple steps. Even with a capable model, missing evidence, unreliable tools, or poorly organized procedures can prevent successful task completion. Harness optimization improves this external support through observation and action interfaces, execution workflows, and reusable experience. Interfaces determine what the model can observe and how it interacts with the workspace. Workflows organize execution, verification, recovery, and delivery, while context management, memory, and skills preserve task progress and useful procedures across interactions. Execution traces reveal where these components need improvement, such as missing information, repeated tool errors, or unnecessary rework. content: 4.3.1 Observation and Action Interfaces Observation interfaces determine what information an agent can inspect before making a decision. For work agents, this often involves locating relevant evidence within large repositories, documents, or tool outputs. SWE-agent introduces agent-oriented repository operations that make software files easier to search, inspect, and edit [3]. TACO further improves observations by discovering terminal-output filters, refining them during execution, and reusing effective rules across tasks [225]. These filters reduce unnecessary output while preserving relevant state and error information. The main consideration is whether an interface provides the evidence needed for the next decision without consuming excessive context or requiring repeated inspection. Action interfaces determine how an agent translates its decisions into operations on files, applications, and services. Unclear tool descriptions or inconsistent argument conventions can cause repeated errors, even when the intended operation is appropriate. Trace-Free+ trains a tool-description generator, gradually moving from supervision based on execution traces to generation using tool descriptions alone [226]. JTPRO jointly optimizes global instructions and tool descriptions using execution feedback [227]. The former learns tool-use conventions that can transfer across tool sets, while the latter coordinates instructions within a particular environment. Both aim to improve tool selection and argument generation, helping agents carry out the operations required by a task. Executable support can also correct errors during tool execution. PRISM analyzes tool traces, state changes, and errors to improve prompts, middleware, or both [228]. Middleware can correct arguments, check prerequisites, and provide error information that supports recovery. These mechanisms are particularly important when work agents modify shared records or related objects. For example, checking a file version before writing helps ensure that an edit applies to the same object the agent previously inspected. Tool responses should also indicate what changed so the agent can decide whether to continue or recover. Evaluating interfaces with the same model and tasks helps isolate improvements from external support. In the Mercor/SkyRL study, correcting tool behavior and observation handling improves the base agent before weight training, while the training gains also transfer to a held-out code-based harness [208]. Such comparisons help distinguish improvements in the execution environment from improvements learned by the model. 4.3.2 Workflows and Execution Control Workflow optimization improves how an agent organizes and executes work across multiple steps [241, 242]. The editable components range from prompts [243–245] and connections between model calls [246, 247] to executable harness code [248, 249]. Prompt optimization can use feedback-guided revision [250, 251], reinforcement learning [252], or evolutionary search [253, 254]. More recent approaches extend these ideas to complete execution procedures. GEPA uses execution traces and outcomes to refine prompts [229], AFlow searches over workflow graphs [230], and Meta-Harness modifies harness code [231]. These methods provide different levels of control over how an agent performs work [255]. For example, an improved workflow may inspect additional evidence before editing, verify intermediate results before dependent operations, or introduce a recovery step after failure. Its effectiveness should be measured by whether these changes improve execution on subsequent tasks. Artifact production illustrates how feedback from individual tasks can improve reusable workflows. AutoDesign uses rendering, validation, and critic feedback to revise a poster, then analyzes recurring failures to propose changes to its design harness [232]. This separates improving the current deliverable from improving the procedure used for future tasks. JIT-Agent takes a related approach by training a separate model to construct task-specific harnesses using execution reward, latency, and cost from a frozen executor [233]. The designer learns how to organize execution and produces an explicit procedure for the acting agent. These approaches show how experience from completed work can guide the design of more effective workflows without requiring changes to the underlying executor. Execution control must also preserve progress when work is interrupted, requirements change, or responsibilities are transferred. For ongoing tasks, a workflow needs clear conditions for continuing, revising previous results, and determining when delivery is complete. These conditions relate to the requirements and responsibilities discussed in Section 2. For example, a report awaiting source confirmation should retain that dependency, while 34

content: a completed deliverable should be checked against the latest requirements before the task closes. Repeated inspections, retries, and human corrections provide evidence of where workflow changes could reduce delays and rework. Methods based on retrospective self-preference, adaptive curricula, and task-dependent harness routing further use feedback to select and deploy suitable procedures [256–258]. Evaluating both the quality of accepted results and the effort required to produce them helps ensure that workflow optimization improves real task execution. 4.3.3 Long Context, Memory and Skills Context management determines which parts of a growing work history remain available for each decision. Work agents may accumulate lengthy tool outputs, repeated observations, and information that becomes outdated as the workspace changes. A larger context window alone does not resolve these issues. MemGPT manages information between active context and external storage, while TACO adjusts the amount and form of tool output retained during execution [225, 234]. For ongoing work, the active context must also preserve current requirements, relevant object versions, and unresolved dependencies. These records help agents determine whether earlier observations and decisions remain valid. Effective context management therefore supports efficient access to information and reliable continuation after interruptions or revisions. Memory optimization focuses on preserving useful experience across tasks. ReasoningBank extracts strategies from successful and failed attempts for later retrieval [235], while ACE maintains an evolving playbook through generation, reflection, and curation [236]. Skills extend this idea by representing reusable procedures that guide future execution. SkillOpt improves procedural documents through validated edits [237], SkillAlpha learns editing policies and evaluates them through downstream execution [238], and CodeSkill extracts, revises, and maintains a library of coding skills [239]. These approaches allow agents to reuse lessons from previous work rather than rediscovering procedures for every task. Execution feedback also helps determine which instructions remain useful and which should be revised as new situations arise. As reusable experience accumulates, agents must decide which procedures to retain, how to combine them, and when to apply them. SkillSmith addresses interactions and dependencies among skills under a limited context budget and considers which operations should be represented as skills or executable tools [240]. Stable operations can be implemented as tools, while skills provide guidance on when and how to use them. This distinction is important for work agents that repeatedly perform related tasks with different materials and constraints. Task-specific state and reusable experience also require different update schedules. A change to a source workbook should immediately update the current task record, while a revised reporting procedure should be validated across multiple tasks before broader reuse. Recording the sources and dependencies of both enables targeted updates. For example, a reporting skill may describe how to reconcile information from several workbooks, while the task record identifies which workbook version has been checked and which approval remains pending. Maintaining this distinction allows agents to reuse established procedures while keeping their execution aligned with the current workspace. 4.4 Model--Harness Coupling and Joint Optimization The effectiveness of a work agent depends on how well its model and harness work together. The model must learn to use the information and tools provided by the harness, while the harness must offer interfaces and procedures that the model can use reliably. This raises an important question of where improvements should be implemented. A capability may be learned through model training, provided through retrieved context, encoded as a reusable skill, or implemented directly in control code. We examine how models are trained within a harness, how the two components can be optimized together, and how repeated execution can improve both the system and its optimization process. Environment evolution and optimizer-level recursion WorkRover [168] Paper Environment components in E; separate policy post-training. VERSE [270] Paper § Code Executor harness h and optimizer procedure G; model weights fixed. Controlled study, test accuracy (%): baseline 39.20; verification only 39.81; self-evolution only 31.79; both 41.05. One evolution run per condition. 4.4.1 Harness-Aware Policy Training A training harness determines what a policy can observe and do. Tool schemas define available operations and their arguments, context management controls access to previous interactions, and execution rules determine how actions affect the workspace. Harness-aware training allows models to learn under these conditions. Spreadsheet-RL trains agents with a spreadsheet runtime and toolset, while UI-Copilot provides structured observations, progress summaries, and a copilot for retrieval and calculation [129, 259]. Through these interactions, the policy learns when to rely on internal reasoning and when to use external tools. The deployment harness must therefore provide the interfaces and support that the policy has learned to use. Training systems can also optimize a policy while preserving the agent’s existing execution process. Agent Lightning connects policy optimization with agent execution, allowing the harness to manage interactions while the training system learns from the resulting decision records [260]. The available tools, memory access, and execution rules all influence the experience collected during training. For example, a model trained with compressed observations needs to learn how to retrieve information that is no longer available in its active context. The training harness therefore shapes the situations and decisions the policy learns to handle, even when only model weights are updated. Models can also learn to construct tools for future tasks. SMITH alternates between tool construction and tool use, adds generated tools to a reusable pool, and rewards their validity and downstream usefulness [271]. As the available tools evolve, the policy learns how to use the capabilities it creates. For work agents, this provides a way to turn repeated operations into reusable executable tools while learning when to construct and invoke them [272]. Feedback from subsequent execution helps determine which generated tools are useful, allowing the model to improve based on their contributions to later tasks. 4.4.2 Joint Model--Harness Adaptation Joint adaptation coordinates model learning with changes to external support, which can be revised at a different pace [273]. BetterTogether alternates between prompt and weight optimization, while Co-Harness uses improved harnesses to generate model-training trajectories and then adapts the harness to the updated model [261, 263]. Fast-Slow Training similarly alternates prompt search with blocks of reinforcement-learning updates [262]. In these approaches, each component is optimized using experience collected with the current version of the other. This interaction matters because a procedure that compensates for an earlier model’s limitations may become unnecessary after training, while a stronger model may be able to use workflows that were previously unreliable. 37

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: Memory and skills provide concrete components for joint adaptation. UI-Mem extracts experience during GUI reinforcement learning and updates memory guidance as the policy improves, while SkillRL maintains a skill library alongside policy training [264, 265]. VERA alternates rubric-guided model updates with validated additions, revisions, and removals in a skill library organized around work stages [175]. SIA uses execution trajectories and reward changes to decide between scaffold editing and policy reinforcement [267]. These approaches allow improvements to target the model, its external support, or both, depending on the observed failures and the capabilities already available. An important question is where learned experience should be stored. Component Routing compares experience incorporated through weight updates with the same experience provided as context [274]. In its evaluated GUI settings, recurring patterns for locating interface elements favor weight updates, while state-dependent procedures and facts benefit more from context. The effectiveness of transferred procedures also depends on the receiving model. For work agents, this suggests learning recurring behavioral patterns in model weights while keeping changing facts, task commitments, and operating rules in external records. To evaluate these choices, we propose comparing (M0, H0), (M1, H0), (M0, H1), and (M1, H1) under consistent task conditions and compatible interfaces. For ongoing work, each configuration can resume from the same saved workspace after an identical source change or user intervention. Comparing these runs with fresh starts would reveal whether updates preserve unfinished dependencies, support necessary rechecks, and improve task completion while accounting for verification costs and human intervention. 4.4.3 Self-Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement Work agents may operate over extended periods while the environments in which they work continue to change. New tools, data formats, business rules, and organizational processes can gradually make previously reliable procedures less effective. Although context and memory can help agents recognize these changes, substantial shifts may require persistent updates to their models, workflows, skills, and verification mechanisms. Self-improvement addresses this need by using execution experience to adapt the agent and its supporting environment. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) goes further by improving the mechanisms through which the system identifies limitations, develops new capabilities, and evaluates its own progress. These two directions offer complementary benefits for work agents. Self-improvement supports continued adaptation to changing work, while RSI offers a potential path toward more fundamental growth in agent capabilities. Adapting the source of practice. Self-improvement allows agents to accumulate experience and revise the capabilities and procedures they use in later work. Socratic-SWE extracts strategies and recurring failures into a skill registry, then alternates task generation and solving through a shared policy with role-specific objectives [269]. Generated tasks guide subsequent training, while new execution traces inform later task generation. CurateEvo uses development failures to improve data augmentation and filtering [173], while SkillRL and SLIM update a procedural library alongside policy training [265, 266]. These methods improve future behavior by changing what the agent practices and which procedures it can reuse. Beyond benchmark tasks, DMRL learns a policy that edits the skill instructions of a frozen advertising-system agent using online outcomes and estimates of longer-term effects [268]. Such feedback connects self-improvement to operational needs, where an agent must adjust its behavior as requirements and working conditions evolve. Maintaining reliable training environments. Continued learning also requires environments that provide valid tasks and feedback. GraphForge revises generated tasks and rubrics using execution feedback before collecting training trajectories [143], while WorkForge constructs and filters environments through a forward generation pipeline [160]. WorkRover supports repeated environment repair by diagnosing compatibility failures and testing candidate changes through Factorial Compatibility Replay [168]. It selects the smallest repair set that satisfies fixed requirements and preserves necessary dependencies, then validates the result through fresh execution. Its natural-defect study reports 70.3% safe repairs, compared with 60.7% for full regeneration, with rates remaining within 70.3–72.4% across three repair generations. Table 7 further compares regressions and token costs. These methods highlight the need to distinguish failures caused by the policy from defects in the training environment. An incorrect decision may require further learning, while missing materials or inconsistent verifiers require environment repair. Maintaining reliable learning environments helps agents improve from experience as their training needs change. 38

content: From adaptive improvement to RSI. Self-improvement can also be guided directly by the outcomes of real work. DMRL learns a policy that edits the skill instructions of a frozen advertising-system agent using online outcomes and estimates of longer-term effects [268]. This illustrates how business feedback can guide improvements to reusable procedures. RSI introduces a further possibility by allowing the optimization process itself to evolve. VERSE explores this direction by keeping the executor and optimizer model weights fixed while modifying the executor harness and the optimizer’s prompts, skills, tools, hooks, and notes [270]. Its controlled comparison evaluates execution verification and optimizer self-evolution separately and together, with the combined setting achieving the best results. Without executable checks, self-evolution selects the initial harness and produces a lower test result. Although these results are based on one evolution run per condition, they illustrate how changes to the optimization process can influence subsequent improvements. These studies provide different perspectives on how improvement should be evaluated. DMRL connects procedural updates to business outcomes [268], WorkRover examines the reliability and cost of repeated environment repairs [168], and VERSE separates the effects of optimizer evolution and executable verifica- tion [270]. For work agents, we propose extending these comparisons to longer periods and changing work conditions. Self-improvement can be evaluated by how effectively an agent adapts while preserving unfinished responsibilities and maintaining the quality of accepted work. RSI requires an additional comparison between the updated optimizer and its frozen predecessor, testing whether improvements to the optimization process enable more effective responses to subsequent, unseen challenges. Such evaluations should measure task success, adaptation costs, verification effort, and the recurrence of previously resolved failures. Table 8 links observed failures to candidate optimization targets and the work-agent capabilities discussed in Section 2.3. Table 8 Choosing an optimization target from observed failures. Targeted failures can test specific improvements, while held-out workflows and later business tasks can assess their transfer. Beyond immediate task success, evaluations should track preserved dependencies, necessary rechecks, human intervention, and the time and cost of accepted work. For RSI, repeated evaluations should further determine whether improvements to the optimization process help agents acquire capabilities needed for increasingly unfamiliar work. This distinction provides a basis for studying both sustained adaptation and longer-term capability growth. 5 Evaluation and Resources: Assessing Work Agents Rigorous evaluation is essential for understanding the capabilities and limitations of current models on work tasks and guiding the improvement of work agents. By verifying whether delegated work meets explicit acceptance criteria, evaluation reveals where agents succeed, where they fail, and which capabilities require further development. These findings provide empirical feedback for the improvement methods discussed in Section 4. To serve this purpose, evaluation must clearly define the delegated work, specify its acceptance criteria, and collect appropriate evidence of completion. content: workflows have different requirements, so assessment must examine the relevant deliverables, workspace state, and execution process rather than rely on the final response alone. Because measured performance depends jointly on the model, tool interface, execution environment, and verification procedure, benchmark scores must be interpreted alongside the tasks and protocols that produced them. This section covers task construction and domain coverage (Section 5.1), the targets, dimensions, and methods used to evaluate work results (Section 5.2), and the metrics used to summarize those judgments (Section 5.3). It also introduces the execution frameworks and evaluation infrastructure that support task execution and verification (Section 5.4). The final part examines the relationships among task performance, execution cost, and economic value, including how human oversight affects deployment returns (Section 5.5). 5.1 Benchmarks and Task Construction A work-agent benchmark is scoped by two choices: how its tasks are constructed and which work domains they cover [275, 276]. Task construction determines how requests, materials, and execution conditions are produced [277, 278], and thus how realistic and how controllable the resulting tasks are. Domain coverage determines the professional knowledge, work objects, and acceptance requirements involved, and thus how representative the benchmark is of the work agents are asked to perform. 5.1.1 Task Construction Strategies Existing benchmarks mainly use four approaches: expert design, conversion of real requests, construction in interactive environments, and construction from professional workspaces. Each emphasizes a different task source and verification condition; Table 9 lists representative instances. Expert-designed and curated tasks. Researchers or domain experts design tasks around knowledge, reasoning, and operational requirements, and supply reference answers, labels, or explicit acceptance criteria. GAIA, FinQA, and LegalBench cover information-seeking reasoning, financial computation, and legal judgment respectively [21, 40, 101]; CADBench (BlenderLLM) refines modeling instructions into check items such as attributes and spatial relations [85]. This approach makes difficulty and requirements easy to control, but it does not necessarily include every interaction condition of a real delegation. Tasks built from real requests and existing task collections. These methods extract tasks from real problems, user needs, or existing professional data. SWE-bench uses GitHub issues and their associated code repositories, and SpreadsheetBench curates workbook requests from user forums [16, 56]; CADBench (MIT) instead builds program-reconstruction tasks from existing CAD data [86]. The advantage is that real work objects are preserved, although task coverage depends on the data source and the filtering procedure. Tasks built around applications and execution environments. These methods place tasks in interactive software environments, constructing repeatably executable tasks by initializing application state, providing operation interfaces, and setting acceptance conditions. WebArena, OSWorld, AndroidWorld, and AppWorld provide web, desktop, mobile, and multi-application API environments respectively, and verify task results against the actual state after execution [6, 7, 27, 37]. Such methods can assess an agent together with the operations it actually performed, but task coverage remains limited by the environment design and by the states that can be verified. Tasks built from professional activities and workspaces. These methods organize multi-step, multi- object tasks around occupational requests and actual delivery requirements. GDPval supplies professional work tasks authored by occupational experts, TheAgentCompany uses simulated enterprise services, and Workspace- Bench concerns multiple files and their dependencies [31, 36, 279]; StartupBench and BankerToolBench further emphasize complete professional delivery and fine-grained acceptance [280, 281]. Compared with a single operation, these tasks come closer to a complex delegation, but their construction and verification costs are usually higher. Taken together, the four approaches trade controllability for realism. Expert-designed tasks specify require- ments most precisely, whereas workspace tasks reproduce the most of an actual delegation. In between, real requests contribute authentic content and environments contribute executable context. 40

Domain coverage matters because the evidence needed to accept a completed task depends on the work object. In finance, law, and healthcare, the object is mainly an answer or a professional judgment, and acceptance rests on factual grounding, professional rules, and result correctness [21, 101, 116]. In office and document work, it is the delivered file, whose content, native structure, and computational or visual effects must be checked [56, 112]. In customer service and enterprise operations, it is the state of business systems, subject to permissions and operational constraints [139]. Software engineering, data science, and scientific research usually produce executable or reproducible results, verifiable through tests, database queries, predictive outcomes, or scientific conclusions [10, 16, 154, 286, 287]. CAD and 3D graphics additionally require program validity, geometric fidelity, and rendering quality to hold together [85, 86, 130]. Web, desktop, mobile, and API settings, by contrast, are interaction settings reusable across domains; they assess the environment state after an operation rather than professional knowledge, and are therefore listed as a separate group [6, 7, 27, 37]. Cross-domain benchmarks combine several work objects and acceptance requirements: GDPval examines occupational work products, Remote Labor Index authentic remote tasks, and Workspace-Bench and Startup- Bench complex workspace delivery [36, 279, 280, 288]. Table 10 and Figure 8 summarize the work objects and requirements of each group. Together, they illustrate the range from localized question answering to complete professional tasks. We refer to these as the evaluation target, the evaluation dimensions, and the evaluation method. Targets are the actual answers, artifacts, or environment states; dimensions include correctness, completeness, structure, visual quality, and constraint compliance.
