content: submitted answer [148]. Answer-level evaluation suits well-defined outputs, but a correct answer does not establish that the operations behind it, such as CRMArena’s queries, were correct. Artifact-level evaluation. The result is a deliverable the agent created or modified, such as code, a document, or a model file. ScienceAgentBench runs each generated program and checks that it executes and that its output meets task-specific success criteria [10]; OmegaUse-OfficeVal requires Office deliverables to be valid, openable, and editable before scoring them against weighted requirements, with penalties for unintended damage [301]. Because each artifact type has its own requirements of use, text similarity cannot replace structural and functional checks. Environment-state-level evaluation. The result is the state of a website, application, or business system after execution. Terminal-Bench 2.0 tests the final container state rather than the agent’s commands [122], VisualWebArena checks the final webpage state with model-based checks where visual content matters [284], and WorkBench compares five sandbox databases with a ground-truth outcome while counting mismatching side effects [114]. Checking state rather than actions admits different action paths to the same goal, but the check must also catch unintended modifications and violated constraints. Workflow-level evaluation. The result is a multi-step, cross-application, or multi-file delivery, and evaluation covers the final result, intermediate requirements, and dependencies among objects. ToolSandbox matches the trajectory against milestones that must occur and minefields that must not, scoring zero if any minefield is hit [127]. MultiAgentBench uses an LLM-based detector to record which milestones a team reaches and who contributes [309], and Odysseys has an LLM judge assess the full trajectory against each rubric item [310]. This level comes closest to a complete delegation, but it must make clear which process constraints belong to the acceptance conditions. 5.2.2 Evaluation Methods Given the collected evidence, automated benchmarks judge it mainly through rules, LLM judges, or agent judges; occupational experts assess open-ended work products or provide reference judgments. Rule-based evaluation. Programs verify the result by answer matching, execution, or assertions over files and state. AutomationBench checks the end state of simulated business applications with deterministic assertions, including changes that must not occur, and gives no partial credit [140]; OfficeBench saves the file system after each task and applies exact, fuzzy, or execution-based checks [76]. Such checks are clear and repeatable but establish only the requirements their tests cover. LLM-as-a-Judge. A model judges the result against task requirements, reference material, and a rubric, which suits semantic, professional, and visual qualities that resist formalization [318, 319]. MCP-Atlas has an LLM check each required factual claim in the final answer and passes a task at 0.75 claim coverage [307]; Finance Agent v2 uses a jury of three frontier models [290]; and CI-Work judges, entry by entry, whether an agent’s final action conveys required information or discloses sensitive information [303]. These scores depend on the criteria, the reference evidence, and the judge model, and are not objective fact. Agent-as-a-Judge. An evaluating agent gathers evidence itself by reading files, calling tools, or inspecting traces [15]. Workspace-Bench lets its judge inspect output files, inputs, rubrics, and the execution trajectory with shell tools and file parsers [36]; BankerToolBench gives its judge the same tools as the evaluated agent, so it can run code to check spreadsheet formulas [281]; and StartupBench runs a separate judge session per rubric item, which agreed more often with domain experts than a single holistic judge [280]. Agent judges reach evidence scattered across files, but extra tool execution can cause missed checks or unstable judgments. These methods are often combined: WildClawBench pairs deterministic checks and side-effect audits with an LLM or VLM judge for reports and images [311], and CRMArena-Pro scores answers by exact match while a GPT-4o judge assesses confidentiality awareness [302]. For open-ended professional work, expert judgment remains the reference; in Remote Labor Index, trained evaluators and subject experts decide, as a reasonable client would, whether an AI deliverable completes the project at least as well as the human one [288]. Benchmarks use three kinds: task outcome scores, relative comparison metrics, and weighted performance metrics. All measure result quality or degree of completion; resource metrics such as cost, tokens, and latency are discussed in Section 5.5.1. Task outcome scores. These measure whether, or how far, a result meets the acceptance conditions. The most common is the share of successful tasks; in τ-bench, a task succeeds only if the final database matches the ground truth and the agent conveys the required information [29]. Answer-oriented benchmarks use accuracy and matching scores, such as accuracy, F1, or ROUGE-L in LawBench, depending on the task [292]. Rubric scores differ in strictness: GDP.pdf ranks models by a strict pass rate that requires every criterion, alongside a mean rubric score [91]. Some outcomes are continuous, such as year-end total assets after a simulated year of store operation in E-Commerce Bench [33]. Over repeated attempts, pass@k requires at least one of k attempts to succeed, and passk, introduced by τ-bench, requires all of them [29]; APEX-Agents reports both Pass@8 and Pass8 [157]. Because they differ in unit and strictness, these scores are not directly comparable across benchmarks. Relative comparison metrics. Without a unique reference answer, quality can be measured by preferences, win rates, or rankings among candidates. GDPval has occupational experts blindly compare model and professional deliverables, reporting how often the model’s is rated better or as good [279]. CentaurBench turns pairwise judgments from a panel of LLM judges into rankings, separately for automation, where the model produces the deliverable, and augmentation, where it guides a weaker worker model [314]. Such results depend on what is compared and how, and cannot be read apart from the reference set. Weighted performance metrics. These aggregate results with explicit weights on criteria or on tasks. PRBench weights each expert criterion with an integer from −10 to 10, so that undesirable content lowers the score [80]; OmegaUse-OfficeVal weights tasks by recorded human labor time or a task-price proxy [301]. 49

authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 5.5.1 Trading Performance against Execution Cost Task performance and execution cost do not always move together. HAL compares task scores and invocation cost jointly, so that a Pareto frontier can identify competitive system configurations under different cost constraints [324]. The analysis applies both to model comparison and to complete agent systems. HarnessTax further finds that when the same model is run under different harnesses, invocation cost can differ substantially even when task success rates are close [326]. Harness-Bench analyzes how the execution configuration affects task performance [325], and automatic adaptation of instructions, tools, and the execution flow improves the cost efficiency of some smaller models [327]. These results show that the performance–cost trade-off depends not only on the choice of model but also on the design of the harness. 5.5.2 The Value of Professional Work Execution cost reflects the resources needed to complete a task, whereas economic value also depends on the task itself. SWE-Lancer connects software-engineering tasks to real market pay [153]; GDPval has occupational experts compare professional deliverables [279]; and Remote Labor Index evaluates end-to-end automation using actual paid remote projects [288]. OmegaUse-OfficeVal further combines office-artifact quality, human completion time, and a task price proxy [301], while a task-completion time horizon uses human task duration to characterize the scale of work an agent can complete [63]. The task distribution of existing agent benchmarks also diverges from the real labor market [328]. Evaluating work value therefore has to account for task representativeness and professional acceptance, and annotation pay or human working hours should not be equated directly with actual economic return. 5.5.3 Reliable Deployment and Agentic ROI High task performance and low invocation cost do not necessarily produce a positive return on deployment. The position that the real barrier to agent usability is agentic ROI argues that an agent’s practical utility depends on delivery quality, the human time saved, and the cost of use, including the effort users spend describing, checking, and revising the work [329]. READY further brings human oversight into reliability and cost evaluation, finding that agents with comparable autonomous accuracy may require different amounts of human assessment to meet the same deployment requirement [330]. Agentic ROI therefore supplies a conceptual view of user utility, and READY an empirical complement in the form of joint human–machine cost under a reliability constraint. Actual deployment return must also account for failure repair, system integration, and long-term maintenance. Overall, the economic evaluation of work agents needs to distinguish the resource cost of executing a task, the potential economic value of the work produced, and the actual deployment return once human oversight is taken into account. The performance–cost Pareto frontier, the harness tax, and agentic ROI complement conventional task-performance evaluation from the perspectives of system efficiency, execution configuration, and user utility respectively. Section 6 develops how these systems can extend from completing assigned tasks to carrying responsibility as workspaces and requirements change. 6 Frontiers: Toward Next-Generation Work Agents A manager asks an agent to prepare a report for a recurring business meeting. Completing the first report requires finding the right records, resolving discrepancies, and explaining the results. Taking responsibility for later reports means following revisions, obtaining missing information, and acting before each deadline. The manager may also ask for a recommendation that reflects how a trusted analyst would weigh new evidence. Other teams must confirm inputs, resolve shared assumptions, and approve changes before the report can be used. These requests extend delegation in three directions. Sustaining the manager’s goals motivates personal work agents; representing the analyst’s judgment motivates human digital twins; coordinating contributions 53

Each places different demands on what the agent must remember, decide, and verify. 6.1.1 Personal Work Agents A personal work agent helps a user keep an unfinished goal moving across requests. For the manager, this means retaining the purpose of the meeting, gathering materials as they become available, and following up on missing inputs before the deadline. When new information arrives, the agent must decide whether to advance an agreed task, ask the user for a decision, or wait [331]. Proactive-agent research studies anticipation and intervention timing [332, 333]; VibeLifeBench and PAST-Bench examine continuing assistance and gains from retained experience [34, 334]. Such service begins with helping the user specify the work. A manager may know which decision the report should support without knowing which records or analyses it requires. Timely progress on agreed goals with less repeated specification and intervention. Human digital twins (§6.1.2) How can an agent reflect a particular person’s judgment in new situations? Agreement with that person’s decisions under comparable information, assessed separately from task quality. Organizational work (§6.1.3) How can roles, decision rights, and dependencies be coordinated toward a joint delivery? Completed handoffs and end-to-end deliveries with less rework caused by coordination failures. 6.2 Technical frontiers: what makes that delegation possible? Environment (§6.2.1) Which work settings and personal differences must practice represent? Transfer across work settings and correspondence to individual judgments in held-out situations. Persistence (§6.2.2) How should goals, personal judgments, commitments, and feedback guide continuing work? Timely action, retained obligations, and updates consistent with the current basis of delegation. Verification (§6.2.3) What evidence establishes work quality, personal fidelity, and return on delegation separately? Separate measures of deliverable quality, person-specific decision agreement, and benefit relative to cost. 6.3 Interacting loops: how can work continue while capability improves? Work execution (§6.3.1) How can responsibility survive interruptions and changes of executor? Resumed work that preserves confirmed effects, pending dependencies, and agreements. Capability improvement (§6.3.2) Which experience should change memory, skills, harness, or policy? Gains on independent tasks and work settings from targeted updates. Coupling the loops (§6.3.3) Which update scope and timing yield gains after rework and coordination costs? More accepted and used work per total effort, including repair of affected ongoing work. 6.4 Research outlook: where does the system expand useful work? Value under openness and persistence (§6.4) Under which discovery and continuity demands does delegation pay off? A wider range of work completed and used with sustainable demands on people and resources. identify missing inputs, and turn the agreed goal into tasks for specialist executors. Magentic-One’s progress tracking and AutoGen’s configurable agent conversations provide mechanisms for coordinating those tasks [53, 335]. Retaining the open goals, completed work, and events that warrant further action lets the agent resume across reporting cycles with less repeated explanation from the user. Claude Duet, introduced as an experimental release in October 2026, illustrates this direction in a personal service: it checks connected applications, prepares briefings, and continues delegated tasks while the user is away, notifying the user when work is complete or needs a decision [336]. This makes the interval between requests part of the work: the agent must choose what to advance and when the user’s attention is needed. 6.1.2 Human Digital Twins for Professional Work The manager may need a recommendation that reflects how a particular analyst weighs new evidence. A human digital twin aims to represent that person’s judgment across new situations. Two analysts can draw different conclusions from the same records because they use different assumptions or accept different tradeoffs. Professional competence concerns the quality of the work; personal fidelity concerns whose judgment the system represents. Existing studies address parts of this correspondence. LLM-based twin architectures support context- aware knowledge exchange, agents grounded in interviews and questionnaires model individual behavior, and TwinVoice evaluates fidelity to a person’s communication and persona [337–339]. GRACE extends representation into clinical communication through clinician-informed dialogue scripts and retrieved medical knowledge [340]. Extending this correspondence to professional action requires learning how a particular person weighs evidence, handles uncertainty, and chooses among acceptable courses of action. 55

content: Such a twin should be evaluated on held-out cases in which the represented person makes or assesses a decision from comparable information. A personalized professional agent that knows the person’s preferences provides a comparison for testing whether the twin also captures characteristic judgments. The twin’s recommendations also enter work done by other participants. Authenticated delegation provides mechanisms for scoped authority [341], while handoff studies show how constraints can be lost when context is transferred [342]. Passing the analysis to the manager’s agent therefore requires retaining both its assumptions and the authority under which it was produced. 6.1.3 Organizational Work Systems Organizational work joins contributions into a delivery that other people can use. The analyst’s forecast must reflect assumptions agreed with other teams, reach the manager’s report, and arrive before the meeting. MetaGPT provides an example of coordination through structured roles, procedures, and intermediate artifacts in software development [54]. TheAgentCompany places agents in shared applications with simulated colleagues [31]. Failure analyses and controlled scaling studies show how communication structure, verification, and task dependencies affect multi-agent execution [343, 344]. The central challenge is coordinating role responsibilities, decision rights, and interdependent contributions toward a joint delivery. A revised sales estimate may require an analyst to update the forecast, another team to confirm an assumption, and a manager to authorize release. The system must determine who is responsible for each unresolved dependency, which decisions can proceed in parallel, and how revisions affect work already passed to another participant. Human–agent teamwork research and WORKBank’s occupational preferences inform how people choose to share those responsibilities [345, 346]. Progress requires dependable handoffs and conflict resolution that advance the overall delivery while limiting avoidable rework. 6.2 Technical Frontiers for Sustained Delegation The three applications place different demands on sustained delegation: personal agents must advance goals between requests, digital twins must remain faithful to a particular person’s judgment, and organizational systems must coordinate work across roles. Environment research asks how to represent situations that exercise these abilities. Persistence asks how goals, personal judgments, commitments, and dependencies remain available and applicable over time. Verification asks which evidence establishes progress on the delegated responsibility, correspondence to the represented person, and the quality and value of the resulting work. 6.2.1 Environment: Learning across Realistic Work Worlds Environment research must decide what work to represent, which features make the experience realistic, how to run it, and where additional practice is most useful. Occupational coverage and transfer. A teacher, analyst, and procurement specialist may all produce presentations while relying on different knowledge and standards. O*NET organizes occupational requirements; GDPval and the Remote Labor Index connect professional tasks to deliverables; WORKBank adds preferences about delegation [279, 288, 346, 347]. Together with analyses of occupational exposure [348], these resources can guide coverage across domains, occupations, and workflows. Testing held-out combinations would reveal what transfers: reconciling inconsistent records may reuse a common procedure, while deciding why a discrepancy matters may require knowledge of the new profession. Those gaps then guide the construction of further experience. For digital twins, environments should also vary the represented person within the same occupation and task. The same reporting problem may lead two analysts to different choices because they use different assumptions or commitments. Holding the available evidence and authorization constant where feasible would isolate differences in judgment; varying authorization separately would test whether actions remain within the delegated role. 56

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: Decision-relevant realism. Within each kind of work, an environment should preserve the relationships that affect decisions. Workspace-Bench makes file dependencies explicit; business and workspace synthesis methods construct connected entities and evidence relations [36, 143, 163]. Generating workspaces through successive episodes of activity could add the histories behind these relationships. Earlier reports would establish conventions, revisions would create competing versions, and parallel workflows would leave plausible but irrelevant materials. Shared-state settings such as τ 2-bench and Collaborative Gym add participants who change the environment [30, 141], while simulation-to-reality studies examine transfer to real interactions [349]. Varying source ambiguity, dependency depth, and incomplete updates would then exercise the decisions needed to clarify and repair work. Execution infrastructure. These environments need to support repeated practice and continuation from interrupted work [350]. BrowserGym provides common web observations and actions, while Agent Lightning connects harness execution to policy training [260, 320, 351]. DSec separates stateful rollouts from preemptible GPU training [352], and AIOpsLab composes services, workloads, faults, and telemetry for operational tasks [123]. Building on these mechanisms, a work environment could package the application versions, source materials, business state, and events needed to reproduce an episode, together with checks for its outcome. Saved states and records of completed effects would let training and evaluation resume the same unfinished work. Practice allocation. Once environments are available, the remaining question is which experiences deserve the execution budget. Repository environments provide executable practice [353, 354]; Skill2Env targets capability gaps, and AgentGym-RL progressively expands interaction horizons [355, 356]. For professional work, an expensive episode involving clarification and coordination may teach more than many easily scored actions. Comparing learning gains and transfer across these choices would turn the construction methods in Section 4.1 into a curriculum guided by the work agents still struggle to perform. 6.2.2 Persistence: Memory, Initiative, and Adaptation Realistic environments expose changes that unfold between interactions. Handling them requires maintaining an open responsibility: work that remains due even when no agent is currently running. The reporting deadline, pending source confirmation, and authority to release the result must survive the pause. This creates three connected needs: remembering what still applies, deciding when to act, and learning from repeated work. Memory grounded in current work. The agent needs to retrieve relevant decisions and procedures and determine whether they still apply. Personalized workflow prediction studies which procedures fit a user’s context [357]. Memory management and temporal representations support retention and revision [234, 358–361]; A-MEM links and revises notes, while Memory-R1 learns memory operations and selection from downstream rewards [362, 363]. StreamMemBench exposes gaps between storing evidence, using it, and reusing feedback [364]. In the report, a convention may expire when the audience changes while the reconciliation procedure remains useful. Memory should also distinguish a user’s goals and preferences from a represented person’s judgments, existing commitments, and authorization. Linking each item to the relevant person, role, source, and period of applicability would help the agent distinguish a preference about presentation from a commitment governing the analysis or the authority needed to release it. Initiative guided by responsibilities. Retained obligations give the agent a reason to act between requests. Proactive Agent learns from activity traces and judgments of proposed assistance; Proactivity-Gym studies intervention timing and trust [332, 333]. VibeLifeBench examines needs that become visible through inspecting external state [34], and temporal and asynchronous environments provide settings for choosing when to observe, ask, act, or wait [128, 365, 366]. A revised sales record may require several reports to be updated, while an approaching deadline may warrant asking for a missing input. The agent also needs to know which decisions it has been delegated. Collecting a missing input, recommending a conclusion, approving its release, and accepting a new commitment involve different decision rights. It can advance tasks covered by the current delegation and seek a decision when a new choice or commitment lies outside that scope. 57

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: Learning from repeated work. Repeated reporting cycles supply experience for improving source selection, analysis, and explanations. Reflection, experience abstraction, skill libraries, and workflow memory retain reusable lessons [60, 367–369]; SkillRL connects skill evolution to policy learning, and PAST-Bench measures gains from retained experience [265, 334]. Feedback can revise the current report, the procedure used for later reports, or the representation of the analyst. A corrected source value repairs the current result; repeated reconciliation errors motivate a reusable check; feedback from the analyst reveals how that person weighs evidence. Retaining which part of the work each correction concerns gives the agent a basis for later adaptation. Work quality and personal fidelity require separate assessment. Section 6.3.3 examines how procedural updates affect work already in progress. 6.2.3 Verification: Work Quality, Personal Fidelity, and Return on Delegation Continuing service raises three evaluation questions: does the delivery meet its requirements, does a digital twin reflect the represented person’s judgment, and does delegation yield a useful return? These questions require separate evidence about work quality, personal fidelity, and benefit relative to human and computational effort. Verification must follow each as the work and its use evolve. Task and deliverable acceptance. A report may contain correct numbers yet fail to inform the decision it is meant to support. Professional acceptance therefore combines direct checks with judgments about purpose and audience. PresentBench uses slide-specific checklists, PRBench elicits expert criteria, and GDPval uses expert comparisons of occupational deliverables [17, 80, 279]. Agent-as-a-Judge provides mechanisms for inspecting files and execution evidence against requirements [15]. The research task is to connect these checks to the brief: determine which criteria transfer across occupations, which require expert input, and which requirements need clarification. Variation across web benchmarks and evidence of judge bias make consistency across these settings an important evaluation target [370–373]. Personal decision fidelity. A twin’s fidelity is assessed against decisions elicited from the represented person on held-out cases under comparable information. For the same report, two analysts may recommend different forecasts because they weigh uncertainty differently. Both recommendations may meet professional standards, yet only one may reflect the represented person’s judgment. Conversely, a faithful prediction can reproduce that person’s mistake. Evaluation should therefore report decision agreement separately from deliverable quality, record uncertainty or changes in the person’s position, and check execution against the agreed authority. This distinguishes whose judgment the twin represents from the quality of the resulting work. Return on delegation. Measuring the effort of delegation requires tracing the whole delivery process. Agentic ROI considers quality relative to a human baseline, time saved after human interaction, and monetary cost [329]. The relevant effort includes specification, supervision, correction, and integration into later work. Computational cost also depends on the harness: HarnessTax reports similar success rates at substantially different API costs for the same model across harnesses on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0 [326]. Recording these costs by stage would reveal where changes to the model or harness could reduce the effort of obtaining an accepted result. The benefit side requires following what happens to that result. For the report, useful evidence includes whether it supported discussion at the meeting and reduced the work needed to reach a decision. Such benefits depend on the people and process using the artifact. A natural experiment on Change.org found changes in petition language without improved platform-level outcomes after AI writing assistance became available [374]. Comparisons with alternative ways of completing the same work are therefore needed to estimate the benefit attributable to delegation. These observations complement acceptance checks and supply the evidence used in Section 6.4. Evidence over time. New source data may invalidate an accepted analysis, while later use may reveal a missing requirement. StateGuard represents constraints, versioned variables, and conclusions in a validity graph [375]. Linking acceptance checks to the source, artifact, and requirement versions they concern would help identify which results need rechecking. Linking later feedback to the delivery and its use would show 58

content: which procedures need improvement. These two paths lead directly to the interaction between ongoing execution and learning. 6.3 Two Interacting Loops: Delivering Work and Improving Capability Execution and learning share the same workspace. A new analysis procedure may improve future reports while changing an estimate that another team has already used. Introducing it requires tracing how its effects propagate through intermediate results, downstream decisions, and ongoing commitments. The work execution loop advances current responsibilities and records what happened. The capability improvement loop learns from that experience and changes how later work is done. Their connection supplies the evidence for choosing the scope and timing of updates while work remains active. Figure 10 shows how updates return to ongoing execution. A persistent work record retains agreed requirements, source versions, unfinished work, and completed actions. Execution history and feedback from downstream use inform targeted updates. Independent tests assess capability gains, while checks on current work identify affected results and commitments. This evidence guides whether to apply an update, migrate affected work, or retain the current procedure. The benefit of an update depends on its gains relative to the resulting rework and coordination costs. 6.3.1 The Work Execution Loop The execution loop needs a record that lasts across agent runs. A persistent work record can hold the report’s agreed requirements, source versions, pending approvals, and completed actions; case handling provides a precedent for such enduring records [376]. When a revised sales estimate arrives, the agent identifies the affected analysis, updates it, checks the result, and records what remains due. Approval closes that delivery while leaving the next reporting cycle active. Interruptions make the relationship between this record and the workspace especially important. An external action may complete before the agent retains its confirmation [377, 378]. On resuming, the agent needs to inspect the actual effect before deciding to retry or repair, using the execution-state distinctions in Section 2.3.4. Provenance and compensating operations provide mechanisms for reconstructing and correcting these effects [379–382]. The resulting history supports both the next participant taking over the work and the improvement loop diagnosing how it was performed. 59

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 6.3.2 The Capability Improvement Loop The improvement loop uses execution history and feedback from downstream use to identify reusable procedures and changes that could improve later work. If reports repeatedly miss a deadline because the agent discovers inconsistent inputs too late, an earlier source check may be more useful than a stronger drafting model. Other failures may call for professional training, a repaired tool interface, or better timing. The methods in Section 4 provide the update mechanisms; reflection, workflow memory, skill evolution, and harness-aware training offer ways to retain and learn from the experience [60, 260, 265, 369]. The loop then constructs relevant practice, proposes a change, and tests it in independent work settings. For the earlier source check, evaluation would examine whether it catches discrepancies and reduces later rework across different reports. Independent output checks against shared task requirements make gains comparable across changes to both the agent and its grader [383–385]. Environment construction supplies practice that exercises the missing ability; verification tests whether the proposed update improves the resulting work. The remaining question is how to apply a successful update to work already in progress. 6.3.3 Coupling Learning to Open Responsibilities Continual learning studies how updates preserve performance on earlier tasks [386]. During service, other outputs or participants may already depend on results produced by the method being updated. The research problem is to trace the update’s effects through these dependencies. In the reporting example, records should link source versions and analytical assumptions to calculations, conclusions, approvals, and downstream decisions. A new forecasting method may change a budget estimate already used by another team; an additional source check may leave that estimate intact. For a digital twin, these dependencies also include the represented person’s assumptions and subsequent choices. Evaluation therefore follows both task quality and personal fidelity, using the separate assessments in Section 6.2.3. These links define the scope of an update: which results to recompute, which checks to repeat, and which handoffs to reopen. Studies should compare changes to a single check, a reusable procedure, and the full model–harness configuration, measuring how far their effects propagate. This connects capability gains to the repair and coordination needed to put them into use. Audits of self-evolving financial agents further motivate examining how learning changes behavior and its effects [387]. This makes net benefit during service a concrete research target. Studies should vary update scope and timing while tasks remain unfinished, measuring gains in accepted and used work alongside training, inference, rechecking, repair, and human coordination costs over the same period. Comparisons with retaining the current procedure or updating only between deliveries would show when those gains repay the cost of change. The goal is to identify the work conditions and update granularity under which continual improvement pays off, including settings where a stable task template remains the more productive choice. 6.4 Research Outlook: Useful Work under Openness and Persistence The systems above should expand the range of work that people can usefully delegate. Openness and persistence, introduced in Section 2, provide two independent dimensions along which to test that expansion. Preparing a single report in an unfamiliar organization stresses discovery of sources, relationships, and authority. Preparing recurring reports in a fixed environment stresses continuity across revisions and interruptions. Combining the two asks whether an agent can learn its way around changing workspaces while keeping existing work moving. Figure 11 contrasts these settings and the evidence needed to assess them. These conditions create different opportunities and costs. Persistent service can reuse context and procedures across deliveries, but it also requires continued observation, maintenance, and recovery. Open workspaces offer access to tasks whose inputs were never fully specified, while adding discovery and clarification effort. Studies can vary these demands separately and together, using the evidence in Section 6.2.3 and the measures in Section 5.3 over the full period of delegation. The resulting comparisons would show where agents reduce the effort of existing work and where they make previously inaccessible work feasible. 60

The four scenarios illustrate variation in work openness and persistence: single reports from given sources or in an unfamiliar workspace, and recurring reports within a fixed workflow or a changing workspace. Across all four settings, accepted work, value in use, and total human and computational effort provide complementary evidence for assessing delegation. The division of work between people and agents is part of this comparison. In a product-innovation experiment, individuals with AI assistance matched human teams without AI and produced proposals spanning technical and commercial perspectives [388]. In a study of experienced developers, the tested AI tools increased completion time [389]. Alongside experiments on professional writing [390], these findings motivate testing delegation across tasks and working arrangements. Changes to processes and skills can determine whether local gains improve overall productivity [391, 392]. For the reporting process, faster analysis matters when assessment and integration can turn it into a timely decision. This returns the agenda to the two loops. As execution improves, assessment, integration, or human decisions may become the limiting stage [393]. The execution loop must organize work around that stage, and the improvement loop must address the capability or coordination that limits the next delivery. Progress is a wider range of professional work completed, accepted, and used with sustainable demands on people and resources. 7 Conclusion Reliable digital work depends on keeping task requirements, actions, and outcomes connected as work unfolds. The system view developed here makes these connections visible across tasks, domains, and interfaces. As work expands from returning an answer or making a local change to coordinating workflows and related workspace objects, agents must track more dependencies and use the results of one step to guide the next. Openness makes discovery part of this process; persistence carries responsibility across stages and events. The five core capabilities provide a way to understand where the process succeeds and where it breaks down. Work execution supplies observations, procedures, corrections, and feedback that can improve subsequent work. Training can develop reusable knowledge and action patterns, while harness changes can improve access to evidence, execution control, and retained state. Model–harness optimization coordinates these updates as 61

content: the model and the work change. Evaluation checks whether the resulting system produces answers, artifacts, state changes, and workflow results that meet their requirements. Distinguishing the inspected result, the assessed properties, the judging method, and the reported metric helps identify which part of the work an improvement actually advances. Sustained delegation brings execution and learning together. An agent must respond to new information and improve its methods while completing work under existing agreements. Gains on new tasks must therefore be considered alongside the repair of dependent work and the effort of introducing updates. Personal work agents, human digital twins, and organizational work systems bring different tests of this capability: progress on continuing goals, fidelity to a particular person’s judgment, and coordination toward a joint delivery. Advances in realistic environments, persistent coordination, and verification can widen the conditions under which these systems are useful. Their practical value depends on the work people accept and use, the benefits it brings, and the human and computational effort required to obtain it. 62

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
authors: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo
section: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
content: In federated learning (FL), secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of local model updates of N N clients, without revealing any information on the individual model updates to the server, beyond their sum. Different clients may be subject to heterogeneous bandwidth constraints, and consequently may choose different numbers of quantization levels to represent the information they send. Most secure aggregation works require the clients to project the values of their update parameters to a common finite group (or field), which does not directly accommodate heterogeneous precision constraints on their transmitted masked updates. Existing approaches of secure aggregation with heterogeneous quantization levels reveal partial aggregates of model-updates, and can reveal segments of individual model updates, under certain dropout and client-server collusion patterns. To prevent this privacy breach, we propose an information-theoretic secure aggregation scheme that tolerates client drop-outs, and up to T T semi-honest clients that collude with each other and with the server, under heterogeneous quantization at clients. Our protocol utilizes the ( T + 1 , N ) (T+1,N) threshold black-box secret sharing construction, where secret shares of the client updates, despite belonging to distinct algebraic groups owing to different quantization, are generated from identical linear integer systems.

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
authors: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo
content: Federated learning (FL) [ 1 ] , first introduced in [ 2 ] , is a distributed collaborative learning paradigm, which enables a group of clients to train a global model together, while keeping their data on their devices. This framework is widely adopted in healthcare [ 3 ] , smart mobile applications [ 4 ] , and IoT applications [ 5 ] , enabling collaborative learning without directly sharing local training data. In a typical FL algorithm (e.g., FedAvg of [ 2 ] ), the central server initializes and broadcasts a global model to the clients (e.g., mobile devices). The clients, after training this global model based on their local data, send their model updates, such as the difference between the locally trained and broadcast model parameters, to the server for aggregation, and the global model is updated for the next round. However, keeping the training data local does not guarantee privacy by itself. It has been shown that the model updates shared with the server can leak sensitive information about clients’ training data through gradient inversion attacks [ 6 ] . To prevent this, FL was equipped with secure aggregation [ 7 ] , in which the server recovers only the sum of the model updates, while the individual model updates remain private.

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
authors: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo
content: The protocol of [ 7 ] maps the real-valued model update vector of size M M in ℝ M \mathbb{R}^{M} to a vector in a finite integer group ℤ q M \mathbb{Z}_{q}^{M} where ℤ q = { 0 , 1 , … , q − 1 } \mathbb{Z}_{q}=\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\} , for a sufficiently large q q , and masks them using pairwise random masks that cancel upon summation. To handle dropouts, i.e., clients that fail to communicate with the server during aggregation, the protocol requires additional masking and secret sharing. Following this, efforts were made towards reducing the communication overhead incurred in secure aggregation [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , while the fundamental limits on communication load and randomness size for secure aggregation were studied in [ 12 , 13 ] . More recently, [ 14 ] demonstrated secure aggregation in FL by mapping real-valued updates to torus, while assuming no client drop-outs. They choose uniform random variables from the torus, and execute masking via addition modulo 1 1 . A fundamental building block of secure aggregation is Shamir’s ( T + 1 , N ) (T+1,N) threshold secret sharing protocol [ 15 ] , which is applied, for instance, to random masks to handle client drop-outs [ 7 ] , and to model updates to prevent client-server collusion [ 12 ] . This framework distributes a secret into N N shares, such that any T T or fewer shares reveal no information on the secret, but T + 1 T+1 shares are sufficient to reconstruct the secret exactly.

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
authors: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo
content: The aforementioned works on secure aggregation assume a common algebraic domain (e.g., a group, a finite field) both for constructing the masked updates and for reconstructing the aggregate. However, they do not particularly account for client-specific precision constraints arising from heterogeneous communication bandwidths [ 16 ] . To address this issue, [ 17 ] proposes a secure aggregation strategy that supports heterogeneous quantization levels, by partitioning users, and securely aggregating segments of the model updates across these user groups, such that each group admits a given quantization. At the server, the reconstructed aggregate from each such group reveals segments of partial sums of the client updates. Moreover, if all but one clients in a group of securely aggregated segments drop out, segments of that surviving client’s update would be revealed to the server.

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
authors: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo
content: In this paper, we mitigate this problem by proposing a secure aggregation protocol, with privacy against up to T T colluding clients, with up to D D client drop-outs, while supporting heterogeneous client quantization levels. For instance, consider a setting with g g distinct quantization levels and N | g N\mid g . Then, in [ 17 ] , the model updates are split into g ( ≥ 2 ) g(\geq 2) equal-sized segments, where each aggregate comprises updates from N g \frac{N}{g} or 2 ​ N g \frac{2N}{g} clients, thus leaking segments of partial sums. If D = N g − 1 D=\frac{N}{g}-1 , there exists a dropout pattern such that the server learns an aggregate with one surviving client, while the rest have dropped out, and the individual update segment of the surviving client is exposed. Furthermore, the aggregate with 2 ​ N g \frac{2N}{g} clients can potentially leak individual model update segments of the honest client, if the server colludes with T = N g T=\frac{N}{g} surviving, semi-honest clients contributing to the same aggregate. For the same setting, our scheme is information-theoretically secure, and prevents such breaches. We achieve this by normalizing the real-valued model updates, and generating shares of the quantized model updates using ( T + 1 , N ) (T+1,N) secret sharing scheme [ 18 ] on the respective torus groups. Different from Shamir’s secret sharing [ 15 ] , where the secret, the secret sharing coefficients and the secret reconstruction coefficients should all be chosen from the same field, the construction of [ 18 ] uses integer-valued sharing and reconstruction coefficients that are independent of the underlying Abelian group, which the secret belongs to. Consequently, each client can generate shares within the discrete torus, that are transmitted and added at the clients to obtain valid shares of the aggregate of updates. Any T + 1 T+1 surviving clients can then enable exact reconstruction of the sum of the quantized updates modulo 1 1 , by choosing a scaling factor for normalization to prevent the overflow of this sum around 1 1 . To support our results, we demonstrate our protocol for FL with the MNIST dataset [ 19 ] for admissible heterogeneous quantization levels.

content: In this paper, we proposed an information-theoretic secure aggregation protocol, that supports heterogeneous quantization levels for clients, while resisting dropouts and client-server collusion. By leveraging black-box secret sharing on the torus, our scheme enables the clients to directly add shares of all quantized model updates, while the server reconstructs the quantized aggregate. Without the requirement for quantization, the steps of our protocol provides an analog secure aggregation protocol, that tolerates drop-outs and collusion.

title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
authors: Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma
section: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
content: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, judged by three VLM judge panels and validated with blind human preferences. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, the benchmark is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead clearly, yet even the best system fails a core requirement on about a quarter of tasks. Whether a video arrives at all matters as much as its quality, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders started too late, run too slowly or never started. The judges agree with each other and with human preferences on system rankings, but only moderately on individual videos.

content: Figure 1 : VibeVideoBench asks a multimodal agent to turn a self-contained specification into a finished MP4 with sound, using only code. Each panel is one frame of an unedited delivery from our evaluation, made by an off-the-shelf agent in its native harness inside a sandbox within one hour: rendered with three.js, Canvas, SVG or cairo, voiced with TTS, scored with synthesized music and sound effects, and muxed with ffmpeg. authors: Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma
content: Video generation has advanced rapidly through diffusion transformers [ 5 , 15 , 26 , 40 , 45 , 35 ] , and benchmarks such as VBench [ 21 , 48 ] and EvalCrafter [ 30 ] measure how plausible and prompt-aligned the generated clips look. Yet many of the videos people actually make—classroom lessons, paper explainers, data stories, product walkthroughs, assembly sequences, rhythm games—demand properties that pixel generators do not guarantee: exact text and numbers, rule-consistent state changes, multi-minute structure, sound aligned to events , and an artifact that can be revised. These are natural properties of programs . Humans already make such videos with Manim or Remotion, and coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI [ 1 , 33 , 14 ] can now work autonomously for hours, driving a full toolchain—a renderer, a headless browser, a TTS engine, ffmpeg—on their own. Users have begun to ask agents for finished videos this way, which requires a multimodal agent that reads input assets, produces picture and sound through code, and inspects its own renders to correct them.

title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
authors: Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma
content: How good are agents at making videos? Existing evaluations do not answer this. Video-generation benchmarks score short, silent clips from generative models [ 21 , 30 , 18 ] . Code-to-visual benchmarks score single programs or static artifacts such as charts, web pages and SVGs [ 37 , 38 , 47 , 9 ] . Code-based lesson and paper-to-video systems [ 27 , 10 , 50 ] propose purpose-built, single-domain pipelines rather than testing general agents. Agentic benchmarks [ 24 , 32 , 43 ] verify textual or functional outcomes with unit tests, whereas a video is a perceptual, temporal and audio-visual outcome for which no unit test exists. Video therefore tests what text-only agentic benchmarks cannot: whether an agent can check its own output across picture, sound and time.

content: We present VibeVideoBench (Figs. 1 and 2 ), a benchmark that evaluates multimodal agents end to end on code-driven video generation : given a specification and optional input assets, an agent must deliver a finished MP4, built entirely with code, inside a sandbox within one hour, with narration, music and sound effects as each task’s audio policy specifies. Its 239 tasks span 12 categories, from brand promos and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers, in English and Chinese. Building it required solving two problems.

content: Tasks must be realistic yet checkable. We build tasks from four sources—real user requests to code-video tools, real videos (seeded from their dense captions), real asset packs such as 3D scans and game levels, and lecture notes and research papers—and turn each into a self-contained specification that fixes facts, identities, stages, timing and the audio policy while preserving creative freedom.

content: Evaluation must rest on evidence in the video. Evaluation has three layers with different executors. Program checks (L1) automatically verify the delivery spec—resolution, frame rate, duration, audible sound, source project. Rubric checks (L2; about 13k in total) are each traced to the requirement they enforce, separate process shown from result claimed , and are tagged by modality. Quality scores (L3) rate five dimensions—visual quality, aesthetics, content logic, timing and audio—each anchored at 1, 3 and 5 by descriptions written for the task. L2 and L3 are judged by VLM judges in three independent panels: two watch the full video with sound, and the third routes visual checks to a vision model and audio checks to an audio-capable model, so audio checks never reach a judge that cannot hear. We validate the judges against blind pairwise human preferences.

content: To simulate real user settings, we evaluate agents as they are deployed : each model runs fully autonomously in its vendor’s native harness at maximum effort, with no follow-up turns and all tool permissions pre-approved, in identical containers with the same one-hour budget. Users adopt the model and its harness as one system, so we evaluate complete agent systems rather than separating model from harness. Nine frontier systems from six labs yield 2,151 scored rollouts.

content: Video generation: the pixel paradigm. Diffusion-transformer generators [ 5 , 15 , 28 , 40 ] synthesize pixels directly from text or images and are evaluated by dimension-wise suites [ 21 , 48 , 30 ] , learned scorers [ 18 ] , physics probes [ 31 , 3 ] and arenas [ 22 ] ; VideoArgus [ 46 ] , closest in spirit to our rubric checks, builds sample-specific rubrics before seeing outputs. Story-video systems [ 29 , 42 ] add an LLM planner, but a generative model still paints the pixels. We study a different paradigm, in which an agent produces a video by writing programs that drive renderers, TTS and ffmpeg, so that content is exact, editable, and controllable in length and sound. Evaluation that asks whether a few seconds of mostly silent footage look plausible does not transfer to it.

title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
authors: Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma
content: Code as a visual medium: the program paradigm. Programs are an editable, verifiable visual representation of charts, web pages, SVG and 3D scenes [ 37 , 38 , 9 , 16 ] ; ArtifactsBench [ 47 ] grades interactive artifacts from screenshots with checklist-guided MLLM judges. For video, TheoremExplainAgent [ 27 ] , Code2Video [ 10 ] , VisualEDU [ 8 ] and ManimAgent [ 23 ] generate educational Manim videos, Paper2Video [ 50 ] turns research papers into narrated slide talks, and Code2Video-Compass [ 11 ] and an industry benchmark [ 19 ] score short silent clips written in one framework. None of these is agentic in our sense: each video comes from a fixed pipeline built around one renderer or genre, or from a single model call, rather than from an agent that chooses its own tools and renders, inspects and revises its own video.

content: Agent benchmarks. Software and computer-use agents are measured by SWE-bench [ 24 ] , Terminal-Bench [ 32 ] , OSWorld [ 43 ] and PaperBench [ 39 ] , and GDPval [ 34 ] grades occupational deliverables by expert comparison. These verify text, files or functional behavior, whereas a video is a perceptual, temporal and audio-visual outcome for which no unit test exists. AgenticVBench [ 6 ] also runs general agents in vendor harnesses, but on post-production of given footage; in our setting every frame and sound must be constructed by code. Tab. 1 contrasts VibeVideoBench with prior work on who makes the video, what is asked, what is delivered and how it is graded.

content: Judges, rubrics and human preference. LLM and multimodal judges [ 49 , 25 , 7 ] exhibit position and self-preference biases [ 41 ] ; rubric decomposition improves reliability in non-verifiable domains [ 2 , 17 ] , and pairwise human preference with Bradley–Terry aggregation [ 4 , 12 ] is the standard validation. Omni models can see and hear [ 44 ] , but audio-visual benchmarks show they remain weak at fine temporal alignment [ 13 , 20 ] . We therefore route checks by modality, require timestamped evidence, use three panels from different model families, and measure where they fail.

(b) Each task gets a three-level rubric traced to its prompt and its input assets; L2 checks quote their basis and carry modality tags; rubrics go through rounds of model QC and human review until no confirmed finding remains. content: Fig. 2 a shows the pipeline. Sources. Tasks start from four kinds of real-world sources: requests people wrote for code-based video tools (what people ask for), dense captions of real videos (what people actually make), real asset packs such as 3D scans, archival records and game sprites, and lecture notes and research papers. Specification contract. Real requests are rarely self-contained, so a source only seeds a task: LLM drafters with cross-review expand and rewrite it under a shared contract that fixes every fact, number and object identity the video depends on, divides it into stages with dwell times and states a four-channel audio policy, while protecting creative freedom; missing assets are searched for or synthesized. What the contract fixes can be checked, and what it leaves open measures the agent’s own design. Human curation. Humans select checkable tasks over open briefs, rewrite each into a self-contained prompt without authoring traces, verify its facts and remove duplicates across sources. The result is 239 tasks in 12 categories and 43 subcategories, from 8 s to 15 min, with narration, music, effects and ambience, with or without input assets (Fig. 3 ).

content: Fig. 2 b shows how rubrics are built. Every check traces to the final prompt (its requirements, delivery spec d d and audio policy a a ) and to the input assets. Each task is evaluated at three levels: L1 program checks , derived from d d and a a and decided by code; L2 task checks , atomic pass/fail checks that each quote the requirement they enforce as their basis, are marked core or detail, require the process to be shown rather than a result to be claimed, and carry a tag for the modality needed to decide them; and L3 quality , five 1–5 dimensions—visual quality (VQ), visual aesthetics (VA), content logic (CL), timing and motion (TM), and audio quality and A/V sync (AQ)—with anchors written per task. Rubrics go through rounds of model review, which flags over-strict, missing or undecidable checks, and human verification, until no flag holds; since judges never see the input assets, each check states the correct content itself. The final set has 1,449 L1 checks, 12,985 L2 checks (about 54 per task) and 1,195 L3 rubrics.

content: L1: delivery and program checks. L1 is decided by programs alone; no model is involved. A run delivers if it leaves an MP4 that decodes and can be judged; the delivery rate is the share of tasks with such a video. Each delivery is then measured (ffprobe, a full decode, audio levels, VAD and Whisper language ID) and checked by code against the task’s machine-readable delivery spec d d and audio policy a a : every task checks container and decodability, resolution, frame rate ( ± \pm 0.01) and duration within [ t min − 0.5 , t max + 0.5 ] [t_{\min}{-}0.5,t_{\max}{+}0.5] s. The 205 core tasks add a delivered source project, an exact frame count where d d requires it (54 tasks) and an audible audio stream (peak > − 50 >{-}50 dBFS) where a a marks a channel as required (98 tasks under a strict parse). Lessons and papers, which all require narration, add an audible audio stream, narration coverage (VAD), narration language (ASR) and the absence of long black or frozen stretches. This gives 1,449 checks per system (1,177 core, 272 lesson and paper). Spec compliance is the share of tasks whose run passes all applicable checks; a non-delivery fails them all. (The rollout collector also runs a lighter container-level check at collection time, App. C ; we use it only in the behavior analysis of § 5.3 .)

content: L2: rubric checks. For each check a judge returns pass, fail, unknown or n/a, with timestamped evidence. Judges score the 12,985 L2 checks (§ 3.4 ), and we report two metrics. L2 pass pools checks: it is # ​ pass / ( # ​ pass + # ​ fail ) \#\text{pass}/(\#\text{pass}{+}\#\text{fail}) , with unknown and n/a excluded. L2 strict (strict task success) is decided per run: a run succeeds if none of its core checks fails and at least one passes; unknown and n/a do not count against it, and a non-delivery fails. For example, the Super Mario level run (CG01) has 59 checks; a video in which Mario does not grow after touching the mushroom fails the core check “growth is discernible after contact”, so the run fails L2 strict even if the other 58 pass (L2 pass 98%); strict success is thus far more discriminative.

content: L3: quality. The judge scores each of the five dimensions from 1 to 5 against the task’s own anchors, with reasons, strengths and defects; a dimension the judge cannot assess is left unknown and excluded. For CG01, timing and motion (TM) asks whether continuous motion, landings and state changes can be followed with enough time to see key dangers and successes; it scores 1 if key processes are hard to track, 3 if they can be tracked but transitions or holds are awkward, and 5 if key changes are clear and motion serves the task. The overall score is the mean of the five dimensions; it is not a weighted total of L1–L3, which we keep separate.

content: Judge panels. Each delivered video is judged independently by three panels, each given the exact task prompt and the rubric but never the system identity. Judges are told that on-screen or narrated self-declarations are not evidence, and that unsampled instants cannot be asserted. J1 (Gemini 4 Argon) and J2 (Gemini 3.8 Flash) watch the full MP4 with sound (4 fps up to 150 s, adaptively lower for longer videos) and judge everything. J3 splits by modality following the check tags: GPT-5.6 Sol judges visual checks and VQ/VA/CL/TM from 24–300 sampled frames (up to 1280 px), and Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash judges audio and audio-visual checks and AQ from a full-length proxy with the original audio. Audio observations are passed to the vision judge as reference. All three panels contain evaluated models (J1, J2 and J3’s vision judge); J3 shares no family with J1/J2. Each panel’s metrics are computed separately and then averaged; scores are never mixed across panels within a metric ( 3 × 2,151 3\times 2{,}151 run results). Tab. 2 reports the mean over the three panels; per-panel results are in App. E .

content: Human preference. To validate the judges we ran a blind pairwise study on all 239 tasks. Five annotators each saw the full prompt and two synchronized players with videos of two systems on the same task, both playable, and chose A , B , tie or both bad by overall quality and adherence ( N votes, N decisive). Human preference therefore measures the quality of delivered videos, not delivery. We fit Bradley–Terry strengths [ 4 ] on decisive votes (Elo scale, geometric mean 1000) with 2,000-sample bootstrap CIs and measure system-level rank correlation and pair-level agreement with each panel.

Astra and Opus deliver almost every video and stay on top, whereas Gemini 4 Argon, which delivers only 77% of its videos, falls from 4th to 7th. L2 strict success requires every core check of a task to hold, so it spreads systems from 26.6% to 76.3%: even the best system fails a core requirement on about a quarter of tasks. Reliability also has quieter forms: 48 of the 213 playable videos of GPT-5.6 Sol have no audio track, which gives it the lowest AQ on delivered videos (3.71); see App. E for details.

content: Three quarters of the failures (169) are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started; the rest are stalled renders (45, 20%), outputs the agent destroyed itself (7, 3%) and other causes (3). Time management. Agents polish components and previews and launch the full render last: GPT-5.6 Sol’s final full renders in failed runs start at a median of 9 minutes before the deadline, often with frame-by-frame browser capture that needs 5–35 minutes, and 65 runs never start a final render at all. Stalled renders occur only in the two Gemini systems: 33 renders deadlock because the agent’s script pipes frames into ffmpeg while never reading its error stream (one stopped at frame 7,744 of 10,102, about 90 s from completion), and in 12 runs the agent ended its turn while a render ran in the background, which was then cut off. Self-destruction is the most avoidable: DeepSeek verified its video twice, then re-encoded it in place one minute before the deadline and left a truncated 0.26 MB file. The successful systems leave margin. Opus, the only system without a failure, finishes its video a median of 24 minutes before the deadline, against 10–11 minutes for Sol and GLM (Fig. 4 b); it first produces a complete deliverable, then improves only copies and verifies the encoded MP4 itself. A larger budget does not substitute for this: in a budget ablation (App. I.3 ), DeepSeek scores 3.92 with 60 minutes and 3.94 with 120, while using 35 more minutes.

content: The pipeline is always “code → \rightarrow frames → \rightarrow ffmpeg”: runs call ffmpeg in 96–100% of cases, whereas Manim appears in 8 of 2,151 runs and MoviePy in 13. Each system has a preferred rendering stack (Fig. 4 c): Claude agents draw vectors with cairo (46–54% of runs), GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi and GLM rasterize frames with PIL/numpy (43–55%), and Astra, DeepSeek and Gemini 3.8 Flash capture browser canvases and three.js scenes (52–60%). Soundtracks are programmed too: 57–96% of runs synthesize music or effects in code. Cairo and browser-2D runs pass the container-level check most often (88% and 85%) and score highest (3.79 and 3.73), three.js scenes least (78%, 3.00); since renderer and system are coupled, this is an association, consistent with slow frame capture being a main cause of late renders (§ 5.2 ).

content: The three panels rank systems almost identically (system-level Spearman 0.93 0.93 – 0.95 0.95 ), and the three-panel mean ranks them like humans do ( ρ = 0.98 \rho{=}0.98 with human Elo; Tab. 3 ). On single pairs the mean agrees with humans 73.3% of the time, but the agreement depends on the margin: 63% when the panels’ score gap is below 0.2 (about a third of pairs) and 86% when it is 0.5 or more. Judges also miss what humans flag: on pairs that annotators label both bad , the panels give the same scores (3.81) as on other pairs, so judge scores order videos but do not certify them as acceptable. The disagreements concentrate on two systems, in opposite directions: humans prefer GPT-5.6 Sol’s videos 16 points less often than the judges do, as the judges penalize it mainly on audio (AQ), and Gemini 3.8 Flash 11 points more often. Per video, check verdicts reach only κ = 0.44 \kappa{=}0.44 – 0.56 0.56 despite 91–95% raw agreement, overall scores correlate at r = 0.45 r{=}0.45 – 0.51 0.51 , and same-task orderings agree only 66–70% of the time. Panels also differ in strictness: J1 is stricter and J2 more lenient, especially on weaker systems, and strict success, which fails a task on a single failed check, is sensitive to this (Opus: 83.7%, 93.3% and 51.9% under J1–J3), so only the three-panel mean is comparable. Implication: current judges can certify system-level rankings over hundreds of tasks, but per-video verdicts—and per-video rewards for training—need margins, multi-panel consensus or human checks.

Higher spending does not buy a matching score: the rank correlation between cost and the overall score is not significant ( ρ = 0.55 \rho{=}0.55 , p = 0.12 p{=}0.12 , n = 9 n{=}9 ), and score per dollar differs by more than 30 × 30\times , from 0.26 points per USD for Opus to 8.8 for GLM (Fig. 5 b). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 95% of GPT-6 Astra’s score at 5.8% of its cost. Spending is not effort either: Astra produces the fewest output tokens (61k per task, against 77k–289k for the others), and within every system longer runs score lower ( ρ \rho from − 0.22 {-}0.22 to − 0.69 {-}0.69 ), because long runs are runs in trouble. title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
authors: Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma
content: We presented VibeVideoBench, a benchmark of 239 realistic, checkable tasks on which multimodal agents must make complete audio-visual videos with code, evaluated by program checks, task-specific rubric checks and quality scores from three judge panels validated against blind human preferences. Across nine frontier agent systems, the benchmark is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead clearly, yet even the best system fails a core requirement on about a quarter of tasks. Whether a video arrives at all matters as much as how good it is, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders started too late, run too slowly or never started; agents should secure a complete video early and verify the delivered file. Automatic judges agree with each other and with humans on how systems rank, but only moderately on single videos, so per-video verdicts still need margins, multi-panel consensus or human checks.

content: Quality rubric. The five L3 dimensions share 20 observation points: VQ1 key-content legibility, VQ2 stability, VQ3 occlusion/cropping/layering, VQ4 object consistency; VA1 hierarchy, VA2 composition, VA3 unity of visual language, VA4 audience fit; CL1 organization, CL2 key relations, CL3 information load, CL4 channel coordination; TM1 action, TM2 state change and transitions, TM3 dwell on key content, TM4 overall rhythm; AQ1 intelligibility and pronunciation, AQ2 prosody, AQ3 mixing, AQ4 sound–event alignment. Each dimension has task-specific anchors at 1, 3 and 5 ( e.g . , VQ for CG01: 1 = “key content remains unclear or is disrupted by visual defects”, 5 = “key content clear, image stable, details support viewing”); a 2 or 4 must say which anchor it is closer to, and insufficient evidence yields unknown , never a default 3. Intentional pixel-art style, grain or blur is not a defect.

content: Every check quotes the prompt sentence it enforces, and optional language (“may”, “e.g.”) never becomes mandatory ( traceability ). A correct final number or a caption reading “synced” cannot pass a check that requires a visible process ( process over claims ): in a marble adder the sum must be produced by actual contacts. Core and detail are fixed before any output is seen, so cosmetic passes cannot outvote a failed core goal. Timing thresholds state how to measure them under frame sampling: “at least N N seconds” passes only if the lower bound is ≥ N {\geq}N , fails if the upper bound is < N {<}N , and is otherwise unknown. 40–50 checks is a coverage aim, not a quota, and no check may prescribe a production method (45 early “must use CSS”-style checks were deleted).

section: B.3 Rubrics for lessons and papers
content: The 34 lessons and papers (C11, C12) use the same levels and judge interface, but their checks come from the supplied material. L1 adds narration coverage (VAD speech share ≥ 50 % {\geq}50\% , no gap over 20 s), narration language (ASR, ≥ 90 % {\geq}90\% in the target language) and no long black or frozen stretch. L2 has 48–83 checks per task (2,172 in total; 1,566 core): content checks enumerate the knowledge points (each concept, derivation step, worked answer, common misconception and relation to be drawn; for papers the motivation, key idea, method components, key equations, results, evidence and limitations), and narration checks require correct reading of terms, formulas and numbers, explanation rather than reading on-screen text aloud, and synchronization at 4–6 key moments. Because judges never see the note or the paper, 330 checks that referred to them (“consistent with the note”) were rewritten to state the required content, and six audit agents re-derived every number and formula against the source. Each task also has a grounded quiz (404 questions), reported separately (App. I.2 ).

content: Rubrics were refined over many rounds in a closed loop. In each round an independent model reviewed every rubric against its prompt, each finding was re-adjudicated in a fresh context and verified by a human reviewer, confirmed findings were fixed, and the revised rubrics re-entered review until no confirmed finding remained. The most frequent defect was over-specification (a rubric demanding more than the prompt), ahead of coverage gaps; the review also surfaced bugs in the tasks themselves, such as an infeasible inventory or contradictory timing tables, which were fixed in the prompts.

content: Each judge receives the prompt the agent received, the task checks and the quality rubric, but never the system identity, the source code or the agent’s notes. For every check it returns pass, fail, unknown or n/a with the time range and the channel (picture or sound) that support the verdict, and it scores the five quality dimensions against the task’s anchors with reasons. On-screen or narrated claims (“✓ requirement met”) are not evidence, properties of the delivered file are left to the program checks, a judge that sees sampled frames may not assert what happens between them, and insufficient evidence yields unknown.

content: Two of three judges favor their own model, by about a sixth of a point. J2 rates the Gemini 3.8 Flash agent + + 0.16 and J3’s vision judge rates the GPT-5.6 Sol agent + + 0.20 higher than the other panels do; both intervals exclude zero. J1 shows no preference for the Gemini 4 Argon agent ( + + 0.03) and rates the Gemini family lower than the other panels ( − - 0.12). Panels also have tastes of similar size that have nothing to do with themselves: J1 favors the Claude agents and Astra ( + + 0.17 to + + 0.21) and disfavors Sol ( − - 0.32), and J2 disfavors Astra ( − - 0.23) while being lenient on the weaker systems (GLM + + 0.13, Sol + + 0.12), so part of its + + 0.16 for Flash is its general leniency toward weaker systems.

content: The ranking does not depend on it. Scoring each system without the panel that is its own model (J1 for Argon, J2 for Flash, J3 for Sol) changes only the last two places: Flash and GLM, 0.008 apart and statistically tied, swap (Kendall τ = 0.94 \tau{=}0.94 with the headline ranking). Scoring each system only with panels outside its family (the Gemini agents by J3 alone, the GPT agents by J1 and J2), after shifting every panel by its leniency offset on the commonly judged videos ( − - 0.27, + + 0.13 and + + 0.14 against the three-panel mean), leaves the order unchanged ( τ = 1 \tau{=}1 ): the Astra–Opus gap narrows from 0.034 to 0.018 (paired bootstrap P ⁡ ( Astra > Opus ) = 0.74 P(\text{Astra}{>}\text{Opus}){=}0.74 ), and Sol stays above Argon ( P = 0.95 P{=}0.95 ). Without the shift Opus overtakes Astra, but only because the panel dropped for the GPT agents (J3) is a lenient one. A relative score cannot separate a panel’s self-preference from the other panels’ dislike of the same system; only a check-level human calibration could say which panel is right.
