content: Evaluation on generating free-text radiology reports from 3D volumes is similar to VQA, incorporating each frozen tokenizer into the LaMed framework [ 59 ] and training the connector and LLM to generate region-specific findings for three anatomical regions (abdomen, chest, and pelvis). We report BLEU-2, RaTEScore [ 60 ] (entity-level NER-based evaluation), and GREEN [ 61 ] (clinically aware error detection via an LLM judge). Table 6 presents the report generation results. MedVTok achieves the best scores on all metrics. The improvement is consistent across anatomical regions, with particularly strong gains in the pelvic region, which is the most challenging due to its complex anatomy and longer reference reports. Compared with MedITok, MedVTok shows meaningful improvements on clinically aware metrics (GREEN: 0.413 vs. 0.386), suggesting that our tokenizer encodes diagnostically relevant information that translates into more accurate clinical language generation. Additional results are provided in § C.2 .

content: Starting from a baseline without any semantic alignment (E1 in Fig. 5 ), shared-space contrastive learning with a single-expert ℒ shared \mathcal{L}_{\text{shared}} (E2, using MedImageInsight [ 16 ] ) yields an initial improvement in classification and segmentation, confirming that semantic supervision is critical for downstream understanding. Extending ℒ shared \mathcal{L}_{\text{shared}} to multiple experts (E3) further improves both metrics, demonstrating that a panel of modality-specific experts provides more comprehensive semantics. Adding expert-space complementary learning ℒ expert \mathcal{L}_{\text{expert}} (E4) brings an additional +1.53% classification gain by preserving modality-specific nuances that shared-space contrastive learning alone may compress away during the shared-space projection.

authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
content: We present MedVTok, a general-purpose medical visual tokenizer that encodes both 2D images and 3D volumes into a shared representational space through a single transformer architecture. Two complementary supervision mechanisms shape this space at different levels: Slice Differential Regularization preserves inter-slice fidelity that per-voxel supervision misses, and Multi-Expert Representation Alignment injects modality-specific clinical semantics from a panel of experts without requiring paired annotations. MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art results across reconstruction and six downstream tasks, ranging from pixel-level fidelity to report generation, demonstrating that structural fidelity and semantic richness can be jointly optimized within a single tokenizer.

content: We acknowledge several limitations. First, the training data focus on common imaging modalities at present. Other imaging modalities, clinical photos, or illustrations in medical publications remain unexplored. Incorporating these would enhance generalization to non-standard visual inputs encountered in real-world clinical workflows. Second, while MERA uses frozen expert encoders, jointly fine-tuning selected experts or incorporating new ones could further improve domain coverage when the computational budget allows. We hope MedVTok will serve as a useful building block for scalable multimodal medical AI systems that enable patient-level modeling across heterogeneous imaging evidence and clinical tasks.

content: MedITok [ 6 ] combines reconstruction and semantic alignment for 2D medical images. AToken [ 9 ] provides a unified tokenizer for general-domain images, videos, and 3D assets. SAMTok [ 62 ] and HiMTok [ 63 ] encode segmentation masks as compact token sequences for multimodal language models. MedVTok focuses on a shared representation for medical images and volumes, combining depth-wise reconstruction regularization with semantic supervision from modality-specific experts.

content: The encoder and decoder of MedVTok each consist of 27 transformer blocks with a hidden dimension of d = 1152 d=1152 . The encoder is initialized from SigLIP2-SO400M-patch16-NaFlex [ 28 ] , while other components are trained from scratch. The patch size is P t × P h × P w P_{t}{\times}P_{h}{\times}P_{w} , where P t = 4 P_{t}=4 is the depth patch size for 3D volumes and P h = 16 , P w = 16 P_{h}=16,P_{w}=16 are the spatial patch sizes for both 2D images and 3D volumes. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [ 27 ] are derived from 3D patch coordinates ( z , x , y ) (z,x,y) . Before the decoder, each encoded d d -dimensional token embedding is projected to a 96-dimensional output, which is split into mean and log-variance for a diagonal Gaussian posterior, yielding latent codes of dimension d z = 48 d_{z}=48 .

content: All inputs, regardless of spatial resolution, aspect ratio, or dimensionality, are converted into a common concatenated patch format before entering the transformer encoder. Each patch spans P t × P h × P w = 4 × 16 × 16 P_{t}{\times}P_{h}{\times}P_{w}=4{\times}16{\times}16 voxels across the depth, height, and width axes, yielding a per-patch feature vector of dimension P t ⋅ P h ⋅ P w ⋅ C = 3072 P_{t}\cdot P_{h}\cdot P_{w}\cdot C=3072 for C = 3 C=3 channels. For a 2D image of spatial size H × W H{\times}W , the input is first zero-padded along the temporal axis to P t P_{t} images. Patchification then yields ( H / P h ) × ( W / P w ) = H ​ W 256 (H/P_{h})\times(W/P_{w})=\frac{HW}{256} patches ( e.g. , a 256 × 256 256{\times}256 image produces 256 patches). For a 3D volume of depth T T and spatial size H × W H{\times}W , patchification directly operates along all three axes, producing ( T / P t ) × ( H / P h ) × ( W / P w ) (T/P_{t})\times(H/P_{h})\times(W/P_{w}) patches ( e.g. , a 32-slice 256 × 256 256{\times}256 CT volume yields 8 × 16 × 16 = 2048 8\times 16\times 16=2048 patches).

content: All patches from a batch are concatenated into a single flat sequence of shape [ N , 3072 ] [N,3072] , where N N is the total number of patches across the batch. This eliminates dense padding entirely and achieves 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) memory regardless of resolution heterogeneity. Each patch is associated with a coordinate vector ( b , z , x , y ) (b,z,x,y) encoding the batch index, depth position, and spatial position, together with a list of per-sample sequence lengths that enables 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) batch-wise slicing. Because the representation has no global spatial grid, a single batch can freely mix different spatial resolutions ( e.g. , 256 × 256 256{\times}256 and 512 × 512 512{\times}512 ), different depths ( e.g. , 16 and 64 slices), and 2D images with 3D volumes simultaneously.

content: We curate the training set from publicly available medical imaging repositories. Before quality filtering, we impose minimum dataset size thresholds: only 2D datasets containing at least 9,000 images and 3D datasets containing at least 180 volumes are included. This criterion serves two purposes. First, it prevents commonly used small-scale benchmark datasets from entering the training pool, thereby preserving their integrity for downstream evaluation. Second, it avoids highly fragmented data sources that contribute minimal training signal relative to the overhead of integration.

content: We use autoencoding reconstruction as a proxy task to evaluate token fidelity: each input is encoded and decoded by the frozen tokenizer, and we measure how faithfully the tokens preserve the original signal. For 2D images, evaluation is performed at 512 × 512 512{\times}512 resolution. We report PSNR and SSIM between the input and reconstructed images. For 3D volumes, we evaluate on CT and MRI using two datasets. CT intensities are clipped to [ − 1000 , 1000 ] [-1000,1000] HU; MRI intensities are clipped at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles per volume. PSNR and SSIM are computed at the volume level. Only models with native 3D support (PUMIT, MedVAE, AToken, MedVTok) are included in the 3D evaluation.

authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
content: We adopt a k k -nearest neighbor ( k k -NN) protocol on frozen features extracted from the CLS token (or equivalent global representation) of each tokenizer. For tokenizers that do not output such a representation ( e.g. , SDVAE), we concatenate all features along the channel dimension. The feature vectors are L 2 L_{2} -normalized, and classification is performed via softmax-weighted voting over the k k nearest neighbors using cosine similarity with a temperature of T = 0.07 T=0.07 . We sweep k ∈ { 10 , 20 , 100 , 200 } k\in\{10,20,100,200\} on the validation set and report the best accuracy for each model. Image resolution is controlled at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 when possible.

title: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer
authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
content: We evaluate image-to-image retrieval using the same frozen features and benchmarks as classification. The training split of each dataset serves as the gallery, and the test split provides the queries. For each query, we compute the cosine similarity between its L 2 L_{2} -normalized feature vector and all gallery features, rank the gallery by descending similarity, and report Recall@1 (the fraction of queries whose top-retrieved image shares the same label). Image resolution is controlled at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 when possible, consistent with the classification setup.

title: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer
authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
content: We evaluate the quality of frozen patch tokens for dense prediction by training a lightweight linear segmentation head on top of each tokenizer’s output, following the protocol of Siméoni et al. [ 55 ] . The segmentation head consists of a batch normalization layer followed by a 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution. For each tokenizer, we train separate heads under identical settings and select the best-performing one by validation Dice score. Training runs for 50 epochs with AdamW (no weight decay), a batch size of 32, cross-entropy loss, and learning rates searched over { 10 − 2 , 10 − 3 , 10 − 4 } \{10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4}\} . Image resolution is controlled at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 when possible. We report the overall Dice score over segmentation classes. Table 9 further reports Hausdorff Distance at the 95th percentile (HD95), where MedVTok still leads in terms of average performance across modalities.

content: We evaluate how the quality of a tokenizer’s latent space influences text-conditioned medical image synthesis. Each frozen tokenizer is integrated into a latent diffusion framework [ 29 ] as the only variable: a UNet denoising backbone following the Stable Diffusion v1.4 architecture is randomly initialized for each tokenizer (with input/output channels adapted to match the latent dimensionality), and a frozen CLIP-based text encoder provides conditioning. We train separate diffusion models per tokenizer using identical data, architecture, and hyperparameters, ensuring that differences in generation quality are attributable solely to the tokenizer.

content: Training uses 70,000 images from GMAI-VL-5.5M [ 1 ] spanning seven imaging modalities (10,000 images each). The noise scheduler is DDPM with 1,000 timesteps, a scaled-linear beta schedule, and ϵ \epsilon -prediction parameterization. The model is trained with an effective batch size of 256, the AdamW optimizer, a constant learning rate with 5% linear warmup, and classifier-free guidance dropout of 10%. Note that the purpose of this experiment is to compare the generative suitability of different tokenizer latent spaces , rather than to build state-of-the-art text-to-image generative models or to benchmark fine-grained synthesis. The original paired descriptions in GMAI-VL-5.5M are often long and fine-grained; using them directly may introduce confounding factors from text complexity. We therefore simplify the setup, replacing each caption with a controlled template, e.g. , “A medical {modality} image,” and keep this protocol identical for all tokenizers. Under this setting, differences in generation quality more directly reflect how well each frozen tokenizer organizes medical images into a latent space that is compact, learnable, and amenable to latent diffusion.

content: We evaluate each frozen tokenizer as a visual backbone within the LLaVA-Med [ 58 ] framework. Given a medical image, the tokenizer encodes it into patch-level tokens, which are then fed through a two-layer MLP connector into Mistral-7B-Instruct as the language model backbone. We train separate LLaVA-Med variants using identical data and hyperparameters while keeping the tokenizer frozen.

CT intensities are windowed to [ − 160,240 ] [-160,240] HU. content: Fig. 9 shows the effect of the MERA loss weight for values in { 0 , 0.1 , 1 , 2 } \{0,0.1,1,2\} . Without semantic alignment ( λ MERA = 0 \lambda_{\text{MERA}}=0 ), classification and segmentation scores remain significantly low despite strong reconstruction, as the tokenizer only learns the low-level structure without discriminating the high-level semantics. Increasing λ MERA \lambda_{\text{MERA}} monotonically improves semantic metrics, but at the cost of reconstruction fidelity: at λ MERA = 2 \lambda_{\text{MERA}}=2 , PSNR drops by nearly 3 dB and SSIM falls to 0.868. content: Fig. 10 shows the effect of the SliDR loss weight. As expected, 2D reconstruction is unaffected by λ SliDR \lambda_{\text{SliDR}} since SliDR operates only on volumetric data. For 3D reconstruction, both PSNR and SSIM improve substantially when SliDR is enabled. Further increasing the weight to λ SliDR = 0.5 \lambda_{\text{SliDR}}=0.5 yields marginal 3D gains but degrades classification accuracy by 2.6%, indicating that excessive volumetric regularization interferes with semantic learning. We therefore adopt λ SliDR = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{SliDR}}=0.1 , which captures most of the 3D benefit without compromising other objectives.

content: To qualitatively assess the discriminative structure of the learned representations, we visualize t t -SNE embeddings of frozen tokenizer features in Fig. 11 . We compare PUMIT, MedVAE, MedITok, and MedVTok on two datasets: (a) a microscopy blood cell dataset PBC [ 68 ] (covering multiple cell types: basophil, eosinophil, erythroblast, immature granulocytes, lymphocyte, monocyte, neutrophil, platelet), which is an out-of-distribution modality not seen during training, and (b) the JSIEC [ 33 ] fundus dataset. On the PBC dataset, MedVTok produces clearly separated clusters for each cell type despite never seeing microscopy images during training, indicating strong generalization of the learned semantic structure. On JSIEC, MedVTok forms tighter, more coherent clusters for fine-grained retinal conditions compared to the baselines, which exhibit more inter-class overlap. These visualizations corroborate the quantitative classification and retrieval results, confirming that MedVTok encodes semantically meaningful representations that generalize across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution modalities.

content: A general-purpose medical visual tokenizer can accelerate multimodal medical AI research and patient-level modeling by providing a shared, reusable visual interface across imaging modalities. This may lower the barrier for building clinical decision-support tools, particularly for under-resourced specialties or institutions that lack the data and compute. By open-sourcing the model and code, we aim to promote reproducibility and equitable access to medical AI infrastructure.

content: As with any medical AI component, there is a risk that downstream systems built on MedVTok could produce incorrect predictions that, if acted upon without appropriate clinical oversight, may lead to patient harm. We will release MedVTok under the Apache 2.0 license with clear documentation stating that it is intended for research use. We encourage downstream users to rigorously validate performance on their target populations and to comply with applicable regulations before any clinical deployment.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
section: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
content: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Recent speech foundation models have substantially improved multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) through larger training corpora, increased model capacity, and improved training objectives Babu et al. (2022) ; Radford et al. (2023) ; Barrault et al. (2023) . However, extending an existing multilingual ASR model to new languages remains challenging. Expansion often needs to be performed with limited data and computation while preserving performance on previously supported languages, creating a trade-off between target-language adaptation and source-language retention.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: A common expansion strategy is to fine-tune the existing model on the new language, but this can cause catastrophic forgetting. Similar degradation has been observed in connector-based Speech LLMs for ASR, where multilingual projectors are easy to adapt but may substantially harm original-language performance Concina et al. (2026a) ; Concina et al. (2026b) . Replay-based continual learning can mitigate forgetting by interleaving previously supported languages during adaptation, but it requires storing and reusing replay data. When such data is unavailable or impractical to reuse, expansion must rely on replay-free target-language adaptation without gradient-based source adaptation.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Model merging offers an alternative by combining learned parameter updates without additional training Yang et al. (2026) . Methods such as weight averaging and task arithmetic integrate capabilities from different training runs or tasks in weight space Wortsman et al. (2022) ; Ilharco et al. (2022) , but independently learned updates may interfere. TIES-Merging mitigates this interference by removing small parameter changes and resolving sign conflicts between task vectors Yadav et al. (2023) . Language-specific merging has also been explored to reduce training and maintenance costs when adding or updating languages in multilingual models Dmonte et al. (2026) . However, how target-language updates behave in connector-based multilingual ASR expansion remains unclear, particularly without source-language replay during adaptation.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: In this work, we study source-aware multilingual ASR expansion for connector-based Speech LLMs Ma et al. (2025) ; Ma et al. (2024) . Starting from a multilingual base connector Zhang et al. (2026a) , our goal is to adapt the connector to new target languages while preserving performance on the source languages, without replaying source-language training data or performing gradient-based source adaptation during expansion. We focus on two questions: RQ1: How can adaptation and merging balance target acquisition and source retention? and RQ2: How effectively can independent target updates be merged to support multiple new languages?

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: To answer these questions, we conduct controlled experiments with three multilingual base connectors and six target languages. We compare direct target fine-tuning, source-aware parameter-selective adaptation, and TIES-based target-update merging under the same target-language adaptation budget. Our experimental results suggest that source-aware merging substantially improves the adaptation–retention trade-off in single-target expansion, while multi-target expansion requires managing interactions among target-language updates. Joint update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive adaptation can achieve stronger target performance under favorable target orders.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Our main contributions are as follows. First, we introduce a source-aware multilingual ASR expansion setting for connector-based Speech LLMs, where new target languages are added while preserving existing source-language performance without source-language replay or gradient-based source adaptation. Second, we systematically compare target-update construction strategies, including direct fine-tuning, SSU-based parameter-selective adaptation, SSU+FT, and TIES-based target-update merging, to characterize the trade-off between target adaptation and source retention. Third, we extend the study from single-target to multi-target expansion and analyze how target-update interactions and recursive target order shape multilingual expansion.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Large-scale speech foundation models have advanced multilingual ASR through cross-lingual self-supervised learning, weakly supervised recognition, and unified multilingual speech modeling across diverse languages and tasks Babu et al. (2022) ; Radford et al. (2023) ; Barrault et al. (2023) . Recent LLM-based ASR systems further connect pretrained speech encoders with large language models through lightweight connectors, showing that frozen speech and language backbones can support multilingual recognition and benefit from auxiliary multimodal context Fathullah et al. (2023) ; Ma et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024) . These developments motivate connector-based Speech LLMs as a parameter-efficient ASR framework, but leave open how to expand them to new languages while preserving existing multilingual capabilities.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Multilingual ASR systems often need to be expanded after the initial model has been trained, making new-language acquisition and source-language retention a central challenge. Prior work on multilingual ASR expansion has largely framed new-language acquisition and forgetting as a continual-learning problem, covering replay-based retention, parameter-regularized adaptation, and decoder-specific optimization strategies Della Libera et al. (2024) ; Kwok et al. (2024) ; Concina et al. (2026b) . In contrast, our work does not rely on source-language replay or gradient-based source adaptation during expansion. We instead study how target-language updates can be constructed and combined under lightweight source-language calibration, comparing parameter-selective adaptation and target-update merging in both single-target and multi-target connector expansion.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Model merging provides an alternative to continued fine-tuning by combining parameters or parameter updates from separately trained models. Model soups show that averaging the weights of multiple fine-tuned models can improve performance and robustness without increasing inference cost, particularly when the models are fine-tuned from the same initialization Wortsman et al. (2022) . Task arithmetic represents fine-tuning effects as task vectors and shows that these vectors can be added, subtracted, or composed to alter model behavior in parameter space Ilharco et al. (2022) . These approaches suggest that independently learned capabilities can sometimes be integrated without additional training.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: However, merging fine-tuned models separately can introduce interference between parameter updates. TIES-Merging addresses this issue by trimming small parameter changes, resolving sign conflicts among task vectors, and merging only sign-aligned updates Yadav et al. (2023) . In multilingual settings, Dmonte et al. (2026) study language-specific model merging as a way to reduce training and maintenance costs when individual languages are added or updated in multilingual task-specific LLMs. In the speech domain, model merging is explored for adding new tasks Zhao et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2025) , domains Carvalho et al. (2026) , and fairness Lin et al. (2026) ; Bravo-Bravo et al. (2026) . Nevertheless, existing model merging work has not fully examined connector-based multilingual ASR expansion under a source-free setting, where target-language updates must be integrated while preserving source-language performance without access to source-language data during expansion.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Parameter-selective adaptation aims to reduce forgetting by restricting which parameters are updated during task or language adaptation Liu et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Pan et al. (2024) . Instead of updating the full model, these methods identify parameters or structural units that are important for previously learned capabilities and protect them during subsequent fine-tuning. This idea has been explored in continual learning through masking, pruning, and parameter-isolation strategies, where different subsets of model parameters are assigned to different tasks or protected from future updates Mallya and Lazebnik (2018) ; Mallya et al. (2018) .

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Source-Shielded Updates (SSU) apply this idea to target-language adaptation of LLMs by estimating source-language parameter importance and freezing source-important units during target-language fine-tuning Yamaguchi et al. (2026) . This is particularly relevant to multilingual ASR expansion, where adapting to a new language can interfere with previously supported source languages. In our work, we adopt SSU-style source-aware masking for connector adaptation, using a lightweight source-language calibration set only to construct masks.

content: Table 3 reports macro-averaged WER for each base group. The results show a clear adaptation–retention trade-off. Target-only fine-tuning learns the new language effectively, but severely damages the original source languages. For example, on the Germanic base, Target FT reduces target WER from 102.70% to 27.86%, but increases source WER from 22.57% to 69.73%. The same pattern appears for Romance and Slavic, where source WER increases by +55.54% and +54.49%, respectively.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Standard TIES merging does not solve this problem in the single-target setting. Although it preserves the target-language gains of fine-tuning, it retains most of the source-language degradation, behaving similarly to Target FT across base groups. SSU-Wanda+FT is also insufficient on its own, even with source-important parameters frozen during target adaptation, the resulting connector still suffers substantial source degradation. These results suggest that neither conventional merging nor protected fine-tuning alone is enough to recover a balanced source–target solution.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: In contrast, SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the strongest overall trade-off. It keeps source WER close to the base connector while still improving target performance substantially. For Germanic and Romance, source WER increases by only +0.24% and +0.69%, while target WER drops from 102.70% to 35.82% and from 111.16% to 37.36%, respectively. For Slavic, the harder expansion setting, SSU-Wanda+TIES reduces source degradation from +53.95% under TIES to +6.68%, while improving target WER from 110.15% to 51.69%. These results show that strong single-target expansion requires combining source-aware adaptation with update merging.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR

content: We next compare the three SSU masking criteria used with TIES: random masking, magnitude-based masking, and Wanda-based masking. Table 3 shows that all SSU+TIES variants reduce source forgetting compared with Target FT and standard TIES, but they differ in how they balance target adaptation and source retention. SSU-Rand+TIES often preserves stronger target-language gains than SSU-Wanda+TIES, but leaves more source degradation. For example, on the Slavic base, SSU-Rand+TIES reaches 41.69% target WER, but increases source WER by +22.54%. SSU-Wanda+TIES gives a higher target WER of 51.69%, but reduces source degradation to +6.68%. This suggests that random protection can limit update damage, but does not reliably select the directions most important for preserving source-language behavior.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: SSU-Mag+TIES provides a more structured mask than random selection, but it is generally worse than SSU-Wanda+TIES in source retention and overall WER. Across all three base groups, SSU-Mag+TIES causes larger source degradation than SSU-Wanda+TIES, indicating that weight magnitude alone is not sufficient to identify source-important connector directions. By incorporating source-language activations, SSU-Wanda produces a more conservative mask that better preserves the original multilingual capability.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Overall, SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the most reliable source-preserving trade-off. It achieves the lowest source WER and lowest overall WER for all three base groups, although it sometimes gives up part of the target-language gain achieved by SSU-Rand or SSU-Mag. We therefore use SSU-Wanda as the default SSU criterion in the multi-target experiments.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: The results show that base–target compatibility affects expansion behavior, but not through a simple ranking of conditions. Serbian is the most compatible target in our design, with both the same language group and script as the Slavic base, and is comparatively easy to add. SSU-Wanda+TIES reaches 27.63% target WER with only +4.17% source degradation. However, same-group targets are not uniformly easy. Polish and Slovenian are both Slavic languages using Latin script in our setting, but they are harder to add than Serbian, and Slovenian causes much larger source degradation.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: The comparison between Slovenian and Kyrgyz further shows that language-group match alone does not determine expansion difficulty. Slovenian is same-group but different-script, while Kyrgyz is different-group but same-script. Yet SSU-Wanda+TIES preserves source languages much better for Kyrgyz than for Slovenian, with +2.26% versus +21.11% source degradation, even though Kyrgyz remains difficult in target WER. This suggests that source retention and target learnability are related but not identical. A target can be hard to recognize while causing limited forgetting, or linguistically closer while producing a more disruptive update.

authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
section: 4.3.1 Joint Update Merging versus Recursive Adaptation
content: Joint update merging provides a stable source-preserving solution, while recursive adaptation can learn target languages more aggressively but is more order-sensitive. TIES keeps source WER close to the base connector for all three base groups and substantially improves target WER, reducing it from 102.70% to 64.93% for Germanic, from 111.16% to 67.22% for Romance, and from 110.15% to 97.41% for Slavic. This shows that independently trained target updates can be merged jointly without severe source-language forgetting.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
section: 4.3.1 Joint Update Merging versus Recursive Adaptation
content: Source-aware variants of joint merging do not uniformly improve target performance in the multi-target setting. Hard SSU+TIES and Incremental dynamic SSU further protect source languages, but often retain less target-language improvement than TIES. This suggests that source protection can become too restrictive when multiple target updates are combined.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
section: 4.3.1 Joint Update Merging versus Recursive Adaptation
content: Recursive methods show a different trade-off. Recursive FT then SSU achieves the best target WER for Germanic and Slavic, and the best overall WER for Slavic under the configured order. However, its Romance result is much worse, indicating that recursive adaptation can produce stronger target learning but depends heavily on target order. Recursive rebased SSU is even less stable. Although it improves target WER in some settings, it causes large source degradation for Romance and Slavic, suggesting that recursively applying base-anchored target updates can accumulate source-language interference. Thus, unlike single-target expansion where SSU-Wanda+TIES is consistently strongest, multi-target expansion exposes a sharper trade-off between stable joint merging and order-sensitive recursive adaptation.

content: For Romance, the configured order NO → \rightarrow IT → \rightarrow SR gives 57.81% overall WER, while IT → \rightarrow NO → \rightarrow SR improves it to 31.82%, outperforming TIES. Germanic shows a similar pattern, improving from 39.61% under the configured order to 35.05% with IT → \rightarrow SR → \rightarrow NO. authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: These results show that recursive adaptation is not simply worse than update merging. It is a higher-variance strategy that can achieve stronger target adaptation under favorable orders, but can also accumulate interference under poorly matched orders. This is consistent with the target-update conflict analysis in Appendix B.4 , where target updates show low cosine similarity and substantial sign disagreement. Overall, update merging is more stable and source-preserving, while recursive adaptation can achieve better overall WER when the target sequence is favorable.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: In this paper, we studied source-aware expansion for connector-based multilingual ASR, where new languages are added while preserving the original base connector. Our results show that target fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but often overwrite source-language performance, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the strongest single-target adaptation–retention trade-off. For multi-target expansion, update merging is stable and source-preserving, whereas recursive adaptation can achieve stronger target performance under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. Overall, effective multilingual ASR expansion requires both source-aware preservation and careful coordination among target-language updates.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: This work has two main limitations. First, our experiments focus on connector-based Speech LLMs, where the speech encoder and LLM are kept frozen and only the connector is adapted. This setting allows us to study parameter-selective adaptation and model merging in a controlled way, but the conclusions may not directly generalize to systems that update the speech encoder, the LLM, or the full ASR model during language expansion. Second, our multi-target experiments cover a limited number of target languages and target orders. Although the results show clear order sensitivity in recursive expansion, we do not propose an automatic method for selecting the target order. A larger-scale study over more languages and principled order-selection strategies would be needed to fully characterize recursive multilingual expansion.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: Our experiments use publicly available speech data from Common Voice, without collecting new recordings or additional speaker metadata. We do not disclose any personally identifiable information about the speakers. Multilingual ASR expansion may broaden access to speech technologies, but improvements for newly added languages can come at the expense of previously supported languages, potentially reducing service quality for their speakers. ASR adaptation methods may affect languages and speaker groups differently, and improvements in average WER can obscure these disparities. To make differences across languages visible, we report per-language performance on both source and target languages.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: For SSU-Wanda, the calibration set contains 5 minutes of speech from the validation split of each source language, totaling 25 minutes per base. Calibration is therefore balanced by speech duration across source languages. It is used only for forward activation collection and mask construction. Source-language examples are not replayed or used for gradient-based adaptation during expansion. Random and magnitude-based masking do not require activation collection.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: We evaluate both single-target and multi-target expansion. In single-target expansion, each target language is added independently to a base connector, with base–target pairs covering language-group and script match/mismatch conditions (Table 2 ). We compare direct target fine-tuning, TIES without source-aware protection, and SSU variants using random, magnitude-based, and Wanda-based masking.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: In multi-target expansion, we study how multiple target-language updates can form a single expanded connector. For joint update merging, target-specific connectors are independently adapted from the same base connector. Each target update is computed relative to that shared base, and the updates are merged without further gradient-based training. Recursive adaptation instead processes targets sequentially, using the connector produced by the preceding stage as the starting point for the next target. Each stage uses only the current target language for gradient-based training.

title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
content: The configured order is NO → \rightarrow IT → \rightarrow SR for the Germanic and Romance bases, and IT → \rightarrow SR → \rightarrow PL → \rightarrow SL → \rightarrow KY for the Slavic base. We additionally evaluate Recursive FT then SSU under the orders listed in Table 6 . These constitute the evaluated subset of possible orders rather than an exhaustive enumeration.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
content: Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev’s accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27–29% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. This loss of initial successes is substantially larger than under fixed-order repetition, even for highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: A correct choice should depend on candidate content, yet language models can change their answers when only the presentation changes. Reordering options can alter multiple-choice answers ( Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) , and swapping two unchanged responses can reverse an LLM judge’s preference ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . Such selection bias lets presentation influence a decision without adding evidence about which candidate is correct. A question answered correctly in one order may therefore fail in another.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Prompting alone does not reliably remove this bias. Zheng et al. (2024) find residual bias under explicit debiasing instructions and chain-of-thought prompting in the settings tested. Calibration and targeted training offer ways to reduce it ( Li et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , while evidence from multi-document question answering suggests that reasoning models can be less position-biased ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Selection bias is therefore sensitive to how a model is trained and used. This raises the possibility that models designed expressly for candidate selection could better preserve their decisions.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Jev-style System One models make this possibility concrete. They predict a probability distribution directly over candidates supplied with each request. TypeSafe describes Jev as trained for calibrated decisions through Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). 1 1 1 TypeSafe’s model introduction and machine-learning primer describe this training goal; the complete architecture and training recipe remain proprietary. Recent efforts to reproduce this behavior have produced a growing family of models ( Geuter et al., 2026 ; Li and Wagle, 2026 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ) , which we call Jev reproductions . These implementations range from training a decision head with backbone adaptation to extracting candidate probabilities from a frozen LLM. The term denotes a shared behavioral goal, without implying recovery of Jev’s proprietary internals or a common architecture. Candidate representation, probability readout, and decision-specific learning are therefore possible sources of robustness, not guarantees of it.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Existing evidence already challenges the assumption that structured decisions resist bias. Typed decision models can repeat pairwise judgments reliably yet reverse them when the two responses are swapped ( Lukassen et al., 2026 ) . In public Jev-style implementations, option labels can override written definitions, and serialization changes can alter this behavior with model weights fixed ( Azizi et al., 2026 ) . What remains limited is a systematic comparison of Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs as correct choices face repeated reordering in multi-option tasks. A single swap cannot reveal how widely failures spread over further orders, and aggregate accuracy can hide losses that recoveries offset. We therefore ask: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias?

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: We investigate this question with a simple test that shuffles options while preserving question and candidate content. The study compares two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs on SuperGPQA ( M-A-P et al., 2025 ) , LEXam ( Fan et al., 2026 ) , MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and GPQA Diamond ( Rein et al., 2023 ) . Our primary collection pools 1,700 questions from SuperGPQA and LEXam. For each question, we compare the original order, its reversal, and six random permutations with eight requests in the unchanged original order. Tracking first errors reveals how the failure set expands and how many initial successes survive. Every request retains the full candidate menu.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The test reveals no general Jev advantage in preserving correct choices. Jev’s accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27–29%, with first failures continuing into the final presentation (Figure 1 ). Four LLMs preserve more initial successes, including on questions every model initially answers correctly. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash have lower pooled retention, preventing a universal ranking of model families. The central finding is that Jev’s structured decision formulation does not by itself protect answers the model can already get right.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Fixed-order repetition exposes a second distinction: repeatability does not ensure robustness to reordering. Jev repeats choices more consistently than several LLMs, but loses substantially more initial successes under reordering than under repetition at the same call budget. The twelve Jev reproductions make this gap especially clear: 97.7–100% fixed-order agreement coexists with losses of 23.2–64.2% of initial successes under reordering (Figure 2 ).

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The remaining analyses examine where correct choices are most fragile and whether repeated answers can repair them. Difficulty and menu-size comparisons locate this vulnerability. MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond show that it persists where Jev achieves higher accuracy and with only four candidates. Voting offers only modest gains for Jev, and unanimity still admits frequent errors. Together, these results distinguish average accuracy, fixed-order repeatability, and preservation of correct choices. The supporting survey in Appendices A – I organizes differences in representation, learning, and computation that controlled comparisons could isolate to explain the observed behavior.

content: The preceding trajectories vary both the request and the candidate order. Holding the order fixed reveals a different comparison (Figure 1 (b)). Thus, variability across reordered presentations includes variation that can already occur under repetition, and its extent differs substantially across models.

They agree on 97.7–100% of their identity-set questions across eight requests, yet 52.2–78.0% receive the same wrong answer throughout. content: At an equal eight-call budget, Jev varies substantially more under reordering than under original-order repetition (Figure 7 ). On the question set shared by both conditions, its changed-choice rate is 23.6 percentage points higher for version 1.13 (95% interval 21.3–26.0) and 24.6 higher for version 1.14 (22.2–27.0), compared with differences of 2.2–7.2 across the six LLMs. This gap also extends to successful decisions. Jev loses 8.2–9.0% of its initial successes under repetition and 25.1–26.4% under reordering, with paired differences of 16.1 points (13.4–19.1) and 18.1 points (15.3–21.1), while mean accuracy differs by less than half a point. By contrast, GLM-5.3-Flash already loses 39.7% under original-order repetition, with a further 5.7-point difference under reordering. Variation under repetition and additional variation under reordering are distinct failure patterns.

section: Obs. 4. Jev’s errors often extend beyond one distractor per question.
content: If every failed question had one fixed wrong answer, the pair count would grow only when another question failed. Jev 1.14 illustrates why this description is incomplete. Its original presentation produces 746 wrong pairs, one for each incorrectly answered question. After eight presentations, 965 questions have failed at least once, but the model has selected 1,449 distinct wrong pairs. The 703 additional pairs comprise 219 newly affected questions and 484 extra wrong candidates beyond the first per affected question. The latter component includes both initially failed questions and questions that first fail later and then receive another wrong answer.

content: Jev’s distinct wrong-pair count increases by 87.8–94.2%, far more than its 27.3–29.4% increase in failed questions. authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 4. Jev’s errors often extend beyond one distractor per question.
content: Multiple distractors are selected on 337–354 questions for Jev, below Qwen3.8-Flash-Next’s 404 and GLM-5.3-Flash’s 569, and above the 94–222 for the other four LLMs. Their contribution persists late in the sequence. Of Jev’s 41–46 new wrong pairs in the final presentation, 34–38 select a different wrong candidate on a previously affected question, accounting for 82.6–82.9% of the additions. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 show a similar pattern, with shares of 80.8% and 79.6%. Late error discovery therefore mainly broadens the observed ways to fail within affected questions, even as a smaller number of previously successful questions fail for the first time.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 4. Jev’s errors often extend beyond one distractor per question.
content: The expansion is not specific to choosing the original or final presentation as a reference. Relative to the mean wrong-pair count of a single presentation, the full union is 86.2–92.0% larger for Jev and 53.9–214.9% larger for the LLMs. Averaging over all eight ways to omit one presentation leaves 42.4–47.4 unseen pairs for Jev, versus 15.5–125.8 for the LLMs. These comparisons characterize the recorded responses without predicting saturation under further evaluation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 4. Jev’s errors often extend beyond one distractor per question.
content: The recorded errors therefore extend beyond one stable distractor per question. Because every request retains the full menu, these observations do not establish how the model would respond if a wrong candidate were removed.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4 How Does Jev’s Order Robustness Vary Across Tasks?
content: The pooled results establish that Jev’s stable score conceals lost successes. We now ask how broadly this pattern holds across benchmarks, difficulty levels, topics, and menu sizes. Each profile separates changed choices from lost initial successes, since a model can appear stable by remaining wrong. These subgroup comparisons locate vulnerability without isolating its causes.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 5. Jev’s relative stability depends on the task and the LLM comparator.
content: The ordering of models by stability can change across benchmarks (Figure 11 ). On LEXam, Jev changes 39.9–42.9% of choices, below DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017’s 47.1%, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next’s 61.6%, and GLM-5.3-Flash’s 75.5%, but above GPT-6.1-sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5.5. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 instead changes fewer choices than either Jev version on SuperGPQA. GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash remain more stable than Jev on both benchmarks, while Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash remain less stable. Jev’s relative position therefore depends on both the task and the comparator.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 5. Jev’s relative stability depends on the task and the LLM comparator.
content: AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 changes fewer choices than either Jev version on each benchmark, but this does not translate into uniformly better retention (Figure 12 ). On LEXam, its loss of 20.5% lies between Jev 1.13’s 21.7% and Jev 1.14’s 17.9%, despite changing fewer choices than both. The distinction between preserving candidate identity and preserving correct answers therefore matters even within the decision-model group.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 5. Jev’s relative stability depends on the task and the LLM comparator.
content: Lower turnover also need not yield more correct answers. Over half of Jev’s LEXam questions with changed choices remain wrong in every presentation. These always-wrong switches account for 21.7% of all paired LEXam questions for each Jev version, compared with 5.5–20.3% for the LLMs. Such trajectories contain no correct answer for voting to recover, linking the stability analysis to the aggregation results in Section 5 .

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: Hard questions challenge Jev beyond lowering its accuracy. Even conditional on an initially correct answer, 51.5–54.1% later become wrong, compared with 10.2–30.4% for five LLMs and 55.5% for GLM-5.3-Flash (Figure 13 ). An initial Jev success on these questions is therefore more often lost than preserved across all eight presentations. Jev’s overall changed-choice rate also rises from 27.2–30.2% on easy questions to 56.8–59.0% on hard questions. The five LLMs’ rates remain similar or decrease, whereas GLM-5.3-Flash rises from 47.7% to 65.3%. For Jev, the difficulty gradient concerns both the frequency of changing an answer and the fragility of an answer already known to be correct.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: The difficulty gradient extends across the twelve Jev reproductions (Figure 14 ). Every model changes more choices on hard than easy SuperGPQA questions, including within ten-option menus. On hard questions overall, loss of initial successes ranges from 36.8% for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 to 88.5% for StartLux-Decision-v1-4B. High fixed-order agreement thus does not protect a correct answer once the model confronts harder questions in a different order.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: Menu size does not fully explain this gradient. Within ten-option questions, Jev’s changed-choice rate rises from 27.0–29.0% on easy questions to 58.9–60.9% on hard questions; every LLM shows a smaller increase (Figure 13 (d)). Question content and subject composition still differ, so this comparison does not isolate difficulty itself.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: Correct-answer retention shows that the vulnerability is present even on easy questions (Figure 15 ). Within ten-option groups, Jev loses 14.9–18.8% of initial successes on easy questions, 26.0–26.1% on middle questions, and 48.6–48.7% on hard questions. Across all 731 ten-option questions, the loss is 25.2–27.4%, while each version’s accuracy varies by only 2.05 percentage points. Hard questions amplify the discrepancy between stable accuracy and fragile successes; they are not necessary for it to appear.

content: Figure 15: Harder questions amplify Jev’s loss of correct answers. Retention across eight presentations for ten-option SuperGPQA questions: easy, middle, hard, and all difficulties. Each curve starts at 100% and retains a question only while every observed answer remains correct. Panels share a scale; question content differs across groups.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: The same ten-option analysis separates the Jev reproductions (Figure 16 ). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 loses 18.2% of initial successes on easy questions and 44.9% on hard questions. The other eleven lose 66.2–93.3% on hard questions, compared with 50.0–53.4% for the Jev references in this comparison. A common candidate count therefore leaves substantial differences both across difficulty groups and within the Jev-style family.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: Subject profiles help locate this difficulty gradient (Figure 17 ). Engineering and science contain much of Jev’s instability and many of the hard questions: 163 of 399 engineering questions and 142 of 321 science questions are hard, compared with nine of 93 in literature and arts. Their higher changed-choice rates are consistent with the difficulty result, without identifying an independent subject effect. Separating correctness changes from always-wrong switches also reveals which variation includes an answer that aggregation could recover.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.
content: Subject profiles also qualify the relatively favorable pooled result for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 (Figure 18 ). It changes 43.9% of choices in engineering and 44.2% in science. Always-wrong switches account for 15.8% and 18.4% of all questions in those disciplines, respectively. Thus, its residual instability includes both lost or recovered correct answers and variation that never reaches the correct answer; the latter cannot be repaired by voting over the recorded choices.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: LEXam reveals substantial heterogeneity across menu sizes. Larger-option groups combine lower accuracy with more changed choices for every model (Figure 19 ). Jev’s changed-choice rates rise from 22.4–23.3% in the four-option group to 66.9–74.6% in the 32-option group. Both Jev versions exceed DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017’s 65.3% in the latter group, reversing their favorable comparison on LEXam overall. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash vary even more, changing 87.3% and 97.5% of choices. The same group yields 85.6–98.3 extra wrong pairs per 100 questions for Jev, compared with 162.7 for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and 230.5 for GLM-5.3-Flash. Larger menus thus identify a particularly unstable portion of this collection, with wrong-option diversity extending well beyond Jev. The groups contain different questions, however, and do not isolate the effect of adding distractors to a fixed question.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Figure 19: Larger LEXam menus accompany more varied wrong choices. Option-count groups contain 125 questions each; metrics follow Figure 11 . Lines connect model estimates, with pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals. Groups contain different questions, so the comparison does not isolate an effect of option count.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Figure 20: LEXam exposes both varied choices and menu limitations. Profiles include 4-, 8-, 16-, and 32-option questions, using the metrics in Figure 19 . Error bars show pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals. Groups contain different questions.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Every reproduction changes more choices at 16 options than at eight, and more at eight than at four (Figure 20 ). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 rises from 14.4% to 33.6% between four and 16 options, then reaches 55.2% at 32. Across four to 32 options, pplx-decider-v1.1-27b rises from 11.2% to 76.0%; AutoTrust-JEV-35B reaches 92.0% in the 32-option group. The remaining nine reproductions do not support 32-option menus, leaving their conditional stability metrics undefined.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: Jev’s loss of initial successes persists on both sides of an eight-option threshold (Figure 21 ). Across the eight presentations, Jev loses 21.7–23.6% of its initially correct answers on questions with fewer than eight options and 26.9–28.0% on questions with at least eight. The comparison with LLMs also varies across these groups. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 loses 23.9% and 22.4%, respectively: slightly more than either Jev version in the smaller-menu group, but less than both in the larger-menu group. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next loses 35.8% and 33.2%, exceeding both Jev versions in each group. These differences qualify pooled comparisons without isolating an effect of menu size.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: Jev reproductions also lose initial successes in both groups (Figure 22 ). Losses range from 17.8–51.9% below eight options and 25.3–71.6% at eight or more. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 has lower loss than either Jev version in both groups. The other eleven reproductions lose a larger fraction of their initial successes than either Jev version in the larger-menu group, showing that the vulnerability extends across the evaluated implementations.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: The full option-count profile qualifies the LEXam trend (Figure 23 ). Jev’s changed-choice rate and loss of initial successes fluctuate across the four- to ten-option groups rather than increasing steadily with menu size. Composition matters: all ten-option questions are from SuperGPQA, while all 16- and 32-option questions are from LEXam. The profile identifies vulnerable groups without estimating what would happen if distractors were added to the same question.

All observed option counts: (a) mean accuracy, (b) changed choices, (c) loss conditional on initial success, and (d) newly failed questions after O per 100 questions, counted once. Error bars show pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals. Benchmark and difficulty composition differ across groups.

content: Figure 24: Jev reproductions fail across the full range of menu sizes. Four to 32 options; metrics follow Figure 23 . Error bars show pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals. Benchmark and question content differ across groups.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: The pooled profile of Jev reproductions similarly prevents a simple ranking by menu size (Figure 24 ). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 loses 25.6% of initial successes on ten-option questions and 22.6% on 16-option questions, although its LEXam-only turnover increases across menu sizes. These groups differ in both benchmark and question content.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: Small menus do not make repeated reordering uninformative. A four-option question has 4 ! = 24 4!=24 full permutations, so eight presentations need not repeat the same menu order. In the four-option group, 199 of 203 questions have eight distinct observed orders and the other four have seven. Jev 1.13’s cumulative failed-question count rises from 76 to 95, and Jev 1.14’s from 73 to 92. Presentations five through eight still expose four and two first failures, respectively. Counting only the first occurrence of each full permutation leaves both Jev failure trajectories unchanged. These distinct full orders need not place the correct answer in distinct positions. The curves measure robustness across the sampled menu orders, without assuming a new correct-answer position on every presentation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery
content: The number of new failures must also be read alongside the pool of initial successes. On 32-option questions, Jev loses 43.5–70.0% of initial successes, but this amounts to only 8.5–11.9 newly failed questions per 100. The ten-option rates are 25.2–27.4% and 14.5–15.9 per 100. Low initial accuracy leaves fewer successes available to fail, so a smaller cumulative increase can accompany greater conditional fragility. Both measures are needed to avoid mistaking a small remaining pool of correct answers for robustness.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5 Can Aggregating Reordered Choices Correct Jev’s Errors?
content: The same repeated answers that expose failures might also help correct them. Plurality voting could recover a correct answer that appears across several orders, while unanimity could identify a more reliable subset. We test both possibilities, asking whether variation supplies useful correction and whether agreement warrants confidence (Figure 25 ).
