Across eight orders: (a) mean accuracy, (b) plurality gain in percentage points, (c) unanimous coverage, and (d) accuracy among unanimous answers. Error bars show pointwise 95% paired source-group bootstrap intervals, stratified by benchmark. Plurality ties use uniform tie-breaking in expectation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5 Can Aggregating Reordered Choices Correct Jev’s Errors?
content: Figure 26: Voting and unanimity provide limited safeguards for Jev reproductions. Metrics follow Figure 25 , with accuracy and coverage over all 1,700 questions. Unanimous accuracy ranges from 30.2% to 66.3% at differing coverage. Error bars show pointwise 95% paired bootstrap intervals; plurality ties use uniform tie-breaking in expectation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5.1 Voting Recovers Only Part of the Error
content: Combining eight reordered answers gives Jev only a modest accuracy gain: 0.81 percentage points for version 1.13 (95% interval 0.17–1.46) and 0.93 for version 1.14 (0.27–1.60). The reference is mean single-presentation accuracy, avoiding dependence on an unusually weak original round. LLM gains range from 0.42 points for GPT-6.1-sol to 5.03 for GLM-5.3-Flash, with positive lower bounds for all six intervals. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash gain 3.23 points (2.43–4.05) and 5.03 (4.04–6.00), respectively. Their lower pooled retention thus coexists with more effective correction through voting.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5.1 Voting Recovers Only Part of the Error
content: The trajectories help explain why correction is limited. Jev 1.14 gains only 0.27 points on LEXam ( − 0.75 -0.75 –1.28), where many changed choices remain wrong throughout. Such trajectories supply no correct vote; even when the correct answer appears, it must receive enough votes to defeat the alternatives. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash gain 2.90 points (1.19–4.42) and 4.19 (2.35–6.04) on LEXam, while the GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash intervals span zero. The usefulness of variation depends on which candidates are selected and how often, rather than on the amount of disagreement alone.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5.1 Voting Recovers Only Part of the Error
content: The eight-call comparison further limits the practical benefit of Jev’s variation. Voting gain, measured relative to each condition’s mean single-request accuracy, is only 0.75 points higher under reordering for Jev 1.13 (95% interval 0.06–1.49) and 0.96 higher for Jev 1.14 (0.24–1.71), alongside a roughly 24-point difference in changed-choice rates. The direct differences in plurality accuracy between conditions have intervals spanning zero for both versions. Thus, the greater variation under reordering accompanies a small additional voting gain relative to a single answer, without establishing higher final voting accuracy than original-order repetition.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 5.1 Voting Recovers Only Part of the Error
content: Voting gains for Jev reproductions are also modest despite substantial turnover (Figure 26 ). They range from 0.74 points for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 (95% interval 0.18–1.31) to 2.49 for StartLux-Decision-v1-35B-A3B (1.71–3.32), with positive lower bounds for all twelve models. Reordering provides some recoverable correct choices, but the gains remain small relative to the widespread changes it exposes.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 7. More than one third of unanimous Jev answers are wrong.
content: Unanimity raises Jev’s conditional accuracy but leaves substantial error among the retained answers. The two versions select the same candidate in all eight presentations on 59.9–61.0% of questions, with accuracy of 63.2–63.9% on this subset. Thus, 36–37% of unanimous answers are wrong. These persistent mistakes account for 21.6–22.4% of all paired questions, each receiving the same wrong Jev answer eight times. They survive even the strongest agreement requirement available in the recorded trajectories. Such mistakes are not, by themselves, evidence of order bias; they show why surviving the reordering test is insufficient to certify a correct decision.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 7. More than one third of unanimous Jev answers are wrong.
content: The same unanimity rule retains more accurate answers for each LLM, although at different coverage. The retained LLM answers are 17.6–21.4% wrong, compared with Jev’s 36–37%. GPT-6.1-sol has the broadest coverage at 82.6%, with 78.6% conditional accuracy, while DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash retain 65.5–79.0% of questions at 79.5–81.1% accuracy. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash retain fewer questions than Jev, at 49.2% and 37.3% coverage, but reach 81.8% and 82.4% accuracy. Agreement improves conditional accuracy within each model, yet the surviving Jev decisions remain substantially less reliable at these observed operating points. Differences in base accuracy and coverage prevent this comparison from isolating the predictive value of agreement or establishing a ranking at matched coverage.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 7. More than one third of unanimous Jev answers are wrong.
content: The Jev reproductions reinforce this limitation of unanimity. Their unanimous subsets reach only 30.2–66.3% accuracy, with coverage ranging from 24.1% to 63.7% of the full collection. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 has the highest coverage, yet 42.4% of its unanimous answers are wrong; these persistent errors account for 27.0% of all 1,700 questions. Across the twelve models, 12.1–27.0% of questions receive the same wrong answer in every presentation. High agreement under fixed-order repetition therefore cannot certify correctness either before or after reordering.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 6 Does Higher Accuracy Protect Correct Choices?
content: Does higher accuracy protect Jev’s successful decisions? MMLU-Pro provides a setting where Jev answers most questions correctly, allowing us to examine whether those successes also survive reordering. Accuracy uses all 300 questions. The other panels use each model’s fixed set of questions with selections in all fifteen distinct requests. These sets can differ across models, so the trajectories support within-model comparisons rather than rankings on identical questions.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: 6 Does Higher Accuracy Protect Correct Choices?
content: Figure 27: Jev’s higher MMLU-Pro accuracy still leaves correct answers vulnerable. authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 8. Higher Jev accuracy does not eliminate the loss of initial successes.
content: Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 average 86.4% and 86.0% accuracy over the reordered presentations, with ranges of 3.7 and 3.3 percentage points (Figure 27 (a)). Yet their cumulative failure sets grow from 35 to 58 and from 36 to 63 questions, respectively. The additional 23 and 27 failures represent 8.7% and 10.2% of initially correct answers, compared with losses of only 1.1% and 2.7% under original-order repetition. Each version first fails on two more questions in the final presentation. The loss is smaller than on the primary collection, but it persists even when Jev answers most questions correctly.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 8. Higher Jev accuracy does not eliminate the loss of initial successes.
content: All twelve Jev reproductions repeat exactly the same candidate across eight original-order requests, yet lose 8.6–45.0% of initial successes under reordering (Figure 28 ). Thus, the separation between repeatability and preservation of correct choices persists on a different benchmark. As in the primary collection, the comparison describes the evaluated systems without isolating an architectural cause.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 8. Higher Jev accuracy does not eliminate the loss of initial successes.
content: Jev’s unanimous answers are more accurate here than on the primary collection, but agreement still does not certify correctness. They cover 88.3% and 86.0% of questions and reach 91.3% and 91.9% accuracy (Figure 27 (d)); 8.7% and 8.1% of the retained answers are still wrong. Thus, both the loss under reordering and the reliability of agreement depend on the task collection. What transfers is the distinction among average accuracy, fixed-order repeatability, and the survival of individual correct decisions.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 9. Jev’s loss of correct choices is not confined to long candidate menus.
content: Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 average 76.6% and 72.6% accuracy, yet their cumulative failure sets grow from 52 to 76 and from 58 to 89 questions. Reordering loses 16.4% and 22.1% of their initial successes, compared with 4.1% and 7.1% under original-order repetition. All twelve Jev reproductions repeat their original choices perfectly but lose 23.7–66.7% of initial successes after reordering. The gap between repeatability and preservation of successful decisions therefore extends to four-option questions. It does not require the larger menus in the primary collection.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Obs. 9. Jev’s loss of correct choices is not confined to long candidate menus.
content: The observed loss of initial successes varies across the LLMs, from 3.3% for GPT-6.1-sol to 21.7% for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and 44.9% for GLM-5.3-Flash. These results do not establish a uniform family ranking. Repeated errors also need not select the same distractor. Jev accumulates 95 and 112 distinct wrong question–candidate pairs across its 76 and 89 failed questions. The reproductions accumulate 142–281 such pairs. Excluding the two questions with duplicate distractor text preserves the Jev repetition–reordering gap. Short menus therefore remain informative about the survival of correct choices, although comparisons across benchmarks do not isolate candidate count from content or difficulty.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Our results provide no evidence of a general Jev advantage in preserving correct choices across option orders. Four LLMs retain more shared initial successes (Obs. 3.3 ), but Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, GLM-5.3-Flash, and the task-dependent comparisons rule out a universal ranking. The contribution beyond pairwise order-sensitivity studies ( Lukassen et al., 2026 ) is to trace the cumulative consequences: which initial successes are lost, how widely failures spread, and whether further orders still reveal first failures. The magnitude and timing of that loss carry the evidence; monotonic growth of a cumulative set does not.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The Jev reproductions show that a shared decision interface can coexist with substantially different robustness. On the primary collection, AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 retains more initial successes than the Jev references, whereas the other eleven reproductions retain fewer. Their near-perfect fixed-order agreement does not predict this ordering. Explaining the differences requires isolating the choices in representation, learning, and computation that the shared interface leaves unspecified.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Reordering diagnoses failures that agreement may not repair.
content: A useful diagnostic need not be an effective correction. Reordering exposes lost successes and multiple wrong candidates, but voting yields only a small accuracy gain for Jev. Always-wrong trajectories contain no correct vote, and unanimous errors pass an agreement filter unchanged (Obs. 5.2 ). These persistent errors do not themselves demonstrate order bias; they limit agreement as a safeguard. Nor does observing several wrong candidates establish what would happen after one is removed. An adaptive masking study could compare removing the previously selected wrong candidate with removing a random distractor at matched menu sizes, separating targeted correction from the benefit of fewer choices.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Behavioral differences do not identify their mechanism.
content: Original-order repetition characterizes variation without changing the menu. Its comparison with reordering describes behavioral differences without isolating a causal order effect. Candidate identifiers travel with their content while entry order changes, leaving the source of presentation sensitivity unresolved. Prior work distinguishes identifier preferences from position and context effects ( Azizi et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) ; our experiment neither separates these components nor establishes how a proprietary interface represents them.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Behavioral differences do not identify their mechanism.
content: Training, inference, and interface also differ across models, precluding a causal claim about decision heads or generation. The literature offers starting points for controlled comparisons: frozen LLM readouts keep the backbone fixed ( Li and Wagle, 2026 ) , and serialization interventions keep weights fixed ( Azizi et al., 2026 ) . Further comparisons could vary decision-specific adaptation or candidate interaction separately. The supporting survey organizes these distinctions alongside supervision, gradient paths, and execution. The present findings concern observed selections, not a recovered account of Jev’s proprietary mechanism.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The results cover fixed task collections and eight presentations. Domain, language, difficulty, and candidate count vary together, while subgroup intervals are exploratory and do not adjust for multiple comparisons. MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond broaden the evidence, but differences in loss magnitude show its dependence on the collection. Continued first failures establish persistence within the observed sequence without predicting growth under further requests.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Early work on contextual calibration shows that language models carry answer preferences that can destabilize few-shot predictions as prompts and demonstrations change ( Zhao et al., 2021 ) . Option reordering provides a more direct test when question and answer content are held fixed ( Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024 ) . Position and identifier effects must nevertheless be distinguished. Zheng et al. (2024) identify preferences for option-ID tokens as a major source of multiple-choice selection bias, while FairEval and MT-Bench document response-order effects in pairwise judgments ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) . In their study of many-shot evaluation, Song et al. (2025) likewise find that changing response order or the symbols assigned to responses alters GPT-4o’s pairwise judgments; they combine evaluations across both transformations to mitigate these biases. Shi et al. (2025) further separate repetition stability, position consistency, and preference fairness. Our candidate identifiers move with their content, so the present experiment measures behavior across reordered menus without independently identifying these sources.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Mitigation through calibration, training, and reasoning.
content: Contextual calibration and PriDe estimate answer priors to reduce bias ( Zhao et al., 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) . CalibraEval extends label-free calibration to LLM judges through an order-preserving transformation of prediction distributions ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Training offers another route. Strengthened symbol binding improves the association between an option and its identifier ( Xue et al., 2024 ) , while permutation-aware GRPO rewards consistency across rearrangements of the same instance ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Recent work also combines a probability-based permutation metric with LoRA fine-tuning and efficient aggregation ( Guda et al., 2025 ) . These interventions show that selection bias is responsive to both training and inference procedures. Evidence of reduced position bias in reasoning models on multi-document question answering further motivates comparison with current LLMs ( Li et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate the deployed systems without applying an additional debiasing method to any of them.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Methods for reproducing Jev-style decisions differ in candidate representation, readout, and learning. LLM-as-Jev can even extract candidate probabilities from frozen causal LLMs ( Li and Wagle, 2026 ) , so the decision formulation alone does not identify an architectural or training intervention. Lukassen et al. (2026) compare eight typed decision models with seven LLM judges in pairwise evaluations, finding sensitivity to swapping two responses despite strong repeatability. Azizi et al. (2026) trace option-label effects to serialization in several public Jev-style implementations through interventions with weights fixed. These studies already establish that typed decisions need not be unbiased. We examine the cumulative consequences in multiple-choice tasks with four to 32 candidates. Repeated permutations reveal how widely failures spread, how much initial success survives, and whether voting or agreement can recover reliable decisions. Fixed-order repetition and contemporary LLM baselines place those losses in context.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: MT-Bench cautions that a judge can be consistently wrong ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . GRP evaluates each response pair in both orders and counts it as correct only when both judgments match the gold preference ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Asking for the worse response improves this joint criterion, without isolating gains in order agreement from gains in per-trial correctness. Ok et al. (2026) distinguish answer flipping from positional skew and show that aggregation can reduce flipping partly by stabilizing an incorrect answer. Their decomposition applies under balanced rotations, which our sampled permutations do not enforce. Likewise, the permutation metric of Guda et al. (2025) measures changes in candidate probabilities, whereas our analysis follows returned selections. We distinguish variation under repeated requests from variation under reordered menus, then test whether voting corrects errors and whether agreement identifies correct answers for Jev and the LLM baselines.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: A simple reordering test reveals a limitation of Jev-style System One models: stable accuracy and repeatable choices can conceal the loss of successful decisions. Across eight presentations of the primary collection, the two Jev versions’ failure sets expand by 27–29% while accuracy remains nearly unchanged. These losses are substantially smaller under original-order repetition, a gap also observed in highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Comparisons with LLMs establish no general Jev advantage. MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond show that the vulnerability persists at higher accuracy and with only four candidates. Voting offers limited correction for Jev, while unanimous errors show that agreement alone cannot certify correctness. Evaluating Jev-style structure therefore requires following individual correct choices across equivalent presentations; explaining their survival requires controlled comparisons of the designs behind the shared interface.

content: Candidate representations can depend on the request, rival options, and serialization position. Caching constrains their computation but not how later layers combine them: reusable options can support set-dependent decisions, while request-conditioned options can remain isolated from rivals (Figure 32 ). Order invariance and sensitivity to meaningful set changes are therefore separate properties.

section: Independent scores with reusable candidate representations.
content: CLM independently encodes state–instruction and action inputs, then compares their projected representations. If these inputs and the temperature remain fixed, adding an alternative changes the softmax denominator but not the odds between two existing alternatives. MetaEncoder also uses a shared bi-encoder and contrastive training, but supports multimodal requests and updates the encoder ( Cheng et al., 2026a ) . Its request-to-candidate InfoNCE is unidirectional, unlike CLM’s bidirectional objective. Moreover, its closed-set request template can include the alternatives, which are randomly dropped during training. Candidate features remain request-independent, but the request representation need not be independent of the set. Thus a bi-encoder label alone does not establish invariant pairwise odds.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Jeva independently encodes the request and each option, then refines only the request state against immutable option memory ( Li and Wang, 2026 ) . Candidate representations exclude the current request, their position, and other options, enabling reuse across requests. A compact decision stack nevertheless allows the final request state to depend on the entire option set. Shared scoring and symmetric aggregation are designed to make the resulting probability vector permutation-equivariant, while allowing the relative ranking of existing options to change when the set changes. Jeva further separates competition among options from coverage: for closed-set probabilities q i q_{i} and estimated coverage ρ \rho , the open-set output is p i = ρ ​ q i p_{i}=\rho q_{i} with p ∅ = 1 − ρ p_{\varnothing}=1-\rho . A diffuse q q expresses uncertainty among options; low ρ \rho expresses possible answer absence. Their empirical quality still depends on learning and evaluation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Candidate-independent block-causal attention offers a third design ( Amit, 2026 ) . A causal request prefix is shared; each candidate block attends to that prefix and its own tokens, but not to other candidate blocks. Reset positions and a shared local score head aim to remove serialization-order effects. Candidate states therefore depend on the request and cannot generally be cached across different requests, even though their computation excludes other candidates. This is different from both independent bi-encoding and Jeva’s immutable option memory. The reported residual permutation flips also distinguish a structural design objective from exact numerical behavior. Its frozen contrastive baseline uses a different training setup, so that comparison does not isolate attention structure alone.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Prism-1 uses the same separation of a shared causal prefix and isolated candidate blocks, but scores each candidate with the native language-model head’s yes/no log odds at its final token ( Teng et al., 2026 ) . A softmax across these scores produces the choice distribution; LoRA and candidate cross-entropy adapt the model without a separate learned scalar head. Every candidate starts at the same position offset. For a fixed prefix and deterministic computation, isolation and position reuse make scores independent of candidate serialization order and preserve pairwise odds when unrelated candidates are added. The latter is a restriction as well as an invariance: a task requiring an existing option’s score to change with its rivals needs a different dependency structure.

Arrows show dependencies; dashed outlines mark representations reusable with fixed inputs and weights. Odds statements fix request text, candidate text, and calibration.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 3. The supervision source determines what a fitted decision distribution represents.
content: Labels describe outcomes in the training population, contrastive pairs distinguish matched inputs from chosen negatives, and teacher probabilities reflect the teacher’s information and computation. Similar cross-entropy expressions can therefore fit different quantities.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Jeff adds a residual decision head to the original letter readout and trains that head with backbone LoRA using cross-entropy ( Geuter et al., 2026 ) . The supervision mixes ordinary dataset labels, human uncertainty and ordinal annotations, and teacher-provided soft distributions. It is neither a pure hard-label recipe nor an RL method. Per-type temperature fitting follows training. The calibrated frozen model already provides a strong reference on the authors’ decision benchmark, while their knowledge-oriented comparisons still favor Jev. These results motivate a strong baseline; they do not establish equivalence across workloads.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The adapted LLM-as-Jev variant instead preserves the architecture and candidate suffix representation ( Li and Wagle, 2026 ) . Its training loss uses a locally normalized candidate-prefix tree plus KL anchors that preserve the frozen model’s behavior on legal/illegal token mass and outside decision positions. That locally normalized training distribution should not be confused with the globally normalized suffix likelihood in Equation ( 8 ). The recipe uses public human-annotated training data rather than teacher-synthesized labels and studies both full adaptation and LoRA.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Kev illustrates supervised adaptation with a different readout. Its pointer head projects the decision position and each option boundary into a shared space and normalizes scaled dot products over options. The released recipe uses cross-entropy; smaller models use LoRA, while the documented 27B model uses full-parameter adaptation. 8 8 8 Official implementation and recipe: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev . Optional permutation and ordinal losses exist in the code but are not part of the documented released-model recipe.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Intern-Decision instead retains the native vocabulary head and fits hard-label, full-vocabulary cross-entropy only at shifted decision positions ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) . Its input contains the complete ordered schema and an assistant JSON skeleton with <decision> placeholders. The logits immediately before each placeholder predict that field; earlier placeholders remain visible without feeding back gold or predicted answers. Inference restricts these logits to legal options and applies temperature scaling. The language parameters are adapted while the vision encoder and projector remain frozen. Training over the full vocabulary and restricting the inference readout are distinct operations, and the shared causal pass does not imply independence or order invariance across fields.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: MJev-Spatial reuses pretrained query/key projections from the final full-attention layer to match a decision state to option-end states, rather than adding a prediction head ( Qin et al., 2026 ) . Mean scaled inner products across query heads become logits for one candidate softmax. The retained language parameters are trained with cross-entropy while the vision encoder and merger are frozen. Because option states come from a causal sequence, later options can see earlier ones; shuffling options during training does not establish structural permutation equivariance.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Qwen-Audio-Jev uses a different design: a shared audio–language prefix state feeds three affine heads for 64 Choice indices, one binary Noul logit, and ten ordinal Score indices ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . Candidate meanings are specified in the input, and each categorical head is normalized over the valid indices. Supervised training updates the audio encoder, adaptor, backbone, and heads using the observed primitive’s loss: Choice cross-entropy, binary cross-entropy, or ordinal cross-entropy with cumulative-distribution and expected-index penalties.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Contrastive Language Models (CLM) use a frozen Qwen3-8B encoder with learned state and action projection heads. 9 9 9 Original technical blog: https://contrastive-lm.notion.site ; official implementation and reference-model recipe: https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM . Matched state–action pairs supervise bidirectional InfoNCE: the state retrieves its matched action and the action retrieves its matched state among batch alternatives. At inference, state plus instructions and each candidate are encoded independently, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives the candidate distribution. Independent candidate representations can be cached, although different question instructions change the state encoding. This is learned contrastive alignment rather than teacher-probability distillation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: SII-Decision trains a direct readout against a same-size backbone’s reasoning-conditioned predictions ( Duan et al., 2026 ) . For each question, two reasoning chains yield two candidate distributions; their mean becomes the cached student target. 10 10 10 JEVal Section 6.2 specifies a nonthinking-readout fallback for invalid chains, while Appendix F.4 describes excluding truncated, invalid, or top-option-disagreeing chains from added-source training data. Cross-entropy to this target is combined with a KL constraint to the original nonthinking prediction, and ordinal tasks also use an expected-level penalty. The student updates language layers while retaining the original label head, and inference uses a single prefill with no generated rationale. This is offline reasoning-to-readout self-distillation, not student on-policy rollout distillation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Where SII retains reasoning-endpoint probabilities, LDM constructs soft targets from sampled answers ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . In the primary experiments, its SPRD variant draws four reasoning answers from a frozen Qwen3.8-27B teacher for all student sizes and forms a vote histogram normalized by the number of parseable answers. SPRD already requires the top vote share over all four samples to reach 0.75 0.75 ; SPRD-C additionally requires the majority to agree with the label intended during data construction. This checks consistency, not independent correctness. The LDM objective uses supervised NLL on one record type and weighted teacher-to-student KL on another, rather than applying both losses to every example.

content: Teacher computation can also differ in depth rather than in the use of reasoning traces. FunDM freezes the backbone and trains a decision head on an intermediate hidden layer to match the full-depth model’s distribution using KL ( p teacher ∥ p student ) \mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{teacher}}\|p_{\mathrm{student}}) ( Panchal, 2026 ) . Inference can stop before the remaining layers, although the new head still requires training.

section: Black-box imitation of the deployed service.
content: AutoTrust-JEV-27B uses output distributions obtained from TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as its main supervision stream. 11 11 11 Author model card and recipe: https://huggingface.co/autotrust/JEV-27B . Its training corpus also contains programmatic labels and downweighted uniform-placeholder targets. The documented recipe fits LoRA adapters and a decision head using target-to-student KL, with an ordinal ranked probability score (RPS) term. The service-target component is behavioral imitation of a black-box model. Agreement with that teacher is a different outcome from correctness against independent labels, and it does not identify the teacher’s internal training algorithm. External-teacher models such as Eikos and Torchcast provide further distribution-fitting variants, catalogued in Appendix I .

content: Some models are trained to support a particular workflow. LAVOIR adds slot representations and a value-of-information head to Laya, trained with decision cross-entropy and value regression ( Yilmaz et al., 2026 ) . The final recipe sets the inherited RL weight to zero. The model learns both a decision distribution and estimates used by the ask/decide/handoff policy in Appendix E.2.1 .

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: AgentDecision-4B, introduced in JevAgentHarness, trains the decision component on agent states ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) . Its Qwen3-4B LoRA recipe includes post-error states from mistake replay. When Jev’s top option matches the gold label, the supervised target mixes 0.3 0.3 gold one-hot mass with 0.7 0.7 teacher probabilities; otherwise it uses the gold label alone. Cross-entropy plus a Brier term precedes closed-loop GRPO with a fixed LLM, task-success and cost/error rewards, and a KL anchor to the supervised model. Here environment feedback updates the decision model itself. Appendix E.3 examines the different role of a fixed Jev service guiding another learner.

section: Takeaway 4. The probability objective and the random variable receiving credit are separate choices.
content: A proper probability score defines an objective for truthful reporting; a gradient estimator determines how its training signal reaches the parameters. For a distribution p p and outcome y y , log score log ⁡ p y \log p_{y} and negative Brier score − ∑ k ( p k − 𝟏 [ k = y ] ) 2 -\sum_{k}(p_{k}-\mathbf{1}[k=y])^{2} reward truthful probability reports in expectation. A differentiable readout can optimize either score directly. By contrast, rewarding only a sampled answer’s correctness maximizes ∑ k p k ​ q k \sum_{k}p_{k}q_{k} under outcome distribution q q , generally favoring a mode of q q rather than reporting q q . Thus the word “RL” identifies neither the statistical property being optimized nor an advantage over direct proper-score fitting.

authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 4. The probability objective and the random variable receiving credit are separate choices.
content: Figure 34 contrasts direct differentiation, output-space perturbations, and rationale-policy credit. OpenJev-RLCD, the rationale-policy method depicted here, retains generated reasoning at inference; this is a property of that method rather than a requirement of every rationale-based training procedure.

Here b b is a baseline, q q a fixed target, and sg \operatorname{sg} stop-gradient. title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Laya and Chinese-Jev perturb output logits and apply policy-gradient updates in that space; Chinese-Jev combines soft cross-entropy with Gaussian perturbations around detached logits and a group-baseline estimator ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . This does not require a generated chain of thought. The decider-derived this-that-model combines CE and Brier terms with a sampled-outcome Brier reward and a control-variate estimator ( Cheng et al., 2026b ) . Another output-policy variant, decider-2B v10, uses PPO over environment actions with terminal returns and an auxiliary proper-log-score belief objective; the documented 4B and 35B releases do not use that RL stage. 12 12 12 Version-specific recipe: https://github.com/Mapika/decider/blob/main/docs/RL.md . These methods apply stochastic policy updates in output space rather than over generated reasoning. Their estimators, stop-gradient choices, and rewards determine what those updates contribute beyond direct fitting.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Qwen-Audio-Jev makes this distinction explicit with an importance-weighted, pairwise sampled-action estimator for negative Brier score and ordinal RPS ( Fang et al., 2026 ) . Its exploration mixture, leave-one-out baseline, and detached weights yield the direct proper-score gradient in expectation under the stated construction. Thus the estimator need not define a different probability target from direct fitting. This equivalence does not establish an empirical advantage in variance, efficiency, or calibration.

content: OpenJev-RLCD first calibrates an answer distribution conditioned on sampled rationales, then adds REINFORCE credit to the rationale policy using the same proper score ( Gao and Wang, 2026 ) . If

Stage one uses the former; stage two adds the latter, with a baseline and KL regularization. Its main experiments score each rationale’s distribution separately and retain explicit rationales at inference. title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: StartLux combines instant decision learning with an AutoThink variant that allocates reasoning conditionally ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ) . Its instant model makes full-attention layers bidirectional while retaining causal linear-attention layers. RLCD 2 uses a frozen reference model’s before/after probability signal to train a reasoning-token policy. Within groups containing only nonempty traces, the initial-score term cancels under reward centering; empty traces receive zero reward, so this cancellation does not extend to arbitrary mixed groups. PostHog’s Jeeves is another reasoning-policy implementation: its repository combines supervised learning, CISPO-style updates, a pointer head, and a diffusion drafter. Its documented reward uses correct-answer probability with a length penalty, which should not automatically be called a proper scoring rule.

Both affect cost, while routing and output transformations can also change the returned prediction.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 5. The absence of a returned rationale does not imply a fixed computation budget.
content: A direct student may omit its teacher’s reasoning, an intermediate head may omit later layers, and a recurrent model may perform additional hidden steps without generating text. Conditional reasoning introduces another possibility, mixing direct and deliberative requests behind one interface. These choices change different resources, so generated-token count alone cannot compare their computational demands.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Conditional reasoning changes both the path and the prediction.
content: LDM routes low-margin items to the student’s untuned base for one reasoning rollout and adopts its answer; the direct branch keeps the readout’s answer (Figure 35 c; Chen et al., 2026b ). Its threshold is the validation margins’ 30th percentile, which does not fix the routed fraction on unseen data. StartLux AutoThink instead uses the same model weights for the initial causal readout, reasoning, and endpoint readout (Figure 35 d; Zhuang et al., 2026 ). With a maximum initial probability below 0.9 0.9 , it generates up to 4,096 reasoning tokens and returns 0.25 ​ p 0 + 0.75 ​ p 1 0.25p_{0}+0.75p_{1} ; otherwise it returns p 0 p_{0} . These routes differ in the model called, the trigger, and the returned prediction.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Latent loops allocate extra computation without generating a textual rationale. SanSi repeatedly applies a recurrent backbone and reads a decision distribution after each loop ( Gan et al., 2026 ) . The base weights are frozen, while shared LoRA adapters and loop-specific readout corrections are learned. Cross-entropy and Brier losses supervise the loop outputs, with gradients passing through preceding loops. The paper trains with eight loops and evaluates different loop counts. Latent computation thus varies separately from parameter count and generated-token count, and additional loops need not improve every task.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Selective Reasoning instead exposes three control decisions: when to start generation, when to read a partial rationale, and when to accept the current answer ( Zheng and Chen, 2026 ) . A reader is trained on empty and partial reasoning prefixes using a frozen backbone. The start gate estimates correction benefit relative to regression risk, the read scheduler limits costly reader calls, and the accept rule uses the reader’s distribution. An accepted prefix answer cancels generation only if generation is still active. If no prefix answer is accepted, a terminal read returns an answer without a certainty requirement. Thus the entropy threshold governs early acceptance rather than guaranteeing the confidence of every returned answer. The threshold itself measures distribution concentration, not an independently measured probability of correctness.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: FastJEV changes the execution of an existing decision model without weight training ( Ma et al., 2026a ) . It reuses shared context and recurrent states, forks candidate-prefix caches, and selects a candidate-path layer-skipping mask using relative-score perturbations on unlabeled calibration inputs. These mechanisms preserve the context and candidate inventory while changing the work performed on candidate paths. Prefix reuse can reduce computation yet increase latency through execution overhead. Its results therefore support a serving analysis under specified workloads, rather than a universal latency improvement. The OmniJev model evaluated in that paper should not be conflated with the separately named OneJev repository.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Comparing these paths requires accounting for backbone depth, reader calls, generation, caching, and scheduling. Returned-answer length alone does not measure their cost.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: A single-pass primitive can form a sequential predictor.
content: MJev-Spatial illustrates a further distinction between the primitive and the completed prediction ( Qin et al., 2026 ) . A categorical answer uses one decision, while spatial point prediction uses three successive nine-way cell choices. The first two choices determine new crops from the original image, which are re-encoded for the next stage. Training packs teacher-forced stages into one backbone pass, but inference must follow the predicted crops sequentially. The spatial quantization bound assumes the correct cell choices; it is not a bound on model prediction error. Single-pass training, single-pass primitive scoring, and single-pass task inference are therefore separate claims.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 6. Serving choices can change prediction semantics as well as execution cost.
content: The model head is only one stage of a deployed prediction. Postprocessing can move its probability mass, scalar reduction can retain different information, and question batching can change how computation is shared. Behavior observed through a service can therefore reflect transformations applied after training as well as the learned distribution.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The same typed interface can expose different question-processing graphs. Kev’s documented hybrid-backbone implementation processes separate causal question rows and can reuse a state cache in serving (Figure 35 a). Cloudflare Clef instead uses a joint schema head and describes one forward pass for all questions (Figure 35 b). Jeff’s released server evaluates questions serially, while official Jev describes shared-state parallel question processing. These differences determine how computation is shared even when each question returns the same output type.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Documented readouts do not always identify a training recipe. Perplexity’s decider v1.1 describes a separate 255-row readout and saved temperature calibration, but the public model cards for decider and Clef do not specify their training objectives (Appendix I ). JevK5 further describes a one-pass readout only up to its candidate limit and a multi-pass tournament beyond it. Candidate limits and question organization are therefore necessary conditions for interpreting an execution claim.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Jeff illustrates how postprocessing can change the apparent decisiveness of a model. Its default binary “commitment” transformation moves intermediate probabilities beyond the benchmark’s abstention interval. The returned distribution therefore differs from the temperature-calibrated distribution before this transformation, and an evaluation of calibration must specify which one it measures. Reduced abstention under this rule cannot be attributed to the cross-entropy training objective alone.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Appendix E Decision Models in Downstream Workflows
content: The consequence of a decision depends on where it intervenes in a task. We distinguish control of an ongoing trajectory, selection among completed outcomes, acquisition of evidence, and assistance to another learner. These roles carry different error and recovery costs, even when they use the same decision model.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 7. Action control and completed-run selection affect different parts of a trajectory.
content: Online selection changes which state the agent reaches next. Completed-run selection instead chooses among trajectories whose generation cost has already been incurred. Both can use a fast scorer, but only the former changes the actions within an individual run. This distinction determines which generator, candidate budget, and executor must remain fixed to attribute a downstream gain to the decision component.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Jev Ultrafast constructs a dynamic action space from the observed browser state. 13 13 13 Primary implementation: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast , especially “The action space” and “Evidence and limits.” Each observation supplies an indexed table of elements. A single Jev request asks for both an operation and speculative targets for the supported operation types. The executor uses only the target corresponding to the selected operation (Figure 36 a). A small LLM supplies text when the operation requires typing. Ordinary code checks target compatibility and page freshness, executes the action, and obtains the next observation.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: The division of labor depends on enumerating actionable choices from the environment. The decision model selects within that interface, while generation remains available for open-ended content. Selection of a DONE action still needs an independent outcome check. The repository reports a small set of demonstrations and repeated runs on one browser task; these establish an implemented loop, not general reliability or an isolated effect of the decision model.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: JevCoder exposes a related boundary in code repair ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Its components recommend code snippets, guide action types, and judge whether to submit or continue. When Jev selects an action type, an LLM still generates the specific command. A judge that blocks a command does not thereby supply a better one, and some blocking interventions hurt performance. The full-workflow experiments are separate from component studies on selected success/failure panels; they should not be pooled as a single task-success estimate. Each full-workflow task receives one run per condition, which limits what can be inferred about repeated-run variability.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Decision gates within a larger controller.
content: A decision gate can replace a local choice, advise a generator, reject an action, trigger extra work, or escalate uncertain cases. JevAgentHarness implements these roles at tool selection, bounded arguments, memory operations, reflection, stopping, and model routing ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) . Its deployment cascade compares the maximum option probability with thresholds fitted for each decision point using held-out shadow trajectories and intervention costs. Free-form arguments still require an LLM. The gate’s confidence and the harness’s policy jointly determine behavior; a threshold alone does not establish safe execution. The same work also trains a decision model and evaluates controllers, which are distinct contributions (Appendices C.3 and F ).

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Decision gates within a larger controller.
content: Jev-LiteMAS specializes this division of labor to a predefined pool of generative experts ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Jev selects the next expert or, when eligible, STOP, and screens artifacts for acceptance or escalation. On escalation, an LLM reviewer supplies a verdict and textual feedback; an expert revises the artifact, which is then screened again. The decision model does not generate repair instructions, and local artifact acceptance is distinct from stopping the entire workflow. Savings therefore depend on the escalation frequency and on whether the resulting artifacts still satisfy the task.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Decision gates within a larger controller.
content: Jarvis applies typed control to an asynchronous task ledger ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . Runtime code constructs eligible operations tied to task identifiers and versions; the decision model selects among them from the transcript, history, and ledger. Low-confidence cases delegate to a worker without speculative ledger mutation. Code enforces one live version, rejects stale results, revalidates plans, and requires a playback receipt before marking speech as delivered. These invariants belong to the executor, not to the model’s probability estimates. The paper also trains a separate audio LISTEN/DIRECT/DELEGATE gate; that learned gate and the downstream ledger policy should not be treated as one training mechanism.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Decision gates within a larger controller.
content: A penetration-testing harness study illustrates how several decision roles can coexist in one domain ( Barbosa, 2026 ) . Typed decisions support finding adjudication, severity assessment, agent pruning, and bounded confirmation, while the harness retains evidence gates and execution. Its exploratory comparison uses one run per condition on one target, and subsequent retests change the harness. The study demonstrates this division of labor, but the separate effects of the decision model and harness remain unresolved. Establishing a benefit would require comparing the same task decomposition and execution policy with alternative decision components.

content: CLM’s released coding verifier averages state--action cosine scores over the last twelve trajectory steps by default. 14 14 14 Official selector implementation: https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM/blob/main/evaluation/bon_eval.py . The coding evaluation uses domain adaptation; it is distinct from the general typed-question interface. This aggregation is a use of the contrastive scorer, not the softmax over a caller’s candidate menu described in Appendix C.3 . FunDM uses a separately trained coding-agent head to judge a whole run ( Panchal, 2026 ) . Its MCQ head and coding head are distinct, and the repository distinguishes the whole-run judge from an action-trained FunDM-CE variant. 15 15 15 FunDM implementation and reproduction notes: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM . Figure 36 b therefore shows a shared selection operation with different scoring mechanisms. It does not imply shared heads, training data, or directly comparable reported performance.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 8. Clarification and memory control alter the information available to subsequent decisions.
content: The preceding workflows use the available evidence to choose behavior or an outcome. Clarification obtains an external answer, while memory control changes how past evidence is organized and retrieved. These operations can improve a later decision without changing the decision model’s parameters. Their benefits and costs therefore depend on the information acquired, as well as the quality of the local probability report.

content: Clarification changes the source of information available to the model. LDM and StartLux conditional thinking process the existing input through an internal rationale, whereas LAVOIR obtains an external answer. It also goes beyond deferring low-confidence cases by ranking particular missing fields by predicted benefit. The evidence is strongest for synthetic multi-turn dialogues, with limited real single-exchange tests and one training seed. Comparisons against slower value-of-information computation and an LLM agent remain incomplete, leaving open whether the learned acquisition policy offers a better quality–cost trade-off across interaction settings.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: E.2.2 Controlling Memory Construction and Retrieval
content: Jev-Mem places a decision controller between stored observations and an LLM answerer ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Its contribution is the organization of memory operations around fast typed decisions, rather than a new recipe for training the controller. Shared canonical memory nodes participate in semantic, temporal, causal, and entity relation views. Figure 37 separates writing this memory from retrieving evidence, because the decision objects and feedback loops differ.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Writing preserves observations and judges relations.
content: Incoming observations retain their original text and provenance. The controller annotates overlapping memory characteristics, while deterministic vector, lexical, entity, and time search produces a bounded set of candidate neighbors. The controller then judges inferred relations; thresholds determine which edges are added. Reliable timestamp ordering and exact identifiers can be handled directly by code. Thus the normal write path does not ask the model to irreversibly discard observations before their future relevance is known. Maintenance may mark redundancy, contradiction, or obsolescence while retaining original evidence, and textual abstraction can be escalated to an LLM.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Retrieval adapts both where to search and when to stop.
content: Given a query, the controller predicts relevant relation views, multi-hop needs, and recency, which guide budget allocation. Hybrid vector and lexical retrieval supplies anchors. During retrieval, the controller assesses whether accumulated evidence is sufficient and whether further expansion is likely to help. If needed and within budget, bounded graph expansion proposes candidates, which are scored and added to the evidence set. The loop stops on sufficient evidence, low expected additional benefit, or a resource limit. Selected memories then go to the LLM for answer synthesis. The controller affects evidence acquisition; it does not replace the final generative answerer.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Retrieval adapts both where to search and when to stop.
content: The reported evaluation uses LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini as the answer model and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring. These results concern Jev-based control on LoCoMo and do not evaluate the Laya controller or LongMemEval configuration provided by the implementation. 16 16 16 Jev-Mem implementation: https://github.com/libingzheren/Jev-Mem . Separating write and read control is particularly useful for attribution: changing stored relations can affect later answers even if the query-time controller is held fixed.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Evidence expansion without a preconstructed graph.
content: SAG2 instead starts from a local SQLite FTS5/BM25 index, without corpus-time embeddings or a neighbor graph ( Wu, 2026 ) . Jev makes a binary Noul judgment about each passage’s necessary contribution to a supported answer chain, conditioned on the retrieved evidence. This is not a single global Choice over passages. Ordinary code extracts lexical expansion terms from scored seed passages; retrieval and evidence-conditioned rescoring can repeat within a bounded budget. Local diversification then produces the final evidence set. The experiments evaluate retrieval rather than generated answers, and development includes MuSiQue and a synthetic enterprise corpus. The local index does not make the complete system local, because the evidence scorer uses the hosted Jev service. Relative to Jev-Mem, the intervention moves from constructing and traversing stored relations to building query-time evidence chains through lexical expansion.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 9. A decision model can guide another learner without itself being trained.
content: A fixed decision service can also change an agent’s exploration, rewards, or updates during learning. Any resulting benefit may persist in the trained agent after the service is removed. This differs from fitting a replacement decision model to service outputs, as in Appendix C.3 , where training changes the model that will answer future decision requests. The relevant distinction is which model learns from the service and what it learns to do.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 9. A decision model can guide another learner without itself being trained.
content: Ma et al. (2026b) use Jev as an action-policy reference, an exploration source, an auxiliary reward assessor, and a replay-priority signal. These interventions change an agent’s data or updates, so their success is measured in the learned agent. AutoTrust instead fits a replacement decision model to Jev’s probability outputs, making reproduction of the teacher’s predictions a training target.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 9. A decision model can guide another learner without itself being trained.
content: The interventions have different semantics. Policy assistance supplies actions that can be imitated or compared with the learner’s actions by a critic. Exploration assistance replaces some random actions with Jev suggestions. Reward assistance maps rubric judgments to bonuses or gates. Replay assistance reweights stored experience using Jev judgments. The reported replay variant omits importance correction and therefore intentionally changes the effective training weighting. None of these roles makes an ordinal judgment a validated cardinal Q-value merely by converting its label to a number.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 9. A decision model can guide another learner without itself being trained.
content: Information access also matters: Jev can receive structured descriptions beyond the learner’s own observation, and the trained learner can later be deployed without Jev or its auxiliary rewards. The paper’s MiniGrid and Atari experiments provide evidence for particular learning interventions, with three seeds; replay assistance does not uniformly help. The resulting gains or losses concern how the service changes learning. They cannot be attributed to the quality of its decision probabilities without separating added information, changed exploration, and changed objectives.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Joint learning changes the decision model as well as the agent.
content: Dyad spans both levels in a different way ( Zhan et al., 2026 ) . Its language model retains token generation and switches to a typed action distribution at designated interaction positions. The model aligns state and action representations through projector training, then applies environment-reward policy optimization over token and action decisions. Its action encoder may be updated alone or jointly with the state encoder. Action features are reusable only while their environment context and descriptions remain unchanged. Thus the learned architecture belongs to model construction, while the interleaving of language and environment actions defines the downstream workflow; it is not simply a frozen service plugged into another learner.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Appendix F From Local Probabilities to Workflow Reliability
content: A candidate distribution, the action selected from it, and the outcome of a complete task require different evaluations. Accurate probabilities can yield a poor action under an unsuitable decision rule; a correct local action can still fail to secure task success. Our experiment measures selections, leaving calibration and downstream utility unresolved. The studies below identify the evidence needed to connect these levels.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 10. Calibration, distribution fidelity, and decision utility are distinct.
content: Ordinary calibration compares reported probabilities with outcome frequencies among cases receiving the same predicted probabilities. Subgroup calibration additionally requires this agreement within specified groups. Distribution fidelity instead asks whether the complete prediction matches the conditional target for each input. Neither calibration nor fidelity alone specifies the action taken or the cost of an error. A decision rule converts probabilities into behavior, so a utility improvement can arise from a better distribution, a better rule, or both. Comparisons must separate these changes before attributing a gain to learning.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Known distributions separate probability estimation from sampled correctness.
content: ProbabilityBench supplies simulated problems with a known conditional distribution p ∗ p^{*} given the visible input ( Dai et al., 2026 ) . This permits direct comparison with p ∗ p^{*} , rather than treating one sampled answer as the complete probability target. Accuracy evaluated in expectation under these conditional targets is bounded by the Bayes accuracy for the same visible information. Accuracy against sampled test labels can exceed that reference through label-sampling noise. For a predicted distribution q q , the input-averaged KL ( p ∗ ∥ q ) \mathrm{KL}(p^{*}\|q) equals excess expected log loss relative to p ∗ p^{*} . A constant class prior satisfies ordinary calibration while ignoring input-specific information, and need not be calibrated within subgroups. Finite-bin estimates can also hide canceling errors or reflect sampling noise. Exact uncertainty in a synthetic generator is therefore valuable evidence about probability estimation, but does not establish access to the true uncertainty of an arbitrary real task.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Additional computation can sharpen probabilities without improving calibration.
content: SanSi provides a concrete example of why compute allocation and probability quality must be evaluated together ( Gan et al., 2026 ) . Its later loops continue to increase confidence even after most answers have stabilized. On the 9,645 answerable test items, the 1.4B model’s expected calibration error rises from 0.082 ± 0.010 0.082\pm 0.010 at loop three to 0.093 ± 0.012 0.093\pm 0.012 at loop eight. These are means and standard deviations over three training seeds, using ten equal-width confidence bins. The comparison concerns different readout depths within each trained model. It shows that additional latent computation can worsen calibration even within the trained loop range, so a stopping rule needs evidence for the probability or decision objective it serves.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Utility also depends on the decision rule.
content: TypedBench complements this view with policy-generated cases, controlled framing changes, and cost-sensitive evaluation ( Sharma et al., 2026 ) . Its calibration and stress-test protocols distinguish benign framing sensitivity from adversarial perturbation. A change from argmax to the Bayes action under a cost matrix changes the decision rule; the resulting utility improvement cannot all be credited to better calibration. Synthetic labels make some controls possible while limiting direct conclusions about unconstrained natural tasks.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Benchmark scores depend on their evaluation protocol.
content: Published scores differ in both what they measure and how evaluation informs model development. JEVal supplies a benchmark as well as the SII model discussed in Appendix C.3 , but the SII release’s separate evaluation suite does not reproduce that benchmark protocol ( Duan et al., 2026 ) . Inner Jev’s Capability metric differs from ordinary accuracy, and its OpenDecisions results inform recipe selection ( Geuter et al., 2026 ) . LLM-as-Jev likewise uses public JevBench errors to guide data-mixture development ( Li and Wagle, 2026 ) . Metric definitions and evaluation feedback must therefore be accounted for before these scores can support a common ranking.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Benchmark scores depend on their evaluation protocol.
content: Data overlap and execution conditions further limit comparisons. FunDM’s reproduction notes disclose overlap between a CLM post-training collection and its test collection. Local-model and hosted-API latency also reflect different hardware and network conditions. Generalization and efficiency claims therefore require controls beyond matching the reported metric.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 11. Reliable isolated decisions need not remain reliable under composition.
content: An isolated prediction tests one input and output interface. Composing predictions introduces dependencies; changing a request can alter evidence, eligible actions, or numerical computation. Interpreting sensitivity first requires specifying what should remain invariant. Our permutations preserve question content and candidate identities, whereas adding a candidate or revealing evidence can change the decision problem.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Takeaway 11. Reliable isolated decisions need not remain reliable under composition.
content: Coherence studies test probability relationships across related questions ( Joy, 2026 ) , while option-set studies test how predictions respond to changed alternatives ( Rajput et al., 2026 ) . Neither relationship follows from calibration on isolated questions.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: Request context, candidate eligibility, and numerical precision.
content: Chen (2026) distinguishes changes to the questions bundled into a request, the evidence provided, and the eligible candidates. A model whose question compiler produces exactly the same input can be invariant for that reason, whereas a full-schema prompt exposes other questions to the decision computation. The Nimble intervention removes other questions from the prompt and eliminates the observed flips, but is not length-matched. Small Laya shifts largely disappear at higher precision or after rounding. The observed sensitivity can therefore reflect prompt construction or numerical precision as well as architectural dependencies. Conditional odds between retained alternatives separate genuine relative-score movement from the inevitable change in a softmax denominator. When a readout restricts the vocabulary, its allowed-label mass provides additional information lost by normalization.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: From correct choices to correct sequences.
content: Choice2Seq compares native candidate choice with independent-position and serial-prefix output interfaces on paired problems ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . Its serial correctness retention is P ⁡ ( serial correct ∣ native correct ) P(\text{serial correct}\mid\text{native correct}) , not agreement with the native answer or fidelity to a plan. Cases improved by the serial interface and the marginal accuracies are needed alongside this conditional statistic. Gold-copy and self-plan controls address different fidelity questions. Candidate restrictions can also change the available search space and number of calls, so a composition claim requires the relevant interface and information controls.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
content: Robustness studies connect input sensitivity to the consequences of a valid but incorrect choice. DecisionRobust tests label-preserving perturbations and targeted prompt injection on initially correct decisions across text and vision ( Lan et al., 2026 ) . The distinction between observation text and task instructions matters because changing task facts would change the decision problem itself. JevProbe traces the structured response through application logic and tests whether reachable lower-trust context can redirect a program decision while leaving task facts and code fixed ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . Together, these studies show why schema validity is insufficient for reliable execution. They identify failures of input handling and decision use, with modeled program consequences rather than measured real-world losses.

title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
section: The released response can reveal more than the intended decision.
content: TUPLE-Bench studies whether a response about an authorized coarse category reveals a protected finer mechanism in the model’s private evidence ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Choice-only, confidence, full-probability, and native-response releases are derived from the same saved response, separating release policy from model reruns. Its informed decoder receives the gold coarse category and two known fine-grained hypotheses; this is a passive closed-set audit, not an estimate of unrestricted real-world leakage. A separate legitimate consumer sees neither private evidence nor those hidden labels. The proposed workflow-conditioned probability quantization selects codewords that preserve a frozen consumer’s actions, including clarification, with a native-response fallback when no match exists. It can preserve wrong actions as well as correct ones, so action preservation establishes neither improved task quality nor a confidentiality guarantee. The contribution concerns evaluation and release postprocessing, not a new decision-model training objective.
