section: Takeaway 12. Task-level gains depend on the surrounding policy and its total resource use.
content: Ling et al. (2026b) separate changes to the action interface from changes to the decision model in ALFWorld. They compare the original baseline, an LLM using a Choice interface, and Jev using that interface. The first contrast examines the candidate-selection interface; the second compares decision components within it. Their AndroidWorld experiments compare baseline and Jev integrations without this three-way control. Across these workflows, local decision savings do not uniformly translate into better task outcomes. Action granularity also differs in one integration: FastAgent-J takes one tool action per step while its baseline can take multiple actions. The study thus provides evidence about particular integrations while illustrating the controls needed to interpret them.

Its closed-loop tool-selection comparison lets the LLM supply tool arguments and uses unthresholded replacement. That protocol differs from the confidence cascade proposed for deployment, so its outcomes cannot be attributed directly to that cascade. Scripted acceptable actions in DecisionGym and disjoint rollout seeds also do not, by themselves, establish generalization to unseen task distributions.

content: System1-Arena broadens the comparison across static decisions and closed-loop environments under task-specific shared harnesses ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Candidate construction converts otherwise open-ended search, patches, or arguments into finite alternatives; the reported results are conditional on this interface. The static comparison uses 85,305 questions across 94 tasks, a subset of the released collection, and excludes its game and embodied questions. Reported static scores weight tasks equally, with source averaging within a task. Closed-loop scores weight environments equally. For real-time simulations, the environment advances using each model’s measured median latency while retaining the prior action, rather than measuring each call’s realized delay inside the simulation. Probability extraction also differs across native decision models, verbalized-probability APIs, and local label-logit models. These protocol choices enable useful controlled comparisons while limiting a universal ranking across interfaces, hardware, and workloads.

section: Which improvements survive equivalent presentations and related decisions?
content: Takeaways F.1 and F.2 distinguish local probability quality from consistency across requests. The main study finds substantially more Jev variation under reordering than under fixed-order repetition, without identifying the mechanism behind this difference. Independent studies examine disagreement between direct and hierarchical predictions ( Joy, 2026 ) , option-set dependence ( Rajput et al., 2026 ) , serial correctness retention ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , and the limited transfer of local savings to successful agent outcomes ( Ling et al., 2026b ) . Together, they motivate testing whether a local probability improvement persists under transformations that preserve the intended decision problem and predicts utility in a fixed workflow. The intended invariance must be specified first. Independence of irrelevant alternatives is not universally appropriate, since an added option may provide meaningful context or change the task. Prompt serialization and precision require controls ( Chen, 2026 ) , while cacheability must be separated from set-dependent refinement ( Li and Wang, 2026 ) .

section: When does the gradient estimator matter beyond the target and objective?
content: Takeaway C.4 separates statistical supervision from the variable receiving gradient credit. Replacing observed labels with teacher distributions changes the target; adding output noise can replace an unperturbed score with its expectation under perturbation. An estimator comparison therefore requires a fixed objective and perturbation distribution, with pathwise differentiation and score-function credit compared where both apply. Matching the backbone, prompt, candidates, examples, adaptation budget, and validation split would isolate this question, with frozen and temperature-calibrated readouts as starting controls. Whether a gain survives common calibration and probability postprocessing would help establish its source. A negative result would delimit the value of a specified stochastic update without resolving how proprietary Jev is trained.

section: Which aspects of reasoning transfer into a direct readout?
content: Takeaways C.3 and D.1 distinguish the information supplied during learning from the computation available at inference. JEVal reports that reasoning-to-readout transfer differs between evidence-weighing and computation-heavy tasks ( Duan et al., 2026 ) ; earlier System 2 distillation also documents task-dependent transfer ( Yu et al., 2024 ) . Conversely, theoretical work shows that some computations can be internalized under particular architectures and curricula ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . The unresolved empirical question concerns the interaction of training support, novel rule composition, and dependency depth. Correct-label supervision, additional data, intermediate-state hints, and explicit-reasoning controls would help distinguish imperfect targets and learning limitations from residual computational demands. Failure on a task family alone does not prove an impossibility of single-pass reasoning.

section: When does a better decision model improve the complete workflow?
content: Takeaways E.1 – E.3 identify where a model intervenes; Takeaway F.3 shows why that intervention matters for evaluation. A comparison within a fixed workflow can replace only the decision component while holding candidate construction, retrieval, budgets, fallback rules, and answer generation constant. A complementary comparison retains the same model while changing its role or control policy. Jev-Mem motivates separating write control from read control; run selection requires matching candidate-run generation; LAVOIR requires accounting for newly acquired information and the cost of questions. Crossing model and workflow choices can reveal whether local probability improvements transfer to task outcomes and how that transfer depends on the surrounding policy. Existing evidence does not establish that either model quality or workflow design universally dominates.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
section: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
content: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark , a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12 × \times and 5.12 × \times speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark .

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across natural language understanding ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2023 ) , and reasoning ( Kojima et al., 2022 ; Jaech et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , yet efficient inference remains a fundamental challenge. Most LLMs adopt an autoregressive (AR) paradigm, producing each token conditioned on all previous tokens. This strict left-to-right dependency limits decoding parallelism: generating L L tokens typically requires L L sequential steps. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) offer an appealing alternative by generating sequences through iterative denoising. From a partially or fully masked sequence, a dLLM predicts multiple masked positions in parallel and progressively commits them over a series of denoising rounds. Recent models such as LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) demonstrate that this paradigm can attain strong language modeling, reasoning, and coding capabilities while enabling flexible generation orders and much greater potential for parallel decoding ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . However, realizing this potential requires reducing the many iterative model evaluations needed to turn a masked sequence into a complete response.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: A central factor governing dLLM inference efficiency is the unmasking schedule : which token positions should be committed at each decoding round and which should remain masked for subsequent refinement. Given the predictive distributions over all masked positions, a decoder may reveal one token, a fixed number of tokens, or a dynamically selected subset in each iteration. Committing more positions increases parallelism and reduces the number of decoding rounds, but overly aggressive commitments may introduce irreversible errors that contaminate the context used to predict other tokens. Conversely, conservative schedules preserve generation quality but sacrifice much of the computational advantage of parallel prediction. Existing decoding strategies therefore commonly rely on prediction confidence, e.g., committing positions whose maximum token probabilities are highest, under the intuition that highly confident predictions are safer to reveal. While effective as a simple heuristic, this strategy treats each masked position largely by its current local predictability and does not explicitly model how revealing it will change the difficulty of subsequent predictions.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: We argue that this distinction between predictability and utility is crucial for efficient diffusion language generation. The easiest token to predict is not necessarily the most useful token to commit. Consider two masked positions i i and j j . Position i i may already have an extremely peaked predictive distribution, yet revealing it may add almost no information about the rest of the sequence. In contrast, position j j may be moderately less certain but encode a critical semantic, syntactic, or reasoning decision, once j j is revealed, the uncertainty of several other positions may decrease substantially. This is particularly important in structured generation tasks such as mathematical reasoning and code synthesis, where intermediate decisions induce strong dependencies among downstream tokens. A schedule based solely on instantaneous confidence may therefore spend early commitments on safe but informationally redundant tokens, leaving influential positions unresolved for many more rounds. The effective decoding problem is thus not simply which tokens can be predicted now , but which tokens should be committed now so that the remaining sequence becomes easier to predict .

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: Motivated by this observation, we propose dSpark , a novel framework for learning when to commit tokens during diffusion language generation via schedule distillation . Our key idea is to construct informative unmasking schedules according to the downstream effect of each commitment rather than its confidence alone. We evaluate candidate commitments by how much revealing them helps reduce predictive uncertainty over the remaining positions. Tokens whose revelation makes multiple unresolved positions easier to determine are prioritized earlier, allowing useful context to propagate more rapidly. Decoding can thus be viewed as a context-construction process: every committed token not only resolves one position but also modifies the prediction problem of all remaining positions. By accounting for this effect, our schedules favor commitments with high future predictive value , producing trajectories that reduce sequence-level uncertainty faster than conventional confidence-driven schedules. This enables substantially more useful progress within each expensive model evaluation.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: Constructing better schedules alone, however, can add computation if sophisticated token selection must be repeated during inference. We therefore further distill the behavior induced by these schedules into the model itself. The constructed schedules provide training trajectories that expose the model to commitment orders in which informative tokens are revealed early and the remaining predictions are progressively simplified. After distillation, the model can exploit these learned dependencies under efficient parallel sampling without expensive search over candidate schedules at every decoding step. Importantly, aggressively optimizing for fast commitment can alter the model’s original predictive behavior and degrade generation quality. To mitigate this, we introduce a KL-divergence regularizer that keeps the distilled model close to the original model distribution while learning to operate under accelerated schedules. Schedule distillation thus shifts computation from repeated inference-time schedule optimization into training, yielding a practical mechanism for jointly improving parallelism and preserving the generation capability of the underlying dLLM.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: We extensively evaluate dSpark on two representative models, LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks. The results demonstrate that learning when to commit is a powerful yet underexplored dimension for accelerating dLLMs. On GSM8K, our approach achieves 10.12 × \times and 5.12 × \times speedups over the baselines for LLaDA and Dream, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. This shows that generation efficiency depends not merely on how many tokens are predicted in parallel, but on how effectively each commitment restructures the prediction problem for later rounds. content: Diffusion Language Models. Discrete diffusion models generate sequences by reversing a corruption process, and subsequent work developed stronger objectives for language modeling, including SEDD, MDLM, and RADD ( Austin et al., 2021a ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) . LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) scaled masked diffusion to an instruction-following language model trained from scratch, while Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) demonstrated strong reasoning and coding performance with a model initialized from an autoregressive LLM. Other work combines diffusion within blocks with generation across blocks or scales diffusion models further through conversion from autoregressive models ( Arriola et al., 2025 ; Bie et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . These advances establish capable diffusion backbones, but their iterative generation process leaves substantial room to improve inference efficiency.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models

content: Efficient Diffusion Language Decoding. Existing methods reduce either the cost or the number of decoding steps. Fast-dLLM ( Wu et al., 2026b ) , dKV-Cache ( Ma et al., 2025a ) , Elastic-Cache ( Nguyen-Tri et al., 2026 ) , and dInfer ( Ma et al., 2025b ) improve cache reuse and inference execution, while D2F ( Wang et al., 2026 ) and Fast-dLLM v2 ( Wu et al., 2026a ) use block-based generation to support efficient parallel decoding. Other approaches distill generation into fewer steps or enable more aggressive token updates ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Closest to our work, dParallel ( Chen et al., 2026b ) uses certainty-forcing distillation to make tokens ready earlier, whereas d3LLM ( Qian et al., 2026 ) distills pseudo-trajectories and applies multi-block decoding. Training-free approaches such as LEAP ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and Ripple-Pivot Search ( Ye et al., 2026 ) use lookahead to identify tokens worth committing early.

content: Results on LLaDA. On GSM8K, dSpark achieves 10.12 × 10.12\times the decoding parallelism of the base model while maintaining the base model’s accuracy. Compared to d3LLM, it further increases parallelism while closing the accuracy gap relative to the base model, resulting in a 33.3 % 33.3\% improvement in AUP. On MATH, dSpark similarly preserves base-model performance while achieving the highest TPF and AUP. The code benchmarks show that the benefits extend beyond mathematical reasoning. On HumanEval, dSpark matches d3LLM’s pass@1 while decoding more tokens per forward pass. On MBPP, it improves both pass@1 and TPF over d3LLM. Across all four tasks, dSpark makes better use of parallel decoding than the competing methods, with the highest AUP in every case.

content: Results on Dream. On GSM8K, dSpark achieves 5.12 × 5.12\times the base model’s TPF while improving accuracy by 1.5 % 1.5\% . Relative to d3LLM, the larger parallelism gains occur on code generation: TPF increases by 30.4 % 30.4\% on MBPP and 36.4 % 36.4\% on HumanEval, accompanied by higher pass@1 on both benchmarks. These improvements give dSpark a substantial AUP lead on the two code tasks and show that its advantage extends across backbones. On MATH, the gain over d3LLM is smaller, but dSpark still achieves the highest TPF and AUP. On MBPP, dSpark achieves the highest TPF and AUP of all compared methods, while also improving pass@1 over d3LLM.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: Accuracy–parallelism trade-off. Figure 4 shows why dSpark leads in AUP. Methods can decode more tokens per forward pass by accepting a sharp drop in accuracy. dSpark achieves higher TPF while maintaining strong accuracy. This is clearest on GSM8K, where it achieves both the highest TPF and the highest accuracy on LLaDA and Dream. On HumanEval, it exceeds d3LLM’s TPF without losing pass@1 on LLaDA and improves both measures on Dream. The other plots show the same overall pattern: dSpark moves decoding toward greater parallelism while preserving enough task performance to make that gain useful. These results are consistent with the goal of dSpark, which encourages the model to reveal informative tokens earlier so that more of the remaining positions can be predicted together. The KL regularizer helps dSpark retain accuracy under aggressive parallel decoding, giving it an advantage over competing methods at higher TPF.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: Confidence and False Positives. Distillation for parallel decoding makes a model confident enough to commit many tokens per forward pass. The risk is that it also becomes confident about wrong tokens, which a threshold decoder then commits. Table 8 measures this on the natural schedules of 250 test GSM8K samples, recording at every round the prediction at every masked position. The three distilled models are confident about a similar share of correct predictions. Among wrong predictions, however, d3LLM and dParallel are confident for 22.9 % 22.9\% and 21.7 % 21.7\% , while dSpark is confident for 15.5 % 15.5\% , so its confident predictions are correct 91 % 91\% of the time, against 82 % 82\% for the two baselines. Figure 5 breaks these predictions into confidence bins. The base model is well calibrated: in every bin, its accuracy is close to its confidence. dParallel and d3LLM are overconfident at every confidence level; for example, their predictions made with a confidence between 0.8 0.8 and 0.9 0.9 are correct only 51 % 51\% and 52 % 52\% of the time. dSpark stays much closer to the diagonal, at 65 % 65\% in the same bin, although it places slightly more predictions in the top bin than the two baselines. Its expected calibration error is also substantially lower than theirs. This more reliable confidence helps explain why dSpark can commit tokens aggressively without the same loss of accuracy.

content: Ablation Study on Training Recipe. To examine the contribution of each component, we ablate schedule distillation and KL regularization on LLaDA, with results shown in Table 2 . Using ordinary trajectory training without optimized schedule and KL, it achieves the accuracy of 74.9 and TPF of 7.6 on GSM8K, and 37.9 accuracy and 5.2 TPF on Humaneval. Using the schedule alone substantially increases TPF on both GSM8K and HumanEval, but accuracy declines as the model commits more tokens in parallel. KL regularization alone has the opposite effect: it improves accuracy but reduces TPF, leading to lower AUP than the variant without either component. Combining the two gives the best balance. The full recipe retains 10.1 TPF on GSM8K and 6.7 TPF on HumanEval while raising accuracy to 78.9% and 39.6%, respectively. It achieves the highest AUP on both tasks. These results show that the schedule is responsible for the parallelism gain, while KL regularization helps prevent that gain from coming at the expense of accuracy.

content: To validate our choice of training mixture, we ablate the ratio of correct to incorrect trajectories on LLaDA and evaluate the resulting models on GSM8K, as shown in Table 3 . Without incorrect trajectories, the model reaches 11.4 TPF but only 74.19% accuracy. Adding incorrect samples improves accuracy, although a larger share generally reduces parallelism. We choose a 4 : 1 4{:}1 ratio because it retains 10.12 TPF while raising accuracy to 78.94%. Increasing the share further to 1 : 1 1{:}1 brings only a small gain in accuracy, while TPF falls to 7.90. At 2 : 1 2{:}1 , both accuracy and TPF are lower than at 4 : 1 4{:}1 , reaching 78.04% and 9.77, respectively. We also test using a separate, disjoint set of correct trajectories for KL regularization, keeping the same ratio of 4 : 1 4{:}1 . Compared with using incorrect trajectories at the same ratio, accuracy falls from 78.94% to 77.10%, and TPF drops by 30.5%. Together, these results support using incorrect trajectories for KL regularization at a 4 : 1 4{:}1 ratio, which provides a strong balance between accuracy and parallel decoding.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: In this work, we studied efficient decoding for diffusion large language models from the perspective of when to commit predicted tokens. We showed that token confidence alone is insufficient for effective scheduling, since some less predictable tokens can provide more useful context for resolving the remaining sequence. We introduce dSpark enabled by schedule distillation , which constructs informative unmasking schedules based on the downstream utility of token commitments and distills these schedules into the model for efficient parallel inference. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show substantial acceleration, including 10.12 × \times and 5.12 × 5.12\times speedups on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining strong task performance. Our results highlight unmasking schedules as an important learnable component of diffusion language modeling and suggest that better commitment strategies can substantially narrow the gap between the theoretical parallelism and practical efficiency of dLLMs.

title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
content: This work focuses on improving the inference efficiency of diffusion large language models and does not involve human subjects or the collection of sensitive personal data. Our method does not introduce new model capabilities beyond those of the underlying pretrained models and therefore inherits their existing limitations and potential risks, including biased, harmful, or inaccurate generations. By reducing the number of decoding steps required during inference, the proposed approach can also help lower computational cost and energy consumption.

section: A.1 Wall-Clock Throughput and KV Caching
content: TPF counts forward passes, but a forward pass with a longer context costs more time. We measure wall-clock throughput on NVIDIA A100-SXM4 GPUs with batch size 1. Table 4 therefore reports the wall-clock throughput of dSpark on LLaDA, without a KV cache and with the prefix and dual caches of Fast-dLLM ( Wu et al., 2026b ) . dSpark runs with both caches. With the short 0-shot prompt, the caches barely change throughput (253 and 213 tokens/s, against 249 without a cache), since they also increase the number of forward passes (from 24.8 to 29.4 with the prefix cache). With a 5-shot prompt, the prefix cache raises throughput from 92 to 155 tokens/s ( 1.7 × 1.7\times ) at similar accuracy. At 512 tokens, the caches lower accuracy by 1.1–2.7 points without raising throughput. Caching is therefore most useful for long prompts, and dSpark reaches 249 tokens/s without it.

content: A promoted token is committed before the frozen model would commit it on its own, so it is, by construction, a token the model is not yet confident about. The filter in Eq. ( 5 ) therefore does not ask for confidence. It only asks that the reference token be plausible to the model: among its k = 10 k=10 most likely tokens at that position, with a probability of at least p min = 0.02 p_{\min}=0.02 , i.e., a surprisal of at most about 4 nats, the range shown in Figure 1 . The two bounds complement each other. When the model’s distribution is flat, many tokens exceed 2 % 2\% and the rank bound applies; when it is peaked, the tenth-ranked token can have a negligible probability and the probability bound applies.

content: Why not a stricter filter. The tokens that help the other positions most are rarely the confident ones. As shown in Figure 1 , revealing an uncertain token ( p θ 0 < 0.5 p_{\theta_{0}}<0.5 ) makes 5.1 × 5.1\times more other positions ready than revealing a confident one and lowers their surprisal 4.7 × 4.7\times more. A filter that asks for confidence would therefore exclude the most useful promotions. Promoting these low-probability tokens also does not cost accuracy (Table 10 ).

content: Why not a looser filter. Below these bounds, the model has effectively ruled the reference token out given the current context. Promoting such a token would make the schedule depend on knowing the verified answer rather than on the model’s own uncertainty, and would train the student to commit a token that its context does not support. The bounds also keep the search small, since every candidate is scored with its own forward pass in Eq. ( 6 ). We set p min p_{\min} and k k from these considerations and did not tune them in end-to-end training.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
section: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
content: Deep research, or any use of large language models (LLMs) to read a large document collection and produce insights, requires synthesizing information from different sources. In this work, we find that LLMs produce long-form research reports that read as confident syntheses but which fail to accurately reflect the underlying documents. We call this failure smoothing . In collapsing diverse and potentially conflicting sources into a single narrative, the model discards the evidential “jaggedness” of its corpus and asserts conclusions more decisive than the citations can support. We introduce a claim level scoring pipeline, SmoothScore , to quantify this effect. Our pipeline extracts key conclusive claims from model generated reports, then finds evidence relevant to each claim and clusters that evidence along high level aspects. Finally, each claim is scored with respect to the evidence to quantify the degree of smoothing done by the agent. Across 7 systems and 4 datasets, we find that agents consistently produce stronger claims than warranted 1 1 1 Code and data: https://github.com/tiasa2/SmoothScore .

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Figure 1: When synthesizing over many documents, agents can present a claim as well supported when the evidence is actually more mixed. SmoothScore flags these smoothed-over claims and quantifies the degree of smoothing.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often deployed within systems that read across many sources of information and return long-form reports with citations ( Shao et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) . These systems, either general-purpose agents paired with Internet access or special-purpose “deep research” agents, retrieve large volumes of documents and analyze and synthesize this information into coherent reports ( Du et al., 2026 ; Onweller et al., 2026 ) . The skills required to do this go beyond simple multi-document summarization ( Fabbri et al., 2019 ) : agents must weigh evidence, integrate conflicting findings, and determine what the evidence warrants ( Narayanan Venkit et al., 2026 ; Rasheed et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . The resulting reports are typically fluent, well-organized, and densely cited, which makes them read as confident, authoritative syntheses. As a result, users increasingly treat these outputs as substitutes for reading the underlying literature, even when the synthesis misrepresents or overstates what the cited sources actually support ( Li and Aral, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: In this work, we study the prevalence of smoothing in LLM generated reports. We define smoothing as the tendency of LLMs to synthesize claims that are more decisive than supported by the documents they cite. Such claims may, for example, fail to portray mixed evidence or overclaim a result to hold in all circumstances when it has only been shown more narrowly. By contrast, a faithful claim should hedge when the evidence is mixed and narrow its scope when the support is narrow.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: To identify instances of this behavior, we propose SmoothScore , a framework for measuring whether the claims in a synthesized report are calibrated to the cited documents. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that an agent’s report can present a claim as well supported by some of its citations, even though other retrieved evidence shows the claim only holds under certain conditions. The bulk of prior work on claim verification and long-form factuality ( Min et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) can check whether individual claims are supported by their cited evidence, but breaks down for synthesized claims: these systems usually return binary judgments at the claim or subclaim level, but do not handle calibration and scoping across a large body of potentially conflicting evidence.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: To compute SmoothScore , we first decompose each report into its main conclusive claims and identify the documents the report cites. As shown in Figure 2 , for each claim, we run two agents over the report’s cited documents: (a) Support Agent : which surfaces evidence consistent with the claim, and (b) Skeptic Agent : which actively searches for evidence that qualifies, limits, or contradicts the claim. Evidence from both these passes are clustered into aspects reflecting different dimensions of the claim, such as viewpoint, strength of argument, and certainty ( Kargupta et al., 2025 ) . Given the claim and its mapped aspect-evidence pairs, we score the claim’s calibration on a 1–5 scale, reflecting how well its stated strength and scope match the evidence collected across both passes.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Across four benchmarks and seven systems, we find that smoothing is pervasive. On average, for each system at least 25% of generated claims received a SmoothScore ≥ 3 \geq 3 . For most systems over half of claims show at least material smoothing, and up to 35% of Gemini Deep Research’s claims show severe smoothing ( ≥ 4 \geq 4 ). We also find that limited interaction with the cited documents contributes to smoothing: Luna opens only 19% of the pages it cites, and actively engaging with the full documents can help reduce smoothing.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Contributions Our main contributions are: (a) We introduce SmoothScore , a framework for measuring whether the claims in a synthesized report are calibrated to the strength and scope of their cited evidence, rather than merely supported by it and (b) we find this issue to be widespread across frontier systems on 4 different benchmarks.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Given a prompt p p , a retrieval-augmented agent M M produces a long-form response or report y y with inline citations. We collect the full text of the cited documents in the report D = { d 1 , … , d m } D=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}\} . Our goal is to measure if the synthesized conclusive claims in y y faithfully represent what D D supports.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: We call a claim smoothed if it satisfies three criteria:(1) it reflects a conclusion drawn from aggregated evidence; (2) some of the evidence supports at least part of the conclusion; and (3) the conclusion as a whole is stronger or broader than the body of the evidence warrants.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: This goal is closely related to hallucination detection ( Zha et al., 2023 ; Min et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) ; we view it as a special case of hallucination detection. However, typical methods for hallucination detection assume binary factuality judgments. Past work has looked at more nuanced judgments for narrative summarization ( Subbiah et al., 2025 ) and opinion summarization ( Bhaskar et al., 2023 ) , but these methods are designed for simpler settings and do not handle the complexity of smoothing in deep research systems.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Evaluating whether a claim is smoothed requires more than checking whether a report’s statements are supported by individual citations. For instance, in Figure 2 , the extracted claim ‘discrete image-token modeling appears more promising than a Stable-Diffusion-centered architecture’ is a conclusion made by the deep research system (satisfying condition (1) above). It is supported by the cited documents, D 1 D_{1} Emu3 paper ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ) and D 3 D_{3} (the Show-o paper ( Xie et al., 2025 ) ) (satisfying condition (2)). However, we find that the same sources along with other documents, namely D 2 D_{2} (the Transfusion paper ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) ), also contains results that show that the statement is only true under certain conditions present counter evidence (satisfying condition (3)). Therefore, smoothing can occur even when a claim appears supported, and methods producing binary judgments from small evidence sets cannot comprehensively capture the distribution to identify it.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: We propose SmoothScore as a way of measuring the degree of smoothing a conclusion shows. Figure 2 outlines the pipeline. At a high level, first, we extract such claims from a generated report that represent the key takeaways, then find evidence that supports and refutes those claims. However, it is not straightforward to combine this evidence into a final score: counting supporting documents vs. refuting documents does not account for the nuances of how a claim is supported or refuted.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Instead, for the claim c c in the report y y and evidence from a cited document d ∈ D d\in D , we identify a set of dimensions A ⁡ ( c , d ) = { a 1 , … , a k } A(c,d)=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\} that we call aspects , following ( Kargupta et al., 2025 ) . These aspects are consolidated across documents, to capture fine-grained ways in which a claim might be refuted. For instance, in Figure 2 , step 3, we are able to find ‘performance and efficiency of tokens vs diffusion models’ , under which we see some evidence state that ‘tokens match or beat diffusion’ but we also see evidence for ‘diffusion or hybrid set ups are competitive’ . As aspects are discovered per claim and tailored to the claim and its evidence, we use them to score claim against the aspect-organized evidence to quantify its degree of smoothing.

section: Open-source agents produce severely smoothed claims
content: Systems follow similar patterns across datasets. The mean SmoothScore in open-source Deep Research systems like DR Tulu ( Shao et al., 2026 ) and QUEST ( Xie et al., 2026 ) remains comparable or slightly above that Sonnet-5. However, at least ∼ \sim 59% and ∼ \sim 55% of their claims score ≥ 3 \geq 3 , and 7–23% score ≥ 4 \geq 4 . From Table 11 , QUEST draws from among the smallest evidence pools (roughly 10 documents and 40–55k words) so it has the least amount of evidence to compress. Despite this, while closed source systems only generate 1–2% of claims that score = 5 =5 , QUEST generates up to ∼ \sim 7% and ∼ \sim 4% such claims on DeepResearchBench II and ResearchRubrics. Appendix G.1 shows that QUEST often generates outputs that read as summarization rather than synthesis. The resulting claims preserve specifics faithfully while overstating scope enough to drive inflated conclusions.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
section: Closed-source systems vary widely in smoothing severity.
content: Among closed-source agents with Websearch, we see that Sonnet 5 and Opus 5.5 produces almost 1.4–2.5 × \times the fraction of claims that achieve a SmoothScore of 3–4 relative to Luna and Sol in Table 1 . These systems differ in the middle of the distribution rather than at its extremes and neither of the systems produce fundamentally misleading claims (Scored 5) at a meaningful rate, at most 1.1% on any dataset. On the other hand, Luna and Sol generate at least 36% claims that show no smoothing (score = 1 =1 ), 1.5–2.7x more than any other system across datasets.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
section: Closed-source systems vary widely in smoothing severity.
content: Across all systems, Gemini performs the worst, with 85–93% of claims scoring ≥ 3 \geq 3 and an average score of 3.05–3.27. Gemini also draws from significantly more documents (roughly 2–5x) than Luna or Sol with websearch, and produces the longest reports on every dataset (Table 11 ). This gives the agent a much larger surface to synthesize, and despite the added length, the report does not appear to compress this information more effectively. Appendix G.2 lists some examples of claims from the generated reports. They contain language that turns a strong result into a universal or final conclusion.

section: Generation features show limited within-system associations with smoothing.
content: From Table 11 we observe that the number of documents and report length vary across systems, which can influence the agents’ ability to synthesize and therefore SmoothScore . We check if these features of an agent predict SmoothScore in Table 12 . Across systems, systems that cite more documents ( ρ = 0.37 \rho=0.37 , p = .056 p=.056 ) or write longer claims ( ρ = 0.43 \rho=0.43 , p = .02 p=.02 ) smooth more, with Gemini at the extreme, but within a system both relationship are negligible ( ρ = 0.03 \rho=0.03 and 0.02 0.02 ; per-system values are small and mixed in sign). Only report length shows a within system association, with a small ( ρ = 0.12 \rho=0.12 ) but positive correlation in all systems, though not significant in any one alone. Number of claims shows no such connection within or across systems (except a modest negative correlation for Gemini, ρ = − 0.23 \rho=-0.23 ). Overall, while these features show associations with smoothing, within-system behavior suggests that other factors could also influence smoothing.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: We find that query framing influences how the model writes its claims. As seen in Appendix G.1 and G.2 , there are certain categories of questions where smoothing is more pronounced: (1) Comparative questions: if the query is comparative in nature, for example, ‘In multimodal pretraining, the paradigms are based on image tokens and stable diffusion, which appears more promising and why?’ or ‘Which paradigm between RL and distillation appears more promising and why?’ , it can presuppose a choice from the agent where to motivate or justify a choice the agent drops important qualifications, (2) Topic overview questions: queries that require an overview of a topic, for example, ‘Describe the Sunflower conjecture, progress towards a solution, and related problems’ , the agent can assemble multiple results a single conclusion or just generalize from a single finding to the whole topic.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: Table 2 shows three patterns that we observe across systems: (1) Unsupported composition : Agents combine individual fragments of evidence into a stronger conclusion. Although each component may be supported, the claim presents its unsupported composition as a conclusive statement. (2) Scope expansion : A claim takes an established result for a particular setup or experimental condition and removes certain boundaries, so that a the scope for an empirical observation expands into a general conclusion. (3) Premature Closure : Claims often adopt conclusive language, using phrases like ‘strictly preserving,’ ‘the best approach,’ ‘definitively proves’ and ‘most optimal.’ .

section: 5.2 Relevance of evidence collected by SmoothScore
content: While human agreement validates the SmoothScore judge’s final scores, we separately check whether the evidence SmoothScore surfaces (Steps 2–4) is useful. We consider an independent measure, using gold rubrics provided by ResearcherBench created for judging the overall quality of the generated report. We take Luna and Sonnet 5 WebSearch reports on the benchmark, and perform an additional revision step with no web search under three context settings: (1) no additional context, (2) providing all cited documents, and (3) the collected SmoothScore evidence as context. We find that both context settings rise well above the no-context control ( + 0.4 +0.4 and + 1.1 +1.1 ), with the extracted evidence improving rubric scores for both agents (Luna + 4.4 +4.4 , Sonnet + 12.0 +12.0 , both p < .001 p<.001 ), matching or even exceeding revision with the full documents. The evidence achieves this with roughly one-fifth to one-tenth of the tokens of the full documents. While this does not test the quality of the evidence relative to the generated claims, it shows that the evidence captures information that matters to an external, expert-written evaluation independent of the judge’s scores.

authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
section: 6 Lack of engagement with document content
content: The systems we evaluate generate reports with citations from the documents they retrieve. However, the agent’s interaction with the cited material is hard to control. For Luna, the trace shows that the agent works almost entirely from search snippets truncated by the tool (median 585 characters), opening a cited page for only 19% of the documents it cites and in just 20 of 65 reports. Sonnet 5 engages even less, opening only 2% of the links it cites (Table 5 , Appendix F ). As agents rarely read the full documents, an agent may never see the qualifications and countervailing findings in the body of a source, which suggests that smoothing is partly shaped by what information the agent chooses to access.

content: To test whether engaging with the documents reduces smoothing, we regenerate Luna and Sonnet 5 reports under varying setups. The instructions are identical across both evidence settings (prompts in Appendix E.4 , E.3 ). We score all reports with SmoothScore on ResearcherBench.

content: We find that neither intervention is sufficient on its own (Table 6 ). For Luna, the instructions without the documents barely change smoothing (mean σ \sigma 1.95 to 1.88), and the documents alone reduce it modestly (1.80). Sonnet 5 responds more to instructions alone (2.54 to 2.23) but little to the documents alone (2.38). Combined, however, documents and instructions reduce smoothing far more than either does separately: mean σ \sigma falls to 1.52 for Luna and 1.78 for Sonnet 5, and the share of materially smoothed claims ( σ ≥ 3 \sigma\geq 3 ) drops from 29% to 12% and from 61% to 25%, removing more than half in both cases. Severe smoothing ( σ ≥ 4 \sigma\geq 4 ) nearly disappears (0.5% and 2.2%). Instructions to calibrate are thus most effective when the agent has the evidence needed to act on them.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: A standard recipe for verifying long-form text is to decompose it into smaller checkable units and score each against a knowledge source ( Min et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Gunjal and Durrett, 2024 ) . These methods generally return a binary decision per claim, which is a good granularity for factual precision, but it does not work for synthesized claims that can have varying degrees of smoothing. ConflictScore ( Liu et al., 2026 ) is the closest to our setting, and it extends this atomic claim recipe in a direction close to ours. They mark a claim as supported, contradicted or irrelevant per document retrieved, and aggregate these into claim-level conflict measures. However, a claim can be labeled supported by every one of its cited documents and still smooth over information it omits. Our work instead follows Kargupta et al. (2025) in organizing evidence along aspects (e.g., viewpoint, strength, certainty), so that supporting and qualifying evidence on the feature of a claim can be considered against each other.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: In science communication, prior work measures certainty in how findings are stated ( Pei and Jurgens, 2021 ) and models how information changes as findings move from papers to news and social media ( Wright et al., 2022 ) . For LLM summaries of scientific text, Peters and Chin-Yee (2025) test ten widely used LLMs on about 4,900 summaries and find that most produce broader generalizations than the source texts, and that LLM summaries are nearly five times more likely than human-written ones to overgeneralize. In medicine, neural multi-document summaries of clinical trials are fluent but often factually inaccurate ( Wallace et al., 2021 ) , and LLM summaries of medical evidence can misstate the certainty of the evidence or overgeneralize by omitting attributes such as a disease subtype ( Tang et al., 2023 ) . These studies summarize a single document or a small set of abstracts. We extend the concern to long-form, multi-document research reports written by agents, and give a claim-level measure grounded in the documents a report cites.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
section: Correctness evaluation for deep research systems
content: Agentic deep-research systems ( Du et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Sharma et al., 2025 ) pair rubric-based insight coverage with citation grounded factuality checks. Several works audit the reliability of these systems. DeepTRACE ( Narayanan Venkit et al., 2026 ) decomposes answers into statements and finds that deep-research agents remain one-sided on debate queries and include many statements unsupported by their listed sources. Onweller et al. (2026) find that citations that resolve and are topically relevant often still fail a factual check against the cited content. Zhu et al. (2026) show that a single misleading document can induce false conclusions in final reports. Rasheed et al. (2026) argue for claim-level auditability, including whether conflicts in the evidence are surfaced or suppressed. Across this literature, factuality is largely operationalized as citation validity: whether a claim is supported by some retrieved source. Our results show that this is not enough. Reports whose claims are individually supported can still present mixed or conditional evidence as a decisive conclusion, so assessing how faithfully the underlying evidence is presented requires the claim-level, evidence-calibrated analysis we propose.

title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
content: In this work, we studied the propensity of LLMs to smooth their conclusions when generating reports based on sources. They frequently generate oversimplified statements or conclusions that aren’t really backed up by the evidence cited. Our pipeline, SmoothScore , allows us to quantify this and establish its frequency across several state-of-the-art agents. Finally, we find that this models fail to read with their own cited documents, and suggest smoothing can improved by more thorough agents engaging wih their sources.

content: 2a. Supporting-evidence extraction The supporting pass extracts findings that substantiate the claim as stated. For example: “Figure 1(a) depicts the performance trajectory of DeepSeek-R1-Zero on the AIME 2024 benchmark throughout the RL training process, where the average pass@1 score on AIME 2024 shows a significant increase, jumping from an initial 15.6% to 77.9%.” “As reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant paradigm for scaling reasoning capabilities in LLMs.” Across all claim–document pairs, the pass extracts 61 61 supporting items.

content: 2b. Countervailing-evidence extraction The countervailing pass extracts findings that contradict, weaken, or materially restrict the claim. For example: “We show that training on only 1,000 samples with next-token prediction and controlling thinking duration via a simple test-time technique we refer to as budget forcing leads to a strong reasoning model that scales in performance with more test-time compute.” “The rule-based RL training stage of DeepSeek-R1-Zero is narrowly focused on reasoning tasks, resulting in limited performance in broader areas such as writing and open-domain question answering.” Across all claim–document pairs, the pass extracts 77 77 countervailing items.

For example: A1.1: Large gains on tasks with objective checks Supporting evidence: • DeepSeek-R1-Zero’s AIME 2024 pass@1 score rises from 15.6 % 15.6\% to 77.9 % 77.9\% during RL training. • AlphaProof learns to produce formal proofs through RL over millions of auto-formalized problems. Countervailing evidence: • AlphaGeometry2 achieves an 84 % 84\% solve rate using a pipeline centered on language modeling, symbolic reasoning, and synthetic data rather than RL. • AlphaProof’s demonstrated successes remain concentrated in competition mathematics. This node contains 31 31 supporting and 9 9 countervailing items. Across the hierarchy, this is the only node in which supporting items predominate; the remaining dimensions contain substantial countervailing evidence.

content: 5. Smoothing judgment Claim role: General forecast about a field-wide training trend; it can be defeated by evidence that RL with verifiable rewards is unlikely to be widely adopted or that strong, persistent limitations preclude mainstream use. Takeaway: Reinforcement learning—particularly when rewards are verifiable—will be widely adopted as a standard part of training pipelines for reasoning models, though not necessarily the only or exclusive approach. Objections: Important constraints temper the breadth of the forecast. RL scales poorly where no reliable verifier exists; it can underperform or fail to improve smaller models; compute and evaluation costs limit practicality; and verifier imperfections introduce shortcutting and misalignment risks. Strong non-RL alternatives can also match or surpass leading RL-trained systems. These findings show that RLVR will not be universally applicable or singularly dominant across reasoning tasks. Net resolution: The claim largely holds but needs an explicit limitation: RL with verifiable rewards is poised to be mainstream for verifier-evaluable settings, yet adoption will be constrained by verifier availability, safety and shortcut risks, model and compute regimes, and viable non-RL alternatives that will continue to coexist. section: Luna, Sol, Sonnet 5, Opus 5.5, and DR Tulu.
content: Luna and Sol use the OpenAI Responses API web search tool, whose calls are recorded as search, page-open, or find-in-page actions ( OpenAI, 2026 ) . We count a cited link as opened if the returned search results contain that page’s opened content, marked by a Source: open(…) header. These markers capture every page-open and find-in-page action, as well as opens returned inside other calls’ results, so counting the actions alone would miss about three quarters of them. Sonnet 5 and Opus 5.5 run with Anthropic’s web search and web fetch tools. Search results return page content in encrypted form, so we cannot observe what the model sees from search alone, while web fetch retrieves a page’s full text ( Anthropic, 2026b ; Anthropic, 2026a ) . We therefore count a cited link as opened if the system successfully fetched it. As search results are encrypted, this measures full-page retrieval only; we cannot observe how much page content the model receives from search. For DR Tulu, we count calls to its browsing tool ( Shao et al., 2026 ) . All five systems cite mostly from search results rather than pages they open. Luna and Sol open 9–19% and 16–30% of the links they cite (45 of Luna’s 65 ResearcherBench reports open no cited page), Sonnet 5 and Opus 5.5 fetch 1.1–3.5% and 0.2–2.3%, and DR Tulu calls its browsing tool only 5 times across all datasets.

content: QUEST’s visit tool does not return the raw page content to the agent: a separate model (GPT-5-mini) reads the page and returns an extract conditioned on a goal QUEST states for the visit, consisting of selected evidence and a short summary ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . We count a cited link as opened if QUEST issued a visit to it. Its high open rate therefore does not mean QUEST reads what it cites: the agent sees only extracts filtered toward what it was looking for, which is consistent with its high smoothing despite frequent visits.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
section: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
content: Neural architecture search (NAS) remains a challenging optimization problem due to the vast and highly non-linear space of possible artificial neural network (ANN) topologies. Evolutionary approaches have demonstrated the ability to automatically generate ANN architectures; however, their effectiveness is often limited by the difficulty of preserving functional organization under mutation and recombination. In biological systems, complex networked phenotypes emerge from genetic information that has remained evolvable over long evolutionary timescales, suggesting that naturally evolved biological networks may encode organizational principles that facilitate adaptation. Here, we present TRON (TRansfer Of Natural networks), a neuroevolution framework that incorporates experimentally characterized protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks as architectural priors for ANN evolution. Rather than initializing search from randomly generated topologies, TRON exploits biologically derived interaction patterns as reusable structural building blocks. The framework combines classical evolutionary operators with mechanisms inspired by neuroevolution, including speciation, while introducing a species quarantine strategy designed to protect newly generated architectures during an initial maturation phase. We evaluated TRON on three classification benchmarks (CORA, CITESEER, and PUBMED) and three regression benchmarks (DIABETES, FRIEDMAN, and CALIFORNIA), comparing its performance against established evolutionary and neuroevolutionary approaches. Across all classification datasets and most regression tasks, TRON achieved the highest predictive performance among the evaluated methods. Furthermore, the framework exhibited substantially lower variability across independent runs, indicating improved robustness and convergence stability during evolutionary search. While these gains were associated with increased computational requirements, the results consistently suggest that biologically derived interaction networks provide more favorable substrates for neuroevolution than randomly generated topologies. Taken together, our findings support the hypothesis that protein interaction networks can serve as effective architectural priors for ANN evolution. More broadly, this work demonstrates the feasibility of transferring naturally evolved biological network architectures into artificial intelligence systems and suggests a new direction for improving evolvability in neural architecture search through the reuse of biological organizational principles.
