title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Classical EAs applied naively to VertexCover perform poorly. The (1+1) EA and variants thereof need at least exponential time to achieve an approximation factor better than ( 1 − ε ) / ε (1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon for n δ − 1 ≤ ε ≤ 2 n^{\delta-1}\leq\varepsilon\leq 2 , i.e., almost arbitrarily bad approximation ratio ( Friedrich et al., 2010 ; Oliveto et al., 2008 ) . In contrast, the trivial greedy algorithm obtains a 2-approximation in polynomial time. Using more sophisticated EAs and adding more problem-specific information can improve the performance. Kratsch & Neumann (2013) used the number of selected vertices as first objective, and the number of uncovered edges as second objective. With this formulation, a multi-objective EA obtains an optimal vertex cover in expected time O ⁡ ( O ​ P ​ T ⋅ n 4 + n ⋅ 2 O ​ P ​ T 2 + O ​ P ​ T ) O(OPT\cdot n^{4}+n\cdot 2^{OPT^{2}+OPT}) , where O ​ P ​ T OPT refers to the size of the smallest vertex cover. Using the ILP-relaxation as second objective leads to a lower runtime bound. Assuming only problem instances where O ​ P ​ T ≤ k OPT\leq k for some fixed parameter k k yields a polynomial runtime, i.e., the algorithm is a fixed-parameter algorithm. OPT cannot be bounded by a constant in general instances, and the runtime bound is therefore exponential on the entire problem class.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We would like to consider non-trivial combinatorial optimisation problems where the agent cannot rely on published results from the theoretical literature on black-box optimisation algorithms, or on formalisations in Mathlib. We also want to consider problems which we expect to be in P P . We therefore chose the problem of computing a minimum vertex cover in well-covered graphs, which we call WellCoveredVC . Recall that a vertex cover is minimum if the graph admits no vertex cover with fewer vertices. A vertex cover is called minimal (not to be confused with minimum) if no strict subset of V ′ V^{\prime} is a vertex cover. By definition, a minimum vertex cover is always a minimal vertex cover, but the converse is not true for all graphs. Graphs where the minimum and minimal vertex covers coincide are called well-covered graphs.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The fitness function in Eq. ( 1 ) combined with the choice of graph class gives the problem several structural properties that are helpful for search heuristics, and which are provided to the agent in the problem card. Given two search points with different number of uncovered edges, the one with fewer uncovered edges always has higher fitness (exposed as lemma wc_F_lt_of_uncovered_lt in the problem card). Also, if { i , j } ∈ E \{i,j\}\in E is an uncovered edge in x x , then flipping bit x i x_{i} reduces the number of uncovered edges (exposed as lemma wc_uncovered_flip_lt in the problem card). It is also straightforward to see that f f contains no local optima. Consider any non-optimal search point x x . If x x is not a vertex cover, then there must exist an uncovered edge { i , j } \{i,j\} , and a search point x ′ x^{\prime} obtained by flipping bit i i or bit j j in x x has strictly higher fitness than x x . Assume the other case, that x x is a vertex cover but not a minimum vertex cover. Then since the graph is well-covered, x x is also not a minimal vertex cover. Therefore, there exists a vertex i i such that x i = 1 x_{i}=1 and flipping bit i i in x x produces a strictly fitter vertex cover x ′ x^{\prime} . The fitness therefore increases.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: In a first set of experiments, we provided a problem card containing all the structural information described above. In this case, the agent produced an optimisation algorithm similar to a (1+1) EA, but with regime-changing asymmetric mutation rates. As long as the current search point is not a vertex cover (revealed by the fitness being less than − n -n ), the mutation-rates were chosen asymmetrically so that flipping 0-bits into 1-bits was twice as likely as the reverse. Once the current search point represented a vertex cover, the mutation-rate was chosen asymmetrically in the opposite direction, making bit-flips from 1 into 0 twice as likely as bit-flips from 0 into 1. The overall runtime obtained was O ⁡ ( n 4 ) O(n^{4}) . The problem card in the first set of experiments revealed all the structural information needed to design an efficient algorithm. In a second set of experiments, we created an anonymised problem card which does not mention the terms vertex cover or well-covered graphs, only providing raw fitness definitions. An experiment with Fable 5.1 failed to obtain an algorithm in this setting. However, Opus 5.5 successfully generated a (1+1) EA with regime-changing mutation rates. This time, the asymmetry between the rates was more pronounced, with the high mutation rate a factor Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) larger than the small rate. Overall, the obtained runtime was O ⁡ ( n 4 ) O(n^{4}) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The problem BandwidthVC is VertexCover restricted to graphs with bandwidth at most k k . A graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) with vertex set V = { 0 , 1 , … ​ n − 1 } V=\{0,1,\ldots n-1\} is said to have bandwidth k k if for all edges { u , v } ∈ E \{u,v\}\in E , it holds | u − v | ≤ k |u-v|\leq k . A low bandwidth k k implies that edges are only allowed between “nearby” vertices with respect to their numbering. In particular, k = 1 k=1 allows only subgraphs of the path 0 , 1 , … , n − 1 0,1,\ldots,n-1 , while k = n − 1 k=n-1 allows every graph.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Since VertexCover is NP-hard, we did not expect the agent to produce a good algorithm for general graphs. With a flat fitness function, which only reveals whether a search point is a cover and its number of 1-bits ( Appendix F ), the agent instead came up with an algorithm that probes all the Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) potential edges in the graph to learn the problem instance, then without making further queries, computes offline the optimum for that instance, and finally queries the optimum (row 10, Section F.10 ). The overall runtime bound was O ⁡ ( n 3 ) O(n^{3}) . This demonstrates that the agent is able to “cheat” this evaluation framework by exploiting a well-known weakness in how algorithms are evaluated in the black-box scenario: Algorithms are only charged for making fitness queries, and not for offline computation. As the agent shows, the black-box complexity of NP-hard problems is polynomial. On BandwidthVC with the same flat fitness function (row 11, Section F.11 ), the agent used the same strategy but exploited the bandwidth: it probes only the vertex pairs within distance k + 1 k+1 , giving a runtime bound of O ⁡ ( k ​ n ) O(kn) . In both runs, the minimum cover is defined non-constructively in Lean, so the computation between queries is not bounded.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: With the graded fitness function ( 1 ), BandwidthVC proved harder (rows 12–14). Two runs with Fable 5.1 designed asymmetric mutation operators but did not complete the pipeline: one stopped at the mass bound of Stage 10h, which is false for its design ( Section F.12 ), and the other at Stage 10c ( Section F.14 ). The run with Opus 5.5 completed with a window-repair random search ( Section F.15 ), whose bound Θ ⁡ ( 2 n ) \Theta(2^{n}) improves on the random search baseline only by a constant factor.

authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We now turn to the problem of minimising sub-modular functions (SFM), a problem with important applications in machine learning. We represent any subset S ⊆ [ n ] S\subseteq[n] as a bitstring x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x\in\{0,1\}^{n} in the natural way by setting x i = 1 x_{i}=1 if and only if i ∈ S i\in S . We now call a pseudo-Boolean function f : { 0 , 1 } n → ℝ f:\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} submodular if and only if for all subsets S ⊆ T ⊆ [ n ] S\subseteq T\subseteq[n] and v ∉ T v\not\in T , it holds f ⁡ ( S ∪ { v } ) − f ⁡ ( S ) ≥ f ⁡ ( T ∪ { v } ) − f ⁡ ( T ) f(S\cup\{v\})-f(S)\geq f(T\cup\{v\})-f(T) . We will assume that f f is integer-valued with range in the interval [ 0 , B ] [0,B] where B := n c B:=n^{c} for some unspecified constant c c . There exist theoretical algorithms that minimise SFMs in O ⁡ ( n 3 ​ log ⁡ log ⁡ ( n ) / log ⁡ ( n ) ) O(n^{3}\log\log(n)/\log(n)) oracle queries ( Jiang, 2023 ) , i.e., independent of B B . However, the more practically useful Fujishige-Wolfe algorithm has running time O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ B 2 ) O(n^{2}B^{2}) . We are not aware of runtime analyses of evolutionary algorithms for general SFM minimisation, but results for special cases such as the minimum spanning tree problem are available ( Neumann & Wegener, 2007 ) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We expected this problem to be significantly more challenging than the previous problems. We therefore added to the problem card the advice that this is a challenging problem where a naive elitist hill-climber may not work, and where the agent needs to carefully design the potential function and exploit submodularity. Furthermore, we ran several generations of the pipeline. The algorithmic design and analysis produced in a first generation of the pipeline was seeded into the following generation, etc. Through all generations, the agent produced the same class of algorithm, which can be described as projected subgradient descent on the Lovász extension. The first generation returned a runtime bound of 12 ​ n ​ B 2 ​ ( 2 ​ n + 4 ) ​ ( n + 1 ) = O ⁡ ( n 3 + 2 ​ c ) 12nB^{2}(2n+4)(n+1)=O(n^{3+2c}) . The second generation improved the constant factor, reducing the runtime to 16 ​ n 2 ​ B 2 ​ ( n + 2 ) = O ⁡ ( n 3 + 2 ​ c ) 16n^{2}B^{2}(n+2)=O(n^{3+2c}) . The third generation saw a factor- n n speed-up, with a runtime of 32 ​ n ​ B 2 ​ ( n + 1 ) = O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ B 2 ) 32nB^{2}(n+1)=O(n^{2}B^{2}) . Note that this is asymptotically the same as the Fujishige-Wolfe algorithm. Generation four and five only brought constant-factor improvements, leading to the approximate upper bound 8.13 ⋅ B 2 ​ ( n + 1 ) 2 8.13\cdot B^{2}(n+1)^{2} .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: To evaluate the impact of the staged pipeline, we developed an unstaged pipeline consisting of a single stage: Given a problem card, the agent is prompted to construct an algorithm for the problem which type-checks with the black-box framework, and which has better runtime than the seeded algorithm. The agent is not given the drift analysis API, the measurability toolkit, the proof cookbook, and most random stream properties. In order to be able to verify the algorithmic construction in Lean, we provided the agent with Lean-definitions of the black-box optimisation algorithm framework, and definitions of runtime. In order for the algorithm to be able to use the random source, we also provided basic clauses related to sampling from the random stream. Since the ablation only concerned the staged pipeline, we kept the problem cards unchanged. We also provided the agent with the definition of the seeded algorithm (random search).

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: For CycleUncover , Fable 5.1 reproduced the trivial random search algorithm (i.e., it copies the provided algorithm0 with minor syntactic changes). Note that this failure mode would have been caught by the NotRandomSearch guard in the staged pipeline. Instead of relying on drift analysis, the agent applied the tail-sum formula 𝔼 ⁡ [ T ] = ∑ k = 1 ∞ Pr ⁡ ( k ≤ T ) \mathds{E}\left[T\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\Pr\left(k\leq T\right) to the runtime variable T T . The agent recognised that the problem involved a hidden permutation and two global optima, giving a runtime bound of 2 n / 2 2^{n}/2 .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: For BandwidthVC , Fable 5.1 constructed the (1+1) EA, and proved all formalisation properties. However, the model failed to produce a runtime bound. The model attempted to apply a fitness-level argument. This is one of the simplest-to-use techniques for analysing the runtime of the (1+1) EA introduced more than two decades ago ( Wegener, 2002 ) , but it has limited applicability to more complex algorithms and fitness landscapes.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We then investigated weaker models. Claude Sonnet (row 17) passed Stages 0–10g on CycleUncover , but needed between 54 and about 1,000 attempts per stage, and it did not pass the mass bound of Stage 10h, because its Good set is empty at some reachable states ( Section F.9 ). The open-weight models, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B for the formal stages and Gemma 4 26B-A4B for the prose stages (vLLM backend, 256 samples per attempt), did not complete the pipeline on OneMax in any of 14 recent runs ( Section F.1 ). Rows 19–21 of Table 2 are representative. Two runs stop at NotRandomSearch (Stage 4) after 13 and 24 batches of 256 samples, although the statement is true for their PBIL-like designs. The third passes Stage 4 only through a loophole of an earlier pipeline version, since its algorithm is random search, and then stops at PotentialFineGrained (Stage 9d), again on a true statement. Frontier models stop, if at all, at a drift stage, whereas the open-weight models stop much earlier ( Appendix G ), and they generate 25–124M output tokens per run, about two orders of magnitude more than the frontier-model runs.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We have presented a staged pipeline in which an agent designs black-box optimisation algorithms and proves their expected runtime in Lean, with no empirical evaluation. Across 8 problem classes, 12 of 15 runs with frontier models completed the pipeline. Nine of these give a polynomial bound for an algorithm whose computation between queries is explicit; of the other three, two learn a VertexCover instance with polynomially many queries and then solve it offline, at no cost in the black-box model, and one improves on random search only by a constant factor. The agent designed an O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) algorithm for CycleUncover , on which the (1+1) EA needs e Ω ⁡ ( n ) e^{\Omega(n)} , matched the optimal order O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) on LeadingOnes , and rediscovered projected subgradient descent on the Lovász extension for integer-valued submodular minimisation, improving its own bound to O ⁡ ( n 2 + 2 ​ c ) O(n^{2+2c}) over five generations. Without the staging, or with open-weight models, the pipeline did not produce efficient algorithms. The bounds are not yet state of the art; richer drift theorems, more iterations of the design loop, and continuous search spaces are natural next steps.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Only frontier models completed the pipeline. A more complete experimental design allowing for a statistical analysis was not feasible due to the high cost of the runs. The agent was only provided with a simplified drift theorem (Corollary 3.1 ). With standard potential functions, this theorem makes more precise variable drift analyses difficult, leading to non-tight runtime bounds such as O ⁡ ( n 3 ) O(n^{3}) on OneMax for (1+1) EA variants. Furthermore, the search space is restricted to bitstrings.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: This paper addresses the scientific question of whether large language models can generate algorithms together with proofs of their efficiency, so LLMs were used extensively as the object of study. All synthesised algorithms, potential functions, drift certificates and their Lean proofs reported in Table 2 were generated by the models named there (Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet; Goedel-Prover-V2-32B and Gemma 4), and every proof was checked by Lean. In addition, LLMs were used to help derive the combinatorial drift part of the Lean library used by the pipeline ( Section 3 ), whose results are likewise checked by Lean; to translate the Lean definitions of the synthesised algorithms into the human-readable pseudo-code of Appendix F , and to collect the potentials and constants reported there, all of which we checked against the Lean artefacts; and to polish the writing. The author takes full responsibility for the content of the paper.

content: The pipeline Python code was initially based on the Goedel-Prover-V2 codebase ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . Every candidate declaration is checked by Lean 4 on a Kimina Lean server ( Dos Santos et al., 2025 ) , and the Lean errors are returned to the model in the next attempt. The number of attempts allowed before backtracking to a previous stage is determined by a Luby sequence ( Luby et al., 1993 ) L = ( 1 , 1 , 2 , 1 , 1 , 2 , 4 , … ) L=(1,1,2,1,1,2,4,\ldots) . In particular, each stage has its own copy of the sequence with unit 3, so it is allowed 3 , 3 , 6 , 3 , 3 , 6 , 12 , … 3,3,6,3,3,6,12,\ldots attempts on successive visits. When a stage exhausts its allowance, the pipeline backtracks by one stage on the first failure of that stage, and by more stages one each further failure. In addition, the whole pipelinen is restarted from Stage 0 when 200 , L k 200,L_{k} attempts have been used in the k k -th run of the pipeline, or earlier when 100 consecutive attempts make no progress beyond the furthest stage reached. All runs in Table 2 use these parameters.

content: Every stage prompt starts with the same global block, followed by the accepted declarations so far and the task of the stage. The global block describes the framework: the black-box algorithm structure of Algorithm 1 , the problem-class interface and the baseline algorithm, whose definitions the agent can use as a template. It then lists an API of library results, whose signatures are checked against the Lean build. These include samplers that turn the random source into bitstrings, with a fixed or a state-dependent per-bit bias, together with inverse lemmas that construct a random input producing any given bitstring. They also include lemmas about bitstrings, how to access elements of a bitstrings, etc. Furthermore, a measurability toolkit provides two tactics that decompose tuple-, if - and arithmetic-structured step and potential functions into leaves, and gives the idioms that close each kind of leaf. For the drift stages, the block describes the random source, the reachability predicates and an assembly theorem of Stage 10j, and it explains which properties of that theorem constrain the design, e.g. that a single ε \varepsilon and p p must serve every reachable non-optimal state. The problem card ( Appendices D and F ) is spliced in as the only problem-specific part. Finally, a proof cookbook collects recurring Lean pitfalls and their fixes, such as if b then is preferred over if ¬ \neg b , never to call decide on goals involving a symbolic n n , how to show that two state tuples differ, and to prove measurability with the toolkit rather than with aesop , whose fixed search budget times out on nested if s. After a failed attempt the agent sees the failing declaration, the Lean error, its earlier attempts at the stage and a list of facts verified in earlier stages.

authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Row 19 . The frozen design samples each bit with its own bias, initialised to 1 / 2 1/2 ; after an improvement, every bias moves by 0.1 0.1 towards the corresponding bit of the query, clamped to the interval [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] [0.1,0.9] . This is a PBIL-like estimation-of-distribution algorithm ( Baluja, 1994 ) , but with too large margins. Stages 0–3 passed. Stage 4 is true for this design (the biases leave 1 / 2 1/2 after one improving step), but all 13 × 256 13\times 256 samples for it failed: 38% contained no extractable Lean code, 35% left unsolved goals, 10% did not parse and 6% used unknown identifiers. The pipeline backtracked to Stages 3, 2 and 1c, but never to the design stages. 5,896 samples, 25.1M output tokens, 23.8 h.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Row 20 . Both designs, the first and the one proposed after a backtrack to Stage 0, are PBIL-like: per-bit biases, learning rate 1 / n 1/n , clamped to [ 0.05 , 0.95 ] [0.05,0.95] and then [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] [0.1,0.9] . The update moves the biases towards the newly drawn query rather than the evaluated one, so the fitness only decides whether they move. Stage 4 is again true, and all 24 × 256 24\times 256 samples for it failed: 53% left unsolved goals, 17% used unknown identifiers, 11% did not parse and 8% contained no extractable code. The run generated 10,776 samples and 73.1M output tokens, and lasted 23.6 hours.

content: Figure 5 shows where the runs spend their effort. Over the 12 completed frontier-model runs, the drift and runtime stages (Stages 10a–10j) account for 53% of the wall-clock time, algorithm construction (Stages 0–8) for 34% and the potential (Stages 9a–9f) for 13%. The most expensive stages are the pointwise drift and mass proofs: PositiveDrift (10f, 13%), DriftSetMass (10h, 9%) and NegativeDriftAndJump (10g, 8%). Two stages fail at the first attempt in almost every run for technical rather than mathematical reasons: DriftConstantProperties (10c) failed first in all 12 completed runs (81 attempts and 13 backtracks in total), mostly on the normal form of the baseline constants, and StepMeasurability (1c) in 11 of them. The incomplete frontier-model runs stop at a drift stage: rows 8, 12 and 17 at the mass bound (10h), which is false for their designs, and row 13 at 10c. The open-weight models stop much earlier, at NotRandomSearch (Stage 4, rows 19 and 20) and PotentialFineGrained (Stage 9d, row 21), after 13–24 batches of 256 samples at that stage. The Sonnet run (row 17) needed between 54 and about 1,000 attempts at every stage it passed before Stage 10g.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
section: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
content: Many decision-making tasks are inherently multi-objective. Interactive evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms (iEMOAs) are particularly well-suited to help the decision-maker find their most preferred solution. However, many of these algorithms employ black-box preference models. For high-stakes decision-making tasks, like healthcare and defense, a high level of transparency is needed, for instance to support accountability. We propose an interpretable iEMOA which uses active learning to efficiently learn a tree-based preference model directly from pairwise comparisons. The survival operator of NSGA-II and NSGA-III is extended with the learned preference model to guide the algorithm towards the region of interest. An extensive experimental study compares the proposed method to a state-of-the-art black-box model and a state-of-the-art interpretable model. Results indicate that our proposed model outperforms the alternatives in terms of finding the most preferred solution at the cost of a slightly worse average final population. Finally, a case study on a real-life engineering problem illustrates how inspecting the learned model reveals which objectives drive the decision-maker’s preferences.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Many real-life optimization tasks are Multi-objective Optimization Problems (MOPs) involving multiple conflicting objectives. For example, when choosing an investment portfolio, one wants to maximize return and minimize risk. For these problems, there is not a single optimal solution but rather a set of Pareto optimal solutions called the Pareto front. Whilst mathematically speaking all Pareto optimal solutions are equally good, a Decision-Maker (DM) usually prefers some optimal solutions over others. One example is pandemic policy design during COVID-19, where policy-makers needed to simultaneously minimize mortality, economic damage, and social and psychological harm, such as mental health deterioration. These objectives are inherently conflicting, leading to multiple different optimal policies and thus different policy choices across countries. For instance, Sweden adopted relatively less restrictive measures, aiming to limit societal disruption, whereas the Netherlands implemented stricter interventions, including lockdowns and a curfew, placing greater emphasis on controlling infection rates and protecting healthcare capacity.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization Algorithms (EMOAs) are particularly well-suited for MOPs because they maintain a population of solutions, allowing them to approximate multiple trade-off solutions along the Pareto front in a single run. Usually these algorithms first approximate the entire Pareto front after which a DM has to choose their most preferred solution. However, this is computationally costly and when there is a large set of alternatives choosing the most preferred solution is difficult [ 1 ] . Moreover, EMOAs struggle when the number of objectives increases because nearly all solutions become Pareto optimal [ 2 , 3 ] . Alternatively, instead of choosing the most preferred solution after the optimization process, one could introduce a DM’s preference information prior to the optimization. This preference information is used to identify a region of interest (ROI), which reduces the search space, and creates an additional ordering in non-dominated solutions increasing the selection pressure. Yet, a DM’s limited knowledge of the problem prior to the optimization can lead to inaccurate and misleading preferences [ 4 , 5 ] . Interactive methods, on the other hand, alternate optimization with preference elicitation, allowing the DM to get a better understanding of the problem, the objective trade-offs and the feasibility of their preferences which in turn enables them to make a better-informed choice [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: These interactive EMOAs (iEMOAs) ask a DM to elicit some preference information, build a preference model, and adapt the optimization algorithm to use this preference information to converge its population towards the ROI. When building such a preference model, one has to consider that a DM’s time is costly. Additionally, answering questions needs to be cognitively simple. Direct questions, like numerically rating solutions, are too cognitively demanding [ 9 , 10 ] . On the other hand, indirect preference elicitation builds a preference model via easy-to-answer holistic questions. One of the most common approaches is to ask a DM to answer pairwise comparisons. Stating that one prefers solution A over solution B is namely much easier than numerically rating both, especially when needing to be consistent over a large sets of solutions. To not cognitively overload a DM, it is thus important to learn a preference model in as few easy-to-provide (i.e. indirect) preference statements as possible.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Recently, Misitano et al. [ 11 ] have argued for an additional desirable property: explainability. They argue that most current interactive methods can be seen as black-box models. DMs elicit their preferences and obtain a solution, however, they have no idea how their preferences have led to that solution. Yet in critical decision-making tasks it is vital that the decision to be made is well-understood, trusted, and justified. Misitano [ 12 ] even questions whether relying on black-box models in any form of decision-making is ”good” decision-making at all. Besides context requiring transparent models, providing explanations to DMs can help them better articulate and refine their preferences, speeding up the convergence to the most preferred solutions [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Although this need for explainability in AI has long been stressed, explainability in iEMOAs is still a very new research field [ 16 , 17 ] and only a few (post-hoc) explainable or (inherently) interpretable methods exist.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: We propose a novel inherently interpretable iEMOA called DT-PBO-NSGA. Our proposed method uses active learning to build a semi-Bayesian decision tree as preference model. This tree partitions the objective space in a set of leaves and ranks each leaf with a preference value with the highest ranked leaf representing the DM’s ROI. By using the decision tree’s learned ranking within NSGA-II [ 18 ] or NSGA-III’s [ 19 ] survival operator, we direct the population to converge towards this ROI. Experimental results on an extensive suit of synthetic benchmarks show that our model performs similar to state-of-the-art baselines (DTEMOA [ 20 ] and PBO-R-NSGA-III [ 21 ] ) in lower dimensions and is more conservative in reducing its ROI, leading to the ROI more often containing the most preferred solutions whilst having a slightly worse average final population. Moreover, a case study on real-world engineering problem of the crashworthiness of car designs shows the learned preference model’s inherent interpretability.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II , we review a set of iEMOAs in terms of some key characteristics. The review motivates the development of our proposed methodology. In Section III-A , we give a short overview of our interpretable preference model based on interpretable Preferential Bayesian Optimization [ 22 ] . In Section III-B we describe how to integrate the preference model with the well-known NSGA-II [ 18 ] and NSGA-III [ 19 ] algorithms. In Section IV , we discuss the results of our numerical experiments on synthetic benchmarks and in Section V we apply DT-PBO-NSGA to a real-world engineering problem showing its preference model’s inherent interpretability. Finally, in Section VI , we provide our conclusions and introduce interesting directions for future research.

content: Interactive EMOAs differ in the following aspects: the type of optimization algorithm they adapt, the preference model they employ, the preference information they request from the DM, and the way they determine what preference statement to ask next. A summary of these key features for a selection of 20 research studies is shown in Table I . The papers that are selected are a representative subset of interactive EMOAs that utilize indirect preference judgments. This overview of papers is not meant to be a comprehensive survey, but instead shows the main research developments of interactive EMOAs in the aforementioned aspects over the years. For more comprehensive surveys we refer the readers to: Xin et al. [ 23 ] , Larraga et al. [ 24 ] , and Ren et al. [ 25 ] .

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: EMOAs can be largely classified in three classes: dominance-based, decomposition-based, and indicator-based. Many interactive EMOAs are based on dominance-based algorithms. These algorithms use the Pareto-dominance concept to select solutions for survival. In higher dimensions, however, nearly all solutions become non-dominated which severely degrades the selection pressure of the algorithm [ 45 ] . Incorporating preference information into the survival operator can reintroduce this selection pressure by focusing on a small preferred region of the Pareto front [ 33 ] . Recently, more attention has gone towards extending decomposition-based EMOAs with preference information. These methods decompose the problem into a set of single-objective optimization problems, usually via weights representing an instance of a scalarizing function or via reference directions. Each set of weights generates a different single-objective optimization problem and preference information is used to steer the set of weights to represent problems in the preferred regions. Lastly, indicator-based EMOAs use a performance indicator (e.g. hypervolume) to measure the performance of a set of solutions. The survival operator is then fully based on this indicator; the set of solutions that maximizes the indicator is chosen to survive. Only a few interactive indicator-based EMOAs exist, but generally they employ a weighted version of the indicator and adapt the weights to adhere to these preferences. Nearly all methods extend a single type of EMOA with preference information. The only exception is I-EMO/LTR [ 40 ] , where they created a preference-based version for all three types.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Most preference models are based on latent utility functions defined over the objective space ℱ \mathcal{F} . A value or utility function u ⁡ ( 𝐟 ) : ℱ → ℝ u(\mathbf{f}):\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} represents a DM’s preferences over an objective vector 𝐟 \mathbf{f} , where a higher u ⁡ ( 𝐟 ) u(\mathbf{f}) means a more preferred 𝐟 \mathbf{f} . In particular, 𝐟 ≻ 𝐟 ′ \mathbf{f}\succ\mathbf{f^{\prime}} implies u ⁡ ( 𝐟 ) > u ⁡ ( 𝐟 ′ ) u(\mathbf{f})>u(\mathbf{f^{\prime}}) . Over the years, many different utility functions ranging from linear weighted sums [ 26 ] to polynomials [ 27 ] to general quasi-concave functions [ 38 ] have been used. Each utility function is parametrized by a set of weights that are learned from preference statements supplied by the DM. The functional form of these utility functions has become more complicated, enabling more general preferences to be learned. However, this expressiveness comes at the cost of interpretability. Even in a simple linear weighted sum the interpretation of weights is nontrivial [ 46 ] , let alone in complex polynomials or quasi-concave functions.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: More recently, the use of inherently interpretable models as utility functions has been proposed. First, Misitano et al. [ 37 ] proposed INFRINGER, which learns a set of belief rules that aim to represent what entails a good solution. These rules and their associated belief values are then aggregated to get a utility function. The interpretability of the model is not discussed further. Similarly, XIMEA-DRSA [ 41 ] learns decision rules that classify solutions as either good or bad, but restricting all solutions to only two classes limits the expressiveness of the preference model. In DT-EMOA [ 20 ] , a decision tree is used to represent the utility function. The proposed classification tree predicts when one solution is preferred over another which allows for local interpretability. In particular, one can see when one item is better than another, but global interpretability, seeing what items are generally the best or the worst is not directly evident. Moreover, the decision tree is learned on the difference in feature values which implicitly assumes that there is a constant tradeoff between objectives over their entire range. However, human preferences tend to be non-linear [ 47 ] , a difference in feature vectors at the lower hand is not necessarily as desired as the same difference in high ranges. In RF-EMOA [ 43 ] , the authors replace the decision tree with a random forest ensemble to support active learning, but using an ensemble model comes at the cost of interpretability.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: The requested preference information can be either direct or indirect. As direct preference information has been shown to be difficult to supply, the review of papers has solely focused on methods that use indirect preference information. The review shows that most of the methods use pairwise comparisons or polarized solutions (e.g., selecting the best solution out of a set).

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Since a DM’s time and effort is costly, a preference model needs to be learned in as few preference statements as possible. Choosing the next question to ask in a smart way can help reduce the information needed to learn a model. Usually, it is a good idea to present preference options with a high probability of being the most preferred. However, when only greedily asking questions involving the current best solution, one runs into the risk of ending up in a local optimum. Therefore, active learning methods balance exploration with exploitation. To do so, these methods require a probabilistic estimate of the utility function to quantify a degree of uncertainty. Table I show that only RF-EMOA and PBO-R-NSGA-III use active learning. The rest of the reviewed methods still use random question selection, simply select a diverse representation of the current population, or always greedily ask the current best solution.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: The reviewed literature reveals that whilst interpretable iEMOAs have become more common, there are still two important limitations. First, interpretable preference models are often limited in expressiveness or provide only local interpretability. Second, although pairwise comparisons are commonly used for preference elicitation, Table I shows that most approaches select queries using random or greedy strategies rather than active learning. To address these limitations, we extend NSGA-II and NSGA-III with a globally interpretable regression tree preference model that supports active preference elicitation. The model is globally interpretable in the sense that the complete learned preference structure is represented by a single inspectable tree, allowing the decision maker to examine how preferences vary across the objective space rather than being limited to local explanations of individual predictions.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: We use NSGA-II for bi-objective problems and NSGA-III for problems with three or more objectives. For the remainder of this paper we will use NSGA to refer to the applicable variant. We adopt NSGA as the underlying evolutionary algorithms because their front-based selection mechanism naturally aligns with the proposed tree-based preference model. In particular, the preference model partitions the objective space into regions with different predicted preference values, from which preference fronts can be constructed. These fronts can be incorporated directly into NSGA’s existing front-based selection procedure, allowing preference information to steer the search without requiring assumptions about the functional form of the DM’s preferences. The following subsections describe how the preference model is learned from pairwise comparisons, how active learning is used to select informative comparisons, and how the resulting preference model is integrated into NSGA-II and NSGA-III.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: To model the DM’s preferences, we use a recently proposed semi-Bayesian regression tree [ 22 ] . Learning this model from pairwise comparisons requires partitioning the objective space into leaves and find the corresponding leaf estimates. The leaf estimates are represented probabilistically to capture uncertainty and facilitate active learning via Preferential Bayesian Optimization (PBO).

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: The PBO process is illustrated in Figure 1 . Starting from an initial set of pairwise comparisons, a regression tree is learned to model the DM’s preferences. Based on this model and its uncertainty, an acquisition function selects the next most informative pairwise comparison. The selected comparison is presented to the DM, whose response is added to the dataset. The regression tree is subsequently updated using the augmented dataset, after which the process is repeated until a stopping criterion is met. This process can continue until a convergence criteria is reached. The following sections give a brief overview of the three main components: (1) the partitioning of the objective space, (2) finding the probabilistic leaf estimates, and (3) the acquisition function used to determine the next most informative question to ask. For a more comprehensive explanation, we refer the reader to the original paper [ 22 ] . Finally, a working example to illustrate the algorithm’s workings is provided.

content: Interactive optimization procedures alternate preference elicitation with optimization. Our procedure, as visualized in Figure 3 starts with running NSGA to get an initial estimate of the Pareto front. After the convergence criteria (e.g., number of iterations) is reached, we switch to preference elicitation. For the first preference modeling stage, we start with randomly asking a few pairwise comparisons. Based on this information the preference model is constructed. For subsequent stages, we ask the most informative questions according to our active learning strategy. If the convergence criteria is reached we switch back to the optimization procedure and continue this process until the decision-maker is satisfied with the current Pareto front. When the optimization procedure is active with a learned preference model, we use this preference information to guide the population to the ROI. To do so, we adapt NSGA’s survival operator and its mating selection operator to use the learned preference information. Moreover, we maintain a representative subset of the entire Pareto front (called external archive) to prevent ending up with dominated solutions, accommodate between-leaf comparisons, and quickly adapt to preference changes.

Similarly to the survival operator, the goals, in order of importance, are Pareto-optimality, Preference, Diversity. Therefore, our operator first checks whether a solution dominates the other. If not, it checks whether one solution is preferred over the other, and finally if that is also not the case, the solution with the better diversity-based score is selected.

content: Besides changing the survival and mating selection operators, we also maintain an external archive (i.e. a representative subset of non-dominated solutions over the entire Pareto front) for the following reasons: First, due to the interactive optimization process, the current population will converge towards being fully contained in the current best leaf. To ask comparisons of items falling in different leaves we need to store a representative subset of non-dominated solutions over the entire Pareto front. Second, NSGA, especially when including preference information, can end up with dominated solutions when the true Pareto front is disconnected [ 52 ] . Using the external archive in the non-dominated sorting step in the survival operator, can detect these dominated solutions and ensure only non-dominated solutions are returned. Finally, when the preference model shifts towards a new region, for example due to a change of preferences of the DM, the archive can help in quickly determining the new Pareto front. In particular, by merging the current population with the external archive upon a preference shift, we can quickly find solutions close to the new preferred region.

We employ artificial DMs that generate the preference statements used by the algorithms. For robustness, we sample 50 different artificial DMs and use them to run 50 repeated trials for each problem. Code to reproduce all experiments is available at: https://github.com/Thomasq99/DT-PBO-NSGA .

content: We compare our method with two peer methods, one interpretable alternative and one state-of-the-art black-box alternative. First, DT-EMOA [ 20 ] , which is conceptually the closest method to our proposed algorithm. It uses an interpretable decision-tree-based preference model. Specifically, it learns a decision tree over the difference in objective vectors and is therefore less interpretable than our method, which learns a global decision tree directly on the objective space. DT-EMOA uses NSGA-II as the base evolutionary algorithm. Note that there is an extension of DT-EMOA, called RF-EMOA [ 43 ] to include active learning by using a random forest model instead of a decision tree. However, by using an ensemble of models instead of a single decision tree the interpretability is significantly reduced. Therefore, to ensure a comparison with a competitive method that retains a high degree of interpretability, we compare our approach with DT-EMOA rather than RF-EMOA. Finally, DT-EMOA requires a DM to rank a set of q q solutions from which ( q 2 ) \binom{q}{2} pairwise comparisons are generated. To compare to DT-PBO-NSGA and PBO-R-NSGA-III, which both require a DM to answer a set of j j pairwise comparisons, we set the number of items that the DM has to rank to q = j + 1 q=j+1 , as under transitivity, a ranking of n n items can be represented by q − 1 q-1 pairwise comparisons.

Since Gaussian processes are inherently black-box algorithms, the learned preference model is not interpretable. However, Gaussian processes are data-efficient models that allow for active learning, which makes them very suitable as black-box preference models. Before learning the preference model, PBO-R-NSGA-III uses a balanced reference direction with a large region of interest (determined by R-NSGA-III’s μ \mu parameter, μ = 1.0 \mu=1.0 ) and runs R-NSGA-III [ 53 ] . After learning the preference model, the best known point is identified which is then used as the reference direction with a reduced μ = 0.1 \mu=0.1 .

content: To evaluate DT-PBO-NSGA, a diverse set of benchmark problems is employed. The ZDT [ 51 ] suite (ZDT5 is excluded due to its discrete decision variables) is used for bi-objective scenarios, providing test cases with convex, non-convex, multimodal, disconnected, and non uniform Pareto fronts. To evaluate performance in higher-dimensional settings, the DTLZ [ 54 ] and WFG [ 55 ] suites are used. Since holistic pairwise comparisons are only cognitively valid up to 5 dimensions [ 56 ] , the number of objectives is restricted to M ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 } M\in\{3,4,5\} . The DTLZ suite provides problems with a range of Pareto-front geometries and optimization characteristics, including linear, spherical, degenerate, and disconnected fronts, as well as multimodal landscapes. However, its decision-space constructions are generally relatively regular and often separable. The WFG suite complements DTLZ by introducing more complex decision-space transformations, including bias, deception, non-separability, and parameter dependencies. Together, these benchmark suites enable a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm’s ability to converge toward the Pareto front. Inspired by Tomczyk and Kadziński [ 44 ] the problem settings were set as described in Table II .

content: The performance of each algorithm is evaluated using two metrics: mean utility and best-point utility. Mean utility is defined as the average (mean) utility of the final population, whereas best-point utility is the minimum utility of the final population. Below we focus on results aggregated by dimensionality to provide a concise overview of how performance scales with the number of objectives. Both across runs and across dimensionality, metrics are aggregated by the median instead of the mean to mitigate the effect of outliers caused by bad runs. Additional experimental results are summarized below, with detailed information provided in the Supplementary Material.

content: To examine how algorithmic performance changes with the problem’s number of objectives, Table III reports the results of the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests grouped by problem dimensionality. Compared with the interpretable baseline DT-EMOA, our method performs particularly well on bi-objective problems, significantly outperforming DT-EMOA in 21 out of 25 cases for average utility and all cases for best-point utility. For three-objective problems, average utility is approximately balanced between the two algorithms, whereas best-point utility strongly favors DT-PBO-NSGA. As the number of objectives increases to four and five, DT-PBO-NSGA is increasingly outperformed in terms of average utility, whilst maintaining a strong advantage in best-point utility. A similar divergence between the two utility measures is observed when comparing DT-PBO-NSGA with PBO-R-NSGA-III, a black-box baseline. For bi-objective problems, neither algorithm shows a clear advantage on either metric. As the number of objectives increases, PBO-R-NSGA-III increasingly outperforms DT-PBO-NSGA in terms of average utility. In contrast, best-point utility increasingly favors DT-PBO-NSGA from three objectives onward. Overall, these results indicate that, as the number of objectives increases, the relative performance of DT-PBO-NSGA in terms of average utility decreases, while its ability to identify high-utility individual solutions remains strong.

content: Figure 6 illustrates this trade-off in greater detail by visualizing the relative performance compared to standard NSGA. Comparing DT-PBO-NSGA to the baselines, we see that, as the dimensionality increases, DT-PBO-NSGA consistently achieves lower best-point utility at the cost of a slightly higher average utility. On average, for bi-objective problems, DT-PBO-NSGA and PBO-R-NSGA-III have similar performance whereas both outperform DT-EMOA. For three-objective problems they both outperform DT-EMOA but DT-PBO-NSGA has a slightly better best point utility and slightly worse average utility than PBO-R-NSGA-III. The trade-off becomes more pronounced in higher dimensions. Specifically, for 4-objective problems, DT-PBO-NSGA reduces the average utility with approximately 41% at the cost of an increase of best-point utility of 7%. PBO-R-NSGA-III and DT-EMOA reduce the average utility with 48% and 43% respectively, but do so at the cost of 76% and 131% worse best point utility. The additional 7 to 2 percentage point reduction in average utility thus comes at the cost of a large increase of best point utility of 69 and 124 percentage points respectively. For 5-objective problems the effect is similar. DT-PBO-NSGA reduces the average utility with 34% at the cost of a 22% higher best point utility whilst PBO-R-NSGA-III and DT-EMOA reduce the average utility with 53% and 43% at the cost of 109% and 184% best point utility respectively. These results indicate that, in higher-dimensional problems, DT-PBO-NSGA offers a somewhat smaller reduction in average utility but has a significantly higher best-point utility than PBO-R-NSGA-III and DT-EMOA.

content: These results are caused by DT-PBO-NSGA being more conservative in reducing the size of the final population for higher-dimensional problems. Figure 7 shows the reduction of the final population size as compared to standard NSGA. The final population size is measured by the diagonal length of the bounding box spanning the final population for each dimensionality. Compared to the baselines, as the problem’s number of objectives increases, DT-PBO-NSGA retains an increasingly larger bounding-box diagonal, indicating that its final population spans a larger region of the objective space. Thus, the higher average utility of DT-PBO-NSGA is caused by preserving a broader set of candidate solutions, while its lower best-point utility indicates that this broader population more often contains the most preferred solution.

content: To check whether performance differs between artificial DMs based on the Stewart and Chebyshev utility functions, we aggregate the results per utility function. Table IV reports the average ranks of the methods based on the average utility and best-point utility. There is relatively little performance difference between the Chebyshev DM and the Stewart cases 1 and 2 while the limited-compensation cases 3 and 4 differ from the other 3. This is most visible for DT-EMOA, which has its worst best-point ranks on these cases (2.92 and 2.89) and whose average rank drops from best on Chebyshev and Stewart case 2 to worst on Stewart case 3 (2.38) and near worst for Stewart case 4. Figure 15 in the supplementary material helps explain these differences by visualizing each utility function. Stewart cases 3 and 4 have a broad, flat region of near-optimal utility in the middle of the Pareto front and steep increases towards its extremes, where one objective falls below the reference level. The effect of a given change in objective values thus strongly depends on where a solution lies in the objective space. DT-EMOA learns from pairwise differences between objective vectors and therefore cannot represent this positional dependence. For the Chebyshev function and Stewart cases 1 and 2, the utility is closer to locally linear along the front, so pairwise differences remain informative, consistent with DT-EMOA’s good average ranks on these functions. DT-PBO-NSGA is trained on absolute objective values and does not suffer from this limitation, which explains its strong best-point ranks on cases 3 and 4.

content: In the supplementary material additional results are presented. First, for each method we test its robustness against noise. In particular, we generate noisy artificial DMs by corrupting their answers with randomly generated Gaussian noise. Results show that all three methods are relatively robust against noise. Second, across various degrees of noise, we investigate the effect of varying DT-PBO-NSGA’s λ \lambda which controls the degree of exploration vs exploitation. As expected, results show that one should decrease λ \lambda , focusing more on exploration, as the level of noise increases. Third, detailed benchmark results showing performance for each individual benchmark problem are presented. These results show largely the same behavior as described in the main experiments. One noteworthy exception is DT-PBO-NSGA’s poor performance on DTLZ5 and DTLZ6. For these problems, the Pareto front is effectively reduced to a single curve, for which the curvature is difficult to capture using axis-aligned splits. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of each method’s performance on the 3- and 5-dimensional DTLZ1, 2, and 7 problems, showing both convergence plots and population plots.

content: To demonstrate the interpretability of the learned preference model, we conduct a case study on the real-world RE34 problem [ 60 ] . This engineering problem concerns the crashworthiness of a vehicle and has three easily interpretable objectives, all of which are minimized: vehicle weight, crash-induced acceleration/deceleration, and passenger-compartment intrusion. The lower crash-induced acceleration/deceleration reduces the forces experienced by the occupants, while the lower intrusion into the passenger-compartment reduces the deformation of the occupant space and, consequently, the risk of injury. The weight of the vehicle should be minimized as the goal is a lightweight design.

content: To test our algorithm, we use the same algorithm settings described in the main experiments (thus 4 × 3 4\times 3 pairwise comparisons asked) and use a Chebyshev artificial DM. After asking 12 questions in total we get a final population and a learned decision tree. The algorithm’s final population can be found in Figure 8 . It shows that the learned ROI is centered at the DM’s most preferred point and that it is relatively small compared to the global Pareto front. The learned tree can be found in Figure 9 . It shows that according to the DM’s answers the best vehicles have a cabin intrusion lower than 0.07m, a collision deceleration lower than 8.33 m/s and a vehicle weight higher or equal to 1676.34 kgs. The reason that a higher vehicle weight is preferred as the last decision rule is that allowing for a higher vehicle weight results in a lower Collision Deceleration and/or Cabin Intrusion. The least preferred vehicle designs fall on the right side of the tree and are vehicles with a Cabin intrusion higher or equal to 0.07m. Besides the tree partitioning, Pareto optimality also induces some geometry on the final ROI. This is shown in the best leaf where the final identified ROI is the region with Vehicle weight between 1676.42-1679.88 kgs, Collision deceleration between 7.42-8.33 m/s and Compartment intrusion between 0.06-0.07 meters. Additionally, the bar graphs in the best leaf show the ROI size and location compared to the global Pareto front. For this specific artificial DM the identified ROI focuses mostly on lower Cabin intrusion, medium vehicle weight and low to medium Collision Deceleration. The preference model’s interpretability enables the DM to get valuable insights and make changes if desired.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: We proposed a novel interactive evolutionary algorithm DT-PBO-NSGA that uses an interpretable tree-based preference model. The model is learned from pairwise comparisons and supports active learning. Its decision-tree structure provides an interpretable partitioning of the objective space based on the DM’s preferences. Each leaf is ranked and this information is used to adapt NSGA’s survival and mating selection operators to guide the population towards the identified ROI. Specifically, a preference-based sorting step is added in between NSGA’s dominance-based and diversity-based sorting.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Extensive experiments across the ZDT, DTLZ, and WFG benchmark suites comparing DT-PBO-NSGA with another interpretable alternative DT-EMOA and a black-box algorithm PBO-R-NSGA-III showed that DT-PBO-NSGA performs particularly well on lower-dimensional problems and maintains a favorable trade-off as the number of objectives increases. While its performance in terms of average utility is slightly worse than DT-EMOA and PBO-R-NSGA-III in higher dimensions, DT-PBO-NSGA has a much better best-point utility. This behavior is mainly caused by its more conservative reduction of the final population, preserving a broader region of the objective space and thereby increasing the likelihood of finding the best solution. Furthermore, results aggregated per utility function show that DT-EMOA performs particularly poorly on Stewart utility functions of type 3 and 4. DT-EMOA cannot model these based on the difference in objective vectors. DT-PBO-NSGA, on the other hand, learns directly from the objective vectors and can therefore model these positional dependencies. Overall, these results show that DT-PBO-NSGA is competitive and interpretable, particularly when finding the most preferred solution is more important than finding a set of final solutions that are all good. Additionally, a case study on the real-world RE34 vehicle crashworthiness problem demonstrated the interpretability of the proposed approach. DT-PBO-NSGA identified an ROI close to the most preferred solution, while the learned decision tree revealed that the artificial DM’s preferences were primarily driven by minimizing cabin intrusion.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
content: Future work could focus on many interesting directions. First, future work could extend decomposition- and indicator-based algorithms with DT-PBO’s preference model. Secondly, the tree-based preference model makes axis-aligned splits and can thus have difficulty accommodating preference functions that do not follow these axes. Third, the learned decision tree does not inherently enforce monotonicity, even though preferences in MOPs are generally assumed to be monotonic with respect to the objectives. Incorporating this assumption directly into the model could improve learning efficiency by eliminating the need to infer these relationships from the preference data. Finally, experiments using real-world decision-makers can be done to validate the learned preference model’s interpretability and its performance in real-life settings.

content: In practice, there is no guarantee that DMs give consistent answers. Therefore, we test each algorithm’s robustness against inconsistencies. To do so, we introduce Gaussian noise into the artificial DM’s value function, such that ( v noise = v + ϵ ) (v_{\text{noise}}=v+\epsilon) , where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) . For each object, noise is independently sampled, and the resulting noisy values are used to determine the DM’s preference statement. We repeat the experiments for different values of σ \sigma , with larger values corresponding to increasingly noisy DM responses. The results are shown in Figure 10 . Although performance generally decreases as the noise level increases, all three methods, including DT-PBO-NSGA, remain relatively robust to moderate levels of noise.

content: DT-PBO-NSGA has a hyperparameter λ \lambda that determines the level of exploration vs exploitation. A lower value of λ \lambda focuses more on exploration and a higher value on exploitation. Figure 11 shows the averaged (by median) best-point utility and average utility (lower is better) of all problems and utility functions when varying both the level of noise σ \sigma and λ \lambda . For one noise level, one can see that the average utility decreases when λ \lambda decreases. For the best-point utility this is reversed. This is expected, as with a higher λ \lambda more exploitation happens, which reduces the size of the region of interest which in turn reduces the average utility. At the same time, reducing the size of the region of interest can cause it to miss the most preferred solution, therefore, increasing the best-point utility. For noiseless DMs, a very high λ \lambda has the best tradeoff, compared to a balanced λ = 1.5 \lambda=1.5 the median best-point utility is worsened by 0.03 0.03 but the average utility is improved by 0.21 0.21 . For noisy decision-makers (e.g. σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 ), a very high λ \lambda is generally outperformed by a conservative or balanced λ \lambda . For example, λ = 1.5 \lambda=1.5 improves the best-point utility by 0.15 0.15 whilst having the same average utility. The optimal choice of λ \lambda thus depends on the level of inconsistencies present in the DM’s answers.

content: For completeness, we have included detailed benchmark results. Specifically, for each benchmark problem we have aggregated on the utility functions and runs. The medians of the average utility of the final population, standard deviations of average utility, and average ranks are shown in Table V . Similarly, for the best-point utility the results can be found in Table VI . The results largely follow the same trend as presented in the main paper. Namely, compared to DT-PBO-NSGA, as the problem dimensionality increases, both PBO-R-NSGA-III and DT-EMOA get an increasingly better average utility but also an increasingly worse best-point utility. The main exception to the trend are the problems DTLZ5 and DTLZ6, for which DT-PBO-NSGA performs poorly. These problems both have a Pareto front geometry that largely reduces to a curve in high-dimensional space. Since DT-PBO-NSGA makes axis-aligned splits it has trouble making rectangular splits that follow the curvature of the Pareto front.

section: A-D Detailed Analysis of DTLZ1,2, and 7
content: As the benchmark suite is too large to provide a detailed analysis for every individual problem, we focus on a small diverse subset. Specifically, we select DTLZ1, 2, and 7, as these problems have different Pareto front geometries. They are linear and multimodal, concave, and disconnected respectively. Moreover, for these results we only use Chebyshev generated artifical DMs. Figure 12a and Figure 12b show convergence behavior by plotting the average utility and best-point utility over the amount of iterations ran. One can see that before any preference information is included DT-EMOA’s base optimizer, NSGA-II, struggles with converging towards the Pareto front. This is caused by all solutions becoming non-dominated in higher dimensions. After introducing preference information, selection pressure is reintroduced and DT-EMOA’s performance improves. However, for DTLZ1 it remains far off the other methods.

title: An Interactive Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization Algorithm Based on Interpretable Active Preference Learning
authors: Thomas Quadt, Boris Čule, Roy Lindelauf, Herman Monsuur, Mark Voskuijl
section: A-D Detailed Analysis of DTLZ1,2, and 7
content: The average utility convergence plots nicely illustrate what happens after preference information is introduced. Shortly after each preference round (denoted by the dashed vertical black lines), the average utility sharply drops as the model converges to the identified ROI. One can also see that those drops are usually smaller for DT-PBO-NSGA, indicating that the identified ROI is still larger than that of DT-EMOA and PBO-R-NSGA-III. The best-point utility plots, on the other hand, show that the best-point utility can actually increase after a preference elicitation round. This occurs when the ROI does not contain the most preferred solution.

content: The final population plots for the three-objective problems shown in Figure 13 show the same trend observed before. DT-EMOA and PBO-R-NSGA-III find very small ROIs which reduce the average utility substantially. However, often the small ROIs do not actually contain the best point itself. For example, DTLZ 2 trial 0 both PBO-R-NSGA-III and DT-EMOA find ROIs far away from the most preferred solution. DT-PBO on the other hand maintains a much larger ROI but more often contains the best point. 5-dimensional population plots are included in Figure 14 . These plots generally show the same trend, but also have some noteworthy differences. First, for DTLZ1 trial 2, DT-EMOA’s final population diverges away from the Pareto front. This is likely caused by NSGA-II’s poor performance in high-dimensional settings. For DTLZ2 trial 2 one can see that PBO-R-NSGA-III has a very concentrated ROI but it is very far from the most preferred solution. DT-PBO-NSGA, on the other hand, has a much broader ROI but does include the Most preferred solution.

content: In Figure 15 , we visualize the utility values along the Pareto front of ZDT1 for five randomly generated instances of each utility function type. The Chebyshev utility is piecewise linear, with a single kink at the most preferred point. Stewart cases 1 and 2 vary more gradually along the front, although case 2 shows sharp local steps close to the optimum. Stewart cases 3 and 4, in contrast, exhibit long, flat valleys of near-optimal utility bounded by steep increases towards the extremes of the front, which level off near the boundary in some instances. For these cases, the effect of a change in objective values on utility therefore depends strongly on the position of a solution along the front.
