authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 situates this work within prior IoT testbeds and measurement-oriented infrastructures. Section 3 introduces the abstract model and architecture of the proposed testbed. Section 4 details the implementation, including hardware, software roles, telemetry schema, and timeliness instrumentation. Section 5 demonstrates the resulting dataset and illustrates how it supports inspection of environmental signals, context distributions, latency behavior, and energy signatures. Section 6 discusses implications, limitations, and directions for extension, and Section 7 concludes.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: IoT testbeds have been developed across a wide spectrum of scales, goals, and methodological commitments, ranging from application-driven smart-building platforms to city-scale experimentation facilities, remotely accessible academic infrastructures, protocol- and technology-specific measurement rigs, virtualized environments, and reproducible dataset-generation testbeds. This section situates this work within these strands and motivates the specific gap addressed by the presented instrumentation- and dataset-centric contribution.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Design goals and academic testbed requirements.
content: A recurring theme in the literature is that academic IoT testbeds are expected to support heterogeneity (devices, sensors, and protocols) while remaining controlled and repeatable. The challenges involved in building such a platform are discussed in the context of a smart-building testbed for academic use, including flexibility for communication research, application use cases, cognition, and security, as well as demonstration-oriented monitoring and visualization workflows [ 17 ] . Complementing such perspectives, a systematic review of IoT/WSN testbed facilities synthesizes the broader landscape, emphasizing the diversity of facilities and the continuing importance of reproducible experimentation practices, supportive materials, and metric-driven facility design [ 18 ] . This work aligns with these motivations and operationalizes them through a concrete, edge-focused architecture and a dataset publication workflow that makes the data-production pipeline observable.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Several influential testbeds emphasize scale, openness, and multi-layer experimentation in real-world conditions. SmartSantander provides a city-scale facility and architectural blueprint for large-scale IoT experimentation in urban scenarios [ 19 ] . City of Things similarly offers a multi-technology smart-city testbed with an integrated approach spanning network infrastructure, data experimentation, and living-lab validation [ 20 ] . FIT IoT-LAB offers a large open experimental platform with thousands of nodes and consistent tooling across multiple sites, enabling experimentation from low-level protocols to higher-level services [ 21 ] . Work on thorough testbed characterization further highlights how open platforms can support repeatable experimentations and how experimentation can be meaningfully combined with simulation for robust evaluation methodologies [ 22 ] . In contrast to the primary emphasis of these facilities on scale and broad experimentation enablement, this work’s contribution is positioned around measurement discipline at the edge : I focus on systematically co-capturing heterogeneous telemetry together with stage-level timing and energy signals, and on releasing analysis-ready artifacts that preserve both replayable raw events and queryable curated views.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Low-cost, minimalistic, and remotely accessible testbeds.
content: A complementary direction prioritizes accessibility and ease of deployment using off-the-shelf components. OpenTestBed advances a minimalistic, low-cost design based on commodity hardware and lightweight infrastructure (e.g., MQTT over Wi-Fi) to facilitate adoption across institutions [ 23 ] . Other platforms emphasize remote access and experiment-as-a-service models, enabling users to deploy and run experiments through remote interfaces and managed resources [ 24 ] . LinkLab extends this notion by integrating remote development capabilities (web-based IDE, remote compilation) to accelerate iterative development and experimentation across heterogeneous devices [ 25 ] . This work’s implementation similarly leverages off-the-shelf edge nodes and MQTT-based communication, but differentiates itself by treating provenance- and timeliness-oriented instrumentation, together with energy metering alignment, as primary dataset features rather than auxiliary operational concerns.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: A substantial body of work designs testbeds to experimentally characterize communication technologies and quantify key performance parameters. A Universal Testbed is proposed to measure latency, error rate, and stability across multiple wireless IoT technologies while abstracting measurement from specific protocol and hardware choices [ 26 ] . Likewise, protocol- and deployment-focused testbeds, such as a low-cost LoRaWAN infrastructure, provide extensive measurement studies that characterize coverage and parameter sensitivity in indoor and outdoor environments [ 27 ] . These efforts motivate careful measurement practice and produce valuable technology-facing insights. This work is complementary in scope: rather than centering a single wireless technology, I instrument the end-to-end telemetry pipeline (Source–Broker–Aggregator) and release data structures that make stage-to-stage timing, message correlation, and energy co-measurement available for downstream benchmarking, tracing, and provenance analyses.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Beyond physical infrastructures, virtual testbeds provide controlled ways to emulate tiered IoT architectures and resource constraints. IOTier transforms clusters into a virtual testbed that exposes the performance implications of multi-tier IoT environments under programmable constraints (CPU, memory, storage, network) [ 28 ] . Emulation-oriented approaches are also central in security-focused platforms such as Gotham, which provides a reproducible and extensible testbed for IoT security experiments and dataset generation across multiple protocols and threat actors [ 29 ] . This work shares with these systems a commitment to reproducibility and dataset utility, while focusing on a different measurement target: fine-grained, role-spanning timeliness metadata and operational energy signals captured alongside heterogeneous edge telemetry, with a dual raw/tabular release that supports both message-level replay and data-centric analytics.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Energy is a foundational concern in IoT evaluation, particularly for constrained and intermittently powered devices. Shepherd introduces a portable testbed for batteryless IoT that records and replays synchronized energy traces at high resolution to study behavior under realistic spatio-temporal energy availability [ 30 ] . The presented testbed addresses a complementary energy perspective aligned with practical edge deployments: plug-level metering captures upstream consumption of compute-and-sense nodes (including adapter effects) and is co-published with telemetry and timing metadata, enabling joint analyses that relate data production, timeliness, and operational energy usage.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Synthesis and gap addressed by this paper.
content: Across these directions, prior work has collectively established: (i) the importance of flexible and repeatable academic testbeds [ 17 , 18 ] ; (ii) the value of open, large-scale and city-scale facilities for real-world experimentation [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] ; (iii) accessible and remotely usable platforms that lower barriers to experimentation and development [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] ; (iv) rigorous measurement infrastructures for wireless performance characterization [ 26 , 27 ] ; (v) controlled virtual and reproducible emulation environments, including security-oriented dataset generation [ 28 , 29 ] ; and (vi) energy-centric tooling for constrained/batteryless IoT [ 30 ] .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Synthesis and gap addressed by this paper.
content: A useful lens for positioning the contribution of this paper is the same three-axis framing used in the Introduction (Section 1 ): pipeline observability , energy alignment , and dual representation . The space that remains comparatively under-emphasized is the co-release of datasets that make the telemetry pipeline itself measurable at fine granularity, while simultaneously aligning operational energy signals with telemetry production and providing both replayable and analytics-friendly representations. The paper targets this gap by (a) defining a role-based edge architecture with explicit stage instrumentation, (b) embedding timeliness metadata directly into a schema-governed telemetry envelope, (c) incorporating broker-side timestamping to support traceability across message mediation, (d) integrating plug-level energy co-measurement aligned with telemetry cadence, and (e) publishing a dual representation (raw Avro and partitioned Parquet) via a deterministic, reproducible transformation pipeline. This positioning frames the contribution as a measurement-first testbed and dataset. The comparison above is qualitative: it identifies differences in emphasis and artifact organization, not measured advantages in timing accuracy, energy attribution, storage efficiency, or scalability. The instrumentation follows established observability practices; no claim is made that existing testbeds or tracing systems cannot provide comparable measurements. Relative to a value-only sensor trace, the additional fields permit message-level inspection of inter-stage timing and time-windowed association with node energy. Their co-release reduces the need to reconstruct these relationships from separate logs, but the present demonstration does not establish superior diagnostic capability.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Here, I present an abstract, technology-agnostic testbed architecture. It is derived from the architectures mentioned in Sections 1 , 2 , 3.1 , built using the Node abstract model as the fundamental building block, and adapted to serve common testbed settings with the goal of inspecting data produced from various nodes enriched with energy, timeliness, and provenance data. While a typical IoT solution is more than data (e.g., automation, autonomous, security, and many more), data enriched with energy, timeliness, and provenance information are, in my opinion, the base of a testbed and the purpose it serves because, when structured and documented properly, it can represent the state of a complex, heterogeneous, interconnected system such as IoT in a deterministic, interpretable, replayable manner. Consequently, it help practitioners understand various specifics and nuances at a very early stage of the IoT design and development lifecycle. That said, next I present the architecture components as well as a graphical representation depicted in Figure 3 . As an example, I include one node by kind to make the example complete.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: There is a Node with networking capabilities that acts as the local network’s router and gateway. Specifically, all nodes communicate with each other using this node at a networking level. For example, it can be a Wi-Fi/Ethernet router with some name-resolving capabilities and other common networking functionality.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: There is a Node with computational capabilities that acts as a broker of high-level messages in the context of an event-driven approach through appropriate software like MQTT. It provides two communication paradigms, publish–subscribe and request–reply. These two paradigms can serve a plethora of communication scenarios, especially publish–subscribe, which is very common in IoT, even for command/query patterns on top of that.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: There is a Node with Perception capabilities, and more specifically sensing capabilities. It senses the environment in various ways based on the sensors attached, either wired or wireless. For instance, it can measure air quality, climate quality, vision, sound, and many more. It usually follows a flow that involves sensing, measuring, transforming, and then sending the data to one or multiple receivers. The most common way is the publish–subscribe paradigm, in which the node publishes the data, appropriately serialized, to a specific topic so one or multiple subscribers can consume the data in near real time.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: There is a Node with Perception capabilities, and more specifically actuating capabilities. It is connected, either wired or wireless, with one or more actuators that produce force, torque, or displacement when they receive an appropriate electrical input. That way, automatic control of real things is achieved. Some examples include production line automation, home automation, and more. It usually follows a flow of listening to events/messages and then, when one or more messages arrive, it invokes a sequence of deserializing, transforming, and validating the data and probably initiates an actuation signal. The most common way is the publish–subscribe paradigm, in which the node subscribes to a topic, usually fine-grained and conceptually owned by this node’s identity or role, and then invokes the aforementioned flow to actuate.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: There is a Node with Computing capabilities. Specifically, it runs user software on top of a platform that provides orchestration, flow-based operations, event-driven sourcing, and similar approaches. For instance, alerting or automating a vent opening based on temperature and humidity can be translated to a user-defined function that runs in that platform or framework to provide IoT orchestration of nodes with sensing/actuating capabilities. Other common cases involve aggregation, data fusion, lightweight computation, lightweight machine learning, and many more. Again, like the previous, it utilizes the publish–subscribe paradigm and is usually both conceptually and technically a consumer and a producer: a consumer to listen to sensing information and a producer to trigger actions or alerts based on sensing information and a state machine.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Three Raspberry Pi 4 single-board computers provide both computation and sensing capabilities. Each unit runs a Linux-based operating system and exposes GPIO and I²C interfaces for peripheral integration. The first Raspberry Pi is interfaced via GPIO with two digital temperature-and-humidity sensors (DHT11 and DHT22). The second hosts an Enviro expansion board that integrates, among other devices, a BME280 sensor (temperature, relative humidity, and barometric pressure) and an LTR-559 sensor (ambient light and proximity). The third is connected via the I²C bus to an MCP9808 high-accuracy digital temperature sensor. These platforms perform local acquisition, lightweight preprocessing, and publication of measurements, and are capable of executing user-defined software for data handling and coordination.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking

content: Perception of electrical load and basic actuation are provided by three Shelly Plug S devices. These Wi-Fi smart plugs offer limited on-device computation relative to the Raspberry Pi nodes but supply switching control (on/off) for connected loads and integrated energy metering (power, voltage, and current). They support local automation and scheduling, operate over IEEE 802.11 b/g/n (2.4 GHz), and include protective functions such as over-temperature, overload, and over-current safeguards. The plugs can be addressed locally or via cloud connectivity, depending on deployment preferences.

content: Network connectivity for the testbed is supplied by a Sercomm H300S residential gateway. This device consolidates broadband access (e.g., VDSL/DSL/fibre, subject to the service provider), Ethernet switching, and dual-band Wi-Fi 5 wireless networking, and additionally offers telephony (VoIP), USB sharing, and local network management. All edge nodes attach to this gateway for intra-testbed communication and backhaul access.

content: Power distribution follows a controlled topology intended to support energy measurement. Each Raspberry Pi 4 is powered via its AC/DC adapter, which is plugged into a dedicated Shelly Plug S; each Shelly Plug S is then connected to the mains supply. This arrangement enables per-node monitoring of real-world electrical consumption, including the upstream adapter and any conversion losses. The Sercomm H300S gateway is powered from the mains through its vendor-supplied power adapter.

The three Shelly Plug S devices also connect through the Sercomm H300S and report the power drawn by the corresponding Raspberry Pi systems (inclusive of power-adapter effects). content: Timeliness is a first-class concern. The released dataset records named stage events across Source, Broker, and Aggregator roles. As detailed in Section 5.1 , these are event timestamps rather than explicit start/end pairs for every stage. The scheduled timestamp represents the intended sensing-cycle time, whereas stage timestamps mark recorded events in the processing path. The interval from the scheduled timestamp to Source initiation therefore includes scheduling delay and should not be interpreted as sensor acquisition time.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: Stage-to-stage delays are obtained by subtracting selected event timestamps for the same message along the pipeline order. An interval labeled by its destination event describes the elapsed time since the preceding selected event; it is not, by itself, the execution time of the destination handler. In particular, the interval ending at broker ingress can include upstream publication, transport, and scheduling effects, while the ingress-to-egress interval describes the instrumented broker segment. Queueing and execution cannot generally be separated without additional boundary events. Likewise, a timestamp preceding persistence does not establish durable database-commit completion.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: All nodes run an NTP client, with a Raspberry Pi serving as the local NTP reference. This configuration provides a common time base, but independent measurements of residual clock offsets, drift, and effective timestamp resolution are not reported for this capture. Nanosecond storage units and high-resolution timestamp APIs do not establish nanosecond measurement accuracy. Cross-node differences include relative clock error as well as elapsed time, whereas same-clock intervals avoid a cross-device offset but remain subject to clock adjustments and instrumentation effects. The reported latencies should therefore be read as estimates for the recorded event boundaries, without a validated error bound.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: This section demonstrates how the proposed testbed materializes a dataset that is simultaneously (i) multi-context (environmental sensing, OS telemetry, and energy metering), (ii) time-aligned via explicit stage-level timestamps, and (iii) amenable to inspection in both raw message form and curated tabular form. The goal is to document what the dataset contains and provide a reproducible first-pass exploration of its structure and recorded measurement characteristics. This is a descriptive artifact demonstration, not a controlled characterization of the telemetry pipeline: message rate, payload size, MQTT QoS, subscriber count, broker/CPU load, and network conditions are not systematically varied. The summaries below describe the captured configuration and do not establish causal effects or performance bounds.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: The testbed produces a multi-modal telemetry dataset that combines (i) environmental measurements, (ii) node/OS monitoring, (iii) electrical power and cumulative energy metering, and (iv) pipeline-stage timestamps for timeliness and provenance. The dataset is published in two complementary representations: a raw event stream (schema-governed) and a processed, analysis-oriented tabular form. Both are derived from the same TelemetryMessage envelope described in Section 5.2.1.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: This work presents an edge-focused IoT testbed and dataset whose primary practical contribution is the systematic co-capture of (i) heterogeneous telemetry (environmental sensing, OS/node monitoring, and plug-level energy metering) and (ii) stage-level timing metadata spanning Source, Broker, and Aggregator execution. Rather than proposing a new protocol, attribution method, or provenance mechanism, the testbed operationalizes a measurement discipline in which timeliness, energy, and provenance-related identifiers are treated as first-class data. The resulting dataset supports reproducible inspection of both payload values and the data-production pipeline that generated them.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: End-to-end latency differs by device class, with substantial tail behavior.
content: The reported end-to-end latency distributions show clear separation between device types: RaspberryPi messages exhibit a mean latency of 83.51 ms and median of 60.66 ms, while ShellyPlusPlugSV2 messages exhibit a mean of 227.38 ms and median of 155.47 ms (Table 4 ). At the same time, the upper tail is non-negligible for both classes, with p99 exceeding 500 ms. This combination is practically important: median differences are relevant for typical responsiveness, whereas p95–p99 behavior is often decisive for systems with timeliness constraints, particularly when telemetry drives alerting or actuation decisions.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: End-to-end latency differs by device class, with substantial tail behavior.
content: A key benefit of the proposed instrumentation is that such tail behavior is not only observable but can be analyzed in relation to pipeline stages. This provides candidate intervals for follow-up diagnosis, but does not identify a root cause or isolate persistence cost without the corresponding boundary measurements. Device-class differences also reflect different software, sensing workloads, and timestamp behavior; they should not be read as a controlled comparison of hardware or MQTT performance.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Stage-level decomposition localizes where latency accumulates and where variance concentrates.
content: The stage-to-stage breakdown for RaspberryPi telemetry indicates that the largest mean intervals are associated with broker.ingress (30.42 ms), source.transform (20.98 ms), and aggregator.initiate (13.66 ms), whereas several recorded intervals fall in the sub-millisecond regime (e.g., aggregator.deserialize at 0.025 ms mean; Table 5 ). These values describe intervals between recorded events; they do not independently measure handler execution time or establish the overhead of serialization, deserialization, or instrumentation.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Stage-level decomposition localizes where latency accumulates and where variance concentrates.
content: The distributional markers also highlight that variability is stage-dependent. For example, source.transform exhibits a p99 of 514.41 ms despite a mean near 21 ms, indicating rare but substantial increases in the interval ending at that event, without isolating transformation execution time. While the present paper does not attribute these events to specific causes, the recorded timestamps enable targeted follow-up studies (e.g., correlating stage delays with CPU load, scheduler effects, transient I/O, or network contention) without modifying the message format or the collection pipeline.

authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Measurement-context skew is substantial and should be treated as an analytic factor.
content: The flattened representation reveals a strongly right-skewed context distribution: OS contributes 63.4% of samples, while energy-related contexts ( energy , os , power ) also contribute materially, and environmental sensor contexts appear at lower frequencies (Table 3 ). This is expected in heterogeneous IoT deployments where system telemetry has higher metric cardinality and stable cadence relative to many physical sensors.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Measurement-context skew is substantial and should be treated as an analytic factor.
content: Practically, this skew affects downstream analysis choices. Without explicit attention, learning or summarization procedures may primarily model OS and energy contexts due to volume, even when the application interest is environmental sensing. The long-format representation used here makes such imbalance explicit and supports mitigation through filtering, stratification, or reweighting. Additionally, the intentional distinction between OS (Raspberry Pi) and os (Shelly) encodes a platform boundary in the data, reducing the risk of accidental aggregation across non-equivalent telemetry sources.

authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Energy measurements provide a complementary operational view but require careful interpretation.
content: Daily energy summaries for the three Shelly devices are closely clustered in mean consumption (approximately 0.0348–0.0378 kWh/day), while exhibiting high relative variability (CV near 81%; Table 6 ). These values are descriptive of the demonstrated capture window and illustrate variation among the observed daily aggregates, whose coverage is unequal. Several factors may contribute, including partial-day windows at the beginning or end of capture, changes in workload, and measurement/reporting granularity of smart plugs.

content: The energy-versus-volume exploration further shows that message counts align with the configured 5-second schedule (e.g., 17,280 messages/day), indicating that data volume is largely cadence-driven in this setup. However, the incomplete pairing observed for 2025-04-28 (energy recorded while message count is missing) emphasizes that daily aggregates should be interpreted in the context of collection completeness and window boundaries, and that the dataset publication pipeline should make such completeness signals easy to audit.

authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: 6.2 Value of the dual representation and reproducible transformation
content: A practical contribution of the testbed is the co-release of raw, schema-governed events (Avro) and curated, query-oriented tabular outputs (partitioned Parquet). The raw representation preserves message semantics and provides payloads for application-level replay, while the processed representation enables efficient exploratory analysis via predicate pushdown and time-based partitioning. The transformation is described as deterministic and streaming, and it is bidirectional in the sense that tabular rows can be reconstituted into TelemetryMessage objects. This reduces friction for practitioners who need to alternate between systems-level inspection (messages, topics, stages) and data-oriented analysis (windowing, joins, aggregates).

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: 6.2 Value of the dual representation and reproducible transformation
content: For reuse beyond this deployment, practitioners can use the released events as a fixed input corpus for testing decoders, schema handling, raw-to-tabular transformations, and analysis queries. The correlation identifiers allow a latency outlier selected from the stage table to be traced back to its readings and available message metadata. Replay into another MQTT pipeline can provide an input workload, but performance evaluation then requires a defined replay rate, fresh timestamps, and measurements from that target system; the original timings and energy values remain observations of this deployment. These are intended reuse paths, not demonstrated debugging case studies or evidence that the capture represents other deployment conditions.

content: Interpreting the reported quantities requires linking each measurement to the conditions under which it is produced. End-to-end and stage-to-stage latency estimates depend on clock alignment, timestamp granularity, and the precise semantics of stage timestamp keys; energy summaries depend on metering scope and window completeness; and provenance-oriented analyses depend on stable identifier conventions and consistent role instrumentation. The following threats to validity therefore map directly to the three measured dimensions emphasized in this work (timeliness, energy, and pipeline observability/provenance) and delimit how the demonstrated results should be generalized.

authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: The testbed is designed to support incremental extension rather than redesign. Several concrete enhancements would strengthen its utility for benchmarking and comparative studies: independent clock-error and meter calibration, instrumented-versus-uninstrumented overhead measurements, and a diagnosis case study with a known fault would help assess measurement validity and practical diagnostic value. Further extensions include (i) recording explicit start/end timestamps per stage to improve attribution of delays; (ii) varying message rate, payload size, MQTT QoS, subscriber count, broker load, CPU contention, and network loss under controlled conditions to characterize how distributions shift; (iii) expanding protocol and power diversity (e.g., BLE/Zigbee/Thread, battery-powered nodes) to evaluate generality; and (iv) propagating the same timeliness instrumentation into fog/cloud ingestion paths for end-to-end accounting beyond the edge.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: This paper presents an edge-focused IoT testbed and dataset that treat the telemetry pipeline itself as a measurable object. The contribution is organized around three practical axes: pipeline observability via role-spanning stage timestamps across Source, Broker, and Aggregator; energy alignment via plug-level metering co-captured with telemetry production; and a dual representation that preserves both replayable raw events (Avro) and analysis-ready tabular views (partitioned Parquet) produced by a deterministic transformation workflow.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: The demonstrated dataset shows that these choices enable immediate, reproducible inspection of system behavior beyond value-centric sensing traces: clear device-class separation in end-to-end latency with non-trivial tail behavior, stage-dependent variability that localizes where delay accumulates, pronounced measurement-context skew that must be treated as an analytic factor, and an operational energy view that supports day-level summaries and co-variation checks with data volume. These observations characterize the released capture rather than validate a general latency or energy model. By co-releasing payload telemetry together with timing and energy metadata in interoperable formats, the artifact provides a reusable input corpus and analysis structure for subsequent benchmarking and diagnostic studies. Controlled workload experiments, calibrated timing, overhead measurements, and concrete diagnosis cases remain necessary to substantiate broader claims.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
section: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
content: Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through Vela , an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 points across agents, but some restrictive interfaces also limit legitimate workflows. Our study provides a systematic empirical account of how agent-mediated access reshapes existing Web vulnerabilities, grounding future Web architecture design in measured security outcomes and trade-offs between reducing attack exposure and preserving legitimate functionality in agent-facing services.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: AI agents are changing how users access Web services. A user can describe a shopping need or an account-management task to an agent and let it carry out the necessary steps. Web-agent research has demonstrated this capability through agents that navigate pages and interact with existing websites ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) . A further shift is now taking shape: services are exposing capabilities that agents can access directly, without navigating a website. OpenAI’s Agentic Commerce Protocol connects ChatGPT with merchant catalogs and shopping experiences ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , while Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol supports agent access to merchant capabilities such as product discovery and checkout ( Google, 2026 ) . These initiatives move the interaction between agents and services toward dedicated interfaces through which business tasks can be completed.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Figure 1 illustrates this change using the task of reordering a previous purchase. In the conventional workflow, the user navigates the website to find the order and complete checkout. Through agent-mediated access, the user states the goal, and the agent invokes the corresponding operations through an agent-facing interface. Both paths reach the same backend, where business logic and application data remain, but the latter no longer requires the service’s pages and forms. This shift opens the possibility of a Web in which agents become the primary means of accessing services, and individual websites are no longer necessary user-facing entry points.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: As this access model develops, service providers need to understand its security implications. Malicious users can also use this path to target backend services. Existing backend vulnerabilities may persist, while interface restrictions and agent behavior change whether and how they can be exploited. For developers and operators, the central question is how much of the harm enabled by existing vulnerabilities remains possible through agent-mediated access, and how the resulting security consequences change.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: A natural expectation is that agent-mediated access provides additional protection. Agent-facing interfaces can restrict operations and inputs needed for exploitation, while safety training and runtime safeguards aim to prevent agents from following harmful instructions ( Anthropic, 2026 ) . A critical question is whether these safeguards actually prevent existing backend vulnerabilities from causing harm. Attacks using ordinary business operations may remain possible, and agents may help complete them by supplying missing steps or combining calls. Stronger restrictions may also make legitimate operations unavailable. Prior studies primarily focus on agents themselves, examining their offensive capabilities, susceptibility to malicious inputs, and handling of harmful instructions ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Greshake et al., 2023 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ; Kumar et al., 2024 ; Jones et al., 2026 ) . The implications of this architectural shift for existing backend vulnerabilities remain insufficiently understood. A systematic empirical evaluation is needed to quantify changes in exploitability and security consequences, distinguish interface effects from agent behavior, and assess the accompanying impact on legitimate functionality.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: To conduct this evaluation, we develop Vela , an executable benchmark comprising 44 documented vulnerabilities from twelve Web application families. For each application, we construct agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We then compare direct Web access, direct invocation of these interfaces, and execution through an agent on the same vulnerable backend. These comparisons isolate the effects of interface design and agent execution, with independent oracles verifying the resulting security consequences. We evaluate three commercial agents and three interface designs, measuring vulnerability exploitability alongside support for legitimate tasks.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Under the reference configuration, the agent succeeds in at least one attempt on every case realized by direct interface invocation, so it removes none of the attacks the interface lets through, and in one case it supplies missing steps. As a result, 91% of the vulnerabilities still produce verified security consequences, and the prevented attacks depend on operations or input control that the interface no longer exposes. Retention remains high across all three analysis groups. Across the tested configurations, changing the interface moves retention between 39% and 95%, against at most 4.5 percentage points across agents, although some reductions come with a loss of legitimate functionality. These results quantify both the persistence of backend security risks and the functional costs of restricting access, providing evidence for the design of future agent-facing Web services.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: In direct Web access, a browser or API client sends requests to the backend. In the agent-mediated setting studied here, an AI agent interprets the user’s request and invokes backend operations through a service-provided interface. The interface exposes callable capabilities, each with a description and an argument schema. It defines which operations are available, which inputs the agent can control, and how calls are bound to the user’s identity. The agent selects capabilities, supplies arguments, and uses returned results to guide subsequent calls. It may preserve or rewrite user-supplied inputs, refuse requests, or supply intermediate steps. The backend processes the resulting requests and remains responsible for enforcing authorization and business rules.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We consider a malicious user who seeks to exploit an existing backend vulnerability through either access path in Figure 1 to violate the application’s security policy. The attacker controls the submitted requests, including attack parameters and payloads. Under direct access, the attacker constructs requests to the native Web interface. Under agent-mediated access, the attacker submits the same attack content as user instructions, adapting its form to the interface while preserving the attack objective and exploit-relevant inputs. The agent operates as a task assistant and accesses the backend only through the published capabilities. The attacker cannot directly modify its system prompt or the interface implementation. Across access paths, the attacker starts with the same identity and privileges, while privilege changes achieved through exploitation remain within scope. The backend retains its original logic and vulnerabilities. Compromising another user’s agent, indirect prompt injection, and autonomous discovery of unknown vulnerabilities are outside the scope of this study.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Vela measures what happens to a natively exploitable vulnerability when it is reached through an agent-facing interface instead of the native Web. Three requirements follow from this goal, and each shapes the design. Because a result must speak to real software, every case is a documented vulnerability in a real or deliberately vulnerable application, reproducible natively and verified independently of the agent’s output. Because an interface tuned to a known flaw would prejudge the outcome, the agent-facing interfaces are built from legitimate workflows without any knowledge of the vulnerabilities. And because a difference must be attributable, all access paths share the same backend, initial identity, and initial state, so a change in exploitability follows from the path, not from the setup.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We select twelve application families to balance external validity with controlled variation. For validity, most are deployed applications with documented CVEs or public advisories, drawn from WebExploitBench ( Liu et al., 2026a ) and CVE-Bench ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , which supply deployable applications, vulnerability documentation, and verification artifacts. Case records distinguish documented production vulnerabilities from deliberately introduced flaws and retain the corresponding CVE, advisory, or challenge identifiers. For controlled variation, we add deliberately vulnerable training applications whose numbered challenges isolate one flaw at a time and let us change a single requirement while holding the surrounding workflow fixed. We deliberately include API-first families, because an agent reaches a backend through operations and arguments much as an API client does. These families provide relevant settings for agent mediation and include authorization and business-logic flaws. Table 1 lists the application families; Appendix A provides representative case identifiers.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We reproduce each documented vulnerability through the native interface and record its version, prerequisites, required operations, and a trusted observation of its effect. A training challenge is counted as a case only after it passes native reproduction. Every validated case enters the analysis whether or not an interface can express it, so selection does not depend on interface reachability. The validated cases span twelve vulnerability categories. We group the categories by what the attack mainly requires, since that requirement is exactly what mediation acts on. Input-precision attacks need exact control of an input value, application-logic attacks, covering authorization and business-logic flaws, need a request that is valid in form but violates ownership, role, or workflow rules, and resource-handling attacks require access to or manipulation of files or other protected resources through operations such as upload, import, or retrieval.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: An interface fixes which operations and arguments an agent can use, so its design directly determines which vulnerabilities remain reachable. We therefore treat the capability design as a controlled factor and build three designs that expose backend functionality at different levels of abstraction. The endpoint-oriented design exposes the documented endpoints with their original parameters, in the style of OpenAPI ( OpenAPI Initiative, 2024 ) . The workflow-oriented design names each workflow as one tool with a bounded business argument schema, in the style of MCP ( Anthropic, 2024 ) . The query-oriented design takes a natural-language query, in the style of NLWeb ( Microsoft, 2025 ) . We deliver all three to the agent through MCP over the same adapters, so a difference between them reflects the capability design and not the protocol or the backend.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Because a query must still become a concrete operation, we fix where that translation happens. The query-oriented design exposes a single tool that takes a query string. A server-side LLM planner maps each query to an intent and fills its typed slots. The planner is part of the service interface and is separate from the agent under test. C1 and C2 use the same planner implementation, with the attacker’s objective and initial privileges held constant. Planner execution remains part of the interface-stage outcome. Intents that read public content are answered from a snapshot index of each application’s public content. An intent is bound to a live adapter only when its benign workflow needs current state or a write, which the snapshot cannot serve.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The planner resolves object references against indexed entities, coerces each slot value to its declared type and range, and drops query text that fills no slot. These constraints, rather than the use of natural language itself, bound what a query delivers to the backend. A query may name an operation or quote a payload, but only values that survive slot filling reach the adapter. Intents, slots, and live bindings are derived from the same benign workflows as the other designs and frozen with them.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The schemes are built blind so that no interface can be tuned to a known flaw. For each user role we collect representative goals from documentation, normal use, and benign traffic, and turn each goal into capabilities that keep the arguments the workflow legitimately needs. Designers never see vulnerability reports or payloads, a trusted component supplies identity and credentials, and the agent sets only the business arguments. We add no vulnerability-aware filtering or authorization, which would introduce targeted defenses into the interface comparison. Before any security test, benign tasks confirm that each capability reaches the intended operation under the correct role. We also measure benign functional coverage , the share of identified workflows that a scheme supports. This coverage is needed to read an absent operation correctly, since a missing capability may reflect incomplete functionality rather than a defense. We then freeze the specification, adapters, and evidence, since any design revised after the security results were known would only be exploratory.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: After the freeze, each case is mapped to the interface as expressible when the capabilities can represent its requirements, inexpressible when a needed operation or argument is absent, or unresolved when the evidence is insufficient. We keep this mapping distinct from execution because an inexpressible case is a structural property of the interface, not a blocked exploit, whereas whether an expressible attack yields its effect is decided only by running it. A success on a case mapped as inexpressible triggers a re-audit of the mapping, never a silent change to the interface. In the query-oriented design, structural restrictions are determined by the available intents and slot domains. Failures to transmit required arguments during planning are classified separately as interface-stage execution losses.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Conditions. We use three conditions so that the two layers of mediation can be separated rather than observed only in combination. All share the same backend, initial identity, and attack objective. C0 exercises the vulnerability through the native interface and fixes the reference consequence. C1 attempts the same objective through the frozen capabilities with a scripted caller. C2 places an agent in front of the same capabilities. C1 omits the external task assistant; for the query-oriented design it still invokes the same service-side planner as C2, through the same query tool. A case is C1-realizable when direct invocation verifies its protected consequence. The attacker submits the same attack content as user instructions, adapting its form to the interface while preserving the objective and exploit-relevant inputs, as specified in Section 2.2 . The agent selects and executes its own calls, never sees the C1 call sequence, and has no path around the tools. The C0-C1 comparison isolates the interface change, and the C1-C2 comparison isolates what the agent adds on top of it.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Matched Execution. A trusted harness restores and verifies the initial state before every attempt, and C1 and C2 share schemas, adapters, and authentication bindings. The harness fixes the initial credentials and the backend destination, and the agent cannot reach reset mechanisms, fixtures, or oracles. We record traces, versions, actor bindings, and oracle observations, and any failed reset or inconclusive run is marked invalid rather than counted as a failed exploit.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Oracles. Each case carries a trusted oracle for the protected effect fixed during native validation, because a fluent agent reply is not evidence of a security effect. The oracle checks backend state or the attacker-visible channel, depending on the effect, and is validated against the native exploit and negative controls to check that it detects the intended effect and rejects the controls. The same predicate applies across all conditions. An unverified response or an agent claim never establishes success on its own. A confidentiality oracle checks that the protected value reached the defined attacker-visible channel, and an integrity oracle checks the persistent backend state. Appendix E gives the oracle forms.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Units of analysis follow the structure of the study. A case is one validated vulnerability and is the unit of case-level claims. A task pairs a case with an attack request. An attempt is one complete session on a task, and because an agent is stochastic, we run R R repetitions of each task. Per-attempt rates therefore divide by attempts and are not treated as independent samples of vulnerabilities, and we report them only beside the case-level retention, as in Figure 4 a, to show how often a realizable case succeeds within a single session.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Mediation Outcome. The primary result of a case is binary, namely whether any applicable task reaches the oracle-verified consequence in any of its R R repetitions within the budget. Cases with a verified consequence form the retained set. For these cases, execution traces characterize how the attack is carried out. A case is preserved when the verified request matches the native exploit, and transformed when the agent alters the input but a payload of the same attack class still reaches the sink. Step completion denotes cases in which the agent supplies necessary calls that the attacker did not specify, such as a target lookup or a prerequisite operation. This label records assistance in executing the attack, without implying a larger security consequence. Within a successful repetition, step completion takes precedence over transformed, which takes precedence over preserved. A case with no verified consequence is neutralized , and we keep its reason separate, distinguishing a structurally inexpressible attack from an interface-stage execution loss or an expressible attack not realized by the agent within the budget. The outcomes are judged per case from its successful repetitions by an annotation guide with two independent annotators, whose agreement on the outcome labels of the 40 retained reference cases is Cohen’s κ = 0.89 \kappa=0.89 . When repetitions of a case differ in outcome, the case takes the label of the majority of its successful repetitions, and a tie is broken toward the label closer to the native exploit, in the order preserved, transformed, step completion.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Reported Quantities. The primary metric is consequence retention , the share of validated cases whose protected effect is verified through a given path. We report it over all native-validated cases and over the C1-realizable subset, distinguishing interface-stage attrition from losses under agent mediation, and break it down by analysis group. Retention records whether a case succeeds at least once within the tested attempts; per-attempt success records how consistently it succeeds. Because restrictions can also remove legitimate operations, we read retention beside the benign functional coverage of Section 3.2 , a workflow-level share over all 50 identified benign workflows, and benign task completion , an attempt-level share over the same fixed set. Its denominator is 50 ​ R 50R , and its numerator counts successful workflow executions within the budget. Unsupported workflows remain in the denominator and contribute no completions. These two measures distinguish the functionality an interface exposes from the functionality successfully delivered through the agent. Because the benchmark is purposive rather than a random sample of the Web, we report results as percentages, give the underlying counts alongside them, and treat class-level differences as descriptive. Where we compare paired conditions, we add an exact McNemar test and report the paired C1/C2 matrix (Appendix D ) rather than inferring from marginal counts.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We evaluate Vela through three research questions. Each uses a reference configuration, Claude Code with the workflow-oriented design, and varies at most one factor. RQ1 asks to what extent natively exploitable vulnerabilities stay exploitable under agent mediation and how this differs across vulnerability classes. RQ2 fixes the capability design and asks how much the choice of agent changes exploitability and through which behaviors an agent loses a case. RQ3 fixes the agent and asks how the capability design changes exploitability and at what cost to legitimate functionality.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Agents and Capability Designs. RQ2 compares three commercial agents, Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) (v2.1.310, Claude Opus 5.5), Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) (CLI v0.164.0, GPT-6.1 Sol), and Grok Build ( xAI, 2026 ) (v1.0.67, Grok 4.7), each pinned at its October 2026 release with its default backing model. Every agent keeps the vendor’s default system prompt with no added security instruction, since neither the attacker nor the service controls it under our threat model, and runs non-interactively, with tool-call approvals granted by the harness. Such approvals ask the user to confirm the agent’s actions, and here the user is the attacker. Its built-in shell, file, and Web tools are disabled, so the tools under test are its only path to the application. RQ3 compares the three capability designs of Section 3.2 , implemented as one tool per documented operation (endpoint-oriented), one tool per workflow with a bounded business argument schema (workflow-oriented), and one query tool whose server-side planner maps each query to an intent over a snapshot index or a live adapter (query-oriented). All three reach the agent as an MCP server over the same adapters, with different operations and arguments exposed to the agent. Benign functional coverage and task completion are read against a fixed set of 50 identified benign workflows across the twelve families, collected before any security test. Task completion uses all 50 workflows as its denominator across repetitions, including workflows that an interface does not support, as defined in Section 3.4 . The reference configuration pairs Claude Code with the workflow-oriented design. RQ1 runs on it, and RQ2 and RQ3 each change one factor.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Requests and Procedure. Before execution we fix the applicable attack requests and their exact wording for each case, following Section 2.2 . Requests preserve the original attack objective and exploit-relevant inputs while adapting their form to agent-mediated access. We distinguish input-bearing requests containing crafted values from goal-oriented requests stating the intended malicious outcome, applying each form where it preserves the case’s attack requirements. A case is attempted under every applicable form, an inapplicable form never counts as a failure, and a case is retained if any applicable request succeeds in at least one repetition. Each C2 task is repeated R = 5 R=5 times under caps of 15 tool calls, 30,000 tokens, and 5 minutes per attempt, whereas C1 receives one scripted pass with the validated inputs, submitted as queries for the query-oriented design. The harness restores the application from a verified snapshot before every attempt. Only an oracle-verified effect counts as success, and a refusal counts as a valid failure only when the oracle confirms that no effect occurred. A budget sweep shows that doubling every cap recovers no additional case under the reference configuration (Appendix C ).

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Of the native-validated cases, 91% are expressible through the workflow-oriented interface, and both direct invocation (C1) and the agent (C2) reach the oracle-verified effect in all of them (Figure 3 ). Retention is therefore 91% of all native cases and 100% of the expressible subset. The remaining 9% are inexpressible because a needed operation or argument is not exposed, and no case remains unresolved. C1 and C2 agree on every case (exact McNemar p = 1.0 p=1.0 ), so all case-level attrition is structural.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The 91% figure reflects what the reference interface exposes, and RQ3 shows that other designs move it between 39% and 95%. The C1–C2 agreement, by contrast, is not implied by the design, since C2 is where the agent can refuse or rewrite the request. Even for input-precision payloads and goal-oriented requests that state the malicious outcome, no case-level loss is attributed to refusal or input normalization (Section 4.3 ).

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Retention stays high across vulnerability classes (Figure 4 a): 17/18 input-precision, 14/15 application-logic, and 9/11 resource-handling cases. Given these group sizes, the gap is descriptive. It traces to the interface, since resource-handling attacks need operations such as upload, import, or retrieval, and missing operations or arguments account for two of the four inexpressible cases. In the retained cases, fixed identity and routing determine who acts and where, while the exposed business arguments still carry exploit-relevant values to the vulnerable handler.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Of the retained cases, 35 are preserved, 4 transformed, where the agent rewrote a non-essential input such as an outer file name while a payload of the same class still reached the sink, and one exhibits step completion. Input-bearing and goal-oriented requests yield identical retention on cases eligible for both (Appendix B ).

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The single step-completion case concerns crAPI’s refund-eligibility flaw (Challenge 8 ( OWASP Foundation, ) ), where a customer can obtain a refund through an order-status update without returning the item. The request specified only the submission; the agent looked up the order and initiated the return first, and the oracle verified the credit. Replaying only the submission produced no credit (Appendix C ), while the complete C1 sequence succeeds, so the agent reached nothing the interface forbids but spared the attacker from specifying the prerequisite steps in the request.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Retention by class is 94 percent for input precision, 93 percent for application logic, and 64 to 82 percent for resource handling across agents. The agents retain 86 to 91 percent of cases overall. The capability designs retain 95, 91, and 39 percent for endpoint, workflow, and query designs, alongside decreasing benign coverage and completion.
