section: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
content: Discrete nonlinear dynamical systems arise in population models, iterative optimization, and numerical simulations, where computing many iterations can be costly in high dimensions. We study Carleman embedding for forced quadratic discrete systems and its application to quantum state preparation. Under explicit stability and initial-state assumptions, we prove that the truncation error decreases geometrically with the embedding degree, uniformly over all iterations. A central obstacle in discrete time is that the lifted update can become dense even when the original coefficient maps are sparse. We overcome this obstacle by constructing an exact auxiliary linear-system representation that applies the coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time, with row and column sparsities bounded independently of the truncation degree. After rescaling, the associated history system has a condition number that grows linearly with the iteration count, uniformly in the truncation degree. These results yield a quantum algorithm for preparing an approximation to the normalized n n th iterate with constant success probability. Under coherent input-access assumptions, and for fixed sparsity, stability parameters, and a known positive lower bound on the final-state norm, the oracle query complexity is linear in n n and polylogarithmic in the inverse accuracy. Numerical experiments in one and three dimensions illustrate the convergence of the truncated embedding.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: Discrete nonlinear dynamics are ubiquitous in scientific computing. They arise whenever a state is updated by a map 𝒙 n + 1 = F ⁡ ( 𝒙 n ) \bm{x}_{n+1}=F(\bm{x}_{n}) . Such recurrences model populations with nonoverlapping generations [ 1 ] and time-stepping schemes for fluid dynamics [ 2 ] . Discrete nonlinear dynamics also arise naturally in machine learning, including gradient-based optimization [ 3 , 4 ] , recurrent neural networks [ 5 ] , and the fixed-point formulations underlying deep equilibrium models [ 6 ] . The stability and convergence of these iterations play an important role in the design and analysis of learning algorithms [ 5 , 7 ] . These examples are inherently specified by discrete updates: a discrete dynamical system need not be a sampling or numerical discretization of any continuous-time evolution. Even a low-degree map can exhibit behavior that is difficult to infer from a single update, while a high-dimensional map can be costly to iterate or probe over many steps. These observations motivate algorithms that exploit the structure of F F to access a later state or a selected observable. We focus on a stable quadratic regime in which the iterates converge to a fixed point.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: A natural route toward quantum algorithms for nonlinear recurrences is to represent their updates as linear evolution in an enlarged space. For polynomial maps, Carleman embedding provides precisely this representation: introduce the monomials of the state, represented here by tensor powers 1 , 𝒙 , 𝒙 ⊗ 2 , … 1,\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\otimes 2},\ldots , and expand their updates under 𝒙 n + 1 = F ⁡ ( 𝒙 n ) \bm{x}_{n+1}=F(\bm{x}_{n}) to obtain an infinite linear recurrence [ 8 ] . Truncating this hierarchy yields a finite linear approximation to the original nonlinear dynamics. This construction connects nonlinear iteration with quantum algorithms for linear algebra, provided that the approximation error and the cost of accessing the enlarged system can be controlled.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: Quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs) make this connection computationally useful. Beginning with the algorithm of Harrow, Hassidim, and Lloyd [ 9 ] , these methods prepare quantum states proportional to solutions of linear systems, with subsequent developments improving the dependence on accuracy and conditioning [ 10 , 11 ] . For a truncated Carleman recurrence, the lifted states at successive iterations can be coupled through a single history linear system, following the general strategy used in quantum algorithms for differential equations [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Solving this system prepares a state encoding the lifted history, from which a state proportional to the desired nonlinear iterate can be extracted, subject to the truncation error. Under suitable sparsity and coherent-access assumptions, the linear-system solver can have only polylogarithmic dependence on the enlarged dimension.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: Realizing this potential requires more than a finite-dimensional approximation. The truncation error must remain controlled over the iteration horizon, the lifted operator must admit efficient quantum access, and the history system must have manageable conditioning. The cost of extracting the desired physical state from the lifted history must also be included. These requirements are coupled: increasing the truncation order enlarges the representation and may increase its implementation cost, even when it improves the approximation. The central question is therefore whether a convergent Carleman approximation can be combined with a quantum implementation whose total cost remains controlled. We address this question for a stable class of quadratic discrete dynamical systems.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: Other quantum approaches to nonlinear problems include evolution of multiple copies of a state through a mean-field approximation [ 16 ] and Koopman–von Neumann representations of classical dynamics [ 17 ] . Homotopy perturbation has also been used to construct quantum algorithms for dissipative nonlinear ordinary differential equations [ 18 ] and for quadratic nonlinear algebraic systems [ 19 ] . The latter solves for a root of a nonlinear equation, whereas our task is to prepare a state associated with the n n th iterate of a nonlinear map. These methods suggest different ways to expose linear structure, with distinct requirements for approximation, state preparation, and output recovery.

content: This paper studies Carleman embedding for discrete dynamical systems under specific assumptions. The discrete setting creates the sparsity challenge: The update of each tensor power contains products of the coefficients of F F , including terms absent from a continuous-time Carleman generator. Moreover, sparse coefficients need not give a sparse truncated update: for F ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = A ​ 𝒙 F(\bm{x})=A\bm{x} , its degree- N N block is A ⊗ N A^{\otimes N} , whose row sparsity can grow as s A N s_{A}^{N} if A A has row sparsity s A s_{A} . A convergence bound for the truncation therefore does not by itself yield an efficient sparse-access quantum implementation. This motivates a representation that applies the original coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time, without expanding their tensor products.

[ 21 , 22 ] studied truncated Carleman propagation for discrete-time stochastic polynomial systems and established approximation-error bounds. Deterministic polynomial maps are included as a special case of that setting. These results provide direct precedents for discrete lifting and truncation analysis.

content: Liu et al. [ 3 ] developed Carleman-based quantum algorithms for discrete gradient updates. Their supplementary analysis treats truncation error, history linear systems, conditioning, sparsity, and corrections arising from the discrete product rule. In particular, it includes an error bound independent of the iteration count under a contraction assumption on the chosen lifted update. Their main construction uses a small-learning-rate approximation, while the supplement also derives the higher-order discrete corrections. Our analysis instead treats the exact forced quadratic update throughout and derives its guarantees directly from explicit bounds on the original coefficient maps and initial state.

content: In fluid dynamics, Sanavio and Succi [ 23 ] applied Carleman lifting to the discrete collision and streaming updates of the lattice Boltzmann method, constructed quantum circuits, and numerically investigated the accuracy of low-order truncations. Sanavio et al. [ 24 ] subsequently developed matrix-access oracles and block encodings for the discrete Carleman update. They reported sparsity growing exponentially with truncation order and low success probabilities that hinder repeated time stepping. These works provide direct precedents for quantum implementation of discrete Carleman dynamics and motivate controlling the implementation cost as the truncation degree increases.

content: More recently, Jennings et al. developed a discrete Carleman formulation for lattice Boltzmann dynamics and examined time-stepping, conditioning, and data extraction through an end-to-end complexity analysis [ 2 ] . They also numerically investigated truncation convergence, but did not establish a rigorous convergence guarantee for that application. Our work considers forced quadratic maps under explicit stability assumptions and provides an exact sparse auxiliary realization of the truncated Carleman update, a truncation-error bound uniform in the iteration count, and a history-system analysis with sparsity independent of the tensor degree. The resulting quantum algorithm prepares an encoded solution state. Observable estimation and full classical readout incur additional costs.

content: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we formulate the quadratic iteration and its Carleman embedding, then establish a truncation-error bound that is uniform in the number of iterations. In Section 3 , we construct an auxiliary sparse system that represents the truncated Carleman update exactly, without explicitly forming its potentially dense matrix. In Section 4 , we develop the rescaled history-system formulation and analyze its conditioning, the recovery of the physical state, and the quantum algorithm’s query complexity. Finally, Section 5 presents numerical experiments illustrating the convergence of the truncated embedding. All of the proofs are deferred to appendices.

content: We studied the Carleman embedding of forced quadratic discrete dynamical systems. Under explicit stability and initial-state assumptions, the degree- N N truncation approximates the original trajectory with an error that decreases geometrically in N N , uniformly over all iterations. In particular, for fixed stability parameters, a degree logarithmic in the inverse accuracy suffices, regardless of how many steps the system is evolved.

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: A finite Carleman lift is not automatically efficient to implement: even sparse coefficient maps can produce dense blocks when their tensor products are formed. We addressed this by representing the truncated Carleman update exactly through an auxiliary operator whose layers apply the coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time. The resulting linear system has row and column sparsities bounded independently of the truncation degree. This separates the accuracy needed for the Carleman approximation from the sparsity of the system used to compute it.

authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
content: We then rescaled the auxiliary representation and assembled the updates into a history system. Its condition number grows as Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) , with constants independent of the truncation degree. Combined with the uniform error bound, this gives a quantum algorithm for preparing a state close to the normalized n n th iterate. Under the stated coherent-access assumptions and a positive lower bound on the norm of that iterate, the query complexity is linear in n n and polylogarithmic in the inverse accuracy when the stability parameters are fixed. The result concerns state preparation. Estimating observables or recovering the full iterate classically requires additional queries. Finally, the numerical experiments illustrate the predicted decrease in truncation error for one- and three-dimensional examples.

On the other hand, there are plenty of nonlinear discrete systems are not in polynomial in machine learning, optimization and physical models. Whether Carleman embedding guarantees error convergence for broader classes of functions is an interesting future direction. Extending the stability and error analysis, estimating the preparation and measurement cost will also help establish end to end cost.

authors: Adam Quinn Jaffe, Congwei Yang, Nicolás García Trillos, Bodhisattva Sen
section: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry
content: While the goal of classical statistical theory is to minimize the variance of unbiased estimators, an additional goal of some recent research is to minimize or constrain other notions of the instability of estimators. In particular, a subset of the authors recently introduced a notion of instability termed “sensitivity”, which represents the expected amount that an estimator would change if its inputs were infinitesimally perturbed. In this work, we study the multiobjective problem of minimizing both the variance and sensitivity over unbiased estimators in a given statistical model, and we aim to determine Pareto optimal tradeoffs between these two objectives. Our main results show that the Pareto front for these tradeoffs is precisely determined by endowing the statistical model with the Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry, which interpolates between the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries that are known to be associated, respectively, with the separate minimization of variance and sensitivity. We also develop a Z Z -estimation technique which constructs estimators that asymptotically achieve Pareto optimal pairs of variance and sensitivity. While computing the Pareto front and constructing the resulting estimators in practice requires solving a continuum of partial differential equations, we fully execute this program in some parametric examples of interest where the analysis is already non-trivial. Our results also shed light on some classical statistical problems, for example by showing that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves the smallest asymptotic sensitivity among all estimators achieving the optimal asymptotic variance.

content: As discussed above, the classical Cramér–Rao theory of variance is associated with Hellinger (equivalently, Fisher–Rao) geometry [ Ama85 ] , while the Wasserstein–Cramér–Rao theory is associated with Wasserstein geometry [ GTJS25 ] . This suggests that lower bounds on convex combinations of variance and sensitivity should be associated with some combination of the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries, but it is not immediately clear what is the appropriate way to combine these two geometries. Interestingly, the naïve approach of directly combining the distances does not work; instead, the appropriate construction is to consider a suitable combination of the Riemannian metric tensors , which leads naturally to the Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry [ LMS16 , LMS18 , CPSV18 ] . This geometric insight allows us to derive a comprehensive theory describing Pareto optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity and constructing Pareto optimal estimators in a variety of statistical models of interest.

This family of geometries describes the evolution of measures as a combination of two mechanisms: a change in mass governed by a scalar field (as in the Hellinger geometry), and movement of mass governed by a vector field (as in the Wasserstein geometry). As such, and as discussed above, the HK \mathrm{HK} geometries have a parameter 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1 0\leq\lambda\leq 1 describing the relative strength of the mechanisms, and which interpolate between the Wasserstein ( λ = 0 \lambda=0 ) and Hellinger ( λ = 1 \lambda=1 ) geometries.

Nonetheless, we can compute the HK \mathrm{HK} score functions in various models of interest (Laplace location family, uniform scale family, various Gaussian models) which we revisit as running examples throughout the paper. Indeed, absolute continuity with respect to the HK λ \mathrm{HK}_{\lambda} metric turns out to be closely related to solutions of the transport-source equation ( 3 ); see [ LMS16 , LMS18 ] . To be explicit, we note that there are three reasons that we use absolute continuity rather than differentiability in this work. First, although the HK distance admits a static formulation (see Appendix A ) which can be used to define a notion of differentiability in the HK \mathrm{HK} sense (denoted DHKS), solving equation ( 3 ) is typically easier than computing the static formulation; this contrasts the Hellinger and Wasserstein cases, where the static formulations can be easily computed via the score functions and the optimal transport maps, respectively. Second, we show (Proposition 2.7 ) that absolute continuity with respect to at least one of Hellinger or Wasserstein metric automatically implies absolute continuity with respect to HK λ \mathrm{HK}_{\lambda} for all 0 < λ < 1 0<\lambda<1 , hence all statistical models studied in the classical theory can be analyzed within our framework. Third, we show (Theorem 2.8 ) that θ ↦ 𝔼 θ ​ [ T n ] \theta\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[T_{n}] can be differentiated for a broad class of estimators T n T_{n} , whenever θ ↦ P θ \theta\mapsto P_{\theta} is absolutely continuous with respect to HK λ \mathrm{HK}_{\lambda} ; this both simplifies and generalizes the result [ GTJS25 , Proposition 2.2] from the Wasserstein case, and may be of independent interest.

content: We can also use HKZE to construct estimators which asymptotically achieve any prescribed Pareto optimal pair of variance and sensitivity (Example 4.9 ). As expected, the HK λ ZE interpolates between the sample mean and the sample median as λ \lambda ranges from 0 to 1, and each intermediate HK λ ZE is an M M -estimator with a strictly convex loss function hence it is easy to compute. It is also natural to compare the HK λ ZE with Huber’s M M -estimators from robust statistics [ Hub64 ] , which provide a ubiquitous family estimators interpolating between the sample median and the sample mean; it turns out that these families of estimators are distinct, but the HK λ ZE indeed has a “Huber-like” loss function (i.e., with quadratic growth when | x − θ | → 0 |x-\theta|\to 0 and linear growth when | x − θ | → ∞ |x-\theta|\to\infty ). As we discuss in Appendix B , it is also possible to define a notion of λ \lambda relative efficiency for the multiobjective problem of minimizing the variance and sensitivity, and it happens that Huber’s M M -estimators are extremely close to being optimal; their worst-case λ \lambda relative efficiency, over 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1 0\leq\lambda\leq 1 , is approximately 0.954 0.954 .

content: As discussed above, our work contributes to a growing theory of “stability” of statistical estimation, which includes stability under various perturbations of the model or data. Classical examples include stability under model contamination [ Hub64 , LB20 , GMB26a , GMB26b ] , subsampling [ Bre96a , Bre96b , SFBW24 , SFBW26 ] , and more, and in this work we specifically focus on the notion of sensitivity from [ LZ23 , NM25 , GTJS25 ] which is connected to various statistical applications [ CS90 , LB20 , DJW18 , BDOW21 ] . We note also that, in some instances, stability is used only as a tool to study accuracy, e.g., in some applications of algorithmic stability [ BE02 ] ; in this work, we take the perspective that stability itself is a goal. We thus view our results to also contribute to the theory of the PCS framework of veridical data science [ Yu13 , YB20 ] , which advocates that various notions of stability should inform the design of estimators and statistical procedures more broadly.

title: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
authors: Adam Quinn Jaffe, Congwei Yang, Nicolás García Trillos, Bodhisattva Sen
content: Another literature in which our results can be situated is the study of tradeoffs between statistical accuracy and other desiderata, which has become a fundamental aspect of modern research in statistics and machine learning. For instance, much is known about computational-statistical tradeoffs [ BR13 , ZWJ14 , MW15 ] , fairness-accuracy tradeoffs [ LLMO26 , LM24 , FJU25 ] , tradeoffs between statistical inference and distributed communication [ ZDJW13 , GMN14 , BGM+16 ] , and more. In this vein, our results are most similar to the recent work [ CLFB26 ] which studies stability-accuracy tradeoffs (although for a different notion of stability); yet, we emphasize that [ CLFB26 ] studies tradeoffs between the rates of convergence of stability and accuracy, whereas we study the tradeoffs in the optimal pre-factor for models with parametric rates of convergence.

title: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
authors: Adam Quinn Jaffe, Congwei Yang, Nicolás García Trillos, Bodhisattva Sen
content: From the geometric point of view, our results further develop the philosophy from [ GTJS25 ] that different geometries on the space of probability measures allow one to control different notions of instability. This is an extension of the perspective of information geometry (see [ Ama85 ] and the references therein), whereby the Cramér–Rao lower bound admits a geometric interpretation in terms of the Hellinger and Fisher–Rao metrics, and was initially applied to the Wasserstein geometry in [ LZ23 , AM24 , NM25 , GTJS25 ] . Our work may be interpreted as an instance of this paradigm with respect to the Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry which was introduced in [ LMS16 , LMS18 , CPSV18 ] and studied in many subsequent works (e.g., [ CCST22 , LMS23 ] ). The Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry is also closely related to the concept of unbalanced optimal transport, which has been used in various problems in statistics and machine learning [ CAG20 , FSFC21 , YWR24 ] .

Indeed, while the use of “Kantorovich” versus “Wasserstein” is only cosmetic [ Vil09 , Chapter 6, Bibliographic Notes] , the terms “Hellinger” and “Fisher–Rao” refer to different geometries, but which have the same infinitesimal structure for probability measures and hence lead to the same lower bounds; see [ GTJS25 , Subsection 2.2] for a discussion. content: In this section we describe the fundamental lower bounds on the pair of variance and sensitivity that can be achieved by any unbiased estimator in a sufficiently regular statistical model. We let X 1 , … , X n X_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be i.i.d. samples from P θ P_{\theta} where the goal is to estimate the unknown θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta . More precisely, we define a particular notion of regularity that we will require from our statistical models (Subsection 3.1 ), we state a simultaneous lower bound on the variance and sensitivity of any unbiased estimator (Subsection 3.2 ), and we study various aspects of the finer structure of this lower bound (Subsection 3.3 ).

section: Appendix A Differentiability in the Hellinger–Kantorovich sense
content: In this appendix, we introduce a notion of differentiability with respect to the Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry. This notion is analogous to the notions of differentiability in quadratic mean (DQM) (see [ vdV98 ] ) and differentiability in the Wasserstein sense (DWS) (see [ GTJS25 ] ) of statistical models. To introduce this notion of differentiability, we first discuss a static formulation of the Hellinger–Kantorovich distance that is reminiscent of the static version in terms of transport maps of the Wasserstein distance. We remark that the form of this static formulation differs from its Wasserstein counterpart. For the Wasserstein geometry, Brenier’s theorem identifies conditions under which the optimal Kantorovich plan is induced by a deterministic transport map and in particular provides sufficient conditions for the equivalence between Kantorovich’s and Monge’s formulations of the Wasserstein distance (see [ Vil09 ] ). In contrast, in the Hellinger–Kantorovich geometry mass may also be created or destroyed, and therefore the corresponding Monge target must encode mechanisms for both spatial displacement and mass creation/destruction. We first recall the static and cone formulations of the Hellinger–Kantorovich distance, then introduce optimal transport–growth pairs through a Brenier-like theorem, and finally introduce the notion of differentiability of a statistical model in the Hellinger–Kantorovich sense, which we write DHKS for short.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
section: Data-Driven Stochastic Optimal Control of air-conditioning Systems with Delayed Activation Thanks: Corresponding author ∗
content: We consider a stochastic optimal control problem arising in the operation of industrial air-conditioning systems with delayed activation effects. The delayed transition between inactive and operational regimes induces a non-Markovian structure in the controlled dynamics. We derive a regression-based discrete dynamic programming algorithm on nested state-control grids. We give a probabilistic proof of convergence of the idealized time-discrete dynamic programming problem to the continuous-time value function. Numerical experiments based on calibrated multidimensional forecast-tracking Ornstein–Uhlenbeck models illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
content: The operation of large-scale air-conditioning systems in industrial and scientific environments requires the reliable maintenance of strict environmental conditions over long time horizons. Typical examples include airport infrastructures, semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and pharmaceutical laboratories in which deviations from prescribed temperature and humidity regimes may result in substantial operational losses or production failure [ 16 , 2 ] . In such systems, heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning infrastructure constitutes one of the dominant sources of operational energy consumption, often accounting for a substantial fraction of the total facility energy demand [ 20 , 23 ] . Simultaneously, failure to maintain the required environmental conditions may compromise product quality, interrupt sensitive production processes, or damage critical infrastructure, thereby inducing severe economic consequences [ 2 ] . Consequently, the operation of industrial air-conditioning systems naturally gives rise to a sequential control problem balancing the energy costs associated with active cooling against the economic penalties caused by violations of prescribed environmental conditions.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
content: A central difficulty in the mathematical modeling of such systems is the delayed response of the cooling infrastructure. Existing optimization and stochastic control approaches for HVAC systems typically assume that control decisions affect the environmental dynamics instantaneously, while uncertainty enters only through exogenous disturbances such as weather conditions or occupancy fluctuations [ 22 , 11 ] . In practice, however, large-scale cooling systems frequently exhibit substantial activation delays. After being switched on, the air conditioning system does not immediately enter the operational regime, but instead undergoes a warm-up phase during which energy costs are already incurred while the environmental conditions may still violate admissible operating thresholds. Consequently, the resulting control problem exhibits an intrinsic delay structure. In particular, the future operational state of the system does not only depend on the present switching state, but additionally on the elapsed time since the most recent activation event. Delayed reaction and execution lags have been studied in stochastic impulse-control settings. The contribution here is an HVAC-oriented stochastic switching formulation that combines an explicit warm-up clock, weak compactness-based analysis, regression-based dynamic programming on the augmented state, and calibration to forecast-tracking environmental data. content: On the numerical side, we construct a hybrid grid and regression-based dynamic programming algorithm. The delay structure is incorporated through a clock variable, leading to a state representation suitable for discrete dynamic programming. The idea is that under sufficiently small time steps, this algorithm produces ε \varepsilon -optimal feedback controls within the framework of open-loop control. The treatment is related to several distinct strands of the stochastic control literature. Impulse control problems with delayed reaction have been studied, for instance, by reducing the delayed intervention problem to a sequence of no-delay optimal stopping problems [ 17 ] . Closely related finite-horizon impulse control problems with decision lag and execution delay have also been analyzed through time-discontinuous optimal stopping formulations and discrete-time approximations [ 19 ] . Separately, regression Monte Carlo methods have been developed for stochastic impulse control, where continuation and intervention functions are learned from simulated trajectories [ 15 ] . The weak-convergence argument used below to pass from the discrete dynamic programming problem to the continuous-time value function follows the general philosophy of Markov-chain approximation methods for continuous-time stochastic control [ 13 ] .

content: The convergence properties of regression-based dynamic programming methods for discrete-time stochastic control problems with continuous state spaces have already been studied rigorously in [ 3 ] . For this reason, the present work does not further analyze the statistical convergence of the regression procedure itself, but instead focuses on the complementary question of convergence of the underlying discretized delayed control problem to the original continuous-time value function.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
content: The stochastic dynamics used in the numerical examples are calibrated on forecast and observation data obtained from OpenWeather [ 18 ] through a multidimensional Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model with correlated noise structure. We adopt the idea of [ 7 ] to regard the deviation of the environmental parameters from their forecast as a zero-mean stochastic process. The real-data simulations are implemented within a rolling horizon framework over sufficiently short decision intervals, so that the progressive deterioration of forecast quality over longer horizons can be neglected within each optimization window. The use of Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics is consistent with established stochastic models for environmental variables such as temperature processes [ 4 ] . More general bounded diffusion models, such as Wright–Fisher dynamics, are equally compatible with the theoretical framework developed in the present work and may be particularly natural when modeling bounded quantities such as relative humidity. In fact, [ 7 ] also develops a rigorous calibration methodology for such models. However, application of the latter to our case would unnecessarily enlarge the numerical study.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
content: The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. First, we formulate the delayed air-conditioning problem as a weak stochastic optimal control problem. Second, we develop a rigorous foundation for the resulting delayed stochastic control problem. We introduce a regression-based dynamic programming algorithm adapted to the delayed switching structure and establish optimality of the associated idealized discrete dynamic programming formulation within the class of open-loop controls. Most importantly, we prove convergence of the idealized discrete dynamic programming value functions to the value function of the original continuous-time stochastic control problem. Finally, we combine the method with a calibrated forecast-tracking model and demonstrate its practical performance in a rolling-horizon study based on real environmental data, providing a complete pipeline from forecast uncertainty quantification to delayed stochastic control and operational cost comparison.

content: The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we formulate the delayed stochastic control problem. Section 3 develops the regression-based dynamic programming approximation and establishes optimality of the corresponding discrete dynamic programming principle. Section 4 establishes convergence of the discrete approximation scheme. Finally, Section 5 presents calibration procedures and numerical examples for air-conditioning systems with delayed operational regimes.

content: In principle, this recursion completely characterizes the discretized optimal control problem. However, exact evaluation of the conditional expectations appearing in the continuation operators is infeasible. To overcome this difficulty, we build upon the regression-based approximate dynamic programming approach introduced by Longstaff and Schwartz in the seminal work [ 14 ] . More precisely, we use Monte Carlo simulation and regression to approximate the conditional continuation values associated with the stochastic state process X X . The clock variable ζ \zeta , on the other hand, evolves deterministically once the control is fixed. Its attainable values are therefore induced directly by the control grid and can be tracked explicitly during the backward recursion. In particular, this avoids the need to introduce randomized controls in the numerical procedure. The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1 . We note that the clock process can be capped at τ \tau without any effect. We make use of this to limit the number of regressions in the numerical procedure in Algorithm 1 , but leave the clock process uncapped in the remaining theoretical discussion for ease of notation. The resulting dynamic programming recursion can be solved in a single backward pass and avoids the need for policy iteration procedures such as Howard’s algorithm [ 8 ] . In the implementation considered below, the continuation functions are approximated through polynomial regression, where the polynomial basis is chosen sufficiently rich to capture the geometry of the decision boundaries while maintaining numerical stability of the backward recursion. We emphasize that polynomials are merely a choice of convenience.

For these plots, we again condition on the true temperature and humidity forecast for June 15, 2023, and independently sample environmental trajectories around this forecast from the calibrated June model. content: The test trajectories are generated independently of the 8000 8000 trajectories used to compute the policy. For each representative realization, the figures show the sampled temperature and humidity trajectories together with the true forecast and the corresponding comfort intervals. The final panel displays the binary control process, with value one indicating that the air-conditioning system is switched on. The plots thereby illustrate how the computed policy responds to possible realizations of the environmental conditions around an actually observed forecast, and in particular how forecast uncertainty, comfort violations, the one-hour activation delay, and switching costs interact in the resulting control decisions. The comparison in Figures 3 and 2 shows the qualitative effect of the delay. When ζ = 0 \zeta=0 , activation must occur before the boundary of the comfort region is reached. Otherwise the system would still be in the warm-up phase when the violation occurs. Once ζ = 1 \zeta=1 , the controller reacts more carefully, since the system is already in regime and turning off carries a larger risk. This anticipatory behaviour is one of the main qualitative consequences of the delayed switching structure.

content: We finally evaluate the rolling-horizon control strategy on real weather data for Berlin over the full year 2024. This constitutes an out-of-sample experiment: the stochastic forecast model is calibrated exclusively using data from the years 2021–2023, while the subsequent policy evaluation is performed on forecasts and observations from 2024. In contrast to the preceding experiments, where environmental trajectories were sampled from the calibrated stochastic model around a real forecast, the policy is now evaluated along the actually observed temperature and relative-humidity trajectories. The stochastic model is used only for computing the control policy: at every rolling-horizon iteration, future environmental scenarios are sampled conditionally on the currently available real weather forecast. The comfort region is the same as in the previous section.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
authors: Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
content: The controller is implemented in a rolling-horizon fashion. At each optimization time, the corresponding real Berlin forecast is used as the deterministic forecast trajectory μ \mu . The forecast-tracking stochastic model is parameterized using the calibration associated with the respective calendar month, obtained from the 2021–2023 calibration data. Conditional on the current forecast, 8000 8000 trajectories are simulated from the calibrated model and used to solve a 12 12 -hour stochastic control problem. The resulting policy is applied to the real observed state only for the first 6 6 hours, after which a new forecast is used and the optimization problem is solved again. Both the observations and control decisions are taken on the original hourly time grid. The continuation values are approximated using polynomial regression of degree 10 10 , and the clock state is carried forward between successive rolling-horizon problems. The complete rolling-horizon procedure is illustrated schematically in Figure 7 .

content: The resulting out-of-sample control trajectory is shown in Figure 8 . The upper panels display the realized temperature and relative humidity together with the corresponding comfort bounds, while the lower panel shows the control selected by the rolling-horizon policy. The control activity is concentrated primarily during periods in which violations of the comfort region become relevant, while the controller remains inactive for extended periods when the observed environmental conditions do not require service.

title: Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems

content: To assess the economic performance of the policy, we compare it with an always-on benchmark. In addition to the total and cumulative costs, we record comfort violations and the number of switching events. The average daily cost is also computed separately for each calendar month. The resulting monthly comparison is shown in Figure 9 . The savings are moderate but systematic within the considered ambient service-demand model. Given the illustrative cost parameters and the high penalty assigned to violations of the prescribed comfort region, the resulting control policy tends to favor conservative operation. These findings should be interpreted as model-based operating-cost comparisons rather than validated indoor comfort improvements or measured facility energy savings.

content: As shown in Table 2 , the estimated savings increase from approximately 0.41 % 0.41\% under operational forecasts to 3.33 % 3.33\% under retrospectively constructed synthetic forecasts. This indicates that the performance of the proposed methodology is sensitive to the forecast information supplied to the controller and suggests that improvements in forecast quality may offer additional opportunities for operational cost reduction. However, the experiment does not isolate forecast uncertainty from other sources of approximation error, including regression, time discretization, receding-horizon optimization, and environmental-model inaccuracies. Accordingly, these results should not be interpreted as establishing that forecast error is the dominant limitation of the proposed methodology.

This suggests that, in the present implementation, the practical performance is limited more by forecast accuracy than by the control methodology itself.

authors: Frank E. Curtis, Xiaoyi Qu, Daniel P. Robinson
section: A Stochastic Proximal-Gradient Method for Regularized Generally Constrained Continuous Optimization
content: A stochastic proximal-gradient method is proposed and analyzed for solving regularized optimization problems subject to nonlinear equality constraints and nonnegativity bounds. The objective function’s values and gradients are available only through inexact stochastic oracles. The method decomposes each trial step into one component that reduces linearized infeasibility and a second component that seeks optimality while preserving that reduction. Trial steps are accepted or rejected through a relaxed sufficient decrease condition subject to stochastic merit function evaluations. Without assuming unbiasedness of stochastic gradient estimates, it is proved under reasonable assumptions that the method reaches an ϵ \epsilon -KKT point within 𝒪 ⁡ ( ϵ − 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) iterations with high probability. This guarantee further implies almost-sure termination in finitely many iterations and an 𝒪 ⁡ ( ϵ − 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) bound on the expected iteration complexity.

content: Recently, several algorithms have been proposed for solving problem ( 1 ), including augmented Lagrangian methods [ 15 , 23 ] , a proximal-point method [ 4 ] , a proximal-gradient method [ 5 ] , and a successive convex approximation method [ 12 ] . Their theoretical guarantees have been established in terms of expected iteration complexity, i.e., the number of iterations required for a stationarity measure to fall below a prescribed accuracy (in expectation). Results in expectation, however, do not control tail events: the iterations required to reach an approximate stationary point can still be arbitrarily large with nonzero probability. To address this limitation, a separate line of work [ 2 , 8 , 10 , 13 , 16 , 21 ] has developed high-probability iteration complexity bounds that characterize the number of iterations needed to reach an approximate stationary point with a prescribed failure probability. These guarantees have been established in a variety of settings, including nonconvex stochastic optimization [ 8 , 13 , 16 ] , nonsmooth stochastic optimization [ 10 ] , equality constrained stochastic optimization [ 2 ] , and stochastic variational inequality problems [ 21 ] . To the best of our knowledge, however, no previously existing method for problem ( 1 ) provides high-probability iteration complexity guarantees.

This excludes without-replacement schemes such as random reshuffling [ 11 ] , which are standard in practice but yield biased mini-batch gradients within an epoch [ 18 , 19 ] . Together, these limitations motivate the development of an algorithm for solving ( 1 ) that achieves high-probability iteration complexity guarantees without having to assume that the stochastic gradient estimator is unbiased.

content: In this paper, we analyzed a proximal-gradient method for solving regularized stochastic optimization problems with general constraints, where exact objective function and gradient evaluations are inaccessible. We established a high-probability complexity bound under assumptions that accommodate noisy tail distributions commonly encountered in machine learning applications. Our analysis yields three main results: (i) explicit high-probability iteration complexity bounds for both subexponential and bounded-noise settings (Theorem 3.18 and the discussion following that theorem), (ii) almost-sure termination guarantee that an ϵ \epsilon -KKT point is found in a finite number of iterations (Corollary 3.19 (i)), and (iii) an expected iteration complexity of O ⁡ ( ϵ − 2 ) O(\epsilon^{-2}) (Corollary 3.19 (ii)). These results extend the high-probability analysis framework found in [ 14 ] from unconstrained smooth problems to the setting of constrained nonsmooth problems.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
section: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
content: Estimating travel behavior parameters is essential for understanding current travel patterns and for forecasting how travelers may respond to future changes in transportation systems. However, reliable estimation remains difficult when behavior must be inferred from sparse and aggregate observations, especially when jointly recovering several behavioral components. In this paper, we develop a bi-level estimation program for a combined destination, mode and route choice model with congestion. The inner level is a convex program at given scale parameters, and returns the taste coefficients as its dual variables together with the equilibrium travel pattern. The outer level selects the scale parameters by out-of-sample prediction, measured by how well the modeled travel pattern predicts observations withheld from estimation. To solve the bi-level problem at scale, we propose a matrix-free Hierarchical Lagrangian Dual algorithm as the inner solver and an outer search by implicit differentiation, which uses the sensitivities of the inner solution to enable efficient search over the scale parameters and reaches the calibrated scales in a handful of iterations. We validate the approach on Los Angeles County using public origin–destination, mode-share and traffic-count data. Our approach scales to a county-level problem with 2.7 million variables and substantially improves computational efficiency over a general-purpose conic solver. Compared with the fixed-scale benchmark, the calibrated model improves predictive performance at the destination and mode levels, with consistent gains across complementary goodness-of-fit measures.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: Estimating travel behavior parameters is essential for understanding current travel patterns and for forecasting how travelers may respond to future changes in transportation systems [ 1 ] . However, reliable estimation remains challenging when inferring behavior at population scale. Household travel surveys provide rich individual-level information, but their inherently limited sample sizes introduce sampling uncertainty and make reliable population-wide expansion difficult. Meanwhile, increasingly available aggregate data, including origin–destination (OD) matrices, mode shares, and traffic counts, offer complementary population-level observations. These sources, however, are aggregates over different levels of the same travel decision (e.g., destination, mode, and route), so integrating them into a unified behavioral model remains challenging [ 2 ] .

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: A recent line of work addresses this challenge by treating the network equilibrium model itself as the object to be learned: a forward problem describes the equilibrium travel pattern, and an inverse problem selects the parameters under which that pattern best reproduces the observations [ 3 ] . Within this line, the combined convex framework developed in [ 4 ] represents destination, mode and route choices jointly with congestion, so that the equilibrium pattern and the behavioral parameters that generate it are obtained from a single program. Three challenges stand between this framework and practice, and they coincide with questions the inverse-learning perspective [ 3 ] leaves open. First, the scale parameters of the choice hierarchy are not identified by aggregate observations and remain to be calibrated. Second, the inverse problem must be solved at full real-world scale, where the forward problem alone is a county-sized equilibrium with millions of unknowns, making general-purpose solvers impractical in both memory use and computation time. Third, whether the framework can recover meaningful behavioral parameters from limited public data and deliver out-of-sample predictions remains an open empirical question. This paper addresses the three challenges, in that order. Our contributions are as follows.

authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: Related work. Combined destination, mode and route choice models with congestion are classical in transportation planning and go back to the entropy and equilibrium formulations [ 8 , 9 ] . Their parameters are conventionally estimated from individual survey records [ 1 ] . Estimation from aggregate data usually draws on observations at a single level of the travel decision, link counts for the OD matrix and a route-choice coefficient [ 10 ] , mode choice from market shares [ 11 ] , and link counts and travel times for route preferences [ 12 ] . Joint estimation of all three levels from aggregate data is less studied, limited to maximum likelihood on a small network [ 13 ] , and more recently, convex estimation on a larger network but with fixed scales [ 4 ] . The inverse-learning perspective of [ 3 ] unifies these estimation problems as inverse problems over a forward equilibrium model, solved at the scale of a city network by a multiconvex reformulation of user equilibrium [ 14 ] . In the control of transportation networks, the same equilibrium models serve as plant models for routing control [ 15 ] , and their calibration from sparse data is addressed as the inference of link latency functions from observed equilibria [ 16 ] . Across the above literature, the scales are normalized or fixed by convention except in [ 13 , 10 ] , the observations rarely enter at more than one level of the travel decision, and no instance reaches a metropolitan region on its full road network. Our paper calibrates the scales, integrates observations from all three levels, and solves the problem for Los Angeles County, a metropolitan region.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: Commuting flows. For the origin–destination flows and the destination attributes, we use LODES 2019 [ 5 ] , which records the census tract of residence and of workplace of 3.69 million workers of Los Angeles County. We use 2,475 of the county’s 2,498 census tracts because the remaining 23 tracts carry no or negligible commuting. The destination choice set 𝒥 i \mathcal{J}_{i} of an origin i i consists of the workplace tracts that receive at least 5 of its commuters. LODES data also gives the jobs and the resident workers of each tract by 20 industry sectors, from which the job counts A ^ j \widehat{A}_{j} and the sector match κ ^ i ​ j \widehat{\kappa}_{ij} are computed.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: Mode shares. For the mode level, we use the American Community Survey (ACS) aggregated five-year estimates for 2015–2019 [ 6 ] , which report the split s ^ i ​ m \widehat{s}_{im} of its workers across modes m m for each tract of residence i i , i.e., driving alone, carpooling, transit, walking and bicycling. Since LODES carries no mode information, we construct the mode-specific counts as T ^ i ​ j ​ m = T ^ i ​ j ​ s ^ i ​ m \widehat{T}_{ijm}=\widehat{T}_{ij}\,\widehat{s}_{im} by assigning each origin tract’s mode shares to all of its destinations and renormalizing over the modes available for each pair, with walking and bicycling only available within 5 and 15 km.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: Network and traffic counts. The road network is OpenStreetMap [ 27 ] , with free-flow speed and capacity as link attributes, and the transit network is built from GTFS feeds [ 28 ] . Driving alone and carpooling choose among three generated routes per pair, while transit, walking and bicycling move at fixed speeds of 22, 4.8 and 15 km/h on their own connections. PeMS [ 7 ] supplies average weekday counts at 1,593 mainline freeway detectors, summed over the morning commute window of 6–10 am. The PeMS counts include trips of all purposes, whereas the model loads commuting trips only, so the two differ by a common factor. The flow loss of Section II removes this factor by subtracting the mean log ratio, so the counts need no rescaling. Each detector is matched to the sequence of consecutive network links it observes, 3.4 links on average, and its modeled flow is the mean over those links.

The estimation origins carry 1.71 million commuters over 143,418 origin–destination pairs and 1.23 million routes, which with the mode and link states makes 2.7 million variables in ( 7 ), and the validation origins carry 184,630 commuters over 15,006 pairs and 129,006 routes.

content: All computations run on a server with two 96-core AMD EPYC 9655 processors and 1.5 TB of memory. As a computational baseline, we formulate the inner problem ( 7 ) as an exponential-cone program and solve it with the interior-point solver of MOSEK [ 30 ] running on 184 parallel threads. The baseline runs the same outer search, except with cold starts in place of warm starts and finite differences in place of implicit differentiation, since MOSEK offers neither. Table I reports the total time of the calibration from 𝐬 ref \mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{ref}} and the time and memory of one cold inner solve. HLD stops each inner solve by its own residual test, at which its destination loss is within 10 − 4 10^{-4} of that at the optimal solution of the baseline. On the full county, a cold inner solve takes HLD 7.5 minutes and 6.6 GB, against 194 minutes and 446 GB for the baseline. The memory of the baseline grows with its number of threads, so part of this memory comes from the 184 threads. With 16 threads, the baseline still needs 277 GB. HLD completes the calibration at every scale, in 0.74 h on the full county, whereas the baseline completes it only at 100 origins, in 8.1 h, and does not finish within 24 h from 200 origins on. The gap comes from the design of HLD, which warm-starts every inner solve after the first and differentiates its optimality conditions cheaply. The baseline cold-starts every solve and, with optimality conditions too large to differentiate, needs additional cold solves per outer step for the sensitivities.

Since the taste coefficients themselves depend on the scale, we report their products with the corresponding scales, which determine the choice probabilities and are directly comparable across scale specifications. The recovered coefficients in our calibrated model have the expected signs and plausible magnitudes: doubling the jobs at a workplace raises its odds of being chosen by a factor of 1.6, a workplace 20 km away has 40% lower odds than one 10 km away, and a 0.1 increase in the sector match multiplies the odds by 1.6. At the mode level, an extra hour of travel time lowers a mode’s odds by 26%. Most importantly, at the reference scales ( λ = 1 \lambda=1 ), the time coefficient is positive, showing that incorrectly fixed scales can yield behaviorally implausible estimates and motivating the outer calibration.

title: Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
authors: Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
content: In this paper, we propose a bi-level program that estimates a combined destination, mode, and route choice model with congestion, from aggregate data. It recovers the taste coefficients, the equilibrium travel pattern, and the scale parameters jointly, and we test it at the scale of Los Angeles County with accurate prediction on the validation origins. There are still interesting future directions. First, the inputs of our model are public aggregate data, and whether the behavioral parameters recovered from them agree with those conventionally estimated from individual-level household travel surveys is an open question. Second, activity-based models characterize current travel behavior in rich detail through individual activity patterns and traveler heterogeneity, whereas our trip-based parametric model is parsimonious, interpretable and can be carried into future scenarios. A hybrid framework, in which an activity-based model characterizes the present system and the parametric combined model estimates behavior and predicts future scenarios, is a natural next step.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: We present a method for computing a specific type of matrix decomposition that combines a structured framework with data-driven adaptation. This framework allows for an efficient and stable representation of signals or images using frames by identifying sets of vectors that naturally capture the essential features of the given data. The resulting decomposition enables the development of regularization techniques that enhance the quality of reconstruction by preserving important signal characteristics while suppressing noise. We develop an optimization-based algorithm to compute the decomposition and establish convergence properties of the resulting iterates. Numerical experiments on synthetic data and tomographic image reconstruction illustrate the behavior of the proposed method and its performance compared to conventional spectral regularization methods.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: The motivation for this problem comes from the use of frame decompositions for the representation and inversion of linear operators in Hilbert spaces. This diagonalized structure allows the evaluation and inversion of the operator to be analysed and implemented in terms of frame operators and scalar multiplication. The sparsity property incorporates prior information about the underlying signal class and can help stabilize the representation. Such decompositions have been used, for example, in the regularization of inverse problems [ 22 , 21 , 20 , 27 , 26 , 9 ] .

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: If 𝐔 \mathbf{U} and 𝐕 \mathbf{V} are orthonormal bases for R M \mathbb{R}^{M} and R N \mathbb{R}^{N} , respectively, then 𝐀 = 𝐕𝐃𝐔 ⊤ {\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{V}{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{U}^{\top} is a singular value decomposition. However, the singular vectors generally do not provide sparse representations for a given signal class. They are determined solely by the matrix 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} and therefore cannot be adapted to different signal distributions. In contrast, tight frames provide stable and redundant representations that are well suited for sparse signal representations. Moreover, their dual frames are particularly easy to compute, since the canonical dual of a tight frame differs only by a multiplicative constant. The diagonal matrix 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} plays a role analogous to the singular values and is therefore often referred to as the matrix of quasi-singular values. It represents the scaling action of the operator in the corresponding frame coordinates. Replacing orthonormal bases by tight frames therefore provides greater flexibility in the construction of such decompositions, allowing additional properties to be imposed. In particular, our sparsity condition introduces a data-dependent criterion: rather than constructing a decomposition solely from the algebraic properties of 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} , we seek a frame 𝐔 \mathbf{U} whose coefficients provide sparse representations given the data 𝐗 \mathbf{X} . This is motivated by the observation that suitable representations can capture the structure of signals and images more efficiently and incorporate prior information that is relevant for inverse problems [ 35 , 12 ] . We note in passing that the diagonal matrix decomposition problems has applications far beyond imaging. In fact, frames are widely used for this purpose in applied mathematics, computer science, and engineering, with applications including sampling theory [ 23 ] , data quantization [ 5 , 6 ] , image processing [ 10 , 29 ] , and coding theory [ 40 ] .

content: In this paper, we develop a numerical methodology for solving the structured matrix decomposition (Problem 1 ). Our approach combines an algebraic reduction of the decomposition problem with a new non-smooth and non-convex hierarchical (bilevel) optimization formulation of the original matrix decomposition problem. In particular, we develop from scratch a new bilevel optimization formulation on the Stiefel manifold containing the desired frame matrices.

content: We first show that Problem 1 can be reduced to an equivalent problem involving only positive diagonal matrices for 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} . This reduction allows us to characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on the diagonal matrix 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} for the existence of a decomposition satisfying the prescribed tightness and decomposition constraints. Once 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} is fixed, the remaining problem can be formulated entirely in terms of the frame 𝐔 \mathbf{U} , since the second frame 𝐕 \mathbf{V} is uniquely determined by 𝐔 \mathbf{U} and 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} . The tightness constraint on 𝐔 \mathbf{U} naturally leads to an optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: To incorporate the sparsity requirement, we formulate the resulting problem as a simple bilevel optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold ( 4.1 ). The lower-level problem is a smooth but nonconvex optimization problem whose solution guarantees the tightness of 𝐕 \mathbf{V} and the decomposition property, while the upper-level objective is convex and lower semi-continuous, incorporating the sparsity requirement. The tightness of 𝐔 \mathbf{U} follows directly from the definition of the Stiefel manifold. Although the lower-level problem is convex when considered in the ambient Euclidean space, this convexity is generally lost after restricting the problem to the Stiefel manifold. We address the resulting nonconvex bilevel problem using a penalized subgradient method formulated in a general setting, which therefore applies beyond the specific matrix decomposition considered here.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: We provide a rigorous convergence analysis of both levels of the resulting bilevel scheme. In particular, we establish convergence of the lower-level optimization procedure and analyze the convergence of the iterates to stationary points of the bilevel problem under the stated assumptions. The theoretical results are complemented by numerical experiments that demonstrate the practical behavior of the proposed method and its ability to identify sparse frame representations adapted to the given data.

content: Optimization-based approaches to frame computation have been studied, for example, by [ 41 ] , who develop convex optimization methods for constructing frames with prescribed structural properties. Our setting differs in that the frame is not designed independently of an operator; instead, the frame and a diagonal scaling are jointly required to represent a given matrix while promoting sparsity of its action on a data set. A related line of work concerns scalable frames, where one seeks diagonal scalings that transform a given frame into a Parseval frame; see, e.g., [ 30 ] . Scalable-frame theory typically considers a fixed frame and asks whether a positive diagonal scaling yields a Parseval frame. In contrast, we optimize the frame itself together with the diagonal scaling, with the additional requirement that their product represent a prescribed operator and with a data-dependent sparsity objective.

In convex optimization in Euclidean spaces, prox-penalization and related diagonal-gradient approaches have been studied extensively [ 3 , 4 , 1 , 2 , 38 , 34 ] . In contrast, penalty formulations specifically tailored to optimization on the Stiefel manifold are comparatively less developed. For example, a Lagrangian relaxation approach for optimization with Stiefel constraints is considered in [ 43 ] . Our work combines these ideas by employing a penalty formulation together with a subgradient method on the Stiefel manifold to solve the bilevel frame decomposition problem.

A simple example of a tight frame is the union of p p orthonormal bases, in which case the frame bounds are A = B = p A=B=p . content: For the application to filtered reconstruction of inverse problems, it is not essential that 𝐕 \mathbf{V} be a Parseval or tight frame. Although computing its canonical dual would be more involved, this is not required in our reconstruction method, where only the dual of 𝐔 \mathbf{U} is needed. Nevertheless, the stability of the reconstruction depends, among other factors, on the frame bounds, or equivalently the condition number, of 𝐕 \mathbf{V} . These need not be equal to one, but should remain reasonably well-conditioned. A key requirement for a DFD is that the ill-conditioning of Σ \Sigma , and hence of 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} , is captured by 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} , since the corresponding components are subsequently filtered. To illustrate this, consider the extreme choice 𝐃 = Id K {\mathbf{D}}=\Id_{K} . For any Parseval frame 𝐔 \mathbf{U} , the corresponding frame 𝐕 = Σ − 1 ​ 𝐔 \mathbf{V}=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{U} inherits the ill-conditioning of Σ \Sigma ; in particular, its condition number can be as large as that of Σ \Sigma . Thus, the primary objective in choosing 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} is to ensure that min ⁡ Ψ \min\Psi is zero or sufficiently small, which generally requires 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} to capture the dominant spectral variation of Σ \Sigma . It also specifies conditions on the step sizes and penalty parameters that guarantee convergence to a stationary point of the lower-level problem. The bound depends on the auxiliary parameter λ > 0 \lambda>0 , which must be chosen sufficiently small and is then kept fixed. As λ → 0 \lambda\to 0 , we have λ ​ L λ → 1 \lambda L_{\lambda}\to 1 , while L λ L_{\lambda} , which appears as the coefficient of the quadratic term, becomes arbitrarily large. content: In the following, we use a second-order Taylor expansion of Ψ \Psi on the Stiefel manifold. We assume that Ψ \Psi is twice continuously differentiable. Unlike in Euclidean space, where Taylor expansions are formulated along straight lines, on a Riemannian manifold they are formulated along geodesics, which are the manifold analogues of straight lines. Moreover, tangent vectors at different points belong to different tangent spaces and therefore cannot be directly compared. Parallel transport provides a way to move tangent vectors between tangent spaces while preserving the Riemannian metric.

content: In the second numerical experiment, we consider a discretization of the two-dimensional Radon transform for the matrix 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} . The Radon transform maps a compactly supported square-integrable function to its line integrals over affine lines [ 33 ] . It provides the mathematical foundation for computed tomography (CT) [ 32 ] and is widely used in imaging applications [ 28 , 45 ] . Its discretized version 𝐀 {\mathbf{A}} maps a vectorized image x ∈ R m 1 ⋅ m 2 x\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}\cdot m_{2}} to a vectorized observation (sinogram) y ∈ R n 1 ⋅ n 2 y\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\cdot n_{2}} . The inversion of the Radon transform is ill-posed, meaning that small perturbations in the sinogram can lead to large reconstruction errors. This makes regularization essential for obtaining stable reconstructions from noisy data.

content: Learning a DFD for large-scale problems can be computationally demanding, as it requires the repeated computation of SVDs of high-dimensional matrices. However, this learning step only has to be performed once for a given operator and training data set. Once the DFD has been computed, reconstructing an image from a sinogram requires only two matrix multiplications and the evaluation of the corresponding filter, making reconstruction computationally inexpensive. To keep the computational cost manageable, we conduct the numerical experiments using images of size 20 × 20 20\times 20 , corresponding to 400 pixels, and sinograms of size 20 × 30 20\times 30 . Although this resolution is relatively low for practical image reconstruction, it provides a controlled setting for evaluating the reconstruction performance and error characteristics of the proposed method.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: In this work, we introduced a data-aware approach for constructing diagonal frame decompositions whose frames in the signal space are tight and promote sparse representations of the given data. We formulated the construction as a bilevel optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, where the nonconvex geometry of the feasible set leads to a nonconvex bilevel problem.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: To address this problem, we proposed a penalized subgradient method and established convergence results in a general setting. Under suitable assumptions, we showed that the iterates converge to stationary points at both optimization levels and the derived convergence rates in terms of appropriate stationary measures. The numerical experiments confirm the theoretical behavior of the proposed method and demonstrate its practical ability to construct data-aware DFDs. In particular, the resulting decompositions provide effective regularization tools when applied to inverse problems, where they yield competitive reconstruction results.

title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
authors: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl
content: Future work will include investigating other sparsity-promoting data terms and their practical performance in the construction of data-aware DFDs. From a theoretical perspective, an interesting direction is to extend convergence analysis towards near-stationary guaranties analogous to those established for nonconvex bilevel optimization in the Euclidean setting [ 16 , 11 ] . On the computational side, parallelization and more efficient retractions on the Stiefel manifold could further improve the practical performance of the proposed method.
