A per-task choice in hindsight between the agent alone and the policy alone reaches only 21.3% SR on the high-precision tasks with either policy. section: Gap to the better component from loose coordination.
content: Second, the combination loses part of what its components achieve alone. The per-task choice of the better component would attain 56.2% with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 60.8% with InternW0- Δ \Delta . It would thus exceed the respective harness configuration by 3.1 and 4.8 points over all tasks and by 13.8 and 8.8 points on the high-precision tasks. The harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} exceeds both of its components on only ten tasks and falls below the better one on thirteen. The harness with InternW0- Δ \Delta exceeds both on eight tasks and falls below the better one on eleven. The preceding analyses trace this loss to three sources in how agent and policy coordinate. First, the agent allocates physics steps to the policy by task horizon rather than by the policy’s competence on the task, as shown in Section 6.5 . Second, each policy segment conditions on the task instruction and the observations listed in Section 6.1 rather than on the agent’s subgoal or the stages already completed, as shown in Section 6.5 . Third, once a policy segment ends, the agent does not command the holding arm to stay closed at the returned finger width, as shown in Section 6.4 .

authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: Invoking a policy also moves computation from the agent into the policy. The agent consumes 1.83M tokens per episode with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 2.22M with InternW0- Δ \Delta , which is 52% and 41% less than the 3.77M under direct control. It also makes 23.7 and 22.7 tool calls per episode instead of 42.6. Per success, it needs 3.5M and 4.0M tokens, which is 57% and 51% fewer than the 8.1M under direct control. The savings concentrate where direct control is most expensive, as shown in Figure 9 . On long-horizon tasks, one success costs 6.2M and 7.5M tokens in the two harness configurations, which is less than two fifths of its cost under direct control. On short-horizon tasks, the cost per success falls by only a quarter to a third. Within each configuration, unsuccessful episodes still consume 2.6 and 2.4 times the tokens of successful ones, because tokens grow with the number of calls in the harness as well. At the published tariff of GPT-6-Astra, the agent’s tokens cost USD 16.82 per success under direct control but only 4.99 and 5.49 in the two harness configurations, as detailed in Appendix C.3 . In exchange, the policy adds 45 inferences of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 135 of InternW0- Δ \Delta per episode.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: This report profiles GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness. The agent observes the scene under the same visual and proprioceptive protocol as post-trained policies and acts first under direct control and then in a harness with a post-trained VLA or WAM. Under direct control, the capability boundary of the agent lies between flexible task interpretation and reliable physical execution. Without robot-specific post-training of the MLLM, the direct-control agent draws on multimodal pretraining and one annotated demonstration for each task to compete with post-trained policies overall, with particular strengths in visual grounding, robustness to generalization shifts, adaptation to failures during an episode, and zero-shot composition of skills. Physical execution, by contrast, exposes a tension in how the agent controls the robot. The agent chooses its corrections between waypoint chunks, whereas grasps, contacts, and the alignment of parts evolve within each chunk, so precise contact, bimanual coordination, and long horizons limit its success. Because each correction also resends the accumulated context, the unsuccessful and long-horizon episodes that this tension produces account for most of the agent’s token cost. The same unconstrained execution also drops held objects outside the agent’s deliberate grasp tests and at times produces abrupt wrist rotations that risk damaging physical hardware.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: Invoking a post-trained policy moves part of this boundary. With InternW0- Δ \Delta , the harness with policy reaches the highest SR and score in Table 1 , and with either policy the agent needs far fewer tokens per success on long-horizon tasks, where direct control is costliest. However, two shortfalls of the combination indicate where further progress is needed. First, precise contact limits the agent and each policy alike, so combining them leaves this ceiling in place. Second, the combination falls short of its better component on many tasks, because the coordination between agent and policy remains loose. The agent delegates without regard to the policy’s competence, the policy pursues the task instruction rather than the agent’s subgoal, and when control returns from the policy, the agent often leaves the holding arm unmaintained, allowing grasped objects to slip. These limitations motivate us to explore several directions.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
section: Designing subtask interfaces and training policies as learnable tools.
content: In the evaluated harness, the agent passes the policy only a step count, so it decides when the policy acts but can neither assign a subgoal nor receive a report of its completion. A finer interface would not only expose learned skills as tools that a planner selects ( RLinf, 2026 ) but also pass an explicit subgoal to the policy, verify the entry and exit conditions of each subtask ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and return whether the subgoal was reached. Such an interface also requires a policy that can serve it. The evaluated policies are post-trained on complete EBench task trajectories under the task instruction, whereas the harness invokes them mid-episode from states that the agent has reached and for subgoals that the agent has chosen. The policy itself therefore has to be trained as a learnable tool of the harness. This training spans three levels and can build on the subtask instruction following of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) and on the subtask descriptions and execution feedback that the authors of InternW0- Δ \Delta list as future extensions of its interface ( Miao et al., 2026 ) . First, the policy should follow the agent’s subgoals rather than only the task instruction. Second, it should be trained on the mid-episode states in which the agent transfers control, including disturbed and displaced ones. Third, it should end each segment on subgoal completion or failure, returning structured feedback to the agent and leaving any held object in a stable grasp. The agent, in turn, can be trained to delegate a subtask according to the policy’s competence on it and to use the proprioceptive state returned at every control transfer to keep a held object grasped.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
section: Grounding exploratory experience into reusable memory and tools.
content: Within an episode, the agent diagnoses slips and displaced objects and revises its strategy, yet every new episode starts again from the same static prompt. Recent work turns such experience into reusable assets. Language-model programs compose perception and control APIs into robot behavior ( Liang et al., 2023 ) , and recent harnesses synthesize task programs around post-trained policies ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , expose embodiment-specific primitives ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , or extend their control interfaces during deployment ( Li et al., 2026c ) . To admit only experience that generalizes, recent work also validates candidate skills on held-out episodes ( Lu et al., 2026 ) and isolates the evaluation from the agent that revises its own prompt and tools ( Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ) . For embodied agents, two questions follow: which recoveries generalize beyond a single trial, and whether experience accumulated with one MLLM serves other MLLMs as well. The stated reasons of the agent offer a natural starting point, as each names a diagnosed failure together with the revised action that follows it. Validated pairs of failure and revision can be retained across episodes as memory or compiled into tools that wrap closed-loop control.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
section: Transferring the agent’s exploratory and corrective strategies to smaller policies.
content: The recorded rollouts contain corrective strategies such as withdrawing for a wider view after a slip and lowering a sweep that missed the beans. The agent produces these strategies at the latency and token cost of a frontier MLLM. Distilling them into smaller models that run at deployment speed would pair failure states with the agent’s revised strategies and their outcomes, including corrections that did not succeed. Such distillation would thereby extend behavior cloning from trajectories toward the intentions behind them. Policies already improve from their own experience and from corrective interventions ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , and an LLM agent can run the cycle of training and evaluating a VLA without a human in the loop ( Yu, 2026 ) . Because agent rollouts carry the reason for every correction, they extend such training data to corrections that the agent discovers on its own.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
section: Coupling geometric perception with active safety constraints in execution.
content: Precise contact and safe execution both depend on geometry that the agent infers from RGB views without depth. On insertion, threading, and seating, the agent has to judge the height of a surface, the clearance of a part, and the onset of contact from images, and its commands reach the robot without checks against the table, the workspace bounds, or the speed of the motion. The harness can therefore pair perception tools with a safety layer. Perception tools such as depth estimation, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation, and visual checks of the terminal state can estimate these quantities from the same camera views. The safety layer can check each command against workspace, reachability, and velocity limits and interrupt chunk execution on slip or collision. On real hardware, a queryable model of the robot’s body already lets an agent convert functional targets into control targets ( Lou et al., 2026 ) , and such a model can supply the kinematic limits that this safety layer enforces. Reporting safety events beside SR and score would let benchmarks measure this progress.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: This report mainly studies the capability profile of one frontier MLLM, GPT-6-Astra, as the core of an agent on one simulated benchmark with synchronous execution, both under direct control and in a harness with two post-trained policies. Natural extensions include measuring the agent’s execution time, asynchronous execution in which the scene keeps evolving while the model deliberates, self-improvement of the agent with or without training the post-trained policy, a full evaluation of other frontier MLLMs as agent cores under the same protocol, and deployment on a physical robot. Appendix B.2 lists the protocol of each run.

content: Complete this single task yourself using the tools: Take out one of the three bowls and stack it on the plate. Robot: manip/lift2/R5a, two arms and a movable planar base. Left arm is left in the overlook view. EEF poses are local to each arm’s planner base: +X forward, +Y robot-left, +Z up; quaternion order wxyz. [...] There is no supplied depth, object pose or camera calibration. Only RGB and measured robot EEF/gripper/base state are available. [...] Use execute_eef sequentially, not parallel calls. Use observations to judge motion and object manipulation. The server determines task success independently. Do not start another episode. Resource limits: unlimited tool calls, physics deadline enforced by the server; no hard token limit; [...] When finished, state the observed outcome concisely. You may call execute_pi05 to delegate a manipulation segment to a learned policy. Choose when to delegate using the current scene. It replans every 30 steps and automatically returns control after the requested segment (at most 300 steps). The pi0.5 prompt is fixed for this task; always pass instruction=null and never invent a per-call prompt. Inspect its returned RGB/state and take over with EEF waypoints or delegate again. [...] The learned policy uses the same current three RGB cameras plus joint/gripper/base state; it receives no object ground truth or demonstration images. Manipulation guidance: after visually aligning, close at a stationary pose and allow settling. A nonzero finger gap on the table is contact evidence, not proof of a secure grasp. Test each grasp by lifting only 0.01 m first, using motion_steps=16 or more, then hold 8..16 steps and request the active wrist plus overlook views. [...] RGB inputs are downsampled: overlook 640x360, wrist 384x288; no crop or object annotation. The saved ICL demonstration remains available through query_icl throughout this episode. [...] Ground actions in the current RGB/state. [... the demonstration: annotation text and ten captioned keyframe images ...] END OF HISTORICAL DEMONSTRATION. The following images and measured state are the CURRENT episode. content: Tables B.2 and B.3 give the SR and score of the agent and the eight post-trained policies on every test task. Relative to the best post-trained policy on each task in Table B.2 , the agent’s SR is higher on three tasks, equal on five, and lower on eighteen. The three higher tasks are all mobile: Bookmark on book, Remote to holder, and Teacup, saucer & teapot. The five equal tasks are Dish, Pen, Perfume to cosmetics rack, Salt to spice rack, and Bottle, which no policy solves. The largest deficits occur on Dishwasher, Flip cup & collect cookies, and Glass into glassbox, where the agent reaches 5%, 10%, and 20% against 90% for the best post-trained policy. These three tasks involve an articulated object, coordinated use of both arms, and two-arm transfer with folding, respectively. The outcome breakdown separates two kinds of shortfall. On Tighten nut, Peg in hole, and Shop, no episode ends with a score of zero, so unsuccessful episodes receive partial credit for completed stages. On Gear installation and Utensils to holder, 15 and 13 of the 20 episodes end with a score of zero, so in these episodes the agent fails before completing the first scored stage.

content: The horizon labels follow the corrected annotation of the benchmark designers, which differs from the grouping displayed on the leaderboard. When the agent ends an episode, the robot is held in place until the evaluation server determines the outcome, and 6 of the 49 direct-control episodes that the agent ended early succeeded during this hold. In the 56 direct-control episodes interrupted by an infrastructure failure, execution resumed from the unchanged simulator state in a new model thread initialized with the recorded action history and the current observations. The direct-control run evaluated Bottle and Shop with a step limit of 3,000 steps, whereas the benchmark’s current protocol, used by both harness configurations, sets a step limit of 5,000 steps for these two tasks. Within 3,000 steps, no episode of either task succeeds in any configuration. Under a step limit of 5,000 steps, the harness with policy solves 3 of 20 Shop episodes with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 1 with InternW0- Δ \Delta , and none of Bottle. These episodes raise the overall SR of the harness configurations from 52.4% to 53.0% and from 55.8% to 56.0%, respectively.

Comparisons between configurations of the agent, and between InternW0- Δ \Delta alone and its harness configuration, pair test episodes that were run at different times, and each configuration was run once per episode. The two harness configurations differ in the policy’s replanning interval and history as well as in the policy itself. The demonstrations include top-camera keyframes that the agent does not observe during execution, and for 31 of the 510 test episodes the demonstration is a recording of the test scene itself. The demonstration of Frame placement records the scene of four of its 20 test episodes. In the comparison with and without the demonstration (Appendix D.3 ), the two conditions were rendered with partly different textures. The recordings shown in the figures were selected to illustrate each behavior.

content: The frequencies of disruptions and grip losses in Section 5 are computed from the finger gaps and commanded finger targets of both arms, recorded after every executed chunk of at most 8 physics steps, and from the stated reasons of all calls in the 510 direct-control episodes, including the segments resumed after an interruption. The finger gap of a hand is the summed opening of its two fingers, which reaches 88 mm when the hand is fully open, or 0.044 m per finger joint in state.gripper . A grip counts as closed on an object when, after a close command, the fingers come to rest between 2 and 80 mm apart over two samples at different timesteps, so that fingertips closed for pushing do not count, and as lost when the gap then collapses while the gripper is still commanded closed. A stated reason counts as reporting a disruption when it names a slip, a drop, a fall, a displacement, or a loss outside a preventive phrase such as “avoid” or “in case”, and words of an intended release such as “released” do not count. A loss counts as occurring in a grasp test when the reason of its call contains test, verify, confirm, or check as a whole word, or names a one-centimeter lift. In a random sample of 20 of the other losses, read together with the arm that loses the grip, 16 occur while an object is lifted or carried, 3 during door manipulation, and 1 during a placement.

content: The speed measures of Section 5.5 use the same chunk records, from all 510 episodes under direct control and from the segments of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in all 510 episodes of the harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , as listed in Table B.5 . Between consecutive chunks of one command, the wrist rotation is the angle between the measured EEF orientations of an arm, and the joint speed is the largest change of any arm joint, both divided by the executed physics steps. The two controllers differ in the tail of the rotation rates, as a single command of the agent can complete a large reorientation within a few chunks. In 38 commands, spread over 31 episodes, a wrist turns through 90 ∘ or more within 24 physics steps, whereas no segment of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} reaches this threshold. Most of these commands reorient or reposition the hand for a new approach. Fast joint motion shows the same contrast, as transitions above 0.08 rad per physics step occur more than five times as often under direct control.

content: Aggregate differences between configurations are tested with a bootstrap over episodes within each task (5,000 resamples), which keeps the task composition fixed, while single-task differences use exact McNemar tests with Holm correction over the 26 tasks. For the harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} against direct control, the 95% SR interval is [ + 2.0 , + 10.5 ] [+2.0,+10.5] points when episodes are resampled within each task and [ − 2.5 , + 15.6 ] [-2.5,+15.6] when tasks are resampled, and the score interval is [ + 0.006 , + 0.071 ] [+0.006,+0.071] . By group, the SR intervals are [ + 6.8 , + 19.0 ] [+6.8,+19.0] for long-horizon, [ + 3.6 , + 19.3 ] [+3.6,+19.3] for tabletop, [ − 8.6 , + 3.2 ] [-8.6,+3.2] for short-horizon, and [ − 11.3 , + 3.8 ] [-11.3,+3.8] for high-precision tasks, and the score interval for high-precision tasks is [ − 0.163 , − 0.029 ] [-0.163,-0.029] . The gain of the harness with InternW0- Δ \Delta over direct control is significant under both resampling schemes, and on the short-horizon tasks this configuration also exceeds InternW0- Δ \Delta alone under both. After Holm correction over the 26 tasks, Glass into glassbox and Dishwasher rise significantly over direct control with either tool, Teacup, saucer & teapot falls significantly with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and against InternW0- Δ \Delta alone, the corresponding harness configuration gains significantly on Apple from shelf and Perfume to cosmetics rack while losing significantly on Shop.

content: The VLA tool is the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} checkpoint fine-tuned on the EBench training set that appears as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on the leaderboard. A call executes 1–300 physics steps. The policy predicts 50 absolute joint and gripper targets per inference and replans every 30 steps under the fixed task instruction, and control returns to the agent after the requested steps with the same observations as an EEF command. The agent’s other tools and its prompt are those of Appendix A .

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: The WAM tool is an InternW0- Δ \Delta checkpoint ( Miao et al., 2026 ) post-trained on EBench data for 77,150 steps. It represents the robot by joint and EEF state and, in 10 denoising steps, predicts 32 absolute joint and gripper targets and base motions, without generating video at inference, of which the first 10 are executed before the next inference. Each inference is conditioned on the three camera views, the proprioceptive state, the first frame of the episode, and the frame 32 steps earlier, under the fixed task instruction. The harness opens one model session per episode with the episode’s initial observation and executes each 10-action chunk as 8 and 2 steps, so that the frame 32 steps back is observed within a call. During the first inferences after the agent’s own control, that frame is unavailable and is padded as at an episode start, which affects 4,276 of the 69,054 inferences. The agent invokes the policy 8.1 times per episode, with 135 inferences, against 45 inferences of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in the configuration with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Its standalone evaluation ran the same checkpoint with the same horizon, execution length, and history on all 510 test episodes with the original inference loop in which the earlier frame is always observed. This standalone evaluation is the entry of InternW0- Δ \Delta on the public leaderboard.

content: Figure C.1 groups the per-task SRs of Table C.1 by the atomic skills that EBench annotates for each task. With π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and InternW0- Δ \Delta alike, mean SR rises most on pushing, pressing, and pulling, by 21 to 70 percentage points, and sweeping improves by 17 and 24 points, respectively. Several tasks require more than one of these skills, as Dishwasher counts toward pushing, pulling, and sweeping, and Glass into glassbox accounts for most of the increase on pressing. Insertion is the only skill whose mean SR drops in both harness configurations, from 36.7% under direct control to 30.0% with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 26.7% with InternW0- Δ \Delta , while the two policies alone reach 23.3% and 18.3%. content: An episode is classified as agent-terminated when the agent stops before the step limit without succeeding. Phrase rules assign its final message to either an unconfirmed completion claim or a reported failure, and a manual check of ten episodes per run confirms this assignment. Table C.2 follows every episode of the agent under direct control to the same scene in each harness configuration. The two harness configurations newly fail 108 episodes that the agent solved under direct control: 59 with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 49 with InternW0- Δ \Delta , on 85 distinct test episodes. Each of these episodes was read call by call, with the executor, the finger widths before and after, the base motion, and the agent’s stated reason of every call. Each was then assigned the incident after which the unfinished stage was never completed, as Table C.3 lists. Each agent-terminated episode is assigned the decisive incident preceding termination: a slip of the agent’s grasp, a loss around a policy segment, or an unmet stage behind a completion claim. A grip counts as held when the fingers come to rest between 2 and 80 mm apart over two samples at different timesteps while commanded closed, and as lost when it collapses while still commanded closed, and a reported slip is a stated reason coded as in Appendix B.2 . An unmaintained grasp is an agent command that follows a policy segment and leaves an arm holding an object unspecified rather than closing it, so that the arm holds its measured finger width. Unmaintained grasps are counted per arm, so the 338 and 316 of Section 6.4 fall in 337 and 313 agent commands. The comparison in Section 6.4 counts unspecified holding arms after the agent’s own commands within the same configuration, and its stratified odds ratios use the Mantel–Haenszel estimator over the tasks on which both kinds occur.

content: Table C.5 compares successful and unsuccessful episodes of the two harness configurations. A motion command is a call of the EEF interface, the gripper command, or the policy, and a transition is a change of executor between two consecutive motion commands. Pooled over episodes, the number of transitions correlates with failure, with point-biserial correlations of r = 0.42 r=0.42 and r = 0.44 r=0.44 , and within the 23 and 18 tasks with both outcomes, unsuccessful episodes make more transitions on 22 and 17 tasks (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 2.1 × 10 − 4 p=2.1\times 10^{-4} and 1.5 × 10 − 5 1.5\times 10^{-5} ). They also issue more motion commands on every one of these tasks, with fewer transitions per motion command on 17 of the 23 tasks ( p = 0.015 p=0.015 ) and 15 of the 18 ( p = 0.06 p=0.06 ). Episodes with a recovery request to the policy fail in 75.5% and 72.0% of cases, against 15.8% and 16.8% without one. Of the 251 and 239 episodes with a disruption report, 227 and 200 contain a recovery request.

content: Using the held state and the losses defined in Appendix B.2 , every physics step between two samples of a held arm counts as a held arm-step of the executor of its call, and rates are given per 1,000 held arm-steps. The harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} holds objects for 278,496 arm-steps under the policy and 146,922 under the agent, with 176 and 321 losses, corresponding to rates of 0.63 and 2.18 per 1,000 held arm-steps. With InternW0- Δ \Delta , the corresponding values are 262,037 and 142,024 arm-steps, with 189 and 315 losses, or 0.72 and 2.22 per 1,000. Of the agent’s losses, 193 and 173 fall in grasp-test calls, and outside these calls the agent’s rates are 0.87 and 1.00. Under direct control, 811 losses over 447,352 held arm-steps give 1.81 per 1,000, and 1.05 outside grasp tests. Among the tasks with more than 2,000 held arm-steps under both executors, the agent’s rate exceeds the policy’s on 13 of 16 tasks with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 15 of 18 with InternW0- Δ \Delta .

authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: Prompt caching dominates the API-equivalent cost of every configuration (Table C.6 ). On each request, the agent resends the growing episode context, including the instructions, the demonstration, earlier observations, and tool results, so most of the input repeats an earlier prefix from the same episode and is billed at the cached-input rate. At the Standard tariff of GPT-6-Astra (USD 10, 1, 12.5, and 50 per million uncached input, cached input, cache-write, and output tokens), cached input covers 91.5–97.0% of the input tokens and still accounts for 44.0–70.5% of the cost per episode despite its tenfold discount. The recorded tokens cost USD 7.82 per episode under direct control and 2.63 and 3.06 in the harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and with InternW0- Δ \Delta , corresponding to 16.82, 4.99, and 5.49 per success. For 44 direct-control episodes the final token record is missing, and the direct-control values here, in Figure 9 , and in Section 5.3 count the recorded tokens. In all three configurations, token use rises with the number of tool calls, with Pearson correlations of 0.88 under direct control and 0.94 and 0.87 in the harness with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and with InternW0- Δ \Delta . No request exceeds the 272k input tokens above which the tariff raises input and cache rates twofold and output rates by half. Only the direct-control run records cache writes, because part of its episodes ran through the API rather than the subscription route, which reports none.

content: Figure D.6 compares rollouts of the GPT-6-Astra-based agent, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and OpenWAM- α \alpha on the two tasks summarized in Section 5.6 . In Teacup, saucer & teapot (Figure D.6 a), the agent first approaches the cup handle and refines its wrist and gripper configuration over successive attempts before grasping and placing the cup onto the saucer. When subsequent manipulation of the teapot inadvertently displaces the cup from the saucer, the agent detects that the completed subgoal has been invalidated, re-grasps the cup, and restores it to the saucer rather than continuing the remaining action sequence. By contrast, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} repeatedly approaches and retracts without completing the cup transfer, whereas OpenWAM- α \alpha fails to grasp the cup and proceeds to place the teapot onto the tray while leaving the cup off the saucer.

On Frame placement (1/20 successes zero-shot vs. 13/20 with the demonstration, mean score 0.283 vs. 0.800), under zero-shot control the agent reaches and displaces the frame, but repeatedly adjusts its approach trajectory and wrist orientation without achieving stable placement. content: Like the direct-control Dishwasher episode of Figure D.5 a, the Gear installation episode of Figure E.1 a with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ends with an unconfirmed completion claim. The agent closes the left hand on the gear hub and lifts the gear by 1 cm (calls 3 and 4, finger opening 29.9 and 30.0 mm), then invokes π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} for transport and seating in three segments of 180, 180, and 120 physics steps. In the second segment (call 6, stated reason “Continue fine alignment and seating of the blue gear on the middle axis”), π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} opens the left fingers from 29.9 to 86.2 mm beside the large gear. The agent then withdraws the open left hand and closes it (calls 8 and 9), requesting only the overview image for both commands, in which the board occupies a small part of the frame. It ends the episode at 828 physics steps with the final message “The blue gear is in the middle position between the white gears and remained there after the hand withdrew”, and the episode scores 0.5. On the same scene, the agent under direct control releases the gear, inspects the assembly from a more vertical wrist view (call 12), re-approaches the hub to correct a forward offset from the spindle (call 13), and withdraws only after the spindle becomes visible through the gear bore (call 16), solving the scene in 821 physics steps.

title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
content: In the recorded episodes, an object that leaves the reachable workspace is not recovered for the rest of the episode, as when the apple of Figure D.4 b falls and the agent under direct control searches outside the workspace. In the Detergent episode of Figure E.1 b, the agent drops the first bottle to the floor when it resumes control during a bimanual handover. InternW0- Δ \Delta closes the right hand on the first bottle while the left hand still holds it (call 4, 250 physics steps), ending with a fully closed finger command and a measured finger opening of 32.9 mm. The agent then opens the left hand (call 5) without commanding the right hand to stay closed, so the right fingers remain at their measured opening of 32.9 mm (Section 6.4 ), and the bottle tilts in the right hand while the left hand opens. In the 1 cm lift test that follows (call 6, stated reason “Check whether the receiving hand retained the bottle using a small lift”), the right fingers close from 32.8 to 2.2 mm within the first 8 physics steps, and the bottle falls from the counter to the floor. InternW0- Δ \Delta places the two other bottles in the basket by physics step 2,348, but the next 20 calls (calls 19 to 38) and 2,020 physics steps fail to recover the bottle on the floor: seven EEF waypoints directed toward the floor end 11 to 20 cm from their targets, and three InternW0- Δ \Delta segments of 300 physics steps each end with the fingers closed at 0.0 to 0.1 mm. The agent ends the episode at 4,368 physics steps with the final message “The blue/red bottle fell to the floor, and recovery attempts failed”, and the episode scores 0.67. Under direct control, the agent solves the same scene in 1,681 physics steps, carrying each bottle in the left hand without a transfer between the hands.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
section: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
content: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without any real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3 × \times faster and 17 × \times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. We demonstrate that ZAP also generalizes to completely new objects, goals, strategies, and language by seating a test tube in a rack (and choosing a different hole in the rack when prompted), handing a test tube between arms mid-air, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing chess. These goals and types of manipulation don’t appear in our training data. Furthermore, ZAP also transfers to an unseen embodiment. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.

content: We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), which adds motion to a small pretrained vision-language model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), entirely in simulation. We evaluate how these skills carry over to new tasks, real hardware, and a new embodiment. Existing methods tend to trade off performance in one of these areas for the others, and broadly fall into three groups (Table 1 ).

content: Models that directly output robot actions. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) learn semantic reasoning & motion control from robot action data [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Because diverse action data is scarce, both skills end up tied to the training distribution: the policy often generalizes poorly to new prompts, objects, scenes and goals, and a new task usually means training again.

content: Code that directly drives the robot. In Code as Policies [ 5 , 6 ] , a language model writes a program that composes perception and control APIs. This is quick and reliable when the situations it will face can be anticipated when the program is written, but struggles outside that script, for example with an unexpected failure, an unfamiliar object or an ambiguous instruction. Adapting to a new task or scene means rewriting the program.

content: ZAP combines semantic reasoning from vision-language pretraining with motion control learned entirely in simulation. We start with Qwen 3.6 27B [ 10 ] , which contributes world understanding and reasoning. We then teach the model motion control in simulation - first SFT on its own mined successful traces, followed by RL across 40 pick-and-place, stacking, and reorientation tasks. Neither stage uses real-world robot demonstrations. At test time, the policy combines pretrained semantic reasoning with learned motion control to perform real-world tasks it was never trained to execute, generalizing to new objects, goals, and robot embodiments.

content: Composing reasoning and motion. Task-and-motion planners compose symbolic operators that ground into geometric motion [ 11 , 12 ] . Large language models then proved to be better high-level planners, sequencing a library of learned skills [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] or handing subgoals to low-level policies [ 16 , 17 ] . ZAP keeps the split between reasoning and motion but drops the fixed skill library. Motion is a skill the model learns itself, through a minimal harness that leaves scene reasoning and action sequencing to the model rather than imposing macros that simplify familiar tasks but limit generalization.

content: End-to-end policies. VLAs and WAMs fold reasoning and motion into one network trained on robot actions [ 1 , 3 , 18 , 4 ] . Several studies show that these policies keep the intent of an instruction but fail to execute it on new tasks, perturbations or skill combinations [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . ZAP instead inherits the reasoning and language ability of a pretrained LLM and learns only motion, in simulation. It never has to learn language from action data, so it is not tied to the instructions that data happens to contain, and it follows what an instruction means rather than how it is worded.

content: Foundation models as robot agents. Code as Policies and its successors compose perception and control APIs into programs [ 5 , 23 ] , and frontier agents now act directly as closed-loop policies through tool harnesses [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . They bring reasoning for free, but they are slow, expensive and not trained to move a robot. The closest work trains compact tool-calling agents, mostly by distilling a frontier teacher: Guava into a 4B agent with object-referenced grasp and align tools, refined with GRPO on two tasks [ 24 ] , RACaP into an 8B model over evolved policy APIs [ 25 ] , and Robo-Harness K1 into a 9B student evaluated in simulation [ 9 ] . ZAP uses no teacher: its fine-tuning data are its own successful rollouts, and RL trains it on all 40 tasks, so no teacher sets its ceiling. It commands complete end-effector poses rather than grasp macros. Guava’s unseen tasks recombine the grasp, place and push primitives it was trained on; ZAP composes motions it never practiced, such as a mid-air handoff and a marker stroke, and runs on a different robot without retraining.

section: 3.1 One interface across simulation and hardware
content: ZAP controls two 6-DoF (degrees-of-freedom) YAM arms with parallel-jaw grippers [ 26 ] . It commands absolute end-effector poses and gripper openings, rather than joint angles, trajectories, or action chunks. We frame tasks as a conversation between the model and its environment through the harness: the model first writes a plan and names the objects to locate based on camera views of the environment, then repeatedly issues perception and movement tool calls to complete its task.

section: 3.1 One interface across simulation and hardware
content: The harness uses SAM 3.1 [ 27 , 28 ] to segment the objects named in the model’s perception queries in each camera stream. These masks are combined with calibrated depth cameras to yield each object’s 3D centroid, height, and principal axes. This process runs continuously and asynchronously in the background: the model steers perception by changing its queries, and receives object measurements and annotated camera images.

section: 3.1 One interface across simulation and hardware
content: The model controls the robot and manages the episode through five tools, two of which move the robot: move_to sets a complete end-effector pose for one or both arms, and set_gripper sets each jaw opening. change_query sets what perception looks for, update_todo keeps a short plan in view across turns, and done ends the episode. There are no grasp macros or motion primitives, so every approach, grasp, lift and release is a sequence of these two motion tools that the model plans itself.

content: Learning motion control on simulated tasks. We design 40 simulated tasks, none of which appear in RoboLab-120, that exercise the same families of everyday object manipulation skills: grasping and lifting, single- and multi-object pick and place, stacking, and reorientation. The goals are deliberately simple, and none requires heavy reasoning. This lets us test whether motion control learned on simple tasks can combine with pretrained semantic reasoning to solve unseen tasks with new goals and strategies.

content: GRPO with dense rewards. The GRPO run is initialized from the checkpoint detailed in § 3.3 and trains on all 40 tasks (hyperparameters in Appendix C ). Binary reward based on task success is inefficient since some tasks start with zero successes, and therefore a pass/fail reward would provide zero advantage and contribute no gradient. We instead shape a dense ladder of partial credit judged on the final state of the scene, manually designed per task type.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: For example, for pick and place tasks, approaching the object earns up to 0.2 in proportion to the gripper fingertip-to-object distance closed; grasping earns 0.2 and lifting up to a further 0.55, in proportion to height up to 8 cm. Transport raises the total to at most 0.9, in proportion to the distance to the goal closed. Completing a task earns 5.0, minus a small length penalty which penalizes the model for taking too many turns to complete the task. The specific numbers for partial credit were not ablated and instead holistically chosen: our guiding principle was that final task success must have a much higher reward than partial reward; otherwise, the model settles for collecting partial credit. The success checker is hardened against reward hacking, for example, by requiring that the goal hold for at least half a second.

content: We penalize turns where either no tool call is made, or where invalid motion is proposed and doesn’t pass certain validation checks (see Appendix A ). These turns (but not the whole sequence) receive a negative advantage, regardless of the episode’s score. In earlier runs without these penalties, the corresponding error rates reached as high as 4% and 34%, respectively. With penalties, these rates fall to 0% and 3%.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Seeding the model with its own successes. A model which is on-distribution for its task space helps reduce variance during RL training, so we first fine-tune on successful agent traces. That raises the question of how to collect them. One option is rejection sampling from either our fixed base model or a larger open model. However, this is prohibitively inefficient, and many tasks never succeed even after hundreds of attempts per task. Instead, initializing from the base model, we run a short GRPO warm-up run of several dozen steps and over-sample the harder tasks, and mine its successful rollouts for SFT. As the policy improves, harder tasks start to yield successes, so the data comes from a slightly evolved version of the model itself, a self-distillation loop that is close to on-policy.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent

content: Prefix-tree search. For tasks that still never succeed, we perform a tree-search over partial episodes (Appendix Figure 8 ). A node is created after each physical action settles; to expand it, we reset the simulator to the task’s deterministic start, replay the node’s stored actions, restore the agent’s context, and sample a new continuation. A best-first rule favors high dense reward and less-explored nodes and prunes failing branches, with up to about 1,000 leaves per task. This found successful traces for several tasks that RL sampling never solved, and these traces are added to the fine-tuning data.

content: Where the VLA breaks. MolmoAct2’s failures follow the meaning of the instruction more than the difficulty of the motion (Appendix Table 6 ). For example, we evaluate the model’s ability to pick & place a Rubik’s cube in different locations. When asked to place in a bowl, it places it successfully 3/3 times. But when prompted to place the cube behind the bowl, it never succeeds (0/3), often still placing it into the bowl. In another task, the VLA must place exactly 3 bananas in a bin and always places too many. The motions are nearly the same; what changes is a spatial relation or count, reflected in the prompt. A VLA can only learn what words like behind or exactly three mean from its robot action data, whereas ZAP already understands them from vision-language pretraining.

From the agent’s perspective, only the system prompt describing the embodiment changes; the harness stays exactly the same. The Franka differs from the YAM in most of the ways that matter to a policy that outputs joint angles or action chunks: one arm instead of two, seven joints instead of six, a different gripper, different reach, and different cameras. We compare two SFT runs: one using 455 successful traces mined early in GRPO, and one using 3.9k traces mined more aggressively after GRPO runs longer, especially on harder tasks. RoboLab-120 success rises from 17.2% to 58.3% (Table 5 , left), a gain of 41.1 points from the same recipe with better data. section: 5 Composing the skills on new tasks
content: A new object and a new task: the test tube. We ask the model to vertically lower a test tube into a rack (Figure 3 ). Both objects and the goal are unseen in training. The model constructs the strategy itself: it grasps the tube lying on its side, turns the gripper so the tube is vertical, and lowers it into a hole. This is challenging because, at the moment of placement, the hole is hidden from every camera. A VLA would typically need task-specific demonstrations of each of these steps; ZAP receives only a single text instruction and, without demonstrations or parameter updates, infers the required motion.

section: 5 Composing the skills on new tasks
content: Steered by the instruction. The model brings the language understanding of its pretrained LLM into its actions. VLAs often respond poorly to changes in their prompts [ 35 ] . ZAP is able to follow precise instructions; on the same starting scene, we replace the instruction with a request to place the tube in a hole at the top left of the rack. With the default prompt, the model picks a hole on its own; with the new one, the tube ends up in the top-left corner (Figure 4 ).

section: 5 Composing the skills on new tasks
content: A new strategy on request: bimanual handoff. We then ask for a completely different way to reach the same goal: hand the tube from one arm to the other in mid-air, then place it in the rack (Figure 5 ). The prompt describes the handoff in writing, but training contains no bimanual interaction even close to a handoff. The model orients the tube-cap up and brings it, held by one arm, to the middle of the table; brings the other arm over the tube and descends from above, just far enough to grasp the cap but not so low that it hits the first arm; closes the receiving gripper, then opens the giving one; moves the giving arm out of the way; and lowers the tube into a hole. Getting this right means timing the two grippers against each other: if the giving arm lets go too early the tube falls, and if the receiving arm comes in too low the grippers collide.

section: 5 Composing the skills on new tasks
content: Complex reasoning: tic-tac-toe and chess. The last two tasks require the model to reason about what a goal means before it can act (Figure 6 ). For tic-tac-toe, we prompt the model to draw an X in the center of a tic tac toe game drawn on a whiteboard. It picks up the marker, recognizes what a tic-tac-toe board is and where its center square lies, and draws the X: it keeps enough contact to leave a line through each stroke, without pressing so hard that it breaks or dislodges the marker. The instruction determines both a place on the board and the motion needed to draw there.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
section: 5 Composing the skills on new tasks
content: For chess, we prompt the model that it is black to move, with mate in one. It observes the board, reasons about the rules of chess to find the single mating move, and then picks up the correct piece and sets it on the target square to complete the checkmate. Through reasoning, the model has determined which piece to grasp and where to put it.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: A robot policy does not need to learn reasoning and motion together from scarce robot data. A 27B VLM brings world understanding and reasoning from pretraining, and SFT followed by RL on 40 simple simulated tasks adds the skill of moving a bimanual robot. A checkpoint trained exclusively in simulation reaches 96.7% success on real hardware tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness while running 3 × \times faster and 17 × \times cheaper, and transfers to a single-arm Franka. Its skills also compose on new real tasks, objects, language and goals: seating a test tube, choosing a different hole when asked, performing a mid-air handoff, drawing an X on a tic-tac-toe board, and playing a checkmate. Because the motion skill comes entirely from simulation, extending it calls for more simulated tasks rather than more robot demonstrations.

content: Tools. ZAP has five tools. move_to moves one or both arms to a complete end-effector pose; naming both arms in one call produces a single synchronized motion. set_gripper sets each jaw opening, from 0 (closed) to 1 (fully open). change_query sets the text descriptions of the objects that perception segments. update_todo writes a short plan that is repeated in every later observation, so it survives when old turns are dropped from context. done ends the episode.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Poses. Each move_to gives an absolute position of the tool center point, in meters, and a full orientation, in a world frame shared by both arms. Perception reports object positions in the same frame and units, so a measured centroid can be used directly as a target. The harness has no relative moves, grasp macros or approach primitives. In earlier versions, such macros raised success on the objects they were designed around but got in the way on everything else. Without them, the model plans the approach, grasp, lift, transport and release itself, and the motions it learned on pick and place carry over to rotating a tube, a mid-air handoff and drawing with a marker (§ 5 ).

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Orientation. Orientation is given by three angles, each measured counterclockwise from world + x +x (Figure 7 ). Slot yaw ψ \psi is the heading of the jaw slot, the axis a held object lies along. Tilt τ \tau is the angle of the tool axis from straight down: 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} is top-down and 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} is horizontal. Tilt direction ϕ \phi is the compass direction the fingertips point toward. We use these instead of Euler angles or quaternions for two reasons. Neither of those states directly where the gripper points or how its jaws are aligned, the two quantities that decide a grasp. And a horizontal tool, as in a side grasp, lies at an Euler singularity, where a few degrees of physical error can show up as a change of about 100 ∘ 100^{\circ} in the reported angles. Our angles are ambiguous only when the tool points straight down or straight up, where tilt direction has no physical meaning.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Observations and perception. Each turn adds one observation to the conversation: one downscaled RGB image from each of the three cameras (for bimanual YAM, overhead and one per wrist), the perception results, the measured tool pose and jaw opening of each arm, and the remaining step budget. Perception uses SAM 3.1 [ 27 , 28 ] , which runs continuously in the background on every camera stream rather than as a tool the model calls and waits on. It segments the objects named by the current queries, draws their masks and numbered boxes on the images, and uses depth to compute each object’s 3D centroid, height and principal axes in world coordinates. The model controls perception only through change_query , which it can call at any time, for example to find a missed object or to segment part of one, such as the cap of a tube. Detections are not fused across cameras; the model decides which ones refer to the same object. In simulation, perception runs on the rendered images and depth, as it does on the real cameras, and never reads any privileged information such as object poses that would be unavailable on hardware.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Validation. Before a move_to call reaches the controller, the harness checks it against limits declared for the robot, such as tilt range and workspace bounds. A call that fails a check is refused rather than clipped to a nearby feasible value, and the model receives the reason as an error message so it can try something else.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Controller and outcome reports. The controller turns a valid pose into a straight-line Cartesian path, solves inverse kinematics densely along it, and refuses the motion if the resulting joint path cannot be validated. When the arm comes to rest, the controller reports one of five outcomes per arm: reached (execution completed and the arm came to rest within tolerance), short (the arm came to rest outside tolerance), incomplete (execution began but did not finish, for example because of a stall), not attempted (nothing moved, for example because no valid path exists) or unknown (the outcome could not be determined). Any outcome other than reached also reports its cause, whether it arose in planning or execution, and the measured position and orientation errors.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: One harness for simulation and hardware. The harness is the same in simulation and on the real robot. Everything specific to a robot, such as joint limits, cameras and workspace bounds, comes from a declarative embodiment description. Moving from the simulator to the real rig, or to the Franka, means swapping that description and the low-level backend, and nothing else. This is why a policy trained only in simulation runs on the real robot without changes.

content: Figure 7: Slot yaw, tilt and tilt direction. The gripper orientation parameterization used by move_to (§ 3.1 ). Left: slot yaw ψ \psi turns the jaw slot (blue), the axis a held object lies along, about the vertical. Middle: tilt τ \tau leans the tool axis (teal) away from straight down; 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} is top-down and 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} horizontal. Right: tilt direction ϕ \phi sets the compass direction the fingertips tip toward. Each angle changes exactly one thing about the gripper that can be seen. All angles are measured counterclockwise from world + x +x .

section: Appendix B A real-robot episode, turn by turn
content: To make the agent loop of § 3.1 concrete, we step through one complete episode of ZAP on the real bimanual rig. The task is “pick up both blocks”. The episode succeeds in 9 turns and 74.6 s of wall-clock time, with 4 robot actions, 118,985 input tokens and 1,920 output tokens. Each image is the observation the agent received at the start of that turn (left wrist, overhead, right wrist); from turn 2 on it includes the SAM 3.1 masks and numbered boxes for the current perception queries, computed in the background. The overhead camera faces the arms from across the table, so its image-left is the robot’s right. Below each image we give an excerpt of the model’s reasoning, the single tool call it emitted, and the result the harness returned, which reaches the agent as the tool message at the start of the next turn. Reasoning is abridged with […]; tool calls are verbatim.

content: Compositional reasoning in robotics. Classical robotics composes behavior explicitly. Task-and-motion planners search over symbolic operators that ground into geometric motion [ 11 , 41 , 12 ] . Learned variants acquire the operators, their abstractions or their programs from data [ 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] , or chain learned skills with generative models [ 46 ] , or compose diffusion policies across tasks and domains [ 47 ] . Coding agents can also synthesize generalized TAMP programs [ 48 ] . Language models later took over the high-level planner: they plan zero-shot in language or as programs [ 49 , 50 ] , sequence a library of learned skills [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , hand subgoals to RL-trained or local low-level policies [ 16 , 17 ] , or supply open-world constraints to a TAMP solver [ 51 , 52 ] . ZAP keeps the split between reasoning and motion but drops the fixed skill library. The interface is a set of tools in physical units, and motion is a skill the model learns itself, so a grasp learned on pick and place can be reused as a tube rotation or a marker stroke.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: End-to-end policies and their compositional limits. Embodied multimodal language models [ 53 ] and vision-language-action models (VLAs) fold reasoning and motion into one network trained on robot actions, increasingly pooled across embodiments [ 54 , 55 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 4 ] . World-action models (WAMs) additionally predict future observations alongside actions, using video as a dense representation of how the world evolves [ 18 , 59 , 60 ] . Zero-WAM uses in-context human videos to guide unseen tasks [ 61 ] , while ObjDream uses object-level representations and future object-state prediction to improve generalization to new layouts and backgrounds [ 62 ] . Some recover a hierarchy inside the model through embodied chain-of-thought or a high-level policy [ 63 , 64 , 65 , 66 ] . Several studies show that these policies keep the intent of an instruction but fail to execute it on new tasks, held-out perturbations or new skill combinations [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 67 ] . Recent diagnoses also find that current VLAs struggle with instructions specifying how to carry out a task [ 22 ] . One reason is that compositional coverage in action data is expensive to collect [ 68 ] . Benchmarks now measure compositional generalization directly, from compositional RL suites [ 69 ] to arm-wise composition in dual-arm VLAs [ 70 ] , alongside standard manipulation benchmarks [ 71 ] and real-to-sim evaluation [ 72 ] . ZAP learns no reasoning from action data; it learns only motion, and only in simulation.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Foundation models as robot agents. Code as Policies and its successors compose perception and control APIs into programs or value maps [ 5 , 23 , 73 ] , in the style of tool-using agents [ 74 ] . RAX compiles a coding agent’s online exploration into robot programs that run without the agent [ 75 ] ; MoCaP uses passive human videos to guide code-as-policy for mobile manipulation [ 76 ] . Multimodal language-model agents remain weak at low-level manipulation when used off the shelf [ 77 ] . Recent work nonetheless uses frontier agents directly as closed-loop policies: on real YAM arms [ 7 , 8 , 32 ] , including head-to-head comparisons with VLAs on bimanual tasks [ 78 ] and in simulation [ 79 ] , through general agent frameworks [ 80 , 81 ] , through a visual interface [ 82 ] , through in-context learning [ 83 ] , through primitive motion commands [ 84 ] , or with perception tools and test-time simulation [ 9 , 85 , 86 ] . SEAR compares code-as-policy, agent-as-policy and VLA auto-research, with controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts and larger budgets [ 87 ] .

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Other work improves the harness, with evolving code, skill libraries or playbooks [ 88 , 89 , 90 , 91 , 92 , 93 ] . URAI lets frontier agents write, call and evolve reusable robot tools [ 94 ] , while ChunkAct chains primitives into action chunks to reduce model calls [ 95 ] . Some harnesses surround a VLA: Cracking Mobile Manipulation adds planning, navigation and local-motion interventions around a fixed policy [ 96 ] , and CarryOn adds planning and execution loops with reusable recovery skills [ 97 ] . AdaRSI first improves the harness, then fine-tunes the executor on sub-steps that remain unreliable [ 98 ] .

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Concurrent work adapts frontier-agent skills from simulation to hardware without weight updates [ 99 , 100 , 101 ] . SimEX develops a robot toolbox in simulation, then adapts it and the simulator through a few physical trials [ 102 ] . ZAP trains the motion skill into an open 27B model that runs 3 × \times faster and 17 × \times cheaper than the frontier model it matches.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: VLMs that directly predict actions. EASG projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera image and lets a pretrained VLM generate continuous translations and rotations as text [ 103 ] . This grounds the action space for zero-shot manipulation, and the same interface supports fine-tuning on robot trajectories. ZAP also uses the model’s native text generation to command motion, learning full absolute end-effector poses through SFT and RL entirely in simulation.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Small trained robot agents. The closest work trains compact agents. Guava distills frontier-model trajectories collected in simulation into a 4B agent using semantic grasp and align tools [ 24 ] . RACaP evolves reusable policy APIs, then distills frontier-model ReAct decisions into an 8B model for efficient deployment [ 25 ] . Show-Harness fine-tunes a 2B model on discrete action units, partly on RoboLab [ 104 ] . Robo-Harness K1 distills a 9B student, evaluated only in simulation [ 9 ] . CaP-RL trains a 7B code-writing model with GRPO in simulation and transfers it to cube lifting and stacking [ 6 ] .

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Other work fine-tunes VLM agents for manipulation question answering [ 105 ] or calls a small agent-ready action model through tools [ 106 ] . ZAP trains mainly with RL on its own multi-turn simulation rollouts to command full robot poses. Beyond Guava’s tested recombinations of familiar skills, ZAP shows new real-world strategies, including a mid-air handoff and marker drawing, and transfers the same checkpoint from bimanual YAM to simulated Franka without retraining.

authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: RL for language-model agents and embodied reasoning. Online RL can ground language models as policies in text and simulated environments [ 107 , 108 , 109 ] . Multi-turn agent RL has since scaled with GRPO-style objectives [ 36 , 110 , 111 , 112 , 113 ] . In robotics, RL has sharpened embodied and physical reasoning in VLMs, for example pointing and keypoint prediction [ 114 , 115 , 116 ] , has fine-tuned VLAs in simulation [ 117 , 118 , 119 ] , and has trained agentic recovery decisions over VLA execution [ 120 ] , including at scale for sim-to-real transfer [ 121 ] . ZAP applies multi-turn GRPO to a VLM tool agent whose actions are real robot motions.

content: Sim-to-real. Domain and dynamics randomization made simulation-only training viable for low-level control [ 122 , 123 , 124 ] . Large procedurally generated simulations now transfer manipulation policies zero-shot [ 125 ] , and object-centric abstractions narrow the gap further [ 126 ] . We use Isaac Sim and RoboLab [ 29 , 127 , 30 ] . Our tool interface acts as the abstraction: the observations and actions the model sees are the same in simulation and on hardware [ 128 ] . As a result, only dynamics and perception, not the interface, differ between the two.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Academic publishing serves a dual purpose. First, it provides a lasting record of scientific discoveries and a means for scholars to share, evaluate, and build upon others’ work. The second purpose is less explicit. Publications have long served as an indicator of an author’s understanding of their field. A paper in a respected peer-reviewed journal was generally taken as evidence of expertise, often without closer examination. This particular aspect of publishing shapes academic job prospects for early-career academics. Graduate students and postdocs seek to publish in prestigious journals, motivated both by the scientific value of their work and by the recognition that publication brings. For an early-career scientist, publishing is thus both a means of advancing knowledge and a way to build the reputation needed to compete for academic positions. Academic recruiters, in turn, have long relied on strong publications as evidence of a candidate’s depth of understanding.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: With the advent of highly capable and easily accessible AI, however, producing high-quality research papers is no longer so rare. For example, AI models can now make progress on long-standing problems across several mathematical fields [ 20 , 21 , 2 ] . Their users can therefore produce impressive research without developing the depth of understanding that was once necessary to produce the same output [ 29 ] . This effect is most pronounced in mathematics and in the theoretical branches of science and engineering. Specifically in these domains, AI has weakened the once-tight link between producing strong results and understanding one’s field.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: In response to AI, academic communities are now reconsidering how they evaluate their researchers. A summit of mathematicians discussing the future of the math Ph.D. recommended placing less weight on dissertation texts, and more weight on in-person assessments and thesis defenses [ 23 ] . A working group in theoretical computer science proposed reviewing at most three works per applicant, and also recommended ‘chalk talks’ to assess technical depth [ 25 ] . The free and open-access preprint server arXiv has introduced a monthly quota of two submissions per individual [ 4 ] . These measures echo calls to cap researchers’ publication rates [ 22 , 9 , 6 ] .

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Other responses focus on research norms. Some mathematicians have pledged to work without AI [ 3 ] . Others oppose hiring colleagues who substitute AI output for their own work [ 19 , 32 ] . Joint statements and policies address attribution, disclosure, and AI’s effects on mathematical practice [ 1 , 24 , 17 , 26 , 7 ] . Early-career mathematicians must navigate these changing expectations while building their careers [ 28 ] . At the same time, departments and other recruiters of researchers must decide how to evaluate applicants whose preparation responds to those very decisions. Each side’s best choice therefore depends on that of the other, and neither can be settled in isolation. Game theory is designed to analyze exactly this kind of strategic interdependence.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: In this paper, we study a game-theoretic model of the incentives on both sides of the academic job market in the age of AI. Applicants differ in potential and choose one of two trajectories: deep study or shallow study with AI. Deep study builds theoretical understanding but costs more to the applicant than shallow study with AI. Furthermore, deep study may reduce paper output for applicants who are not of high potential. Shallow study with AI is cheaper and produces high output without building understanding. How much more deep study costs also depends on the applicant’s potential. Recruiters observe only an applicant’s paper output and the result of a possibly imperfect test of understanding, such as an interview, which the applicant either passes or fails (the likelihood to pass is much larger if an applicant understands ). Because an applicant’s potential and their study choice remain hidden from recruiters, recruiters must infer understanding from two signals: paper output and the applicant’s performance in the test. The recruiters’ hiring decisions depend on how much they value output and understanding, and they may reward either one or both. We ask how applicants of different potentials should choose their study trajectories, and how recruiters should decide when presented with a publication list and a test result.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: We characterize all pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibria of this game. These equilibria identify patterns of study and hiring that neither side has an incentive to unilaterally change. We then examine which behaviors emerge under a learning process, such as payoff-based imitation and rare exploration. This evolutionary analysis helps distinguish possible equilibria from outcomes that tend to emerge through learning. We also relate proposed institutional reforms [ 23 , 25 , 4 ] to changes in the model’s parameters. This yields conditional predictions about how those reforms could affect study and hiring.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Section 2 defines the game, and Section 3 characterizes its equilibria. Section 4 examines evolutionary selection among outcomes. Section 5 discusses institutional implications, related work, and limitations. The Appendix (Section A ) gives the evolutionary methods.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
section: 2 Game-theoretic model of academic effort and hiring
content: Game description. We study an effort-and-hiring signaling game between applicants and recruiters. A candidate (say, a graduate student) shows up to a job interview with a resume that highlights the academic papers they have under their belt. We classify profiles with a binary variable y y , with y = 0 y=0 denoting few papers and y = 1 y=1 denoting many papers. We assume it is impossible to fake a profile. That is, a hiring committee can reliably check if a candidate is lying on their resume.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
