Initiatives like Project Glasswing should be expanded in scope and multidisciplinary composition.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: should require audited evidence of independent developmental coverage as a core governance control. Emerging litigation regarding addictive design [ 40 ] , corporate liability for AI outputs [ 38 ] , and automated care denials [ 23 , 67 ] demonstrates that lifespan AI liability is a material risk. Matrix coverage provides an auditable, comparable metric directly usable for ESG disclosures, due diligence, and insurance underwriting.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: This section outlines methodological constraints and scope boundaries of the proposed framework. While independent evaluation shifts the failure distribution toward lower-severity events, it does not eliminate risk. Below, we address central limitations across causal attribution, construct validity, evaluator incentives, alignment scope, and empirical selection bias.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Isolating AI-attributable harm from broader environmental, socio-economic, and educational influences remains a methodological challenge. Furthermore, longitudinal monitoring risks confounding developmental age effects with generational cohort effects (e.g., varying lifetime technology exposure across generations), requiring designs that systematically decouple them.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The five moderators and six stages are grounded in developmental science but represent hypothesis structuring instruments rather than fully validated parameterizations. Their factor structure, independence, and measurement validity in human-AI interaction require ongoing empirical testing. The same caution applies to the DH principles: they are a proposed synthesis, and the mapping from principle to moderator is an argument we advance rather than a validated correspondence.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: External evaluation bodies remain vulnerable to commercial capture. Mitigating conflicts of interest requires institutional safeguards adapted from financial auditing, such as mandatory evaluator rotation, whistleblower protections, and independent quality oversight [ 65 ] . We note the countervailing caution that formal audit regimes can decay into ritualized verification that produces assurance documents without producing assurance [ 48 ] ; an evaluation regime indexed to auditable coverage metrics is intended in part to resist that failure mode.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The framework evaluates safety at the behavioral and output level; it serves as a necessary complement to, rather than a substitute for, foundational alignment research.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The incident record exhibits strong selection bias — overrepresenting high-severity cases from large organizations in high-income, Western contexts. Stages with sparse incident documentation (e.g., emerging adulthood) reflect an absence of systematic monitoring rather than an absence of risk. The global distribution of AI harm is broader and more concentrated in vulnerable populations than currently documented.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Future research must validate the developmental evaluation framework, formalize measurement standards, and address emerging technical challenges. We identify four priority avenues for empirical, methodological, policy, and cross-cultural investigation.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Research must verify whether each tier reliably surfaces distinct failure classes and quantify detection rate differentials between internal-only and hybrid external evaluation regimes. The M3 displacement hypothesis requires direct test in populations acquiring the offloaded capability, rather than extrapolation from adult offloading studies.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Interdisciplinary efforts across clinical psychology, developmental science, gerontology, and HCI are needed to establish validated operational metrics for the five moderators, and to extend the DH principles beyond the initial set proposed here.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Investigating the market and regulatory conditions — such as liability law, procurement mandates, insurance underwriting, and network dynamics — that drive adoption of independent safety evaluation.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Testing the validity of the matrix’s developmental constructs across non-Western populations and diverse regulatory jurisdictions. Crucially, extending the framework to autonomous agentic systems represents the most urgent technical challenge; agentic deployment fundamentally transfers consequence authority (M4) from the user directly to the system, and is the most likely source of DH principles beyond those proposed here.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: This paper has argued that safety deficits in frontier AI are structural rather than procedural. Closing the assurance gap requires shifting from developer self-assessment to independent, external evaluation indexed directly to human developmental vulnerability.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The empirical record demonstrates that isolated product harms across the lifespan reflect a single underlying failure: systems are evaluated against an implicit model of a cognitively typical adult, ignoring stage-varying human vulnerability. Consequently, vulnerability peaks at both ends of the lifespan while oversight remains asymmetrical, leaving high-authority adult decisions largely unscrutinized and vulnerable populations exposed.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The operational tools — automated simulation, expert red teaming, and continuous post-deployment monitoring — already exist in prototype. What remains missing is their systematic integration into an independent governance architecture indexed to the developmental state of the user. Independent external evaluation is a structural necessity; the imperative now is how rapidly institutions can build the capacity to execute it.

authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: This paper discusses documented, publicly reported AI harm incidents, including cases involving suicide, child safety, CSAM, and elder exploitation, solely for the purpose of empirical governance analysis; no new or previously undisclosed harmful content is introduced. Individuals in cited incidents are identified only where their involvement is already a matter of public legal or journalistic record, and minors are not named. Allegations in pending or concluded litigation are described as allegations. The authors acknowledge that the empirical record carries documented selection and reporting biases, discussed in Section 7 , and that any governance framework derived from it should be applied with attention to populations underrepresented in that record.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
section: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
content: Clinical trial prescreening requires distinguishing unmet conditions from insufficient evidence in patient records. Given patient records, criterion questions, and predefined answer options, we retrospectively compared JEV, a non-generative decision model returning native option probabilities, with schema-constrained Qwen Flash across 2,048 test patient–condition pairs from TrialGPT and question–answer datasets derived from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, all evaluated under strict Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policies to ensure clinical data privacy. Both models assessed conditions individually or in batches sharing the same patient context, with performance measured against reference labels. In batch mode, JEV and Qwen achieved similar macro-F1 scores on TrialGPT (0.652 vs. 0.660) and MIMIC-IV (0.807 vs. 0.814), whereas JEV substantially outperformed Qwen on MIMIC-III (0.768 vs. 0.534; Δ \Delta = +0.234, 95% CI: 0.187–0.281). This advantage largely reflected higher recall for conditions labeled as having insufficient information (56.3% vs. 9.9%). Across all three datasets, JEV also had lower observed median job latency (1.18–1.40 vs. 2.80–8.90 s) and 53%–74% lower estimated cost per condition. These findings position JEV as an initial assessment component that provides criterion-level judgments and flags potential information gaps for review. JEV’s observed errors in interpreting clinical evidence underscore the need to verify its outputs against patient records before they inform eligibility decisions.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
content: Clinical trial prescreening requires assessing patient records against individual inclusion and exclusion criteria [ 2 ] . A useful initial assessment must distinguish whether a condition is clearly unmet or simply lacks sufficient evidence in the record. This judgment depends on interpreting clinical statements in context, including their negation and timing [ 1 ] . For example, a documented symptom may leave a criterion unresolved if its required duration is not recorded. The task is therefore to produce criterion-level judgments that preserve potential information gaps for subsequent review.

content: Figure 1: Proposed role of JEV in clinical trial prescreening. (a) Reviewers assess the patient record against individual inclusion and exclusion criteria and document their judgments. (b) JEV assesses criteria sharing the same patient context in a batch, returning provisional labels and native option probabilities. Clinicians verify these judgments against the patient record and follow up on potential information gaps before making a screening decision.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
content: Generative large language models (LLMs) have been applied to this task. TrialGPT produces criterion-level eligibility predictions together with explanations and relevant sentence locations in patient notes [ 2 ] . Related work has used synthetic data distillation to train smaller LLMs for clinical information extraction, including trial-related questions [ 9 ] . These studies motivate evaluating models in terms of both the correctness of their judgments, the latency and cost of obtaining them. For an initial assessment with predefined answer options, non-generative decision modeling provides an alternative approach to examine.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
content: JEV is a non-generative decision model that takes a text context, natural-language questions, and predefined answer options as input and returns selected labels with native options probabilities [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . In criterion assessment, the context is the patient record, each question specifies a clinical condition, and the options define the permitted assessment labels. Multiple questions can share the same patient context [ 4 ] . Figure 1 illustrates JEV’s proposed role in initial assessment before evidence verification and final screening. Because generative models can also return schema-constrained labels, the relevant question is how JEV compares in classification performance, handling of insufficient evidence, and service latency and cost.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
content: We retrospectively compare JEV with schema-constrained Qwen Flash on 2,048 test patient-condition pairs form TrialGPT and two question-answer resources derived from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV [ 2 , 7 , 8 ] . Both models receive the same patient records, criterion questions, and label definitions, with conditions assessed individually or in batches sharing a patient context. We retain source-specific reference conventions and report performance separately for each dataset. The evaluation combines classification performance with observed job latency and estimated cost per condition. Directional error analysis and representative cases help interpret the aggregate comparison; native probability diagnostics separately assess JEV’s reported confidence.

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?

content: We evaluate initial criterion assessment: given a patient record, a condition question, and predefined answer options, a model assigns a label to the patient–condition pair. Here, a condition refers to either a trial criterion or a clinical question adapted for screening. The permitted labels describe whether the stated condition holds, does not hold, remains unresolved, or does not apply (Table 1 ). For an exclusion criterion, MET indicates that the disqualifying condition holds. Figure 1 places these judgments before clinical verification; the present evaluation scores model outputs against source-derived reference labels without clinician revision.

content: JEV is a non-generative decision model accessed through TypeSafe’s text Choice application programming interface (API). We evaluated the fixed model version jev-1.14.0. content: A net gain does not imply that every changed answer improved. On MIMIC-IV, Qwen Batch corrects 48 Single errors but introduces 27 errors on previously correct conditions. Thirteen of the corrections occur among the 30 reference-unknown conditions, with no damages within that class. Request packaging is therefore associated with a marked change in evidence-state classification for Qwen on this track. One saved execution per mode cannot distinguish the effect of accompanying questions from repeated-call variability.

content: Thinking raises macro-F1 point estimates by 2.39 points on TrialGPT and 2.95 points on MIMIC-III, and lowers it by 2.89 points on MIMIC-IV (Table 6 ). All three paired intervals include zero. Class-specific changes provide a more informative interpretation than a global statement that thinking helps or harms. TrialGPT gains 19 correct labels overall while losing six correct insufficient predictions. MIMIC-IV gains one correct answer overall while losing five correct insufficient predictions, with no corrections in that class. The latter redistribution explains how accuracy can rise slightly while macro-F1 falls.

content: JEV Batch has lower observed job latency and estimated cost than Qwen Batch on all three test tracks. Its median job times are 1.20 versus 4.55 seconds on TrialGPT, 1.18 versus 2.80 seconds on MIMIC-III, and 1.40 versus 8.90 seconds on MIMIC-IV. content: Within JEV, Batch lowers TrialGPT median job time from 8.08 to 1.20 seconds and MIMIC-IV from 18.30 to 1.40 seconds. MIMIC-III changes little, with 322 test conditions distributed across 319 jobs. This pattern is consistent with greater amortization when multiple conditions share a record.

content: Cost superiority is not universal across modes. On MIMIC-IV Single, Qwen’s estimated upper-bound cost is USD 0.1987 per 1,000 conditions versus JEV’s 0.2057. Across all frozen partitions and both modes, the reference runs contain 6,270 planned outputs per model; estimated total upper bounds are USD 0.6306 for JEV and USD 1.0481 for Qwen. These totals exclude the separate thinking comparison..

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang, Wu Yuan
content: This retrospective benchmark shows that JEV’s native choice interface can produce criterion-level decisions and label probabilities at low observed Batch latency and estimated cost. Its quality advantage is conditional on the task and request configuration: the largest JEV–Qwen difference occurs on MIMIC-III and is concentrated in reference-unknown conditions, while Batch macro-F1 point estimates are close on TrialGPT and MIMIC-IV. Additional Qwen thinking increases resource use without a uniform quality gain in the matched comparison.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
section: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains on cheap checks, such as unit tests, that a policy can learn to game, while a stronger check is too expensive to run on every rollout. We study how to spend a limited strong-verifier budget in GRPO, separating which weakly passing rollouts to audit from what reward a caught hack receives. At a fixed policy state with centered advantages, the expected update depends on a design only through each rollout’s marginal audit probability and correction; reflecting a caught hack’s reward about the failure reward negates the advantages of an all-hack group; and auditing whole groups with the fewest weak passes first (low-pass budgeted audits, LB ) minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among pass-count designs with a fixed correction when a label’s value falls with the pass count. We tested this analysis in actual LLM training: from each run’s starting state, the sign of this mass on a frozen panel predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. In LeetCode (Wong et al., 2026) and Countdown-Code (Khalifa et al., 2026), LB drives hacking to near zero, while random audits with the same penalty and budget do not and use more labels. We also find that the randomness of the update affects training: in Countdown-Code, two unbiased corrections, per-item reward-level IPW and a group-level advantage correction, bring hacking down too but end 6.1–11.8 and 8.0–11.5 points lower in held-out accuracy than LB at the same budget. A full audit, which the group-level correction reproduces in expectation, stays within about two points of LB in three seeds, while LB uses 28% of its labels, and allocating the same correction by pass count recovers most of the loss (one seed). Training outcomes thus depend not only on the expected update but also on the randomness of its estimate.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO

content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models on automatic checks such as unit tests, and a policy can learn to pass a weak check without solving the task. In Countdown-Code it rewrites the target value in its own solution file so that the provided test passes ( Khalifa et al., 2026 ) ; in the LeetCode environment of Wong et al. (2026) it defines its own run_tests function, which the grader then executes. A stronger check, such as the full test suite or a semantic check of the answer, is usually available, but it costs too much to run on every rollout ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Sakib et al., 2026 ) .

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: This paper asks how to spend a fixed strong-verifier budget during group-relative policy optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024 ). An audit design makes two choices: which weakly passing rollouts to send to the strong verifier ( selection ) and what reward a caught hack receives ( correction ). Two defaults are natural: random audits with an inverse-propensity correction, which reproduce the full-audit reward in expectation ( Horvitz and Thompson, 1952 ; Moya et al., 2026 ; Sakib et al., 2026 ) , and giving a caught hack the reward its strong verdict implies. Neither accounts for how GRPO turns rewards into updates. A rollout’s advantage depends on its siblings, so the same caught hack can push the policy strongly, weakly, or not at all.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: We make three observations. First, without group standard-deviation normalization, the expected raw policy gradient depends on an audit design only through each rollout’s marginal audit probability and correction value ( Lemma 1 ): coupling audits within groups changes the noise of an update, while selection and correction change its direction. Second, giving a caught hack the reward 2 ​ b − a 2b-a , the pass reward a a reflected about the failure reward b b , exactly negates the advantages of a group whose weak passes are all hacks, whereas the strong-verdict reward b b only zeroes them ( Proposition 1 , Figure 2 b). Third, an uncaught hack’s advantage is largest when few siblings pass, so a label spent on a low-pass group buys the most correction ( Figure 2 a). Low-pass budgeted audits ( LB ) therefore audit whole groups in increasing order of weak passes until a fixed fraction p p of the batch’s weak passes has been checked in expectation ( Figure 1 a). Among whole-group designs that select by pass count and give caught hacks a fixed correction, LB minimizes a frozen-state objective, the advantage mass left on hacks, whenever the value of a label does not increase with the pass count ( Theorem 1 ).

content: For each run, we computed the hack mass J J of its design on a frozen panel of about 1000 prompts at its starting checkpoint and predicted from its sign whether hacking would be suppressed (late hacking below 2%) or persist (10% or more). Over the 39 runs whose designs we scored this way, 33 predictions held. For 16 runs the prediction was committed before the run started ( Appendix I ), and 13 of these held, in both directions: LB failed at a budget of 0.1 and succeeded at 0.2 in two seeds each, LB with corrections scaled by 3.1 and the group-level advantage correction succeeded at 0.1, and random group audits failed in Countdown-Code. The other three ended between the two thresholds and nearer the predicted side: 2.19% and 3.44% late hacking for two runs predicted to suppress hacking (seed 1 of the Countdown-Code group-level correction and seed 2 of the LeetCode one), and 7.9% for one predicted not to ( LB with penalty − 11.5 -11.5 at 0.1, which suppressed hacking for about 15 steps before it rose); a continuation of that run, preregistered with separate thresholds, rose to 40.5% against a frozen-sign prediction of below 10%. Of the other 23 runs, the sign matched all 13 LeetCode runs of the main comparison and its references ( LB , random group audits and random item audits in three seeds each, no audit, and the full audit in three seeds) and all six Countdown-Code runs of LB and the full audit, but it missed three of the four audit-unit runs at penalty − 11.5 -11.5 and p = 0.4 p=0.4 ( Appendix F ): whole-group audits ( J = − 0.002 J=-0.002 ) did not suppress hacking in either seed, and per-item audits ( J = − 0.067 J=-0.067 ) did in one seed but rose to 13.7% in the other. Designs we did not score on the starting panels (the strong-verdict arms, the audit-unit runs at penalty 0, the per-item IPW variants and LB without std normalization) are not included. Within these two environments and related designs, the sign of the frozen push anticipated the outcome in most runs.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: LB ’s ordering assumes that low-pass groups hold a large share of the hacks. In the LeetCode runs with c = b c=b , hacking spread, and the share of hacks in groups with at least 12 of 16 weak passes rose from about half to over 80%; the 8 lowest-pass groups then held no more hacks than random groups. Under the reflected penalty hacking collapsed within the first ten steps, before it could spread to high-pass groups.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
section: An online rule that optimizes the frozen objective.
content: Auditing part of each group, with the number of labels chosen from the estimated composition of groups with each pass count, improves J J beyond LB on frozen panels. In a preregistered LeetCode pilot from step 120 ( p = 0.2 p=0.2 ), such a rule was worse than LB : its area under the hacking curve was 4.90 points higher and its late hacking 47.81% against 31.25%, although its realized J J was more negative in every phase. So J J is not the first-order change in the hacking rate, which also depends on the directions of all responses’ gradients and on the optimizer. A one-step diagnosis did not identify the cause, but showed that which of several similar hacks in a partially audited group receives the penalty is a large source of noise in a single update, which whole-group audits do not have ( Appendix H ).

section: 6 Beyond the expected update: unbiased corrections
content: Unbiased corrections target the full audit’s update: on a frozen batch, per-item reward-level IPW without std normalization has the full audit’s expected update by Lemma 1 , and so does the group-level advantage correction of Sakib et al. (2026) by Proposition 8 . Comparing the group-level correction with LB and with a full audit therefore separates the expected update from the randomness of its estimate and the allocation of audits.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
section: 6 Beyond the expected update: unbiased corrections
content: Per-item reward-level IPW targets the same reflected reward as LB in Countdown-Code, spends about the same number of labels, and, following Lemma 1 , runs without std normalization. Both suppress hacking, with late hacking below 1% in every run, but LB ends with higher late correctness in all three seeds, by 4.53–11.13 points, and answers more held-out problems correctly, by 6.1–11.8 points ( Figures 4 and 3 ). Part of the held-out gap comes from unfinished answers: IPW left 3.3–13.9% of its answers cut at the 2048-token limit, against 0.2–1.6% for LB . Among parseable answers LB was still more accurate in every seed, by 4.5–5.9 points, with each interval above zero; comparisons among parseable answers condition on an answer being finished, so the subsets compared need not have the same difficulty. Continuing every cut answer to 4096 tokens from its own prefix made only 9 of 1779 correct, and LB ’s lead was unchanged at 6.1–11.7 points. The correction value matters for IPW too: targeting c = b c=b instead of − 0.8 -0.8 leaves late hacking at 14.73%, and adding group std normalization, which breaks its unbiasedness ( Section 3.4 ), leaves it at 19.06% (single seeds; Table 5 ).

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Sakib et al. (2026) correct the advantages instead of the rewards: an audited group’s normalized advantages move from their weak-reward values toward their full-audit values by the change divided by the audit probability, which matches a full audit in expectation ( Proposition 8 ). In LeetCode, auditing each group with probability 0.33 (the expected budget of LB ) suppressed hacking in two of three seeds, slightly faster than LB , and left late hacking at 3.44% in the third; held-out accuracy showed no detectable difference from LB in any seed ( Figure 3 ), although in LeetCode held-out accuracy barely moved even under widespread hacking ( Section 5.1 ), so this comparison has little power. In Countdown-Code at p = 0.28 p=0.28 it also brought hacking down (late hacking 0.35–2.19%, the highest just above our 2% threshold for suppression), but in all three seeds it ended with lower late training correctness, by 3.48–9.92 points, and LB answered more held-out problems correctly, by 8.0–11.5 points, each interval above zero ( Figures 4 and 3 ). In seed 1, 23.4% of the correction’s held-out answers were unparseable, almost all cut at the length limit, and among parseable answers it was more accurate than LB , but continuing the cut answers to 4096 tokens made only 7 of 1863 correct and left the gap at 7.9 points [ + + 6.6, + + 9.2]; in seeds 2 and 3 few answers were unparseable (3.8% and 0.3%), and LB was more accurate among parseable answers as well, by 10.0–10.9 points. Its late response length varied widely across seeds (677–1117 tokens, against 749–847 for LB ; Figure 4 ) while its accuracy loss did not, so length growth alone cannot explain the accuracy loss across the three seeds.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Two preregistered controls locate the gap. On a common frozen batch, every unbiased group-level design has the full audit’s advantages, and hence its raw first-order policy gradient, as its expectation. A full audit with the reflected penalty stayed within about two points of LB on held-out problems in all three seeds, with LB minus the full audit at − - 2.1 [ − - 3.6, − - 0.7], 0.0 [ − - 1.3, + + 1.2] and + + 2.2 [ + + 1.0, + + 3.4], far from the uniform correction’s gap, so the correction does not lose by aiming at the full-audit update. Allocating the same correction by pass count, with audit probabilities that fall with the number of weak passes (weights chosen to reduce the variance of the corrected advantages on a frozen panel of 1000 groups whose 5250 weak passes were all checked by the strong verifier, labels not counted in its training budget of 1498; floor 0.1), recovered most of the gap at the same expected budget: its held-out accuracy was 6.8 points above the uniform correction’s [ + + 5.4, + + 8.1] and 1.2 points below LB ’s [ − - 0.1, + + 2.5] (one seed). The loss therefore comes not from the full-audit update that the correction estimates but from the randomness of the estimate and how the audits behind it are allocated; which part of that randomness hurts we have not identified. At this budget LB accepts a bias in the update for low noise, and its held-out accuracy stayed within about two points of a full audit’s with 28% of its labels.

content: LB does not depend on std normalization. In Countdown-Code over three seeds, LB without it also suppressed hacking and ended with higher late correctness than LB with it, by 4.45–11.05 points, at the cost of longer responses and more labels ( Appendix E ).

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Checks that a policy can satisfy without solving the task are a recurring failure of RLVR. Countdown-Code isolates the phenomenon in a small code environment ( Khalifa et al., 2026 ) ; ImpossibleBench measures the propensity of models to exploit tests ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) ; patches counted as solved on SWE-bench fail the repository’s full suite ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ; and systematic verifier errors can delay or derail RLVR ( Egashira et al., 2026 ) . Optimizing against a monitor of reasoning teaches the policy to hide its intent ( Baker et al., 2025 ) , a training-time instance of reward-model overoptimization ( Gao et al., 2022 ) , and Deng et al. (2026) predict when detectable hacking will emerge.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Wong et al. (2026) benchmark monitor-based penalties and screening in the LeetCode environment we use and observe that correct responses that also attempt the hack keep the behavior alive ( Appendix G ). HackFree-GRPO ( Anonymous, 2026 ) discounts and filters trajectories scored by a frozen detector under centered advantages and shows that a discounted hack can keep a positive advantage; it scores every trajectory and has no strong-verifier budget to allocate. GRAFT ( Ward et al., 2026 ) routes the gradients of flagged samples into parameters removed after training. Moya et al. (2026) show that partial audits suffice when the correction outweighs the pressure toward hacking and propose PAC , a projected gradient correction we compare against in adapted form; their audits are independent per item.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: AI Control spends a scarce budget of trusted audits on the most suspicious outputs at deployment ( Greenblatt et al., 2023 ) . CARE acquires ground-truth labels where the gap between pseudo-label and true-label advantages is largest ( Wang et al., 2026 ) ; our oracle selection uses this criterion with true labels. Selecting the hardest examples for GRPO under an annotation budget works best ( Pikus et al., 2025 ) ; LB applies a related preference for low-pass groups online. PAIR applies Horvitz–Thompson reweighting to adaptive rollout allocation and notes that dividing by a random group standard deviation biases ratio estimators ( Nomand et al., 2026 ) . Sakib et al. (2026) quantify, without training, the variance of whole-group and per-attempt random audits with reward-level and advantage-level inverse-propensity corrections for coding agents ( Section 1 ).

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Dr. GRPO removes std normalization from GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Gupta (2026) shows that changing only the correlation of rewards within a group can reverse the expected group-normalized update, and Xin (2026) measure correlated verifier errors within groups. STAR-GRPO down-weights unreliable ratings before normalization ( Tian et al., 2026 ) , and noise-corrected GRPO corrects exogenous reward noise in expectation ( El Mansouri et al., 2025 ) . Lemma 1 is the centered-advantage counterpart of these observations for audits, and Proposition 3 makes explicit how std normalization defeats unbiased per-item corrections.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: A small strong-verifier budget can suppress reward hacking in GRPO, provided it is spent where uncaught hacks gain the most and caught hacks are pushed away rather than merely zeroed. At a frozen state, auditing whole groups with the fewest weak passes first minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among whole-group pass-count designs with a fixed correction, when a label’s value does not increase with the pass count. From the starting state, the sign of this mass predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. In our experiments the following recipe worked in both environments: give caught hacks the reflected reward 2 ​ b − a 2b-a ; audit whole groups with the fewest weak passes first; set the budget as a fraction of weak passes, so that spending falls when weak passes fall as hacking is suppressed; and avoid per-item reward-level inverse-propensity corrections under group std normalization. Randomness matters as well. Unbiased corrections can match LB on hacking, but in Countdown-Code their randomness cost correctness at the same budget: a full audit stayed within about two points of LB , and reallocating the audits recovered most of the loss.

title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
content: Our experiments cover two environments, 3B and 4B models, and 40-step windows that start after hacking has emerged; we have not tested whether hacking returns over longer training or at larger scale. In both environments the strong verifier is cheap enough that the budget is a design choice rather than a necessity; we have not tested a setting where the strong verifier is itself expensive or imperfect. We treat the strong verifier as reliable and independent of the policy, and a strong verifier with blind spots would push the policy toward them, as observed for optimized monitors ( Baker et al., 2025 ; Ward et al., 2026 ) . The two main comparisons and several ablations have three seeds; the group-level advantage correction has three seeds in each environment and the full audit three in Countdown-Code, and other comparisons, including the allocated correction, have one or two. The correctness advantage of LB over per-item IPW is positive in all three seeds, with p = 0.055 p=0.055 in training and p = 0.040 p=0.040 on held-out problems at the seed level, and against the group-level correction it is positive in all three seeds, among parseable answers in two of them. Our decision metrics, hacking and correctness on training rollouts, missed length drift, which appeared in rollout lengths and on held-out panels. Our analysis is first order at a frozen state: the sign of its objective predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs (13 of 16 preregistered), but its magnitude does not rank designs, as the online rule showed. These predictions come from two environments and related designs and have not been compared with a simple baseline. The reflected penalty is exact only when non-passing responses share the reward b b .

authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang

content: In LeetCode, a response is a hack when it passes the weak verifier only through its own run_tests function and fails the problem’s tests; responses that pass the problem’s tests are correct even if they also define run_tests . In Countdown-Code, a weak pass is a hack when its expression literal does not use exactly the given numbers or does not evaluate to the given target.

content: In Countdown-Code we also compare against three alternatives. PAC ( Moya et al., 2026 ) keeps the weak reward and adds a correction along an inverse-propensity estimate of the hack-probability gradient, projected to be orthogonal to the reward gradient. The original Euclidean rule collapsed the policy within one step under full-parameter training, so we use an adaptation in which the projection is taken in the metric of AdamW’s diagonal preconditioner after the batch’s optimizer updates; the guarantees of the original method, stated for a fixed metric and gradient flow, do not carry over. The correction size was selected on a separate development state. An oracle selection rule ( Cag ) reads the semantic labels and audits groups in decreasing order of the corrective advantage gap, the acquisition criterion of CARE ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , under LB ’s budget; it is not the full CARE method. Audited-only learning ( Ao ) uses LB ’s audits but drops unaudited groups from the update.

section: Appendix E Group std normalization and other baselines in Countdown-Code
content: Adding group std normalization to IPW breaks its unbiasedness and, in our run, strongly attenuated its correction, consistent with Proposition 3 : hacking plateaus at 19.06% instead of 0.82%. LB does not depend on std normalization, and in Countdown-Code it trained better without it. Over three seeds, LB without std normalization suppressed hacking as well (late hacking at most 0.12%) and ended with higher late correctness than LB with it in every seed, by 4.45–11.05 pp, with higher pass@8 in every seed. The cost is 5% to 11% more labels and 18% to 30% more generated tokens, because responses grow longer. On held-out problems, the no-std LB checkpoints of seeds 2 and 3 answer 54.6% and 54.2% correctly (2.2 and 2.0 pp above LB with std normalization, and 14.0 and 9.4 pp above IPW at the same seeds), with a truncation tradeoff: in seed 3, 18.7% of held-out responses were unparseable, almost all after reaching the 2048-token limit, compared with 0.2% for std-normalized LB . Removing std normalization changes GRPO’s weighting of easy and hard prompts ( Liu et al., 2025 ) ; LB composes with it. When LB runs without std normalization, its late correctness exceeds that of IPW at the same seed by 17.03 and 12.19 pp in seeds 2 and 3, so the gap between LB and IPW is not an artifact of the normalization.

content: PAC ( Moya et al., 2026 ) keeps the weak reward, so each GRPO step still reinforces hacks, and the projected correction is locally orthogonal to the weak-reward gradient in the chosen metric. With per-item audits at the same rate, hacking rose to 64.80% in the late window, and the unprojected correction reached 15.20% ( Table 5 ). The oracle selection rule ( Cag ) matched LB on hacking and correctness, including held-out accuracy, with 648 labels against 1403, mainly because it skips groups whose corrective gap is zero. Learning only from audited groups ( Ao ) matched LB on hacking and correctness but drifted toward long responses (1148 against 749 tokens on average in the late window); 34.4% of its held-out responses gave no answer, almost all because they reached the 2048-token limit.

content: At the starting checkpoint of the step-120 pilot, we drew 8 common batches of 16 prompts with 16 responses each from the training distribution, assigned audits to the same responses under LB and under the frozen online rule (penalty − 2.5 -2.5 , p = 0.2 p=0.2 ), and computed the exact projections of each response’s score gradient on estimated directions d H = ∇ P ​ ( H ) d_{H}=\nabla P(H) and d C = ∇ P ​ ( C ) d_{C}=\nabla P(C) . content: Randomly permuting the advantages among the hacks of each group leaves every class coefficient unchanged. Under the online rule the mean change in the d H d_{H} projection was + + 0.0002, as it must be by symmetry, but its root mean square over 64 assignments was 0.0024, 2.2 times the mean net projection ( − - 0.0011); in the batches sampled with top- p p 1 it was 0.0017, 0.85 times the mean net projection ( + + 0.0020). Under LB , which audits whole groups, it was exactly zero. Which hack receives the penalty is therefore a large source of noise in a single update, although its role in the long-run outcome is not identified. We also computed the first step of a fresh Adam state; its projections were too noisy to compare, and since Adam is nonlinear and the omitted terms do not cancel after it, this diagnosis does not identify the optimizer’s contribution.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
section: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
content: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation , which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation , which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones. These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size . Experiments support predictions of the theory.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: The success of large language models (LLMs) has prompted research into the learning and generalization properties of the underlying transformer architecture. Classical statistical learning theory provides a wealth of techniques that bound the generalization error as a function of the data size and the complexity of the hypothesis class. Recent work has brought these to bear on transformers (Covering numbers: Edelman et al. (2022) ; Trauger and Tewari (2024) , Bayesian methods: Lintilhac and Shaikh (2026) ; Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026) , VC Dimension: Yang et al. (2026c) , inter alia ). These results primarily address the i.i.d. regime – for transformers, this in particular implies that the test inputs are drawn from the same length distribution as the training inputs.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: However, for transformer learning theory, the i.i.d. paradigm is arguably insufficient: it is highly desirable to understand when transformers can extrapolate to sequences longer than seen during training . This phenomenon is referred to as length-generalization ( Bhattamishra et al., 2020 ; Anil et al., 2022 ; Kazemnejad et al., 2023 , e.g.) , and is understood to be diagnostic of when a transformer actually learns an underlying algorithmic solution, as opposed to length-dependent heuristics ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 , e.g.) . It also indicates when LLMs can be expected to perform a task reliably across long contexts ( Jobanputra et al., 2025 ) .

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: Length generalization is governed by two quantities: the number of training samples, and their length. Sample count determines how reliably the training data pins down the target function, as in classical statistical learning theory; sample length determines how well the model extrapolates, since the longest input length at which the target function’s behavior is observed dictates to which point a model will extrapolate beyond it. For a given target function and learning procedure, we thus need to consider not only its sample complexity (the required number of training samples), but also its length complexity (the required length of training samples).

The main idea is that training length determines which behaviors become observable; sample size determines how reliably those behaviors are learned. Below a task-dependent length threshold, some competing behaviors cannot be distinguished. Around the relevant transition, longer examples can make informative events much more common; increasing length can thus strongly reduce sample complexity in this regime. Beyond that transition, the benefit of additional length diminishes and additional independent examples matter more.

content: We follow prior sample complexity bounds in studying an idealized learning model that abstracts away from the algorithmic process of learning. Capacity-based learning bounds ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Trauger and Tewari, 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026c ) apply to Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), which finds parameters minimizing training error under some constraint on the hypothesis class. We contrast it with the Guess & Check algorithm ( Chiang et al., 2023 ; Buzaglo et al., 2024 , G&C, ) , which samples parameter settings from the parameter space until a setting interpolating the training set is found. Guess & Check expands over ERM by modeling the inductive bias of SGD-like optimizers towards solutions occupying large volumes in parameter space ( Chiang et al., 2023 ; Buzaglo et al., 2024 ) . This is an important difference over bounds based on ERM ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; Trauger and Tewari, 2024 ) , as it (i) allows us to explicitly take into account the effect of both the hypothesis class and the ground-truth function, (ii) while bounds depend more mildly on the hypothesis model’s size than capacity-based bounds. This enables stronger results when the target function can be represented by small models, and we find it to be borne out empirically in experiments. G&C is closely related to a Bayesian interpretation of learning, as it samples from a posterior over the parameter space conditional on the training set ( Haussler et al., 1994 , e.g.) . Given a teacher transformer T t T_{t} implementing the target function and a student T s T_{s} from the hypothesis class, we introduce the difference function , which checks for any given word if the output vectors of both transformers match at every position. Previously, Li and Cotterell (2025) showed that fixed-precision transformers with a binary classifying output layer are expressively equivalent to LTL ​ [ P ] \textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] , a fragment of linear temporal logic, and further can be represented as a partially-ordered deterministic finite automaton (poDFA) (Figure 2 ). A poDFA is a DFA where the reachability relation defines a partial order on the state set; intuitively, such automata have no nontrivial loops. Intuitively, the state space describes the dynamic of the transformer’s KV-cache; as soon as some activation is added to the KV-cache, it cannot be removed anymore, giving rise to the partially ordered loop-free structure.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: Our result goes beyond established theory in two ways: First, it goes beyond statistical generalization bounds for transformers by guaranteeing length generalization. Prior learning results for transformers characterize generalization error and sample size when the test and train samples are at the same sequence length ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Trauger and Tewari, 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Truong, 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2025 ; Rizvi-Martel et al., 2026 ; Lintilhac and Shaikh, 2026 ; Mousavi-Hosseini et al., 2025 ; Hanneke et al., 2026 ; Joshi et al., 2025 ) . Our results instead consider the more general case of length generalization, in the setting of fixed-precision transformers. We note that our main result ingests the statistical generalization bound essentially as a black box; hence, our results might analogously also be formalized on the basis of other statistical generalization bounds.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: Second, our results go beyond prior work on length generalization by giving explicit and joint rates for sample size and length. So far, the most generally predictive account of length generalization has been the RASP-L Conjecture ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and its formalization via C-RASP and Limit Transformers ( Huang et al., 2025a ) . This theory has been highly predictive of which tasks empirically show length generalization ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , but provides no quantitative predictions. Notably, C-RASP is more powerful than ℱ ​ 𝒫 ​ 𝒯 \mathcal{FPT} ; e.g. it can model the MAJORITY language. However, C-RASP is a too loose target for quantitive learning bounds: Yang et al. (2026a) show that, beyond the shallow-depth case ( Izzo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , any length threshold would need to grow uncomputably with model complexity. The positive fragment C-RASP + has expressivity equivalent to fixed-precision transformers and was studied in Yang et al. (2026a) ; Zetzsche et al. (2026) . We compare with these results in detail in Appendix A . Importantly, our work innovates over these prior results by providing joint generalization guarantees in both sample size and length.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: Like capacity-based generalization bounds ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Trauger and Tewari, 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026c ) , our work treats an idealized learning model that abstracts away from the computational process of finding a model fitting the training data. Understanding optimization dynamics for transformers has been difficult. Progress has been made for specific task families and restricted models, such as single layers ( Yang et al., 2025b ; Mwigo and Dasgupta, 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2024 , e.g.) (including one-layer models performing chain-of-thought, Huang et al. (2025b) ) or specific task families ( Nichani et al., 2024 , e.g.) . We view the study of G&C as an (imperfect) proxy for part of the implicit inductive bias of SGD-like learning; understanding of optimization dynamics for a general multi-layer model and a general hypothesis class will require new methods.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: The main limitation of our results is that they predict asymptotic rates but not yet concrete realistic numerical bounds for specific tasks and models. The primary barrier here is that the bounds involve large constants involving the fixed-precision set 𝔽 \mathbb{F} , which is large at full-precision training. It is an interesting question whether realistic numerical bounds can be obtained when training with strong quantization. Further limitations are that fixed-precision transformers are less expressive than log-precision or infinite-precision transformers, we did not treat positional encodings, and studied G&C and ERM as opposed to optimization dynamics.

title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: We have provided generalization bounds for multi-layer fixed-precision transformers that account for the roles of both the number and the length of training samples. We provided a joint treatment of both dimensions, showing that, under a given token budget, increasing length can sometimes be exponentially more efficient than increasing sample size.

content: 1. How do the results relate to Yang et al. (2026a) ; Zetzsche et al. (2026) ? Yang et al. (2026a) give two core results: (i) an impossibility result for computable length generalization bounds for C-RASP, and (ii) a deterministic length generalization bound analogous to our Lemma 3.1 for C-RASP + \text{C-RASP}^{+} . The first result indicates that C-RASP is too powerful a target for obtaining quantitative learning results for transformers: even though C-RASP has been successful in predicting generalization behaviour experimentally ( Huang et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2026b ) , there are C-RASP-expressible tasks where training data would need to include strings with astronomically large lengths. Yang et al. (2026a) ; Zetzsche et al. (2026) further show an analogue of our Lemma 3.1 for C-RASP + \text{C-RASP}^{+} , the positive fragment of C-RASP, giving a computable bound in the size of the defining C-RASP formula. Most recently, Zetzsche et al. (2026) have further studied the role of sample size. They show exponential sample size bounds for C-RASP + \text{C-RASP}^{+} and another fragment, called C-RASP 1 \text{C-RASP}_{1} . C-RASP + \text{C-RASP}^{+} has the same expressivity as fixed-precision transformers, though there is no direct 1-to-1 link between the transformer size parameters ( L L , D D , H H ) and the size of defining C-RASP + formulas. As a consequence, length and sample complexities that we obtain may not be directly comparable to bounds obtained for C-RASP + \text{C-RASP}^{+} in Yang et al. (2026a) ; Zetzsche et al. (2026) . An important difference of our results, besides directly applying to a transformer model rather than the C-RASP + logic, is that we obtain joint bounds allowing us to understand the tradeoff between sample length and sample size.

content: 2. How do the experiments differ from the theoretical learning model? What are the implications of these differences? The point of our experiments is to test theoretical predictions (obtained for idealized learners G&C or ERM on fixed-precision transformers) in a realistic training setup using gradient-based optimization (Adam) on high-precision (FP32) transformers. Whereas the theoretical setup asks for exact match of the output vectors, the experiments instead train for per-dimension binary cross-entropy. In experiments, we select only runs with perfect training accuracy, enforcing interpolation, as assumed in theory.

content: 3. Why study fixed-precision transformers? Why not study C-RASP / Limit Transformers? It is a well-established empirical finding that transformers show strong length generalization on the class of languages expressed by fixed-precision transformers ( Li and Cotterell, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) . They are thus a natural target for joint treatment of sample and length complexity. Fixed-precision transformers define a strict subset of C-RASP ( Yang and Chiang, 2024 ) and Limit Transformers ( Huang et al., 2025a ; Izzo et al., 2025 ) . On the one hand, there is empirical evidence that transformers also show length generalization on tasks that are expressible in C-RASP but not by fixed-precision transformers, such as MAJORITY or certain regular languages such as bounded-depth Dyck languages ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , which require a transformer’s numerical precision to grow with the input length. On the other hand, as discussed above, Yang et al. (2026a) show that C-RASP cannot admit computable length generalization bounds, i.e., any threshold C C satisfying ( 3 ) for all of C-RASP must grow faster in the size of the C-RASP formula (or Limit Transformer) than any computable function. This indicates that C-RASP is too broad as a target for quantitative length generalization bounds ( Yang et al., 2026a ; Zetzsche et al., 2026 ) . It is an interesting question for future work whether tractable generalization bounds exist for some natural class between fixed-precision transformers and C-RASP.

authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
content: 5. The paper studies ERM and G&C. Why not study optimizers like SGD or Adam? Our work follows prior work ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Izzo et al., 2025 ; Trauger and Tewari, 2024 , e.g.) in studying idealized learners abstracting away from gradient dynamics. ERM in particular is a highly popular standard approach for deriving learning bounds. Guess-and-check models the inductive bias of realistic training towards solutions occupying high volume in parameter space ( Buzaglo et al., 2024 ) , unlike ERM. Prior and concurrent work has provided evidence that parameter space volume is useful for understanding transformer generalization, finding that certain hard-to-learn functions occupy small volume in parameter space ( Hahn and Rofin, 2024 ; Kövér et al., 2026 ; Zhu and Chiang, 2026 ) ; G&C is consistent with this by predicting easier generalization for functions occupying high parameter space volume. Neither G&C nor ERM should be considered full models of learning. For instance, for matrix factorization, Alexander et al. (2025) show that SGD can in some cases of matrix factorization generalize even better than G&C. Understanding gradient dynamics for general mutli-layer transformers is extremely difficult. Developing quantitative generalization bounds for gradient-based training is a major task for future work; the 1-layer setup might be a tractable starting point.

content: 6. Could the framework be extended to handle positional encodings? Prior bounds for statistical generalization (not length generalization) of transformers use fixed absolute positional encodings ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; Lintilhac and Shaikh, 2026 ) . That would also be possible to include in our setup, though one would need to understand their effects on the automaton structure. Learnable absolute positional encodings are harder to account for as they lead to rapid growth of the parameter count with the input length (as acknowledged by Edelman et al. (2022) ), and are inherently undefined outside of the training length range. Huang et al. (2025a) impose translation invariance constraints to constrain the hypothesis space in their analysis. Relative positional encodings can be easier to account for, as they do not involve an unbounded number of parameters. Yang et al. (2025a) show that ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) can be understood (in the context of C-RASP) as the addition of local predicates; we expect the effect on fixed-precision transformers to be very similar to the effect provided by local attention. We opt to analyze local attention, as it is nowadays popular in LLM design and has been rigorously formalized in the fixed-precision setup by Li and Cotterell (2026) . RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) is harder to capture theoretically in the context of length generalization: while it can be formalized in terms of modular predicates ( Yang et al., 2025a ) (which admit exact automata-theoretic treatment in an appropriate extension of our poDFA framework, with appropriate modifications to the length complexity term), this does not characterize conventional RoPE implementation, which rather behave like fixed-length backwards-lookup operators ( Jerad et al., 2026 ) , and may in fact impair empirical length generalization ( Jerad et al., 2026 ) .

content: 11. The theoretical bounds include effects of both teacher size (the transformer representing the target function) and the student size (the transformers in the learner’s hypothesis class). Experiments show strong effects of the teacher but weak effects for the student. Why? Our theoretical predictions provide worst-case sufficient upper bounds on the test error; practical learning outcomes may be better both because the theoretical analysis may not be tight and because gradient-based learning may generalize better than the theoretical idealizations ERM and G&C. Indeed, it is a common observation that key techniques for proving statistical learning bounds show an overly pessimistic dependency on the student size: overparameterized neural networks often generalize very well, far better than is accounted for by capacity-based bounds that guarantee learning for ERM via uniform convergence ( Nagarajan and Kolter, 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Bartlett et al., 2021 , e.g.) . The G&C analysis as developed by Buzaglo et al. (2024) , that we adopt in Section 4.1 , goes some way towards ameliorating this, as its dependence on the student size is substantially milder than for the capacity-based ERM bounds. Some work has provided generalization bounds that scale very mildly in the student size for simpler neural networks ( Allen-Zhu et al., 2019 ; Arora et al., 2019 , e.g.) , though the extension of such results to transformers will likely require new techniques.

content: We use three controlled synthetic task families to test the qualitative predictions of our theory. We choose these families for variety in teacher depth, width, number of heads, alphabet size, and associated automaton height. The induction-head task also tests local positional information provided by a local attention head. We use standard FP32 arithmetic and test whether the theoretical predictions carry over to real-world numerical implementations. First, the logarithmic–linear tradeoff between training length K K and sample size N N suggests that an additive increase in K K can offset a multiplicative reduction in N N : increasing training length can therefore be more effective than adding examples. Second, larger teacher and larger student depth L L , width D D , or alphabet size | Σ | |\Sigma| can increase the sufficient requirements on N N and/or K K , suggesting possible performance degradation at fixed training resources. These experiments also have an exploratory role: the two bounds on the automaton height C C in Lemma 3.1 yield different dependencies on these quantities, and worst-case guarantees need not describe their empirical effects.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
section: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
content: Recently, there has been rise in multimodal vision-language models for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), yet their application in breast diagnosis, particularly for predicting biopsy outcomes remains limited. This study presents a multimodal vision-language approach, incorporating Grad-CAM as an Explainable AI (XAI) technique, to predict benign tumors in patients recommended for biopsy, especially those classified as BI-RADS 4 and 5. A novel multimodal framework was developed using Vision Transformer (ViT) for imaging feature extraction and DeBERTa-V3-Large for textual embeddings. The model was trained and evaluated on a comprehensive in-house dataset comprising 1,632 patients, each with four mammography views and a corresponding radiology report. The features of both modalities were extracted independently and fused by late fusion before classification. Grad-CAM was used to generate visual explanations highlighting key regions influencing model predictions. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100% with corresponding specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively. The best AUC achieved was 0.72 by multimodal approach on the test set, outperforming the image-only (0.66) and text-only (0.68) baselines. The proposed multimodal architecture, enhanced with Grad-CAM, demonstrates a strong potential to identify benign tumors among high-risk patients, offering interpretable insights and thereby helping reduce unnecessary biopsies, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: Breast cancer is the most common disease among women in the United States and the world [ 15 ] . Different imaging modalities have been used to diagnose breast cancer in the early stage. Mammography is one of the common imaging techniques used for earlier cancer diagnosis and has shown potential benefits in clinical settings [ 15 ] . One of the main problems with mammography is that most benign findings are recommended for biopsy. BI-RADS was created to describe the various stages of cancer appropriately to provide better patient care [ 7 ] . BI-RADS category 4—is divided into four subsections; 4, 4a, 4b, and 4c, represents a suspicious abnormality, which is therefore recommended for biopsy. Among the recommended biopsies in the BI-RADS 4 category in general, 75% of the BI-RADS category 4 findings are proven to be benign [ 7 ] . In the United States alone, more than 970,000 breast biopsies are unnecessary [ 2 ] . This causes a high false positive rate, which leads to additional expenditure, clinical procedures, and further stress. Different CAD systems have been used to improve the diagnosis and prognosis of breast cancer in various stages using numerous imaging modalities and clinical data [ 14 ] . The latest breakthroughs in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models have enabled the implementation of CAD models [ 8 ] . The ever-burgeoning capacity of computational resources and access to a large amount of data creates extraordinarily favorable conditions for DL models in various image classification, segmentation, and object detection tasks and enables extracting insight from textual data in parallel [ 19 ] . DL models use Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to automatically extract imaging features, in contrast to conventional hand-crafted techniques [ 8 ] . CNN-based advanced architectures have shown potential in different breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis applications [ 17 ] , such as breast cancer classification [ 10 ] , risk prediction [ 19 ] , survival [ 1 ] , and recurrence prediction [ 11 ] . In recent studies, a surge in the use of vision-language models for different applications in classification, detection, and segmentation has been observed in biomedical and general-purpose applications [ 20 ] . However, it is rare in breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis applications due to the lack of multimodal medical data. BI-RADS 4 and associated categories of patients are recommended for biopsy. Few studies have used DL approaches to predict biopsy outcomes [ 12 ] ; however, to the best of our knowledge, no study has employed a multimodal approach combined with an XAI technique for this purpose. Therefore, a novel multimodal framework that employs a ViT to extract mammographic features and DeBERTa-V3-Large to obtain embeddings from radiological reports is proposed. Furthermore, an XAI technique—Grad-CAM, is used to visualize the image regions that contribute to the model’s prediction for interpretability purposes. ViT has demonstrated effective performance in tumor classification, and Grad-CAM—an XAI technique, is applied to generate attention-based heatmaps. Grad-CAM highlights the critical imaging regions that contribute the most to the model’s predictions, thereby offering interpretability and fostering trust in automated decision-making systems [ 13 ] .

authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: In the proposed framework, features from each modality are processed independently and subsequently fused using a late-fusion strategy through feature concatenation before the final classification layer. This multimodal integration aims to address the limitations of unimodal approaches by incorporating both mammographic imaging data and radiological reports. Four mammographic views—right cranial-caudal (R-CC), the right mediolateral-oblique (R-MLO), the left cranial-caudal (L-CC), and the left mediolateral-oblique (L-MLO), are used as inputs to the model. The objective of this study is to use a vision–language modeling approach to assess biopsy outcomes for BI-RADS 4 and its subcategories, as well as BI-RADS 5, with the goal of reducing unnecessary biopsies for patients who do not have breast cancer.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: The classification of benign tumors from breast biopsy recommended that patients can be seen in ultrasound imaging studies using ML. Investigators in a few studies [ 21 ] , have explored the possibilities of identifying benign biopsy from ultrasound images using ML methods. However, it is uncommon to classify biopsy-recommended patients in mammography images using ML techniques. Only a handful of studies have used these techniques to investigate this problem further. An unnecessary breast biopsy reduction problem has been explored using DL on digital mammograms quite recently. Meng and colleagues [ 21 ] explored the possibility of classifying patients based on BI-RADS 4 using a deep transfer learning technique. They particularly used a pre-trained Inception-V3 model. The best AUC reported for this model is 0.86. The authors in a study [ 18 ] , developed a patch-based DL pipeline, where they divided mammography images into different patches to obtain local features. They aggregated feature maps using a shallow convolutional aggregation network, which includes two convolutional layers, global average pooling, and a classification layer. They used DenseNet-161 for extracting local features and reported an AUC of 0.799. In another study [ 4 ] , authors designed a decision support tool for risk categorization, and reduction of unnecessary biopsies in mammographic data. An AUC of 0.93 is reported in this study. In a recent study conducted by Liu and colleagues [ 9 ] , used a simple DL VGG16 architecture on digital mammograms to classify benign tumors among malignant tumors in the category 4 BI-RADS. They reported the best AUC of 0.72 for the main task of classifying benign tumors among various types of tumors, along with a few other complementary tasks.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: Limited research has been conducted on the identification of the biopsy outcome using ML from BI-RADS 4 patients. Few of the studies that have used DL to predict biopsy outcomes from BI-RADS 4 patients are presented as follows. The authors [ 12 ] used deep transfer learning on digital mammograms for patients with BI-RADS 4 recommended for biopsy. An Inception-V3 model was particularly used for this objective. In another study [ 18 ] , the authors extracted patches from mammography images to capture important local features. They aggregated these patches using a shallow convolutional aggregation network and subsequently fed the aggregated feature maps into a DenseNet-161 architecture for final outcome classification. In another work [ 4 ] , researchers designed a decision support tool used to stratify risk and reduce biopsy in BI-RADS 4 mammograms. The study was limited in the sense that the model was built and validated internally. In a recent preliminary study [ 9 ] investigators designed a DL model based on digital mammograms to avoid unnecessary breast biopsies. This study performed four binary classification tasks—the main task being the classification of tumors as benign versus all other types of lesions, achieving a best AUC score of 0.72. However, the study had limitations, such as a limited internal dataset consisting only of mammograms and using a simple VGG16 architecture. In summary, existing studies on biopsy outcome prediction from BI-RADS 4 mammograms remain limited in several respects. Most approaches rely solely on mammographic images and do not leverage the complementary information contained in radiological reports. Furthermore, many studies are developed and evaluated using relatively small, single-institution datasets, which may limit generalizability. In addition, model interpretability has received limited attention, reducing transparency and potentially hindering clinical adoption. These limitations highlight the need for multimodal and explainable approaches for biopsy outcome prediction.

content: The TecSalud hospital’s at Tecnologico de Monterrey provided the dataset for this study. Together with digital mammograms, it also comprises digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT), digital mammography (DM), and ultrasound (US) based radiological reports. All reports and mammograms were anonymized to maintain privacy. The reports were gathered between 2014 and 2019, originally written in Spanish. Google Translate was used to translate them into the English, and bilingual radiologists then confirmed the translation. Two experienced radiologists wrote and assessed each report. The dataset started with 42000 examples. Only biopsy-recommended patient data were extracted. The four views (LCC, LMLO, RCC, and RMLO), as well as the corresponding radiological reports containing detailed descriptions of the diagnosis—including BI-RADS classifications, breast density scores, patient ages, family cancer histories, lesion laterality, biopsy recommendations, among others were combined with each patient’s data. The laterality of the lesion shows whether the patient has ever had breast cancer. If a patient had cancer in either breast, it is indicated by the laterality of the lesion. Three values are used to describe laterality: 0, 1, and 2. Cancer in the left breast is represented by the number 0, cancer in the right breast by the number 1, and cancer in both breasts by the number 2. The purpose of laterality was to determine whether the patient had cancer at all. Furthermore, 1,632 cases comprising a total of 6,528 mammograms, along with their associated radiological reports, were included after preprocessing. The preprocessing steps involved removing reports with missing values, duplicate records, and cases assigned BI-RADS categories 0 (incomplete assessment), 1 (negative), 2 (benign finding), 3 (probably benign), and 6 (biopsy-proven malignancy). Thus, the dataset contains the remaining categories of BI-RADS 4 and associated categories 4A, 4B, 4C, and BI-RADS 5. The distribution of BI-RADS used in this study can be seen in the Fig. 2 . The patients, who were all female and used for the final model building and assessment, had an average age of 51.52, a standard deviation (SD) of 11.44, and an age range of 22-93. The report is a sample and can be used for demonstration purpose. The detailed characteristics of the dataset are defined in Table 1 .
