title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding the capabilities of Web services ( Moslem and Kelleher, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) , from information seeking to complex reasoning and problem solving ( Pesl et al., 2025 ; Izzi et al., 2025 ) . LLM routers have emerged as a key component of agentic infrastructure, selecting suitable models for individual queries to balance response quality and inference cost ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Ong et al., 2025 ) . With the growing adoption of multi-agent systems (MAS) in agentic web services such as Grok Bot and WorkBuddy, routing must extend beyond model selection to jointly determine model assignments, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and the skills and subtasks assigned to each agent. For service providers handling Web queries across diverse domains and difficulty levels, adaptively selecting MAS configurations to jointly optimize reasoning performance and compute cost has become a central research problem.

title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: Existing MAS routing research primarily improves routing decisions through two mechanisms. Parametric policy optimization internalizes execution feedback into router parameters through reinforcement learning or feedback-conditioned distillation, learning policies for model assignment and system orchestration ( Yue et al., 2025b ; Su et al., 2026 ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . Explicit experience evolution updates retrievable execution records, routing rules, or orchestration skills, allowing accumulated experience to guide subsequent decisions without gradient updates to the router ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Rajib et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . Connecting experience reuse with policy learning is particularly challenging for joint MAS configuration: the benefits of a model, collaboration mode, or resource allocation depend jointly on task requirements and the surrounding configuration choices. Reusable experience must therefore preserve these conditions of applicability, while effective policy learning must translate the relevant knowledge into the ability to plan new configurations. As illustrated in Figure 1 , this raises a central open question: How can configuration experience be distilled into reusable knowledge of conditional dependencies and internalized in the router’s pre-execution planning policy to improve the system-level trade-off between accuracy and cost?

title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: Addressing this question presents two challenges, as highlighted in Figure 2 . (i) Discovering reusable routing principles within a complex, multidimensional configuration space. Jointly selecting models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills causes a combinatorial explosion in the configuration space, making exhaustive evaluation computationally prohibitive ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, because configuration benefits depend on both the task and the combination of choices, a single execution trajectory reveals only the outcome under a specific configuration ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . It provides insufficient evidence to identify necessary, redundant, or suboptimal decisions. The router must therefore move beyond learning from isolated outcomes and analyze execution trajectories across tasks and configurations to uncover conditional configuration patterns that generalize to subsequent tasks. (ii) Translating post-execution experience into fine-grained supervision for pre-execution routing. Existing reinforcement learning approaches to routing derive reward signals solely from highly sparse feedback on final task success and computational cost ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Liao et al., 2026 ) . However, a complete MAS configuration involves multiple coupled planning decisions. Terminal rewards provide limited guidance on which decisions are effective, which waste resources, and how individual configuration choices should be adjusted. Even when valuable routing insights can be distilled from historical trajectories, they do not automatically translate into effective action selection at specific decision states of the current routing policy. This mismatch between high-dimensional combinatorial decisions and coarse, sparse execution feedback limits the router’s ability to learn efficiently and improve continually from limited execution experience.

title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: To address these challenges, we propose EvoRouter , an adaptive multi-agent routing framework built around an insight-guided self-improvement loop. To address the first challenge , we conduct preliminary experiments that systematically examine how configuration changes affect reasoning performance and computational cost across tasks, revealing task dependence, diminishing marginal returns, and configuration interdependence. We then design an LLM-based expert that distills routing insights by periodically aggregating configurations, execution outcomes, and costs across tasks. The expert derives conditional insights into task-specific capability bottlenecks, marginal returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. These insights guide exploration according to task characteristics, steering the router toward optimal configurations. To address the second challenge , we develop a router training method that combines privileged on-policy distillation (OPD) with cost-aware reinforcement learning (RL). OPD transforms configuration insights accumulated across trajectories into dense, token-level rewards informed by routing insights, while RL optimizes the performance–cost trade-off using end-to-end execution outcomes. These complementary training signals address the challenge of learning interdependent multi-agent configuration decisions from sparse execution feedback.

authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: LLM routing spans per-query model selection ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Ong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Farahani et al., 2026a ; Farahani et al., 2026b ) and output-budget allocation ( Xue et al., 2026 ) , sequential model invocation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) , and joint MAS configuration ( Yue et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Beyond team design, routers adapt delegation ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ) , agent or context selection ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , and execution state ( Li et al., 2026b ; Rajib et al., 2026 ) . Experience-based approaches retain reusable routing knowledge ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2026 ) or co-evolve routing with worker capabilities ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . RSI-Router ( Li et al., 2026a ) evolves subtask assignments and model-specific skills through Pareto selection. EvoRouter targets pre-execution joint configuration over fixed heterogeneous workers, informed by our analysis of task-dependent scaling and configuration interactions.

title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: LLM post-training commonly combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstrations with preference optimization ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards further develops reasoning capabilities from outcome feedback ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Complementing reward-based optimization, on-policy distillation provides teacher supervision on student-generated sequences and can reduce the training–inference distribution mismatch associated with offline distillation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Recent methods enrich this supervision with textual feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , trajectory-derived skills ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and role-specific coordination feedback ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) . Building on these principles, EvoRouter combines group-relative RL with OPD on student-generated configuration plans, conditioning the teacher on evolving cross-task insights and current execution feedback. The resulting policy operates without privileged feedback at inference.

authors: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong, Haoran Luo
content: We presented EvoRouter, a framework that learns to jointly configure heterogeneous LLM-based MAS from execution experience. Combining cost-aware reinforcement learning with on-policy distillation, EvoRouter internalizes cross-task configuration insights and trajectory feedback into its routing policy, enabling deployment without privileged feedback. Across 21 datasets spanning seven domains, EvoRouter achieves higher average accuracy at lower computational cost than the evaluated routing baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Our current framework is designed for cloud-based agent services. Future work will extend EvoRouter to resource-constrained edge environments through coordinated cloud–edge routing that accounts for device heterogeneity and inter-agent communication overhead.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
section: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
content: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs’ image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline , augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing , to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach’s practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: The idea of controlling robots with natural language has long been a staple of science fiction. However, accomplishing even simple tasks, such as “Clean up the table.” , requires a complex understanding of the world and the robot’s capabilities, as well as drawing on many of the core challenges in robotics, such as perception, manipulation, and planning.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
content: With the recent advances in Vision Language Models (VLMs) [ 1 ] [ 2 ] , significant progress has been made in enabling robot reasoning and planning by leveraging vast amounts of real-world knowledge [ 3 ] [ 4 ] . While VLM-based systems have produced impressive results for tasks in everyday environments (such as offices or homes), they still struggle in more specialized domains, including industrial and scientific applications [ 5 ] [ 6 ] . This is attributable to these domains being underrepresented in the VLMs’ training data. The resulting performance gap is a barrier to the more widespread adoption of VLMs in these fields, in which data collection and annotation is often particularly expensive and time-consuming.

content: A fundamental requirement for VLMs to generate effective robot task plans is the ability to ground their language understanding in the robot’s perception and action capabilities. In other words, the objects and features comprising the robot’s environment must be linked to the semantics used in the given task, and these, in turn, must be linked to the concrete movements and poses necessary to interact with them. General-purpose VLMs often fail at the first step for recondite objects, and their image-level outputs alone do not provide sufficiently reliable geometric targets for robot execution. A practical planning system therefore requires explicit interfaces connecting domain-specific perception, VLM-level semantics, and the robot’s action capabilities.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
content: In this work, we tackle the challenge of VLM grounding in specialized domains by presenting a modular pipeline for VLM-based robot task planning. Rather than fine-tuning the model or replacing the entire existing robot software stack, TrySee compensates the general-purpose VLM’s limitations in object recognition and robot pose generation by connecting its reasoning abilities with replaceable domain-specific perception modules and established motion-planning components. This allows the pipeline to be adaptable to different domains and tasks, through targeted perception models without requiring end-to-end robot demonstrations.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
content: In TrySee, the VLM incrementally generates and verifies short-horizon action sequences, while the perception modules provide semantic object labels, visual masks, and executable target poses. This provides online grounding that is continuously updated as the environment changes. For object-dense environments, the VLM can request preprocessing only for the information relevant to the current verification step.

content: Our approach enables the VLM to generate task plans for a variety of domains. We evaluate the pipeline using tasks across 5 vastly different domains (see Fig. 1 ), including e-waste recycling, a workshop environment, and an agricultural setting. The focus is on complex, multi-step tasks. In order to underline the real-world applicability of our approach, we also implement the pipeline on a real robot and evaluate it in an industrial recycling environment.

content: In recent years, substantial progress has been made in the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Language Models (VLMs) in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots.

content: LLM- and VLM-based task planning: In SAYCAN [ 3 ] , planning is performed by sequentially selecting skills from a predefined library. Candidate skills are scored using both their linguistic relevance and learned affordance functions, grounding their selection in the robot’s capabilities. PROGPROMPT [ 7 ] leverages the code-generation capabilities of modern LLMs by expressing actions, assertions, and plans directly in Python syntax, making them easier to process downstream. SAYPLAN [ 4 ] grounds planning in large environments by traversing a 3D scene graph representation.

content: These approaches represent open-loop task planners and are easily prone to failure in dynamic environments. By contrast, our approach and the remainder of this section discuss closed-loop task planning approaches instead.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: Reactive task planning using LLMs and VLMs: INNERMONOLOGUE [ 8 ] attempts to close the loop of SAYCAN by injecting execution feedback and scene descriptions from visual-question-answering models (or human feedback) into the LLM prompt at each step. ROSLLM [ 9 ] implements a generic ROS-based framework for integrating LLM agents with robotic systems and supports task correction based on feedback cues. REFLECT [ 10 ] maintains a hierarchical memory structure and semantic scene representation, extracted via object detection and CLIP to find relations, to support failure analysis and replanning. However, the LLM itself is only fed textual prompts. BETR-XP-LLM [ 11 ] and REPLAN [ 12 ] employ VLM-based verification and critique mechanisms to detect and correct planning failures. AHA [ 13 ] further studies failure detection through task-specific fine-tuning of VLMs. More recent work investigates VLM-based failure detection and recovery through optimized prompting [ 14 ] , behavior-tree-based reactive failure handling [ 15 ] , and constraint-aware visual monitoring [ 16 ] . Other approaches represent plans as behavior trees [ 17 ] , allowing the resulting policies to be executed directly within established robotic control frameworks [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] .

content: Explicit visual grounding: ConceptGraphs [ 23 ] uses 3D scene graph representations to support language-conditioned planning and spatial reasoning. Other work explores multimodal interfaces between vision-language models and symbolic planners [ 24 ] . Recent segmentation-oriented VLMs such as LISA [ 25 ] show that segmentation masks can be generated from language-based reasoning queries, highlighting the relevance of explicit visual grounding for downstream robotic tasks. Related visual-prompting approaches explicitly annotate candidate image regions: SoM (Set-of-Mark Prompting) uses interpretable marks to improve visual grounding in multimodal models [ 26 ] . Similarly, MOKA employs mark-based visual prompts and point-based affordances to connect VLM predictions to robot manipulation actions [ 27 ] .

This allows the planning system to continuously update its grounding during execution while remaining adaptable to different domains through the replacement of individual perception modules.

content: However, VLA models generally require substantial amounts of training data and are often tied to specific robot embodiments, action spaces, or domains. Adapting them to highly specialized applications remains challenging when representative demonstration data is unavailable. By contrast, our approach operates at the task-planning level and combines VLM reasoning with modular perception and classical motion generation techniques. This enables the reuse of existing robotic software stacks while facilitating adaptation to new domains through targeted perception modules rather than large-scale retraining.

content: For this work, the VLM is employed in two different modes, differing in how they are prompted. The alternating use of these two modes forms the basis of the cyclic planning pipeline . On the one hand, the VLM is used to generate the next planning step based on the task at hand and the current state of the environment. To this end, it is provided with the task description, the list of actions the robot can perform (each of which represents a basic motion primitive, as seen in Table I , which can be combined with others to form more complex behaviors), current images of the environment, and the list of interactable objects and points of interest found therein. In turn, the VLM generates a Thought (a natural language description of the next step to be executed), a sequence of actions from the toolbox, as well as the goal it aims to achieve with the generated sequence (in natural language). The Thought provides an explicit rationale alongside the structured action output. The division of the overall plan into smaller steps is entirely self-directed by the VLM, which is instructed to generate only one major interaction with its surroundings (e. g., picking up an object) at a time.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: Additionally, the same VLM is also used to verify whether the generated plan was executed successfully. This is accomplished by comparing the goal generated in the planning step against current images of the environment as well as images from directly before the execution of the plan. The model first describes the images provided before generating an Observation stating whether or not the expected goal was achieved. The collection of past Observations comprises the memory of the VLM, which is also appended to its input in subsequent planning steps.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: The division of the pipeline into explicit planning and verification steps is a key design choice. It allows the VLM to focus on each step individually, without being overwhelmed by having to perform both of these complex tasks simultaneously. Separate prompts are used for planning and verification so that each invocation has a constrained objective and output format.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: For the purposes of the proposed pipeline, the VLM is treated as a black box, with the models not being fine-tuned or adapted to the specific task at hand. This separates domain adaptation from the choice of reasoning model and allows newer VLMs to be integrated without modifying the perception or execution interfaces. Additionally, while fine-tuning the VLM might improve the model’s innate scene understanding capabilities, external modules would still be required to provide the necessary action grounding.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
content: The modular vision preprocessing is provided by a collection of dedicated computer vision systems, which together aid in grounding the VLM’s language understanding by providing three functions. Despite its name, the module serves both as a visual preprocessing interface for the VLM and as the action-grounding interface for the robot execution layer. Initially, a find_objects function identifies any task-relevant interactable objects in the environment and returns their (expressive, natural language) labels. The VLM then uses these labels to reason about the objects in the environment and to parametrize the resulting action sequence. This creates a shared vocabulary between the VLM and the Vision Preprocessing Module. Secondly, a mask_objects function is used to overlay a segmentation mask of the given object(s) on the input image. The colors of the masks are communicated to the VLM together with the object labels and masked image, allowing it to reason about the spatial relations of the object in the environment. This performs the task of grounding the VLM’s language understanding in the visual input. Finally, a generate_pose function is used to generate a target pose for the given object label. Applying this function for each label used in the task plan enables the robot to actually interact with its surroundings, grounding its actions in the real world.

content: The pipeline starts by taking current images of the workspace and preprocessing them using the find_objects and mask_objects functions introduced above. The resulting images are added to the VLM’s planning mode input, which uses them to generate an action sequence. The generated actions are parsed into a Behavior Tree (BT), whose leaf nodes invoke the corresponding functions from the robot’s action toolbox. The BT provides an inspectable interface between the VLM-generated plan and the underlying robot-control framework. Any object labels parametrizing the plan are mapped to the corresponding robot pose using the Vision Preprocessing Module’s generate_pose function. The mapping is performed using a fresh set of current images from the moment in which the relevant action starts being executed. This reduces sensitivity to small scene changes occurring during VLM inference or the execution of preceding actions, increasing the robustness of the pipeline.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: Once the execution is completed, another new set of images is taken and preprocessed. These new images, along with the initial images that were used to generate the plan, are then passed to the VLM in verification mode. The preprocessing is especially important here, as the VLM must recognize any differences between the two sets of images to ascertain whether they match the plan’s expected goal. However, in dense environments, the sheer amount of information provided to the VLM can be overwhelming. This can lead the VLM to disregard key information by attending to the wrong masks. Instead, we introduce a dynamic preprocessing selection cycle. Initially, the VLM is only provided with the unpreprocessed images, as well as the list of object labels. Using these labels, the VLM can iteratively request additional preprocessed images until it has enough information to generate an answer. This limits the number of simultaneous visual annotations and helps the verifier focus on task-relevant changes in object-dense scenes. Analogously to the Thought step in the planning mode, the VLM first describes the images, focusing on their differences, giving the model space to reason. Then, it decides whether or not it requires more information based on these descriptions. Finally, once the verification process is finished, the model’s Observation is appended to the VLM’s input in planning mode for the next iteration of the pipeline.

content: The evaluation addresses three questions: whether explicit domain-specific visual grounding improves VLM-based planning and verification, whether visual preprocessing provides benefits beyond textual domain descriptions, and whether VLM-directed preprocessing helps verification in object-dense scenes. To investigate these questions, we compare five configurations constituting ablations of the grounding interface of the cyclic planning pipeline. Initially, we evaluate the performance of the pipeline without the modular vision preprocessing (and consequently, without the dynamic preprocessing selection ). This forms our baseline. The second configuration augments the basic VLM inputs with natural language descriptions ( D D ) of the domain-specific objects that can appear in the environment. Next, we introduce the modular vision preprocessing ( V V ) to the pipeline, both with and without the natural language descriptions. Finally, we evaluate the full pipeline with the dynamic preprocessing selection ( S S ), in order to assess its effect on the scalability of the preprocessing in object-dense environments.

content: We manually assess the pipeline at three levels corresponding to its planning and verification stages. Planning Accuracy denotes the proportion of sequences for which the generated plans are judged correct, independently of subsequent verification outputs. Verification Accuracy denotes the proportion of verification decisions matching the known execution outcome and is evaluated for correctly generated plans. Overall Accuracy denotes the proportion of sequences for which both planning and all associated verification decisions are correct.

Nonetheless, the same trends can be observed, with the Vision Preprocessing Module ( V ) (V) providing a substantial boost in both planning and verification accuracies, and the dynamic preprocessing selection ( S ) (S) further improving the verification accuracy. content: The use of vision modules for preprocessing the VLM’s visual input shifts the generalization requirements of the pipeline from the VLM to the dedicated vision model. While this may seem like a minor change, it is important to note that the vision modules can be trained on much smaller datasets than VLMs, and can be easily fine-tuned to new domains with only a few additional examples. Therefore, this shift is a key strength of the pipeline, and significantly increases its modularity and its practical applicability in specialized domains.

content: The controlled image-sequence evaluation uses manually prepared perception outputs and therefore isolates their effect on downstream planning and verification rather than measuring sensitivity to perception errors. The real-robot case study complements this evaluation by demonstrating one complete implementation using learned detection, segmentation, pose estimation, and physical execution. A natural extension would be to expose perception confidence through the same modular interface, allowing uncertain detections to trigger additional observations or controlled recovery actions.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains

content: After visual grounding is provided, the remaining planning failures primarily concern instruction following and logical consistency. This indicates that grounding alone cannot compensate for all limitations of the reasoning model. These errors could be addressed without changing the perception interface, for example through explicit action constraints, validation of generated Behavior Trees, or a structured memory for longer tasks. Within its current scope, TrySee is best suited to structured applications in which domain-specific perception and robot skills are available and the environment changes primarily between actions. For such applications, the proposed architecture provides a practical, flexible, and robust approach to combine evolving VLM capabilities with mature robot-control software and targeted domain knowledge.

content: We presented TrySee, a modular system that connects general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robot execution components. The system incrementally generates and verifies short-horizon plans, while a Vision Preprocessing Module supplies semantic object labels, visual masks, and executable target poses. For object-dense scenes, dynamic preprocessing selection allows the VLM to request only the information relevant to the current verification step.

title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
content: Across five specialized tasks, the complete system achieves 81.8 % 81.8\% Planning Accuracy, 91.2 % 91.2\% Verification Accuracy, and 67.3 % 67.3\% Overall Accuracy, compared with 3.6 % 3.6\% , 50.2 % 50.2\% , and 0.0 % 0.0\% for the ungrounded baseline. The brownfield industrial e-waste disassembly application further demonstrates how the architecture can reuse ROS 2, MoveIt 2, Behavior Trees, and targeted perception models without task-specific VLM fine-tuning. The results show that explicit, modular visual grounding provides a practical route for applying VLM-based task planning in specialized robotic applications while retaining existing robot software and domain-specific capabilities.

title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
authors: Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy, Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane
content: 1 Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews Pujan Pant 1,*, Sagar Newpane 1, Hari Sitaula 2 and Manish Sakhakarmy 3,* 1 Herald College Kathmandu, University of Wolverhampton, Naxal, Kathmandu 44600, Nepal 2 Department of Mathematical Sciences, Montana Technological University, Butte, MT 59701, USA 3 ASI Industrial, Billings, MT 59101, USA * Correspondence: pantpujan017@gmail.com (P.P.); sakhakarmym@gmail.com (M.S.) Abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines can turn visitor reviews into structured data, but generic schemes may miss rituals, sacred spaces, cultural restrictions and emotionally mixed experiences at living sacred heritage sites. We adapted the LLM–Social Computing (LLM-SC) framework to Pashupatinath Temple, Nepal, by specifying a 12-type entity taxonomy (four original LLM-SC types plus eight sacred-heritage types), four relation types and nine aspect-sentiment dimensions in a GPT-4o extraction prompt, which was applied to a fixed random sample of 2,500 English-language Tripadvisor reviews from a processed corpus of 3,939. The exports contain 11,286 entity, 6,232 aspect-sentiment and 5,590 relation records, covering 2,485, 2,487 and 2,433 reviews, respectively; the eight added sacred-heritage types account for 64.8% of entity records. Against an adjudicated two-annotator reference for 200 reviews, exact normalized surface-and-type matching gave provisional entity scores of 41.0% precision, 21.8% recall and 28.4% micro-F1. Aspect-presence F1 was 53.6% and end-to-end aspect-plus-polarity F1 was 42.6%. Human adjudication supported 153 of 194 first-listed relation candidates (one per review; 78.9%), a candidate-level rate that does not estimate relation recall or whole-graph precision. The contribution is a culturally grounded, domain-specific adaptation with component-wise human evaluation and explicit reproducibility and generalization limitations. Keywords: LLM-SC; living sacred heritage; domain adaptation; semantic extraction; aspect-level sentiment analysis; semantic network; human evaluation; tourism reviews 1. Introduction Cultural heritage sites preserve historical, religious and cultural practices while continuing to shape contemporary visitor experiences. In Nepal, heritage is an important part of the tourism landscape, and both the Kathmandu Valley and Lumbini are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List [1,2]. Tourism also contributes substantially to the national economy [3,4], while infrastructure and environmental problems make a systematic understanding of visitor experience increasingly important [3]. Online reviews are an increasingly important source for this purpose because they contain naturally occurring accounts of visitors’ experiences, expectations, satisfaction and complaints [5–9].

title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
authors: Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy, Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane
content: 2 Pashupatinath Temple lies within Pashupati, one of the seven Monument Zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property [1]. As a living sacred heritage site, it functions simultaneously as a place of worship, pilgrimage, cultural practice and tourism. Reviews of the site therefore contain more than conventional assessments of services or facilities: within a single account, visitors may describe rituals, religious actors, sacred spaces and objects, cultural restrictions, spiritual emotions, environmental conditions, crowding and interactions with site personnel. This creates a distinctive semantic challenge for automated review analysis, because a system must represent not only what visitors mention but also the cultural and experiential meaning attached to those concepts. General-purpose review-analysis methods do not necessarily capture these characteristics. When culturally specific concepts such as rituals, religious actors, sacred places and objects, cultural rules and spiritual experiences are forced into broad generic categories, distinctions that matter to visitors can be lost. Sentiment poses a similar problem. A visitor may describe a strongly positive spiritual experience alongside crowding, pollution, restricted access or poor guidance, and a single sacred encounter may itself be described with both positive and negative emotions. A document-level polarity score cannot preserve these distinctions, and a generic aspect scheme may assign them to categories that do not reflect their sacred or experiential meaning. Tourism and heritage research has increasingly applied natural language processing (NLP), transformer models and LLMs to visitor-generated content [5–13]. The LLM-SC framework [5] is a relevant foundation because it combines LLM-based semantic extraction, sentiment analysis and Social Computing network construction. However, a framework developed for one heritage context does not necessarily represent another adequately. When examined against Pashupatinath reviews, the original LLM-SC configuration did not provide sufficient representation for several culturally specific entities and experiential dimensions. The problem addressed here is therefore not simply how to analyze more reviews, but how to adapt LLM- SC so that it preserves the domain-specific semantic structure of living sacred heritage. This study extends LLM-SC by adapting its semantic representation to living sacred heritage while retaining the framework’s core structure. The adaptation has two parts: a 12-type entity taxonomy that keeps four categories from the original configuration and adds eight sacred- heritage categories, and an explicitly guided extraction prompt that defines the entity types, four relation types, evidence requirements and nine aspect-level sentiment dimensions. The resulting structured information is represented as a Social Computing network of typed relations. GPT-

authors: Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy, Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane
content: 3 4o outputs for a fixed sample of 2,500 reviews are evaluated against human-adjudicated reference annotations for a 200-review subset, separately for entity extraction, aspect-level sentiment and selected relation candidates. The evaluation asks whether the extracted content is supported by the review text, conforms to the schema and agrees with human judgments; a larger number of extracted records is not treated as evidence of better performance. Alternative models were screened only qualitatively, so no quantitative ranking of models is claimed. The structured outputs are motivated by recurring review monitoring, but hourly retrieval and live- system performance were not evaluated. The study has three objectives: 1. To adapt the LLM-SC framework to living sacred heritage by developing a domain- specific entity taxonomy, extraction prompt and aspect-level sentiment representation capable of capturing culturally specific entities and complex visitor experiences; 2. To assess GPT-4o outputs against human-adjudicated annotations on a defined review subset, using component-appropriate measures for entity extraction, aspect presence and polarity, and relation support and type agreement; 3. To describe how the resulting structured outputs could support recurring visitor-review monitoring, while keeping this application-oriented motivation separate from any evaluation of live retrieval or system performance. Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 describes the data and methods, Section 4 reports the results, Section 5 discusses them together with the study’s limitations, and Section 6 concludes. 2. Related Work 2.1. User-Generated Content and Online Reviews as Data Sources for Tourism Research The growth of online platforms has made user-generated content (UGC) an important source for understanding visitor behavior, destination experiences and tourism performance. Fronzetti Colladon et al. [12], for example, analyzed more than 2.6 million Tripadvisor forum posts about seven European capital cities and found that forum language complexity and the centralization of the communication network were the strongest predictors of international airport arrivals, whereas models based on simple activity measures produced worse forecasts. Fei [7] similarly highlighted Tripadvisor, Instagram and X as complements to traditional surveys for capturing tourist experiences.

title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
authors: Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy, Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane
content: 4 UGC is particularly valuable for cultural heritage because visitors describe their experiences in their own words rather than responding only to predefined survey dimensions. Research on historical districts in Fujian Province identified visitor priorities involving local culture, historical significance, architecture, food and commercial activity from online reviews [6], and Luo et al. [5] showed that visitor comments on the Forbidden City contain layered relationships among attractions, services and emotional responses that static survey instruments struggle to capture. For living sacred heritage, this naturalistic character is especially important, because reviews can contain spontaneous descriptions of rituals, religious actors, sacred spaces, spiritual experiences, access restrictions, environmental conditions and other factors that shape the visit. The analytical value of UGC, however, depends on what can be recovered from the text. Because a single review covers several dimensions of experience, collecting large volumes of reviews does not by itself yield a structured understanding of visitor experience. Approaches are needed that identify the concepts visitors discuss, determine how those concepts are evaluated and represent their relationships within the wider heritage experience. 2.2. Sentiment Analysis and Aspect-Level Opinion Mining in Tourism Sentiment analysis is widely used to extract visitor opinions from tourism-related text. Early studies combined deep-learning sentiment classification with topic modeling to identify concerns such as local culture, historical significance, architecture, food and commercial activity in cultural heritage destinations [6]. Document-level sentiment is nevertheless a coarse representation, because a single review may praise some aspects of a visit and criticize others. Aspect-level sentiment analysis addresses this by associating sentiment with particular dimensions of an experience. Fei [7] combined transformer-based language models and clustering to identify the tourism attributes associated with visitor satisfaction, including wellness services, natural environments and hospitality. Chen et al. [9] combined aspect-based sentiment analysis with machine learning and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify concerns about overcrowding, accessibility and service quality at a heritage site. LLM- based approaches have also handled implicit and ambiguous opinions in hospitality reviews and approached human-level evaluation in some aspect-sentiment tasks [13]. These studies show the value of moving beyond a single positive or negative label. The distinction is particularly important for living sacred heritage, where a review may express strong spiritual satisfaction alongside dissatisfaction with access, crowding, environmental conditions or other operational factors, and where the same sacred experience may carry both

Aspect-level sentiment for sacred heritage therefore requires dimensions that reflect the domain rather than categories transferred unchanged from hospitality or general tourism. 2.3. Named Entity Recognition in Cultural and Heritage Domains Entity recognition determines which concepts in a review become available for later analysis. This matters in cultural and heritage settings because reviews contain domain-specific terminology, historical references, names and culturally meaningful expressions that may not map onto generic entity categories. Concepts that are not identified and represented correctly can direct downstream sentiment and relation analysis toward overly broad or semantically inappropriate categories. Wang et al. [10] proposed GPT-NER, which reformulates named entity recognition (NER) as a text-generation task and performed strongly in low-resource settings where labeled training data are limited. Levchenko [11] found that GPT-4o recognized person names in Russian cultural-event announcements with higher F1 than transformer-based NER models. In cultural heritage tourism, Luo et al. [5] showed that LLM-driven extraction from Forbidden City reviews identified substantially richer tourism-related subcategories than a conventional NLP baseline. Entity recognition is therefore more than a preprocessing step: it fixes the concepts available to downstream analysis. In living sacred heritage, the required entities extend beyond attractions, facilities and general tourism categories to religious practices, religious actors, sacred locations and objects, cultural restrictions, and spiritual or emotionally complex experiences. The task is to define an entity representation that reflects the semantic structure of the target domain, not simply to extract more entities. In the literature reviewed for this study, we found limited evidence of such a representation for Himalayan or South Asian living sacred heritage. 2.4. Large Language Models and Domain Adaptation in Tourism Text Analysis LLMs are increasingly applied to tourism text because they can interpret context, implicit meaning and domain-specific language without every extraction rule being encoded manually. Roumeliotis et al. [8] compared GPT-4o-family models, before and after fine-tuning, with a BERT baseline for hotel-review classification and reported higher accuracy for the GPT models. Água et al. [13] reported GPT-4o-based aspect-level sentiment results comparable to human analysis for hotel reviews. GPT-NER showed the potential of generative models for low-resource entity extraction [10], and Luo et al. [5] showed that LLM-based analysis gives

content: 6 greater semantic granularity on cultural heritage reviews than conventional rule- or dictionary- based approaches. LLM-based approaches nonetheless remain sensitive to prompt design, computational cost, multilingual and metaphorical language, and the way the target domain is specified. Existing evaluations have often focused on hospitality, wellness or other settings where task-specific annotated resources are available [8,13]. For living sacred heritage, we did not identify a directly comparable public annotated resource for the culturally specific entity and experiential categories required here, which constrains conventional supervised domain adaptation. Prompt-based domain adaptation offers an alternative under this constraint. Rather than assuming that a model’s existing knowledge is sufficient for consistent downstream analysis, domain knowledge can be specified explicitly through entity definitions, examples, sentiment dimensions, relation types and extraction rules. The model’s role is then not simply to recognize religious terms, but to map them consistently into a predefined semantic representation suitable for subsequent analysis. This distinction motivates the adaptation of LLM-SC developed here. 2.5. Social Computing and Semantic Network Analysis in Tourism Research Review-level extraction can be extended through Social Computing and network analysis, which model relationships among entities, behaviors and other elements of tourism systems. Fronzetti Colladon et al. [12] showed that network properties of tourism discussions carry information about online discourse and tourism demand, and Maghsoudi et al. [14] used social network analysis of 162 tourism-related websites in Iran to show that digital tourism services operate as an interconnected ecosystem. Luo et al. [5] combined LLM-based semantic extraction with Social Computing to construct heterogeneous information networks from visitor reviews, representing relationships among attractions, services, visitor concerns and emotional responses. Such representations show how extracted concepts are connected within visitor narratives, which frequency counts or isolated sentiment scores cannot. Network structure, however, depends on the quality and semantic specificity of the underlying extraction. A network built from generic noun phrases and undifferentiated co-occurrence differs from one in which entities carry domain-specific types and relationships are explicitly classified. For living sacred heritage, Social Computing is therefore best treated as a downstream component whose usefulness depends on the domain-adapted representation supplied by the extraction stage, not as an independent analytical layer.

Research Gaps and Positioning of the Present Study The studies reviewed above establish that online reviews provide rich evidence about visitor experience, that aspect-level sentiment captures dimensions obscured by document-level polarity, that LLMs can support entity extraction in low-resource settings, and that Social Computing can represent relationships among extracted concepts [5–14]. Three gaps remain for living sacred heritage. The first is a representation gap. Tourism and heritage approaches commonly use general entity and sentiment categories, whereas living sacred heritage involves rituals, religious actors, sacred spaces and objects, cultural restrictions, spiritual emotions and emotionally complex experiences. The challenge is to represent the concepts visitors actually use, not merely to extract entities. The second is an integration gap. Existing studies demonstrate entity extraction, aspect-level sentiment and network analysis, and some combine several of these. In the literature reviewed here, however, we found limited evidence of an integrated domain-adaptive LLM-SC framework that jointly specifies sacred-heritage entities, domain-specific sentiment dimensions and typed semantic relationships. The third is an operationalization gap. Much of the existing literature evaluates approaches on retrospective datasets, and evidence on domain-adapted LLM-SC for ongoing review monitoring in living sacred heritage is limited. This study considers how its structured outputs could support monitoring, but its evaluation uses a fixed 2,500-review snapshot and does not test live retrieval or the reliability of an hourly monitoring service. The contribution of this study is therefore a domain adaptation of LLM-SC for living sacred heritage, together with a component-wise evaluation of the selected GPT-4o pipeline against human-adjudicated reference annotations. The evidence does not establish that GPT-4o outperforms alternative models or that the adaptation transfers to other sites; rather, it provides an explicit adaptation procedure whose categories and definitions can be tested and refined in related sacred-heritage settings. 3. Domain-Adaptive Taxonomy and Prompt Design The adaptation was implemented through a domain-specific representation scheme rather than by changing the underlying language model. Taxonomy development began with an examination of 200 randomly selected reviews from the eligible corpus to identify recurring concepts relevant to knowledge acquisition; a further 100 reviews were then examined to refine category boundaries and definitions. This review-informed process was complemented by domain knowledge about concepts that required explicit representation. The aim was to extend, not replace, the categories inherited from the original LLM-SC framework. Four categories from the original configuration were retained (scenic_spot, problem, facility_service and general_sentiment, the last corresponding to the original emotions category) because they remained useful for architectural features, complaints, management and service experiences, and general emotional evaluations not specific to sacred practice. The religious_actor category covers people in religious roles, including sadhus (Hindu ascetic renunciants), priests, pilgrims, devotees, monks and yogis. The sacred_space category covers religiously significant locations, including ghats (stepped riverbank embankments used for ritual bathing and cremation), the Bagmati River, sanctums and cremation areas. The festival_event category covers named religious events, cultural_rule covers access norms, restrictions and culturally specific rules, and sacred_object covers physically identifiable religious objects such as offerings, lamps, garlands and ritual implements. Two further categories represent aspects of sacred experience that general-purpose categories would struggle to preserve. The spiritual_emotion category captures an internal spiritual or emotional state explicitly experienced by the reviewer, rather than one attributed to the site or to another person. The dual_valence category captures an experience or entity that the reviewer explicitly describes with simultaneous positive and negative emotional meaning. It was introduced because sacred encounters can be emotionally mixed: a cremation, for example, may be described as disturbing or grief-inducing and, at the same time, as meaningful or transcendent, and treating it as simply positive or negative would discard part of what the review expresses. Category definitions were refined during pilot inspection because some boundaries were initially less precise than consistent extraction required; definitions and examples were clarified to separate closely related concepts, particularly reviewer-felt spiritual emotion and mixed- valence experience. The final taxonomy and prompt were then fixed, and no prompt modifications were made in response to outputs from the 2,500-review extraction. The prompt operationalized the taxonomy through natural-language definitions, examples and extraction rules (Appendix A). In addition to the 12 entity types, it specified four relation types (co_occurrence, causal, description and contrast) and nine aspect-level sentiment dimensions (service, facility, environment, ritual_experience, spiritual_authenticity, access_fairness, sacred_atmosphere, crowd_management and cultural_sensitivity). Exclusion rules were intended to prevent the site and generic contextual terms from being extracted repeatedly: Pashupatinath Temple, Kathmandu, Nepal and similar terms, and generic words such as place, site, visit and experience, were treated as contextual subjects rather than entities. LLM Extraction Pipeline 3.3.1. Model Screening and Extraction Configuration Several candidate approaches were screened qualitatively before the full run, including Llama- family models, a GLiNER-based extraction approach combined with SetFitABSA, and GPT- 4-family models. Screening focused on tasks requiring contextual interpretation: domain- specific entity extraction, identification of reviewer-felt spiritual emotions and recognition of mixed-valence experiences. GPT-4o was selected on this basis. Because matched, reproducible outputs and reference-based evaluations are not available for the other candidates, the screening does not support a quantitative ranking, and quantitative claims in this study are limited to GPT- 4o outputs evaluated against human references. Each review’s text_clean field was inserted into the fixed prompt (Appendix A) and submitted as a single user message through the OpenAI Batch API (Chat Completions endpoint), using the OpenAI Python library (August 2026 release), with the model alias gpt-4o, a temperature of 0.1, a maximum of 900 output tokens and 45 requests per batch. Before adjudication, the two annotators marked 1,162 and 1,532 entity mentions. They agreed on 524 mentions with the same normalized span and type (pairwise F1 = 38.9%), rising to 778 (57.8%) when span variants confirmed by hand are included; where both annotators marked a span, they assigned the same type in 82.0% of cases (Cohen’s κ = 0.80). For aspects, presence agreed in 91.9% of the 1,800 decisions (κ = 0.80), and polarity agreed in 82.3% of the 436 aspects that both annotators marked present (κ = 0.73). For relations, the annotators agreed on whether the candidate relation exists in 80.4% of the 194 candidates (κ = 0.38) and on its type in 67.4% of the 138 candidates both accepted (κ = 0.55). Chance-corrected agreement was lowest for relation existence (κ = 0.38). 4.3. Entity Extraction Against the Human Reference Under the exact normalized surface-and-type matching rule, the GPT-4o entity export yields 373 matched predictions among 910 predictions for the 200 reviews, leaving 537 unmatched predictions and 1,341 unmatched reference mentions (Table 3). Micro-precision is 41.0% (95% CI 37.7–44.4%), micro-recall 21.8% (19.5–24.1%) and micro-F1 28.4% (25.9–31.0%); macro- F1 across the 12 types is 26.5% (23.0–30.2%). These are mention-level surface-and-type scores, not character-offset span scores, because the export contains no predicted offsets. When entity type is ignored, 464 predictions match the text of a reference mention (precision 51.0%, recall 27.1%, F1 35.4%), and 80.4% of these surface matches also carry the reference type. Per-type F1 ranges from 49.4% for ritual to 0% for dual_valence (16 predictions and 3 reference mentions, none matched); general_sentiment reaches only 3.9% because the model rarely extracted it as an entity (13 predictions against 297 reference mentions; recall 2.0%).

Of these, 153 were adjudicated as relations that exist in the source review, a sample-specific support rate of 78.9% (95% CI 73.1–84.5%; Table 5). The sensitivity results are reported separately and do not replace the primary results. 5. Discussion 5.1. Domain Adaptation and Semantic Representation The main contribution of the adaptation is the explicit representation of concepts that are salient in living sacred heritage but are not distinguished by generic entity labels. The eight added sacred-heritage categories account for 64.8% of the entity records in the export (Table 2), so the pipeline uses them extensively. Use is not accuracy or cultural validity, however: the categories must also be judged against the human reference, and both missed mentions and unsupported or mistyped mentions matter. The taxonomy is therefore best regarded as a domain-representation design whose performance is evaluated separately (Section 4.3), not as a taxonomy validated by the fact that the model populated it. 5.2. Separating Detection, Typing, and Polarity The component-level results show why output volume and a single aggregate score cannot characterize a structured-review pipeline. For entities, exact surface-and-type matching penalizes both lexical differences and taxonomy disagreement, and the absence of predicted offsets prevents boundary-level evaluation. Strict matching is also demanding for this task: before adjudication, the two annotators themselves agreed on the same normalized span and type for only 524 mentions (pairwise F1 = 38.9%). Output volume also limits recall directly: the evaluated export contains 910 predicted mentions for these reviews against 1,714 reference mentions, so even perfect matching could not have produced a recall above 53.1%. For sentiment, aspect-presence and end-to-end scores differ because a correct polarity cannot compensate for an omitted or spurious aspect. Conditional polarity accuracy (79.4%) is informative about the polarity step but should not be presented as overall sentiment performance. Neutral labels and noncanonical polarity outputs warrant targeted error analysis before stronger interpretations are drawn.

content: 27 5.3. Interpreting Semantic Relations and Network Structure The semantic network represents model-extracted relations; it does not verify real-world causal mechanisms. In the relation validation, 153 of 194 selected relations (78.9%) were supported by human adjudication, and 106 (54.6%) were both supported and typed as adjudicated. These are support and typed-match rates for selected candidates, not exhaustive precision, recall or F1, because the 200 evaluation reviews contain 450 relation records, of which 194 were adjudicated. The graph analysis distinguishes the 5,926-node inventory, the 5,110-node relation network, the 5,341 typed groups and the 5,221-connection undirected projection (Table 6). Co- occurrence, description, causal and contrast relations have different meanings and should not be collapsed without an explicit reason, and symmetric relations require careful handling of endpoint order. Because names are normalized only for whitespace and case, variants of one concept (cremation and cremations in Figure 2) remain separate nodes, which spreads their connections across several nodes and can affect degree rankings and component counts. 5.4. Implications for Heritage-Review Monitoring A schema-guided pipeline could help analysts organize large volumes of visitor feedback into culturally specific entities, experiential dimensions and candidate relations. Potential uses include triaging recurring concerns about access, facilities, environmental conditions or cultural sensitivity, and identifying review narratives that merit human attention. These are potential decision-support uses rather than demonstrated management outcomes: the study evaluates a fixed snapshot and does not establish the reliability, latency or operational impact of a live monitoring service. Model-generated evidence should remain inspectable, and uncertain or high-impact interpretations should be reviewed by people familiar with the site and its cultural context. 5.5. Limitations Several limitations bound these findings: 1. Data scope. The corpus consists of English-language Tripadvisor reviews of one living sacred heritage site. Platform self-selection, language restriction, review-writing practices, repeated text across distinct platform IDs and the site’s cultural setting limit generalization to other destinations, languages, platforms and visitor populations; 2. Evaluation scope. The human reference covers a random subset of 200 of the 2,500 sampled reviews, so the component scores are estimates from that subset; the bootstrap intervals quantify review-level sampling uncertainty only. The reviews were obtained through a third-party API, and the authors hold no documentation that the provider was authorized by Tripadvisor, whose terms restrict automated retrieval and reuse of content [17]. No legal conclusion is drawn, and review texts are not redistributed. 5.6. Future Work Future comparisons should apply every model to the same reviews, schemas, normalization rules and scoring units. Entity assessment should report mention-level precision, recall, F1 and schema conformance; sentiment assessment should separate aspect detection from end-to-end polarity; and relation metrics should follow a probability-based or exhaustive candidate sampling design. Coverage and invalid or missing outputs should be reported alongside the scores. Replicated annotation, evaluation of relations beyond first-listed candidates and evaluation at related sacred-heritage sites are needed before broader claims can be made. 6. Conclusions This study adapted the LLM-SC framework to reviews of a living sacred heritage site by integrating a sacred-heritage entity taxonomy, nine aspect-level sentiment dimensions and a typed relation schema in one structured extraction workflow. The human-reference evaluation shows why these components should be assessed separately, because entity surface-and-type matching, aspect detection, polarity classification and candidate-level relation validation reflect different sources of error. Entity extraction scores were low and provisional (28.4% micro-F1; 95% CI 25.9–31.0%), and aspect presence and end-to-end aspect sentiment reached F1 values of 53.6% and 42.6%. The relation validation supported 153 of 194 selected candidates (78.9%) and found 106 exact supported-and-typed matches, but its non-exhaustive sampling design does not support full-output relation precision, recall or F1. The graph analysis distinguishes records, typed relation groups, node inventories and topology connections, so the network summaries are reproducible from the released exports under explicit definitions. A post hoc duplicate- handling check changed output and edge counts only slightly, although it added one connected component. For heritage managers, the potential value is a traceable decision-support resource that organizes candidate concepts and visitor experiences for human inspection while keeping uncertain evidence, schema violations and missing outputs visible. The study does not show that the representations are culturally complete or reliable enough for autonomous management decisions. title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
section: O m n i S h o w c a s e : Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
content: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject’s unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K , a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench , a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase

title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Subject-to-video (S2V) generation aims to create videos of a specified subject from reference images while preserving its appearance across time and viewpoints. Recent video diffusion models generate photorealistic videos from text or a single image ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Wan Team, 2025 ; Brooks et al., 2024 ) , and S2V methods use reference images to preserve subject identity in generated videos ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . However, most S2V methods condition on a single reference image, which provides appearance information only for the visible surfaces and leaves other regions unconstrained. As the camera reveals previously unseen sides, generated videos may exhibit inconsistent geometry and appearance, which can lead to changes in silhouette, structure, and surface details. These ambiguities motivate the use of multiple reference views and explicit geometric information. The main difficulty is geometric rather than purely photometric since the model must infer 3D structure that is absent from the input.

title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Recent methods incorporate multiple reference views into S2V generation. MV-S2V ( Song et al., 2026 ) trains a feed-forward model using generated multi-view videos, whereas 3DreamBooth ( Ko et al., 2026 ) performs per-subject optimization using static multi-view images. These efforts motivate two complementary directions: training on geometrically consistent viewpoint changes and providing explicit 3D geometry during generation. For the latter, recent feed-forward reconstruction methods can recover 3D geometry from a few uncalibrated images ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) , making explicit geometry available from the same sparse references used at inference.

authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) are the dominant approach to visual content synthesis, and the shift from convolutional U-Nets to transformer denoisers ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with rectified-flow training ( Esser et al., 2024 ) improved their scalability and sample quality. These advances carried over to video. Early video models extended pretrained image backbones with temporal layers ( Singer et al., 2023 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) ; more recent systems use large diffusion transformers trained on web-scale corpora and generate high-resolution clips of steadily increasing length ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Wan Team, 2025 ; Brooks et al., 2024 ) . Image-to-video (I2V) variants add a starting frame as a condition, giving coarse control over appearance. Our framework builds on a pretrained I2V diffusion transformer and adapts it through low-rank tuning ( Hu et al., 2022 ) .

title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Representing and rendering 3D content from images has been studied through neural fields ( Mildenhall et al., 2020 ) and point-based splatting ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) . To synthesize unseen viewpoints without per-scene reconstruction, one line of work distills 2D diffusion priors into multi-view-consistent generators: image-conditioned models such as Liu et al. (2023) hallucinate novel views of an object, and multi-view diffusion models ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Voleti et al., 2024 ) jointly denoise several views to enforce cross-view coherence. These methods are mostly confined to isolated objects against clean backgrounds and do not model scene-level dynamics. In parallel, feed-forward geometry estimators build on monocular depth foundation models ( Yang et al., 2024 ) and recover dense 3D structure from sparse, uncalibrated images in a single pass ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . This makes it practical to derive explicit geometry from multi-view reference images. We use this capability to supplement coarse 3D information of unseen views as a geometry cue.

authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Personalizing generative models to a user-specified subject originates in the image domain, through identifier-based personalization ( Ruiz et al., 2023 ; Gal et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ) and later encoder- or adapter-based conditioning that injects reference features without test-time optimization ( Ye et al., 2023 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) . These ideas carried over to video, where subject-to-video (S2V) methods keep a reference identity stable throughout a generated clip. Optimization- and adapter-based approaches ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) preserve identity over time, and reference-conditioned frameworks ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) extend this to multiple subjects and flexible prompts. These methods primarily encode the subject through 2D appearance features, leaving viewpoints not covered by the reference unconstrained.

title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: Closest to our setting are recent attempts to move beyond single-view conditioning. MV-S2V ( Song et al., 2026 ) feeds multiple reference views into a video diffusion transformer and uses a shifted positional-encoding scheme to distinguish different views of the same subject. The references provide appearance information from several viewpoints, but do not explicitly encode the 3D surface structure underlying those views. Its training videos for object-centric generation are produced by a camera-controllable video generator, so viewpoint variation is not explicitly tied to a shared 3D asset. 3DreamBooth ( Ko et al., 2026 ) uses static multi-view images for subject-specific adaptation, preserving the pretrained model’s temporal behavior but requiring optimization for each new subject. In contrast, OmniShowcase reconstructs geometry from the input views at inference and uses it directly as a conditioning signal, without subject-specific optimization. content: Our training data are designed to satisfy three requirements: subject identity preservation, geometrically consistent viewpoint changes, and explicit geometry for conditioning. A camera-controllable video generator does not guarantee these properties, because unseen surfaces are still synthesized by the generative prior. Real multi-view capture satisfies the first two but leaves the third to an estimator. Rendering from a 3D asset satisfies all three at once, because one mesh under known cameras produces every frame. However, direct rendering produces clean-background videos. We therefore add a separate scene-compositing stage to introduce realistic backgrounds corresponding to the camera motion. The pipeline used to construct Showcase-4K has two branches: a video-generation branch (Figure a) that produces the target video and a geometry-generation branch (Figure b) that produces the condition.

content: We source 3D meshes from Objaverse ( Deitke et al., 2023 ) and, for real-scanned subjects, from the Digital Twin Catalog ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and Google Scanned Objects ( Downs et al., 2022 ) . A heuristic pre-screen discards degenerate meshes, and a vision-language model inspects four rendered views of each remaining asset and keeps only those with valid geometry, plausible textures and category consistency (rubrics in Appendix ). We use four orbit-family motions (Orbit and Helix-Up/Down/In) with four rotation amounts each and eight additional motions—arc, truck, dolly, and zoom variants—with nine framing transitions each, yielding 88 88 trajectory configurations in total (Appendix ). From the same mesh, Blender renders an 81 81 -frame target video and N = 4 N{=}4 reference views ℛ \mathcal{R} at 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} yaw intervals, so references and target share one underlying shape and appearance.

Subject masks from the render’s alpha channel drive a video inpainting model ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) that synthesizes a coherent background around the fixed subject, while keeping the rendered subject pixels unchanged. The scene prompt combines a location from a language-model-written scene bank with the sample’s camera motion and lighting, and a vision-language gate discards videos whose subject floats, deforms, or departs from the references. content: Datasets and baselines. We evaluate on ShowcaseBench , a held-out benchmark of 50 50 subjects spanning four 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} camera trajectories and sharing no 3D asset with Showcase-4K , and on NAVI ( Jampani et al., 2023 ) with 35 35 subjects. Training and inference settings are given in Appendix . Phantom ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and MAGREF ( Deng et al., 2026 ) are single-view S2V models, and we run them in the multi-reference mode. We refer to these variants as Phantom-MV and MAGREF-MV, where the four reference images are treated as views of the same subject. Appendix also runs both in their original single-view mode, where the four-view extension is the stronger setting on almost every metric, so the multi-view numbers are the ones we report. We further compare against recent methods, MV-S2V ( Song et al., 2026 ) and 3DreamBooth ( Ko et al., 2026 ) . All methods in our main comparison use the same four reference images. For 3DreamBooth, these images are used for both subject-specific optimization and inference. Prompt details are provided in Appendices – .

content: 3D consistency. MEt3R ( Asim et al., 2025 ) scores multi-view consistency between reference and generated views, taking the minimum dissimilarity per reference. We also lift the generated orbit to a point cloud with π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2026 ) and compare it with the dataset’s ground-truth geometry. For ShowcaseBench , the ground-truth point cloud is back-projected from source-mesh depth renders; for NAVI, it is sampled from the 3D scan mesh. We report GT-CD as the symmetric mean nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance between the predicted and ground-truth point clouds, following independent centering, mean-radius normalization, and rigid alignment. We additionally report RotCoverage as an alignment-dependent diagnostic of viewpoint coverage, computed as the mean distance from each reference viewpoint to the nearest estimated generated viewpoint after pose alignment. Appendix gives the evaluation details.

content: Without geometry conditioning the model keeps the reference appearance but is told nothing about how the subject is shaped away from those views, so identity preservation, MEt3R, and GT-CD all deteriorate. The auxiliary RotCoverage score also increases. The textured variant carries the same geometry but paints it with reconstructed colour, which competes with the reference images for appearance: identity barely moves relative to dropping the condition, and text alignment falls furthest of the three on ShowcaseBench . Thinning the turntable preserves the modality but not the coverage, and its cost depends on how reliable the reconstruction is. On ShowcaseBench , Textured gives the lowest GT-CD among the three ablations, while Sparse gives the lowest auxiliary RotCoverage score.
