title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
content: We present OmniShowcase, which pairs an automated pipeline that renders omnidirectional videos from 3D assets with surface-normal turntable conditioning reconstructed from the reference views, requiring no temporal alignment with generated frames. OmniShowcase leads single- and multi-view baselines on subject identity and cross-view 3D consistency on both ShowcaseBench and NAVI. Two limitations remain: the background sometimes looks synthetic, and subjects that are not rigid across the four references are not handled (Figure , Appendix ). We leave both to future work. We will release the data, benchmark, and code.

content: We fine-tune Wan2.1 I2V-14B-480P through its Diffusers implementation. Training applies LoRA to the DiT with rank 128 128 and α = 128 \alpha=128 , and every other weight stays frozen. Each training sample contains a 25 25 -frame normal-condition segment and an 80 80 -frame target segment at 480 × 832 480\times 832 resolution. These segments are encoded separately into 7 7 and 20 20 latent frames, respectively, and concatenated along the temporal axis to form a 27 27 -frame latent sequence. The four in-context reference images are encoded independently. We train for 33,000 33{,}000 steps at a batch size of 2 2 per device over four NVIDIA B200 GPUs with no gradient accumulation, which takes about 50 50 hours. content: RotCoverage is an auxiliary, alignment-dependent diagnostic of viewpoint coverage. After similarity alignment, the generated and reference camera poses are normalized by the RMS radius of the reference camera centers. Each pose is represented by five frustum vertices: the apex and four far-plane corners at depth 0.5 0.5 and half-size 0.25 0.25 . Pose distance is the mean Euclidean distance between corresponding frustum vertices. For each reference pose, we take the minimum distance over generated poses and average across references, yielding a dimensionless score.

content: Showcase-4K is the surviving remainder of a much larger candidate pool. Assets enter from Objaverse ( Deitke et al., 2023 ) , the Digital Twin Catalog ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and Google Scanned Objects ( Downs et al., 2022 ) and pass through four gates: G0 , a model-free heuristic on the mesh and a quick render; G1 , a vision-language check of four rendered views; G2 , the same check on the composited target video; and G3 , on the reconstructed turntable (rubrics in Appendix ). G0 rejected 17 % 17\% of downloaded candidates outright, and G1 kept 4,186 4{,}186 of the 7,016 7{,}016 assets it judged ( 60 % 60\% ). In the most recent production round, 44 % 44\% of 7,438 7{,}438 composited clips passed G2 and 63 % 63\% of those passed G3, so 28 % 28\% of rendered clips survive; most G2 rejections are a changed object structure or physically implausible support. The binding constraint is G2, and we did not relax it. Over-generating and discarding is cheaper than letting a bad sample into training, because a subject that deforms in the target teaches exactly the failure the method is meant to remove. Over all rounds 4,829 4{,}829 clips passed, and 4,000 4{,}000 of them, covering 2,593 2{,}593 assets in 620 620 categories, form the released corpus.

content: The two columns of Figure fail for unrelated reasons. The synthetic look of the background follows from how the training targets are built. Only the subject is physically rendered, and the scene around it is painted in afterwards by a video inpainting model conditioned on the prompt. The corpus therefore pairs a physically shaded subject with a generated background, and the light transport between the two was never consistent to begin with. The model reproduces that statistic, so the subject holds while the surroundings inherit the flat shading and thin material detail of their source.

content: The dynamic case is a property of the conditioning signal itself. The surface-normal turntable is obtained by lifting the reference views into a single static reconstruction and rendering that one shape from every viewpoint. When the four views catch the subject in four different poses, the reconstruction fuses them into one rigid body that corresponds to no pose the subject ever held, and the condition handed to the generator is a static representation of a subject that is not static. Under a static prompt the model follows that condition faithfully, which is exactly why the output settles into an averaged pose. Asking for motion in the prompt does not repair it. The text now requests a pose change that the geometry condition does not encode, so the two disagree, and the model has to interpolate between reference poses in image space with no 3D correspondence to guide it. The tangles appear at those interpolated transitions. Handling non-rigid subjects would require a conditioning representation that varies over the generated sequence, which we leave to future work.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
section: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
content: In eXplainable AI, counterfactual explanations have gained significant traction by offering users direct, intuitive, and actionable insights into model decisions. We introduce CounterFlow, a novel framework based on Conditional Flow Matching that generates visual counterfactual explanations by directly steering a source image toward a user-specified target class. By leveraging target-conditioned vector fields, CounterFlow identifies highly realistic semantic modifications while requiring substantially lower computational overhead than traditional GAN- or diffusion-based architectures. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that CounterFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual realism and target class switching. By working directly in the raw pixel space, CounterFlow offers a more practical solution for real-world deployment.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: Context. On the one hand, in generative modeling, diffusion models currently dominate the landscape for high-quality image, video, and audio synthesis ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ho et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) . However, they are also well-known for their slow training times and their stochastic sampling paths. To address these limitations, Lipman et al. (2023) ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023b) introduced Conditional Flow Matching (CFM). CFM is a generative modeling framework based on Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) that uses standard regression objectives for training. Moreover, instead of relying on diffusion processes, CFM generates examples by integrating the CNF’s ODE along deterministic trajectories. On the other hand, the generative models’ ability to generate complex data distributions and thus to produce realistic examples is particularly appealing for eXplainable Artificial Intelligence ( Dwivedi et al., 2023 , XAI,) , where one aims to produce counterfactual explanations ( Wachter et al., 2017 ) , i.e. , examples (i) close to a given input, (ii) plausible, and (iii) that change the model’s prediction. Unlike adversarial examples that rely on imperceptible noise to fool the classifier, counterfactual examples expose meaningful changes, helping users to trust the model while enabling developers to debug it. Our work leverages CFM to create counterfactual explanations: rather than generating images from random noise, our approach transports an input sample toward a counterfactual conditioned on a user-defined target class, while jointly optimizing for plausibility and proximity; see Figure 1 .

content: Related Work. Prior work on image counterfactual explanations falls into two categories: instance-based and generative approaches. Instance-based methods ( Goyal et al., 2019 ; Keane and Smyth, 2020 , see e.g. ,) select examples from the training set using similarity metrics to modify the input sample 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . However, they require access to the training set at inference and cannot tailor a minimal, plausible edit to a specific example 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . We focus instead on generative approaches, a more recent line of work ( Khorram and Fuxin, 2022 ; Jeanneret et al., 2024 ; Weng et al., 2024 ; Augustin et al., 2022 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) that produces more plausible examples, which we group by generative backbone: GANs, diffusion models, or CFM.

content: • GAN. C3LT ( Khorram and Fuxin, 2022 ) encodes the input (with a VAE encoder) into a latent space, in which it learns two cycle-consistent transformations per pair of classes ( y , y ′ ) (y,y^{\prime}) before decoding with the generator of a GAN. It thus requires one model set per pair, impractical for many classes, and its fidelity is bounded by the VAE’s reconstruction quality.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: • Diffusion. DiME ( Jeanneret et al., 2024 ) generates a counterfactual by corrupting the input and denoising it through the backward diffusion process (an inner loop of several steps); at each outer step, the classifier gradient computed on this denoised estimate refines the corrupted instance, and the process repeats until it converges to a valid counterfactual. FastDiME ( Weng et al., 2024 ) instead computes this gradient directly from the model’s one-step denoised estimate, bypassing the inner loop entirely. ACE ( Jeanneret et al., 2023 ) takes a different route: it builds an adversarial attack against the classifier and lets the diffusion model’s own denoising process project this attack back onto the manifold of realistic images, turning an imperceptible perturbation into a semantically meaningful one. DVCE ( Augustin et al., 2022 ) starts the reverse diffusion from a partially noised version of the input, rather than pure noise, and steers the process by projecting the gradient of an adversarially robust classifier onto a cone around the target classifier’s own gradient direction whenever the two disagree, avoiding non-semantic changes. More recently, MaskDiME ( Guo et al., 2026 ) improves on DiME’s efficiency and spatial precision with a training-free, adaptive dual-mask mechanism guided by classifier gradients that restricts updates to a localized region rather than the whole image. Regardless of the specific guidance scheme, diffusion-guidance methods must reapply their guidance at every one of many denoising steps, making inference slow: DiME’s inner diffusion loop scales quadratically with the number of diffusion steps, and even FastDiME’s one-step approximation, despite yielding a roughly 20 × \times empirical speedup, only reduces this to a linear scaling and remains markedly slower than a single forward pass. ACE and DVCE compound this same per-step cost further, respectively adding an adversarial attack and a robust-classifier gradient computation at every step.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: • CFM. LeapFactual ( Cao et al., 2025 ) builds on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) to generate counterfactuals. It learns a class-conditional generative flow from a Gaussian prior to the latent space of a pretrained VAE, and repurposes this flow for counterfactual generation through a lift-and-land procedure. Given an input, its VAE encoding is first lifted toward the prior under the input class by solving the learned ODE backward, and then landed back into the latent space under the target class by solving the ODE forward. This “leap” must be repeated a dataset-dependent number of times, with each leap requiring a VAE decoding and a classifier query. Our work also builds on CFM, but uses it in a fundamentally different way. We directly learn a transport from an input image to its counterfactual. This avoids (i) the need for multiple costly leaps, (ii) the intermediate traversal through a prior space, and (iii) VAE encoding and decoding, whose reconstruction fidelity can limit the quality of the generated counterfactuals.

content: Datasets. We evaluate CounterFlow on two standard image classification benchmarks: MNIST and CIFAR-10 , MNIST consists of 70,000 70{,}000 grayscale images of handwritten digits belonging to 10 10 classes, with a spatial resolution of 28 × 28 28{\times}28 pixels. CIFAR-10 contains 60,000 60{,}000 color images of size 32 × 32 32{\times}32 pixels, evenly distributed among 10 10 object categories. These two datasets provide complementary evaluation settings, ranging from a simple handwritten digit classification task to a natural image classification benchmark. For all experiments, we use the standard training and test splits provided with each dataset. Section A.4 discusses why we do not extend the comparison to larger benchmarks such as ImageNet.

This fixed-step solver provides a more deterministic evaluation protocol and allows a fair comparison of the computational cost across methods. content: Methods. We compare CounterFlow 2 2 2 The hyperparameters of CounterFlow are listed in Appendix. against three recent counterfactual generation methods: C3LT ( Khorram and Fuxin, 2022 ) , FastDiME ( Weng et al., 2024 ) , and LeapFactual ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , where we use the official implementations. Among diffusion-guidance methods, we retain only FastDiME as a representative baseline: DiME and ACE are prohibitively expensive to run at scale due to their inner-loop or per-step attack computations; DVCE requires an adversarially robust classifier, a constraint that our method does not rely on and that we therefore do not impose in our experiments; and MaskDiME’s masking mechanism restricts edits to a localized region, which conflicts with our evaluation setting where the change may need to affect the whole image. Beyond this choice, neither of the two remaining baselines, namely LeapFactual and FastDiME, is applicable to both datasets. LeapFactual relies on a compact VAE latent space to remain tractable, which does not scale to CIFAR-10 without dominant reconstruction artifacts and a much costlier latent flow, so we evaluate it only on MNIST. Conversely, FastDiME depends on pretrained OpenAI diffusion models built for natural images, so we evaluate it only on CIFAR-10.

content: Following the standard definition of the Fréchet Inception Distance ( Heusel et al., 2017 , FID,) , feature statistics for FID t and FID s are extracted from pretrained image classification networks. For CIFAR-10, we use the pretrained Inception-V3 network available in torchvision . Since ImageNet-pretrained models are not well suited for handwritten digit recognition, for MNIST we instead compute features using the pretrained convolutional classifier employed throughout our experiments. FID is then computed between the Gaussian statistics of the extracted features from the generated counterfactuals and those of the corresponding source or target class, i.e. , FID t on the target class and FID s on the source class. Note that, since these statistics are estimated from the subset of test examples belonging to a single class, rather than from the full test set as in standard, unconditional FID computations, the reported values are higher than those typically observed in unconditional image generation. We therefore focus on relative comparisons between methods under the same evaluation protocol rather than on the absolute reported numbers.

CounterFlow reaches the highest conditional validity ( 99.6 % 99.6\% ) and the lowest target FID while remaining close to the source, confirming that the learned conditional transport reliably reaches the target class with a single ODE integration. LeapFactual stays closer to the source but has the highest target FID, reflecting a more conservative transformation. C3LT performs worst overall and requires by far the largest model, due to its per-class-pair VAE, GAN, and mapping networks.

content: CIFAR-10. CounterFlow is best on all five metrics: it reaches 100 % 100\% conditional validity, nearly halves C3LT’s target FID while also lowering its source FID by a quarter, and needs roughly half the inference FLOPs and an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Improving both FIDs at once is the signature of a near-minimal transport: counterfactuals that fall within the target class without drifting away from the source image. FastDiME reaches only 16 % 16\% conditional validity despite a diffusion backbone 900 × 900\times more expensive per sample, and has the worst FID on both axes; with so few samples switching class, these scores reflect generic realism rather than class transfer.

Pairing semantically similar examples yields simpler transport trajectories that are easier for the conditional velocity field to approximate, whereas random pairing often associates visually unrelated samples, leading to harder-to-learn trajectories and lower-quality counterfactuals. content: Style Preservation. Figure 1 shows five source/counterfactual pairs per dataset. On MNIST, CounterFlow preserves writer-specific style, such as stroke thickness and slant – e.g. , the 4 → 5 4{\to}5 transition retains the source’s thin strokes – and keeps the digit’s orientation, rather than collapsing to a generic class prototype. On CIFAR10, the same near-minimal-path behavior appears at the scene level: the background stays untouched and only the foreground object changes, often preserving its color palette and orientation while altering just the class-relevant structure.

content: Trajectories. Figure 2 visualizes the full integration trajectory for five counterfactuals per dataset, with the border color marking the classifier’s prediction at each step ( red for the source class, green for the target class). In most examples the color flips early, showing that CounterFlow reaches the target class within a small fraction of the path and spends the remaining steps refining the sample within that class rather than driving the decision itself, i.e. , most of the trajectory makes the class change plausible rather than induces it. Intermediate frames stay visually close to both endpoints rather than passing through a degraded intermediate state, confirming at a finer granularity that CounterFlow produces minimal, semantically meaningful edits rather than an unconstrained image-to-image mapping. See Figures 4 and 5 in Section A.5 for additional CounterFlow trajectories.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: Existing image counterfactual generation methods often require heavy generative backbones, including diffusion models or multiple class-specific generative networks, making their deployment computationally demanding. CounterFlow demonstrates that Conditional Flow Matching provides a significantly simpler alternative. By learning a single target-conditioned transport field and requiring only one ODE integration at inference, our method achieves competitive or superior counterfactual quality while substantially reducing computational complexity. We believe this constitutes an important step toward making counterfactual explanations practical for interactive decision-support systems, where explanations must be generated quickly and consistently.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: Despite these encouraging results, several limitations remain. First, our experiments are restricted to relatively low-resolution image datasets. Evaluating CounterFlow on larger-scale benchmarks such as ImageNet or high-resolution generative datasets would provide further evidence of its scalability. Second, our latent-space pairing strategy currently relies on nearest-neighbor retrieval using a pretrained encoder, which introduces an additional preprocessing step. Finally, while Conditional Flow Matching substantially reduces inference complexity compared to diffusion models, solving an ODE remains more expensive than a single feed-forward network.

title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals
authors: Paul Sevellec, Elisa Fromont, Romaric Gaudel, Laurence Roze, Paul Viallard, Laetitia Houeix
content: We presented CounterFlow, a Conditional Flow Matching framework for visual counterfactual explanation generation. Unlike previous approaches relying on GANs or diffusion models, CounterFlow directly learns a target-conditioned transport field between image classes in pixel space. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art counterfactual validity while remaining competitive in image realism and substantially reducing computational requirements.

Future work will investigate its application to larger-scale datasets and other data transformation tasks, including domain adaptation, semantic image editing, and robust model analysis.

content: This work introduces a method for generating visual counterfactual explanations of image classifiers, evaluated on the standard MNIST and CIFAR-10 benchmarks, which do not contain personal or sensitive data. As with other counterfactual-explanation and image-editing methods, the underlying generative technology could in principle be misused to produce misleading edited images of real people; we mitigate this risk by restricting our experiments to non-human-identifying benchmark datasets and by releasing the method as a tool for model interpretability rather than for unconstrained image generation.

content: Explained classifier. A counterfactual method should not depend on the specific classifier it explains. Table 5 therefore keeps CounterFlow unchanged and only substitutes f f , comparing the RepVGG-A2 used throughout the paper with a deliberately mis-specified variant, namely the same network evaluated without its input normalization, which drops its accuracy to 86.3 % 86.3\% , and with an adversarially robust PreActResNet-18 ( Gowal et al., 2021 ) . The mis-specified classifier is explained as well as the original one: validity stays at 100 % 100\% and both FID scores remain within two points of the default, indicating that CounterFlow does not require the explained model to be accurate, only that it defines an exploitable decision boundary. The robust classifier behaves differently: validity drops to 83.5 % 83.5\% , while FID t reaches the lowest value we observe ( 55.72 55.72 ). This is consistent with what adversarial training is designed to achieve, namely flattening the decision boundary and suppressing the small non-robust directions that a gradient-based guidance term can exploit, so that ℒ Cla \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Cla}} pushes less strongly and a fraction of the samples never crosses the boundary. The counterfactuals that do cross must therefore carry a genuine, large-scale semantic change, which is what brings them closer to the target distribution; note that the 16.5 % 16.5\% of samples that remain in the source class can only inflate FID t , so this value is, if anything, pessimistic. Explaining a robust model is thus harder for CounterFlow, but yields more plausible counterfactuals, which is coherent with diffusion-based methods that explicitly require an adversarially robust classifier ( Augustin et al., 2022 ) .

Hence, its ImageNet experiments are qualitative, restricted to five pairs of classes, and use latent codes sampled from a pretrained GAN rather than real images ( Khorram and Fuxin, 2022 ) . LeapFactual relies on a latent space in which inputs can be faithfully encoded, and each of its leaps requires decoding the latent code and querying the classifier; its only large-scale experiment is a binary task on images generated by a pretrained GAN ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
section: Adapt for Planning, Not Just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
content: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner’s goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: Latent world models have demonstrated success across a range of control and planning tasks ( LeCun, 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) . These world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time. Test-time distribution shift can degrade planning performance. A standard approach in adaptive control is to update the dynamics model online as new transitions are observed. This raises the central question: which objective should guide test-time adaptation of a world model?

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: A straightforward choice is to minimize the latent prediction loss on transitions observed at test time. AdaJEPA ( Wang et al., 2026a ) follows this approach for goal-conditioned planning with JEPA world models, updating the model on recent transitions at each replanning step. Compared with a frozen model, this prediction-only adaptation can improve planning success under distribution shift. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, test-time adaptation operates in a closed loop: the planner selects actions by scoring the model’s imagined rollouts, and the resulting transitions are used for the next model update. The model is thus trained to minimize prediction loss only on the outcomes of its own action choices, so it can fit them accurately yet remain wrong about actions that would reach the goal, a closed-loop identifiability problem ( Borkar & Varaiya, 1979 ) . This mismatch between the prediction loss and the planning objective is known as objective mismatch ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) .

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: An early solution to this objective mismatch was reward-biased maximum likelihood (RBMLE), proposed by Kumar & Becker (1982) . RBMLE estimates the model with a joint objective of two terms: the likelihood of the observed transitions and the optimal long-run reward achievable under the model. This objective is both task-aware and optimistic: it favors a model with high achievable reward while anchoring the model estimate to the observed transitions. RBMLE introduces optimism directly through the estimation objective, without the confidence sets or explicit uncertainty estimates required by upper-confidence-bound methods ( Jaksch et al., 2010 ) , making it more amenable to test-time adaptation, where calibrated uncertainty estimates are difficult to obtain for world models under distribution shift. RBMLE has so far been studied mainly in adaptive control and reinforcement learning ( Kumar & Becker, 1982 ; Mete et al., 2021 ; Mete et al., 2026 ) ; in this paper, we propose an optimistic objective for test-time adaptation of world models used for planning.

content: Test-time adaptation is used in a wide variety of settings to address distribution shift ( Sun et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Hansen et al., 2020 ; Liang et al., 2025 ) . Several recent works adapt world models to distribution shift ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . For latent world models used in planning, AdaJEPA ( Wang et al., 2026a ) proposed test-time adaptation by minimizing prediction error on observed transitions. Updating the dynamics model online as new transitions are observed is also standard in adaptive control and model-based reinforcement learning ( Borkar & Varaiya, 1979 ; Kumar & Becker, 1982 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2024 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) .

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: A large number of latent world models are trained and adapted to minimize prediction error, but are then used to select actions for planning or control ( Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . This leads to a mismatch between the model-learning objective and the control objective ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) . To address this mismatch, value-aware model-learning methods train the dynamics model using reward or value information in addition to prediction error ( Farahmand et al., 2017 ; Farahmand, 2018 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) . These methods require a learned reward or value function, which is unavailable when adapting a pretrained world model for goal-conditioned planning. In this paper, we argue that optimism offers a practical solution to objective mismatch in test-time world-model adaptation for goal-conditioned planning.

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: Reward-biased maximum likelihood estimation (RBMLE) ( Kumar & Becker, 1982 ) was proposed to counteract the pessimistic bias that maximum-likelihood estimation can exhibit in closed-loop control ( Borkar & Varaiya, 1979 ) . It favors models with higher optimal reward while anchoring the estimate to the observed transitions. Later, upper-confidence-bound (UCB) methods implemented optimism by optimizing over a confidence set of plausible models ( Auer et al., 2002 ; Jaksch et al., 2010 ) , of which RBMLE can be viewed as a Lagrangian relaxation ( Mete et al., 2022 ) . Uncertainty-based optimistic approaches ( Curi et al., 2020 ; Sukhija et al., 2025 ) rely on calibrated uncertainty estimates, which are difficult to obtain under distribution shift and limited deployment data, whereas RBMLE requires none. RBMLE has since been extended to reinforcement learning ( Mete et al., 2021 ) , linear-quadratic control ( Mete et al., 2022 ) , and, recently, online world-model-based reinforcement learning ( Mete et al., 2026 ) . Whereas Mete et al. (2026) apply RBMLE-style optimism to online reinforcement learning with rewards, OpTTA applies it to test-time adaptation of pretrained world models for goal-conditioned planning.

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn representations by predicting target embeddings rather than reconstructing observations ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . JEPA world models such as PLDM, DINO-WM, temporal straightening, and LeWM ( Sobal et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Maes et al., 2026 ) apply this principle to action-conditioned prediction for goal-conditioned planning. In this paper, we address test-time adaptation of these world models for goal-conditioned planning.

content: Our experiments evaluate the benefits of optimistic, task-aware world-model adaptation for goal-conditioned planning under distribution shift. The evaluation spans three latent world models; manipulation, reaching, and navigation tasks; visual and environment shifts; predictor-only and joint predictor–encoder adaptation; and sampling-based and gradient-based planners.

We evaluate goal-conditioned planning on tasks commonly used in related world-model work ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Maes et al., 2026 ) : object manipulation (PushT and PushObj), reaching (Reacher), and navigation (TwoRoom and maze tasks).

content: On PushT visual corruptions, the optimistic objective yields about 2.5 × 2.5\times the prediction-only adaptation gain in final success for both LeWM and temporal straightening with predictor-only adaptation, and about 2 × 2\times the gain when the encoder is also adapted. With DINO-WM, AdaJEPA and OpTTA yield final-success adaptation gains of 11.8 11.8 and 13.4 13.4 points, respectively, on PushT visual corruptions. On Reacher visual corruptions with LeWM, the ratio is similar: 2.4 × 2.4\times with predictor-only adaptation and 1.9 × 1.9\times with joint adaptation. TwoRoom is a notable exception: under visual corruptions, both TTA objectives reduce final success relative to Frozen under both adaptation scopes, a failure mode discussed below.

content: Figure 4 helps explain OpTTA’s advantage. It does not come from fitting the agent’s own experience better: OpTTA solves more episodes than AdaJEPA, yet its prediction loss on the transitions the agent executes is not consistently lower. The difference shows up instead in what the model predicts beyond those transitions. On Reacher, OpTTA is more accurate than AdaJEPA on a goal-reaching trajectory that the agent never generated; on PushT the two are similar. On both tasks, and especially on Reacher, OpTTA’s model also becomes more optimistic, expecting its chosen plan to close more of the remaining distance to the goal. This is what optimism is meant to do: planning with an optimistic model either reaches the goal or produces transitions that the prediction loss then uses to correct the model.

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
authors: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar
content: We introduce OpTTA, which augments prediction-based test-time adaptation with an optimistic planning loss. Across three JEPA world models, both adaptation scopes, visual and environment shifts, and CEM and gradient-based planners, OpTTA improves final success over prediction-only adaptation in most settings. Our design of the optimism weight α k \alpha_{k} is practical but not necessarily optimal, and its optimal design remains an open question. More broadly, our results suggest that world-model adaptation should account for the downstream planning objective rather than prediction alone, and that optimism offers a simple way to do so.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
content: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models (LLMs) as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human–agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: A central objective of cognitive and developmental robotics is to construct artificial agents that acquire increasingly sophisticated competencies through prolonged interaction with their environment. Inspired by human cognitive development, developmental robotics emphasizes intrinsically motivated exploration, incremental skill acquisition, and the progressive organization of behavior [ 1 , 2 ] . In parallel, the paradigm of Open-Ended Learning (OEL) formalizes the capacity of autonomous systems to continuously generate new goals and expand their behavioral repertoire beyond predefined tasks or datasets [ 3 ] . Together, these perspectives frame autonomy not as the execution of fixed policies, but as an ongoing developmental process.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Within cognitive architectures, such developmental open-endedness is commonly achieved through motivation-based control systems [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . In these systems, behavior is regulated by internal motivational variables that define why the agent acts, allowing goals and skills to emerge as means to regulate internal states. We refer to these domain-independent motivations as robot purposes .

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Robot purposes include designer-embedded needs , such as homeostatic requirements and intrinsic motivations that drive exploration and competence acquisition [ 7 , romero2024autonomous ] , as well as externally derived purposes, or missions , which reflect what human users expect the robot to accomplish during runtime. Both needs and missions are operationalized through drives – quantitative variables encoding the urgency of satisfying a given purpose [ 8 ] . By acting to regulate its drives, the robot autonomously discovers goals and learns skills that are grounded in the robot’s sensorimotor system. Alignment is achieved when the resulting behavior fulfills human expectations [ 9 ] .

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: However, integrating human purposes into a developmental, open-ended system presents a significant challenge. Human intentions are expressed through natural language – ambiguous, context-dependent, and culturally grounded [ 10 ] – whereas motivational architectures require structured, formally defined representations [ 11 ] . This discrepancy creates a semantic gap that may lead to misaligned internal purposes, undermining trust and safety [ 9 ] . Explainability [ 12 ] and grounding strategies [ 13 ] address aspects of this issue, but they do not fully solve the problem of embedding human purposes into the motivational dynamics that drive developmental learning.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide powerful tools for interpreting linguistic instructions and relating them to perceptual context. Nevertheless, employing such models as end-to-end robot controllers raises concerns regarding explainability, controllability, safety, and the absence of explicit motivational structure [ 14 ] . From a developmental perspective, delegating control to monolithic policies risks bypassing the very mechanisms – intrinsic motivation, goal discovery, and incremental learning – that underpin autonomous cognitive growth.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: We therefore adopt a complementary view: LLMs and VLMs are integrated not as end-to-end control policies, but as high-level semantic and cultural knowledge resources that provide structured priors to a motivation-based cognitive architecture. These multimodal models support the interpretation and clarification of human purposes, constraining the space of plausible missions. The discovery of specific goals and skills, however, remains grounded in the robot’s developmental learning processes and regulated by explicit drives. In this way, large models inform but do not replace the motivational dynamics that sustain autonomous development.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: To operationalize this perspective, we propose a multimodal alignment framework composed of three layers: (1) semantic alignment , which interprets and refines human purposes through interactive dialogue; (2) mission generation , which translates aligned purposes into structured, domain-consistent missions; and (3) drive modeling , which transforms missions into quantitative drive functions embedded in the motivational system. An explicit alignment need , implemented as an alignment drive, motivates the robot to seek clarification until a coherent internal representation of the intended purpose is achieved.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The contributions of this work are threefold: (i) a cognitively and developmentally grounded framework for embedding human purposes into a motivational architecture supporting open-ended learning; (ii) the integration of specialized LLM- and VLM-based modules as semantic priors within this architecture; and (iii) experimental validation in simulation and on a physical robotic platform, demonstrating effective human–robot alignment while preserving autonomous developmental processes.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: By combining multimodal semantic mediation with explicit motivational regulation, this work contributes to the design of developmental autonomous systems that can sustain long-term growth while remaining aligned with human intentions.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-A Instruction Following and Foundation Models in Robotics
content: Bridging the semantic gap between high-level human purposes and executable robot behavior has become a central research topic in embodied AI. Recent approaches increasingly leverage large-scale foundation models to interpret user instructions and generate robot actions. For instance, SayCan [ 15 ] combines a Large Language Model (LLM) with a predefined library of robot skills. The LLM ranks candidate skills according to semantic relevance, while a value function evaluates feasibility in the current state. This modular strategy enables execution of long-horizon instructions, provided the required primitive skills are available. However, the system remains constrained by a fixed behavioral repertoire and does not generate new goals or expand its skill space.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-A Instruction Following and Foundation Models in Robotics
content: Other approaches, such as RT-2 [ 16 ] move toward tighter integration by training a unified vision-language-action model on Internet-scale and robotic data. The model directly maps multimodal inputs to low-level actions, enabling impressive zero-shot generalization. Nevertheless, this end-to-end formulation lacks explicit motivational or goal representations. The resulting policies are difficult to interpret, regulate, or adapt structurally, raising concerns regarding transparency, controllability, and long-term alignment in open-ended environments.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-A Instruction Following and Foundation Models in Robotics
content: From another point of view, there are systems that address pragmatic intention understanding. One such case is [ 10 ] , which classifies user instructions according to their explicitness and leverages contextual cues to infer appropriate actions. Another is the work presented in [ 17 ] that consideres introducing an estimation of uncertainty in user commands and tries to increase certainty through dialogue. While improving robustness in human–robot interaction, such approaches typically operate within predefined task templates and do not support autonomous goal discovery.

authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro

content: Finally, shared autonomy methods [ 18 ] adapt robot policies to user preferences through interactive feedback. Although effective for collaboration, they primarily refine existing behaviors rather than reorganizing the agent’s motivational structure or enabling the emergence of new purposes.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-B Developmental Robotics and Open-Ended Learning
content: Developmental robotics investigates how autonomous agents can acquire progressively complex competencies through processes inspired by human cognitive development [ 1 , 2 ] . Rather than relying on externally specified task objectives, developmental systems are driven by intrinsic motivations such as curiosity, competence improvement, or learning progress. These mechanisms support exploratory behaviors, goal babbling, and the autonomous construction of hierarchical skill repertoires over extended interaction with the environment.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-B Developmental Robotics and Open-Ended Learning
content: Motivation-based cognitive architectures operationalize these principles through internal drives that regulate behavior and trigger self-generated goals [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Within the broader Open-Ended Learning (OEL) paradigm [ 3 ] , agents continually expand their behavioral and representational spaces, discovering novel goals and refining predictive models through sensorimotor experience. Crucially, learning remains grounded: goals emerge from embodied interaction rather than from predefined symbolic plans.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: II-B Developmental Robotics and Open-Ended Learning
content: Despite these advances, most developmental approaches assume that high-level purposes are either hard-coded by the designer or provided in structured form. While they excel at autonomous goal discovery and skill acquisition [ 4 , 5 , 11 ] , they do not directly address how abstract, linguistically expressed human purposes can be integrated into the agent’s motivational system without disrupting its developmental dynamics. As a result, the problem of semantically aligning human intentions with intrinsically motivated, open-ended learning processes remains largely unresolved.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Beyond robotics, the AI alignment literature highlights the difficulty of ensuring that artificial agents pursue objectives consistent with human intentions [ 9 ] . Many alignment strategies for large models rely on techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback [ 19 ] or instruction tuning [ 20 ] . Although effective at shaping output behavior, these methods do not necessarily yield explicit, inspectable representations of purpose within the agent’s control architecture. In embodied, open-ended systems, alignment requires mechanisms that integrate human purposes into the internal motivational dynamics governing goal generation and learning.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Taken together, existing research either (i) leverages large multimodal models for instruction following, often through fixed skills or end-to-end policies, or (ii) develops developmental architectures capable of autonomous goal discovery without addressing semantic alignment with human purposes. What remains lacking is an integrated framework in which multimodal models provide semantic and cultural priors while an explicit motivational architecture preserves grounded developmental learning, and alignment.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Our work addresses this gap by embedding LLMs and VLMs as knowledge resources within a motivation-based cognitive architecture that integrates information from different sensing modalities, enabling the transformation of human purposes into aligned drives that guide autonomous open-ended development.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Fig. 1 : Overview of the proposed framework. The Alignment Engine manages human–robot interaction to align human and robot purposes. The Translation Engine converts aligned purposes into missions and drives, which are integrated into the Motivational System of a cognitive architecture to guide autonomous robot behavior.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Translating human purposes expressed in natural language into motivational representations such as missions and drives is not a trivial task. Humans rely on cultural and contextual knowledge to interpret intentions and desires, whereas computational systems lack this implicit background. To bridge this semantic gap, we use LLMs as cultural knowledge bases related to different sensing modalities that, through an alignment process, are able to clarify human purposes.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Fig. 1 illustrates the proposed framework. At the input of the framework there are several elements that allow the user to add multimodal inputs such as an image, language and audio. Next, at its core, the Alignment Engine extracts and interprets the human purpose from multimodal information (ususally speech and vision). In cases of ambiguity, it engages in iterative dialogue with the user to refine the interpretation, seeking confirmation before proceeding. Once the purpose is clarified, it is passed to the Translation Engine , which decomposes it into missions and corresponding drive functions. These are explicitly instantiated within the motivational system of the cognitive architecture, guiding the robot’s autonomous behavior.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The system is designed for non-expert users. Interaction is therefore concentrated at the specification stage: the user expresses the desired objective in natural language, while the architecture autonomously generates the underlying missions and drives. This allows intuitive purpose specification without requiring knowledge of the robot’s motivational structure.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The function and configuration of each of the three instances of the LLMs used are explained in detail below. Additionally, the prompts used in each of the LLM instances, as well as the source code and the results from the design tests are all available in a public repository 1 1 1 GitHub repository .

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: This module manages multimodal inputs to improve the user experience by providing a more intuitive interaction interface. Visual data is processed through a Vision Language Model (VLM), specifically we used GPT-4o by OpenAI. This model is configured through a specialized prompting to generate a detailed scene description and provide an inferred human intent. For audio processing, the system integrates two distinct frameworks: OpenAI’s Whisper model for Speech-to-Text (STT) transcription, and Google Text-to-Speech (gTTS) to handle the system’s vocal responses.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: This first LLM uses an instance of the phi4:14b model by Ollama. It receives the natural language purpose provided by the user and/or a visual description of the environment and reformulates it into a clear, unambiguous specification. When necessary, it engages in a brief interactive dialogue with the user to resolve ambiguities or request missing details.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The prompt used to guide this LLM instance was carefully structured to include all relevant contextual and operational information. It consists of six main components: (1) Context, which introduces the LLM’s task and defines key concepts such as needs, missions and drives; (2) Robot description and general description of its environment; (3) Robot perceptions, specifying available sensory inputs along with their value ranges; (4) Input description, explaining the nature and format of the user-provided purpose; (5) Task constraints, which define what the LLM must do and explicitly limit its scope; and (6) Interaction rules, which describe the expected structure and format of the model’s responses, ensuring consistency and compatibility with downstream components.

authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The input to this module is a purpose expressed in natural language by the user, along with the image description from the Multimodal Input, when used. The user is required to answer questions and provide additional details to the LLM when needed.

authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: To determine when a purpose was fully aligned we looked at how humans clarify intentions during conversation. Often, they ask: “Is this what you meant?” or “Is this what you want?” . Based on this behavior, the user is who decides when the purpose is correctly understood. From a human-robot interaction perspective, this means the human user has full control over when to move to the next stage.

content: The output is a final aligned and refined purpose statement, written as a clear paragraph. If, based on the robot’s capabilities and perceptions, the model determines that the purpose is not achievable, it returns a standard message: “It is impossible to achieve your purpose with this robot”.

content: Once the user purpose has been aligned, a second LLM instance, also using the phi4:14b model, is responsible for decomposing it into a structured set of missions. These missions represent concrete end-states that the robot must achieve in order to fulfill the user’s intention.

content: Each mission also includes an associated weight that indicates its relative importance within the overall task context, reflecting how critical it is for achieving the human’s intended purpose for the robot. The output of this component serves as a bridge between high-level human intent and the motivational structure that will later govern the robot’s autonomous behavior.

content: The prompt for this instance was designed to clearly instruct the model to generate a list of missions that directly correspond to the aligned purpose. It included: (1) Context, which introduces the LLM’s task and defines key concepts such as needs, missions and drives; (2) Robot description; (3) Robot perceptions; (4) Requirements for creating missions and assigning their weight (priority to fulfill the purpose); (5) Interaction rules and output format; and (6) A list of predefined internal needs, introduced by the designer within the cognitive architecture.

content: The input for this module is the refined purpose generated by the Alignment Engine, expressed as text. On the other hand, the output is an array of missions, where each mission is represented as another array. The first element is a descriptive tag of the mission, it should represent a meaningful end-state, for example “object_in_hand” . The second element corresponds to a numerical weight that indicates the relative priority of that mission. title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: A third LLM instance uses the GPT-4.1 model from OpenAI, and is responsible for modeling a mathematical drive function for each mission. A drive function is a continuous, monotonic mathematical expression that quantifies the urgency to satisfy a given mission based on the robot’s current state. This function must return zero only when the mission has been fulfilled, and increase smoothly as the robot deviates from the desired goal-state. The output of this component integrates directly into the robot’s motivational system.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The prompt provided to this LLM was designed to ensure internal consistency with the elements of the cognitive architecture, and alignment with the robot’s perceptual space. It includes: (1) Context definitions for missions, drive functions, and drive values; (2) Robot description; (3) Robot perceptions; (4) Format specification of the missions generated in the previous stage; and (5) Structured instructions for generating a drive function for each mission.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The input to this component consists of two elements. First, the fully refined purpose provided by the Alignment Engine, expressed in text form. Second, the list of missions generated by the previous LLM instance. The output is a list of mathematical drive functions, one for each mission. Each entry follows the structure: Mission: [tag, weight] and Drive: valid Python expression . If the LLM detects that the purpose cannot be fulfilled with the robot’s current capabilities, it returns the message: “It is impossible to achieve your purpose with this robot” .

content: The results of the semantic alignment evaluation are summarized in Fig. 2 , which illustrates the distribution of cosine similarity scores across the different experimental conditions. For the initial low-detail inputs provided by users, similarity scores ranged between 0.4 and 0.6. These values quantify the initial semantic gap, reflecting the fact that human instructions are often underspecified or ambiguous. At this level of similarity, the Alignment Engine cannot reliably translate purposes into well-defined missions and drive functions.

content: When the purpose was interpreted by the LLM without alignment interaction, the cases that included multimodal input showed much higher semantic similarity to the ideal reference. This improvement suggests that the model was able to use visual context about the robot and its environment to enrich the linguistic description. However, despite this increase, the results show that the generated purposes still diverge semantically from the ideal reference. In other words, the improvement is insufficient to guarantee that the generated purpose fully captures the user’s intended meaning.

content: A Mann-Whitney U test was performed to determine whether the use of multimodal resources led to greater improvement in semantic alignment. This non-parametric test was used to evaluate distributional differences between the unimodal and multimodal settings for three cases: the initial inputs, the outputs without feedback, and the outputs with feedback. Statistical differences were observed in the no-human-feedback scenarios for the Arrange apples by color and Classify cylinders by color purposes. In these cases, the p-values were below the α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 threshold, leading to rejection of the null hypothesis. This result indicates that multimodal resources provide a significant improvement mainly in scenarios without human feedback.

authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: When interactive alignment is enabled (pink distributions in Fig. 2 ), cosine similarity scores consistently converge toward high and stable values across all three tasks. Importantly, these scores are significantly higher than those obtained in non-interactive conditions, regardless of whether multimodal resources are available. This result highlights the critical role of user interaction in achieving precise semantic alignment. Iterative clarification ensures that the internal representation of the purpose closely matches the intended meaning.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The contribution of multimodal information (e.g., visual input) is more nuanced. In interactive settings, multimodal resources do not substantially increase the final semantic similarity compared to linguistic-only interaction. Instead, their primary benefit lies in improving alignment efficiency. Specifically, multimodal scenarios required an average of 3 interaction rounds to reach convergence, whereas text-only interaction required 4.5 rounds on average, with some cases demanding up to 11 rounds. Thus, multimodal grounding reduces the interaction overhead needed to achieve alignment.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Overall, these results indicate that multimodal information enhances interpretation quality and reduces clarification effort, but interactive alignment remains essential to ensure reliable semantic grounding before translating purposes into motivational structures.

section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: This test evaluates the Translation Engine’s capacity to transform refined human purposes into structured motivational representations through two interconnected stages: (1) decomposing purposes into missions, and (2) generating mathematical drive functions for each mission. To isolate these stages from spurious effects introduced by the Alignment Engine, no feedback from the mission or drive evaluation was used to further disambiguate the purpose during these tests.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: The inputs to the mission generator were the aligned purposes obtained from the experiment described in Section IV-B . The resulting list of missions was then used as input to the drive generation stage, allowing this second step to be evaluated independently from unrelated input errors. To assess the validity of the missions and drives, an expert manually classified each output as valid or invalid. To this end, several factors were considered. First, we assessed whether the complete set of missions would enable the robot to achieve the intended human purpose and whether the associated weight distribution was appropriate. Additionally, each generated drive function was individually examined to ensure both mathematical correctness and proper implementation in Python. It was also verified that each function reached zero, or decreased, only under the appropriate task conditions. For clarity, Table III presents the set of missions and drives obtained for the ideal Arrange apples by color purpose defined in Table II .

content: A similar manual analysis was conducted for each set of missions and drives. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , scenarios involving human feedback led to a significantly higher percentage of valid missions than scenarios without user intervention. Although the autonomous multimodal configuration (multimodal without feedback) occasionally exhibited superior performance, its success remains highly dependent on the visual context provided and the complexity of the task. Consequently, this setting cannot guarantee consistent reliability. Therefore, only scenarios involving human feedback were used for the final drive evaluation.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: Regarding the generation of drive functions, Fig. 4 shows that validity rates varied across tasks. While the system performed very well on the Classify cylinders by color task, it was less successful on the Stack cylinders by size task, failing in 6 out of 15 instances. Compared with the ideal case, performance on the first two purposes closely matches the ideal results, whereas performance on the stacking task is substantially worse in both the multimodal and unimodal settings. The reason for this behavior is that, as the purpose becomes more complex and requires a more detailed description, the Alignment Engine becomes more prone to producing ambiguous purposes. When these ambiguities propagate to the drive generation stage of the Translation Engine, they lead to inconsistent performance and, in some cases, invalid drives.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: We observed that when the purpose is well specified, repeated runs through the Translation Engine produce essentially the same valid set of drives. However, if the purpose contains ambiguity, repeated runs through the Translation Engine often produce different sets of drives, some of which are invalid. This variability can therefore be interpreted as a signal that the purpose remains underspecified, which could be used to trigger further dialogue between the Alignment Engine and the user.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: In general, these findings demonstrate that the Translation Engine can adequately translate fully defined user purposes into motivational structures. When failures occur, they are usually caused by ambiguities in the purpose definition, which indicates that the Alignment Engine should be triggered to refine that definition.

content: The results shown in Fig. 6 indicate that it consistently reached the goal in 3–4 iterations, which is close to the practical minimum given the initial positions of the objects on the table. Notably, the robot reached the goal with very few iterations, suggesting a more directed behavior than what would typically be expected from novelty-based exploration alone. Moreover, the robot quickly converges to the correct sequence of actions, guided by the rewards induced by the generated drives. These results demonstrate that the generated missions and drives enabled the robot to complete the task accurately and efficiently.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: This paper introduced a multimodal framework for aligning human purposes with the motivational system of an autonomous robot. By integrating three LLM-based components for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling, the approach enables non-expert users to specify goals in natural language while grounding them in a structured, motivation-driven control architecture.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Experimental results demonstrate that interactive alignment significantly improves semantic precision, confirming that clarification dialogue is essential to reduce ambiguity and reliably translate human purposes into executable motivational structures. While multimodal inputs enhance interpretation efficiency and provide contextual information, iterative human feedback remains crucial for robust alignment. The generated missions and drive functions were found to satisfy the required formal constraints and, when embedded in a cognitive architecture, support consistent goal-directed behavior.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Overall, the proposed system shows the potential of large multimodal models to serve as semantic mediators within a developmental, motivation-based architecture, while maintaining interpretability and alignment. Future work will expand multimodal interaction capabilities and investigate adaptive alignment mechanisms that evolve through prolonged human–robot interaction.
