title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: 5.1 Base probes transfer to both successors
content: Figure 2 a shows the main result. On XSTest, the base probe applied unchanged to the distilled model changes its AUC by − 0.003 -0.003 (math-7b), − 0.011 -0.011 (llama-8b), + 0.003 +0.003 (qwen-14b) and + 0.010 +0.010 (qwen-32b), from base-model AUCs of 0.878, 0.908, 0.899 and 0.931. Applied to the instruction-tuned model it changes by − 0.006 -0.006 , + 0.017 +0.017 , + 0.027 +0.027 and + 0.006 +0.006 . No interval for the distilled models excludes zero; for the instruction-tuned models only the qwen-14b gain does. This is similar observed accuracy, not demonstrated equivalence: the lower ends of the nominal intervals are − 0.045 -0.045 , − 0.034 -0.034 , − 0.014 -0.014 and − 0.006 -0.006 for the distilled models, the intervals are too narrow, and the true bounds on a possible loss are somewhat looser. Full numbers are in Table B.1 .

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: The result holds on the independent set.
content: On OR-Bench, which the probes never saw, the change is − 0.010 -0.010 , + 0.042 +0.042 , + 0.011 +0.011 and − 0.015 -0.015 for the distilled models and + 0.016 +0.016 , + 0.024 +0.024 , + 0.053 +0.053 and + 0.011 +0.011 for the instruction-tuned ones (open markers in Fig. 2 a; Table B.2 ). Two of the distilled changes have intervals that exclude zero, one in each direction; the instruction-tuned changes are all gains. With a fixed layer per family instead of per-fold layer choice the XSTest picture is the same (distilled − 0.013 -0.013 to + 0.011 +0.011 , instruction-tuned − 0.006 -0.006 to + 0.027 +0.027 ; Table B.3 ).

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: The successors are slightly easier to separate.
content: A probe trained on the successor itself scores higher than the base model’s probe on the base model in all eight cases: by + 0.003 +0.003 , + 0.023 +0.023 , + 0.024 +0.024 and + 0.026 +0.026 for the distilled models and + 0.021 +0.021 , + 0.040 +0.040 , + 0.052 +0.052 and + 0.016 +0.016 for the instruction-tuned ones ( Table B.1 ). The gains of the transferred probe on the instruction-tuned models, in particular qwen-14b, are consistent with this.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: 5.2 Rotation does not predict the change
content: Distillation rotates the safety direction by 30.5 ∘ to 35.1 ∘ and instruction tuning by 17.1 ∘ to 33.6 ∘ . Figure 2 b sets these angles against the transfer changes: the four largest rotations (30 ∘ to 35 ∘ , all distillation) come with changes of − 0.011 -0.011 to + 0.010 +0.010 , and the two smallest (17 ∘ , qwen-14b and qwen-32b under instruction tuning) with + 0.027 +0.027 and + 0.006 +0.006 ; there is no clear relation between the angle and the change. The rotation is not an artefact of the measurement: it appears at every layer of every network ( Fig. B.1 ), and in the same common coordinate system the alternative conventions change the cosines by at most 0.013 ( Table B.4 ).

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: Unrelated directions rotate by comparable amounts.
content: To ask whether the safety direction rotates more than an arbitrary direction would, we built 38 control directions in exactly the same way from labels that have nothing to do with safety, in the spirit of the control tasks of Hewitt and Liang (2019) : all 35 ways of dividing the 8 prompt groups into one set of 4 groups and the remaining 4 (the label being whether a prompt belongs to the first set), whether the prompt starts with “How”, whether it contains a capitalised word after the first, and whether it is longer than the median. Under distillation the safety direction rotates slightly more than all 35 splits in three families and less than all of them in math-7b, by margins of about 0.01 in cosine; prompt length rotates more than the safety direction in every family ( Fig. B.2 ). So a rotation of 30 ∘ to 35 ∘ is what directions in these models generally undergo under distillation, and the safety direction is not an outlier. The controls show that the rotation is not peculiar to the safety direction, nothing more.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: The probe keeps more separation than the angle predicts.
content: The size of the rotation motivates a prediction. If the transferred probe lost accuracy only because the successor’s safety direction has rotated away from it by an angle θ \theta , and the two classes were spread like two equal round Gaussian clouds, the probe would keep exactly a share cos ⁡ θ \cos\theta of the successor’s class separation ( Section B.1 gives the derivation). For a 30 ∘ rotation that is 87%. The transferred probe on the distilled models keeps 98%, 88%, 92% and 95% ( Fig. 1 c), between 6 and 16 percentage points more than the angle predicts, in all four families (family-level p = 0.035 p=0.035 from four values). Since a probe’s score is the projection of the activation onto its weight vector ( Section 4 ), rotation in directions perpendicular to that vector is invisible to the probe; Lee and Kondor (2026) make the same point. The pattern is consistent with part of the rotation lying in such directions. The AUC changes themselves are much smaller than these percentages because AUC is a compressed scale near 0.9. For the instruction-tuned models the difference has mixed sign ( Table B.5 ). We report this as an exploratory pattern.

content: Figure 3: The probes’ advantage over the prompt text depends on the test set. (a) AUC of the base model’s probe on XSTest (filled; mean over 8 held-out folds, nominal 95% intervals) and on the independent OR-Bench prompts (open; benign but alarming versus toxic, bootstrap 95% intervals), against the best text-only classifier (character 3- to 5-grams; dashed lines: 0.728 on XSTest, 0.640 on OR-Bench). title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: On XSTest the probes clearly beat the words.
content: The best text-only classifier reaches 0.728 AUC (word unigrams 0.679, word bigrams 0.680, prompt length 0.508; Table B.6 ), against 0.878 to 0.931 for the probes ( Fig. 3 a). Fold by fold the probe beats the text classifier in all 8 folds of all 4 families, by + 0.149 +0.149 , + 0.179 +0.179 , + 0.171 +0.171 and + 0.203 +0.203 on average.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: On the independent set the advantage shrinks.
content: On OR-Bench the probes reach 0.747, 0.669, 0.702 and 0.840 AUC, against 0.640 for the text classifier trained on the same XSTest data. The margin is 0.11, 0.03, 0.06 and 0.20; for llama-8b the two intervals overlap. Both classifiers were trained on XSTest; both do worse on OR-Bench, whose prompts were written by other authors with a different recipe, and the probes lose more. This partly reproduces the negative result of Wang et al. (2026) .

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: The probes respond to apparent harmfulness.
content: AUC compares scores; to use a probe as a filter one must also choose a threshold above which a prompt is called unsafe. The logistic-regression probe has a natural one: a score of zero, where its estimated probability of “unsafe” is one half. This threshold was not validated on any data; it is the probe’s default. Figure 3 b shows what each base probe flags at it on the independent set. Of the OR-Bench toxic prompts it flags 59% to 81% (true positives), and of the ordinary Alpaca instructions 0% to 3% (false positives). But of the OR-Bench hard prompts, which sound harmful but are benign, it also flags 29% (math-7b), 35% (llama-8b), 42% (qwen-14b) and 29% (qwen-32b); transferred to the distilled models, the same probes flag 38% to 68% of them. In words: at its default threshold, a base probe would block roughly a third of benign requests that merely sound dangerous. A second threshold shows that scores do not carry across datasets either. If we instead set the threshold on XSTest, at the value that catches 90% of XSTest’s unsafe prompts, it catches only 19%, 22%, 22% and 34% of the OR-Bench toxic prompts, because OR-Bench toxic prompts receive lower scores than XSTest unsafe prompts do. On XSTest the alarming words were present in both classes and the probes still separated them; on OR-Bench, whose benign prompts are built differently, much less of that separation remains.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
content: A probe trained on a base model retained similar observed accuracy on the DeepSeek-R1 distillation and on the instruction-tuned version of that base, in four families, on its training distribution and on an independent one. This is an empirical result across four families and two kinds of successor; whether it holds for other base models or other distillation recipes is untested. The angle between two models’ safety directions was a poor guide to whether the probe still worked, so transfer is better measured directly than inferred from direction similarity. A text-only baseline belongs beside every probe, on the same evaluation and on at least one dataset the probe was not trained on: the probes’ advantage over the words was clear on XSTest and much weaker on OR-Bench. Thresholds need recalibration on each new dataset, and benign prompts that sound harmful are where these probes fail.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
content: The probes are trained on 450 prompts, and any two of the eight XSTest folds share six of their seven training groups, so the XSTest intervals are narrower than the true uncertainty; conclusions should rest on the agreement across families and with the independent set, not on any single interval. The label states what a well-calibrated model should refuse; we measure no model behaviour and run no causal test. The independent set’s labels are OR-Bench’s operational moderation labels, not an independent ground truth for harmfulness, so our conclusions about that set are conclusions about those labels; and the instruction-tuned models were run on raw prompts, outside their chat format. The probes are linear and read one layer, so they can miss information that is encoded non-linearly or spread across layers. All four families have Qwen2.5 or Llama-3.1 bases and one distillation recipe; the two 32B models were loaded in 4-bit precision; the 8-token pooling window was not tuned.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
content: In this work we posed two questions: (A) whether a linear probe for harmful requests, trained on a base model, keeps its accuracy on that model’s successors, and (B) whether such probes read anything beyond the words of a prompt. For (A), across four model families, the base-trained probe retained similar observed AUC on two successors, a distilled reasoning model and an instruction-tuned chat model, even though both rotated the safety direction by up to 35 ∘ ; the answer is yes for these models and evaluations. For (B), on prompts designed to defeat keyword matching the probes beat the words clearly, but on an independent prompt set much of that advantage disappears and benign prompts that sound harmful are often flagged; the answer is only partly.

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
content: This work evaluates linear probes as monitors for harmful requests and reports both where they work and where they do not. Two findings bear on their use: a probe’s decision threshold set on one dataset does not transfer to another, and on an independent prompt set the probes flag 29% to 42% of benign prompts that merely sound harmful. Anyone deploying such a probe should recalibrate it and measure its false-positive rate on their own data. We release no new model or dataset; the prompts used are from the public benchmarks cited in Section 3 .

content: The extraction code takes entries 1 to L L of the hidden_states tuple returned by the HuggingFace model with output_hidden_states=True , where L L is the number of decoder layers; entry 0, the embedding output, is dropped. In the Qwen2 and Llama implementations, entries 1 to L − 1 L-1 are the residual stream after decoder layers 1 to L − 1 L-1 (counting from 1), before any normalisation, and entry L L is the output of the last decoder layer after the final RMS normalisation. Throughout the paper layers are numbered from 0, so “layer j j ” is the raw residual stream after the ( j + 1 ) (j+1) -th decoder layer, except the last layer, which is normalised. Of all layers used in the paper only one is affected: one math-7b fold chose the last layer, 27. Checked in the transformers source, version 5.19.0. The install cell of the Colab runs does not pin a version; a Colab runtime queried in October 2026, after the runs, reports version 5.20.1. Pooling is the mean of the last 8 prompt tokens (left padding, so these are the real final tokens).

title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
authors: Marios Tsatsos
section: A.2 Coordinate systems for comparing directions
content: The probe’s score is w ⋅ x + b w\cdot x+b ( Section 4 ), so comparing two probes means comparing their weight vectors w w , and comparing two models’ safety directions means comparing two vectors; both need the vectors in one coordinate system. A cosine between two vectors is a well-defined angle only if both vectors are written in the same coordinate system. Each model’s activations have their own per-coordinate standard deviations, so standardising each model by its own standard deviations (as the probe does) puts the base model’s and the successor’s directions in slightly different coordinate systems. We therefore compute the headline cosines after dividing both models’ activations by the base model’s standard deviations (“base-scaled”). Two alternatives are reported in Table B.4 : “own-scaled” (each model by its own standard deviations) and “raw” (no scaling). Base-scaled and own-scaled cosines differ by at most 0.013 at the chosen layers and 0.025 at any layer. Raw cosines are higher and unstable, ranging from 0.63 to 0.99 across folds within math-7b, because a raw cosine is dominated by the few coordinates with very large values that residual streams contain ( Sun et al., 2024 ) ; we do not interpret them.

content: Standardisation divides each coordinate by a different number, so the weight vector of a probe trained on standardised activations is expressed in that model’s own units. Dividing each weight by the standard deviation of its coordinate rewrites the probe as one on raw activations with identical scores; we use this raw form when comparing the weight vectors of two probes, so that both are in one coordinate system.

section: B.1 Separation kept by a transferred probe
content: Suppose a classifier’s scores for safe prompts and for unsafe prompts are two Gaussian distributions with the same spread σ \sigma , their means a distance d ′ ​ σ d^{\prime}\sigma apart; d ′ d^{\prime} is the class separation in units of the spread ( Green and Swets, 1966 ; Macmillan and Creelman, 2005 ) . The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen unsafe prompt scores higher than a randomly chosen safe one. The difference of the two scores is Gaussian with mean d ′ ​ σ d^{\prime}\sigma and spread σ ​ 2 \sigma\sqrt{2} , so that probability is AUC = Φ ⁡ ( d ′ / 2 ) \mathrm{AUC}=\Phi(d^{\prime}/\sqrt{2}) , where Φ \Phi is the standard normal distribution function. Inverting gives d ′ = 2 ​ Φ − 1 ​ ( AUC ) d^{\prime}=\sqrt{2}\,\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{AUC}) , which is how we convert each measured AUC into a separation. We define the share kept as d ′ d^{\prime} of the transferred probe divided by d ′ d^{\prime} of the successor’s own probe: the fraction of the separation available in the successor that the base model’s probe still captures. If the classes were such Gaussian clouds and the transferred probe lost separation only because the successor’s safety direction is rotated by an angle θ \theta away from the probe’s, projecting the clouds onto the probe’s direction would shrink the distance between their means by cos ⁡ θ \cos\theta and leave their spread unchanged, so the share kept would equal cos ⁡ θ \cos\theta . The comparison is a reference point under these assumptions, not a model of our data.

content: A middle-layer direction has the residual stream’s width, so it can be passed through the model’s final normalisation weights and output matrix to score every vocabulary token ( nostalgebraist, 2020 , the “logit lens”,) . We project the safety direction in raw coordinates at the fixed layer. In qwen-14b the highest-scoring tokens towards “unsafe” include “anonymous”, “sex”, “rape” and “contraception” for the base model and “anonymous”, “privacy” and “Sext” for the distilled model; in qwen-32b, “dispose” and “Anonymous” for the base and “Anonymous” and “desire” for the distilled model. In llama-8b and math-7b the lists are word fragments with no readable content, although control directions decode to their own content in the same models. In the two families where the tokens are whole words, they are words that occur in unsafe prompts, both before and after distillation, though the specific words differ; no refusal words (“sorry”, “cannot”) appear. This is an indirect reading and carries no weight in our conclusions.

section: Appendix C Preliminary run with reinforcement-learning checkpoints
content: An earlier run of this project, whose pipeline is less fully recorded than the one reported here, also included for each family a checkpoint trained from the base by reinforcement learning alone, from SimpleRL-Zoo ( Zeng and others, 2025 ) : hkust-nlp/Llama-3.1-8B-SimpleRL-Zoo, hkust-nlp/Qwen-2.5-14B-SimpleRL-Zoo and hkust-nlp/Qwen-2.5-32B-SimpleRL-Zoo, the only SimpleRL release for each of those bases; for Qwen2.5-Math-7B three SimpleRL releases exist and the one used was not recorded. Their activations on XSTest were almost identical to the base models’ (mean per-prompt cosine 0.9998 or higher; relative distance 0.006 to 0.018), the base probe’s AUC changed by at most 0.002, and the safety-direction cosine was at least 0.999. In the same run the distilled models’ activations had mean per-prompt cosines of 0.79 to 0.96 with the base models’. A model that has barely changed cannot test whether a probe survives change, so these checkpoints say nothing about reinforcement learning in general and are not used in this paper.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
section: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
content: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent, and use it for research: problems whose answers can be checked by a program or against data. It runs three loops. A discovery loop keeps an archive of scored solutions, and each new candidate is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox, writing and running its own search code and a lab notebook. A catalogue mode searches real data for things nobody has catalogued, judged by a referee rather than a metric. A self-improvement loop lets the system rewrite its own prompts, tools, skills, memory and meta agent behind a gate. An autonomous mode chains everything from a single plain-text goal with no human step: an agent chooses an open problem and writes its verifier; the kernel calibrates that verifier; an adversarial agent audits it; the search runs; an agent that never sees the verifier checks the result; and a final agent writes the report. Proposers see only a public score; where a task has hidden data (held-out instances, later observations), a private split that no agent sees decides what counts. Around this discovery loop the Infinity Machine keeps an editable genome : prompts, tools, skills, an evidence-backed playbook and the meta agent’s own procedure. A kernel that the agent cannot write to gates every change to the genome: it checks policy, compares held-in and held-out performance, and enforces a cost limit. We applied the system to fourteen problems, thirteen of them external, in six days of October 2026, at a total cost of about $180 in model usage. It produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information, each checked by a verifier that the proposing agent did not write:

content: It also cut the added-gate count of the SABRE qubit-routing benchmark from SABRE’s 68,559 to 12,087 (9,312 against the best published 13,044 on the 15 circuits shared with later work), built a 5-parameter transformer that adds 10-digit numbers, closed 24% of the gap between a 20M-parameter language model and the GPT-2 checkpoint on FineWeb validation loss, and surfaced one unconfirmed planet candidate in TESS photometry. In hardware, it redesigned the RTL of an open 8 × \times 8 INT8 systolic matrix-multiply tile. Through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow at a fixed clock, it cut the energy per multiply-accumulate from 578.9 fJ to 128.8 fJ (77.7% lower) with 55% less area. Power was measured from gate-level switching activity, and the design stays bit-exact. In three fully autonomous end-to-end runs ($7.59–$9.97 each, no human step after launch), the system chose its problem, wrote and audited its own verifier, searched, and re-checked its result blind. One audit rejected a task whose cited record was stale. All three runs ended in honest ties with the public record, two of them with documented near misses. In one run the agent-written score pointed the wrong way, and none of the checks caught it. We report as carefully the parts that did not work. The system’s one gated attempt to adopt a playbook it had written for itself was rejected on cost. Proposers gamed lenient scorers, usually within a single iteration, four times. And the operator’s hand-made changes to the harness were decisive for several results. We describe them so the reader can separate what the loop did from what its operator did.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Large language models can now write and run substantial programs, and agents built on them can stay on a task for an hour or more. A system that turns this into discoveries needs two things beyond a capable model. It must have a way of telling a real advance from a plausible-looking one, and a way of keeping what it learns. AlphaEvolve [ 1 ] and FunSearch [ 2 ] show the first. They ground an evolutionary search over programs in automatic evaluation, so that the model’s errors are filtered out by execution, and they reach new results in mathematics and computer science. Work on self-improving agents, including STOP [ 3 ] , the Darwin Gödel Machine [ 4 ] , Hyperagents [ 5 ] and AIDE 2 [ 6 ] , addresses the second. There the object being evolved is the agent itself, and recursive self-improvement [ 7 ] is the long-run aim.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The Infinity Machine 1 1 1 Earlier data deposits call the system EVO; the two names refer to the same system. is a research agent that does both. It is not a program-evolution engine with a fixed harness: the unit of work is a researcher-like agent run, the search can be open-ended as well as score-driven, and the harness that directs those agents is itself under gated self-modification. It is built for a single operator with a laptop and a cloud account. Four design choices define it.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: 1. Agents, not samples. A proposal in the Infinity Machine is a full agent run. A Deep Agents [ 8 ] model with a shell, a file system and up to an hour of wall clock in a fresh sandbox reads the task notes and the parent solution. It writes and runs its own search code and delivers a solution together with a lab notebook. A problem therefore receives a handful to about fifteen proposals, not thousands. The proposer, not the harness, decides whether to write a C tableau simulator, an exhaustive enumeration or a gradient ladder.

authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Figure 1: Architecture. The kernel owns everything whose corruption would make scores meaningless: scorers, private splits, archive, budget and policy. The genome holds everything the system may change about itself. Agents run inside sandboxes that mount the genome and the public split only.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The Infinity Machine is split into an immutable kernel and an editable genome (Figure 1 ). The kernel contains a daemon that owns long jobs and survives the controlling shell, the archive (the genome’s version history as a lineage DAG, with rollback), the scorers, the gate, the strategy and model bandits, reward logging, and the budget middleware. The genome contains the task agent’s and meta agent’s prompts, the meta agent’s procedure and weakness-mining script, tools with tests, skills with fixtures, and an ID-addressed playbook in which every bullet carries evidence run IDs and a confidence. The split follows the rule from harness-engineering practice [ 9 ] : whatever the agent may legitimately want to change is in the genome, and whatever would let it change its own grade is not. The kernel never trusts an agent’s report of what it ran. It records tool calls itself, and scorers read solutions produced in a fresh sandbox.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: A task consists of a specification (problem family, description, scorer, score range and direction, sandbox image and resources, per-run budget, and a brief), a public split (problem statement, notes, tools, a local verifier), a private split and an optional seed solution. The scorer is either a verifier program that the kernel runs in its own sandbox, whose value is mapped linearly onto [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , a test suite, or a retrain-from-code scorer for ML tasks. The brief is the operator’s channel to the proposers: it lists what has already been measured and what to try.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: A discovery session runs N N iterations of the loop of Figure 2 with P P proposers each. The kernel scores the seed and places it in an experience bank . In each iteration it samples P P parents with probability proportional to σ ⁡ ( 10 ​ ( s pub − s ¯ ) ) / ( 1 + c ) \sigma(10\,(s_{\rm pub}-\bar{s}))/(1+c) . Here s pub s_{\rm pub} is the parent’s public score, s ¯ \bar{s} is the mean public score of the top three entries and c c is the parent’s number of children. This is the DGM/Hyra rule [ 4 , 10 ] , which favours good parents that have not been expanded much. Each proposer also receives a named strategy , drawn by a per-family UCB1 bandit whose reward is whether the child beat its parent on the public score; AIDE 2 [ 6 ] found UCB over named strategies to be its most valuable discovered mechanism. The default arms, written for the optimisation family and used by every family without its own set, are conservative , aggressive rewrite , new neighbourhood , data structure and robust/simple . Math tasks use structured construction , exhaustive small case , new objective , scale compute and literature transfer . ML tasks use new architecture family , parameter sharing , embedding budget , connectivity and recipe ; astronomy tasks have five search-oriented arms of their own.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: A proposer is a fresh Deep Agents model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) in a sandbox that mounts the genome, the task’s public split and an inspiration folder: the parent solution and a bank summary that shows public scores only. It works with a shell for up to about an hour. It must keep its solution directory current, because a per-run spend cap ($4 by default), checked before every model call, can end it at any turn. On return, the kernel scores the solution on both splits in a separate sandbox, appends it to the bank and logs the strategy reward. The session’s answer is the best public solution, and its private score is what we report.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Optimisation has a parent to improve; open-ended discovery in real data does not. A task in catalogue mode changes the deliverable to a list of claims plus a search log. The scorer becomes a referee , which re-measures every claim from the raw data, checks it against catalogues of known objects and returns per-claim verdicts. Those verdicts reach the next proposer as feedback. The hidden split is prediction : for the TESS task, the private verifier mounts later observing sectors that no agent can read and checks whether each periodic claim predicts dips there. After each round the kernel merges all accepted claims into one shared catalogue, which every proposer then extends.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The self-improvement loop improves the genome rather than a solution. A UCB or score-child selector picks a parent generation. The meta agent (Claude Opus 5.5), whose prompt and procedure are themselves genome files [ 5 ] , reads an evidence bundle of recent runs and mines weaknesses. It proposes one bounded edit together with a manifest that states the evidence, the root cause and the predicted fixes. The kernel then applies a static policy check (only genome paths may change, kernel-owned files are byte-identical, at most 12 files) and grades the candidate on held-in and held-out tasks. It accepts the candidate only if neither split regresses beyond a noise band of 0.03 and the cost is at most 1.5 times the incumbent’s. A gain larger than 0.3 is parked for human review instead of being activated. Predictions in the manifest are checked against per-task deltas, and a meta agent whose predictions keep failing is sampled less often.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Three further paths feed the genome. Consolidation [ 11 ] reflects on run records and edits playbook bullets by ID. Bullets that a run retrieved are confirmed or weakened by that run’s outcome, and recurring lessons are promoted to skills, which must pass a fixture. Capability requests let a task agent ask for a tool; a toolsmith subagent writes it with tests, and the kernel re-runs those tests before the requester may use the tool. Rewards come from scores and from the operator’s good/bad feedback on individual runs, and update the bandits and playbook confidence. Every path ends in a generation that passes the same gate, so every self-modification is auditable and reversible.

section: 2.5 Autonomous mode: from a goal to a verified report
content: In the modes above a human writes the task: the problem statement, the verifier, the seed and the notes. Autonomous mode removes that step. Its only input is a plain-text research goal; the default goal asks for an open problem whose best known result is an explicit object or number that a program can check exactly. Every phase is an agent run in its own fresh sandbox, and the kernel only validates, routes and records (Figure 3 ).

content: The record CNOT-count/depth points for preparing | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle of the [ [ 23 , 1 , 7 ] ] [[23,1,7]] Golay code were ( 44 , 8 ) (44,8) and ( 45 , 7 ) (45,7) , from RL plus MCTS graph decimation on an A100 [ 24 ] . Session 1 returned the seed from all four runs. In session 2 a proposer under the aggressive rewrite arm rewrote the search in C (about 5 × 10 6 5\times 10^{6} tableau evaluations per second per core). It changed the objective to the number of qubits left mixed after reverse-applying the circuit, which is zero if and only if the state is a product in any local basis, not only in Z Z . It then walked the neutral network at a fixed 44 gates with a penalty on gates beyond the target depth. Depth 7 appeared in about a second and depth 6 in 10–60 seconds; depth 5 and 43 gates were never reached, the latter even after 10 10 10^{10} evaluations and an exhaustive delete-two/insert-one sweep. The ( 44 , 6 ) (44,6) circuit dominates both published points. It was verified up to wire relabelling by stabilizer-tableau checks and a 2 23 2^{23} -amplitude statevector overlap of 1.0 [ 14 ] .

section: Stabilizer rank of | T ⟩ ⊗ m |T\rangle^{\otimes m} .
content: Exact stabilizer ranks are known only for m ≤ 4 m\leq 4 , and the bounds for m ≥ 7 m\geq 7 were products of smaller decompositions [ 25 , 26 ] . Session 1 was null. Two of its six proposers ran no search at all, one calling the task an open research problem and the other “hardening” a seed that was already a record, as its default-arm instruction suggested. After the operator replaced the math arms, a structured construction proposer in session 2 followed a direction the operator’s notes had listed as untried (close a few stabilizer states under qubit permutations) and built a dictionary by closing three seed states under S a × S b S_{a}\times S_{b} -symmetric Cliffords (396–540 vectors). It then annealed over subsets with 1,024 batched chains, reaching r = 12 r=12 in 40 s, r = 11 r=11 in a few minutes, and r = 10 r=10 on the [ 2 , 5 ] [2,5] block family. The decomposition is exact, with coefficients in 1 4 ​ ℤ ​ [ ζ 8 ] \frac{1}{4}\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{8}] , and gives χ ⁡ ( | T ⟩ ⊗ 7 ) ≤ 10 \chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10 and by sub-multiplicativity χ ⁡ ( | T ⟩ ⊗ 13 ) ≤ 60 \chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 13})\leq 60 [ 16 ] . A companion exhaustive small case run found that coordinate descent over the full m = 5 m=5 stabilizer table stalls at residual 0.0647 for five terms, which is evidence (not proof) that χ ⁡ ( | T ⟩ ⊗ 5 ) = 6 \chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 5})=6 .

section: Qubit routing on the SABRE suite.
content: On the 26 circuits and the 43-edge IBM Q20 Tokyo design graph of the SABRE paper [ 27 ] , with SWAP insertion only and three added gates per SWAP, the methods progressed as follows. Two circuits ( qft_13 , qft_20 ) are not in the public benchmark repository and were regenerated (338 and 800 gates against the paper’s 403 and 970), so their reference is our SABRE reimplementation. Session 1 rewrote SABRE in C++ with early-abort randomised restarts and a hill-climb over initial mappings (36,435 added gates), then a receding-horizon rollout router (24,228). In session 2, two proposers independently implemented a direction the notes listed as untried, a beam search over SWAP sequences, whose state is the mapping plus per-qubit progress; together they reached 12,261. Session 3 refined this to 12,087. On identical inputs, Qiskit 2.4.1’s SABRE gives 64,137 (53,418 with heavy trial settings) and pytket 2.18.5 gives 35,685. On the 15 circuits reported by later routing papers, the best published counts (HAIL, 2025 [ 28 ] ) total 13,044, against 9,312 here, and our count is lower on every one of those circuits [ 17 ] . Beam search for routing is not new. The routers also spent minutes to an hour of CPU per circuit, against seconds to minutes for the stock baselines (up to 23 minutes per circuit for heavy Qiskit), the run-to-run spread is about 8%, and the graph is the design graph rather than the 35-coupler device, so this is a statement about headroom in a widely used benchmark, not a fair comparison of algorithms.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: On the internal TSP task (hidden instances, n n from 600 to 2000, scored against a BHH optimum estimate), two iterations with two proposers each raised the private score from 0.58 to 0.88. The proposers converged on chained 2-opt with Or-opt and segment-swap kicks. While calibrating this family we found that any reference built from a hand-written local search was matched by the agent within one session, so references must come from optima or stronger solvers.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The task is to find the smallest transformer that adds two 10-digit numbers with full accuracy [ 29 ] . Working from the rules alone, a proposer designed a 5-parameter model in one 8-minute, $1.05 run. It has one attention layer and two heads keyed on a period-11 sinusoidal positional encoding, a scalar tied embedding and read-out, and a sigmoid carry gate; the carry arises only through autoregressive feedback. It passes the upstream verifier on 10,010 of 10,010 additions across three seeds. A parallel proposer found an independent 6-parameter design. The next session gamed the parameter counter (Section 4 ).

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The task was to find an architecture of at most 20M parameters, embeddings included, that beats the OpenAI GPT-2 124M checkpoint on FineWeb validation (1.0658 bits per byte), training only on FineWeb-10B (GPT-2 itself was trained on WebText). The scorer retrains each candidate from its code on one H100 for 10 9 10^{9} tokens, so a gain must come from the architecture or recipe. The seed was a scaled-down modded-nanogpt [ 30 ] at 1.3376. Session 1 reached 1.2868 with recipe changes and learnable residual mixing; it made no architectural change, because the bandit drew only opt-era arms. After the operator replaced the ML arms, session 2 reached 1.2716 with four unique blocks looped twice over eight layers. That closes 24% of the gap. The Modal workspace spend limit then stopped the session. This is the clearest case in which the Infinity Machine did not reach its target.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
section: 3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile
content: The final design uses 7.7 mW at the same clock and throughput, and is 77.7% lower in energy per MAC than the original RTL. It is also 55% smaller, with setup and hold slack of + 5.2 +5.2 and + 6.3 +6.3 ps. A same-run ablation attributes about 43 fJ of the last step to the ring buffer and 16 fJ to writing the weights in place. Two of the agents’ own observations shaped the search. The first was that the 64 input bits are the narrowest point of the pipeline, so it is cheaper to delay the activations than to register partial sums. The second was that flops, and the clock that drives them, dominate the power. The search also found negative results: a radix-4 Booth multiplier with activations encoded once per row was worse (300.8 fJ), and eight rows per stage would not close timing at 600 ps. One proposer declined to ship a 1.6% better variant because its hold slack was only + 0.197 +0.197 ps, reasoning that a gate failure on the private run would score zero.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
section: 3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile
content: This result has clear limits. ASAP7 is a predictive PDK, so these are modelled, not measured, energies. There is one flow, one clock and one synthetic workload distribution. The gate-level simulation is zero-delay, so glitch power is not counted. The ring-buffer design relies on the protocol’s weight load of exactly eight w_valid cycles per tile, which the testbench uses but which a different host could violate. The comparison is against the original RTL, not against a hand-optimised design. The operator built the evaluator, wrote an “already measured” table between sessions, corrected the score range twice, and reseeded session 2 with session 1’s best design (Section 4 ).

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: We pointed catalogue mode at TESS [ 33 ] light curves of about 17,000 stars: 9,779 director’s-discretionary targets and 7,474 M dwarfs within 40 pc observed only in full-frame images. Four sessions cost about $58. The referee was rewritten four times: twice to close loopholes that proposers exploited (Section 4 ), once after the operator’s manual vetting found blends, eclipsing binaries and aliases, and once to fix a cadence bug the operator found. The final referee accepts 47 of 60 known TOIs and 30 of 49 known FFI planets, and accepts none of 80 random fake claims. One candidate survives: G 249-11 (TIC 417732194), an M4.5 dwarf at 29 pc with a 3 ppt, 0.9 h transit-like signal at P = 5.307425 P=5.307425 d, which implies R p ≈ 1.6 ​ R ⊕ R_{p}\approx 1.6\,R_{\oplus} . An ephemeris fitted to two sectors predicted dips in two later sectors that were never used for selection, with p ≈ 0.002 p\approx 0.002 from 400 full-pipeline nulls [ 18 ] . That is about 3 ​ σ 3\sigma , and a bound eclipsing binary and a faint neighbour are not excluded, so we report a candidate, not a planet. An independent read-only reviewer agent caught a 1000-day error in the reference epoch and an independence error in the first vetting report.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: On the Einstein Arena [ 34 ] Sidon (4,5)-set problem, the Infinity Machine found 13 new sets tying the 4/7 record but none below it. The operator’s feasibility analysis (not the agent’s) shows that within the verifier’s range only n = 16 n=16 or n = 18 n=18 could beat 4/7. On the 51 × 51 51\times 51 Hadamard maximal-determinant problem, proposers established that the record [ 35 ] is a fixed point of every local method they tried. Their best alternative family ( ℤ 5 × ℤ 5 \mathbb{Z}_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{5} blocks) reaches 43.2310 against the record’s 43.3013. A further exhaustive argument ruling out one circulant family was again the operator’s. For the largest seven-qubit distance-two code ( 24 ≤ K ≤ 26 24\leq K\leq 26 [ 36 , 37 ] ), hundreds of restarts all land on one plateau per method. For four bases in ℂ 6 \mathbb{C}^{6} , every proposer did basin hopping around the known optimum [ 38 ] , and about 35,000 re-ascents returned to it. Where the published record is a robust optimum of random-restart search, the Infinity Machine did not improve it, and the useful output was a measured negative.

content: Table 4 summarises both runs. Both tied the record. In both, the scout’s selection reasoning was specific and checkable, the verifier survived its audit, and the final report declined to claim anything. Their near misses are informative but are not results: a network that leaves one input unsorted is not a sorting network. Four things went wrong.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: • A reversed score in run 2, missed by every check. The kernel’s minimising scorer gives score 1 at the first end of the task’s score range and 0 at the second. The scout wrote the range as 186 to 175, intending the opposite. As installed, the 186-comparator Batcher network scored 1.0, the record 0.455, and a record-beating 179 would have scored 0.364, below its parent. Kernel validation checked values but not the direction of the score. The auditor read the mapping as intended and reported 0.545 for the record. The reporter noticed the mismatch between 0.545 and 0.4545 but not its cause. No proposer shipped a larger network, so the outcome was unaffected. Had one found a 179, though, the bandit and the parent sampler would have treated it as a regression. Worse, the independent check and the report take the highest-scoring solution, so the 179 would have stayed in the bank unreported. The operator had made the same mistake on the chip task (Section 4 ). Validation should check that calibration cases with better values score higher.

section: The self-improvement gate rejected the one self-derived generation.
content: Graded by the self-improvement gate ($8.22, 57 minutes), the generation with these bullets scored 0.944 on held-in tasks against the incumbent’s 0.927, and 1.000 on held-out tasks against 1.000. Its cost was 2.02 times the incumbent’s, above the gate’s 1.5 limit, so it was rejected . The bullets made the agent run more experiments, which bought a small gain at twice the spend. No meta-agent proposal ran in that session, because the single iteration was spent validating this pending candidate; in an earlier smoke run the meta agent proposed no change. Every discovery result in Section 3 was therefore produced by the initial genome. The gate behaved as designed. Whether 2 × 2\times the cost for + 0.017 +0.017 is worth it is a policy question for a human, and with one seed the gain is within noise. We do not yet have evidence that the Infinity Machine improves itself on these problems.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
section: Strategy arms mattered, but a human chose them.
content: Over the first 16 runs the bandit’s data were unambiguous. Data structure earned a mean reward of 0.4 over 5 pulls, and every other arm earned 0 over 11. Conservative and robust/simple pulls on a record seed were pure no-ops: proposers shipped the seed unchanged, at about $0.8 in total. The bandit would have learned to avoid those arms eventually, but on problems with only 4–6 pulls per session it could not. The operator replaced the arms by hand for math and ML (and wrote the astronomy arms). For math (structured construction and the others), the first session afterwards produced χ ⁡ ( | T ⟩ ⊗ 7 ) ≤ 10 \chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10 . For ML (architecture family, parameter sharing and the others), the next session produced the looped model. Under the rule that lessons must enter through the system’s own loops, these were kernel changes, not self-improvement, and we report them as such. A version of the Infinity Machine that proposed its own strategy arms through the gate is the obvious next step.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: A system that edits its own harness and runs code it wrote needs containment that does not rely on the model’s cooperation. The Infinity Machine enforces the following structurally, in the kernel.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: • Sandboxing. Every proposer and every scorer runs in a fresh container or Modal sandbox. Network is off by default, the root file system is read-only, and data volumes, where needed, are mounted read-only. Kernel code, private splits, scorers and credentials are never mounted, so an agent cannot read its hidden grade or change how it is graded.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: • Human gates and their machine replacement. A self-modification whose gain exceeds the anomaly threshold is parked for review instead of activated. Every generation can be rolled back. Outside autonomous mode, proposed evaluators are inert until a human approves them. In autonomous mode that approval is automatic only after three checks: kernel calibration on known cases, an adversarial audit whose exploits are replayed, and a blind independent re-check of the final result. The approval and its basis are logged. A verifier written by one agent is therefore never trusted on that agent’s word alone. In the first of the three autonomous runs, this chain rejected the first task.

content: What we observed is mostly in Section 4 . Proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and in two cases said so openly: once when asked for review risks (AdderBoard), and once in a notebook (TESS). We saw no attempt to read hidden splits or to escape a sandbox. However, unlike STOP [ 3 ] , we did not audit traces systematically for such attempts, so this is an absence of observed incidents, not a measured rate. The main residual risk is not the agent but the harness: our private splits were only as good as the verifiers the operator wrote, and two of them were exploitable for a full iteration before they were fixed.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: FunSearch [ 2 ] evolved short Python functions scored by an evaluator. AlphaEvolve [ 1 ] scaled this to whole files, rich prompts and many problems, and Georgiev et al. [ 39 ] applied it to 67 problems in mathematical analysis, geometry and combinatorics. ShinkaEvolve [ 40 ] and Hyra [ 10 ] are open, sample-efficient variants; Hyra uses agentic proposers and lets the evaluator evolve. AIDE [ 41 ] searches over ML code with a tree of drafts. The Infinity Machine shares their reliance on automatic evaluation but differs in kind: its proposals are hour-long agent runs rather than sampled programs, it also searches open-endedly in real data, and its own harness is subject to gated self-modification.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: STOP [ 3 ] improved its own scaffolding program. The Darwin Gödel Machine [ 4 ] evolved coding agents with an archive and documented reward hacking of its own tests. Hyperagents [ 5 ] made the meta agent editable. AIDE 2 [ 6 ] rewrote a research agent’s harness under a private grade it never sees. Prime Agent [ 42 ] and Continual Harness [ 43 ] keep typed supplemental state with rollback by ID, building on recursive language models [ 44 ] . ACE [ 11 ] curates an itemised playbook. Weng [ 9 ] surveys harness engineering for self-improvement. The Infinity Machine combines an editable meta agent, an archive, a cost-aware gate and an ACE-style playbook, and adds an honest report that, so far, its discovery results come from the unmodified genome.

content: Two others implemented directions the notes listed as untried: a symmetric dictionary instead of annealing over all stabilizer states (stabilizer rank), and a beam over SWAP sequences instead of a greedy SWAP choice (SABRE). The public/private split and adversarially calibrated verifiers, not instructions, kept the outputs honest. The same idea carried over to autonomous mode. When an agent writes its own evaluator, the evaluator is trusted only after machine checks that a different agent and the kernel perform. In the first end-to-end run these checks caught a stale record that would otherwise have become a false discovery. The approach also carried over to hardware. With power measured from gate-level switching activity on a routed design, and correctness checked bit-exactly at both RTL and gate level, the proposers cut energy per MAC by 77.7% through architectural changes (dataflow, storage structure, clock gating, generated arithmetic) rather than tuning.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Self-improvement has not yet earned its name in our data. The one self-derived generation was rejected on cost, the most consequential harness changes were the operator’s, and cross-session memory ran through hand-edited notes. Where a record is a robust optimum of random-restart search (MUBs, Hadamard, the seven-qubit code), the Infinity Machine reproduced the record and produced negative evidence, not progress. Proposers sometimes found an object without understanding it, as with the product structure of the qutrit state. All three fully autonomous runs ended in ties with public records. The first scout chose a crowded problem, and the first run’s final round was wasted on conservative no-ops. Research arms and narrower goals in runs 2 and 3 produced real searches and near misses, but no improvement, and two proposers still declined to search. In run 2 the machine checks that replace human approval passed a task whose score was reversed. They test whether a verifier accepts the right objects, but not whether the score ranks them the right way round.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: All results come from a single operator, a single proposer model and one to three sessions per problem. There are no repeated seeds, ablations or matched-compute comparisons. Several problems were chosen because they looked search-shaped, so the success rate is not representative. The quantum results are lower bounds or explicit constructions with stated claim boundaries, not optimality results. The SABRE comparison is not compute-matched. The TESS candidate is unconfirmed. The accelerator result rests on a predictive PDK, one flow, one clock, one synthetic workload and zero-delay gate-level simulation, and it compares against the original RTL rather than a hand-optimised design. End-to-end autonomy has been demonstrated three times, all with null results, and in runs 2 and 3 the operator named the table to search. The fifteen operator-led campaigns that produced the results above were not run in autonomous mode, so none of their results is an autonomous end-to-end discovery.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: Next we plan to: run autonomous mode repeatedly with open goals, with a scout that also checks leaderboards and discussion threads before choosing, a validation step that checks the score’s direction on calibration cases, and a brief that forbids returning the parent without a search; repeat the accelerator task on a second PDK, at several clocks and workload seeds, with timing-annotated simulation; let the meta agent propose strategy arms and brief templates through the gate; replace operator-written “already measured” tables with consolidation output, and measure whether the next session does better; run matched A/B comparisons of gated generations on held-out problem families (imp@ k k [ 5 ] ); and add a reviewer round to every catalogue-mode session.

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The problems studied are in mathematics, quantum information, compilers, machine learning, astronomy and digital hardware design, and carry little direct potential for harm. The broader concern with self-improving agents is that they may optimise a proxy in unintended ways. We observed exactly this on a small scale (Section 4 ) and report every instance. All external claims went out under the author’s name after host-side verification, with AI involvement disclosed in each deposit, and none was posted by an agent. The TESS candidate is reported as unconfirmed, and no follow-up request was sent on the agent’s behalf.

content: For every published result, the Zenodo deposits contain the solution object, the verifier, the task text given to the agents, the agents’ notebooks and search code, and SHA-256 sums. Anyone can re-check the results without our harness. Appendix C lists every discovery session with its configuration and spend, Appendix D the strategy-arm texts, and Appendix F the gate configuration and the self-derived playbook. For each autonomous run, the session directory keeps every artefact: the goal, each scout round’s task, the validation reports, both audits with their exploit files and replay results, the automatic approval record, the search bank, the independent checker’s code and verdict, and the final report and claim. Appendix B summarises it. Model runs are not deterministic: rerunning a session will produce different proposals, and we report only one session sequence per problem. The model versions were Claude Sonnet 5.5 for proposers and Claude Opus 5.5 for the meta agent.

authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: The design is the LogikBench 8 × \times 8 weight-stationary INT8 systolic array (signed 8-bit activations and weights, 32-bit outputs) shipped as asap7/tpu with OpenROAD-flow-scripts [ 31 ] . A tile loads eight weight rows (one per w_valid cycle), streams activation rows, and returns each output row 15 cycles after its activation row. The host idles 2 ​ N − 1 = 15 2N-1=15 cycles between tiles. A candidate must keep the ports and this cycle-level protocol, so it computes 64 MACs per cycle at the fixed clock. There is no published record for this tile; the reference is the original RTL.

At 600 ps the power is 4.34 mW internal, 3.33 mW switching and 0.04 mW leakage (7.71 mW in total, against 34.66 mW). content: • Session 1, it00-p0. It removed the per-PE activation registers and broadcast each activation along its row, delaying row i i by 7 + i 7+i cycles at the input so no output de-skew is needed. It narrowed the partial sums to 16–19 bits per row (sign-extended at the output) and dropped datapath resets (346.9 fJ). It then added latch+AND clock gates per pipeline depth, enabled from the valid pipe derived from a_valid , and a w_valid gate for the weights (274.9 fJ). Flops fell from about 4,200 to about 2,300. A parallel run ( robust/simple , $1.81) instead wrote an explicit Baugh–Wooley multiplier with a 3:2 carry-save tree and a Brent–Kung adder, because Yosys maps + and * to Kogge–Stone structures (285.2 fJ, area 2,935).

title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: • Session 2, it02-p0. It replaced the activation shift chains (13 or 14 stages of 64 bits, every flop toggling every cycle) by a 13-entry ring buffer. Each entry is written once through its own latch+AND clock gate under a shared one-hot pointer, and read through an AND-OR mux into the valid-gated input register; rows 0–3 read with the pointer rotated by one (delay 13), rows 4–7 without (delay 14). It also replaced the shifting weight register by direct per-row writes, with one clock gate per row and a one-hot pointer that advances on w_valid . Result: 128.8 fJ. An ablation in the same run (ring buffer only) gave 144.6 fJ.

section: B.2 Choosing the goals of runs 2 and 3
content: Before runs 2 and 3, five research agents, directed by the operator, surveyed published tables of explicit, exactly checkable records for low current activity. They looked beyond quantum information. Their top picks were Brouwer’s mixed binary/ternary code tables (quiet since 2013), qutrit stabilizer-code gaps, sorting-network sizes for 25–40 inputs, real Grassmannian packings and ternary codes A 3 ​ ( n , d ) A_{3}(n,d) . They advised avoiding tables already worked by many agents: the V3R1T4S list, binary and constant-weight codes, most Einstein Arena problems and the QIQC zoo. The operator wrote one goal sentence for each of the first and third picks, naming the table and the improvement wanted, and asked the scout to choose the cell and confirm that it was current. Both jobs ran with 3 iterations, 2 parallel proposers, a $30 budget and the research math arms. The first launch of the pair collided on a session directory (Section 3.8 ) and was cancelled within a minute; the relaunches below are the runs reported.

content: (02:40–02:58, $2.03). It chose n = 31 n=31 : record 180 comparators in 14 layers, bounds 141 ≤ S ⁡ ( 31 ) ≤ 180 141\leq S(31)\leq 180 , table source “Batcher odd-even merge”, with no 31-input size change since the 2017 draft (page dated 10 October 2026). Its reason was that the entry is the 32-input merge network minus one wire, never improved by search, while the entries for n = 28 n=28 –30 had been improved beyond the wire-removal bound. Before choosing, it ran its own wire-removal beam search from all record networks for n = 25 n=25 –40; this beat no entry (for n = 30 n=30 it gave 173 against the record 172). The verifier is an exact check of all 2 31 2^{31} binary inputs by bit-slicing (about 8–15 s). The seed is the record network. There were eight calibration cases. The three valid ones were the 186-comparator Batcher network, the record and the record plus a redundant comparator (181). The five invalid ones were an index out of range, a malformed list, the record with one comparator dropped, a reversed comparator and a 30-input network. Scoring was minimised over the range 186 to 175, which in the kernel’s convention is reversed (Section 3.8 ).

authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
content: (02:40–03:27, $4.66). It chose N ⁡ ( 4 , 5 , 3 ) N(4,5,3) : words in { 0 , 1 } 4 × { 0 , 1 , 2 } 5 \{0,1\}^{4}\times\{0,1,2\}^{5} (3,888 in all) at mixed Hamming distance at least 3, with bounds 186–216. The lower bound dates from Brouwer, Hämäläinen, Östergård and Sloane (1998), and the upper bound 216 is 3 ​ N ​ ( 4 , 4 , 3 ) 3N(4,4,3) . Its reasons were the 16% gap and the fact that neighbouring cells, among them N ⁡ ( 3 , 5 , 3 ) N(3,5,3) , N ⁡ ( 5 , 5 , 3 ) N(5,5,3) , N ⁡ ( 3 , 6 , 3 ) N(3,6,3) and N ⁡ ( 4 , 7 , 3 ) N(4,7,3) , were improved by forum posters in 2010–2013 while this one was not. It fetched the page (Last-Modified 17 October 2026); its arXiv search was blocked by HTTP 429. It wrote coset.c , a clique search over unions of cosets of an additive subgroup. This reproduced 186 as 62 cosets of ⟨ ( 0000 | 10101 ) ⟩ \langle(0000|10101)\rangle in seconds, along with other table entries ( N ⁡ ( 7 , 3 , 3 ) = 192 N(7,3,3)=192 , N ⁡ ( 8 , 3 , 3 ) = 384 N(8,3,3)=384 , N ⁡ ( 5 , 6 , 5 ) = 96 N(5,6,5)=96 , N ⁡ ( 6 , 5 , 5 ) = 66 N(6,5,5)=66 ). Its own searches over subgroup orders 2, 3, 4, 6 and 9 and a 16k-step LNS did not beat 186. There were twelve calibration cases. Four were valid: the record, a 150-word subcode, the same code in string format and a single word. Eight were invalid: a binary symbol 2, a duplicate, an empty code, float symbols, a near miss at distance 1, the record plus a conflicting 187th word, the wrong cell and the wrong length. Scoring was maximised over 150–188, so the record scores 0.947 (correct direction).

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
section: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
content: We introduce ExCal , a normal-only multivariate time series anomaly detector that combines raw state retrieval, a signal/derivative subspace, and robust statistics across temporal scales. Each expert map receives a high normality floor from the training prefix. During scoring, positive excess is retained, attenuated for broadly firing maps, and combined with a small rank term. The method fits reference memories and projections without gradient optimization or anomaly labels. Prevalence and ranks depend on the complete scored sequence, making inference batch and transductive rather than online. On 180 series from 17 TSB-AD-M families, ExCal obtains AUC-PR 0.421 ± 0.37 0.421\pm 0.37 and VUS-PR 0.452 ± 0.37 0.452\pm 0.37 over three seeds, ranking second among 24 methods. Holm-adjusted paired tests detect no significant difference from AxonAD or StreamVAE, which are the two leading non-pretrained methods on TSB-AD-M, on either primary metric, while finding significant positive differences against the other 21 baselines. A separate single-run probe over three series measures median model-wrapper time of 0.0662 0.0662 s. Ablations associate the largest primary-metric changes with raw retrieval and excess-magnitude preservation. The evaluated score is decomposable by expert, but its diagnostic utility and online suitability remain untested.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: Multivariate telemetry may deviate through unusual operating points, broken cross-channel relations, changes in local dynamics, or events visible only at particular durations. With only a normal training prefix, no single representation is assured to expose all of these departures. Neural forecasting, reconstruction, and attention methods offer expressive alternatives [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , but require optimization and architecture choices. Classical approaches offer transparent normality tests based on isolation, density, projection, or retrieval [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Combining these heterogeneous signals remains a calibration problem because their score scales differ.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: We propose ExCal ( Ex cess Cal ibration), which derives temporal scales and normality references from the prefix, evaluates absolute raw state, derivative-aware subspace, and multiscale statistic maps, and combines their standardized excess above expert-specific floors. Prevalence damping attenuates maps firing broadly over the scored sequence, and a small rank term preserves sub-floor ordering. An optional context-centered shape branch is evaluated but excluded from the base configuration. Fig. 1 illustrates map calibration and the resulting score, while Fig. 2 details the architecture.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: ExCal is optimization-free: it performs no gradient updates or neural learning, but fits PCA projections, reference banks, and quantiles. The primitives are established. The contribution lies in their explicit excess-preserving calibration and fusion, evaluated using TSB-AD-M [ 17 ] , range-aware metrics [ 18 ] , ablations, paired tests, seed repeats, and a small timing probe. The study does not isolate causal component effects or establish generalization beyond this benchmark.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: Forecasting and reconstruction methods infer anomaly evidence from the discrepancy between an observed sequence and a learned normal model. LSTM predictors use future prediction error [ 1 ] . Donut models seasonal web-service KPIs with a variational autoencoder [ 2 ] , whereas OmniAnomaly and sequential variational models represent stochastic dynamics and temporal smoothness [ 3 , 4 ] . USAD combines autoencoding with adversarial training [ 5 ] . TranAD uses transformer encoders, self-conditioning, and adversarial learning for multivariate detection [ 6 ] .

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: Attention-based methods explicitly model temporal interactions. Anomaly Transformer uses association discrepancy to distinguish anomalous points [ 7 ] . TimesNet discovers multiple periods and maps one-dimensional variation into a two-dimensional representation [ 8 ] . AxonAD models causal attention-query dynamics [ 19 ] , and STREAM-VAE separates slow and fast telemetry dynamics with dual-path variational routing [ 20 ] . ExCal shares the objective of covering multiple temporal mechanisms, but replaces end-to-end learned fusion with explicit normality tests and calibration on the training prefix.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: Isolation-based, density-based, histogram-based, and copula-based detectors offer simple alternatives to iterative neural training [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Robust principal component analysis (PCA) provides a low-rank model that tolerates sparse corruption [ 14 ] . K-means and nearest-neighbor constructions supply additional geometric views of normal data [ 21 , 15 ] . PyOD exposes many such detectors through a common interface [ 22 ] . ExCal follows the same transparent geometric spirit but applies its references to overlapping temporal windows and explicitly combines absolute state, derivatives, and local statistics.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: The TSB-AD benchmark emphasizes that aggregate anomaly-detection results depend on dataset heterogeneity, class imbalance, and the evaluation protocol [ 17 ] . Area under the precision–recall curve (AUC-PR) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) evaluate score ordering without selecting one threshold, while volume under the surface for precision–recall (VUS-PR) and receiver operating characteristic (VUS-ROC) extend this idea to range-aware behavior across a volume of parameters [ 18 ] . We therefore treat AUC-PR and VUS-PR as the primary metrics and use the remaining reported measures as complementary diagnostics.

content: Both f i f_{i} and rank01 \operatorname{rank01} are statistics of the complete scored sequence, which under the benchmark protocol includes the training prefix. The final score is therefore a batch, transductive quantity rather than an online or causal one: the score at time t t depends on the distribution of map values over the entire sequence being scored, and identical points embedded in different scored sequences can receive different scores. All normal-reference quantities (normalization statistics, temporal scale, exemplar banks, subspace, statistic references, and floors) remain prefix-only. Because the prevalence and rank terms read only the unlabeled input sequence, and because every semisupervised method in the benchmark scores the same complete sequence, this is a statement about the deployment form of the detector rather than label leakage in the comparison. content: We report per-dataset deltas between ExCal and selected baselines in addition to aggregate means. The intervals in Table V are nonparametric 95% bootstrap intervals for the mean delta, based on 10,000 resamples of the 180 dataset-level seed means and a fixed bootstrap generator seed of 2026. The win–loss counts and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon values use the same paired dataset-level observations. The bootstrap interval describes uncertainty around the arithmetic mean effect. The Wilcoxon test evaluates the signed-rank distribution. A skewed set of differences can therefore produce a positive mean without a significant majority-dataset advantage. The two viewpoints differ concretely for PaAno_PAI on AUC-PR: the bootstrap interval contains zero, while the adjusted Wilcoxon p p -value is 0.042 0.042 . The interval reflects uncertainty in the mean difference, whereas the test reflects the signed ranks, which favor ExCal on 106 of 180 datasets.

content: ExCal has a positive mean delta relative to StreamVAE, PaAno_PAI, USAD, CNN, and AnomalyTransformer on both primary metrics. The interval for the AxonAD comparison contains zero on both metrics, and the paired tests are nonsignificant. These results do not establish equivalence. The StreamVAE intervals are positive even though ExCal wins on fewer datasets than it loses. This indicates a skewed effect distribution in which a smaller number of larger gains outweigh more numerous smaller losses. The Wilcoxon test remains nonsignificant after correction, which does not establish equivalence. Against AnomalyTransformer, ExCal has higher scores on 148 of 180 datasets for AUC-PR and 145 for VUS-PR, with positive mean deltas and small adjusted p p -values.

authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: The second-place aggregate ranking coexists with heterogeneous family results and modest Kendall’s W W values. Corrected tests do not distinguish ExCal from AxonAD or StreamVAE on either primary metric. The score decomposition identifies contributing normality maps, not physical root causes. Batch prevalence and rank statistics and a three-series, single-run timing probe preclude claims of online or real-time readiness.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: The evaluation covers one TSB-AD-M split, three seeds, and correlated performance metrics. The timing probe includes three series with one measured repetition and excludes loading, metrics, memory, and energy. A clean normal prefix is assumed. Contamination can alter reference banks and floors, while legitimate regime changes can trigger broad excess. A single detected period may miss nonstationary or multiperiodic structure. Moreover, batch prevalence and rank normalization change a point’s score when the surrounding sequence changes, so a causal deployment variant remains unevaluated. Score decomposition has not been tested for operator diagnosis, and benchmark F1 values do not establish deployment thresholds. Relevant next steps include independent telemetry datasets, contamination studies, causal fusion references, threshold and detection-delay evaluation, and larger resource studies.

title: ExCal: Optimization-Free Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Excess Calibration
authors: Kadir-Kaan Özer, René Ebeling, Markus Enzweiler
content: ExCal combines prefix-fitted raw retrieval, signal/derivative subspace residuals, and multiscale robust statistics through magnitude-preserving excess fusion without gradient optimization. Prevalence and rank terms make its inference batch and transductive. Across 180 TSB-AD-M series, the detector ranks second among 24 methods on AUC-PR and VUS-PR, although paired tests find no significant difference from AxonAD or StreamVAE. Ablations associate the largest score changes with raw retrieval and magnitude-preserving fusion. The runtime probe is preliminary, and operational performance and causal scoring remain untested.
