title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
content: Multi-fidelity training, which combines abundant low-fidelity data with scarce high-fidelity labels, is increasingly common in atomistic modeling, but its effect on predictive uncertainty remains largely unexplored. We investigate this question using deep ensembles of mean–variance MACE models trained on ANI-1x, contrasting high-fidelity training from scratch with low-fidelity pretraining followed by fine-tuning. We characterize aleatoric, epistemic, and total uncertainty throughout training and under two distribution shifts: unseen molecular systems and higher-energy configurations. We find that pretraining reduces prediction error and improves uncertainty-based ranking across all test sets, but does not yield well-calibrated predictive variances; calibration deteriorates more severely under energy extrapolation. Training-dynamics analysis localizes most of this calibration degradation to high-fidelity optimization, during which the learned aleatoric variance becomes overconfident on held-out data. Moreover, multi-fidelity fine-tuning produces a more effective uncertainty-based acquisition function than high-fidelity training from scratch. These findings show that uncertainty ranking and calibration capture distinct properties and must be assessed separately in multi-fidelity atomistic models, especially under extrapolation.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential in atomistic machine learning, where models are routinely deployed beyond their training distribution, for instance in active learning and molecular dynamics ( Podryabinkin and Shapeev, 2017 ; Unke et al., 2021 ; Perego and Bonati, 2024 ) . Recent work has investigated ensembles, calibration and the decomposition of predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components for atomistic models ( Valdenegro-Toro and Mori, 2022 ; Tan et al., 2023 ; Busk et al., 2023 ; Dai et al., 2025 ; Grasselli et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, multi-fidelity ( Musil et al., 2019 ; Tran et al., 2020 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Gardner et al., 2025 ; Ko and Ong, 2025 ) and transfer learning ( Falk et al., 2023 ; Rocken and Zavadlav, 2025 ; Novelli et al., 2025 ; Radova et al., 2025 ) have emerged as practical strategies for combining abundant low-fidelity (LF) data with scarce high-fidelity (HF) labels, typically obtained at different levels of electronic-structure theory ( Smith et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Zaverkin et al., 2023 ) . Yet, how multi-fidelity training shapes predictive uncertainty remains largely unexplored.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: In standard statistical settings, the aleatoric–epistemic decomposition separates irreducible data noise from uncertainty about the model ( Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006 ; Kendall and Gal, 2017 ) . Its interpretation is less straightforward in atomistic modeling, where reference energies are deterministic and data coverage is highly structured. Moreover, uncertainty is commonly evaluated only at convergence and through a single score, conflating two distinct properties: whether uncertainty correctly ranks configurations by prediction error, as required for acquisition and filtering, and whether its magnitude matches the error, i.e. whether the error bars are calibrated ( Kuleshov et al., 2018 ; Rasmussen et al., 2023 ) . These properties need not evolve together across fidelity changes, distribution shifts, or training stages. The latter is particularly relevant in practice because deployment ultimately relies on a checkpoint selected during training.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Contributions. Using ANI-1x data ( Smith et al., 2020 ) , with DFT as low fidelity and CCSD(T)/CBS as high fidelity, we compare LF-only, HF-only and pretrain-then-fine-tune (LF → \rightarrow HF) training of mean–variance MACE ensembles. We evaluate two distribution shifts: unseen molecular systems and higher-energy configurations of known systems. Across five independent data splits, we follow aleatoric (AU), epistemic (EU) and total uncertainty (TU) throughout training. Our study uses theoretically grounded mean–variance deep ensembles ( Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017 ; Kendall and Gal, 2017 ) and, to our knowledge, provides the first systematic analysis of how multi-fidelity training affects uncertainty dynamics. We find that: (i) LF pretraining consistently improves predictive accuracy and the error ranking induced by AU, EU and TU across all test sets, but does not always improve calibration ; (ii) unlike system shift, energy extrapolation decouples ranking from calibration: models rank high-energy errors more effectively while underestimating their magnitude more severely, and in-domain isotonic recalibration does not repair this; (iii) along training, most of the calibration is lost in the HF stage in both training protocols, and the loss emerges faster after pretraining: AU becomes markedly overconfident on unseen data, whereas EU mitigates the resulting degradation in TU; (iv) pretraining makes uncertainty a better guide for data acquisition: despite starting from higher accuracy, the pretrained model benefits more from uncertainty-guided selection than a model trained from scratch. We release splits, protocols, and evaluation code at https://github.com/matteotolloso/mace . Related work is reviewed in Appendix A .

content: For a structure 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , defined by its atomic species and positions, with reference energy y y , predictive uncertainty quantifies the reliability of a prediction y ^ ​ ( 𝐱 ) \hat{y}(\mathbf{x}) before computing y y . It is represented by the predictive distribution p ⁡ ( y | 𝐱 , 𝒟 ) p(y|\mathbf{x},\mathcal{D}) conditioned on training data 𝒟 \mathcal{D} ( Murphy, 2012 ) , and it is commonly decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components ( Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ) . Epistemic uncertainty captures uncertainty in the predictor, arising from limited data coverage, model misspecification, or extrapolation, and is in principle reducible with additional data. Aleatoric uncertainty is conventionally associated with irreducible observation noise. However, since reference energies of a given electronic-structure method are deterministic ( Helgaker et al., 2013 ) , we instead interpret it operationally as input-dependent residual variability, or configuration-dependent difficulty. Whether the two terms actually behave as irreducible and reducible uncertainty is tested in Section 4.2 .

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Data and fidelities. All experiments use the ANI-1x data set ( Smith et al., 2020 ) , which provides molecular configurations labelled at several levels of theory. The low-fidelity (LF) target is the ω \omega B97x/def2-TZVPP DFT energy and the high-fidelity (HF) target is the CCSD(T)/CBS coupled-cluster energy, which is available for far fewer configurations (the ANI-1ccx subset ( Smith et al., 2019 ) ). Only energies are used. Each split has 50,000 DFT and 5,000 CC training configurations, 10,000 DFT and 1,000 CC validation configurations, and 5,000 CC configurations per test set; CC configurations are a subset of the DFT ones.

content: Distribution shifts. The system-level shift holds out 40% of the molecular systems entirely: System-ID tests on unseen configurations of the training systems, System-OOD on the held-out systems (Appendix D ). The energy-based shift ranks the configurations of every system by their relative DFT energy, with within-system quantile q s ​ ( x ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q_{s}(x)\in[0,1] . Configurations with q s ≤ 0.5 q_{s}\leq 0.5 are used for training, validation and the Energy-ID test, configurations with q s ≥ 0.55 q_{s}\geq 0.55 form the Energy-OOD test, and the band in between is discarded (Appendix E ).

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Training protocols. LF-only models are trained on DFT energies and HF-only models on CC energies, both from scratch for 300 epochs. LF → \rightarrow HF models are LF-only models fine-tuned on CC energies for 100 epochs with a tenfold smaller learning rate; every fine-tuned member starts from the LF-only member with the same split and seed. All protocols use the Gaussian NLL, the same architecture and M = 10 M=10 ensemble members (Appendix F ). The checkpoint of each member is selected by its validation NLL; test sets are never used for selection. This selection criterion retains HF-only members after 30–111 of 300 epochs and LF → \rightarrow HF members after one to three fine-tuning epochs (Appendix F ).

content: Replication and statistics. The pipeline, from data splitting to ensemble training, is repeated on five independent dataset splits, the unit of replication. Metrics are computed within a split from its ten-member ensemble and summarized by the five-split mean with a two-sided 95% Student-t interval (4 degrees of freedom); ENCE, RMSE and ratios use geometric means with log-space intervals.

content: Metrics. Both errors and uncertainties are normalized per atom, i.e. energies are divided by the number of atoms and variances by the square of the number of atoms. Accuracy is the RMSE of the ensemble mean. Ranking is measured by the area under the sparsification error curve (AUSE) ( Lind et al., 2024 ) , which compares discarding configurations by uncertainty with discarding them by their true error and rewards identifying the largest errors (lower is better); calibration by the expected normalized calibration error (ENCE) ( Levi et al., 2022 ) , 1 B ​ ∑ b | MV b − MSE b | / MV b \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}|\mathrm{MV}_{b}-\mathrm{MSE}_{b}|/\mathrm{MV}_{b} over B = 15 B=15 equal-count bins of predicted variance, with mean variance MV b \mathrm{MV}_{b} and mean squared error MSE b \mathrm{MSE}_{b} (Appendix C ). A bin where the variance overestimates the error contributes less than one, so ENCE above one can only come from overconfident bins. Note that, because TU is the predictive variance and AU and EU are its two components, the three cannot all match the magnitude of the error at once: calibration is expected of TU, while the ENCE of AU and EU only shows how much of the error each part accounts for. Our figures therefore highlight TU when showing calibration. All metrics exclude the handful of Energy-OOD configurations (13–16 of 5,000 per split) that are compressed below any interatomic distance seen in training (Appendix G ).

We then examine the full multi-fidelity training trajectory (Section 4.2 ) and compare its high-fidelity stage with HF-only training (Section 4.3 ). Finally, we present a small acquisition experiment (Section 4.4 ). All results are replicated over five data splits; figures show 95% intervals, and the complete set of metrics, reliability diagrams and training curves is in Appendices I and H .

section: 4.1 Pretraining improves ranking but not always calibration
content: Figure 2 compares the HF-only and multi-fidelity training. As expected, pretraining reduces the prediction error (RMSE), most strongly in domain but also out of domain. Instead, the other metrics reveal a different behavior of the uncertainty components. On the one hand, pretraining consistently improves ranking (AUSE) (panel b): across all three signals and on all four test sets, pretrained ensembles order prediction errors more effectively than ensembles trained only on HF data. Notably, multi-fidelity training reshapes the uncertainty decomposition rather than merely improving prediction accuracy. Indeed, there is a change in the ranking capabilities of the individual components: in HF-only, EU is the weakest ranking signal on every test set; with pretraining, EU ranks as well as or better than AU on three of the four test sets and approaches the ranking quality of total predictive uncertainty (see also Appendix I.2 ).

content: By contrast, pretraining has a mixed effect on calibration (ENCE; panel c). The relevant uncertainty (TU) is slightly better calibrated after pretraining in domain and on unseen systems, but substantially worse on Energy-OOD. Its components also diverge: EU improves across all test sets, while AU deteriorates. Thus, pretraining lowers error and improves ranking, but does not necessarily produce uncertainties with the correct magnitude.

section: 4.1 Pretraining improves ranking but not always calibration
content: Notably, we find that the relationship between ranking and calibration depends critically on the type of distribution shift. To highlight this, Figure 3 places each test set in the calibration–ranking plane and connects every in-domain result to its out-of-domain counterpart. Under system shift, moving from ID to unseen molecular systems improves ranking with little change in calibration. Under energy shift, however, where OOD means higher-energy configurations, ranking improves while calibration error increases several-fold: for TU, by approximately 4 × 4\times with HF-only training and 7 × 7\times with LF → \rightarrow HF. The Energy-OOD behavior in Figure 2 c is therefore not specific to pretraining. Both protocols rank high-energy errors better than in-domain errors, yet underestimate them more severely. In other words, the models largely identify which high-energy configurations will incur larger errors, since those errors are larger and easier to order, but not by how much . Ranking and calibration can therefore move in opposite directions along some extrapolation axes, and isotonic recalibration fitted in domain does not repair this (Appendix I.3 ).

authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.2 Uncertainty signals evolve differently during training
content: To better understand how uncertainty components behave in different training schemes, we examine their evolution over the course of training. Figure 4 follows the full LF → \rightarrow HF trajectory on the model’s own training data (a, b), the ID test set (c, d) and the OOD test set (e, f). On the training set, ranking changes little during DFT pretraining and improves markedly during CC fine-tuning (panel a) while the calibration of TU remains stable along the training epochs (panel b). HF-only models behave the same way on their training data (Appendix H ).

authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.2 Uncertainty signals evolve differently during training
content: On the ID test set, ranking performance improves for all three uncertainty signals during pretraining (panel c). The change from the low- to the high-fidelity target produces a sharp discontinuity; during the subsequent fine-tuning stage, the ranking performance of EU and TU recovers, whereas that of AU changes little. Calibration follows the opposite trend (panel d): TU becomes better calibrated during pretraining but progressively less calibrated during fine-tuning. This deterioration is driven primarily by the aleatoric component, whose calibration error increases by approximately two orders of magnitude over the fine-tuning stage.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.2 Uncertainty signals evolve differently during training
content: A similar ranking behavior is observed on the OOD test sets (panel e): ranking improves during pretraining under both distribution shifts and approaches a plateau during fine-tuning. The evolution of ENCE, however, depends on the type of shift (panel f). During pretraining, TU remains reasonably well calibrated on unseen molecular systems but progressively drifts on higher-energy configurations. Once fine-tuning begins, its calibration error increases under both shifts. However, the two uncertainty components behave differently: the calibration error associated with EU remains comparatively stable and ends near its pretraining level, whereas AU becomes strongly overconfident, with its predicted variance falling one to two orders of magnitude below the squared prediction error. The evolving balance between the two components is examined in Appendix H.1 . Although the poor reliability of aleatoric uncertainty under distribution shift is well documented ( Valdenegro-Toro and Mori, 2022 ) , its deterioration on the ID test set indicates that the effect is also associated with high-fidelity training and is accelerated by pretraining (Section 4.3 ). A plausible explanation is that the variance head follows the shrinking residuals of the training configurations and transfers these small variance estimates to held-out configurations whose errors have not decreased, a known failure mode of mean–variance training ( Nix and Weigend, 1994 ; Seitzer et al., 2022 ) . Because the reference energies are deterministic, this behavior suggests that the aleatoric term acts less like irreducible noise and more like a reducible estimate of in-sample residual difficulty.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.3 Pretraining speeds up both the gain in ranking and the loss of calibration
content: Having examined the full training dynamics of LF → \rightarrow HF, we now compare its high-fidelity stage with HF-only training (Figure 5 ), focusing on out-of-distribution performance. Under both distribution shifts and for all three uncertainty signals, the LF → \rightarrow HF models achieve a lower AUSE than the HF-only ones already from the first epoch. For both protocols, AUSE then decreases and levels off over the course of high-fidelity training.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.3 Pretraining speeds up both the gain in ranking and the loss of calibration
content: Calibration follows a different trajectory (panels c and d). For HF-only training, ENCE initially decreases before increasing again, whereas for LF → \rightarrow HF it is lowest near the beginning of the high-fidelity stage and then grows with fine-tuning. As observed above, this deterioration is driven primarily by the aleatoric component. Pretraining therefore does not appear to cause the degradation, but it accelerates it considerably: within 100 fine-tuning epochs, the AU ENCE reaches about 80 80 on System-OOD and 200 200 on Energy-OOD, compared with about 14 14 and 70 70 , respectively, after 300 epochs of HF-only training. The epistemic component behaves differently: its calibration error ends close to or below its initial value in all four settings, limiting the deterioration of total uncertainty relative to that of the aleatoric component. Overall, these results show that uncertainty ranking and calibration follow distinct, partially decoupled trajectories during training: ranking can continue to improve even as calibration deteriorates. Checkpoint selection should therefore not rely on prediction error alone, but should jointly monitor accuracy, uncertainty ranking, and calibration throughout training.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: 4.4 Pretrained uncertainty estimates improve single-round acquisition
content: Finally, we compare single- and multi-fidelity training in a setting where uncertainty is used to acquire new data. We perform a single acquisition round on Energy-OOD, selecting 500 configurations either at random or according to the highest AU, EU, or TU scores. After adding the corresponding high-fidelity labels to the training set, each model continues training and is evaluated on a disjoint held-out set (Appendix J ). All uncertainty-based acquisition strategies outperform random selection (Figure 6 a). However, all three uncertainty signals yield larger improvements for the pretrained ensembles than for those trained only on high-fidelity data: relative to random selection, their RMSE decreases by about 2.3 2.3 – 2.5 2.5 meV/atom, compared with 0.8 0.8 – 1.6 1.6 meV/atom for HF-only training. This is notable because the pretrained ensemble is already more accurate before acquisition, with an RMSE of about 59 59 meV/atom on the held-out set compared with 75 75 meV/atom for the HF-only ensemble, yet it benefits more from uncertainty-guided selection. The two protocols select configurations with similar energy-quantile distributions (Figure 6 b), indicating that the larger improvement after pretraining cannot be explained simply by selecting systematically higher-energy configurations. Instead, it suggests that pretraining produces a more informative uncertainty-based acquisition function within comparable energy ranges.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: We studied how low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning shapes the ranking, calibration, and decomposition of predictive uncertainty in atomistic models. Low-fidelity pretraining improves predictive accuracy and the error ranking for every uncertainty signal across all test sets, but does not consistently improve total uncertainty calibration. It also changes the uncertainty decomposition: without pretraining, the epistemic component is the weakest ranking signal; after pretraining it approaches total uncertainty on three of the four test sets ( RQ1 ). Under both shifts, errors are ranked better out-of-domain than in-domain, whereas only energy extrapolation degrades calibration ( RQ2 ). Along training, most calibration loss arises during the high-fidelity stage under both protocols, and develops faster after pretraining: aleatoric uncertainty remains conservative on the training data but becomes strongly overconfident on unseen configurations, while epistemic uncertainty mitigates the degradation of total uncertainty ( RQ3 ). Finally, pretrained ensembles yield more effective uncertainty-based acquisition functions than HF-only models ( RQ4 ).

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: These findings lead to clear practical implications. Ranking and calibration should be evaluated separately, and total uncertainty calibration should be monitored on held-out data throughout training because it may deteriorate even as ranking improves. Checkpoint selection should therefore account for uncertainty ranking and calibration in addition to prediction error. Aleatoric estimates obtained after training on scarce high-fidelity data require particular caution on unseen configurations, and in-domain recalibration should be validated explicitly before use under extrapolation (Appendix I.3 ). Although our analysis is limited to energy prediction, one uncertainty estimator, and a single acquisition setting (Appendix K ), it establishes a broader conclusion: uncertainty in multi-fidelity atomistic models is not a static property, with its ranking, calibration, and decomposition changing across fidelity transitions, distribution shifts, and training stages.

content: Recent surveys and perspectives provide broad overviews of the uncertainty quantification (UQ) field, covering Bayesian methods, ensembles, calibration strategies, active learning, and the relationship between uncertainty, dataset composition, transferability, and model robustness ( Dai et al., 2025 ; Grasselli et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) . These works highlight that benchmarking and interpretation of UQ methods remain open challenges, especially in transfer and multi-fidelity settings.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: A large body of work has focused on practical uncertainty estimators for neural network potentials. Ensemble-based methods remain among the most widely used and robust approaches. For instance, Tan et al. (2023) compare ensembles against single-model uncertainty methods such as mean-variance estimation, evidential regression, and Gaussian mixture models, finding that no method uniformly dominates across datasets and metrics, while ensembles remain strong for robustness and generalization. Other work has proposed more efficient ensemble variants, including multi-headed architectures, committee models, shallow or last-layer ensembles, and shared-representation ensembles, to reduce computational cost while retaining useful uncertainty estimates ( Carrete et al., 2023 ; Kellner and Ceriotti, 2024 ; Beck et al., 2025 ) .

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Several works have specifically addressed calibration and uncertainty decomposition in atomistic models. Busk et al. (2023) propose a framework for calibrated aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in graph neural network potentials, using deep ensembles to decompose total uncertainty and post-hoc recalibration to improve agreement between predicted uncertainty and observed error. More generally, Valdenegro-Toro and Mori (2022) study disentangled aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty across different UQ methods, showing that the interaction between these components can be non-trivial, that aleatoric uncertainty may become unreliable under distribution shift, and that ensembles provide the most consistent decomposition. In molecular property prediction, Heid et al. (2023) further analyze uncertainty sources by separating epistemic uncertainty into bias and variance contributions, showing that different sources of error dominate depending on noise level, dataset size, model architecture, and representation.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: A related line of work studies multi-fidelity learning in atomistic modeling. Gardner et al. (2025) investigate multi-fidelity training strategies for atomistic models, including pretraining–fine-tuning and multi-headed training, showing that fine-tuning can improve accuracy but that learned representations may remain method-specific, while multi-headed models can learn more method-agnostic representations across fidelities. More broadly, multi-fidelity UQ has been studied in surrogate modeling and materials design, often using Gaussian process models to combine information across fidelity levels while quantifying predictive confidence ( Tran et al., 2020 ) .

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Finally, the interpretation of uncertainty depends strongly on the evaluation metric. Rasmussen et al. (2023) ; Lind et al. (2024) analyze common regression UQ metrics, including AUSE, calibration error, Spearman correlation, and NLL, showing that they capture different properties and can lead to different conclusions.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Overall, existing work has made substantial progress on uncertainty estimation for atomistic models, uncertainty decomposition, calibration, efficient ensemble methods, and multi-fidelity training. However, these directions have largely been studied separately. In contrast, our work provides a controlled empirical analysis of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty across multi-fidelity training regimes, system-level and energy-based distribution shifts, and training dynamics. This allows us to study not only whether uncertainty is accurate at convergence, but also how its components evolve and whether they can serve as diagnostic signals for model behavior under changing fidelity and data regimes.

Two known properties of the estimator matter for our results ( Skafte et al., 2019 ; Seitzer et al., 2022 ; Stirn et al., 2023 ; Sluijterman et al., 2024 ) . First, the head is fitted to training residuals, which shrink as the network fits its training set, so on unseen configurations it can inherit the scale of the training error rather than that of the test error; this is the behavior of AU observed in Sections 4.2 and 4.3 . Second, the gradient with respect to the mean is weighted by 1 / σ 2 1/\sigma^{2} , so configurations that the head already deems easy dominate the fit of the mean ( Seitzer et al., 2022 ) . We use the plain Gaussian NLL, without the modifications proposed in these works.

authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Models are trained on the Gaussian NLL of the energy, with the term of each configuration divided by its number of atoms, using Adam (AMSGrad), batch size 64, weight decay 5 ⋅ 10 − 7 5\cdot 10^{-7} and a reduce-on-plateau learning-rate schedule (factor 0.8 0.8 , patience 50 epochs), without stochastic weight averaging or an exponential moving average of the weights. LF-only and HF-only models are trained from scratch for 300 epochs with learning rate 10 − 2 10^{-2} . LF → \rightarrow HF models are initialized from the weights of the LF-only member with the same split and seed after its last pretraining epoch, including the mean–variance readout, and fine-tuned on CC energies for 100 epochs with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} ; the atomic reference energies are refitted on the CC training set, and the optimizer and learning-rate schedule start afresh. For every member, the checkpoint with the lowest validation NLL is kept; test sets are never used for model selection. Across the 50 members of each experiment, the selected epoch has a median of 60 (range 30–111) for HF-only under system shift and 67 (34–111) under energy shift, and a median of 2 (range 1–3) fine-tuning epochs for LF → \rightarrow HF under both shifts.

content: Energy-OOD contains a small number of configurations compressed far below the repulsive wall covered by training. For each split we compute the smallest interatomic distance occurring anywhere in that split’s DFT and CC training and validation sets, and we exclude every test configuration whose smallest interatomic distance falls below it. The rule reads geometry only: it never inspects predictions, errors or uncertainties, and it removes the same configurations for every protocol, signal and metric within a split. It removes 13–16 of the 5,000 Energy-OOD configurations per split, at most two Energy-ID configurations, and none on the system split, whose training data already cover compressed geometries.

content: The filter matters because all our metrics average squared errors or variances. On the excluded configurations the models extrapolate very poorly, and a single one of them can dominate the RMSE, the ENCE of a bin or the AUSE of a whole test set. We therefore treat them as outside the domain of validity of the models rather than as evidence about the quality of uncertainty. The same rule is applied to the acquisition experiment (Appendix J ).

content: Four regularities recur. First, ranking on held-out data settles within a few dozen epochs, while calibration keeps changing: during HF-only training the TU calibration error on the ID and OOD sets passes through a minimum and then rises for the rest of the run, driven by the aleatoric component, and during fine-tuning the aleatoric calibration error rises from the first epoch. Second, on the training set the calibration error of every signal stays close to, and below, one throughout, without the rise seen on held-out data. Third, on the training set RMSE and NLL keep decreasing, whereas on the ID and OOD sets they flatten early; the gap opens most clearly during CC fine-tuning, where the training error keeps falling while the held-out error barely moves. This widening gap between training and held-out error is plausibly what the variance head, fitted to the training residuals, fails to capture. Fourth, the validation loss (Figure 11 ) keeps improving over 300 epochs for LF-only training, reaches a minimum after a few dozen epochs for HF-only training and then slowly worsens, and stops improving within the first few epochs of fine-tuning while the training loss keeps falling, which is why validation-based selection keeps such early fine-tuning checkpoints (Appendix F ). System-split pretraining also shows a transient instability around epochs 50–60 in two of the five splits, visible in every metric and in the EU/AU ratio of Appendix H.1 .

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: For each signal we fit an isotonic regression from predicted variance to squared error on the ensemble’s validation predictions in each split ( Kuleshov et al., 2018 ; Busk et al., 2023 ) , and apply it to the test sets. The map is monotone and is held constant beyond the range of validation variances. Recalibration changes only the predicted variances: the ensemble mean, and hence the RMSE, are those of Figure 2 , and AUSE and Spearman change only through the ties that the piecewise-constant map introduces. In domain it works as intended, reducing TU ENCE from 0.444 0.444 to 0.196 0.196 (HF-only) and from 0.427 0.427 to 0.150 0.150 (LF → \rightarrow HF) on Energy-ID, and from 0.401 0.401 to 0.250 0.250 and from 0.342 0.342 to 0.174 0.174 on System-ID. Figure 15 shows the OOD test sets. Under system shift, recalibration repairs the badly scaled epistemic signal ( 2.02 → 0.44 2.02\to 0.44 for HF-only, 1.49 → 0.35 1.49\to 0.35 for LF → \rightarrow HF), with mixed effects on TU ( 0.391 → 0.330 0.391\to 0.330 for HF-only, 0.319 → 0.508 0.319\to 0.508 for LF → \rightarrow HF). Under energy extrapolation it inflates the calibration error of AU ( 3.25 → 7.19 3.25\to 7.19 and 6.70 → 10.2 6.70\to 10.2 ) and TU ( 1.64 → 6.42 1.64\to 6.42 and 2.97 → 8.11 2.97\to 8.11 ) for both protocols, and improves EU only slightly ( 14.5 → 9.93 14.5\to 9.93 and 13.3 → 10.6 13.3\to 10.6 ). Because the map preserves the ordering up to ties, ranking is essentially unchanged (Energy-OOD TU Spearman 0.556 → 0.547 0.556\to 0.547 for HF-only and 0.640 → 0.632 0.640\to 0.632 for LF → \rightarrow HF). The failure appears to be one of scale: high-energy errors exceed anything seen in the validation set, and a map that is constant beyond the validation range cannot extend the variance scale to them.

content: Figures 16 and 17 show the reliability diagrams after recalibration. In domain, all three signals of every protocol collapse onto the diagonal, and on System-OOD they stay close to it. On Energy-OOD the three signals become nearly indistinguishable but remain far above the diagonal, because the recalibrated variances cannot exceed the largest value seen on the validation set.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: For each split, the 5,000-configuration Energy-OOD CC test set is divided, stratified by molecular system, into an acquisition pool and a held-out test set of 2,500 configurations each; the held-out half is not a higher-energy half. The pool labels are hidden. Each strategy selects 500 pool configurations: uniformly at random (one batch per split, shared by both protocols), or the 500 with the largest AU, EU or TU under the converged HF-only or LF → \rightarrow HF ensemble. Every member of the corresponding ensemble is then warm-started from its converged checkpoint, with a fresh optimizer and learning-rate schedule, and trained for 50 additional epochs with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} on its CC training set plus the 500 acquired configurations. Checkpoints are selected on the original validation set. Gains relative to random selection are computed within each split before averaging over splits. The training-support filter (Appendix G ) removes 6–10 held-out configurations per split. In addition, one held-out configuration of one split, on which the LF → \rightarrow HF ensemble extrapolated catastrophically, was removed after inspection; that split therefore has 2,499 held-out configurations before filtering.

authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Figure 6 a shows the RMSE reduction on the held-out configurations relative to random selection. Uncertainty-guided acquisition beats random selection for all six combinations of protocol and signal. The benefit is larger after pretraining, roughly 2.3 2.3 – 2.5 2.5 meV/atom against 0.8 0.8 – 1.6 1.6 meV/atom without it, and the difference between the two protocols is resolved for every signal. Without pretraining, EU is the best signal, ahead of AU by 0.80 ± 0.55 0.80\pm 0.55 and of TU by 0.46 ± 0.41 0.46\pm 0.41 meV/atom (paired over splits); after pretraining the three signals are indistinguishable. Figure 6 b shows why uncertainty helps: every signal concentrates its batch on the high-energy end of each molecule’s range, where the model is weakest.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: Appendix K Limitations and future work
content: We focus only on energy prediction. While energies are central to atomistic modeling and provide a clean setting for uncertainty analysis, practical molecular simulations also require accurate and reliable forces. Extending the analysis to force uncertainty is an important direction for future work, especially because force errors are local, vector-valued, and directly affect molecular dynamics stability.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: Appendix K Limitations and future work
content: We use mean–variance deep ensembles as our uncertainty estimator. This choice provides a strong, theoretically founded, and widely used baseline for decomposing predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, but it is computationally expensive because it requires training and evaluating multiple models. Future work should investigate whether cheaper alternatives, such as shallow ensembles, last-layer ensembles, multi-head models, evidential methods, or approximate Bayesian approaches, reproduce the same uncertainty dynamics observed here. We also do not ablate the parts of the estimator, for example by training ensembles with a squared loss, using a single mean–variance model, or resetting the variance head at the start of fine-tuning.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: Appendix K Limitations and future work
content: Our analysis relies on operational definitions. With deterministic labels, there is no ground truth for the aleatoric and epistemic terms separately, so we judge calibration on TU and use the ENCE of AU and EU only as a diagnostic (Appendix B ). The comparison between HF-only and LF → \rightarrow HF is one of data access: LF → \rightarrow HF also sees the DFT labels, including the geometries of the CC training set, and we do not separate the effect of this additional information from that of the change of fidelity. Likewise, the two shifts use different training sets, so we compare each OOD test set with the ID test set of its own split rather than the two shifts with each other in absolute terms.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
section: Appendix K Limitations and future work
content: Our main experiments are based on ANI-1x and on controlled system-level and energy-based splits. This design is useful for isolating the effect of data fidelity and distributional shift, but it does not capture the full complexity of realistic simulation workflows, where chemical composition, molecular size, temperature, conformation, and energy can shift simultaneously. Evaluating the same questions on larger and more diverse datasets, including materials and biomolecular systems, would test the generality of our conclusions.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: This work is primarily methodological and focuses on understanding predictive uncertainty in atomistic machine learning models. As such, it does not directly introduce new capabilities for generating data or making decisions affecting individuals or groups, and its societal impact is indirect.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: On the positive side, improving the understanding of uncertainty in atomistic models can contribute to more reliable simulations in chemistry and materials science. This has potential downstream benefits in areas such as drug discovery, energy storage, and materials design, where more accurate and trustworthy models can accelerate scientific progress while reducing computational cost. In particular, better uncertainty estimation can enable more efficient data acquisition strategies, reducing the need for expensive quantum-mechanical calculations and lowering the environmental footprint of large-scale simulations.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Potential negative impacts are limited but not entirely absent. More efficient and reliable atomistic modeling tools could be used to accelerate the design of harmful chemical compounds or materials if applied inappropriately. Additionally, incorrect or misinterpreted uncertainty estimates could lead to overconfidence in model predictions, potentially resulting in flawed scientific conclusions or unsafe downstream applications. However, our work explicitly highlights the limitations and regime-dependent behavior of uncertainty estimates, which may help mitigate such risks by discouraging overreliance on poorly calibrated models.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
authors: Matteo Tolloso, Davide Bacciu, Luigi Bonati
content: Overall, we believe the primary impact of this work is to improve the transparency and reliability of uncertainty estimation in atomistic machine learning, contributing to safer and more informed use of these models in scientific and engineering applications.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
section: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
content: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to improve next-item prediction in a target domain by leveraging user behavior from auxiliary source domains. However, real-world deployment faces two critical challenges: business constraints that isolate interaction data across domains, and user heterogeneity, where many users lack cross-domain activity. This makes existing cross-domain methods difficult to apply. In this paper, we propose a simple and practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendations that transfers information exclusively through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. We introduce a lightweight adapter that projects the source-domain user representation into the target-domain embedding space and integrates it with the target interaction sequence. Importantly, when source data is unavailable (i.e., the user observed only in the target domain), the model seamlessly defaults to a robust target-only sequential recommender, retaining benefits from joint training across all users. Extensive experiments were conducted under two setups; one targets benchmarking against previous baselines, while the other focuses on realistic and scalable conditions. Both sets of experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains for shared and unshared users.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Sequential recommender systems have become a central component of modern information platforms, enabling personalized prediction of a user’s next interaction based on their historical behavior. Recent advances in deep sequential models, such as Transformer-based architectures, have significantly improved recommendation quality within a single domain ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ; Xie et al., 2021 ) . However, in many real-world scenarios, user interaction histories in an individual domain are sparse or incomplete, limiting the effectiveness of even the most expressive sequential models.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) addresses this limitation by transferring knowledge across domains in which the same users interact with different item spaces, such as e-commerce, media consumption, or online services ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . By leveraging behavioral signals from a source domain, CDSR methods seek to improve recommendation performance in a target domain, particularly for users with limited interaction histories. Existing CDSR approaches commonly rely on shared item spaces, joint training on merged interaction data, or pretraining and fine-tuning strategies. While effective in controlled settings, these methods often require strong assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in practice, such as user/item alignment across domains or unrestricted access to raw interaction data ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, parameter-transfer approaches may suffer from negative transfer or catastrophic forgetting when domain distributions differ substantially ( Ju et al., 2025 ) .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Practical deployment of CDSR systems, therefore, faces two fundamental challenges. First, interaction data transfer across domains is often prohibited due to storage or data ownership concerns, making centralized modeling of raw interaction sequences from different domains infeasible ( Tian et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We formalize this setting as a vertical federated learning (VFL) problem ( Yang et al., 2019 ) , where domains possess distinct feature spaces (item sets) but partially overlapping users, and only intermediate representations rather than raw interaction sequences may be exchanged. Second, user overlap between domains is typically partial, and many users may have no interaction history in the source domain at all ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) . Effective CDSR models must consequently operate under restricted data sharing assumptions and remain robust to missing source-domain information .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer

content: To address these challenges, we propose FLADRec ( F ederated L earning Ad apted Rec ommender), a representation-level cross-domain sequential recommendation framework. Our key idea is to transfer cross-domain knowledge exclusively through learned user representations , rather than raw interactions or shared item embeddings. In the proposed framework, the source-domain encoder produces a fixed-dimensional user representation from its interaction sequence.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer

content: To enable effective transfer, we introduce a lightweight fusing mechanism that conditions target-domain sequence modeling on a projected source-domain user representation. The transferred representation is aligned to the target embedding space and injected directly into the target sequence, allowing the target encoder to adapt its internal dynamics based on cross-domain user preferences . This design enforces strict separation between domains while enabling early and flexible integration of source-domain information.

content: Importantly, the proposed framework naturally supports users without source-domain interaction histories. In such cases, the model reduces to a standard single-domain sequential recommender, while still benefiting from joint training with users for whom cross-domain information is available . As a result, the approach improves recommendation quality not only for shared users, but also for users observed exclusively in the target domain .

content: In this section we describe the experimental setup. We evaluate our method in two complementary settings to balance reproducibility against prior work and realism in deployment conditions .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: We conduct our benchmarking experiments on three datasets used by previous work ( Bian et al., 2025 ) . These datasets are derived from the Amazon reviews datasets 2 2 2 https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~jmcauley/datasets/amazon/links.html ( McAuley et al., 2015 ; He and McAuley, 2016 ) , representing three pairs of domains: Food-Kitchen (FK), Beauty-Electronics (BE), and Movie-Book (MB). These datasets serve as established testbeds that enable direct comparison with published baselines under identical preprocessing, user filtering, and evaluation protocols (e.g., sampled metrics with 999 negatives, last-item split, and full user overlap). While essential for reproducibility, such benchmarks exhibit known limitations : (i) they are not native cross-domain datasets, interactions originate from a single platform (Amazon), and domain separation is imposed post hoc based on product categories, (ii) artificially high user overlap (only shared users retained), (iii) evaluation via negative sampling—which distorts ranking quality ( Krichene and Rendle, 2022 ; Cañamares and Castells, 2020 ) , and (iv) non-temporal or inconsistent data splits that risk temporal leakage ( Gusak et al., 2025 ) . We elaborate further on these pitfalls in Section 7.2 , recommending critical guidelines to advance benchmarking of CDR models.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: To address these shortcomings and assess performance under realistic conditions, we additionally evaluate on two industrial-scale, multi-domain datasets: TenRec ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) and Zvuk&MegaMarket (Zvuk&MM) ( Shevchenko et al., 2024 ) . Both capture authentic cross-domain user behavior across distinct services (e.g., music streaming and e-commerce) with naturally partial user overlap and million-scale item catalogs. Crucially, we employ full-catalog ranking without negative sampling and enforce strict temporal splits, thereby eliminating key biases inherent in benchmarking evaluations. As summarized in Tables 1 and 2 , this dual-evaluation strategy allows us to validate competitiveness against prior approaches on standard benchmarks , and demonstrate robustness and scalability in settings that reflect real-world cross-domain recommendation challenges .

For benchmarking datasets, we optimize models using the full Cross-Entropy (CE) loss ( Klenitskiy and Vasilev, 2023 ) . However, for large-scale datasets with extensive item catalogs, full CE becomes computationally infeasible. Therefore, for scalability experiments, we adopt the Scalable Cross-Entropy loss ( Mezentsev et al., 2024 ) during both the pre-training and adaptation stages.

content: The ablation study results for the tuned source encoder are presented in Table 7 . The full-transfer (full) setting achieves the best performance in both the source-tuned and source-frozen scenarios. When the source encoder is tuned, random embeddings (rand) slightly outperform the no-embedding baseline (none) for the shared subset of users, likely because they introduce user-discriminative signals that complement the adapted encoder weights. Not surprisingly, the metrics in the (full) and (none) settings for the unshared users are identical, since no source embeddings exist to transfer for these users, whereas injecting random source embeddings for unshared users degrades performance. Conversely, when the source encoder is frozen, random embeddings perform worse than no embeddings, as the fixed representation space cannot adapt to the injected noise, leading to uncontrolled perturbations.

In this configuration, the source representation remains fixed as initially pretrained on its native task, while only the target encoder and fusing layer parameters are updated. This experimental setup isolates the contribution of source encoder fine-tuning to the overall performance gain.

Compared to the tuned-source setting, the frozen-source configuration yields lower NDCG@10 for both shared and unshared users, with particularly pronounced drops for shared users under full transfer. content: Single-domain recommender systems have achieved significant progress through deep learning architectures like Transformers ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) and self-supervised learning techniques ( Zhou et al., 2020 ; Xie et al., 2021 ) , which effictively capture the dynamic user preferences.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: For the case of many domains, particularly with partial user overlap, sequential cross-domain recommendation have emerged. These method concentrate on transferring knowledge from source domains to improve recommendation quality in the target domain ( Chen et al., 2024 ) for the next-item prediction task.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: A common line of work assumes the presence of users shared across domains and transfers knowledge through shared user representations. Models such as CD-SASRec ( Alharbi and Caragea, 2021b ) , DCDIR ( Bi et al., 2020 ) , and MIFN ( Ma et al., 2022 ) employ domain-aware encoders or attention mechanisms to fuse sequences from multiple domains. More recent CDSR approaches focus on transferring knowledge at the representation level, by aligning latent user embeddings via contrastive objectives or partially sharing model parameters across domains. C 2 DSR ( Cao et al., 2022 ) utilized contrastive learning through domain-specific and domain-invariant tasks. ABXI ( Bian et al., 2025 ) uses task-guided LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) modules to identify domain-invariant user interests and finetune the models in both source and target domains. AutoCDSR ( Ju et al., 2025 ) utilizes self-attention to optimize the cross-domain knowledge transfer and combat the negative transfer caused by imbalanced signals from domains. These methods typically rely on joint training over all domains, including the usage of merged interaction sequences across domains and exploit shared users to bridge domain gaps.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: The increasing focus on privacy has spurred research into federated recsys, where models are trained across decentralized data sources without exchanging raw user interactions. PPCDR ( Tian et al., 2024 ) proposes a scheme that shares user embeddings protected by local differential privacy technique. However, this method provides learning schemes for domains with full user overlap, which rarely happens in real-world services. FedCDR ( Meihan et al., 2022 ) addresses cross-domain recommendation in federated settings but focuses on rating prediction rather than sequential next-item prediction, limiting its applicability to modern sequential recommendation systems.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Our approach bridges critical gaps between cross-domain recommendation and privacy-preserving learning. Unlike prior CDSR methods that require sharing raw sequences or item mappings, our framework transfers knowledge exclusively through distilled user representations, never exchanging raw interactions or embedding tables between domains. Unlike methods that assume full user overlap, our architecture naturally accommodates partial overlap through a fusion mechanism that seamlessly converts to single-domain recommendation when source data is missing.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Our lightweight adapter enables cross-domain knowledge transfer while maintaining strict domain separation, making it deployable in federated learning scenarios where existing methods fail. Furthermore, our framework uniquely benefits all users, not just those with cross-domain activity. Through joint training with shared parameters, target-domain-only users indirectly benefit from the regularization effect of cross-domain signals, achieving performance gains. This dual benefit represents a practical advance toward deployable cross-domain recommendation systems that respect privacy boundaries while maximizing utility.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: FLADRec was essentially designed to achieve cross-domain knowledge transfer between different subsidiaries (services) under a shared ecosystem. The federated training process operates in a distributed storage environment with mild privacy restrictions. Thus, the proposed architecture lack a dedicated mechanism to prevent user history reconstruction attacks. However, we obtain a representation-transfer mechanism that naturally operates effectively whether representations are exchanged via secure channels (VFL) or directly (non-VFL), without architectural modification . To secure the training process where gradients are transferred back to the source domain, stronger privacy guarantees, such as formal differential privacy, can be integrated into the federated training protocol.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
section: 7.2. Toward A Fair, Sustainable CDR Benchmarking Protocol
content: In this section, we identify and analyze five prevalent pitfalls in benchmarking pipelines for cross - domain recommendation models, which substantially undermine their practical reliability in industrial settings when compared with single - domain baselines. As illustrated in our scalability experiments (Section 4.2 ), we took steps to avoid as many of these pitfalls as possible.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Large companies such as Amazon and Douban release anonymized user-item datasets split into categories, which researchers repurpose to simulate cross-domain recommendation. However, these datasets originate from a single platform, where a shared environment and shared models have access to all data simultaneously. Recently, more "honest" datasets have been released, notably the MegaMarket–Zvuk pair ( Shevchenko et al., 2024 ) and TenRec ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) are collected from genuinely separate platforms and therefore produced by independent models.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Most CDR research assumes shared users or items across domains and links their representations accordingly. In practice, overlap is limited, creating non-uniform conditions under which models must handle shared and non-shared users differently. Most researchers in the CDR field run experiments on datasets with unrealistically high or even full user overlap, and insufficiently discuss the disparity in quality improvement between shared and unshared users. Notably, recent work has begun addressing quality fairness between shared and non-shared users ( Chen et al., 2025 ) .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Many recent CDR papers still rely on small, heavily processed datasets ( < < 300k interactions), especially when controlling the user overlap ratio. Replicating most such models in real-world settings is typically computationally infeasible. Since recommender systems research is inherently practical, comparisons against baselines evaluated only on small datasets are of limited value, even when those baselines appear to outperform others in that restricted regime.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Sampled metrics have grown popular because they enable fast computation by ranking relevant items against a random subset of negatives rather than the full catalog. However, this approach can distort model comparisons, and several works have proposed corrections for this bias ( Krichene and Rendle, 2020 ) .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Sampling each user’s most recently interacted item is a common evaluation practice in recommender systems. It is, however, frequently applied to non-temporal or temporally inconsistent data splits, introducing a risk of temporal leakage ( Gusak et al., 2025 ) . Nevertheless, temporal leakage across multiple domains remains insufficiently investigated to date.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Specifically, the Zvuk/MegaMarket experiment satisfies all the criteria discussed above, but to a lesser extent with respect to the overlap ratio, as a 50% user overlap remains relatively high. In addition, the TenRec experiment also does not meet the requirement of a strict temporal split, since the dataset originally lacks absolute timestamps.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Nonetheless, we argue that enforcing the optimal condition for each of the aforementioned considerations is overly demanding in the context of fast-paced academic research, even though it would promote stronger alignment with industrial applications. We further argue that the partial overlap and scalability conditions are the most critical aspects to prioritize in future CDR research.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: In this work, we introduced a practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendation that transfers knowledge through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. Our SASRec-based architecture, combined with a lightweight fusing layer and vertical federated fine-tuning of the source encoder, enables effective alignment of source and target user preferences under realistic privacy and deployment constraints. Extensive experiments across five datasets, including two industrial-scale benchmarks and three established academic benchmarks, demonstrate consistent improvements over strong single-domain and cross-domain baselines, for both shared and target-only users, confirming that representation-level transfer not only avoids negative transfer but also benefits the entire user population. Future work includes extending the framework to multi-source and multi-task settings, exploring alternative fusion mechanisms and backbone architectures, and integrating privacy-preserving mechanisms to protect the exchanged data during learning.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: Unsafe deserialization turns untrusted data into attacker-controlled execution, and a single vulnerability can admit diverse exploit variants that evade defenses tailored to a known exploit. Existing defenses typically operate at a single enforcement point with limited visibility into the full attack. Combining controls across layers offers complementary protection, but coordinating them to preserve legitimate functionality and adapting them to new variants requires substantial expert effort.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: We propose Janus , a red-blue adversarial framework for automated cross-layer defense synthesis. Starting from a known exploit, Janus iteratively refines deployment-specific policies in an isolated offline environment. A black-box attacker probes the current policy for exploit variants using only externally observable feedback. The defender summarizes each verified variant into its security-relevant effects, uses counterfactual replay to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement, and jointly selects and scopes controls across layers. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: We evaluate Janus on sixteen vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications against gateway, application, system, and cross-layer defenses. Janus reduces held-out attack success to 6.2%, compared with 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and preserves 98.4% of benign functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 latency increase.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Unsafe deserialization poses a persistent and critical threat to Web security ( OWASP Foundation, 2021 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . When applications reconstruct objects from untrusted data, attacker-controlled types and field values can trigger chains of existing methods that lead to remote code execution (RCE) ( Sayar et al., 2023 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Existing defenses constrain specific steps of this process, for example by restricting the classes permitted during deserialization ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; David et al., 2024 ) . However, a single vulnerability may admit multiple gadget chains drawn from application dependencies, so filters targeting known gadgets can be bypassed by alternative chains ( Cao et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2022 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . Mitigation is also deployment-specific: the deployed libraries and runtime determine which chains are viable ( Kreyssig and Bartel, 2024 ) , whereas legitimate features determine which deserialization behaviors must remain available ( Huang et al., 2016 ) .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Motivation. As shown in Figure 1 , defenders can intervene at three layers with distinct visibility and established enforcement mechanisms. At the gateway, a Web application firewall (WAF) inspects and filters incoming request representations ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) . Application-level deserialization filters constrain the types and object structures accepted during reconstruction ( Oracle, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; David et al., 2024 ) . System-level policies restrict the resulting operations through system-call filtering or container isolation ( Bulekov et al., 2021 ; Lei and Shue, 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Each layer nevertheless observes only part of the attack: narrow restrictions may miss exploit variants, while broader restrictions risk disrupting legitimate features ( Sayar et al., 2023 ; Demetrio et al., 2020 ) .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Combining these layers offers complementary protection ( Rubel et al., 2005 ) , but requires coordinating their policies. We define a multi-layer composition as a joint selection of controls with deployment-specific parameters and enforcement scopes. Constructing an effective composition is challenging because upstream blocking can obscure downstream coverage, overlapping controls may introduce redundant overhead, and policy interactions can disrupt legitimate workflows in ways that isolated checks do not reveal. Moreover, a composition that blocks known exploits may still admit variants using different gadget chains or payload representations. Existing automated mitigations support the generation of security workarounds, deserialization restrictions, or runtime policies ( Huang et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) , but these capabilities alone do not establish how controls should be jointly configured and revised to cover adaptive exploit variants while preserving legitimate functionality.

content: Figure 1. Motivating example. Each layer’s defense stops some exploit variants, but one variant passes all three layers and reaches RCE, while the legitimate request is served. An attacker and a user send requests down through gateway, application, and system bands. Three attack attempts stop at different bands, one reaches RCE, and the user's request is served.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Our Approach. We present Janus , a red-blue adversarial framework for synthesizing deployment-specific multi-layer defenses against unsafe deserialization. The framework pairs an attacker agent with a defender agent on an isolated replica of the deployment. Starting from a known exploit, the attacker adapts its gadget-chain selection and payload representation to achieve a specified consequence, such as command execution within the application container. The defender uses execution evidence and benign-workflow feedback to jointly revise controls across layers. Through this offline interaction, the agents expose and address weaknesses beyond those revealed by the initial exploit. The attacker observes only what an external attacker could observe and serves as a source of counterexamples. The technical contributions of Janus lie on the defense side, in how the defender interprets these counterexamples and coordinates controls to cover them.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Realizing this process raises three technical challenges. ❶ Exposing Variants Under Black-Box Observation. A defense is only as robust as the variants it is checked against, yet an external attacker cannot distinguish a gateway rejection from an incompatible gadget chain. Janus ’s attacker parameterizes reviewed fixtures whose prerequisites match the deployment, treats ambiguous feedback as hypotheses, and submits candidates to an independent oracle that it cannot observe. ❷ Interpreting Exploit Effects and Defensive Coverage. Raw system-call traces are too low-level for policy reasoning, and upstream blocking hides the protection of downstream controls. Janus condenses execution evidence into attack-effect summaries expressed as security-relevant capabilities, each tied to the control that can intercept it, if any, and uses counterfactual replay with upstream rules disabled to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement. ❸ Coordinating Controls Under Functional Constraints. Controls that are individually acceptable may break legitimate workflows when combined, and some improvements require coordinated changes across layers. Janus jointly selects and scopes controls from a bounded catalog of deployable mechanisms and accepts a candidate only if it blocks all verified exploits and meets the functionality and latency thresholds on the benign-workflow regression suite.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Evaluation. We compare Janus on 16 deployments across six applications against ModSecurity with OWASP CRS ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) , Datadog RASP and OpenRASP ( Datadog, 2025 ; Baidu Security, 2024 ) , Kintsugi ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , and Tetragon ( Cilium Authors, 2025 ) . Janus lowers held-out attack success to 6.2%, versus 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and is breached on 5 of 48 unseen-attacker/deployment pairs, while passing 98.4% of functionality tests. A recorded run on CVE-2026-84645, a recent Jenkins RCE, illustrates the refinement loop.

authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Unsafe deserialization allows attacker-controlled data to trigger unintended method invocations during object reconstruction. A sequence of existing methods leading to a sensitive operation constitutes a gadget chain ( Dahse et al., 2014 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . A vulnerable entry point may admit multiple chains ( Park et al., 2022 ; Cao et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , whose viability depends on the deployed libraries and runtime ( Kreyssig and Bartel, 2024 ; Cao et al., 2023b ) . Exploit variants can differ in where serialized data enters, how it is encoded and framed, or which execution path leads to the consequence.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Each of the three defensive layers has a characteristic blind spot. Gateway controls ( G ) such as reverse proxies and WAFs ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) inspect request representations rather than reconstructed objects, so representation changes can bypass them ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Demetrio et al., 2020 ) . Application controls ( A ) restrict accepted classes or object-graph properties where the parser exposes them ( OpenJDK, 2016 ; Oracle, 2024 ) , yet may still permit malicious uses of allowed classes. System controls ( S ) restrict process creation, file access, or network communication ( Docker, 2024 ; Bulekov et al., 2021 ) , limiting consequences without preventing deserialization, often for a whole process or container. These controls also differ in availability across deployments, so an effective composition must account for both the controls a deployment supports and the legitimate behavior within their scopes.

authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: We consider a Web deployment D D with a known, unpatched deserialization vulnerability and a validated seed exploit that achieves a specified security consequence. The defender operates on isolated, resettable replicas with representative benign workflows.

The offline attacker agent operates under the same restrictions and receives no internal execution-stage feedback.

content: Stopping and Freezing. Refinement stops at budget exhaustion , at stagnation after k k consecutive rounds without a new verified bypass, or at catalog exhaustion , when every eligible fixture and permitted variation has been tried against the incumbent. None of them proves that no bypass exists. Finalize re-checks the last incumbent on a fresh replica and returns it as π ⋆ \pi^{\star} if it is still accepted, or RefinementFailure otherwise. Held-out attacks and test workflows are used only to evaluate π ⋆ \pi^{\star} .

Both agents sample from an LLM, so runs from the same seed may return different configurations, whereas verification, replay, and regression checks are deterministic given the snapshot. content: We implement Janus in about 9,800 lines of Python. Each deployment runs as a Docker Compose project behind an NGINX reverse proxy and is restored from a snapshot before every replay. Oracles and workflow assertions run outside the application container, and failed replays are retried rather than counted as blocks. No application code is modified.
