authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: Our work. To tackle these challenges, we propose a neuro-symbolic framework, RAINFALL ( RA nk IN g F unction gener A tion with LL m), within the generate-verify-refine paradigm, which combines the generative capabilities of modern LLMs with the rigor of symbolic techniques. This integration enables RAINFALL to discover richer termination arguments and prove termination for a broader class of loop programs. We remark that LLM fine-tuning could also be adopted, as demonstrated by PROTON 2.1. We avoid fine-tuning because it is not only cost- and resource-intensive, but also requires large-scale, high-quality training datasets, which otherwise risks overfitting.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: Specifically, to address the first challenge, RAINFALL first transforms the synthesis of ranking functions into a code-assertion generation problem, motivated by the observation that LLMs are very effective in code and specification generation. This transformation avoids requiring LLMs to interpret complicated definitions of ranking functions and improves the quality of the generated candidate ranking functions. Second, we embed expert knowledge about termination arguments (e.g., lexicographic and multi-phase ranking functions) with few-shot examples into structured prompts which can enhance the reasoning ability and in-context learning of LLMs for code-assertion generation.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: To address the second challenge, we present a symbolic verification pipeline which checks whether the LLM outputs satisfy the required correctness criteria, thereby providing soundness guarantees. In this pipeline, we first ensure that the LLM does not modify the original program by applying a lightweight, syntactic equivalence check. This step prevents potential cheating where the LLM modifies the program and generates assertions that hold only in the modified version. After this, we check the completeness of the generated code-assertion statements required to induce a ranking function (e.g., whether assertions include strict decrease, non-negativity and termination conditions). Without these conditions, valid ranking functions cannot be extracted even if the program satisfies the assertions (e.g., an LLM outputs true as the assertion, which would not be useful). Finally, we verify whether the program satisfies the assertions via safety checking. To repair incorrect outputs with minimal interactions, we re-prompt LLMs by incorporating fine-grained diagnostic information (e.g., the detected program modification, missing ranking function conditions, or counterexample produced by the safety verifier). The corresponding ranking functions can then be extracted and used as a witness to program termination. Remark that we do not copy the LLM-generated code-assertions into the original program and then verify them using the later checks because such code-assertions typically cannot induce a valid ranking function and subsequent checks would incur substantial computational overhead.

content: We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using MiniMax (V2.7) ( Min, 2026 ) , RAINFALL generates verifiable ranking functions for 323 programs (90.22%), outperforming six state-of-the-art tools such as AProVE ( Lommen and Giesl, 2025 ) (78.77%), UAutomizer (79.05%), LOOPY (73.74%) and PROTON 2.1 (86.87%). Ablation studies confirm that formulating ranking-function synthesis as a code-assertion generation task, together with few-shot examples and diagnostic information feedback is critical to this performance. We further show that RAINFALL remains effective across LLMs (e.g., proved more programs in less time using GPT V5.5 ( GPT, 2026 ) and Claude-Opus V4.7 ( Cla, 2026 ) ) and complements other tools (e.g., a 96.65% success rate, solving 346 tasks when combined with the symbolic counterpart of PROTON 2.1).

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: Single ranking function synthesis. The most standard approach to proving program termination is via ranking functions that decrease along every loop iteration. Podelski and Rybalchenko ( Podelski and Rybalchenko, 2004 ) gave a complete method for synthesizing linear ranking functions on linear loops. Later work relaxes the strict decrease requirement, e.g., by eventual linear ranking functions ( Bagnara and Mesnard, 2013 ) . These approaches typically reduce the synthesis problem to constraint solving (via, e.g., Farkas’ lemma), but are limited in expressiveness.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: Template-based ranking function synthesis. Template-based approaches synthesize ranking functions by reducing the problem to constraint solving over predefined templates. For a chosen ranking function class, a parameterized template with unknown coefficients is fixed, and synthesis amounts to finding coefficient values that satisfy the required conditions. Common templates include linear ( Leike and Heizmann, 2015 ) , multiphase ( Ben-Amram and Genaim, 2017 ) , and lexicographic ranking functions ( Bradley et al., 2005a ; Bradley et al., 2005b ; Alias et al., 2010 ; Ben-Amram and Genaim, 2014 ) , as introduced in Section 2 . For example, to synthesize a single linear ranking function for a loop with guard ϕ \phi , one can use an affine template f ⁡ ( x → ) = a → ⋅ x → + c f(\vec{x})=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{x}+c , where a → \vec{a} and c c are unknown. The synthesis task reduces to determining a → \vec{a} and c c such that the ranking function conditions hold for all program transitions and f ⁡ ( x → ) ​ ¡ ​ 0 ⟹ ¬ ϕ f(\vec{x})<0\implies\neg\phi . Leike and Heizmann ( Leike and Heizmann, 2015 ) reduce the synthesis problem of common ranking functions above to solving nonlinear constraints via SMT. More expressive templates may use polynomial or rational expressions, or multiple components as in multiphase and lexicographic ranking functions. Thus, the effectiveness of template-based methods depends heavily on choosing suitable templates, a task that aligns well with the strengths of LLMs.

content: Data-driven techniques. Some learning-based approaches predict termination without formal guarantees ( Alon and David, 2022 ) , while others adopt a learn-and-check paradigm ( Nori and Sharma, 2013 ; Urban et al., 2016 ; Xu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . Neural approaches, in particular, learn candidate functions from execution traces and validate them using SMT ( Giacobbe et al., 2022 ; Abate et al., 2021 ) . However, these methods rely heavily on the availability of high-quality execution data.

content: Other symbolic approaches. Alternative approaches reason about transition relations and exploit transition invariants. Key techniques include size-change analysis ( Lee et al., 2001 ) , refinement ( Chawdhary et al., 2008 ; Cook et al., 2006 ) , variance analysis ( Berdine et al., 2007 ; Podelski and Rybalchenko, 2005 ; Kroening et al., 2010 ) , abstract interpretation ( Cousot and Cousot, 2012 ) , temporal reasoning ( Le et al., 2014 ; Le et al., 2015 ) , and interprocedural summarization ( Chen et al., 2018a ) . Some techniques further address complex data structures, e.g., heaps ( Berdine et al., 2006 ) , pointers ( Cook et al., 2006 ) , and lists ( Hensel and Giesl, 2023 ) .

content: Termination checking tools. AProVE ( Lommen and Giesl, 2025 ) uses integer transition systems (ITS) and integrates KoAT ( Lommen and Giesl, 2026 ) for inferring complexity bounds of ITS. Both UAutomizer ( Heizmann et al., 2014 ; Chen et al., 2018b ) and T2 (and its predecessor Terminator ) ( Cook et al., 2006 ; Cook et al., 2013 ; Brockschmidt et al., 2016 ) iteratively prove termination by analyzing cycles; UAutomizer employs automata-based reasoning to discover new cycles, while T2 reduces the problem to safety checking. FreqTerm ( Fedyukovich et al., 2018 ) enumerates candidate ranking functions, whereas ddlTerm ( Xu et al., 2022 ) adopts a data-driven approach to learn loop bounds. PROTON 2.1 ( Mukhopadhyay et al., 2025 ) leverages fine-tuned LLMs to handle cases not solved by PROTON 1.1.2 ( Metta et al., 2024 ) , a bounded model checking-based tool. Other tools include DynamiTe ( Le et al., 2020 ) and FuncTion ( Urban, 2015 ) . Related work also addresses non-termination ( Gupta et al., 2008 ; Chen et al., 2014 ; Han and He, 2023 ) and LLM-based prediction ( Sultan et al., 2026 ) , which is not our focus.

content: RAINFALL consists of two main phases: preprocessing and iterative generation-verification . In the preprocessing phase (cf. Section 4.1 ), RAINFALL performs program instrumentation and prompt construction . It first automatically instruments 𝒫 \mathcal{P} by inserting four predefined code and assertion placeholders at selected locations for each loop, resulting in an instrumented program 𝒫 𝚒𝚗𝚜𝚝𝚛 \mathcal{P}_{\tt instr} . This reduces ranking function synthesis to a code-assertion generation problem on 𝒫 𝚒𝚗𝚜𝚝𝚛 \mathcal{P}_{\tt instr} . Next, it constructs a structured prompt ℳ 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 \mathcal{M}_{\tt init} based on 𝒫 𝚒𝚗𝚜𝚝𝚛 \mathcal{P}_{\tt instr} , natural language descriptions and few-shot examples of ranking functions, and queries the LLM accordingly.

content: In the iterative generation-verification phase (cf. Section 4.2 ), RAINFALL generally alternates between symbolic verification and prompt construction with diagnostic feedback. It first queries the LLM with the initial prompt ℳ 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 \mathcal{M}_{\tt init} (from the preprocessing phase), to produce a candidate program 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} by infilling the code/assertion placeholders. Despite the structured prompt, 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} may still be incorrect or incomplete, and thus is analyzed by a symbolic verification pipeline.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: The symbolic verification pipeline comprises three components: syntactic equivalence checking , which ensures that the original code in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is not modified by the LLM; code-assertion completeness checking , which verifies that the generated assertions cover strict decrease, non-negativity, and termination conditions; and assertion checking , which validates the correctness of these assertions. If 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} passes all three checks, the LLM-generated code-assertions induce a valid ranking function f f , and RAINFALL returns 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} as 𝒫 𝚙𝚛𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt proved} . Otherwise, diagnostic information is incorporated into the ℳ 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 \mathcal{M}_{\tt init} , leading to the prompt ℳ 𝚏𝚋 \mathcal{M}_{\tt fb} for the subsequent iteration (a new interaction with the LLM using ℳ 𝚏𝚋 \mathcal{M}_{\tt fb} ), to refine the LLM output. This process repeats until a valid ranking function is found, or the resource budget is exhausted.

content: Semantic assertion checking is thus necessary to verify the LLM-generated code-assertions as a valid ranking function. Specifically, the program 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} is verified using a safety verifier (e.g., UAutomizer ). Intuitively, this step checks whether the original program 𝒫 \mathcal{P} terminates under the candidate ranking function induced by the code-assertions in 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} . This procedure is sound because (1) the equivalence checking ensures that the original code of 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is not modified in 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} , and (2) the completeness checking ensures that all the required code-assertions have been properly instantiated in 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} . Consequently, if the assertions are valid in 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} , they collectively induce a valid ranking function for proving termination of 𝒫 \mathcal{P} .

section: 4.2.4. Prompt Augment with Diagnostic Information Feedback.
content: To address the issues identified by the checks, we augment the initial prompt ℳ 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 \mathcal{M}_{\tt init} with the incorrectly generated program 𝒫 𝚌𝚊𝚗𝚍 \mathcal{P}_{\tt cand} and the corresponding diagnostic information. This combined text forms a complete context for the next new interaction with the LLM. The diagnostic information is tailored to each type of check. For syntactic equivalence checking, it reports mismatched statements with their locations. For code-assertion completeness checking, it highlights the incorrect/incomplete variable declarations and code within each placeholder slot. For assertion checking, it provides the location of the violated assertion along with a counterexample, as reported by the underlying safety verifier.

content: Benchmark. We consider two public benchmark suites provided by LOOPY and FreqTerm , denoted by BS-L and BS-F, respectively. BS-L consists of 188 terminating C programs (after deduplicating 93 programs with identical ASTs but different lines of code), while BS-F contains 170 terminating C programs, after removing a non-terminating instance. These benchmarks were originally collected from the termination category of SV-COMP, covering a range of typical loop patterns, including linear, non-linear and conditional branches. (Note that one of them uses a for-loop, which is transformed into an equivalent while-loop.) We do not evaluate on the entire SV-COMP Termination benchmarks mainly because of the high token cost of LLM-based experiments. Nevertheless, the selected benchmarks are sufficiently large and diverse for a meaningful evaluation. In particular, ddlterm ( Xu et al., 2022 ) (ICSE 2022) evaluates exclusively on the BS-F benchmark suite; similarly, CondTerm ( Huang et al., 2026 ) (ICSE 2026) uses only the 170 terminating programs from BS-F.

content: Overall, RAINFALL outperforms all baselines, solving the largest number of tasks across both benchmark suites. In particular, RAINFALL solves 12 more tasks than PROTON , the best-performing baseline and winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. PRO-LLM solves only 11 tasks on BS-F and 4 on BS-L, all of which are already solvable by PROTON without invoking its fine-tuned LLM. Compared to the LLM-based tool LOOPY , which uses the same LLM (i.e., MiniMax) to generate ranking functions instead of code-assertions, RAINFALL solves 59 additional tasks. In terms of efficiency, RAINFALL not only solves more tasks but also requires fewer LLM queries than LOOPY .

RAINFALL outperforms all baselines with most LLMs; the only exception is Qwen-Plus, for which RAINFALL performs worse than ddlTerm and PROTON . title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites, and its effectiveness may differ on other benchmarks or real-world programs. Because modern LLMs are typically trained on large corpora containing publicly available code, these benchmarks may have been included in their training data, raising the possibility of benchmark contamination. We mitigate this concern by synthesizing code assertions rather than directly generating ranking functions. To the best of our knowledge, no public benchmark contains the code assertions used by our framework. Evaluating RAINFALL on additional benchmark suites and real-world programs remains an important direction for future work.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: We presented RAINFALL , a novel neuro-symbolic framework for ranking function synthesis. Our approaches formulates ranking function synthesis as a code-assertion generation problem using dedicated placeholders, enabling seamless integration of modern LLMs within an iterative generate-verify-refine workflow. We showed that incorporating expert knowledge of ranking functions, few-shot examples and diagnostic information into prompts can significantly enhance generation accuracy. To ensure soundness, we developed a symbolic verification pipeline tailored to our LLM-generated code-assertion. Experimental results show that RAINFALL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and complements existing symbolic termination analysis tools.

title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
authors: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu
content: More broadly, this work demonstrates the promise of combining the generative capabilities of LLMs with the formal rigor of symbolic verification for ranking-function synthesis. As LLMs continue to improve, we expect this neuro-symbolic paradigm to become an increasingly effective approach to automated termination proving.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
section: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
content: Recovering an object’s 3D structure and camera motion from a few uncalibrated views is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Classical structure from motion methods recover 3D geometry consistent with the input images but cannot recover unseen regions; native generation methods produce plausible 3D objects which are related but not necessarily faithful to the input images. Methods simply concatenating reconstruction and generation allow error to cascade across the two stages, instead of producing a 3D object consistent with both the distribution and the input. We propose GenSfM , which integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model. In particular, we use a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise the shape latent and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention, grounding generated geometry in the observed views while using object-level priors to infer unobserved regions. A compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization keeps the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. On Toys4k and GSO, for 4 4 uncalibrated views, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2 3.2 – 4.5 4.5 dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8 2.8 – 3.8 × 3.8\times over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over 96 % 96\% Acc@ 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} without any external pose-estimation backbone, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics. Project page: https://dotb1ue.github.io/GenSfm/ .

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
section: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
content: Figure 1 : Generative object shape and camera motion recovery. Given multiview input images, GenSfM recovers the object shape and camera poses in a unified 3D space. A diffusion transformer performs multi-view reasoning through iterative structure-and-pose denoising (the trajectory of the camera), emulating an end-to-end SfM process. The denoised cameras ( blue ) align accurately with the ground-truth poses ( red ) and the recovered 3D structure gives a holistic object representation.

authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Recovering 3D structure and camera motion from images is a foundational problem in computer vision. Classical Structure-from-Motion and Multi-View Stereo pipelines Schönberger and Frahm (2016) ; Schönberger et al. (2016) ; Furukawa and Ponce (2009) estimate camera poses from multi-view correspondences and reconstruct geometry through photometric or geometric consistency, often regularized by hand-crafted priors. While effective when input views provide sufficient texture, overlap, and coverage, this geometric paradigm becomes brittle in sparse object-centric settings, where only a few uncalibrated views are available and large object regions go unrecovered.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Such settings are common in practice, from robotic manipulation to AR capture and content-creation pipelines, all of which need a holistic 3D representation to reason about occluded surfaces and contact regions. Sparse-view 3D object recovery therefore requires more than triangulating visible evidence: it must infer a complete 3D explanation that is both consistent with the input images and plausible as an object, jointly answering what the object is and where each view was taken from.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Recent learning-based methods relax the texture and overlap assumptions of classical pipelines by introducing large-scale data-driven priors. Feed-forward reconstructors Wang et al. (2024) ; Leroy et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) predict camera parameters and pixel-aligned 3D representations jointly, while pose-centric works Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Sinha et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) estimate relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity. Both threads remain primarily observation-driven: they recover what the input views support but do not explicitly model the distribution of complete object shapes, leaving outputs incomplete in unobserved regions when input coverage is poor.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: A complementary line of work introduces generative priors learned from large-scale 3D datasets Deitke et al. (2023) into sparse reconstruction. View-based generative SfM Zhao et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Xu et al. (2024a) ; Zhao and Tulsiani (2024) casts structure and motion as a generative problem in view space, while reconstruct-then-generate pipelines Ardelean et al. (2025) ; Huang et al. (2026) ; Chang et al. (2025) ; Team et al. (2025) ; Siddiqui et al. (2026) pair feed-forward reconstructors with native 3D generators Tochilkin et al. (2024) ; Xiang et al. (2025) ; Zhao et al. (2025b) . The latter family in particular has shown that 3D generative priors can complete hidden geometry that observation-driven methods cannot. These systems remain cascaded: an external module predicts poses or image-aligned representations and the 3D generator only completes the result, propagating errors across stages and preventing joint optimization of a single 3D hypothesis that explains all input views.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: In this paper, we invert this pipeline: instead of using a generative prior to complete the output of a feed-forward reconstructor, we treat the 3D generative prior itself as the primary reasoning mechanism for sparse-view reconstruction. We propose GenSfM , an end-to-end framework that formulates joint recovery of complete object structure and per-view camera motion as a single conditional inference problem in a native 3D diffusion model, as shown in Fig. 1 . The diffusion prior operates directly on a native 3D representation throughout inference, simultaneously denoising shape and per-view pose under joint self-attention. This grounds the generated object in the observed views while using object-level regularities to infer unobserved geometry.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Realizing this formulation requires a single diffusion transformer that jointly denoises a shared 3D shape with a per-view pose latent bound to its input image, while keeping the per-view pose-token overhead small as views are added. We adopt CUPID ’s Huang et al. (2025) 3D-native UV-volume pose tokenization, but compress each view’s pose latent to a compact token grid, since the dense volume over-parameterizes a low-DoF perspective projection. A learned view embedding tags each view’s pose latent and image tokens, binding pose to its source image. Since neither stream natively carries cross-view information, we prepend a small set of register tokens to the shape stream as a shared channel for all views to communicate through self-attention.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Instead of relying on back-projection to recover surface texture like feed-forward methods ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , we add a second stage of native 3D refinement and texturing ( Xiang et al., 2025 ) so that hidden regions stay coherent with the observed views. We design a pose-aware fine stage that, using the cameras predicted in the coarse stage, projects every active voxel into the input views and conditions denoising on per-voxel semantic and texture features sampled and averaged across views.

What requires both visible and hidden object structure, while where requires the camera motion relating the input views. content: Pose-centric approaches Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Sinha et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) target the where side, regressing relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity, but leave what largely untouched. More general feed-forward reconstructors Wang et al. (2024) ; Leroy et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) predict dense pointmaps, correspondences, and camera parameters jointly, addressing camera motion and visible geometry; hidden geometry, however, is recovered only indirectly through learned priors.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Native 3D generators trained on large 3D corpora Deitke et al. (2023) , such as TripoSR Tochilkin et al. (2024) , TRELLIS Xiang et al. (2025) , and Hunyuan3D Zhao et al. (2025b) , are strong on what : complete object structure is modeled explicitly and hidden geometry is hallucinated from the prior. They do not target where : camera motion is typically assumed and only weakly encoded through cross-attention, so applied directly to uncalibrated sparse views they can produce plausible but misaligned geometry.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: View-based generative SfM Zhao et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Xu et al. (2024a) ; Zhao and Tulsiani (2024) casts what and where as a joint generative problem in view space; DiffusionSfM, for instance, diffuses ray origins and endpoints to recover per-view geometry and camera motion jointly. Because diffusion operates over view-based quantities (rays, pointmaps, depths), hidden what is recovered only insofar as it can be back-projected from individual views.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Reconstruct-then-generate pipelines Ardelean et al. (2025) ; Huang et al. (2026) ; Chang et al. (2025) ; Team et al. (2025) ; Siddiqui et al. (2026) ; Yao et al. (2025) couple feed-forward reconstruction with native 3D generators: e.g., ReconViaGen Chang et al. (2025) injects VGGT Wang et al. (2025) geometry tokens into a 3D generator. These pipelines recover hidden geometry through the generative prior while grounding camera motion and visible structure with feed-forward geometry, but solve what and where in separate stages, so errors from the reconstruction backbone propagate into a 3D hypothesis that need not remain coherent with all input views.

content: We train our model on four public 3D-asset datasets: Objaverse-XL Deitke et al. (2023) (GitHub and Sketchfab partitions), HSSD Khanna et al. (2024) , 3D-FUTURE Fu et al. (2021) , and ABO Collins et al. (2022) . After TRELLIS ’s aesthetic filter ( ≥ 4.5 \geq 4.5 ), about 430 430 K instances remain. Each is rendered following TRELLIS ’s protocol, with 24 24 condition views at 1024 × 1024 1024{\times}1024 from cameras uniformly sampled on the upper hemisphere. We evaluate on two held-out test sets, Toys4k Stojanov et al. (2021) (synthetic) and GSO Downs et al. (2022) (real-captured), neither overlapping the training corpus.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: We assess photometric fidelity, 3D geometry, and camera-pose accuracy. Each test set uses its first 400 400 objects with two disjoint 4 4 -view sets, { 0 , 6 , 12 , 18 } \{0,6,12,18\} and { 3 , 9 , 15 , 21 } \{3,9,15,21\} , yielding 800 800 object–viewset instances for aggregation. As baselines fall into three capability families, we apply the most suitable evaluation protocol to each: (i) least squares on predicted vs ground-truth input-view pointmaps for feed-forward reconstruction, tight only with accurate predicted geometry and poses; (ii) similarity ICP on sampled point clouds for 3D generation; and (iii) gauge-invariant pairwise relative-pose comparison on unordered input-view pairs for pose-predicting methods. GenSfM is reevaluated under each applicable protocol; comparisons are restricted to methods sharing a table and protocol. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS Zhang et al. (2018) on 512 × 512 512{\times}512 novel views at the 8 held-out condition-view indices { 2 , 4 , 8 , 10 , 14 , 16 , 20 , 22 } \{2,4,8,10,14,16,20,22\} ; bidirectional Chamfer Distance (CD; reported as the median across objects, since a few severe failures dominate the mean) and F-scores at τ ∈ { 0.01 , 0.05 } \tau\in\{0.01,\,0.05\} ; and Relative Rotation Error (RRE) with Acc @ ⁡ { 5 ∘ , 15 ∘ } @\{5^{\circ},15^{\circ}\} , Relative Translation Error (RTE), and mean absolute FOV error (RFOV; only for methods that predict intrinsics). See App. A.1 for the full alignment protocol and App. A.2 for the pose metric definitions.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion

content: We compare against a representative set of multi-view image-to-3D baselines: (a) TRELLIS -S Xiang et al. (2025) : TRELLIS run as a single-image generator on each input view independently, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (b) TRELLIS -M Xiang et al. (2025) : TRELLIS with multi-view input in stochastic mode, where each denoising step is conditioned on one randomly chosen input view; (c) SAM 3D Team et al. (2025) : a single-image-to-3D generator run once per input view, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (d) FreeSplatter Xu et al. (2024b) : predicts per-view pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians together with input camera parameters in a pose-free setting; (e) LucidFusion He et al. (2025) : predicts per-view relative coordinate maps that are fused into a 3D Gaussian output; (f) ReconViaGen Chang et al. (2025) : combines feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement, using VGGT-derived geometry tokens to condition a 3D generator; (g) VGGT Wang et al. (2025) : a transformer that jointly regresses per-view pointmaps and camera extrinsics/intrinsics from uncalibrated images. Our table appear in three families: 3D generation (a,b,c,f), feed-forward reconstruction (d,e,f), and pose prediction (d,f,g).

content: Tab. 2 and Fig. 3 compare against feed-forward reconstruction baselines under input-view pointmap LSQ alignment. GenSfM outperforms every baseline on every metric and on both datasets, with the gap widening at the strict F@ ​ .01 \text{F@}.01 threshold and qualitatively in the form of alignment artifacts and surface noise. Feed-forward methods compound any disagreement between their predicted geometry and predicted poses, while a generative 3D-native model refines it away.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Tab. 3 and Fig. 4 compare against 3D generation models that produce a canonical, pose-free output, under similarity-ICP alignment. GenSfM leads on every metric, with the largest margins on the strict-threshold geometry metrics ( F@ ​ .01 \text{F@}.01 , CD-med). Pose-free baselines hallucinate plausible but mismatched detail on unseen sides; the two strong multi-view baselines ( TRELLIS -M’s stochastic per-step view conditioning and ReconViaGen’s feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement) still trail GenSfM by large margins, indicating the gain comes from joint shape–pose denoising rather than late-stage view sampling.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Tab. 4 reports camera-pose accuracy on baselines that predict input-view extrinsics. GenSfM achieves substantially lower rotation and translation errors, with Acc.@ 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} saturating; baselines commonly fail on symmetric objects whose orientation depends on low-level visual cues. Our model also recovers intrinsics accurately (known-intrinsics row shown for reference); VGGT, not trained on varying-FOV synthetic data, incurs large RFOV despite strong extrinsics, whereas GenSfM keeps RFOV under 3 ∘ 3^{\circ} on both datasets while saturating Acc.@ 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} . Thus, RFOV confirms reliable intrinsic recovery under varying FOV, but its margin over VGGT also reflects training-distribution coverage, not architecture alone.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: We ablate each design choice on Toys4k in Tab. 5 , with rows added cumulatively. In Stage 1, full cross-attention enables cross-view information sharing and improves all metrics; visual feature conditioning sharpens photometric fidelity and pose accuracy with only marginal geometry gains, suggesting appearance cues primarily help rendering and pose grounding; shared register tokens aggregate global information and contribute most to pose accuracy and the strict F@ ​ .01 \text{F@}.01 threshold. In Stage 2, a fine decoder trained natively on multi-view data sharpens photometric fidelity, while 3D geometry is already saturated. The decoder swap leaves raw coarse-stage cameras unchanged but shifts geometry-aligned pose metrics because their similarity fit depends on the final pointmap. Fig. 5 corroborates these trends qualitatively: surface details (e.g., the screwdriver cap, the snake’s head) sharpen left-to-right and the full model best matches GT.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: We presented GenSfM , which recasts a native 3D diffusion model as the primary inference mechanism for sparse-view object reconstruction, jointly denoising shape and per-view camera poses in a single multi-modal diffusion transformer. Three choices keep the formulation tractable: a UV-volume pose latent compressed to a compact token grid, a unified multi-modal sequence that places shape and per-view pose tokens in a single self-attention, and a pose-aware fine stage that conditions each voxel on features sampled at its pose-aligned image projection. On Toys4k and GSO, GenSfM outperforms feed-forward, 3D-generation, and pose-prediction baselines on photometric, geometric, and pose metrics simultaneously, recovering both extrinsics and intrinsics to high accuracy without any external pose estimator or post-hoc optimization.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Our results are restricted to object-centric inputs at N = 4 N{=}4 ; extending to larger view counts, scene-level inputs, and in-the-wild captures with looser segmentation is a natural next step. Under distribution shift, large pose/calibration errors may misregister fine-stage image features, degrading local refinement while the coarse 3D prior preserves global completion. The model also inherits the object distribution and resolution limits of its TRELLIS backbone, so scaling the underlying generator should directly improve sparse-view recovery.

content: Our baselines differ in what they natively output (input-view pointmaps, canonical pose-free 3D, or input-camera poses), so a single shared alignment would unfairly discard the structure each method already provides. We therefore align each prediction with the protocol best matched to its output family before evaluating, and GenSfM is evaluated under each applicable family using that family’s protocol so all comparisons within a table are like-for-like.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: This protocol applies to feed-forward reconstruction methods (LucidFusion, FreeSplatter, ReconViaGen), which already place geometry in a noisy estimate of the input-camera frame. For each input view, we back-project the per-pixel predicted depth at the predicted camera into 3D, alpha-mask the result, randomly subsample to at most 50K points per view, and pair it with the GT pointmap obtained by back-projecting GT depth at the GT camera. Stacking the per-view pairs with equal aggregate weight per view yields one set of 3D-to-3D correspondences per object, which we fit with a closed-form Umeyama similarity ( Umeyama, 2002 ) . The resulting transform is applied once to the full predicted 3D before all photometric and geometric evaluation; we log the per-object LSQ residual as an alignment-fidelity diagnostic. Note that this protocol exercises both halves of feed-forward reconstruction: the matched correspondences require the predicted geometry to align with the predicted cameras, so a method with weak geometry, weak pose recovery, or any mismatch between the two will produce noisy correspondences and a loose Umeyama fit, inflating all downstream metrics.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: This protocol applies to 3D generation methods (TRELLIS-S, TRELLIS-M, SAM 3D), which output a canonical pose-free 3D, and to GenSfM when evaluated under the same family. To obtain the prediction-side point cloud uniformly across output formats (whether the prediction is a mesh or a set of 3D Gaussians), we render depth from a set of orbiting random views around the prediction and back-project the depth maps into 3D, which yields a well-covered surface point cloud without surface-sampling biases specific to the underlying representation. The GT-side cloud is sampled directly on the GT mesh surface. We initialize alignment by sweeping the 24 orientation-preserving signed axis permutations of the PCA-aligned bounding box and keep the candidate with the lowest post-ICP residual; we then refine with similarity ICP and use the resulting transform to map the prediction into the GT frame for evaluation.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Different pose-predicting baselines fix their world frame in different ways (some anchor to the first input view, some to an internal canonical frame, others through their own internal similarity fit), so absolute predicted extrinsics cannot be directly compared to GT extrinsics. To bypass this gauge ambiguity entirely, all metrics in Table 4 are computed on unordered pairs of input views: for each pair, the relative pose between the two views cancels any global rotation, translation, and scale that affects all views jointly, leaving only the camera geometry intrinsic to the pair. We adopt this pairwise form uniformly for both rotation and translation rather than anchoring to one reference view, which would entangle every error with the chosen anchor. For each object, we average each metric over the N ⁡ ( N − 1 ) / 2 N(N{-}1)/2 unordered pairs and then average across objects. Relative Rotation Error (RRE) is the geodesic angle (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative rotations of the pair; Acc.@ 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} / Acc.@ 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} is the fraction of pairs whose RRE falls below the corresponding threshold; Relative Translation Error (RTE) is the angular error (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative-translation directions, an angular form chosen because absolute translation magnitude is itself gauge-dependent (a global similarity scale can be reabsorbed by any consistent rescaling of all camera centers); and Field-of-View Error (RFOV) is the mean absolute difference (in degrees) between predicted and GT FOV, computed directly on intrinsics without any pose alignment, since intrinsics are independent of the world frame. To score baselines with a coarse front/back chirality ambiguity on geometric correctness rather than chirality alone, all angular metrics (RRE, Acc.@ { 5 ∘ , 15 ∘ } \{5^{\circ},15^{\circ}\} , RTE) are read off after collapsing R pred ​ R gt ⊤ R_{\text{pred}}R_{\text{gt}}^{\top} under the diag ⁡ ( ± 1 , ± 1 , − 1 ) \mathrm{diag}(\pm 1,\pm 1,-1) sign-flip equivalence class. The same rule is applied uniformly to all methods, including ours, to compare geometric recovery under a shared front/back equivalence. Chirality remains relevant for camera-dependent applications, so we explicitly note that this metric does not assess that failure mode.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: The pose VAE is a 3D-convolutional encoder–decoder over a 64 3 64^{3} voxel grid with a deliberately aggressive bottleneck: four 2 × 2{\times} spatial downsamples compress the input into a 4 3 4^{3} token grid with 8 8 channels per token. This compression is feasible because each per-voxel target is a smooth function of voxel position and a low-DoF camera, so the latent does not need to absorb high-frequency content. Per voxel the encoder receives three input channels (a binary in-frustum indicator plus the two pixel coordinates obtained by projecting the voxel center under the input camera), and the decoder emits the same three channels through a classification head (visibility mask) and a regression head (pixel UV).

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: We use a dice loss on the visibility classifier and an L1 loss on the UV regression, with a small KL weight ( 10 − 3 10^{-3} ) so the latent stays close to a standard Gaussian for the downstream diffusion stage. The training distribution matches inference: each minibatch sample takes a real camera pose from the multi-view renders of a sampled training object and projects it on the fly into the 64 3 64^{3} voxel grid. We optimize for 1 1 M steps with AdamW (lr 3 × 10 − 4 3{\times}10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} ) on a cosine schedule.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
content: Voxel centers can project outside the input image. We handle this by clamping target UVs to [ 0 , 1 ] 2 [0,1]^{2} rather than dropping out-of-frame voxels, keeping the decoder output well-defined everywhere. The visibility channel encodes the same in-/out-of-frame information as a binary indicator with a small 1 % 1\% inset margin ( 0.01 ≤ u , v ≤ 0.99 0.01\leq u,v\leq 0.99 ); the inference DLT solve uses this channel to restrict to in-frustum voxels, so saturated boundary UVs never contaminate the recovered pose. The UV reconstruction loss is applied uniformly to all voxels rather than only the in-frustum subset, keeping saturated-boundary regions consistent between encoder and decoder.

We encode each held-out 64 3 64^{3} ground-truth UV volume to the chosen latent grid, decode back, and recover camera pose via a DLT solve over in-frustum voxels. UV Dist. is the per-voxel L2 distance in normalized image coordinates; RRE , RTE , and RFOV are the standard rotation, translation-direction, and FOV errors in degrees. All three latent resolutions deliver near-identical pose accuracy (within a few hundredths of a degree on RRE/RTE/RFOV), and even the worst row stays an order of magnitude below the downstream pose-prediction residuals in Table 4 , so the latent is not the bottleneck on overall pose accuracy. We adopt the 4 3 4^{3} latent in the main paper as the most compute-efficient operating point, since the larger grids carry 8 × 8\times and 64 × 64\times more tokens at no measurable pose gain.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
section: Coarse stage: dual-stream encoder and token fusion.
content: Each view is encoded by two complementary streams that fuse into a single per-view token sequence for the coarse DiT to cross-attend to. A frozen DINOv2-L/14 with registers at 518 × 518 518{\times}518 produces 1374 1374 tokens per view (CLS + 4 registers + a 37 × 37 37{\times}37 patch grid) at 1024 1024 channels, supplying object-level semantics. In parallel, a lightweight 4-level CNN at 296 × 296 296{\times}296 ( 5 × 5 5{\times}5 convolutions, strides { 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 } \{1,2,2,2\} , output channels [ 6 , 6 , 6 , 8 ] [6,6,6,8] ) is patchified down to the same 37 × 37 37{\times}37 grid, with per-token contributions [ 384 , 96 , 24 , 8 ] [384,96,24,8] channel-concatenating into a 512 512 -dim local-texture feature. We append the 512 512 local channels onto the 1024 1024 semantic channels at every patch token (non-patch tokens zero-pad on the local side), giving a uniform per-token width of 1536 1536 and a cross-attention key/value of length N × 1374 N\times 1374 . The two streams are deliberately complementary: semantic anchors pose to image content, while local texture restores the pixel-faithful appearance cues the semantic encoder has discarded, letting cross-attention recover accurate cameras without polluting the joint self-attention with raw image tokens.

section: Fine stage: visual pyramid and per-voxel projection.
content: The fine stage refines up to L ≤ 32,768 L\leq 32{,}768 active voxels at 64 3 64^{3} under the cameras already recovered by the coarse stage. Cross-attending every voxel to thousands of image tokens per view is intractable, so we replace cross-attention with per-voxel pixel-aligned feature sampling: each voxel projects to 𝐮 j , i \mathbf{u}_{j,i} in view i i under the predicted camera, and visual features are bilinearly sampled at that pixel. The visual encoder is a ConvNeXt-style pyramid run once per view at 256 × 256 256{\times}256 : four stages, each one ConvNeXt block with a 7 × 7 7{\times}7 depthwise kernel at internal width 32 32 , with a 2 × 2{\times} downsample between stages. Each stage exposes a 4 4 -channel tap (LayerNorm + 1 × 1 1{\times}1 Conv); the four taps sampled at 𝐮 j , i \mathbf{u}_{j,i} and channel-concatenated yield a 16 16 -channel multi-scale texture feature 𝐜 j tex \mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{tex}}_{j} . We pair it with an 8 8 -channel semantic feature 𝐜 j sem \mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{j} : the coarse-stage DINOv2 patch tokens (reused, no extra DINOv2 pass) are bilinearly sampled at the same per-voxel projection and re-encoded through the frozen SLat encoder, placing them on the SLat target’s latent manifold and giving a compact 24 24 -channel per-voxel conditioning vector. This keeps fine-stage cost proportional to active voxels rather than view tokens, while the multi-scale taps let each voxel combine coarse contour cues with fine local texture without inflating the per-voxel width.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Large organizations now consume large language models (LLMs) from several vendors at once, and each vendor brings its own API dialect, credential model, streaming protocol, pricing and release cadence. Integrated directly, this heterogeneity yields credential sprawl, format lock-in, unbounded spend and inconsistent governance. We present the design and production operation of the Cosmos LLM Gateway , the governed entry point for enterprise LLM traffic at PayPal. The gateway is built on Envoy and splits work by latency profile: I/O-bound control decisions (authentication, credential brokering, policy and budget evaluation) run in an out-of-process external-processing service, while latency-sensitive payload work (wire-format translation, token metering and prompt-cache shaping) runs in-proxy as a Rust WebAssembly filter, so that, by default, streamed response body chunks never wait on an out-of-process call. Models, providers and prices are largely a validated data model rather than code. Governance is declarative policy evaluated by Open Policy Agent and managed through a control plane with role-scoped authoring for platform and business-unit administrators, approval workflows, scheduled activation, limited-access model releases, cohort-based pilots, shadow-mode rollout, configurable usage notifications and versioned policy-bundle distribution. For use cases that require it, a data-loss-prevention layer that combines pattern rules with an internally hosted detection model can block, redact or reversibly pseudonymize detected sensitive content before it reaches a provider. Every spend scope is a view over per-model usage counters, so a new budget applies to spend already recorded in its window without data migration, and every governed request is designed to yield one deduplicated usage record in the analytics warehouse. As of September 2026, the gateway serves more than 12,000 developers and hundreds of business use cases, including real-time voice support with more than 2,000 concurrent calls. It handles millions of requests and roughly 200 billion tokens per day across more than 100 models from multiple providers, at 99.999% availability to business. In a benchmark of the core request path against a synthetic upstream, it adds a median of 4 ms and a p99 of 11 ms of overhead at more than 2,200 requests per second on two 4-vCPU instances, with no failed requests across the tested range. We report the architecture, the policy model, an evaluation, and the lessons we would carry to any enterprise standardizing access to multiple AI providers.

content: Programmable proxies. Envoy [ 6 ] is a widely deployed layer-7 (L7) proxy with mature TLS, HTTP/2, WebSocket, load-balancing and telemetry support. It offers two extension mechanisms that matter here. The external processing filter (ext_proc) [ 7 ] streams request and response phases to a gRPC service that may inspect and mutate headers, bodies and trailers and may return an immediate response; it runs out of process and can be configured to fail open or closed. Proxy-Wasm [ 21 ] runs sandboxed WebAssembly modules inside the proxy’s worker threads, which suits per-byte work on streaming bodies.

content: LLM gateways. Open-source LLM proxies provide a unified API across vendors, typically as an application-level service [ 20 ] . Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) [ 1 ] and agentgateway [ 2 ] build AI-specific routing on top of proxy data planes, and cloud providers now offer managed AI gateways [ 5 , 13 ] . The closest design to ours, Agent Router, performs request translation, upstream authorization and token metering in an external processor, and names Envoy dynamic modules as a possible higher-performance alternative [ 1 ] . A single streamed response can carry thousands of chunks, and we did not want to pay a network round trip to an external process for each of them. We therefore keep only I/O-bound decisions out of process and run per-chunk translation and metering in-proxy as WebAssembly (section 5 ). We evaluated an off-the-shelf proxy before building. Basic routing worked, but at the time of evaluation it did not meet our requirements for real-time (WebSocket) traffic, identity-aware authorization, enforceable user- and organization-level budgets, or workload-identity-based cloud credentials. Our design shares the proxy-native approach of these projects. It differs mainly in the governance layer: organization-anchored policy, retroactive spend scopes, and a managed policy lifecycle.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Authorization and policy as code. Zanzibar [ 19 ] established relationship-based authorization at global scale. Open Policy Agent (OPA) [ 17 ] popularized declarative, side-effect-free policy evaluated against injected data. We use OPA as the decision engine. The gateway gathers state and performs effects, which keeps decisions pure, testable and replayable (section 9 ).

content: Cost-aware model use and serving. FrugalGPT [ 4 ] and RouteLLM [ 16 ] route queries across models to trade cost against quality. Serving systems such as vLLM [ 12 ] and SGLang [ 24 ] optimize inference itself. These lines of work complement ours: a gateway is the natural place to enforce the budget decisions that a router optimizes for, and it sits above the serving systems that host open-weight models.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: Figure 1: Architecture. One governed entry point fronts enterprise LLM traffic. On the unified API, the control service makes I/O-bound decisions out of process and fails closed, and the Wasm filter translates and meters in process. Real-time sessions use a connection-oriented path tuned for long-lived streams. The control plane publishes versioned policy bundles that the data plane enforces on every request. The shaded region is PayPal’s private network: self-hosted open-weight models run inside it, and external providers are reached with brokered credentials.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Figure 1 shows the system. A single TLS listener terminates all traffic and routes it by path through the same Envoy pod. Unified API requests pass through the control path (authentication, policy, data protection and credential brokering), translation and metering in the Wasm filter, and an upstream call with a brokered credential (section 5 ). Real-time voice APIs run over WebSocket; for these, Envoy holds each long-lived connection on its event loop and forwards audio frames as they arrive, without body buffering (section 12 ).

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: Behind the data plane sit three supporting planes. The control plane holds the authoritative model registry, prices and governance policy, exposes a management API for platform and business-unit (BU) administrators, and publishes versioned policy bundles. The identity plane mints verifiable JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) for platforms that call the gateway on behalf of users. The telemetry plane carries metrics, traces and durable per-request usage records into the analytics warehouse.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: Deployment. The gateway runs on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in multiple regions with disaster recovery. Closed-weight models such as Gemini and Claude are served, where supported, through the global endpoint of Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI Platform), which avoids dependence on a single regional endpoint. Open-weight models run on an internal GKE inference stack built on vLLM [ 12 ] , SGLang [ 24 ] and NVIDIA Dynamo [ 15 ] . Other providers are reached over the network with brokered credentials. The caller does not need to know where a model runs.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: The most consequential design decision was to refuse the trade-off between governed and fast . Governance decisions are I/O-bound: they need identity validation, the organizational hierarchy, spend counters and secret material. They therefore run out of process in a Go ext_proc service that scales independently of the proxy. Payload work is CPU-bound, sits on the critical path of every streamed byte, and needs no network I/O. It therefore runs inside Envoy as a Rust Proxy-Wasm filter, so that a streamed response is translated and metered chunk by chunk without waiting on any out-of-process call.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Below, the control service is the Go service behind the control ext_proc, the metrics service is the service behind the metrics ext_proc, and the Wasm filter is the in-process translation filter (translate.wasm in fig. 1 ). The HTTP filter chain runs in a fixed order: (1) the control ext_proc, configured to fail closed, which receives the buffered request body because the routing key ( model ) is in the body; (2) a metrics ext_proc, configured to fail open, which runs after control and therefore observes the request as authorized and rewritten; (3) the translation Wasm filter; (4) a small buffer filter that restores Content-Length after translation, because some upstreams reject chunked request bodies and Proxy-Wasm cannot set headers during the body phase; and (5) the router. Table 1 lists the ext_proc processing modes. The metrics service runs in Envoy’s observability mode , in which bodies are mirrored to it asynchronously and never held. The control service buffers only the request body, skips response headers and bodies entirely, and is invoked again only for response trailers, where it reads usage. By default, the streamed response body therefore sits on the blocking critical path of exactly one extension, the in-process filter; the metrics service sees a non-blocking mirror, and the control service is consulted again only for the trailers at the end of the stream. In production, the metrics service derives metrics from mirrored bodies without persisting their content.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Figure 2 traces a unified request. In the request-headers phase the control service records the entry wire format (from the path) and the caller’s credential; Envoy then delivers the buffered, size-bounded body. In the request-body phase it authenticates the caller, extracts the model, resolves it through the registry, evaluates model access, brokers the upstream credential, evaluates rate and spend policy, sets the handoff headers for the Wasm filter, rewrites the path, and asks Envoy to clear its route cache so that Envoy re-selects the vendor route and cluster for the rewritten request. It also attaches attribution metadata for the access log. The Wasm filter then translates the request into the upstream format. On the response, the filter translates each chunk back into the client’s format, taps token usage from the stream, and emits usage as response trailers. In the response-trailers phase the control service prices the request from the registry, records spend, attaches cost metadata, and invalidates a cached upstream credential if the vendor returned 401 or 403.

content: The Go control service and the Rust filter communicate only through a small, versioned contract of gateway-internal request metadata and response trailers, which carry the entry and upstream wire formats, the upstream model, token usage, a count of unclassified fields and the tools the model invoked. The contract lives in one machine-readable file that also names the access-log metadata fields (section 11 ). Test suites in both languages assert their constants against it, so any drift fails the build, and an unrecognized value is never reinterpreted. In practice, this explicit cross-language contract removed a class of integration bugs that otherwise surfaced only in end-to-end tests.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: Each component on the request path had to answer one question: if this breaks, what happens to the request? Table 2 summarizes the answers. The asymmetry is deliberate. An access or data-protection rule that silently stops enforcing during an outage is not a rule, so those decisions fail closed. A telemetry outage must never become a traffic outage, so observability fails open. New budgets are rolled out in shadow mode first, which is designed to keep a defect in a newly introduced policy from taking AI tooling offline for the whole organization. Together these rules make degradation graceful and predictable: telemetry failures never reach the caller, a failed policy update leaves the last good revision in force, and an invalid configuration is rejected before it serves traffic.

content: Early versions encoded vendor selection, upstream paths and capability flags in code. That made every new model a deployment, and nothing could be edited by an administrator. We replaced it with a registry : a typed, declarative model of everything the gateway supports. Model resolution, upstream paths, capability gating and prices all come from the registry. The code keeps a path-template substitutor, the credential resolvers (which perform I/O), and a small number of provider-specific adaptations for vendor quirks, such as session-affinity headers.

A price may also define a long-context tier that applies when the prompt (input, cache-read and cache-write tokens) exceeds a threshold. For a request with token counts n k n_{k} and the applicable tier’s rates p k p_{k} , the cost in micro-dollars is ∑ k n k ​ p k \sum_{k}n_{k}p_{k} . A price change is therefore a registry edit that takes effect within one publication cycle, and the management API validates prices on every write: units come from an allow list, every rate is non-negative, and unknown keys are rejected.

content: From file to database. The registry began as a version-controlled file and now has a durable store behind the management API (section 10.1 ). A leader-elected projector rebuilds the served registry deterministically whenever the store’s epoch changes and publishes it through the same bundle channel as policy (section 10 ). The data plane validates the projected registry when it loads it; an invalid or missing bundle fails configuration. Registry and policy epochs are independent, so a catalog change never requires rewriting policy rules, and vice versa; registry and access data are published in the same bundle.

content: A canonical IR: N N codecs, not N ⁡ ( N − 1 ) N(N-1) converters. Every wire format decodes into, and encodes out of, one canonical intermediate representation (IR). An any-to-any conversion is decode → \rightarrow IR → \rightarrow encode . Each codec translates only between the IR and one wire format, with no knowledge of other formats, so adding a format costs one codec rather than one converter per existing format. The system has five general-purpose codecs, plus raw adapters for a small number of internal formats.

content: Both fast paths are lossless for client content because they never build the IR. Table 3 shows the plan for the main entry and upstream pairs. OpenAI Chat to OpenAI Chat is a deliberate exception to identity. Gemini, served through an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, returns a thought_signature [ 9 ] on each tool call (in a vendor extension field, extra_content ) and requires it to be sent back on the next turn; some agent clients drop unrecognized fields when they echo the conversation, which would break multi-turn tool use. On the response, the codec therefore reversibly encodes the signature into the tool-call identifier, which clients must echo verbatim to correlate tool results. On the next request, it decodes the identifier, restores the original ID and reinstates the signature in the extension field before forwarding upstream. The mechanism is stateless and applies only to signatures attached to tool calls; the Anthropic Messages and OpenAI Responses codecs use the same identifier encoding.

content: Streaming. Server-sent event streams are converted incrementally. A decoder maps wire chunks to IR stream events (message start, content-block start, text and tool-argument deltas, block stop, usage, message stop), and an encoder maps those events to the target’s event grammar. Per-stream decode and encode state carries partial bytes across chunk boundaries, maps the wire stream’s content-block indices onto the IR’s indexed blocks, and buffers nothing beyond an incomplete event. Reasoning signatures that some vendors require to be echoed on the next turn are carried through the IR, so multi-turn tool use survives a format change. Token usage is tapped from the stream and reported in trailers without altering the passthrough bytes. Because Proxy-Wasm forbids header writes during the body phase, all metadata produced while streaming leaves the filter as trailers.

content: Gateway-side prompt caching. Coding agents resend long, stable prefixes (system prompts, tool definitions, conversation history) on every turn. The filter injects cache breakpoints on the last tool definition, the system prompt and the most recent content block, within the vendor’s limit of four breakpoints [ 3 ] and without removing breakpoints the client already set, and it requests an extended (one-hour) cache lifetime for all of them. This shaping applies on the Anthropic-on-Vertex upstream path. For providers that support it, the control service can also add a stable, hashed session-affinity key derived from the caller’s identity (and the client’s session where available), enabled per provider or for a configurable share of traffic, so that repeated turns land on warm caches. Clients get these benefits without changing any code; the effect is reported in section 13 .

Business applications present an application credential bound to a registered application, so that usage is attributed to that application rather than to an individual. Platforms that act on behalf of users present tokens from the mint service described below. Personal and platform-minted tokens resolve to a person, whom the policy layer evaluates against the organizational hierarchy; application credentials resolve to the registered application.

content: Detection inside the enterprise boundary. Detecting sensitive data in free text is harder than matching patterns: the same date or number can be harmless in one sentence and sensitive in the next. Detection therefore combines deterministic pattern rules with an internally hosted, purpose-trained detection model that uses the surrounding context. Both run inside the enterprise boundary, so content is inspected before any vendor call is made. Detection is probabilistic, and accuracy varies by entity type. DLP therefore reduces exposure rather than guaranteeing that no sensitive value is ever sent, and it complements, rather than replaces, use-case data classification and provider contractual controls.

content: Policy-driven actions. Each use case is configured with its own DLP policy, because data classification, security zone and tolerance for false positives differ between use cases. From most to least restrictive, a policy can block a request that contains sensitive data; redact the sensitive spans by masking or removing them; or pseudonymize them, replacing each value with a realistic surrogate of the same format and restoring the original values in the response. For these use cases the gateway also handles the response body: the original values that were swapped out are held for the duration of the request and substituted back for their surrogates before the response is returned to the client. Redaction is simple but can distort the task (a model asked to apply an age-based rule cannot reason about a masked date). Pseudonymization preserves the format of each detected value while the provider never sees the detected originals, which makes it well suited to conversational use cases.

content: Operational properties. DLP is integrated into the gateway API and is enforceable per use case: an application adopts it through per-use-case configuration and a request-level enforcement flag rather than an extra service call or SDK change. Inspection fails closed: if a check cannot complete, the request is not sent. DLP events are logged for security monitoring and audit. Together with a mediated path, attribution and consistent usage records, these are technical controls that can contribute to the organization’s broader compliance programs; the gateway does not by itself establish compliance with any regulatory framework.

content: Access is layered (table 4 ). Each access layer can only narrow what the layers above it allow (an authoritative pilot’s cohort lists decide access for its enrolled users, section 10.2 ), and each is evaluated before any vendor credential is issued. Spend caps work differently: an approved business-unit override can raise a platform cap, but only within the platform’s locks (sections 9.2 and 10.2 ). Model restrictions name organization leaders rather than teams: a model may carry a leader deny list, an optional leader allow list, and explicit per-person exemptions. A caller belongs to a leader’s organization when that leader appears in the caller’s upward reporting chain. The chain is resolved from the people directory through a cache, with the organization snapshot distributed in the policy bundle as a fallback (section 10 ). Because rules name leaders rather than team lists, a reorganization that moves a team automatically moves its access and budgets, with no policy edits.

content: Actions compose. Block is stateless and recomputed per request, so it clears automatically when the window rolls over. Pause blocks for a fixed duration and fires at most once per rule and window, so a user who returns hours later is not penalized again. Message adds a live status line, and email notifies the user or, as a deferred digest, the leadership chain (section 10.3 ). A separate no-promote action can bar a population from self-service tier promotion (section 9.3 ).

content: This formulation has a property that matters operationally. Because tags are resolved at evaluation time over counters keyed by immutable model identifiers, a newly created tag or rule immediately governs spend recorded earlier in the current window, before the rule existed . No backfill, key rewrite or migration is needed. A business-unit policy such as “cap each person in this BU at a monthly amount for Opus-class models” (a vendor’s largest model family) is a single data change that takes effect over the month to date. Business-unit policies are entries whose population predicate selects that unit; their caps apply per person (section 10 ). Retroactive scope is not retroactive repricing : counters are already denominated in micro-dollars at the price in force when each request completed, so a later price change affects only subsequent requests. The same property lets a draft rule be dry-run against current usage before it is enabled (section 10 ). Appendix B shows the rule language.

content: We moved policy evaluation from imperative code to OPA [ 17 ] and its policy language, Rego. The dividing line is strict: the gateway gathers state and performs effects; Rego decides . Before evaluation, the control service assembles an input document containing the caller, canonical model, tier, organization chain, the summed spend per (scope, window), pause state, window boundaries and the enforcement switch. Evaluation returns a decision (block or allow, the limiting entry, a retry-after hint and per-limit utilization). The gateway then performs any side effects: updating counters, recording pauses and one-shot notifications, and queuing emails. Listing 1 gives a simplified illustration.

The pilot module is deliberately isolated from platform and BU policy documents, and the policy test target checks that separation. On the request path, an enrolled pilot decision overrides the platform and BU decision only when pilot enforcement is authoritative.

content: Keeping decisions pure gave us four practical benefits. Policies are unit-testable, and the policy suite requires coverage of every production module. A “what-if” admission query can preview a proposed change without touching live state. The policy and organization data are distributed as a versioned bundle (section 10 ), so every data-plane replica evaluates the same revision. And the migration itself was safe: the previous Go engine and the OPA engine ran side by side behind a selector while a parity suite checked identical decisions across all combinations of engine and enforcement mode, together with hot-reload tests of updated rules.

content: Roles and trust. Administrators authenticate through corporate single sign-on, and the gateway maps each administrator onto one of two canonical roles. Platform administrators act organization-wide. BU administrators act only within the business units they have been granted.

content: Onboarding a model is a sequence of validated data changes through the management API (fig. 5 ). A platform administrator creates the model (brand, API family, entry formats, aliases, tags, capabilities) and then its deployments, each with provider, region, priority and price. Every write is validated against the registry topology, capability and pricing rules; updates and deletes require an entity-tag precondition (missing returns 428, stale returns 409), and an idempotency key makes retries safe. Until it has an enabled deployment, a model is staged and not served. A new model can first be released as limited access to a bounded named roster, with its own spend windows, amounts and expiry, or through a pilot. It is then graduated , which clears the roster and makes the model generally available. Because policies can select models by tag, a newly tagged model is covered by existing restrictions and budgets within one publication cycle, with no policy edit. A model cannot be deleted while a live policy references it, and every step is recorded in the activity log.
