content: Platform policies set organization-wide controls: per-person runaway-cost limits, per-model caps, model-access decisions, and locks that BU policies cannot exceed. Conflict checks scan the complete active set before a change is accepted, and caps must be strictly ordered across windows (a monthly cap exceeds the weekly cap, which exceeds the daily cap).

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: BU policies let business-unit administrators set per-person and per-model caps and model toggles for their own organization, within the platform’s locks: an unlocked BU cap takes precedence over the platform baseline, a request above a locked maximum is rejected (and any stored cap is clamped to that maximum when policies are applied), and an exact lock rejects any change. BU model toggles take effect without approval but cannot re-enable a model the platform has locked. Controls can select models explicitly or by tag, and tag selections follow the registry.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Approvals and scheduling. BU cap changes are either submitted to an approval queue, where they do not affect enforcement until approved, or auto-approved where the platform allows it. Decisions are restricted to platform administrators, self-approval is forbidden, a rejection must include a comment, and an approval can be bound to the reviewed diff so that edits arriving in between are detected. Changes can be scheduled to activate at midnight in a given timezone. A leader-gated scheduler applies them, expires stale requests, and re-projects whenever the store’s epoch is ahead of the served bundle, so the durable record and the enforced bundle converge.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Pilots. New models and new budget regimes are introduced through pilots : named, date-bounded programs of a small number of cohorts. Each cohort has its own cost controls, model-access lists, BU assignment, alerts and exceptions. Cohorts that share a leader and window but have distinct amounts form a tier ladder . An enrolled user is governed by the lowest tier whose exceptions do not cover them, so an exception promotes a user up the ladder rather than removing the cap. Validation returns every violation at once (double enrollment, duplicate controls, duplicate tier amounts, unknown or empty tag selections), and writes serialize across replicas under a database advisory lock. Pilot enforcement has its own switch: off , shadow (evaluate and log only) or authoritative .

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Users should learn that they are approaching a limit long before they hit it. Notification points are configurable at two levels. In the rule language, any entry can attach an email or status-line action at its own threshold; the typical pattern is a warning email at 90% of an allowance and a block plus email at 100% (appendix B ). In managed policies, each control carries alerts at administrator-chosen percentages (1–100%), each with at least one channel (email or in-tool message) and a template. Templates are managed through the API, are scoped to the platform or to a business unit, and support placeholders such as utilization percentage, threshold, resume time, model, window, person and business unit. Delivery is deduplicated per policy owner, window instance, threshold, template and channel, so a user receives one email per crossing rather than one per request. Status headers on every response report the governing limit’s utilization, status, scope, reset time and any pause, and coding agents and the developer CLI render them as a live status line. Leadership notifications are deferred into one digest per leader after the window boundary. The usage API reports utilization as percentages.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Shadow first. Usage tracking is always on, and enforcement is a separate switch, set globally and per pilot. New controls are therefore rolled out in shadow mode against real traffic, with utilization visible to users and administrators and nothing blocked, until their effect is understood. Because scopes are views over current-window counters, a draft rule can also be dry-run against current usage before it is enabled. A rule enabled directly while enforcement is on applies to the window to date and can block at once, which is why new controls go through shadow mode or a pilot first.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Distribution. The durable store is the system of record. A leader-elected projector builds a deterministic bundle containing policy, registry-derived access data and the organization snapshot, and serves it with an entity tag. Data-plane replicas poll conditionally and hot-reload. A failed reload keeps the last good revision, and an engine whose initial bundle fails to compile refuses to serve. API responses distinguish the saved revision from the enforced revision, so administrators can see when a change is live.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Audit. Every mutation writes an append-only activity record; policy changes write it in the same transaction as the change. Records can be filtered by category, outcome, actor and role; platform administrators see all records, and BU administrators see their own business units.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Metrics and traces. Envoy’s native statistics (upstream health, circuit breakers, connections, latency and response classes) and application metrics (requests, latency, token counts by kind, cache reads and writes, cost, rate-limit events, and schema-drift counts) are exported through OpenTelemetry [ 18 ] . Labels identify the canonical model, vendor and entry path, and aliases collapse to canonical identifiers so that each logical model is counted once. Per-caller dimensions are limited to a small set of governance events (such as limit blocks); full per-request attribution lives in the usage record, which keeps metric cardinality bounded and identity data in an access-controlled store.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: The access log as the system of record. We initially emitted usage events from the control service through an asynchronous in-memory queue. That design lost data silently: when the queue was full, after retries were exhausted, during pod shutdown, and when a client disconnected before the trailers arrived. We moved the durable record to Envoy’s access log, which Envoy writes for every stream, including resets, immediate rejections and control-service outages. The control service contributes attribution (user, application, tier, platform, workflow, harness, requested and canonical model, entry and upstream formats) and the priced cost breakdown as metadata assembled from in-memory state only. Assembling this metadata adds no I/O to any ext_proc phase. The Wasm filter contributes per-field token counts as trailers. Interrupted streams still produce a usage record. Blocked requests (4xx immediate responses for authentication failures, invalid requests, access denials and limits) carry the same attribution, which makes rejected traffic visible to abuse and chargeback analysis. The earlier event pipeline was run in parallel during migration so the two could be reconciled.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: From log line to warehouse. Each record is one JSON line on standard output. A node-level logging agent ships it to a managed log service, from which the records are routed to the analytics warehouse. Rows are projected into a typed usage table, partitioned by day and clustered by caller and model, and a view deduplicates on the gateway-generated request ID, which clients cannot spoof. From the logging agent onward, delivery is at-least-once with read-time deduplication, barring node loss. Once a line reaches standard output it sits on node disk under the container runtime’s management, so a crash of the gateway process afterwards does not lose it. The residual loss window is bounded: a hard proxy crash can lose at most one flush interval of buffered entries (below), and a node failure can lose seconds of unshipped agent buffer. This replaced the unbounded, silent loss modes of the earlier in-process queue. The schema is additive-only and versioned, so new fields require no infrastructure change. These records, one per request with tokens and cost by component, drive chargeback and usage analytics. Appendix C lists the fields.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Implementation details that mattered. First, Envoy silently drops dynamic metadata returned by an ext_proc service unless the filter allow-lists the receiving namespaces. Without the allow list, every metadata-derived column is null, and only an end-to-end test against a real Envoy caught it. Second, Envoy is configured to flush access-log entries every few seconds for streams that are still open, rather than only when a stream closes, which bounds what a hard proxy crash can lose on a long stream at negligible I/O cost. Periodic entries preserve the record and its attribution; usage is carried by the entry written when the stream ends. Third, Envoy is configured not to preserve client-supplied request IDs, so a client cannot poison the deduplication key.

content: Context-engineering signals. The Wasm filter reports which tools a model actually invoked. Combined with the tools a client declared, this lets the platform identify MCP servers and tools that a user keeps declaring across requests within a 24-hour session window but that the model never invokes, and return per-user recommendations with the estimated token savings per request of removing them.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
content: Voice changed the problem. Our previous gateway was built for short request–response exchanges behind a request-oriented L7 load balancer. Chat traffic suited it, because each request released its resources almost immediately. A voice call is different: one WebSocket held for the whole conversation and streaming audio in both directions. Two thousand concurrent calls of up to 30 minutes each pinned per-session resources for the life of the call in a service sized for sub-second requests. In addition, a load balancer that balances requests is a poor fit for long-lived connections . Envoy resolves both problems: a call becomes a connection multiplexed on Envoy’s per-worker event loops, and connection lifecycle is a first-class proxy concept.

title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

content: A connection-oriented path. Real-time routes are tuned for long-lived sessions: frames are forwarded as they arrive, with no body buffering and no request timeout, and an idle timeout reclaims abandoned connections. Real-time sessions are recorded in the same access log and proxy metrics as other traffic, and real-time model endpoints are available in more than one region.

content: Regional placement and failover. The gateway runs in multiple regions with disaster recovery and load balancing. Where a data-residency endpoint is configured for a vendor, it is the default. Automatic fallback to another endpoint is a single retry, limited to connection-level failures and service-unavailable responses; other errors are returned to the client rather than retried, which keeps retries from amplifying load during a vendor incident.

content: Migration without a big bang. The gateway reached its current form without asking any team to change its integration. First, Envoy was placed in front of the existing service, so nothing behind it changed. Then authentication, credential brokering, translation, spend and policy moved into the new data plane one capability at a time, behind the same entry point, following a strangler-fig pattern [ 8 ] . Progress was measured continuously, and the previous implementation is being retired capability by capability.

content: Method. We measured the latency the gateway adds with a Locust load generator (user ramp of 500 users/s, think time 0.5–1 s) against a synthetic upstream with a fixed 110 ms latency. Each instance has 4 vCPU and 8 GiB, split evenly between one Envoy pod and one control-service pod. Load steps use 1,000 and 2,000 virtual users. Every request carries a unique payload, and each load step runs for five minutes. Overhead is the time from the start of the client request to the start of the upstream response, minus the upstream service time, both recorded by Envoy at microsecond resolution; it therefore measures the request path up to the upstream call and excludes response-body work. We ran two and four instances with 1,000 and 2,000 virtual users (about 1,100 and 2,300 requests per second) against the unified chat-completions path.

content: Effect of centralization. Several outcomes were not achievable under direct integration. Governed AI traffic now flows through one mediated entry point, and model calls carry per-user or per-application, per-platform and per-workflow attribution and a priced usage record. Model choice is configuration: switching the vendor or region behind a model requires no application change, and onboarding a new model or changing a price is a validated data change. Budgets are organization-aware, shadow-testable and retroactive within their window, and users are typically warned before they reach a limit. Engineers reach approved models through their supported entry formats with no vendor keys to manage and no per-team provisioning. Gateway-level prompt-cache shaping reached hit rates of up to 96% on agentic coding workloads, which lowers input cost, since cache reads are billed at a discount [ 3 ] , and can reduce time to first token, with no client changes.

content: The gateway is security- and cost-critical, so we treat its correctness as a product requirement. Continuous integration runs the Go and Rust test suites with a coverage floor, the policy test suite (which requires coverage of every production policy module), bundle validation, and the cross-language contract tests for the handoff, together with a build-failing coverage test for codec field classification. An extended suite adds database-backed tests for the control-plane stores and engine-parity tests between the previous Go engine and the OPA engine. A synthetic upstream service lets end-to-end tests and benchmarks run without vendor spend. The data plane, control plane and identity services comprise roughly 45k lines of Go and 7k lines of Rust, with about 35k further lines of Go tests.

content: Several limitations remain. Centralizing access also concentrates risk: the gateway brokers credentials for every provider, so it is a high-value target whose own access, secret handling and change control must meet the standard of the most sensitive workload it serves. Our experience comes from one large organization, and other environments may weigh these trade-offs differently. Our overhead benchmark covers the core request path, and production overhead depends on the policies and features enabled for a workload. Data-loss prevention relies on a learned detector whose accuracy varies by entity type, so it reduces rather than eliminates exposure. Budget thresholds, notification points and data-protection policies are organization-specific and require ongoing tuning against real usage; the mechanisms described here make that tuning safe, but do not remove the need for it.

content: The Cosmos LLM Gateway shows that, in one large enterprise, the problems of LLM access (credential sprawl, format lock-in, ungoverned spend and uneven governance) could be addressed at a single layer while adding a median of a few milliseconds of measured request-path overhead (section 13 ) for the developers and products that depend on it. The architecture rests on a few choices: governance out of process and translation in process; models, prices and policy as validated data; spend scopes as views over counters keyed by immutable model identifiers; pure policy decisions distributed as versioned bundles and introduced in shadow mode, with users normally warned before they are blocked; and a durable, priced usage record written where it is hardest to lose. Viewed this way, an enterprise LLM gateway is neither just a router nor just a policy engine. It is the platform layer that absorbs vendor multiplicity, credential variability and format heterogeneity into one governed substrate, so that a developer writes against one API, presents one identity, and reaches the right model through its supported entry formats with governance, attribution and observability applied by default.

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
section: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
content: Trajectory-based confidence estimation has shown promising performance for large language models (LLMs) by leveraging rich signals from their reasoning processes. However, we find that such confidence estimators can degrade substantially after agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) as it induces substantial shifts in the reasoning trajectories. More importantly, despite these shifts, we uncover a reliability structure that is largely preserved across Base and RL models: more stable trajectories remain more likely to produce correct answers . This preserved relationship provides a transferable, label-free reliability signal for post-RL confidence adaptation. Building on this finding, we propose StaR-TTA , a stability-guided framework for label-free test-time confidence adaptation. StaR-TTA jointly learns from correctness supervision and stability-derived reliability supervision on labeled Base trajectories, establishing the connection between trajectory stability and answer reliability. At test time, it reuses stability-induced reliability rankings from unlabeled RL trajectories to adapt confidence scores to the shifted trajectory distribution, without requiring target correctness labels. Across four QA benchmarks, StaR-TTA achieves an average AUROC of 0.721 0.721 , with consistent improvements across unseen datasets, model families and scales, and different Agentic RL algorithms.

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift

content: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications, particularly for reasoning tasks where plausible outputs can still be incorrect ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; de Oliveira et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2023 ; Turpin et al., 2023 ; Guan et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Recent approaches increasingly estimate confidence from reasoning trajectories, which reveal how a model arrives at its answer ( Khanmohammadi et al., 2025 ; Subramani et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, LLMs are increasingly optimized through agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL), which can substantially reshape their reasoning and tool-use behavior ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025c ; Singh et al., 2025 ; Matsutani et al., 2026 ) . This raises a critical question: do confidence estimators learned from a base model remain reliable after Agentic RL?

authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: We find that they often do not. Confidence estimators that perform well on Base-model trajectories can degrade substantially when directly transferred to their RL-trained counterparts. Through controlled analysis, we identify post-RL trajectory shift as an important source of this degradation: even with tool results and final answers controlled, replacing RL trajectories with their Base counterparts recovers a substantial portion of the lost confidence-ranking performance. Retraining requires post-RL correctness labels, while direct transfer suffers from trajectory shift. We therefore ask: can a confidence estimator adapt to post-RL trajectory shift without target correctness labels?

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: Our key observation is that, although Agentic RL shifts trajectories, it does not destroy all reliability structure. Across both Base and RL models, trajectory stability remains positively associated with answer correctness: answers that remain more stable under repeated sampling are consistently more likely to be correct. Crucially, unlike correctness labels, trajectory stability can be obtained directly from model outputs without human annotation. This creates a useful supervision bridge across the RL shift: correctness labels can ground the stability-reliability relationship on the source model, while stability remains available as a label-free reliability signal after RL .

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: Building on this insight, we propose StaR-TTA , a label-free test-time confidence adaptation framework via Sta bility R anking. During source training, StaR-TTA jointly learns from correctness supervision and stability-derived reliability supervision, explicitly aligning confidence scores with the reliability ordering induced by trajectory stability. At test time, correctness labels are unavailable, but the preserved stability–correctness relationship provides a transferable supervisory signal. StaR-TTA extracts stability from unlabeled RL trajectories, constructs reliability rankings, and uses them to adapt the confidence scorer to the shifted trajectory distribution while preserving the source-learned confidence scale. The adapted scores are then mapped to correctness probabilities by a frozen confidence calibrator. In this way, the same stability-based reliability structure learned alongside correctness on the source model becomes the supervision for label-free adaptation after RL.

content: Confidence Estimation. Confidence estimation predicts the probability that an LLM answer is correct ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) . P ⁡ ( True ) P(\mathrm{True}) provides a self-evaluated signal ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) . Beyond self-evaluation, CCPS ( Khanmohammadi et al., 2025 ) predicts correctness from hidden-state perturbation features, while MICE ( Subramani et al., 2025 ) uses logit-lens comparisons between intermediate and final predictions for tool-using agents. At the process level, HTC ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) estimates answer confidence for tool-using agents, whereas P ⁡ ( Sufficient ) P(\mathrm{Sufficient}) ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) probes whether accumulated multi-turn information is sufficient for answering correctly. DACA ( Luo et al., 2026 ) instead calibrates post-trained model confidence through agreement and disagreement with its pre-trained counterpart, without correctness labels. These methods exploit hidden representations, intermediate predictions, trajectory behavior, and so on, but how reliably these signals transfer under model and trajectory distribution shifts remains an open question.

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: Agentic Reinforcement Learning. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) trains LLM policies through multi-step interactions with environments, tools, or other agents, using trajectory-level rewards ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Common training algorithms include Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Havrilla et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . Unlike supervised fine-tuning on fixed reasoning traces, Agentic RL lets models learn when to reason, search, verify, and use tools through interaction. For example, Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025b ) trains a base LLM to interleave reasoning with search, issue multiple queries, and incorporate retrieved evidence before answering. It uses multi-turn rollouts, retrieved-token masking, and outcome-based rewards without step-level annotations. Other work applies Agentic RL to self-reflection and verification ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , tool use ( Singh et al., 2025 ) , and search without supervised reasoning traces ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . These methods can change action patterns, tool use behaviors, reasoning structure, and hidden representations, shifting the trajectory distributions on which confidence estimators rely.

content: We use Qwen2.5-3B ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) as our test model and Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025a ) as the Agentic RL framework. We evaluate effectiveness on TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2021 ) , and PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) . For cross-dataset generalization, we train on TriviaQA and test on NQ, 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , and Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) . We also test different model scales and families using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct ( Meta AI, 2024 ) ; and different RL algorithms: PPO ( Havrilla et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . We compare with five baselines: CCPS ( Khanmohammadi et al., 2025 ) , MICE ( Subramani et al., 2025 ) , HTC ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , P(Sufficient) ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and DACA ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . MICE-LR and MICE-RF share internal features but use logistic regression and random forests, respectively. We report AUROC for ranking, ECE for calibration, and Brier score and NLL for probability quality ( Fawcett, 2005 ; Guo et al., 2017 ; Brier, 1950 ; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . We set λ a = 0.1 \lambda_{a}=0.1 , λ h = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{h}}=0.5 , λ r = 1.0 \lambda_{r}=1.0 , and λ s = 0.5 \lambda_{s}=0.5 (details can be accessed in Appendix A.3.1 and Appendix A.3.2 ).

content: We evaluate confidence transfer in Table 3 . For each dataset, we train the confidence estimators on Base-LLM trajectories and evaluate them on Agentic RL trajectories. Across four datasets, our method achieves the best average performance: AUROC ( 0.721 0.721 ), ECE ( 0.069 0.069 ), Brier ( 0.187 0.187 ), and NLL ( 0.573 0.573 ). In terms of AUROC, only HTC outperforms our method on the MuSiQue dataset. Appendix A.4 compares the performance on both Base and RL trajectories, indicating that the poor performance of baselines is mainly due to the shift of Agentic RL. We further visualize the representation shift induced by Agentic RL. Fig. 4 shows that the Base and RL representations occupy visibly different regions of the feature space, indicating that RL training alters the internal representation adopted by the confidence estimator. We further report the baseline that directly uses stability information; the results are shown in Appendix A.2 , which indicate that stability provides useful information but stability alone is insufficient. These results show that our method improves both confidence ranking and probability estimation under the influence of Agentic RL.

authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: Our TTA procedure uses stability-based pairwise rankings to adjust confidence scores. More unlabeled target questions can provide more informative comparisons and make results more reliable. We therefore vary the number of questions used for adaptation, as shown in Table 9 . With only a small number of adaptation samples (e.g., N = 2 N=2 or N = 4 N=4 ), the results become unstable and even decrease. Performance gradually recovers and stabilizes as we increase the number of unlabeled questions for adaptation. The average AUROC rises from 0.7035 without TTA to 0.7155 with 64 questions. We can find that only a small number of samples (e.g., 64) during TTA is sufficient. These results suggest that additional unlabeled examples improve the reliability of ranking-based adaptation, with diminishing gains as the sample budget increases. We further analyze the additional cost introduced by our method in Appendix A.5 . The results show that the stability signal only introduces an extra token overhead of merely 0.8%.

title: Test-Time Confidence Adaptation under RL-Induced Trajectory Shift
authors: Zhenzhen Ren, Xiaoqing Zhang, GuoBiao Li, Bowen Fang, Yanxi Wang, Xinpeng Zhang, Ke Han
content: We studied why confidence estimators trained on Base LLM trajectories degrade after Agentic RL. We find that RL-induced trajectory shifts account for a substantial fraction of the degradation. Despite this shift, trajectory stability remains predictive of answer correctness in both Base and RL models. This preserved relationship motivates StaR-TTA, a label-free method that adjusts confidence scores on Agentic RL trajectories at test time. Across four datasets, StaR-TTA achieves an average AUROC of 0.721 0.721 . It also generalizes across datasets, model families, and PPO- or GRPO-trained agents. These results suggest that StaR-TTA may provide a useful starting point for further research on confidence estimation in Agentic-RL trained LLM agents.

content: To analyze the contribution of different components in our framework, we conduct ablation studies on both the trajectory representation and the test-time adaptation strategy. For trajectory feature construction, we incorporate three types of signals: internal representations h m h^{m} , external descriptors d m d^{m} , and stability vectors c m c^{m} . Since using hidden-layer representations h m h^{m} as trajectory features is a natural choice, we further investigate whether the additional stability and statistical signals provide complementary benefits.

Each ablation retains the other input features and follows the same source-training and calibration protocol. Stability signals remain available to the SRM, training losses, and TTA. Table 10 shows that removing stability inputs worsens all four metrics on every dataset. Removing interaction statistics also lowers AUROC on all four datasets, although ECE improves on three datasets and MuSiQue obtains lower Brier score and NLL. section: A.4 Confidence Estimation on Base and RL Trajectories
content: Table 15 compares confidence estimation on held-out Base and RL trajectories. We evaluate our source-trained TCS and frozen calibrator on Base trajectories, and report the full TTA method on RL trajectories. Several baselines achieve strong performance on Base trajectories but deteriorate substantially when transferred to RL trajectories. For example, CCPS achieves AUROC values of 0.7868 0.7868 on TriviaQA and 0.7329 0.7329 on HotpotQA before transfer, which drop to 0.4197 0.4197 and 0.4381 0.4381 after transfer. Similarly, MICE-LR and MICE-RF exhibit lower AUROC on RL trajectories across all four datasets, despite their strong performance on Base trajectories. These comparisons show existing estimators can successfully estimate confidence on held-out trajectories from the Base model, yet their learned confidence signals become less reliable after Agentic RL changes the trajectory distribution.

content: We distinguish standard source training and confidence scoring from the additional costs of stability estimation and test-time adaptation. At test time, we freeze TCS and CC then update only a linear corrector using unlabeled target examples. Paired Base and RL trajectories are required only for training the corrector. Once corrector is trained, confidence scoring uses RL trajectories alone, without running the Base model on subsequent questions. Table 9 shows that 64 adaptation examples improve average AUROC from 0.7035 to 0.7155, compared with 0.7208 using all available examples. Thus, a small adaptation subset can provide useful gains while limiting the cost of Base-model execution. Other confidence estimators may need to perform retraining on a large collection of RL trajectories (e.g., tens of thousands). Without this retraining, they undergo substantial performance degradation.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
content: Software engineering agents resend their entire trajectory to an LLM at every turn, which motivates work on online trajectory reduction. Prior work shows that even randomly deleting 75% of the tokens in old turns may preserve the agent’s effectiveness, but it remains unclear why this is the case, what the agent does to compensate for missing content, and whether trajectory reduction actually reduces costs. This paper presents an empirical study of 42 trajectory-reduction configurations, focusing on their effects on effectiveness, agent behavior, and cost. Our study systematically explores the effects of deleting content from old turns by varying the scope, granularity, amount, and timing of deletion across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on the SWE-bench Verified dataset. We find that deleting large amounts of trajectory content (e.g., up to 100% of reasoning text) can preserve overall effectiveness. Importantly, such deletion needs to be applied with a delay, as deleting content immediately after it is generated tends to significantly degrade effectiveness. Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, which can increase both the number of turns an agent takes to solve a task and the number of input and output tokens. Whether trajectory reduction reduces LLM costs depends on the pricing model: Under a flat pricing model, where all input tokens are billed equally, estimated costs fall in 26 of 42 evaluations across both agents. Surprisingly, under a caching-aware pricing model, none of these 42 evaluations yields lower estimated costs, since reducing the trajectory breaks the cached prefix, whose tokens are billed at a lower rate. Our findings have several important implications: First, token counts alone are misleading; trajectory reduction techniques must instead consider overall costs under a realistic pricing model. Second, studies of trajectories are important for understanding agent behavior, as focusing only on end-to-end effectiveness can hide important behavioral differences, such as excessive re-fetching of deleted content. Finally, these results highlight the need for future work on memory management, that is, deciding which trajectory content to keep or delete and when to delete it, to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Software engineering agents based on large language models (LLMs) increasingly automate software engineering tasks by inspecting repositories, modifying code, and validating patches [ 1 ] . Such agents retain prior reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs in a trajectory that grows as they work. This growth increases the context processed by the model and can eventually exceed its context window [ 2 , 3 ] , making trajectory management an important challenge.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Prior approaches reduce retained trajectories by discarding messages or tool outputs, selecting content to remove, or summarizing earlier interactions [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . For example, AgentDiet reports that randomly deleting up to 75% of eligible trajectory tokens can preserve much of an agent’s effectiveness [ 2 ] . These studies demonstrate that agents can tolerate substantial trajectory reduction.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: However, existing results do not show how the individual design choices in trajectory deletion affect agents. A deletion policy must decide what to remove, how much to remove, whether to remove whole turns or individual tokens, and whether to protect recent turns. Because trajectories contain diverse information, from intermediate reasoning to tool observations, these choices may affect agents differently. A systematic study that isolates deletion scope, granularity, amount, and timing can clarify how each choice affects task solving.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Trajectory reduction requires broader evaluation than final task success or token counts alone. An agent may complete a task by revisiting files, repeating commands, or retrieving deleted information, adding work even when the outcome is unchanged [ 5 , 6 ] . Token counts also do not establish cost savings: prompt caching discounts reusable input prefixes, and rewriting a trajectory can invalidate part of that prefix [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 6 ] . Evaluations thus need to measure task effectiveness, subsequent agent behavior, and execution cost together.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of trajectory deletion in software engineering agents. We vary scope, granularity, amount, and timing across 42 deletion configurations, evaluating each on two popular agents (Mini-SWE-agent [ 10 ] and Trae agent [ 11 ] ). Half of the configurations delete with a two-turn delay and half without it, which gives 42 evaluations per timing across both agents combined. The study covers 100 SWE-bench Verified [ 1 ] tasks and 9,400 runs. We measure effectiveness as tasks solved, analyze how agents behave after content is deleted, and estimate execution costs under both flat and caching-aware pricing. More specifically, we address three research questions.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ1: How do deletion scope, granularity, amount, and timing affect effectiveness and execution length? We find that the timing of trajectory reduction is critical. With a two-turn delay, 37 of 42 evaluations do not statistically significantly reduce the number of tasks solved. In contrast, immediate deletion significantly reduces the number of tasks solved in 19 of 42 evaluations. The kind of deleted content also matters: Removing reasoning usually does not affect effectiveness, but deleting tool output is more harmful. Finally, we observe that trajectory reduction tends to increase the number of turns an agent needs (in 21 of 42 and 34 of 42 evaluations with delayed and immediate deletion, respectively).

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ2: How does trajectory deletion affect agents’ subsequent behavior, particularly the repeated retrieval of previously observed information? Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it. For example, deleting tool outputs raises the re-fetch rate to as much as 7.5 times (with delayed deletion) and 10.6 times (with immediate deletion) compared to the baseline.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ3: How does trajectory deletion affect estimated execution cost under flat and caching-aware pricing? The answer heavily depends on the pricing model. Assuming a flat pricing model, where all input tokens are billed equally, 26 of 42 evaluations with the delay reduce estimated costs across both agents. However, the results change under a caching-aware pricing model, where cached input prefixes are billed at a lower rate. In this case, none of these 42 evaluations reduce estimated costs, and 26 evaluations are significantly more expensive than the uncompressed baseline.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Our findings have several important implications for future work. First, trajectory reduction should be evaluated not only in terms of task success and token counts. Instead, evaluations should also consider execution length, retrieval behavior, and estimated costs under realistic pricing models. Second, it is important to study the behavior of agents after trajectory reduction, as they may compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, which can increase execution length and costs. Finally, we expect the detailed results across our 42 deletion configurations to inform future research on trajectory reduction techniques, including memory management strategies that decide what to keep or delete and when to delete it.

authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: An LLM-based agent solves tasks, such as GitHub issues, through repeated model calls and repository interactions [ 10 , 13 , 11 ] . At each turn, the model produces reasoning text and tool calls, such as commands to inspect files, modify code, or run tests. The agent executes these calls and records their outputs. A turn comprises one model call, its reasoning, tool calls, and resulting outputs. The sequence of turns forms the agent’s trajectory [ 14 ] . An agent retaining its complete trajectory includes previous interactions and newly acquired information in each request, so the prompt grows during execution. Tool outputs, including file contents, search results, and test logs, contribute to this growth. Since input-token processing is a major part of coding-agent costs [ 15 ] , reducing the retained trajectory offers a way to limit context consumption.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Trajectory-reduction approaches rewrite old turns before resending them and differ in what they remove and retain. Masking replaces old tool outputs with a placeholder [ 10 , 16 ] . Selection uses a model to identify and remove irrelevant content [ 2 , 17 ] . Summarization (compaction) replaces a span of turns with an LLM summary [ 18 , 19 ] . Recently, agents have been trained to decide when and what to compact [ 3 , 4 ] . Our study builds on AgentDiet [ 2 ] , in which a reflection model removes content classified as useless, redundant, or expired from every turn longer than 500 tokens once it is two turns old. AgentDiet’s random baseline deletes 75% of eligible tokens and solves almost as many tasks as its model-based reduction approach. These results motivate studying agents’ compensation for deletion and the resulting additional execution costs.

section: II-C Prefix Caching and Its Pricing
content: A model computes key and value vectors for prompt tokens and stores them in a key–value (KV) cache. When a prompt repeats the previous prompt and appends a turn, inference engines reuse cached states for the matching token prefix [ 20 , 21 ] . Prefix reuse ends at the first token that differs because each cached state depends on the preceding tokens. OpenAI , Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek discount input tokens served from matching cached prefixes. When the cache is available, an agent appending turns without rewriting history pays the cached price for the repeated prefix. Rewriting an old turn changes the prefix and prevents reuse of the cached states from the first change onward (Figure 1 ). Under the caching-aware pricing model used in this study, these tokens incur the full input price. SWE-agent’s documentation warns that eliding old observations breaks prompt caching [ 22 ] , and Anthropic’s documentation states that clearing tool results or reasoning invalidates the cached prefix [ 19 ] . Section VI evaluates whether token savings offset the cost of processing tokens beyond the matching prefix.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: We evaluate two agents with different tool interfaces. The first is Trae agent [ 11 ] , the agent used by AgentDiet [ 2 ] , which we include to support comparison with AgentDiet. Trae agent features a structured file viewer, an editor, and a shell environment. The second is Mini-SWE-agent [ 10 ] , a setup restricted to a single shell tool, which provides a contrast to the specialized tools of Trae agent. Both agents use the same model, DeepSeek-V4-Flash [ 23 ] . We choose this open-weight model to support self-hosted inference, complete call logging, and execution of 9,400 runs (Section III-E ).

content: The tasks are the fixed 100-instance subset of SWE-bench Verified [ 1 ] used by AgentDiet [ 2 ] . Each task corresponds to a real GitHub issue and has a hidden, human-validated test suite. Using AgentDiet’s subset [ 2 ] supports direct comparison and limits the experiment to 4,700 runs per agent.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: A turn yields three pieces of information: (i) reasoning text produced by the model, (ii) one or more tool calls suggested by the model, and (iii) the outputs of those tool calls. The trajectory contains information from all completed turns and forms part of each subsequent model request. We vary four dimensions of deletion: scope, granularity, amount, and timing. Each configuration assigns values to each dimension, and is evaluated on both agents. Deletion rewrites eligible turns before a model call, conforming to the configuration.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Scope. The scope is the part of a turn eligible for deletion. We evaluate three scopes: (i) reasoning text, (ii) tool output, or (iii) both, including the tool call. The third scope therefore covers the entire turn. We do not consider the tool call itself as a scope because it is usually short. Reasoning includes observations, plans for subsequent actions, and hypotheses about the cause of a bug. Tool outputs include file contents, search results, and test logs.

content: Granularity. Turn-level deletion (Turn in the tables and figures) drops the scoped content of a turn entirely, with probability p p , and replaces it with a one-line note indicating deleted content. Token-level deletion (Token in the tables and figures) removes 100 ​ p % 100p\% of the scoped tokens of a turn, chosen at random, and keeps a note together with the surviving tokens. At the same p p , both granularities delete approximately the same expected percentage of scoped tokens. Token-level deletion retains some tokens in each eligible turn, whereas turn-level deletion either removes or retains all scoped content.

For token-level deletion, the procedure tokenizes the scoped content with a fixed tokenizer and removes ⌊ p ⋅ n ⌋ \lfloor p\cdot n\rfloor of its n n tokens, sampled uniformly without replacement.

We use 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% for turn-level deletion, to cover the range from light to total deletion, and 25%, 50%, and 75% for token-level deletion since at 100% the two granularities coincide. This gives 3 × ( 4 + 3 ) = 21 3\times(4+3)=21 combinations of scope, granularity, and amount.

content: Timing. A turn becomes eligible for rewriting after a fixed delay. With delayed timing, the delay is two turns, so the last two turns are always intact. The two-turn delay follows AgentDiet [ 2 ] . With immediate timing, the delay is zero. This configuration tests the effect of removing the retention delay. Immediate deletion rewrites a turn before the next model call, so the agent never observes the original content of a deleted output. The procedure considers each turn once, when the turn becomes eligible. Therefore, a turn that survives the turn-level draw stays intact, while a rewritten turn stays rewritten for the rest of the run. Figure 2 illustrates the two granularities and contrasts immediate and delayed timing on a real Trae agent trajectory. The 21 combinations at each of two timings yield 42 configurations. Evaluating every configuration on both agents gives 84 evaluations, with 42 evaluations per timing.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ1. Effectiveness: How do deletion scope, granularity, amount, and timing affect effectiveness and execution length? To answer RQ1, we evaluate all 42 configurations (Section III-B ) on both agents and the same 100 tasks (Section III-A ). Furthermore, we add five uncompressed runs per agent. Because inference is not deterministic, the repeated baselines characterize execution variability without deletion. For each run, we track four metrics: (1) a task is solved when the patch passes its associated test suite. A failing patch, no patch, or a run that ends with a context-length error counts as not solved. We report the number of tasks solved, or the solved rate when expressed as a percentage; (2) run length is the number of turns, which we summarize by its median across tasks; (3) a run is capped when it reaches the 200-turn budget. A capped run can still solve the task if it already holds a working patch while testing it; (4) a run loops when it repeats an identical tool call at least ten times in a row. We compare each configuration with the uncompressed runs (Section III-D ). We first examine scope, granularity, and amount under delayed deletion, following AgentDiet [ 2 ] , and then compare delayed and immediate deletion to assess the effect of timing.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ2. Behavior: How does an agent compensate for content deleted from its trajectory? To answer RQ2, a rule-based labeler classifies each tool call as a read, edit, test, script, or other operation. The labeler identifies file reads performed through shell commands or Python scripts. We manually verify the labels for ten randomly sampled logs, five per agent. For each agent, the five sampled logs comprise one uncompressed run and runs from two delayed and two immediate configurations. The labeler assigns 851 of the 855 labels correctly (99.5% accuracy). The replication package includes the classifier and the ten manually verified logs. We then mark each read as a re-fetch or an initial read: a read is a re-fetch when at least 80% of its distinct lines already appear in the output of an earlier read in the same run. We exclude outputs under five lines to avoid accidental matching. The re-fetch rate is the number of re-fetches divided by the number of reads, per run, reported as a ratio to the uncompressed runs (Section III-D ). Normalizing by the number of reads supports comparison across configurations with different run lengths. The analysis also compares re-fetching of deleted and retained outputs and characterizes run behavior. Furthermore, we measure on the uncompressed runs how far back an agent reaches for content. For a re-fetch, we count the turns since its lines last appeared in a read. For an edit, we count the turns since the agent last read the file. The percentage of re-fetches and edits whose source lies within the last k k turns indicates what a deletion delay of k k turns would leave intact.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: RQ3. Cost: How does trajectory deletion affect estimated execution cost under flat and caching-aware pricing? To answer RQ3, we calculate token counts from the logs (Section III-E ) and estimate each run’s cost relative to the uncompressed baseline under two pricing models. Under flat pricing , every prompt token costs the input price. Under caching-aware pricing , only the longest prefix identical, token for token, to the previous call’s prompt costs the cached price, and all remaining prompt tokens cost the input price (Section II-C ). Both models bill completion tokens at the output price. An uncompressed trajectory preserves the prefix, whereas a rewrite re-bills tokens from the first change onward. Turn-level deletion breaks the prefix only when a turn is selected for deletion. Token-level deletion breaks it at every call with an eligible turn.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: Depending on the provider, a cached token costs 0.05 to 0.5 times the price of a new input token [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . We pick a price ratio of 1 : 0.1 : 5 1:0.1:5 for input, cached input, and output tokens. The cached-input ratio of 0.1 lies within this range. The caching-aware model ignores cache-write premiums and assumes that every matching prefix is served from the cache, so its cost estimate is a lower bound on realistic costs.

authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: The reference for every comparison is the five uncompressed runs of the same agent. For tasks solved and the re-fetch rate, we compare a configuration with the per-task mean of the five runs. Run length and cost have long-tailed distributions, including capped runs, so we summarize these metrics with medians. For these two metrics, we take the median of the configuration over the 100 tasks, divide it by the median of each uncompressed run, and average the five ratios.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
content: We make two kinds of comparison. The first is a configuration against the reference, as above. The second compares two configurations that differ in one dimension, on the same agent: delayed against immediate timing (RQ1 and RQ2), or turn-level against token-level granularity at the same scope, amount, and timing (RQ1). Every comparison is paired by task, and its uncertainty is a paired bootstrap confidence interval over the 100 tasks. We resample the 100 tasks with replacement 10,000 times. On each resample, we compute the statistic of the configuration on the drawn tasks and the statistic of the reference on the same drawn tasks (the mean task-solving outcome, or the median of turns or cost), and then their change or ratio. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these 10,000 values form the 95% interval. A change is significant when its interval excludes zero (for a change in tasks solved) or one (for a ratio of turns, re-fetch rate, or cost).

section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Tasks solved. Only five of the 42 delayed-configuration evaluations (in bold) show a significant loss, while the confidence intervals for the other 37 include zero change. Three of these five solve more than ten fewer tasks than the baseline, and all three delete reasoning and tool output together: Mini-SWE-agent loses 14 tasks and Trae agent 32 when every turn is deleted whole, and Trae agent loses 15 under token-level deletion of 75% of both. The other two drops are seven tasks for Mini-SWE-agent with 50% token-level deletion of both scopes and eight for Trae agent with 75% token-level deletion of tool output.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Scope. Delayed reasoning deletion shows no statistically significant decrease in tasks solved or increase in run length. Across the 14 evaluations of reasoning deletion, the change in tasks solved ranges from − 5 -5 to + 4 +4 relative to the baseline. Some Trae agent configurations reduce median run length by up to 15%. At a fixed deletion percentage, reasoning deletion removes fewer tokens than deletion of tool output or both scopes (Section VII ). The experiment therefore does not isolate the effect of scope from the number of tokens removed.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Granularity. Granularity primarily affects run length in these comparisons. Only one pair differs significantly in tasks solved by the paired bootstrap: Trae agent, both, 75%, where turn-level deletion solves 69 tasks and token-level deletion 60. Granularity also affects run length. Token-level deletion produces longer runs than turn-level deletion in ten of the twelve pairs that delete tool output. The difference increases with the deletion percentage. At 75% deletion of both scopes, Trae agent’s median run reaches the turn cap under token-level deletion, compared with a 92% increase over the baseline under turn-level deletion. In the six reasoning pairs, runs are equal or shorter under token-level deletion.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Amount. Up to 50%, only one evaluation (Mini-SWE-agent) loses tasks significantly. At 75%, three evaluations on Trae agent solve six to 15 fewer tasks, all involving tool output deletion. Deleting 100% of both reasoning and tool output significantly reduces tasks solved for both agents. Increased deletion is also associated with longer runs. Of the 28 evaluations that delete tool output, 21 have significantly longer runs, compared with none of the 14 evaluations that delete reasoning alone. Under turn-level deletion of both scopes, Trae agent’s median run grows from 15% above the baseline at 25% deletion to the cap at 100%. The number of capped runs increases from four to 92 out of 100, whereas tasks solved decrease significantly only at 100% deletion, from a baseline mean of 74.6 to 43. Longer runs also occur without a statistically significant decrease in tasks solved. Under turn-level 100% deletion of tool output, Trae agent solves 70 tasks, compared with a baseline mean of 74.6, while median run length increases by 73% and 29 runs reach the cap. Reporting only tasks solved thus hides longer runs and budget exhaustion.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Comparison with AgentDiet. AgentDiet [ 2 ] evaluates two fixed baselines on Trae agent, on the same 100 tasks and with the same two-turn delay: one deletes 75% of the tokens of a turn at random and the other deletes the turn entirely, both applied to reasoning and tool output together [ 2 ] . They correspond to our token-level deletion of 75% of both and our turn-level deletion of 100% of both. Both studies agree that deleting the whole turn costs more tasks and more turns than deleting 75% of its tokens. The magnitudes differ: AgentDiet reports 1 and 7 fewer tasks solved against our 15 and 32, and 13% to 14% more turns where our runs reach the cap. Three design differences limit direct comparison: AgentDiet rewrites only turns longer than 500 tokens rather than every turn, uses Claude 4 Sonnet rather than DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and limits runs to 50 turns rather than 200. Answer to RQ1: Delayed deletion. With delayed deletion, 37 of 42 evaluations show no statistically significant decrease in tasks solved. However, runs lengthen significantly in 21, all deleting tool output.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-A Delayed Deletion: Scope, Granularity, and Amount
content: Implications for future work. Our results call for evaluations of trajectory reduction that measure tasks solved, execution length, and budget exhaustion under common turn limits, since agents can preserve effectiveness through additional work. The contrast between reasoning and tool output deletion also motivates memory-management policies that treat these content types differently. Future comparisons should match the number of tokens removed to determine whether such policies improve the tradeoff between effectiveness and execution effort.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Without the delay, a deleted output is rewritten before the first call that would show it, so the agent never sees it intact. At 100% of tool output or of both, the agent therefore never sees any tool output at all. Immediate deletion raises significant losses in tasks solved (in bold) from five to 19 of the 42 evaluations per timing, and significantly longer runs from 21 to 34. No immediate configuration has significantly shorter runs than the baseline. Paired bootstrap comparisons of configurations that differ only in timing show significantly fewer tasks solved with immediate deletion in 16 of the 42 comparisons. The two agents fail differently. In the eight Trae agent configurations with fewer than 60 tasks solved, 33 to 100 of the runs loop, against two to five in the uncompressed runs. In the six Mini-SWE-agent configurations with fewer than 35 tasks solved, 38 to 94 of the runs end without a patch, and Mini-SWE-agent loops in at most one run in any configuration.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Turn-level deletion. At 25% and 50%, no turn-level configuration differs significantly from its delayed value, although runs are up to twice as long as the baseline when deletion affects tool output. Two of these configurations, Mini-SWE-agent with both and Trae agent with reasoning deleted at 50%, are about six tasks below the reference. At 75% deletion, the effects differ between agents. Mini-SWE-agent loses 14 tasks when tool output is deleted, while Trae agent keeps its delayed value but loops in 41 to 60 of its runs, with a median run close to the cap. At 100% deletion of tool output or both scopes, Trae agent solves no tasks, and with both deleted, it repeats one directory listing until the cap in every run. Mini-SWE-agent solves two tasks with both deleted and 14 with tool output deleted, without ever observing file contents. Its 14 successful patches warrant further analysis to distinguish reliance on issue descriptions, memorized fixes, and other explanations.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Token-level deletion. Immediate token-level deletion of tool output reduces Trae agent’s tasks solved at every deletion percentage, to five at 75%, with most runs capped from 50% onward. Mini-SWE-agent shows no significant difference from delayed deletion up to 50% deletion and solves 27 tasks at 75% deletion. With both scopes deleted, Mini-SWE-agent solves 31 tasks at 25% against 69 under delayed deletion. Of the immediate runs, 45 end without a patch, and none reach the cap. Compared with delayed deletion, Trae agent solves 13 fewer tasks at 25% deletion. It solves 34 and five tasks at 50% and 75% deletion, respectively. The content left by each granularity offers an interpretation of this difference, drawn from Trae agent’s traces and not an established cause. Turn-level deletion replaces the removed content with an explicit deletion notice, whereas token-level deletion leaves fragments that the agent sometimes reads as repository corruption and attempts to repair. Loop counts are consistent with this interpretation. At 50% of tool output, 67 of Trae agent’s runs loop under token-level deletion against eight under turn-level deletion, compared with nine and six looping runs under delayed deletion and two to five in the uncompressed baseline.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Reasoning deletion. Immediate and delayed reasoning deletion yield similar numbers of tasks solved. Confidence intervals include zero change in 13 of the 14 evaluations. The exception solves six fewer tasks than the baseline. Run length shows a different pattern. No delayed reasoning evaluation has significantly longer runs, but seven of the 14 immediate ones do, by under 20% in all but three. Mini-SWE-agent’s runs are 49% longer under token-level deletion of 75%, and turn-level deletion of 100% lengthens Trae agent’s runs by 35% and Mini-SWE-agent’s by 105%. At 75% deletion, the corresponding increase is 13% for Mini-SWE-agent, with no significant change for Trae agent.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Answer to RQ1: Immediate deletion. Without the delay, 19 of 42 evaluations show significantly fewer tasks solved than the baseline, and 34 have significantly longer runs. While reasoning deletion and turn-level deletion of up to 50% of tool output generally retain their delayed effectiveness, token-level deletion of tool output does not.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: IV-B Immediate Deletion: The Effect of Timing
content: Implications for future work. The timing comparisons motivate studies of memory management that jointly vary retention delay and deletion scope. Such studies should test whether reasoning and tool outputs require different protection periods and measure tasks solved, execution length, and failure behavior under each policy. Analyses of loops, missing patches, and budget exhaustion would clarify how retention choices affect execution beyond the final task outcome.

content: Scope. Deletion scope affects re-fetching similarly to the pattern for run length in Section IV . Deleting both scopes triggers the most re-fetching, followed by tool output, then reasoning. At matched amounts and granularities, deleting both scopes yields higher re-fetch ratios than deleting tool output in all Trae agent comparisons and most Mini-SWE-agent comparisons.

authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen

content: Granularity. Agents re-fetch more under token-level deletion than under turn-level deletion in 21 of the 24 pairs that delete tool output or both, at the same scope and amount, and the other three are ties.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: V RQ2: How Does the Agent Compensate for Deleted Content?
content: Amount. Section IV shows that run length increases with the percentage of tool output deleted. The additional turns include repository exploration, testing, and editing. Table II identifies re-fetching as one source of additional work that increases when deleting tool output. Under delayed turn-level deletion, Trae agent’s ratio grows from 1.7× at 25% to 7.5× at 100% for both, and from 1.5× to 4.6× for tool output. The corresponding ratios at 100% deletion for Mini-SWE-agent are 2.4 × 2.4\times and 1.6 × 1.6\times , respectively. Of the 28 evaluations that delete tool output at each timing, all 28 show a significant increase with the delay and 27 without it. The exception, Mini-SWE-agent at 100% of tool output without the delay (1.0×), never receives any tool output and explores unread content rather than re-reading: in its 41 capped runs, 36% of all calls read content not seen before, 35% are scripts, and 7% re-read content already seen.

title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: V RQ2: How Does the Agent Compensate for Deleted Content?
content: Timing. Immediate deletion produces significantly higher re-fetch rates than delayed deletion in 25 of the 42 paired bootstrap comparisons, 18 of 21 for Trae agent and seven of 21 for Mini-SWE-agent. The increase is largest in the token-level rows. Trae agent goes from 3.7× with the delay to 7.0× without it at 75% of tool output, and from 3.9× to 8.8× at 50% of both. For Mini-SWE-agent, tool output re-fetch ratios differ little between timings below 100% deletion. The highest value in the table, 10.6 × 10.6\times , is Trae agent under immediate turn-level deletion of both at 100%.

authors: Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Islem Bouzenia, Michael Pradel, Leon Moonen
section: V RQ2: How Does the Agent Compensate for Deleted Content?
content: Reasoning. Delayed reasoning deletion produces no consistent increase in re-fetching. Re-fetch ratios range from 0.7 to 1.2 across the 14 evaluations, and the four significant differences from the baseline are small, point in opposite directions (two below one, two above one), and show no trend with deletion percentage. Two immediate configurations stand out. In both agents, turn-level deletion of 100% reaches 1.9 × 1.9\times , and token-level deletion of 75% reaches 1.5 × 1.5\times . Under both granularities, removing the latest reasoning increases re-fetching; removing reasoning older than two turns does not.

content: Deleted versus retained outputs. A higher re-fetch rate can mean that the agent retrieves deleted content again or that it retrieves both deleted and retained content more. To distinguish these explanations, we compare subsequent retrieval of deleted and retained outputs within each run. Under turn-level deletion, independent random draws determine retention. Assignment therefore does not systematically select outputs by age, file, or position, supporting interpretation of differences in subsequent retrieval as responses to deletion. Table III gives the percentage of kept and of deleted reads whose output is re-fetched later, for the turn-level configurations that delete tool output or both at 25% to 75%.
