section: 3.1 Translator Evidence Conditions and the Cultural-Effectiveness Metric
content: Four translator input conditions form an intervention on evidence accessibility: Text Only provides only the text; Multimodal provides the native image matching the sample; Random Image provides an image drawn from another sample, used to distinguish relevant evidence from a generic multimodal input effect; and Human Caption provides a human-verified image description as evidence that does not participate in translation, used to relieve the visual-perception burden ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . Each condition keeps the translation instruction unchanged; the full prompts are given in Appendix D .

section: 3.1 Translator Evidence Conditions and the Cultural-Effectiveness Metric
content: Cultural effectiveness is judged by the domain-specialized Chinese Judger trained in this work ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , loaded on self-hosted vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) with 8 8 -way tensor parallelism ( tp = 8 \mathrm{tp}=8 ), using a fixed deterministic decoding configuration on the judge side to ensure reproducible and consistent scoring. Following the rubric of the CULTURE-MT ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , we report two metrics: the mean score is the average of the 0 0 – 3 3 scale, and the cultural-effectiveness rate is the proportion of samples scoring 2 2 or above ( 2 2 – 3 3 , i.e., semantically and pragmatically adequate), with 0 0 – 1 1 counted as ineffective; the visual gain Δ \Delta is the difference of the multimodal condition over the text-only condition on these metrics.

content: The core of the protocol is to separate “what evidence the sample contains” from “what evidence the translator can access.” The Judger always reads the same human-verified image description for all translator conditions ( Liao et al., 2025 ) , because that description characterizes the sample’s ground truth rather than any single translator’s input; the evidence intervention occurs only on the translator side. We do not provide the judge with an enumerated “ambiguous word → \to correct meaning” answer ledger, to avoid degrading scoring into answer matching. With the judge’s information fixed, score changes across conditions can be interpreted as differences in the translator’s acquisition and use of evidence, providing a common reference for the subsequent failure attribution.

The Judger is built on a Qwen3.5-27B ( Team, 2026 ) base and aligned to the 0 0 – 3 3 human standard of cultural effectiveness through two-stage supervised fine-tuning ( Kim and Kang, 2026 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2025a ) ; the full training configuration is given in Appendices D and G . content: The visual benefit is evidence-selective, not a generic multimodal dividend. Figure 4 and Table 5 show that across 17 configurations, the average gains on Symbol, Visual, and Hybrid are + 0.050 +0.050 , + 0.280 +0.280 , and + 0.197 +0.197 , respectively. While Visual and Hybrid show positive gains for every configuration, Symbol remains small and unstable, with 5 configurations showing no gain or a drop. Images thus help consistently only when they provide information missing from the text; when translation relies mainly on shared cultural knowledge, they are often unhelpful and may distract. The lower gain on Hybrid further confirms this: jointly dependent samples retain symbolic difficulty that images cannot resolve, which persists in 4.3.2 even with human descriptions.

content: Visual access alleviates the information bottleneck but does not close the capability gap. Text-only and multimodal scores are highly consistent across models (Pearson r = 0.989 r=0.989 , computed from Table 5 ), with strong models remaining ahead after receiving images. Images mainly restore missing sample-level facts, while final quality remains constrained by language generation, pragmatic inference, and cultural transfer. Visual evidence thus alleviate input-side information constraints but cannot guarantee quality translation.

For the Qwen3.5 dense series (4B/9B/27B), the multimodal mean rises from 1.623 1.623 to 1.785 1.785 to 2.171 2.171 , while gains are + 0.229 / + 0.225 / + 0.267 +0.229/+0.225/+0.267 ; for Qwen3-VL (8B/32B/235B), the mean rises from 1.564 1.564 to 1.890 1.890 to 2.129 2.129 , with gains of + 0.197 / + 0.251 / + 0.211 +0.197/+0.251/+0.211 . Scaling therefore raises the performance ceiling but does not guarantee better image use, making evidence use an evaluation dimension independent of scale and modality architecture.

Gemini-3.1-pro (high) achieves 2.424 2.424 multimodal with only + 0.108 +0.108 gain; Qwen3.5-27B scores lower ( 2.171 2.171 ) but achieves the highest gain ( + 0.267 +0.267 ); GPT-5.6 achieves both the highest multimodal score ( 2.432 2.432 ) and a large gain ( + 0.211 +0.211 ). Lower baselines tend to yield larger Δ \Delta (see Table 5 ), so a large Δ \Delta may reflect effective image use or simply greater room for improvement. Thus, the multimodal score measures translation quality, while Δ \Delta measures how much vision closes the information gap, jointly distinguishing translation quality from visual reliance.

content: Mismatched evidence cannot substitute for missing evidence. On 4 4 representative configurations, the average change of random images over text-only is Symbol − 0.074 -0.074 , Visual − 0.005 -0.005 , Hybrid − 0.077 -0.077 (overall − 0.052 -0.052 ), whereas the same models with real images improve Visual and Hybrid by + 0.297 +0.297 and + 0.232 +0.232 . The main result is thus not a “one extra input modality” effect: models do read the image, but only visual evidence matching the current text can reconstruct the omitted contextual meaning, while a mismatched image is at best unhelpful and even introduces noise that distracts generation (Table 6 )—in sharp contrast to the visual-redundancy phenomenon of classic MMT, where randomly swapping the image is almost lossless.

content: The real-image condition requires a model to both recognize visual facts and use them for translation, and the two failures are hard to separate. The Human Caption condition directly provides human-verified visual facts, bypassing perception; comparing it with Text Only and Multimodal roughly distinguishes whether failure comes from “visual facts not recovered” or “facts obtained but target-language transfer not completed.” The judge input is kept identical across the three conditions.

content: Having visual facts available does not equal completing cultural transfer. On 4 representative configurations, the overall mean under Human Caption ( 2.201 2.201 ) is slightly higher than direct image reading ( 2.161 2.161 ), as is the score on Visual ( 2.316 2.316 vs. 2.242 2.242 ), suggesting that models may miss some task-relevant visual facts, but the gap is limited. Meanwhile, Hybrid under Human Caption reaches only 2.035 2.035 , below Visual’s 2.316 2.316 . Since the two groups are not strictly matched, this gap is not a pure causal estimate of cultural ability, but it shows that even with visual facts textualized, jointly dependent samples retain additional difficulty beyond what images can provide (Table 6 ).

title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
content: We move beyond the conventional view of whether images improve translation and argue that culturally effective social-media translation is fundamentally meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence . Culture-MMT uses three evidence-dependence types and controlled interventions to diagnose model failures across three stages: inaccessible evidence, insufficient fact recovery, and insufficient cultural adaptation. Experiments across 17 models show that visual perception and cultural knowledge are not interchangeable: the former recovers omitted facts, while the latter enables pragmatic adaptation. This perspective provides standardized evaluation and diagnostic tools for studying complex pragmatic representation in next-generation multimodal models.

title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
content: Multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to mitigate textual ambiguity ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Hatami et al., 2025 ) . However, standard benchmarks assume semantically self-contained text, leading prior work to question the necessity of vision ( Futeral et al., 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2025 ; Xiong and Zhao, 2025 ) . While recent studies incorporate cultural awareness and visual grounding ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Villa-Cueva et al., 2025 ; Satar et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , they conflate multimodal perception with cultural understanding. In contrast, Culture-MMT reframes UGC translation as meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence . Crucially, visual fact recovery and cultural adaptation represent distinct, non-interchangeable bottlenecks: accessing visual facts does not guarantee pragmatic adequacy. Through evidence-dependency categorization and controlled interventions, Culture-MMT systematically disentangles model failures across evidence access, visual grounding, and cultural transfer.

title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
content: Recent studies investigate cultural awareness in text-only translation ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Liao et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025b ) and extend it to multimodal contexts through visual grounding and meme transcreation ( Villa-Cueva et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . In user-generated content (UGC), however, prior work largely focuses on colloquial noise or multimodal dialogue ( Michel and Neubig, 2018 ; Liang et al., 2022 ) , while cultural benchmarks like Culture-MT ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ) assume the source text is semantically self-contained. In contrast, we extend cultural evaluation to visually dependent UGC where essential meaning is omitted from text. By introducing Symbol as a text-only control and applying controlled evidence conditions, Culture-MMT systematically disentangles visual fact recovery from cultural adaptation.

content: Language and Cultural Scope. Culture-MMT focuses exclusively on the Chinese-to-English direction. Although the theoretical framework of distributed evidence is generalizable to other high-context online communication, Chinese social media exhibits highly specific cultural memes and elliptical patterns. Validating whether the observed evidence-utilization trends generalize to other typologically distinct language pairs and cultural spaces remains future work.

However, its statistical power is limited for finer-grained sub-analyses across the 20 verticals or visual grounding mechanisms (e.g., OCR text, scene disambiguation, and cultural metaphors).

content: Evaluation Ceiling of Textual Proxies. To prevent perceptual errors and hallucinations of multimodal judges from confounding evaluation, our Judger evaluates translations against human-verified textual descriptions rather than raw images. While this protocol ensures reproducible and controlled scoring across conditions, it inherently shifts the evaluation ceiling to the descriptive granularity of human annotations—subtle visual nuances omitted in the captions cannot be credited.

The human-caption condition does not resolve the error, suggesting that the visual fact is available but is not correctly integrated with the textual reference.

title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
section: D.1 Why the Judge Needs Visual Evidence
content: We assess cultural effectiveness with the domain-specialized Judger we train (on aQwen3.5-27B ( Team, 2026 ) base). Unlike a generic LLM-as-a-judge ( Fu and Liu, 2025 ) , this task additionally requires the judge to determine whether a translation recovers information carried by the image but not made explicit in the text. If the judge saw only the source text, it might misjudge a correct visual completion as an unfounded addition; and if different translator conditions corresponded to different judge evidence, the change of evaluation condition would be confounded. We therefore fix the judge input across all translator conditions: the Judger always receives the same human-verified image description, fixing the judge’s basis on the sample’s attributes so that between-group differences correspond to the evidence the translator can access. The agreement of the Judger with human scoring and the comparison results are given in 3.3 .

content: The Judger rates a translation on a 0 0 – 3 3 scale for semantic accuracy, linguistic naturalness and cultural fit: 0 0 means serious errors with core semantics not conveyed; 1 1 means the main idea is recognizable but there are clear mistranslations, omissions or expression problems; 2 2 means the main information is accurate and grammar is largely correct, but there is slight unnaturalness, cultural infelicity or stylistic weakening; 3 3 means accurate semantics, natural expression and fit to the English social-media context ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Beyond the overall score, the prompt specifies format constraints, eight error types, three severity levels, a structured output format and three scoring examples. For image-dependent samples, the judge reads the human-verified Chinese image description, the Chinese source and the English translation simultaneously, and uses the image description to judge whether the translation recovers visual information not explicit in the text. The image description states only task-relevant visual facts and contains no answer to the translation point; all translator conditions use exactly the same judge input, keeping the scoring basis consistent.

section: E.2 Candidate Filtering and Differential Verification
content: The filtering stage aims to obtain the three evidence-dependency types separately. The first stage is a feature-based coarse filter with no LLM call: keeping only samples of length 5 5 – 30 30 characters containing Chinese characters, removing catch-all phrases (e.g., “thanks / so cute / amazing”) and templated content and discarding the Easy tier, then keeping, by regular-expression features (code-switching, elided reference, named entities, visual signals), candidates with a visual dependency or a strong textual signal, and filtering out pure cultural-symbol noise. The second stage performs differential verification on Visual and Hybrid candidates: a Gemini multimodal model generates an image text description, a text-only translation and a multimodal translation, and our text Judger (a 0 0 – 3 3 scale, the same scoring rubric as the main experiment’s judge) scores the two translations under the same image-description context; when the score difference of the multimodal translation over the text-only translation reaches the threshold ( gap ≥ 1 \mathrm{gap}\geq 1 ), the candidate enters human re-review, sorted by descending gap. Symbol candidates are not retained by visual gain, but are confirmed by humans to require internet-culture knowledge while not depending on the image. title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
content: Machine learning models are now widely used to predict environmental variable dynamics in domains like hydrology, climate science, agriculture, and ecology. These models are usually compared on fixed benchmark datasets using a single average accuracy score. As models improve, their scores become very close when averaged over large regions and long time periods, so the benchmark can no longer tell them apart, and a single number hides where and when a model fails. Three failures are common across environmental domains: models get worse as the climate shifts (non-stationarity), models fail at unmonitored sites (spatial extrapolation), and models miss rare but important regimes such as floods and droughts.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
content: We present EvoBench , a benchmark framework that shows where a model fails, tracks failures over time, and evolves to focus on model capability gaps. We apply EvoBench to daily streamflow prediction as a case study ( CAMELS-Evolve , about 9,000 U.S. basins, 1985–2024) and compare an operational physical model (NWM), a conceptual reference (HBV), and several data-driven models. No model wins on every testing scenarios (e.g., in terms of average accuracy, performance at low flows and unmonitored basins). Also we observe that all data-driven models under-predict floods. Additionally, we show that targeted fix based on the reported failures could mitigate weaknesses the benchmark identified in certain scenarios. EvoBench turns model evaluation from a saturated ranking into a moving map of model limitations.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Machine learning (ML) has been widely used in environmental modeling to predict streamflow, greenhouse-gas fluxes, air quality, soil moisture, and crop yield, and they are often reported to exceed traditional process-based models in terms of both accuracy and computational ( Kratzert et al., 2019a ; Tran et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Yu et al., 2025b ) . To compare these models, researchers have built large benchmark datasets with fixed training and test splits, and they usually report a single accuracy score such as RMSE, Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), and KGE.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: This way of evaluating models has several issues. As models improve, their scores become very close to one another. When many models reach nearly the same number, the benchmark saturates : the score can no longer tell good models from bad ones. More importantly, despite a better overall score, ML models are known to struggle in out-of-distribution and data-sparse scenarios, which could be obscured by averaging performance over large regions and long time periods. For scientific use, knowing the failures matters more than knowing the average.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Three types of failure are particularly common in machine learning applications across environmental domains. The first is non-stationarity : a model that works well on past data can get worse as the climate and land surface change, but a random train/test split hides this because it mixes easy and hard years together. The second is spatial extrapolation : sensors are sparse and unevenly placed, so a model that does well at monitored sites may fail at unmonitored ones, yet most benchmarks only test monitored sites. The third is regime-specific error : because models are trained to minimize average error, they tend to miss rare but important regimes such as floods and droughts, which contribute little to an average score. A useful benchmark should therefore be diagnostic (it should show where a model fails) and evolving (it should keep tracking failures as models and the environmental conditions change). Since these problems are shared across many environmental domains ( Karpatne et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2025a ) , the benchmark should be designed to be generalizable and adaptable across domains.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: In this work, we introduce EvoBench , a diagnostic and evolving benchmark framework for environmental modeling. We then apply it to daily streamflow prediction as a detailed case study, which we call CAMELS-Evolve . We build the case study on the CAMELSH dataset ( Tran et al., 2025 ) , which provides daily weather forcing, observed streamflow, and catchment attributes for about 9,000 river basins across the contiguous United States from 1985 to 2024. Hydrology is a good first case for three reasons: it shows all three failure modes above, it has strong physical and operational baselines to compare against, and new observations are being collected over time and can be used as ground truth. Unlike benchmarks in language modeling and computer vision, environmental ecosystems keep producing new test data. Every new day of observed streamflow is an example that no model could have seen during training. This makes it natural to test models in a rolling, forward-in-time fashion, which better reflects real-world deployment and reduces the risk of benchmark overfitting. Moreover, over the rolling evaluation, the benchmark is expected to actively find the conditions under which models fail — certain basin types, flow regimes, or time periods — instead of reporting one overall performance score. Later rounds then concentrate on these open problems rather than rewarding cases that models have already solved. In this way the benchmark keeps steering attention toward the frontier of what current models cannot yet do.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: In this case study, we use EvoBench to several physical models (NWM, HBV) and data-driven models (e.g., LSTM, EA-LSTM ( Kratzert et al., 2019b ) , Transformer, TCN, DLinear ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) , TSMixer ( Chen et al., 2023c ) , and PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2022 ) ). We find that no single model is best at everything. The LSTM and GRU surpass NWM in average NSE and the LSTM is also best at low flows, the EA-LSTM generalizes best to unmonitored basins, general-purpose time-series architectures fall near or below a simple conceptual model, and all data-driven models badly under-predict floods, where NWM remains far ahead. We also perform two additional tests for these baseline models, by (1) iteratively improving the model using evaluation feedback from each round to identify and address its specific weaknesses, and (2) incorporating memory across successive rounds, enabling it to retain insights from previous evaluations and refinements and leverage them to guide subsequent improvements.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Finally, we show that the benchmark’s findings are useful in practice: when it points to a specific weakness (dry and snowy basins), one of two plausible targeted fixes (over-sampling those basins) clearly improves both cells at no cost to overall accuracy, while the other (re-weighting low flows in the loss) does not help. In short, EvoBench turns model evaluation from a single, saturated ranking into a moving map of model limitations.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Large-scale datasets and benchmarks now exist for many environmental problems, including streamflow ( Addor et al., 2017 ; Kratzert et al., 2023 ) , greenhouse-gas and carbon fluxes ( Cheng et al., 2026c ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , and air quality ( Betancourt et al., 2021 ) . Most of them report average scores on a fixed test set. As a result, they tend to run into the same issues we target, including scores saturate, performance drops over time, and models that look good at monitored sites fail at new ones ( Nearing et al., 2024 ) . EvoBench is an evaluation layer that addresses these issues and can be applied across such benchmarks.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: CAMELS ( Addor et al., 2017 ; Newman et al., 2015 ) provided catchment attributes and daily data for 671 U.S. basins. Caravan ( Kratzert et al., 2023 ) extended this idea globally, CAMELSH ( Tran et al., 2025 ) provides hourly and daily data with attributes for about 9,000 U.S. basins, and recent extensions add weather nowcasts and forecasts to support operational, forecast-time evaluation ( Kratzert et al., 2024 ) . On these datasets, LSTM models ( Kratzert et al., 2018 ) and the entity-aware LSTM (EA-LSTM) ( Kratzert et al., 2019a ) , which uses static attributes to help a model generalize across basins, became the standard baselines; transformers and other advanced machine learning models have been tested more recently ( Koya and Roy, 2024 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026a ; Yu et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2022 ) . In particular, several previous works have targeted extreme events and unseen scenarios ( Frame et al., 2022 ; Nearing et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2023a ) —exactly the regime and spatial-transfer failures EvoBench isolates. General-purpose time-series foundation models ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2024 ) have also been applied to environmental series, which makes a diagnostic, evolving evaluation even more useful.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: NSE ( Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) and the Kling–Gupta efficiency ( Gupta et al., 2009 ; Kling et al., 2012 ) are the standard accuracy measures in hydrology. Flow-duration-curve signatures ( Yilmaz et al., 2008 ) measure the bias in high flows and low flows separately. We use these measures and add a skill score against a re-runnable reference so that results stay comparable across rounds. Recent work has also explored using large language models to mimic human expert preferences in evaluation ( Cheng et al., 2026b ) .

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: A growing body of work keeps benchmarks fresh so they do not saturate or become contaminated. Recent examples span modalities: collecting new data over time (MMBench-Live ( Anonymous, 2026b ) , LiveHouse-TS ( Wen et al., 2026 ) ), scraping freshly discovered problems to stay ahead of model cutoffs (Live-kBench ( Anonymous, 2026d ) , SWE-MERA ( Anonymous, 2025d ) ), generating harder items automatically ( Anonymous, 2025b ) , and updating labels as evidence improves ( Anonymous, 2026a ) . Recent surveys catalog these dynamic and contamination-resistant designs but note there are still no agreed standards for evaluating them ( Anonymous, 2025c ; Anonymous, 2025a ) , and some argue live benchmarks lose value once events are resolved ( Anonymous, 2026c ) . Our setting is different and offers a clear advantage. The test items come from the physical world, so there is nothing to generate and nothing to leak, and old rounds remain valid because the observed record only grows. To our knowledge no evolving benchmark has been built for environmental modeling.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Recent benchmarks use language-model agents to build or check test items ( Anonymous, 2026b ; Anonymous, 2026a ) . We use an agent in a narrow and auditable way. Specifically, all the performance scores in our framework are computed deterministically. The agent only decides whether a failure is a true model weakness or a data problem, and a model-independent water-balance check backs up that decision. The agent’s outputs inform updates to the evaluation protocol across iterations but do not directly determine the final evaluation scores, avoiding the additional uncertainty that agent-driven scoring could introduce.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: EvoBench requires multiple input components that most environmental-modeling tasks can provide: per-site time series of driver data, a few static attributes describing each site, a physical or empirical model to use as a reference, and a conservation law (such as a mass balance) to check whether the observations are physically plausible. In this section, we explain each part through the streamflow case study, CAMELS-Evolve . Fig. 1 illustrates the overall pipeline. Table 7 in the appendix shows how the same parts map to other domains.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: We build the case study on CAMELSH ( Tran et al., 2025 ) , which contains 9,008 U.S. river basins with daily records from 1985 to 2024. For each basin and day it provides 11 weather forcing variables, observed streamflow, and 44 static catchment attributes (such as climate indices and soil and land-cover descriptors), which are fixed in time. It also includes simulations from the National Water Model (NWM). Because basins differ in how much observed streamflow is available, we use two groups of basins: a strict core group (162 basins with at least 90% observation coverage over 1985–2024) and a larger extended observation group (1,139 basins with at least 80% coverage).

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Dynamic input features. Each data-driven model reads a 180-day history of five daily meteorological forcing variables, all derived from the NLDAS-2 reanalysis: precipitation ( Rainf ), air temperature ( Tair ), downward shortwave radiation ( SWdown ), downward longwave radiation ( LWdown ), and potential evapotranspiration ( PotEvap ). These five variables drive the dominant water-and-energy balance that governs runoff. Precipitation and temperature set the input and the rain/snow partition; the two radiation terms and potential evapotranspiration set the energy available to evaporate water and to melt snow.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Static catchment attributes. To let a single regional model adapt to each basin, we concatenate 18 static attributes to the inputs, which capture the basin’s time-invariant climate, topography, soil, and land-cover characteristics. Specifically, they fall into four groups. Climate : mean precipitation, mean potential evapotranspiration, aridity (their ratio), precipitation seasonality, the fraction of precipitation falling as snow, and the frequency and duration of high- and low-precipitation spells. Topography : drainage area, mean elevation, and mean slope. Soil : sand, silt, and clay fractions, soil permeability, and the baseflow index (the share of flow sustained by groundwater). Land cover : forest fraction. These attributes are exactly the axes along which we later define failure cells (Section 3 ), so aridity, snow fraction, area, baseflow index, and degree of regulation serve both as model inputs and as diagnostic groupings.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Target and preprocessing. The prediction target is daily specific discharge (mm day -1 ), i.e. observed streamflow normalized by basin area, which makes basins of very different size comparable. Forcings, attributes, and target are standardized to zero mean and unit variance using statistics computed only from each round’s training window, so no future information leaks into the inputs. Days with missing streamflow are excluded from training and scoring.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: We evaluate models in rounds . Each round covers five water years, i.e., the most recent year plus the previous four years and the window moves forward by one year between rounds. A model may use only data from before its round’s window, and it is then scored on the full five-year window. We use five years rather than one because a single year could be dominated by year-specific conditions, e.g., whether it happened to be wet or dry, while a five-year window is more stable and almost always contains both floods and droughts. In our data, five-year rounds reduce the round-to-round variation compared with one-year rounds (in scores by about 60%). Because neighboring rounds share four years of data, we treat a sequence of rounds as a trend rather than as independent samples.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: A failure cell is a group of basins that share a common property. Specifically, we group basins by five attributes, each linked to a known weakness of data-driven models: aridity (dry basins and low flow), snow fraction (snowmelt), basin area (long memory and routing), baseflow index (flashy response), and degree of regulation (dams and human control). The 2-D version additionally splits each basin’s record by flow regime—low, medium, high, and peak—using that basin’s own flow-duration curve. The 2-D view is important because a single average score can hide large errors that occur only in specific regimes. When analyzing predictive bias, opposite errors in different regimes can cancel out. For example, a model may over-predict low flow and under-predict peaks at the same time, which looks only “average” overall but is clearly wrong once the two regimes are separated.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 3.4. The evolving loop and its guardrail
content: Each round, the loop finds the failure cells where even the best model does poorly and promotes them, i.e., keeping them as the focus for the next round. The loop also retires cells that a model has solved (median NSE at least 0.5). Over time, attention moves toward the problems that remain unsolved. However, a loop that simply chased the largest errors would drift toward meaningless cases that cannot be possibly predicted by any models given the available data, such as dammed basins or bad gauges. Hence, the promotion of failure cells must pass a guardrail with three checks:

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 3.4. The evolving loop and its guardrail
content: (1) Agreement across independent models. We first require the failure to be shared across multiple models, rather than being specific to a single model, to ensure that it represents a meaningful limitation worth highlighting in the benchmark. If a single model fails while the others succeed, that is a weakness of that model, not a capability gap worth promoting for the field. In our implementation, we flag a cell only when at least two independent data-driven models fall below a preset skill threshold, which filters out the artifact of any one architecture or training run.

section: 3.4. The evolving loop and its guardrail
content: (2) A reference floor. We then ask whether the target is even learnable from the available data, by comparing against the per-basin-calibrated HBV reference and the physical NWM. If HBV or NWM predicts the cell acceptably while the learned models fail, the signal clearly exists in the data, so the failure is a genuine learned-model capability gap and should be promoted. If instead every model—including the calibrated HBV—fails, the cell is more likely limited by its data than by the models, and promoting it would chase an unlearnable target. To make this judgment, an LLM agent reads a short, structured evidence summary for the cell—the per-model skill scores, the HBV reference floor, the degree of regulation, and other static attributes—and labels it capability gap , regulation effect , data problem , or needs external information .

authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 3.4. The evolving loop and its guardrail
content: (3) Physical plausibility. Finally, a model-independent check tests whether the observations themselves are trustworthy, using a conservation law rather than any prediction. Over a long record runoff cannot exceed precipitation, so the runoff ratio, i.e., total runoff divided by total precipitation, must not exceed one. A value above one often indicates a wrong drainage area, an inter-basin transfer, or a gauging error, and thus the basin will be removed as a data artifact. Even if the data meet the runoff ratio requirement, it could be flagged if we observe that an runoff ratio very close to one, an implausibly high ratio for an arid basin, negative flows, or a long constant-value segment. These flags mark a basin as suspect but cannot by themselves say whether the data are wrong. For example, a long constant-value segment could be either a stuck sensor (bad data) or a managed, constant reservoir release (a real flow). Only these ambiguous cases are referred to a verification agent, which uses the basin’s regulation context to make the final decision. In the previous example, a flat segment in a heavily regulated basin is read as a managed release and kept, whereas the same pattern in an unregulated basin is treated as a faulty sensor.

authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 3.4. The evolving loop and its guardrail
content: Only a cell that passes all three checks, i.e., a failure shared across models, shown to be learnable by the reference, and backed by physically plausible data, is promoted. A key consequence is that the guardrail does not blindly promote the flood regime. For example, when every model fails on peak flows and the reference gives no signal, the cell is labeled a data problem. This could be because high-flow observations are themselves uncertain (e.g., rating curves extrapolated beyond the measured range). It is noteworthy that the agents used in our framework only make decisions and do not produce performance scores. All performance scores are computed by a deterministic process, which mitigates the impact of LLM stochasticity and improves the reproducibility of the benchmark results.

content: If a specific round is hard, both the model’s error and the reference’s error grow together, so their ratio stays stable. The reference must be runnable in any period. In this work, we use HBV ( Seibert and Vis, 2012 ) , a simple process-based hydrology model that we calibrate once per basin and can then run on any input. HBV is meant to serve only as a modest baseline, not a strong competitor.

authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Many existing works holds out only time in evaluation. To measure true spatial generalization, we group basins into six clusters by their attributes and hold out one whole cluster at a time, training on the rest and predicting the held-out basins. We report the spatial gap , the drop in NSE from gauged to ungauged prediction. For the reference, HBV’s drop from local calibration to using neighbors’ parameters gives a baseline that learned models should beat.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: We compare ten models. Two are process-based models: the operational NWM and the HBV reference. Eight are data-driven baselines. Four are models commonly used in hydrology: LSTM, EA-LSTM ( Kratzert et al., 2019b ) , a GRU (lighter gated recurrent model), and a small encoder-only Transformer (2 layers, model width 64, about 69k parameters). The other four are popular general-purpose time-series architectures: a TCN (dilated causal convolutions), DLinear (trend–seasonal decomposition followed by linear maps over time) ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) , TSMixer (all-MLP mixing across time and features) ( Chen et al., 2023c ) , and a simplified PatchTST (a 2-layer Transformer encoder over 30-day patches) ( Nie et al., 2022 ) . The training data covers all the data before the testing window in the current round. Each data-driven model reads the input of a 180-day history of five weather variables plus 18 static attributes and predicts daily streamflow. Every data-driven model is trained for one epoch, i.e., one expected pass over all of its training samples, so the number of iterations grows with the size of the training set; full training details are in Appendix A . We report results on the core group (162 basins) and the extended group (1,139 basins). We use five metrics: NSE and KGE ′ for overall accuracy, log-NSE for low flows, peak-day percent bias for floods, and the skill score of Eq. ( 2 ) against HBV.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: This comparison uses a single fixed temporal split rather than the sliding rounds of Section 3.4 . All data-driven models are trained on all data before the test window (water years 1986–2010) and evaluated on 2011–2022, a held-out future period, matching the protocol of the sliding rounds. The HBV reference is calibrated per basin on the same pre-test record (water years 1986–2010). NWM is scored from NOAA’s NWM v3.0 retrospective simulation over the test period; it is an external operational benchmark whose parameters were calibrated by its developers rather than under our protocol. Every reported value is a median over basins.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Table 1 shows the comparison. The ranking changes with the metric. On overall accuracy, the LSTM (NSE 0.674) and GRU (0.665) surpass NWM (0.644), and the LSTM also has the best KGE ′ (0.711) and the best low-flow skill (log-NSE 0.595). Here note that NWM is an external operational benchmark whose calibration period may overlap our test years, which would favor NWM. NWM remains by far the best at floods: every data-driven model under-predicts peak days by 27–44%, while NWM is at − 13 % -13\% . The EA-LSTM (0.633) comes close to NWM on NSE, while the GRU, despite its high NSE, is weaker at low flows (log-NSE 0.545). Among data-driven time-series architectures, only the TCN (0.595) is competitive with the recurrent models; DLinear, PatchTST, and TSMixer fall below the HBV reference on NSE and have strongly negative log-NSE, i.e., they largely fail to learn low flows. The Transformer lies in between on the 162-basin core group (NSE 0.558). At the larger scale of the extended group (Table 2 ), most models score lower, because this group admits harder, lower-coverage, and more regulated basins. The LSTM (0.637), GRU (0.630), and EA-LSTM (0.586) all surpass NWM (0.562), by a wider margin than on the core group, and the LSTM is again the best at low flows (log-NSE 0.606). NWM keeps the best KGE ′ (0.664) and peak-day bias ( − 14 % -14\% , against − 29 % -29\% to − 45 % -45\% for the data-driven models). A single-number leaderboard would hide all of these differences: the best model depends on whether one asks about average skill, low flows, or floods.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Our absolute NSE values are lower than the strongest LSTM results reported on the standard 531-basin CAMELS benchmark, where well-tuned, ensembled models reach a median NSE of roughly 0.74–0.76 ( Kratzert et al., 2019a ; Feng et al., 2020 ) . Several deliberate choices explain the difference. We train a single model using a reduced input set (five forcings and 18 attributes), and maintain the same training budget across all ten models, so that differences reflect the models rather than tuning effort. We also evaluate on CAMELSH with a different temporal split, and our extended group deliberately includes low-coverage and heavily regulated basins that the 531-basin benchmark excludes, both of which lower the median. Also note that our aim is to expose relative , regime-specific behavior rather than to maximize absolute skill. Stronger absolute performance could be produced by model-specific tuning, ensembling, and augmentation of input variables.

Each fold model is trained over its own training basins. Although EA-LSTM is worse on monitored basins, its drop to unmonitored basins is about 45% smaller than the LSTM’s (0.105 vs 0.191), and it becomes the best data-driven model once ungauged (NSE 0.529). This matches the design of the EA-LSTM, whose use of static attributes is meant to help it transfer across locations. Conversely, the LSTM, the best model on monitored basins, loses the most among the strong models (gap 0.191), followed by the TCN (0.175) and GRU (0.165). All data-driven models fall well below their gauged scores, and only the EA-LSTM, GRU, and LSTM stay clearly above the HBV regional reference (0.416); the Transformer and PatchTST, with the largest gaps (about 0.25), fall below it. The very small or negative gaps of DLinear and TSMixer reflect weak gauged skill rather than good transfer.

content: Here we use the fixed-split predictions on the extended group (1,139 basins), which gives enough basins per cell for stable estimates. The 1-D grid consistently ranks the hardest basin types across models: at the larger scale, snow-dominated basins (n = = 109; LSTM NSE 0.47), arid basins (n = = 492; 0.50), and baseflow-dominated basins (0.57). Heavily regulated basins are hard for NWM (0.49 vs. 0.60 on natural basins) and for the EA-LSTM and Transformer, but barely for the LSTM (0.63 vs. 0.64). The 2-D grid (Figure 2 ) explains why the LSTM looks only average on arid basins: it makes two opposite errors that cancel in a single score. It over-predicts low flow by about 219% and under-predicts peaks by about 30%. The only cell where the LSTM is worse than the HBV reference is arid low flow (skill relative to HBV − 0.31 -0.31 ). Because the simple reference succeeds there, the signal exists in the data, so this cell passes the reference-floor check of the guardrail as a genuine model capability gap. On the peak cells, in contrast, the LSTM beats HBV (skill about + 0.3 +0.3 ) yet still under-predicts peaks by 30–37%, while NWM is at about − 14 % -14\% ; since the physical reference captures floods much better from the same weather, the flood shortfall is also a learnable capability gap rather than a pure data limitation, although high-flow observations, which come from rating curves extrapolated beyond the measured range, add uncertainty for every model. The 2-D grid also reveals differences between models that an average score hides: on arid low flow the LSTM over-predicts ( + 219 % +219\% ) while the Transformer under-predicts ( − 62 % -62\% ). The two models fail in opposite directions.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: We run the 5-year window forward for five rounds, retraining every data-driven model from scratch to each round’s cutoff (Figure 3 , Table 4 ). The rounds test water years 2016–2020, 2017–2021, …, 2020–2024. In each round a model is trained on all data before its window (round 1 on ≤ \leq 2015, round 5 on ≤ \leq 2019), and we evaluate on both the core and the extended group, with HBV recalibrated to each round’s cutoff as the reference. We see four things. First, the ranking is stable over time: the LSTM surpasses NWM in every round on both groups and has the best overall NSE in all rounds but one (core round 2, where the GRU is marginally ahead), and the GRU surpasses NWM in every round except round 3 on the core group. The EA-LSTM and TCN follow, while the Transformer and the other general-purpose architectures stay near or below HBV. Second, the strongest models are stable across rounds: the LSTM varies by less than 0.02 NSE over the five rounds on both groups, even though the rounds include harder recent years. Less stable models still swing between rounds: the EA-LSTM dips in the middle rounds on the core group (0.649 in round 1 to 0.585 in round 3), and the Transformer collapses in single rounds (0.343 in round 4 on the core group, 0.154 in round 5 on the extended group). A fixed split would average such swings away. HBV stays a flat, low baseline and keeps the skill scores comparable. Third, arid and snow basins remain the frontier, and they show the retire mechanism at work. On the core group, no data-driven model reaches the retirement threshold (median NSE 0.5) on arid basins in any round, and NWM reaches it only once (round 2). On the extended group, the LSTM reaches it on arid basins in rounds 1 and 4 (0.502 and 0.506) and on snow basins in rounds 1, 4, and 5 (0.525, 0.504, 0.559); because these cells sit right at the threshold, they alternate between retired and open across rounds, which is why retired cells stay in a regression set rather than being dropped. Averaged over rounds, the LSTM matches NWM on core arid basins (0.410 vs. 0.409) and exceeds it on extended arid (0.480 vs. 0.381) and snow basins (0.505 vs. 0.265); the core group has too few snow basins (n = = 6) for stable estimates. Fourth, the NWM retrospective ends in January 2023, so in rounds 4 and 5 NWM is scored only on the early part of the window. Its drop in round 5 (extended overall 0.530, snow − - 0.099) therefore should not be read as a real decline. This is why the benchmark uses HBV, which can be rerun on any new window, as its reference.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 4.3.2. Enhancing model based on benchmark feedback.
content: Finally, we test whether the benchmark’s findings can be acted on, using the fixed split on the core group. The benchmark flags that the LSTM over-predicts low flow in arid basins (by about + 63 % +63\% on arid low-flow days) and that arid and snow basins remain its weakest cells. In response, we apply two simple changes to training: we give low-flow days three times more weight in the loss, and we additionally sample arid and snow basins three times more often. Because single runs are noisy, each configuration is trained with three seeds (Figure 4 ). The low-flow loss does not help: the arid-cell NSE is unchanged (0.381 to 0.378), the arid low-flow bias barely moves ( + 63 % +63\% to + 61 % +61\% ), and the snow cell gets worse (0.09 to − 0.08 -0.08 ). Over-sampling, in contrast, lifts the arid cell from 0.381 to 0.473, more than twice the seed spread (standard deviation 0.03–0.04), and the snow cell from 0.09 to 0.28, with no loss in overall NSE (0.668 in both cases). The arid cell thus moves close to the retirement threshold, crossing it for one of the three seeds, but it stays open on average and is carried to the next round. The experiment also shows that the benchmark can tell which of two plausible fixes actually addresses a diagnosed weakness, and why it reports seed spread: the per-seed arid low-flow bias ranges from + 8 % +8\% to + 130 % +130\% for the same configuration, so bias changes from a single run would be unreliable.

section: 4.3.3. Diagnosis, intervention, and memory in evolving tests.
content: We now ask whether this loop generalizes. For each data-driven baseline we run three conditions over the five sliding rounds on the core group. (1) Baseline : a fresh model each round, no intervention. (2) Targeted : a fresh model each round, but intervened on the previous round’s promoted failure cells (a low-flow-weighted loss plus over-sampling of basins in those cells). (3) Targeted+memory : the same intervention, but the model is carried across rounds (warm start) with cheap incremental updates (20% of a one-epoch training per round, about 1,300–1,500 iterations instead of 6,400–7,300). Round 1 is identical for all three, since there is no previous round to diagnose. Tables 5 and 6 report the mean over the five rounds. Each cell is a single run, so given the seed spread measured above (about 0.01 for overall and 0.03–0.04 for arid NSE), we only read differences larger than these as real. (The baseline column differs slightly from Table 4 because here input normalization is fixed from the round-1 window for all rounds, so that a warm-started model sees consistent inputs.)

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
section: 4.3.3. Diagnosis, intervention, and memory in evolving tests.
content: Three patterns are observed. First, the targeted intervention helps most models on the cell it aims at. On arid basins it clearly raises the GRU (0.360 to 0.442, and 0.469 with memory) and the EA-LSTM (0.361 to 0.401, and 0.422 with memory), and with memory also the TCN (0.240 to 0.294); it lifts the linear and all-MLP models from very low levels (TSMixer − 0.50 -0.50 to − 0.15 -0.15 , DLinear − 0.41 -0.41 to − 0.27 -0.27 with memory). The LSTM, which already has the best arid score (0.457), does not gain further, and the Transformer does not benefit at all. Second, cross-round memory gives the best overall score for five of the eight models while using about a fifth of the compute per round: the LSTM (0.680 to 0.690), GRU (0.668 to 0.679), EA-LSTM (0.629 to 0.637), TSMixer (0.355 to 0.375), and PatchTST (0.465 to 0.512). For the three recurrent models this gain is small, close to the seed spread, so memory mainly matches full retraining at a fraction of the cost. Third, the interventions do not help every family: they lower the Transformer’s overall score (0.503 to 0.484), and memory slightly lowers the TCN (0.579 to 0.569). In short, the loop “diagnose → \to intervene → \to update with memory” helps most baseline models on the evolving benchmark, but whether a given intervention helps also depends on the model family.

authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: We presented EvoBench , a benchmark framework for environmental modeling that is both diagnostic and evolving, and we validated it through a streamflow case study ( CAMELS-Evolve ) on CAMELSH. EvoBench breaks performance into failure cells by site attribute and regime, measures prediction at unmonitored sites, slides a time window forward to track which failures remain, and uses a small agent with a physical consistency check to tell true model weaknesses apart from data problems.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: Across the base models in our tests, we found that no model is best at everything. Also all data-driven models under-predict floods. A single number would hide all of these differences. Finally, evolving the benchmark by sliding the window forward showed varying model performance, a sign of non-stationarity that a fixed split hides, while snow and arid basins remained the hardest cases, with the best models only beginning to retire them in some rounds. This shift—from a single ranking on a static dataset to a moving map of model limitations—is useful for environmental ML benchmarks in general, where the real environmental ecosystems keep supplying new benchmark data.

In addition to extending to other environmental domains, we will also consider a forecasting setup with forecast inputs and the addition of time-varying disturbance data.

content: The LSTM, EA-LSTM, and GRU use hidden size 128 and dropout 0.4, with a last-step linear readout. The Transformer is encoder-only with d model = 64 d_{\text{model}}{=}64 , 4 heads, 2 layers, feed-forward 128, and sinusoidal positional encoding ( ∼ \sim 69k parameters). The TCN has three residual blocks of dilated causal convolutions (64 channels, kernel 3, dilations 1, 2, 4, dropout 0.3). DLinear decomposes the window into trend (25-day moving average) and seasonal parts, applies one linear map over time to each, and joins the result with the static attributes in the output head. TSMixer uses two blocks of alternating time-mixing and feature-mixing MLPs (dropout 0.2) followed by temporal mean pooling. The simplified PatchTST splits the window into six 30-day patches, embeds each, and runs a 2-layer Transformer encoder ( d model = 64 d_{\text{model}}{=}64 , 4 heads, feed-forward 128, dropout 0.3) over the patch tokens. All learned models take a 180-day sequence of five NLDAS-2 forcings ( Rainf , Tair , SWdown , LWdown , PotEvap ) plus 18 static attributes and predict standardized specific discharge (mm/day). Static attributes are concatenated to each timestep, except that the EA-LSTM feeds them only to its input gate and DLinear adds them at the output head. Training uses Adam ( 10 − 3 10^{-3} ) with batch 256.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: A 10-parameter HBV-light model (snow, soil-moisture, and two response reservoirs) is vectorized over a 60-sample Monte-Carlo ensemble and the KGE ′ -best parameter set is cached per basin. It is calibrated on the same data as the learned models, i.e., all data before the test window: water years 1986–2010 for the fixed split and up to each round’s cutoff in the sliding rounds. The first calibration year is a warm-up excluded from the objective, and every evaluation run starts with a one-year spin-up so that the snow, soil, and groundwater stores are not cold-started on the first scored day. Because it can be run on any evaluation window, HBV serves as the forward reference in Eq. ( 2 ).

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
authors: Yiming Sun, Yuan Zhang, Qi Cheng, Yingda Fan, Runlong Yu, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia
content: The interventions add two knobs, each a response to a benchmark diagnosis: a low-flow-weighted loss ( 3 × 3\times weight on each basin’s bottom-30% flow days of the training window) and 3 × 3\times over-sampling of basins. In the fixed-split experiment the over-sampled basins are the arid and snow basins, and each configuration is trained with seeds 0–2 (one epoch each). In the three-condition experiment the over-sampled basins are those in the previous round’s promoted cells; the baseline and targeted conditions train from scratch each round (one epoch), while targeted+memory warm-starts from the previous round’s model and trains for 20% of an epoch. There, input normalization is fixed from the round-1 training window so that a warm-started model sees consistent inputs. Only the intervention knobs change between conditions; data, architecture, and seed are identical.

content: Each agent follows the pattern “deterministic core emits an evidence bundle → \to LLM returns a strict-JSON verdict → \to a deterministic rule proxy is the fallback.” The data-quality auditor’s decisive checks (runoff ratio > 1 ⇒ >1\Rightarrow exclude) are deterministic; only borderline cases (e.g. long flatlines in regulated basins) are referred to the LLM judge. Verdicts are stored as JSON and never enter any score.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
content: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation . We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Medicine is, at its core, a distributed enterprise. The expertise required to manage a complex patient rarely resides in a single clinician, department, or institution. A rural primary care physician develops pattern recognition for atypical presentations under resource constraints that an academic specialist never encounters; a community cardiologist accumulates experience with medication titration across diverse socioeconomic contexts; a home health monitoring system learns to distinguish clinically significant decompensation from benign fluctuations in daily vital signs. This distributed expertise, forged through thousands of diagnostic encounters across heterogeneous clinical environments, represents the most valuable and least utilized knowledge asset in healthcare.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has contributed to growing interest in agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), which seeks to extend AI systems beyond static information retrieval toward perception, reasoning, and action in dynamic environments. Prior work has reported promising results in complex domains such as software engineering, mathematical theorem proving, and scientific hypothesis generation Yang et al. (2024) ; Baba et al. (2025) ; Gottweis et al. (2025) ; Lange et al. (2025) . In healthcare, where clinical reasoning demands synthesizing heterogeneous evidence under uncertainty, agentic AI promises to augment human expertise by orchestrating knowledge-intensive diagnostic and therapeutic workflows.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Early applications of agentic AI in medicine established foundational approaches to algorithmic clinical reasoning. Systems such as those in Ferber et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2024) ; Rose et al. (2025) ; Hao et al. (2025) employ LLMs as centralized orchestrators, using modular decomposition to partition clinical queries into sub-tasks spanning evidence retrieval, differential diagnosis, and treatment recommendation. While effective for localized decision support, these systems operate as isolated instances constrained by static reasoning templates and single-institution deployment. Recent work has advanced toward hierarchical multi-agent systems enabling dynamic collaboration for symptom assessment, diagnostic interpretation, and treatment recommendation, simulating multi-turn clinical consultations Almansoori et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Qin et al. (2025) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) .

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: However, a fundamental architectural tension pervades current systems: clinical expertise is inherently distributed across institutions, specialties, and care settings, yet agentic AI remains stubbornly centralized. This tension is deeper than the well-known challenges of data fragmentation and privacy regulation, though it encompasses them. We identify three dimensions of this mismatch, each reflecting not merely a data problem but an expertise problem.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The conventional framing of healthcare data silos emphasizes regulatory barriers to data sharing. Though real, this framing obscures a more fundamental issue: even removing regulatory barriers would not pool clinical expertise . The diagnostic insight a rural emergency physician develops managing acute coronary syndrome without catheterization access is not encoded in the EHR; it resides in the physician’s reasoning process and outcomes observed. A centralized system trained on pooled records acquires statistical patterns but not the situated reasoning constituting clinical mastery. The challenge is therefore not merely to share data across institutions but to share the experience of navigating clinical complexity.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The advancement of LLMs has been predicated on access to ever-larger corpora of human-generated text, yet recent analyses suggest this paradigm is approaching asymptotic limits as high-quality medical data becomes increasingly scarce Villalobos et al. (2024) ; Muennighoff et al. (2023) . In healthcare, where rare conditions, evolving treatment protocols, and longitudinal patient trajectories demand continuous learning, reliance on static datasets creates systems that are perpetually outdated. More critically, static training data captures declarative medical knowledge such as facts, guidelines, and associations, but not the procedural knowledge of how to apply it under the uncertainty and time pressure of clinical practice.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Autonomous agents handling Protected Health Information (PHI) must comply with HIPAA, IVDR, and GDPR Neupane et al. (2025) ; Müller et al. (2022) ; Voigt and Von dem Bussche (2017) , yet compliance is only one dimension of a broader sovereignty challenge. Healthcare institutions increasingly assert governance over not only their data but their institutional knowledge (i.e., clinical protocols, reasoning conventions, and accumulated expertise) as competitive and intellectual assets. Current architectures offer institutions a binary choice: contribute data to centralized systems or remain isolated. What is needed is an architecture that enables institutions to contribute to and benefit from collective intelligence while retaining sovereignty over their clinical assets , sharing insights without surrendering the experiences from which those insights derive.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: These challenges are compounded by the computational realities of deployment. State-of-the-art agents rely on multi-model toolchains: EchoAgent Daghyani et al. (2025) orchestrates domain-specific vision models for echocardiogram interpretation, while Echo-CoPilot Heidari et al. (2025) leverages EchoPrime Vukadinovic et al. (2025) and PanEcho Holste et al. (2025) for multi-view cardiac analysis. Centralizing such systems incurs substantial inference costs Zhang et al. (2025a) , while naive distribution faces severe infrastructure heterogeneity.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Such converging pressures cannot be addressed by existing distributed learning paradigms. Federated Learning (FL), the prevailing privacy-preserving approach, aggregates model parameters through gradient averaging, operating at the wrong level of abstraction for clinical expertise. Gradients encode statistical correlations rather than reasoning strategies, require architectural homogeneity, and provide no mechanism for transferring the procedural knowledge characterizing clinical mastery.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: In this Perspective, we propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS) as an alternative paradigm: a framework wherein distributed agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence through the sharing of abstracted reasoning trajectories, while concurrently self-evolving through the reciprocal incorporation of network-wide experiential knowledge into local reasoning capabilities. We formalize the architectural principles underlying DAS (Section 3 ), examine the deployment landscape and governance requirements for real-world adoption (Sections 3.5 and 4 ), and articulate the critical open challenges (Section 5 ).

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: The transition toward decentralized agentic architectures represents a necessary evolution aligned with fundamental shifts in how AI acquires knowledge. LLMs’ progress has been predicated on scaling human-curated datasets, a paradigm approaching asymptotic limits as high-quality clinical data grows scarce Villalobos et al. (2024) ; Muennighoff et al. (2023) . In healthcare, this constraint is particularly acute: medical knowledge is continuously generated through diagnostic encounters, treatment adaptations, and clinical judgments across thousands of institutions, accessible only in part to any centralized system. We argue that the next frontier lies in enabling AI agents to learn directly from distributed clinical experiences, transforming ephemeral diagnostic interactions into durable, shareable intelligence.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: Experience differs fundamentally from data. Data represents static records, laboratory values, imaging findings, documented diagnoses. Experience, by contrast, encompasses the dynamic process through which an agent perceives clinical signals, reasons about their significance under uncertainty, selects among possible interventions, and observes outcomes Silver and Sutton (2025) . Consider the difference between a dataset of electrocardiograms labeled with diagnoses and the experience of an agent that detects a subtle ST-elevation pattern, retrieves relevant patient history, considers confounding factors, and refines its interpretation based on downstream clinical confirmation. The former provides declarative knowledge, facts about the world; the latter generates procedural knowledge, that is, how to navigate clinical reasoning itself.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: Each institutional agent continuously generates experiential feedback through clinical interactions. A cardiology-focused agent may develop nuanced expertise in distinguishing Takotsubo cardiomyopathy from acute coronary syndrome in post-menopausal women; a primary care agent may learn to recognize atypical thyroid dysfunction in elderly populations. Such experiences represent the contextual, procedural knowledge unavailable in static datasets. The challenge lies in synthesizing this distributed intelligence into collective clinical wisdom without violating data sovereignty constraints.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: To address this, we propose DAS as a framework for agent-centric insight aggregation. Unlike FL McMahan et al. (2017) , which aggregates numerical model parameters through gradient averaging, DAS operates at a higher abstraction level: the sharing of semantic trajectories . We define a semantic trajectory as a structured record comprising an agent’s reasoning path: observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and inferential steps, together with environmental feedback that validated or refuted its conclusions. Exchanging these traces rather than raw data or model weights enables knowledge transfer that is both privacy-conscious and semantically meaningful, forming the substrate through which individual agentic nodes continuously self-evolve: each agent refines its local reasoning capabilities by assimilating experiential knowledge distilled from across the distributed network.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Why existing federated approaches are insufficient.
content: Gradient-based approaches assume homogeneity in model architectures, data distributions, and task definitions, while assumptions rarely hold across diverse healthcare settings. Semantic trajectories abstract away these implementation details to capture the core reasoning process. An insight such as “in patients presenting with chest pain and elevated troponin but atypical ECG findings, consider requesting strain echocardiography before concluding myocardial infarction” transfers meaningfully across institutional contexts regardless of underlying architectures or data distributions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Why existing federated approaches are insufficient.
content: DAS is distinct from FL variants that partially address the limitations of FedAvg McMahan et al. (2017) . Federated distillation Lin et al. (2020) ; He et al. (2020) exchanges soft predictions or logits, reducing architectural coupling. Split learning Gupta and Raskar (2018) partitions computation across clients and servers. Personalized FL T Dinh et al. (2020) ; Fallah et al. (2020) accommodates heterogeneous data distributions through local adaptation. Each addresses a specific limitation of gradient-based aggregation, yet all share a common constraint: they operate at the level of model parameters or outputs, not at the level of reasoning .

authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: DAS relates to, but differs from, several active research directions. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Lewis et al. (2020) enhances LLM reasoning by retrieving relevant documents; DAS can be viewed as a federated extension of RAG where the retrieval corpus consists of validated reasoning trajectories from distributed agents. Chain-of-thought distillation Ho et al. (2023) ; Magister et al. (2023) transfers reasoning via training on reasoning traces; DAS extends this from a teacher-student relationship to a network of peer agents sharing experiential knowledge. Experience replay in multi-agent reinforcement learning Foerster et al. (2017) enables learning from stored interactions; DAS adapts this to healthcare where experiences comprise clinical reasoning under real-world constraints.

authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The aggregation of validated semantic trajectories enables what we term collective self-evolution : the emergence of shared diagnostic intelligence exceeding any individual agent’s capabilities. This evolution occurs not through centralized retraining on pooled data but through continuous refinement of reasoning strategies based on cross-institutional experience. When an agent successfully navigates a novel presentation to correct a diagnosis, that trajectory becomes available network-wide, enriching the collective repertoire of clinical problem-solving once abstracted and validated.
