section: Appendix C Physical Relations and Constants
content: The specification axioms evaluate closed-form relations of conceptual aircraft design [ 71 ] (Table ). Table C.1 gives the constants of the relations and of the International Standard Atmosphere (ISO 2533:1975) with the initial values of the graded degrees, and Table C.2 the remote-sensing constants with the Airplane Design Groups of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) 3 3 3 FAA Advisory Circular 150/5300-13B, Airport Design, March 31, 2022. . The train prior widens each per-class range of a derived quantity over the 44 clean training aircraft to [ 0.88 ​ min , 1.12 ​ max ] [0.88\min,\,1.12\max] , as the oracle does; these initial bands are then learned with their slopes (Section ), and business jets, absent from training, start from the band of all training classes. The learned bands act as tolerances learned from the fleet. On specification records, 45.7% of them keep both edges inside the training fleet range widened in the same way, and the others extend beyond it (Appendix G.9 ). In the remote-sensing stratum, 103 of the 144 learned group bands (the 18 bands of R2 for military roles, R3 and R4 in each of the 8 seeds) extend beyond the clean training range widened on each side by 12% of its width. The initial bands of R2 for military roles, R3 and R4 (Table C.2 ) were set from the annotations and from knowledge of the aircraft types to contain every clean annotation, those of test and unseen sites included, and the generator oracle of the satellite benchmark was fitted on the clean annotations of every site, so both may carry held-out information; the satellite benchmark was not regenerated, nor the remote-sensing stratum retrained, without them.

section: Appendix D Data and Benchmark Details
content: This appendix describes the specification records and the benchmarks built from the records and images of Section : the corruption operators with their realized magnitudes (Table D.1 ), the realized instances per type and split (Appendix D.1 ), the frame of the cross-dataset runs and the rule that chose the examples of Figure . Every generator is deterministic given its seed. The 107 specification records cover seven classes: wide-body (17 aircraft of 8 families), narrow-body (18 of 6), regional jet (13 of 6), regional turboprop (11 of 8), business jet (19 of 17, the unseen class), general-aviation turboprop (12 of 11) and general-aviation piston (17 of 15). They were compiled from the type-certificate data sheets of the aviation authorities of the United States, the European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom and France and from manufacturer documents (airport-planning manuals, specification sheets and flight-manual excerpts), with other public sources used for cross-checks. The 67 jets declare thrust and the 40 propeller aircraft shaft power, and 18 records, all general-aviation aircraft, declare the stall speed; every record passed a loose screening with the verifier’s physics module, so the clean records were checked against the relations that the verifier evaluates; the intervention labels, set from the edit alone, bypass this dependence. Table D.1 lists the corruption operators. A candidate that the oracle does not flag is generated again with its magnitude doubled, for at most six attempts (Section ), so the realized magnitudes reflect the oracle tolerances and extend beyond the declared grid of 5 and 10%. They extend furthest for performance corruptions, whose Breguet tolerance must absorb the largest residual among the clean records.

In the cross-dataset runs of Appendix G.5 , a knowledge base fitted on one source scores the other through a 23-field unified frame (Figure (c)) with only the axioms R2 to R4, which both sources can evaluate; a specification record takes its role and design group from its clean wingspan. On the records of each split, the report prints the class of the nearest clean training record (Section ; example in Figure ): this proximity names the class of a record from an unseen family and attributes each business jet, a class absent from training, to its nearest training class.

section: E.1 Proof of the Exact Reduction
content: Proof. (a) Fix α \alpha . A masked axiom has α k = 0 \alpha_{k}=0 , and the implementation sets its degree (for a cross-modal axiom, its truth) to 0 by selection before any sum; its term and its weight therefore vanish from the numerator and from the denominator of Eq. ( ), which reduce to the sums over 𝒮 ′ \mathcal{S}^{\prime} . If 𝒮 ′ \mathcal{S}^{\prime} is empty, a tabular stratum takes V 𝒮 = ln ⁡ 2 V_{\mathcal{S}}=\ln 2 by definition and the cross-modal stratum has γ 𝒜 ​ 𝒳 = 0 \gamma_{\mathcal{AX}}=0 . Every degree and its derivatives are finite, because undeclared fields carry a finite placeholder and degrees are capped at 10 4 10^{4} , so the selection passes no value and no gradient from the degree v k v_{k} , or the truth sat k \mathrm{sat}_{k} , of a masked axiom. The stratum verdict therefore has zero derivative with respect to them, and a field read only by masked axioms does not affect it. (b) Without an image, no cross-modal axiom is available. Then, as when every cross-modal axiom is masked, γ 𝒜 ​ 𝒳 = 0 \gamma_{\mathcal{AX}}=0 , and since λ 𝒯 > 0 \lambda_{\mathcal{T}}>0 , Eq. ( ) reduces to feas 𝒯 = exp ⁡ ( − V 𝒯 ) \mathrm{feas}_{\mathcal{T}}=\exp(-V_{\mathcal{T}}) ; the implementation returns feas 𝒯 \mathrm{feas}_{\mathcal{T}} itself in this case, so the equality holds bit for bit. Otherwise, the cross-modal stratum enters both sums of Eq. ( ) with weight λ 𝒜 ​ 𝒳 ​ γ 𝒜 ​ 𝒳 \lambda_{\mathcal{AX}}\gamma_{\mathcal{AX}} and the tabular stratum keeps λ 𝒯 \lambda_{\mathcal{T}} , which is the stated renormalization over the strata present. □ \square

content: This appendix completes the setup of Section : it lists the comparators and the configuration, states how the configuration was selected and which choices used data beyond the training split, and reports how the vision results change when the part detector’s visibility threshold is re-selected on validation data alone. Table F.1 orders the comparators by the knowledge they receive; each shares the partitions, the labels and the evaluation code of NeSySpec, with settings selected on validation data within a budget fixed before its runs, and one planned arm, the language model in its thinking mode, has no result: in a pilot run too few of its answers could be parsed, below the parse rate fixed before the runs. Table F.2 gives the configuration of every module of NeSySpec, of its optional settings and of the baseline detectors; bands, slopes, latents, visual heads, read-outs, operating thresholds and checkpoints are fitted or selected on data, and every other value was set once. The class bands of the generator oracle are fitted on all 107 aircraft, test and out-of-distribution aircraft included, and reach training through the generator labels and per-constraint targets (Section ); Appendix G.9 refits the oracle without test or out-of-distribution aircraft.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: NeSySpec’s configuration was selected on validation data and on held-out training classes; during development, earlier configurations were also evaluated on the test splits. Validation data selected the configuration of both tabular strata, the largest-violation key, the abduction and repair rules and the optional settings, and held-out training classes also selected the key and the critical-field alert (Appendix G.9 ). The rule that reads each constraint as held or violated has no tuned parameter. The part detector’s visibility threshold was moved from 0.25 to 0.20 on a 240-image stratified subset including test and out-of-distribution images, by an informal trade-off, with no numeric criterion and no saved tuning output. The results of this paper use 0.20.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: Re-selected on 240 stratified validation images alone, under a criterion declared beforehand that keeps propeller detections on jets, which have no propeller, at or below 10% of jet images, the threshold becomes 0.25, as in 197 of 200 resampled subsets: at 0.20 those detections reach 17% on validation, against 7% on the original subset. Weighing part visibility and those detections equally keeps 0.20. Without retraining, 0.25 turns 12.1% of the part flags of training, validation and test images to not visible, 2,794 flags, 1,618 of them on the wing.

content: Retrained at 0.25 with the same code, configuration and 8 seeds (even seeds on the RTX 5090, which trained the original module, and odd seeds on the RTX 4090; the even seeds alone give the same accuracy and pointing readings), the photograph module keeps its macro head accuracy (0.916 on test and 0.944 on unseen families, as at 0.20) and at most one collapsed head per seed on test. It also keeps its pointing lead over the network without a localization term ( + 0.671 +0.671 ) and with permuted masks ( + 0.414 +0.414 ), its lead over RRR, GradMask and Pukdee et al. on PASCAL-Part ( + 0.568 +0.568 , + 0.676 +0.676 and + 0.469 +0.469 , every interval above zero) and the nine overall readings of the cross-modal stratum against Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B on test, unseen families and the unseen class. Of the 21 readings by pair type, 4 change by one step under each of the two bootstrap streams of that comparison, 3 of them to the disadvantage of the stratum. The networks without a localization term or with permuted masks, RRR, GradMask and Pukdee et al. were trained with the flags at 0.20 and not retrained. At 0.25 the cross-modal AUROC is 0.693 on test (0.692 at 0.20) and slightly lower on unseen families (0.716 against 0.733) and on the unseen class (0.827 against 0.844); the axiom on engine placement and tail configuration (AX4) is available on 0.784 of the test pairs scored for detection, instead of 0.956. Pointing on pseudo-masks is slightly lower on test (0.774 against 0.780) and on unseen families (0.778 against 0.784): there the seed-bootstrap and the image-and-seed bootstrap intervals include zero, while the intervals over paired seeds, [ − 0.010 , − 0.001 ] [-0.010,\penalty\ -0.001] and [ − 0.010 , − 0.004 ] [-0.010,\penalty\ -0.004] , do not. On PASCAL-Part human masks pointing is slightly lower with 3 runs (0.711 against 0.737, − 0.026 -0.026 [ − 0.051 , − 0.002 ] [-0.051,\penalty\ -0.002] ) and lower over 8 seeds (0.708 against 0.729, − 0.020 -0.020 [ − 0.037 , − 0.005 ] [-0.037,\penalty\ -0.005] ). The auxiliary loss at weight 0.3, retrained at 0.25 with its 3 seeds, falls on PASCAL-Part as the axiom does (0.708 against 0.739, − 0.031 -0.031 [ − 0.055 , − 0.005 ] [-0.055,\penalty\ -0.005] ). With both at 0.25 the two stay on par in localization on test pseudo-masks ( − 0.009 -0.009 ), out of distribution ( − 0.027 -0.027 ) and on PASCAL-Part ( + 0.003 +0.003 [ − 0.028 , + 0.032 ] [-0.028,\penalty\ +0.032] ), while the axiom keeps its out-of-distribution accuracy lead ( + 0.016 +0.016 [ + 0.010 , + 0.021 ] [+0.010,\penalty\ +0.021] ). With all 8 seeds of the axiom, the axiom’s pointing on test pseudo-masks is slightly lower than that of the auxiliary loss at 0.25 ( − 0.019 -0.019 ) and lower at 0.20 ( − 0.026 -0.026 ). A first check against the auxiliary loss still at 0.20, added after the results, had shown the axiom lower on PASCAL-Part ( − 0.028 -0.028 ); the like-for-like comparison attributes that difference to the threshold.

content: NeSySpec is tested against 14 groups of comparators (Table F.1 ), from knowledge-free detectors, residual learners and tabular foundation models to solvers, constraint losses and prompted language and vision-language models, on six benchmarks, four of them labeled independently of the generator oracle (Table ). Specification records carry two label families, generator and intervention labels, and are evaluated on three splits (test, unseen families and the unseen class), satellite pairs on two (test and unseen sites); each stratum of NeSySpec is trained with eight seeds (seeds 0 to 7, Table F.2 ) and the satellite backbone grid with three seeds per backbone. Unless the text or a table note names another scheme, every interval on specification records rests on 5,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples at each of the two cluster levels (seed 20261002); the removals of Table G.9 use 2,000, and the curve over the number of constraints in Appendix G.8 resamples the subsets of each size and the seeds of each drawn subset (5,000 draws). Tables G.1 to G.4 print 168 contrasts with both intervals, and Table G.8 prints 41, of which 36 are not in Table G.3 . Every primary diagnosis contrast of the largest-violation key keeps its reading in all 20 alternative bootstrap streams, except two on intervention labels, which keep it in 19 and 17 of the 20. So do 11 ablation contrasts, the unseen-class contrasts with half the fields hidden, also under each of 10 further bootstrap seeds of that analysis, and every primary localization and repair contrast except two on the record repair error.

content: NeSySpec’s constraint verdicts reach a macro-F1 of 0.795 on generator-label test and, without retraining, 0.575 on intervention-label test (Table G.5 ), from a rule fixed by the semantics (a degree above ln ⁡ 2 \ln 2 ) with no tuned parameter; comparator thresholds were chosen on validation rows only. Against the network trained with the DL2 loss on the same residuals and per-constraint targets, their macro-F1 is higher in all six split and label-family cells, with every interval above zero: on test by + 0.134 +0.134 [ + 0.086 , + 0.242 ] ⋅ [ + 0.099 , + 0.264 ] [+0.086,\penalty\ +0.242]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.099,\penalty\ +0.264] with generator and + 0.149 +0.149 [ + 0.090 , + 0.268 ] ⋅ [ + 0.095 , + 0.276 ] [+0.090,\penalty\ +0.268]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.095,\penalty\ +0.276] with intervention labels, on unseen families by + 0.243 +0.243 and + 0.250 +0.250 and on the unseen class by + 0.164 +0.164 and + 0.121 +0.121 . In all six cells they also find every labeled violation of a corrupted record more often (on generator-label test 0.934 against 0.522, + 0.413 +0.413 [ + 0.367 , + 0.460 ] ⋅ [ + 0.371 , + 0.510 ] [+0.367,\penalty\ +0.460]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.371,\penalty\ +0.510] ) and reach a higher micro recall (0.959 against 0.635 on generator-label test). Their micro precision is on par on test and lower on the unseen class (0.458 against 0.577 on generator and 0.517 against 0.639 on intervention labels), and their exact-set agreement is higher on unseen families (0.721 against 0.508 and 0.373 against 0.221) and on par on test and the unseen class. Over the 8 seeds, NeSySpec’s generator-label test macro-F1 spans 0.767 to 0.808 (sd 0.013) and its exact-set agreement 0.446 to 0.549, the network’s macro-F1 0.442 to 0.838; the intervals average the seeds. The network reports fewer false violations on clean-labeled and control records on test and on the unseen class (0.020 against 0.074 on generator-label test, 0.041 against 0.125 on the unseen class), and the crisp edits are on par in macro-F1 on generator-label test (exact-set agreement, macro-F1 and false-violation rate 0.569, 0.829 and 0.036 against 0.504, 0.795 and 0.074; macro-F1 − 0.034 -0.034 [ − 0.114 , + 0.075 ] ⋅ [ − 0.132 , + 0.064 ] [-0.114,\penalty\ +0.075]\cdot\allowbreak[-0.132,\penalty\ +0.064] ) and below the constraint verdicts in macro-F1 on intervention-label unseen families (0.569 against 0.694, + 0.125 +0.125 [ + 0.053 , + 0.187 ] ⋅ [ + 0.035 , + 0.186 ] [+0.053,\penalty\ +0.187]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.035,\penalty\ +0.186] ); beyond the verdicts, NeSySpec also returns the altered field and a repair from the same degrees.

content: • Largest-violation key: the available constraint with the largest violation degree, selected on held-out training classes. Second head: the monotone read-out on the degrees, kept as the secondary key. SHAP: grouped exact Shapley values of the residual model, one group per constraint. Oracle and worst tie-break: ties among the optimal localizations broken toward and away from the altered field. Repair errors, on single-field corruptions: log-space error of the altered field, plus the change of the correct fields for the record; clean records changed: share of the 48 clean and control test records. Class-I PiShield-style ordering: sequential projection onto the crisp constraints, fields in ascending order of their class-I residual. Detection gate: imputation only on the records that the class-I residual flags, a residual outside its 95% prediction interval. Residual-MLP alarm and own alarm: the residual MLP or the verdict at its validation threshold; with the alert, the verdict or NeSySpec’s optional critical-field alert.

content: NeSySpec’s record verdict reaches a test AUROC of 0.979 ± 0.002 0.979\pm 0.002 on generator labels, from 0.937 on cruise to 1.000 on geometric corruptions by corruption type, each type scored against the 48 clean-labeled test records (16 clean records and their 32 noisy-but-coherent copies; means of 8 seeds), and each of its flags names the violated constraint, the altered field and a repair proposal. Table G.7 groups the detectors of Section by the knowledge they receive, with what each returns. On test the record verdict is on par with TabPFN v2 and close to the residual MLP, LightGBM and the one-class SVM on the residuals and ahead of the learners on the raw fields, the rule checkers, the Mahalanobis distance, the DL2 method and the language model (Table G.3 ). On the unseen class five learners on the residuals rank higher in record-level detection (residual MLP 0.978, TabPFN v2 up to 0.984); there, with NeSySpec’s optional rank-then-explain setting, the residual MLP raises the alarm and NeSySpec explains it with the violated constraint, the altered field and a repair, flagging and correctly diagnosing 0.849 ± 0.043 0.849\pm 0.043 of the corrupted unseen-class records (Table G.6 ).

authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: Without an image, NeSySpec’s fused verdict equals the record verdict bit for bit in 9 of 9 satellite cells, against 0 of 207 learned method and cell rows, and its second head with ConvNeXt-T (8 seeds) reaches 0.998 ± 0.001 0.998\pm 0.001 on test and 0.991 ± 0.003 0.991\pm 0.003 on unseen sites over all pair types. On the satellite pairs of Section , the best learned comparators rank the pairs higher after learning from labeled pairs: CatBoost on knowledge-base truths on test swaps, TabPFN on visual posteriors and image embeddings on unseen-site swaps, and late fusions on knowledge-base truths over all pair types on unseen sites (nine runs of three backbones). Learned heads also rank the pairs higher in the contrasts of Tables G.2 and G.3 , where NeSySpec’s fused verdict differs by − 0.012 -0.012 from the late fusion trained with swaps on test swaps and by − 0.031 -0.031 from CatBoost on knowledge-base truths with 30% of the images hidden. The fused verdict, instead, aggregates NeSySpec’s strata without labels and names the contradicted axiom; on photographs, Qwen3-VL-32B ranks unseen-family pairs higher than the cross-modal stratum ( − 0.094 -0.094 ). With 30% of satellite images hidden, the fused verdict (0.947) keeps the exact reduction; the read-out trained with modality dropout ranks the pairs at 0.973 without keeping it. When a visual stratum trained on ground photographs scores satellite crops, the record verdict alone (0.796) is the fallback across sensors without labels: the fused verdict reaches 0.724 and an out-of-domain abstention restores the record level, while the fusion selected with satellite labels reaches 0.786 and a refit trained on satellite labels, a reference with privileged access to them, reaches 0.979. Fitted on specification records and applied without satellite training through the shared axioms R2 to R4 (Appendix D.1 ), the knowledge base reaches 0.767 ± 0.007 0.767\pm 0.007 on satellite test annotations and 0.764 ± 0.008 0.764\pm 0.008 on unseen sites, against 0.796 and 0.812 for the remote-sensing record verdict trained on these annotations; fitted on satellite annotations and applied to specification records, it reaches 0.541 ± 0.003 0.541\pm 0.003 (8 seeds, no interval); the military roles, absent from the records, keep their prior bands. Comparators on satellite pairs were not retrained or retuned, and those that read knowledge-base truths (CatBoost and TabPFN on knowledge-base truths, the best fusion and the fusion selected without satellite labels) keep the truths of the saturating-envelope variant of the remote-sensing stratum they were fitted on (the specification-record row of this ablation is in Table G.8 ). NeSySpec’s graded remote-sensing stratum was selected on validation among eight candidate configurations; it trains with per-constraint targets that the end-to-end, fusion and vision-language comparators do not receive, and its validation split serves both early stopping and the choice of configuration.

content: Each of the 736 falsification problems inflates one capacity of a genuine held-out record, the range, the cruise speed, the maximum take-off mass or the ceiling, by 5, 10, 20 or 40% (46 records: the 16 clean test records, 11 of unseen families and 19 of the unseen class). A bare lie submits the inflated record; a cover-up also edits up to five further declared fields within the ranges of the fleet, found by a black-box search that reads only the detector’s score; an omission withholds up to two declared fields other than the inflated one. A lie evades a detector when the submitted record scores below the detector’s validation threshold, and evasion is the share of evading lies among the problems whose genuine record the detector accepts; the smallest number of further edits that covers a flagged lie is censored at six.

content: NeSySpec with the critical-field alert, an optional setting, flags a record when the verdict or the alert fires. Under black-box falsification, a lie flagged by NeSySpec’s record verdict is covered less often than one flagged by the residual MLP: with up to five further edits 0.936 of cover-ups pass against 1.000 (Table G.4 ), and 0.247 of its flagged bare lies cannot be covered, against 0.000. The smallest cover of one of its flagged lies has 2.69 further edited fields on average (2.68 with the critical-field alert), against 1.01 to 1.63 for the learned detectors (on the residuals, MLP 1.38, LightGBM 1.37 and TabPFN v2 1.63) and more for the Mahalanobis distance and the pooled rules (3.45 and 3.62; point estimates, censored at six). On the 72 problems that the verdict and the residual MLP flag on every seed, 0.413 of the verdict’s flagged lies cannot be covered, against 0.000, with 3.76 edits per cover against 1.58. On omissions of up to two fields and on bare lies some comparators are evaded less often (Table G.4 : on omissions the residual MLP + 0.026 +0.026 , the residual one-class SVM + 0.143 +0.143 and the Mahalanobis distance + 0.119 +0.119 ; on bare lies residual LightGBM + 0.052 +0.052 and residual TabPFN v2 + 0.105 +0.105 ). A withheld field masks the axioms that read it (Proposition ); with the optional critical-field alert, which names the undeclared field and the constraints it leaves unchecked, NeSySpec is evaded less than the residual MLP with the same alert on unseen families ( − 0.074 -0.074 ) and more on the unseen class ( + 0.125 +0.125 ). On this fleet a rule without the knowledge base (an alert on any undeclared field that the record’s class, or its engine type for classes with fewer than five training records, declares in at least 95% of the training records, whether or not an applicable axiom reads it) gives the alert’s protection with the same false alerts on the genuine records; NeSySpec’s report also names the constraints that each withheld field leaves unchecked.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: To measure what each constraint contributes, NeSySpec was retrained with subsets of its 12 specification constraints. A removed constraint is unavailable for every record in training and scoring, while the record labels of training stay unchanged. The record verdict was then scored on intervention labels, which no constraint defines, and on generator labels, which the same constraints define, so that a removal hides the corruptions of its constraint by construction (Figure in Section , all panels on intervention labels; Table G.9 ). Over 96 subsets of 1 to 11 constraints, all 12 of sizes 1 and 11 and 8 random ones of each size from 2 to 10, with 3 seeds each, and the full knowledge base, the intervention-label AUROC averaged over test, unseen families and the unseen class has a mean per size that rises from one size to the next, from 0.535 with one constraint to 0.723 with all twelve (Spearman 0.93 [ 0.90 , 0.95 ] [0.90,\penalty\ 0.95] ), by steps whose intervals include zero at 5 of the 11 steps. The returns diminish: a logarithmic trend fits better than a linear one ( R 2 R^{2} 0.87 against 0.84; on the unseen class alone the two fit equally), the gain is about 0.028 per constraint up to six and 0.008 beyond, and the twelfth still adds a small gain (0.009 [ 0.003 , 0.015 ] [0.003,\penalty\ 0.015] ). The AUROC grows linearly with the share of edits that alter a field read by some active constraint ( R 2 R^{2} 0.88, against 0.74 for a logarithmic trend), a share that goes from 0.22 with one constraint to all edits with twelve, while on the edits of fields the constraints read it stays between 0.70 and 0.75 at every size: the gain follows the coverage of the edits. The residual MLP on the same subsets gains from the same knowledge (0.540 to 0.706), with no trend in its gap to NeSySpec. Removing one constraint from the full knowledge base lowers the intervention-label AUROC for A5 and A2, slightly for A4, A7 and A8 and for A4 with A4P together, and leaves it on par for A1, A4P, A9 and A10 and close for A3, A6 and A11; removing A1 lowers it on the unseen class and raises it slightly on test, and no removal raises it averaged over the three splits. Stall speed, engine count and fuselage length, the fields that only A6, A9 and A11 read, are never edited alone in the intervention records, and stall speed is never edited at all; A3, A4P and A10 read only fields that other constraints also read, as do A2, A4, A7 and A8, whose removal still lowers the AUROC, slightly for A4, A7 and A8. On generator labels the removal of A1, A2, A4, A4P, A5 or A8 lowers the AUROC, that of A7 or A10 slightly, and that of A3 raises it slightly (0.001); abduction is lower without A1 (0.187), A5 (0.077), A3, A4, A4P, A8 and A11, slightly lower without A2, A7 and A10, and on par without A6 and A9. In Figure c the darker line gives the aircraft interval and the lighter the family interval, with filled points where both exclude zero.

authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: The diagnosis key was selected on held-out training classes: with each of the six training classes left out in turn, the verifier retrained and every statistic, prior and head recomputed without it, the largest-violation key ranked a violated constraint first in 0.802 of the held-out corrupted records (mean over the six classes), against 0.630 for the second head, with a higher mean on each held-out class (differences from 0.006 to 0.432); on validation records of the seen classes the two keys differ by 0.0008, and the second head is kept as the secondary key. NeSySpec’s optional critical-field alert was selected because, on validation, it lowered evasion by an attacker who knows the alert from 0.949 to 0.739 and fired on 2 of the 17 genuine validation records, and because, with each training class held out in turn, it fired on 0.028 of that class’s genuine records (mean over six classes; limit 0.25; largest rate 0.091, against 0.263 on the unseen class). Validation selected the abduction rule, the smallest-change rule of Table F.2 , and its feasibility threshold 0.9, also chosen in 7 of 8 leave-one-seed-out selections. With threshold 0.8, abduction reaches 0.750 on single-field test corruptions, its readings against minimum-cardinality localization unchanged and still ahead of the Class I residual on test. The largest-feasibility rule of Table G.2 , which ranks every field by the lowest verdict it reaches, gives 0.692 on test, 0.747 on unseen families and 0.660 on the unseen class, on par with the Class I residual on test. On intervention labels every reading holds under both alternatives except the margin over the oracle tie-break ( + 0.112 +0.112 and + 0.095 +0.095 ). For a class without training aircraft NeSySpec reads fleet statistics; five alternative reference statistics (engine-type or declared-mass pools with the union or weighted mean of class bands, and the nearest training class), compared on held-out training classes, met no adoption rule, and on the business jets each flags every clean record (1.000 against 0.322 with fleet statistics) with a detection AUROC of 0.836 to 0.906 against 0.934; under the mass pools and the nearest class a withheld field changes the reference class of 16.0, 21.7 and 1.8% of masked held-out records.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: On generator labels, every band alternative that places more of NeSySpec’s learned bands inside the training fleet range widened by 12%, [ 0.88 ​ min , 1.12 ​ max ] [0.88\min,\,1.12\max] , lowers validation detection by more than 0.005: the learned bands act as tolerances learned from the fleet, 45.7% of them with both edges inside that range. The alternatives project the band edges onto that range after every step, or pull them toward it with a penalty of weight 0.01, 0.1 or 1.0 (eight seeds each). Retrained on intervention labels, the four alternatives hold 68.5, 86.7, 96.5 and 100% of the 46 counted bands per seed (those with a training fleet range) inside the range and stay within the validation margin; the projection reaches 0.804 on test, against 0.807 for NeSySpec retrained on the same labels. The penalty of weight 0.01, the alternative selected on validation, keeps its share at 45.7% and was not adopted; it reaches on generator-label test a detection AUROC of 0.977, on par with 0.979, the same diagnosis top-1 (0.942), a localization top-1 of 0.728 against 0.742 and a false-positive rate on the controls of 0.082 against 0.086, and on the unseen class a detection AUROC slightly lower, 0.932 against 0.934; with weight 1.0 (53.8% inside) unseen-class detection is lower, 0.924 against 0.934. These alternatives are sensitivity analyses of NeSySpec.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
section: Oracle bands fitted on the training aircraft.
content: With the class bands of the generator oracle fitted on the 44 clean training aircraft alone (business jets, which have no training aircraft, on the band of all training aircraft), and the generator, its seed and the family splits unchanged, the benchmark holds 1,239 instances instead of 1,312. These bands flag 38 of the 63 clean held-out aircraft, 15 of the 16 in test, mostly on A1, A9 and A11; controls must stay clean under the oracle, so the test controls fall from 32 to 4. NeSySpec was retrained with its selected configuration on 8 seeds, as were the residual MLP and TabPFN v2 with their full selection protocol and the DL2-loss network with its selected hyperparameters, whose search was not repeated; the crisp edits and minimum-cardinality localization were recomputed, and the rule diagnosis, TabPFN v2 on intervention labels and the alternative bootstrap streams were not rerun (Tables G.10 and G.11 ). The validation rule of the crisp edits now selects per-class bands without pooling (validation AUROC 0.919 against 0.915), the bands of the new label oracle itself, with which the crisp edits lead NeSySpec on generator labels in key and macro-F1 on every split; the tables keep the pooled bands of the paper, and on intervention labels NeSySpec is on par with the unpooled crisp edits in macro-F1 on test ( − 0.006 -0.006 ) and ahead on the other two splits. On intervention labels, whose records are the same under both oracles, NeSySpec stays ahead on every split of the DL2-loss network in macro-F1 ( + 0.045 +0.045 [ + 0.012 , + 0.142 ] ⋅ [ + 0.012 , + 0.163 ] [+0.012,\penalty\ +0.142]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.012,\penalty\ +0.163] on test), of Fellegi-Holt and Z3 in diagnosis ( + 0.126 +0.126 and + 0.092 +0.092 on test) and of minimum-cardinality localization with random tie-break ( + 0.226 +0.226 on test); on test it is on par with the oracle tie-break ( + 0.079 +0.079 ) and with the crisp edits in macro-F1 ( − 0.016 -0.016 ), and the DL2-loss network has the higher exact-set agreement ( − 0.149 -0.149 ) and fewer false violations. NeSySpec’s own test levels there are lower, with more false violations, every paired interval excluding zero: macro-F1 0.488 against 0.575, exact-set agreement 0.070 against 0.283, false-violation rate 0.219 against 0.084, key 0.732 against 0.786 and abduction 0.532 against 0.593, while detection is on par (0.695 against 0.701). On unseen families key, abduction and detection are on par and macro-F1 comparable (0.666 against 0.694), exact-set agreement is lower (0.255 against 0.373) and the false-violation rate slightly higher (0.088 against 0.028); on the unseen class the verdicts, abduction and detection are on par and the key is lower (0.743 against 0.778). Trained on the flags of these bands through its per-constraint targets, NeSySpec learns narrower bands where the oracle’s bands narrow. Over the 46 counted bands, the median ratio of its learned widths to those learned under the paper’s oracle is 0.903 (seed-bootstrap interval [ 0.897 , 0.911 ] [0.897,\penalty\ 0.911] ), and 64% of the bands narrow, with a moderate rank correlation with the oracle’s width ratios over 45 class bands (Spearman 0.43). The narrowing is largest for the thrust bands of A9 and the passenger-density bands of A11 (median 0.71), which carry the largest rises in false violations on the 16 clean test aircraft ( + 0.35 +0.35 and + 0.33 +0.33 ; 0.061 to 0.208 over all constraints), followed by A2 ( + 0.26 +0.26 ), whose learned bands shift. Seven of its eight seeds reached their best epoch by epoch 22, against 80 to 100 for the paper’s seeds; the seed whose best epoch is 93 shows a similar narrowing on the bands of A3 and the thrust bands of A9 (0.78 and 0.74) and a smaller one on the passenger-density bands of A11 (0.78). On generator labels the records differ between the two benchmarks: the held-out corrupted records keep the violations their clean origin already has under the narrower bands, and the clean record itself stays labeled clean. There the residual MLP is slightly higher in detection on test (0.950 against 0.910, − 0.040 -0.040 [ − 0.075 , − 0.010 ] ⋅ [ − 0.071 , + 0.001 ] [-0.075,\penalty\ -0.010]\cdot\allowbreak[-0.071,\penalty\ +0.001] ) and on unseen families ( − 0.013 -0.013 ), as is TabPFN v2 on unseen families ( − 0.020 -0.020 ), and stays slightly ahead on the unseen class (0.986 against 0.959), where TabPFN v2 is now on par ( − 0.008 -0.008 ). The key reaches 0.944 on test and 0.931 on unseen families (0.973 before), slightly ahead of Fellegi-Holt and Z3 on test ( + 0.102 +0.102 ) and on par with them on unseen families ( + 0.094 +0.094 ); on the unseen class, where the pooled crisp bands equal those of the label oracle, Fellegi-Holt and Z3 lead ( − 0.094 -0.094 ). The verdicts stay ahead of the DL2-loss network in macro-F1 on every split ( + 0.288 +0.288 on test), are on par with the crisp edits on test and unseen families and below them on the unseen class ( − 0.125 -0.125 ), with more false violations than the crisp edits on every split. Abduction is now ahead of the oracle tie-break on test ( + 0.199 +0.199 [ + 0.042 , + 0.370 ] ⋅ [ + 0.052 , + 0.528 ] [+0.042,\penalty\ +0.370]\cdot\allowbreak[+0.052,\penalty\ +0.528] ) and stays ahead of random tie-breaking on every split. The repair still lowers the error on the altered field on every split (0.126 against 0.236 without repair on test); as the verifier now rates almost every clean and control test record as violating, its target is reached on 0.036 of single-field test records (0.555 before) and it proposes a change for 0.988 of the clean and control test records (0.588 on unseen families and 0.707 on the unseen class); the repair rule re-selected on the new validation split (feasibility threshold 0.8 instead of 0.9) reaches the target on 0.190 and changes 0.894 of them. Bands fitted on all 107 aircraft cover the range of the fleet the records describe, which bands fitted on 44 aircraft do not.

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
section: Oracle fitted on training and validation aircraft, tolerances chosen out of family.
content: Fitted on the 61 clean training and validation aircraft, the oracle had each of its three tolerances set, by a rule declared before any result, to the smallest value of a grid that flags at most 5% of the clean aircraft when their family is held out in turn: the range margin, the relative widening of each class band ( [ 0.88 ​ min , 1.12 ​ max ] [0.88\min,\,1.12\max] at 0.12), becomes 0.50 instead of 0.12 (2 of 61 aircraft flagged, against 24 at 0.12); the equality factor, which multiplies the largest absolute log-residual of the clean records of each class for the identities A1, A5 and A6, becomes 1.25 instead of 1.15 (3 of 60, at the limit of the rule); and the mass-balance margin of A7, subtracted from the smallest clean mass-balance margin, stays at 0.05; with these values 5 of the 61 aircraft are flagged by some tolerance. This oracle flags 14 of the 46 clean test and out-of-distribution aircraft: 11 of the 16 in test, 10 of them narrowbodies on A1, whose class tolerance rests on 3 aircraft of 2 families, 3 business jets on A9, judged by the band fitted on all 61 aircraft, and none of the unseen families; its wider bands let the generator escalate further (median magnitude 0.8 against 0.4), and the benchmark holds 1,260 instances with 10 test controls. Retrained on its labels as above (Tables G.10 and G.11 ), NeSySpec on intervention labels keeps its false violations at the paper’s level on test (0.073 against 0.084, on par), with fewer on the unseen class (0.087 against 0.128), and its exact-set agreement on par on test and unseen families and slightly higher on the unseen class (0.206 against 0.155); its macro-F1 is lower on test (0.537 against 0.575) and unseen families (0.636 against 0.694), its abduction on test (0.491 against 0.593) and unseen families (0.508 against 0.594), and its key on the unseen class (0.735 against 0.778) and slightly on test (0.738 against 0.786), while detection is on par on test and unseen families and close on the unseen class (0.711 against 0.719). Against the comparators on intervention labels it stays ahead on every split of Fellegi-Holt and Z3 in diagnosis and of minimum-cardinality localization with random tie-break, ahead of the DL2-loss network in macro-F1 on unseen families, slightly on test ( + 0.037 +0.037 ) and on par on the unseen class, with the network keeping fewer false violations on test and the unseen class. In macro-F1 it is on par with the crisp edits on test and unseen families and slightly ahead on the unseen class ( + 0.029 +0.029 ), and, against the bands with a 25% margin, small classes pooled, that the validation rule of the crisp edits now selects (validation AUROC 0.943 against 0.942), on par on test and ahead on the other two splits. In abduction it is on par with the oracle tie-break on every split, and against the Class I residual on par on test, lower on unseen families ( − 0.096 -0.096 ) and ahead on the unseen class. On generator labels, with larger corruptions, NeSySpec reaches a detection AUROC of 0.976 on test, slightly below the residual MLP (0.994), and on the unseen class slightly below the residual MLP and TabPFN v2 (0.988 against 0.999 for both); its macro-F1 is on par with the DL2-loss network on test and the unseen class and ahead on unseen families, ahead of the crisp edits on test, slightly ahead on unseen families and below them on the unseen class; its key, 0.955 on test, is ahead of Fellegi-Holt on every split and of Z3 on test and unseen families, and on par with Z3 on the unseen class; abduction is on par with the oracle tie-break on every split and ahead of random tie-breaking; the repair lowers the error on the altered field on every split, reaches its target on 0.570 of single-field test records and changes 0.418 of the clean and control test records; and 109 of the 154 corrupted test records carry a violation their clean origin already has. Under these tolerances the bands widen, the training corruptions grow and training stops earlier (best epochs 15 to 27, against 80 to 100), so their effects on the key and abduction levels are not separated.

content: Figure in Section shows the training curves of the axioms; two readings complete it. At the frozen checkpoint, restored at the best validation epoch, the mean truth of each specification constraint is lower on corrupted than on clean-labeled records in 46 of 46 split and constraint pairs with available evidence, by as little as 1.0 × 10 − 5 1.0\times 10^{-5} on the unseen class. content: This appendix gives the results and the protocol of the comparison with explanation supervision summarized in Section . Under the protocol described at the end of this appendix, the grounding axiom localizes the annotated parts more than RRR [ 57 ] , GradMask [ 58 ] and Pukdee et al. [ 61 ] , with every cluster-bootstrap interval of the difference above zero on the FGVC pseudo-masks, on PASCAL-Part human masks (levels in Figure G.1 b) and on two further human-mask datasets. Against RRR, GradMask and Pukdee et al., in this order, its pointing exceeds theirs by + 0.725 +0.725 [ + 0.700 , + 0.750 ] [+0.700,\penalty\ +0.750] , + 0.779 +0.779 and + 0.618 +0.618 on the FGVC test pseudo-masks, by + 0.594 +0.594 [ + 0.559 , + 0.630 ] [+0.559,\penalty\ +0.630] , + 0.702 +0.702 and + 0.496 +0.496 on PASCAL-Part, by + 0.523 +0.523 [ + 0.475 , + 0.571 ] [+0.475,\penalty\ +0.571] , + 0.631 +0.631 and + 0.420 +0.420 on PartImageNet and by + 0.483 +0.483 [ + 0.359 , + 0.595 ] [+0.359,\penalty\ +0.595] , + 0.636 +0.636 and + 0.446 +0.446 on the 40 items of UDA-Part, with wider intervals on the last two; Pukdee et al. is run at the calibration of the protocol, which flattened their teacher toward the uniform prediction. The intervals of all 27 differences, nine mask configurations by three baselines, lie above zero, also under an independent bootstrap seed. Across the weights 0.3, 1 and 3 the axiom keeps at most one collapsed head, a head whose F1 is at most 0.05, against up to 5.7 on average for the auxiliary loss. At weight 1 it keeps an out-of-distribution accuracy lead of + 0.016 +0.016 [ + 0.012 , + 0.020 ] [+0.012,\penalty\ +0.020] over the auxiliary loss at its validation weight 0.3; test accuracy, by contrast, is degenerate (a constant predictor scores 0.926).

title: NeSySpec: Neuro-Symbolic Technical Intelligence for Auditing Engineering Specifications with an Application to Aircraft
authors: Pier Mattia Basciano, Gianvito Antenori, Cristiano Andolfi, Giovanni Farina, Salvatore Monteleone
content: A first set of runs of RRR, GradMask, RES [ 59 ] (its RES-L variant, adapted to these part masks) and Pukdee et al. used λ = 1 \lambda=1 and penalties coupled across a batch through batch normalization [ 94 ] in training mode. The comparison retrains RRR, GradMask and Pukdee et al. with per-example penalties, the normalization constants held fixed, selects λ ∈ { 0.1 , 1 , 10 } \lambda\in\{0.1,1,10\} times a calibration constant on validation with one seed per value, and evaluates three seeds at the selected value. RES-L is not retrained: on these masks its adapted objective does not reward localization, so its pointing does not measure what RES can localize. title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
section: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
content: The rapid proliferation of Industrial Internet of Things devices has led to increasingly large-scale and non-stationary time-series data, posing significant challenges for time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). Existing approaches often focus on reconstructing or forecasting observations while overlooking the role of trend dynamics, which constitute a major source of non-stationarity and contain valuable information for anomaly identification. To address this limitation, we propose AdaTrendLike, a TSAD framework that directly estimates trend likelihoods for anomaly detection. Specifically, we introduce Standardization Embedding to capture local statistical characteristics as latent representations and AdaDetrending to adaptively decompose input series into trend and detrended components. The detrended component is processed through a Fast Fourier Transform and a complex-valued convolutional neural network to learn normal periodic patterns, while TrendEst models the distribution of the trend component. Based on the estimated distribution, TrendLike computes anomaly scores by measuring the likelihood of observed trends, enabling effective detection of deviations from normal behavior. In addition to improving detection performance, the proposed framework provides feature-level interpretability by identifying anomalies through deviations in the estimated trend distribution. Extensive experiments on five public benchmark datasets demonstrate that AdaTrendLike consistently outperforms state-of-the-art TSAD methods, validating its effectiveness and robustness across diverse application scenarios.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: With the widespread deployment of Industrial Internet of Things devices, the volume of time series data has grown rapidly, creating a pressing need for robust Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) tools for large-scale sensory data. In cybersecurity systems, malicious activity is flagged when the network exhibits unusual temporal behavior. In cyber-physical systems, which integrate digital and physical infrastructure, TSAD methods are utilized to detect physical anomalies caused by cyber intrusions in domains such as water treatment plants [ 1 ] and unmanned aerial vehicles [ 2 ] . In IT infrastructures, monitoring systems track server metrics to detect anomalies indicative of system failures or resource bottlenecks [ 3 , 4 ] . Despite differences in anomaly types across domains, the core challenge remains detecting deviations from normal behavior in temporally dependent, non-stationary time series.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: Classical methods such as Local Outlier Factor (LOF), Isolation Forest (IF), and One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] are widely used. However, with the increasing scale and complexity of time series data, these methods struggle to capture temporal dependencies and high-dimensional feature interactions. Consequently, learning-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging representation learning to model complex temporal and feature relationships [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . These learning-based approaches typically rely on reconstruction errors to identify anomalies, which can be unreliable because normal variations or seasonal trends may be misclassified as anomalies. Moreover, this approach does not consider predictive uncertainties, which are crucial for informed and interpretable anomaly detection, such as identifying the features that contribute to anomalies.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: Non-stationarity in real-world time series arises from multiple factors and can obscure the distinction between normal and abnormal patterns [ 11 ] . One of these factors is the trend component, which represents the progressive long-term behavior of the data and can be leveraged in two main ways: as a dominant feature for modeling and as a means to detrend the series, promoting local stationarity. Trends can be extracted using traditional statistical models, but their effectiveness is limited because these models rely on the assumption of local stationarity [ 12 ] . In contrast, learning-based decomposition methods address this by incorporating mechanisms that extract the trend component within the inner blocks of the models [ 11 , 13 , 14 ] . Although the inner blocks provide rich representations that capture underlying trends, these methods rely on trend separation mainly to improve reconstruction rather than explicitly exploiting the trend component for TSAD.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: To address these challenges, we propose AdaTrendLike, an Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring method for TSAD. Our method first employs a Standardization Embedding (SE) module that encodes the local statistical properties of time series as latent embeddings. To further handle non-stationary behaviors, we propose Adaptive Detrending (AdaDetrending), a hierarchical module that progressively extracts trend components through multiple layers. At each layer, local trends are estimated using moving averages, and the residuals representing the detrended components are processed through a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), followed by a complex-valued Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). This combination enhances the model’s capability to accurately capture normal behavior in time series exhibiting periodicity via frequency representations and local dependency via convolution. Finally, the trend components extracted from all layers are aggregated and modeled by the Trend Estimator (TrendEst) to estimate a global trend distribution, while the Trend Likelihood Scoring (TrendLike) module computes anomaly scores based on the likelihood of observed trends. By explicitly modeling the distribution of the trend component and performing anomaly detection through likelihood estimation, the proposed framework achieves improved robustness under non-stationary dynamics. Unlike existing methods that primarily exploit trend information to facilitate signal reconstruction, AdaTrendLike directly integrates trend modeling into the anomaly detection process. Specifically, deviations from the estimated trend distribution are treated as anomaly evidence, enabling effective detection of trend-related anomalies while enhancing robustness to non-stationary time-series data. content: Classical methods such as IF [ 5 ] , OCSVM [ 6 ] , and LOF [ 7 ] have been widely used for unsupervised anomaly detection. Building on these foundations, advanced models like Deep-SVDD [ 15 ] , which jointly train a neural network with Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) [ 6 ] to enclose normal data in a minimal hypersphere, and THOC [ 16 ] , which employs dilated recurrent neural networks with skip connections for multi-resolution features, have emerged. COUTA [ 17 ] further introduces uncertainty quantification and anomaly perturbation to enhance confidence in detection. However, detecting anomalies as deviations from the learned data manifold remains challenging in high-dimensional spaces due to the curse of dimensionality.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: Deep learning methods often incorporate inductive biases, such as specific training objectives or architectural constraints, that favor the reconstruction of normal patterns. The resulting reconstruction errors are then used to identify anomalous segments. For instance, TranAD [ 18 ] employs an adversarial training procedure to amplify reconstruction errors, while EvoAAE [ 19 ] optimizes a variational autoencoder–adversarial framework through particle swarm optimization. However, in both cases, the reliance on reconstruction-based objectives can lead to over-generalization, enabling anomalous patterns to be reconstructed too accurately and thereby masking their detection [ 8 ] . MoARNN-AM [ 2 ] similarly uses a genetic algorithm to optimize the hyperparameters of recurrent neural network variants and attention mechanisms. However, it is designed for multi-class anomaly detection and relies on labeled anomalies, which are typically scarce in real-world settings [ 20 , 17 ] . Rather than depending on extensive hyperparameter optimization or labeled data, other methods introduce model-specific inductive biases. AT [ 9 ] amplifies normal–abnormal scores using the discrepancy between an association vector from a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a prior association vector based on a Gaussian distribution. MEMTO [ 8 ] employs a Transformer encoder to extract latent representations, along with a gated memory module that is incrementally updated to capture prototypical normal patterns. Although these models are designed to reconstruct normal patterns effectively, they are trained exclusively on normal data. Consequently, variations arising from aleatoric uncertainty may be mistakenly flagged as anomalies.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: Instead of focusing on model design, some approaches improve detection performance by refining anomaly scoring criteria. DAGMM [ 21 ] employs a Gaussian Mixture Model for anomaly scoring, NSPR [ 20 ] scores anomalies based on point-wise and sequential reconstruction deviations, and TranAD [ 18 ] uses adversarial reconstruction errors. Although these strategies achieve strong empirical performance, they lack an explicit mechanism to account for deviations from the normal data distribution, limiting their robustness to non-anomalous variations.

title: AdaTrendLike: Adaptive Hierarchical Detrending and Trend Likelihood Scoring for Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Van Kwan Zhi Koh, Songnan Lin, Rongmo Luo, Zhiping Lin, Bihan Wen
content: Learning from dominant decomposed components in time series analysis involves separating signals into key components, such as trend, seasonality, and residuals, to improve representation learning [ 14 , 13 , 22 , 11 ] . TransDe [ 23 ] , SDDformer [ 24 ] , and Time-Frequency analysis based TSAD (TFAD) model [ 22 ] are methods that incorporate time-domain decomposition for TSAD. These methods primarily employ time-domain decomposition to separate temporal components, making the learned representations dependent on predefined decomposition assumptions, limiting their ability to capture complex temporal dynamics. Therefore, recent methods perform decomposition in the latent space. Autoformer [ 14 ] extracts trend components directly from latent representations, while D3R [ 11 ] decomposes latent representations into trend and stable components before recombination. Although these models effectively learn trends to facilitate representation learning, they do not explicitly exploit trend information as an anomaly cue for TSAD. As a result, they fail to leverage the valuable information encoded in the trend component, where deviations from the underlying temporal trajectory can serve as strong indicators of anomalous behavior.

content: Typically, FFT is applied directly to the input time series to transform time-domain signals into the frequency domain, enabling the capture of frequency-based patterns [ 22 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . MAGE [ 27 ] transforms the input time series into the frequency domain using FFT, followed by a graph neural network to learn the feature topology. Similarly, TFAD method applies FFT to the decomposed components before modeling. Instead of raw or decomposed features, recent studies perform FFT on latent representations [ 28 , 13 ] . Fedformer [ 13 ] combines FFT with transformer self-attention, selecting random frequency components to capture dominant patterns. FreTS [ 28 ] applies FFT to latent features and processes them with a complex-valued multilayer perceptron (MLP) to model global spectral components. Furthermore, existing approaches are primarily designed for TSF, with limited exploration in TSAD. In contrast, our method introduces frequency-learning biases to improve anomaly separability and employs a Complex CNN to capture frequency-domain periodicity and local temporal dependencies.

content: This study utilizes five publicly available datasets from real-world applications: the Server Machine Dataset (SMD) [ 4 ] , the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) and Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) datasets from NASA [ 32 ] , the Secure Water Treatment (SWAT) dataset [ 1 ] , and the Pooled Server Metrics (PSM) dataset [ 3 ] . Missing values are handled via forward filling, where the most recent non-null value is propagated to fill gaps. For SMD, MSL, and SMAP, which consist of multiple entities, the data are preprocessed by concatenating entities along the time-step dimension. Each dataset comes with predefined training and testing splits, with anomalies appearing exclusively in the test sets. Each dataset is provided with predefined training and testing partitions, with anomalous samples confined to the test partition. All datasets are normalized using min–max scaling to the range [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , with scaling parameters estimated exclusively from the training data.

All models are evaluated on the provided datasets, except for D3R, which is designed to operate only on datasets with continuous-valued features. Experiments for THOC, AT, MEMTO, COUTA, NSPR, and D3R are conducted using publicly available implementations, while the remaining models are evaluated using the Multivariate TSAD toolkit [ 33 ] . A common evaluation practice, known as point adjustment, treats a predicted anomaly as correct if it falls within any truth anomalous segment [ 8 ] . However, several studies question this practice, as it enables even trivial or adversarial algorithms to achieve inflated performance scores [ 20 , 11 ] . Consequently, we evaluate our model strictly based on its raw predictions, without applying point adjustment. In addition, we report threshold-free performance using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) to provide a complementary evaluation.

content: The main results are summarized in Table IV-B1 , where bold values indicate the best results. Our proposed AdaTrendLike achieves the best performance on 4 out of 5 datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in TSAD. While deep learning approaches have been proposed, classical methods such as IF and LOF remain strong baselines. Deep One-Class methods, such as THOC and COUTA, which extend classical architectures, offer only marginal gains over classical methods. AT and MEMTO employ inductive biases to foster diverse representations; however, this may cause over-generalization that negatively impacts anomaly detection accuracy. DAGMM and NPSR employ unique anomaly scoring mechanisms that yield strong performance, highlighting the crucial role of effective anomaly scoring strategies. NPSR achieves highly competitive results by leveraging sequential pattern comparison to characterize normal behavior. Similarly, our model specifically utilizes trend information. D3R performs decomposition but relies on reconstruction loss, whereas our method employs TrendLike for anomaly scoring, achieving better results.

content: Notably, AdaTrendLike achieves the best performance on four out of five datasets, demonstrating strong effectiveness for TSAD. On SMD, the performance gain is less pronounced, likely due to its highly imbalanced anomaly distribution, with only 4.16% anomalous time steps (Table I ). As shown in Fig. 4 , many anomalous observations closely follow the underlying trends of normal data, resulting in weak anomaly evidence. In addition, SMD exhibits substantially shorter anomaly segments, with a mean length of 90 90 , compared to MSL ( 216 216 ), SMAP ( 826 826 ), SWaT ( 1561 1561 ), and PSM ( 339 339 ). Since our model focuses on learning trends that capture long-term temporal patterns, short anomaly segments provide limited evidence for reliably estimating trend deviations, thereby reducing the effectiveness of TrendLike-based anomaly scoring. Nevertheless, AdaTrendLike still achieves the second-best AUC on SMD, indicating competitive ranking performance. Overall, these results highlight the advantages of the proposed hierarchical detrending framework, frequency-domain modeling, and TrendLike-based anomaly scoring.

content: Anomalies may arise from various features and time steps, but identifying which features are responsible is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the input data. Our model addresses this by providing a visual comparison between the estimated trends and trend reconstruction. From the SWAT dataset, four labeled scenarios, with feature names (e.g., P102) following the dataset documentation, are summarized in Table IV . ‘Attacked features’ indicate features subjected to external changes, while ‘Expected feature changes’ indicate features for which changes are anticipated. As shown in Fig. 2 , scenarios 1, 2, and 4 show deviations between estimated trends and expected feature changes. Notably, MV303 in scenario 1 shows an unexpected deviation, suggesting a link to the attacked feature. For scenario 3, which involves gradual changes, our model does not detect this anomaly segment, likely because the trend-learning mechanism treats such changes as normal behavior.

content: Based on these scenarios, practitioners can assess anomalies from deviations along the estimated trend, highlighting contributing features and detection likelihood. For further analysis, trend estimation on other datasets are presented in Fig. 3 . The MSL and SMAP datasets contain frequent short-term spikes, whereas the SWAT and PSM datasets exhibit smoother patterns. Our model captures these spikes within the estimated trend distribution, adapting to such patterns. The temporal vector provides a global representation of the features within a segment, capturing patterns such as sudden drops, mean shifts, and high-frequency fluctuations. During anomalous segments, it highlights noticeable changes in these characteristics, which can serve as indicators of anomaly occurrence.

content: This section analyzes the performance of the three anomaly criteria: MSE computes the anomaly score using the reconstruction loss in ( 10 ), where the ground-truth trend 𝐓 \mathbf{T} is replaced with 𝝁 T \boldsymbol{\mu}_{T} during both training and anomaly score computation; Exclude 𝝅 ^ \hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}} removes the temporal vector from TrendLike in ( 12 ) and from the likelihood loss in ( 11 ); Exclude Summation omits the summation over adjacent time steps in ( 12 ). As illustrated in Fig. 6 , our proposed TrendLike method produces distinct and consistent anomaly scores. In contrast, variants that exclude the temporal vector tend to overestimate anomaly durations, yielding anomalous segments that exceed the ground-truth boundaries and thus increase false alarms, whereas those that exclude the summation exhibit random spikes even during normal segments. Table VII shows that TrendLike consistently delivers superior results. While our anomaly criterion achieves the best overall performance, it still fails to detect certain anomalous segments, as illustrated in Fig. 6 , corresponding to the trend estimation in Fig. 7 . The detected anomalies typically involve multiple features within the same time segment and are accompanied by abrupt changes, whereas undetected segments, highlighted in green, exhibit only minor deviations within the estimated trend distribution, indicating a limitation in capturing subtle anomalies.

content: Each hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is conducted by varying one parameter over a predefined range while keeping all other parameters fixed, as listed in Table II . Across datasets, the PSM dataset exhibits the greatest sensitivity to hyperparameters, potentially due to its higher anomaly ratio. Accordingly, hyperparameter tuning may improve model fitting and enhance anomaly detection performance in datasets with higher anomaly ratios. As shown in Fig. 8 , the sensitive hyperparameters are mainly L L , d m d_{m} , and n d n_{d} . For L L , shorter input lengths yield better performance, which declines as the input length increases. Meanwhile, increasing d m d_{m} may improve performance, but there is a trade-off between accuracy and model complexity. Varying the number of n d n_{d} layers allows the model to capture both local and global trends. For certain datasets, particularly SMAP and PSM, it has a significant impact, suggesting that proper tuning is necessary. The hyperparameter g cnn g_{\text{cnn}} has little effect on most datasets except PSM, suggesting that larger values can be used to reduce computational complexity while maintaining accuracy. The remaining hyperparameter exhibits low sensitivity and can be set to constant values with minimal impact on performance. Overall, tuning the parameters L L , d m d_{m} , and n d n_{d} is generally sufficient to identify near-optimal hyperparameter settings for most datasets.

content: Table IX summarizes the training and inference computational complexity and runtime of the four baseline models (IF, LOF, TranAD, and NSPR) in comparison with our proposed model on the SWaT dataset. For consistency and fair comparison, all deep learning (DL) models, including TranAD, NSPR, and the proposed model, are trained with a fixed batch size of 64, whereas IF and LOF do not require batch-wise training. Runtime is reported as training time per epoch, and inference time is measured per sample, where each sample corresponds to a window of 100 time steps. Among the baseline methods, IF incurs the lowest training cost. Although LOF is more computationally expensive, it remains relatively efficient compared to deep learning (DL) approaches, which require multiple training epochs. For per-sample inference, IF achieves the fastest runtime due to its shallow tree traversal. In contrast, LOF is the slowest among the baselines, as it requires computing k-nearest neighbor distances and estimating local densities for each sample. DL models, including TranAD, NSPR, and our model, entail higher training costs but maintain competitive inference efficiency.

content: The TrendLike module is the primary computational bottleneck. In particular, the final covariance reconstruction 𝐋 σ , l ​ 𝐋 σ , l ⊤ \mathbf{L}_{\sigma,l}\mathbf{L}_{\sigma,l}^{\top} introduces a computational complexity of 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ​ d x 3 ) \mathcal{O}(Ld_{x}^{3}) . This term becomes the primary bottleneck when d x d_{x} is large. TranAD [ 18 ] employs a standard Transformer architecture with attention complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( L 2 ​ d m ) \mathcal{O}(L^{2}d_{m}) , while NSPR adopts Performer [ 35 ] , a linearized Transformer variant with attention complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ​ r ​ d m ) \mathcal{O}(Lrd_{m}) , where d m ≫ r d_{m}\gg r . All DL models include a feedforward network (FFN) with computational complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ​ d m 2 ) \mathcal{O}(Ld_{m}^{2}) . When d m ≫ L , d x d_{m}\gg L,d_{x} , the FFN term dominates across all methods, leading to similar overall computational costs. When L ≫ d m , d x L\gg d_{m},d_{x} , TranAD scales quadratically with L L and becomes the most expensive, while NSPR remains the most efficient. Our method scales linearly with L L but complexity depending on feature dimension d x d_{x} . When d x ≫ L , d m d_{x}\gg L,d_{m} , our model becomes the most computationally expensive. In this regime, NSPR remains the most efficient, while the relative ordering between TranAD and our method depends on the specific values of d m d_{m} and d x d_{x} . TranAD may incur higher practical runtime due to its two-stage training procedure, while its inference speed remains competitive. NSPR introduces overhead from stacking multiple linearized Transformer blocks, which increases runtime despite its lower theoretical complexity. In contrast, the TrendLike module is computed in a single forward pass, enabling efficient training and inference. Despite its additional computational cost, our approach remains competitive with existing methods.

content: To assess the impact of different distributional assumptions, we conduct an ablation study using four alternatives: an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Gaussian distribution (G-dist), an i.i.d. Student’s t-distribution (t-dist), and quantile prediction. These variants are implemented by replacing the TrendEst ​ ( ⋅ ) \text{TrendEst}(\cdot) module without altering the overall model architecture. For i.i.d. G-dist, each element of the L × d x L\times d_{x} time series is modeled independently by a Gaussian distribution, with the mean 𝝁 ∈ ℝ L × d x \boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{x}} and standard deviation 𝝈 ∈ ℝ L × d x \boldsymbol{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{x}} estimated using 1DCNNs, the latter with a softplus activation. For the i.i.d. Student’s t t -distribution, an additional 1DCNN with a softplus activation is employed to estimate the degrees of freedom (DOF). Both variants are trained by maximizing the log-likelihood formulation. For quantile predictions, a 1DCNN estimates q = 100 q=100 quantiles and is optimized using the pinball loss [ 36 ] . The multivariate Student’s t t -distribution (Multi t-dist) follows the same estimation procedure as the multivariate Gaussian distribution, with an additional 1DCNN using a softplus activation to estimate a time-dependent DOF parameter, producing an L L -dimensional vector. For all variants, the computation of the temporal vector and detrended reconstruction losses remains unchanged. Table IV-C7 shows that the i.i.d. assumption consistently yields the poorest performance, as it fails to capture the feature dependencies inherent in real-world time series. In contrast, the multivariate and quantile-based distributions achieve comparable and substantially better results, with the multivariate formulation exhibiting greater robustness across datasets. These findings underscore the importance of distributional modeling in TSAD, suggesting the multivariate formulation as a reliable default choice, while the most suitable distribution may still depend on the characteristics of the dataset.

content: We further assess the validity of the Multi G-dist assumption on the SMD and PSM datasets, which are selected as representative cases of relatively poor and strong anomaly detection performance, respectively. Under a Multi G-dist, the standardized residuals 𝐫 i = 𝚺 ^ T , i − 1 2 ​ ( 𝐭 ^ i − 𝝁 ^ T , i ) , \mathbf{r}_{i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{T,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{T,i}\right), where i i denotes the time step, are expected to follow a standard normal distribution. Therefore, we compute the standardized residuals, aggregate them across features at each time step, and pool the resulting values over all sliding windows of length 128 for evaluation using Q–Q plots. As shown in Fig. 9 , the SMD dataset exhibits greater deviations from normality than the PSM dataset, indicating a poorer fit to the Multi G-dist. This is consistent with its comparatively poorer anomaly detection performance. Conversely, the PSM dataset exhibits good agreement with normality in the central region of the Q–Q plots. Overall, the Multi G-dist provides a reasonable approximation of the underlying trend distribution. Nevertheless, as the estimated trend distributions may deviate from the Multi G-dist assumption, feature-level interpretation is considered a secondary analysis and is applied only to segments identified as anomalous by the anomaly score.

content: Since evolving trends are a major source of time-series non-stationarity, we investigate whether sensitivity to imperfect trend estimation increases with dataset non-stationarity. The non-stationarity level is quantified using the average Wasserstein distance between consecutive Gaussian distributions parameterized by the sample mean and covariance of sliding windows with a length of 128 and a stride of 32, yielding scores of 0.198 (SMD), 0.187 (MSL), 0.266 (SMAP), 0.336 (SWAT), and 0.125 (PSM). To evaluate robustness under imperfect trend estimation, synthetic trend perturbations are introduced into the test set by injecting random level shifts and slope changes with varying magnitudes into randomly selected temporal segments, affecting 10%–50% of the time steps and features. As shown in Fig. 10c, although imperfect trend estimation causes performance degradation, the proposed model remains robust, with highly non-stationary datasets such as SWAT and SMAP exhibiting smaller performance degradation.

content: In conclusion, AdaTrendLike provides an effective framework for non-stationary time series by explicitly modeling trend and detrended components as distinct dominant elements. Hierarchical detrending facilitates estimation of their distribution and clearer separation from the ground truth. Complementing this, frequency-based convolutional neural networks further process the detrended component, improving anomaly detection performance. Together, these enable direct estimation of trend likelihood and provide feature-wise interpretability with actionable insights into which variables are affected by anomalous behavior. Despite these advances, datasets with subtle anomalies remain challenging, motivating future work to incorporate additional time-series components, such as cyclic and seasonal patterns, alternative distributional assumptions, and feature-wise anomaly scoring.
